Canadian anti-Israel group to host Wikipedia edit-a-thon honoring ‘martyred’ Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:13:30 UTC
04:13:30 KST

A Canadian pro-Palestinian organization is hosting a Wikipedia editing event on October 22, inviting participants to "populate Wikipedia entries honoring martyred Palestinian artists and exposing the Canadian, Zionist backers of genocide."
Jewish Onliner was the first to report on this 'Free Palestine Wiki edit-a-thon,' but it was independently confirmed by The Jerusalem Post.
The group, Artists Against Artwashing (AAA), says the evening will begin with Palestinian short films, followed by a Wikipedia 101 session and hands-on editing.
While anyone can contribute to Wikipedia, organizing editing sessions around a predetermined political objective like 'honoring Palestinian martyrs' risks taking the site away from its formal core policy known as the Neutral Point of View (NPOV).
'That is canvassing [and] they should be blocked'
Wikipedia co-founder Larry Sanger said, "If you are organizing people to take a controversial point of view on Wikipedia, that is canvassing [and] they should be blocked."
Independent investigator WikiBias said, "Wikipedia claims neutrality. Their mission of “remedying the narrative” tells a different story."
Artists Against Artwashing describes itself as a group of "arts workers across so-called-Canada demanding cultural institutions divest from settler colonialism and genocide."
Its main campaign is focused on pressuring arts institutions into cutting ties with the Azrieli Foundation, the charitable counterpart to the Azrieli Group, Israel’s largest real estate company.
AAA held another Wikipedia editing workshop earlier this year, in April, specifically targeting articles associated with the Azrieli Foundation.
According to Wikipedia’s public revision history, changes to the Azrieli Group article were made at 7:30 p.m. Toronto time on April 28, coinciding with the editing workshop.
The user who made the edit - 'Sure-thing-no-problem' - was registered that day, has no user page, and made exactly one edit.
Other accounts made further edits to the page, especially removals, throughout May.
Similar to 'Sure-thing-no-problem,' an account named 'subterra6677' carried out edits on the Azrieli Group and David Azrieli pages only, before being warned in June of edit warring.
Edit warring on Wikipedia occurs when editors repeatedly undo one another’s changes to an article, often over disputed wording, sources, or political framing. Wikipedia’s three-revert rule generally prohibits editors from reverting the same page more than three times within 24 hours, although edit warring can violate policy even before that threshold is reached.
On June 25, subterra6677 received a message from another user noting that the former had made several edits in order to restore a version of Azrieli Group.
"The impulse to repeatedly undo an edit you disagree with is understandable, but I wanted to make sure that you're aware of Wikipedia's edit warring policy. Repeatedly undoing the changes made by other users in a back-and-forth fashion like this is disallowed, even if you feel what you're doing is justifiable," subterra6677 was warned.
Training participants to edit Wikipedia is a relatively common activity in pro-Palestine/anti-Israel spaces.
Hamas-linked organization, Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, has run several training sessions teaching Gazans to edit Wikipedia pages about the Israel-Hamas War as part of its “WikiRights” program.
Training covers creating, developing, and updating content
It launched the third edition of the WikiRights project in the Gaza Strip in February 2026. The project targets 12 young Palestinian men and women and provides them with “in-depth training in human rights research and documentation, as well as professional editing on Wikipedia.”
The training covers creating, developing, and updating content and involves using editing and contribution tools in both Arabic and English.
Additionally, the Anti-Defamation League's (ADL) Center for Technology and Society released a new report Thursday titled Damage Done: Wikipedia Leaves Biased Edits Unchecked Despite Editor Bans, which found that uncorrected past biased edits remain embedded across Wikipedia's most-read pages concerning Israel, Zionism, Hamas, and Jewish history.
This follows an initial investigation released in March 2025 titled Editing for Hate, which documented a coordinated campaign by approximately 30 bad-faith editors to manipulate entries related to Israel, Jewish history, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Israeli ad firm weaponises commercial network to deploy mercenary spyware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:08:46 UTC
04:08:46 KST

Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech weaponised a vast commercial ad network to harvest personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant reported.
"The core finding is the weaponisation of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterised by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting," Confiant said in its investigative findings on Thursday.
The coordinated operation enabled US-blacklisted Israeli spyware company Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos to exploit commercial ad inventory across major global platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia's Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers termed "AdFection."
Devices belonging to staff at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through the weaponised ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
Surveillance
Discover-Tech operated a specialised system called Controlium that converted routine commercial advertising auctions into an expansive surveillance apparatus.
After analysing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS in dozens of countries during four months.
"Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies," said Confiant.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens, and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations strictly barred processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also revealed that an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, utilised Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecom providers, matching digital advertising identities to physical phone numbers to deanonymize mobile subscribers en masse.
Focus on Palestine
Geographic telemetry revealed sharp traffic spikes pointing to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2 percent of all digital advertisements in the territory, peaking at roughly 10 percent on April 7, with one in every 36 Android ads originating from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also landed directly on sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister’s Office, international bodies, judicial agencies, universities and defence organisations.
Investigators detected surgical handoffs to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56 percent of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain, and others.
After the joint investigation was disclosed, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi severed Discover-Tech's access to their digital advertising systems.

Justice Dept. sues California, seeks to stop state from counting 20,000 ballots

Justice Dept. sues California, seeks to stop state from counting 20,000 ballots
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Many of the flagged voters are in L.A. County. State officials say the federal data are unreliable and the demand comes too close to the election.
- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has alleged that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California.
The Trump administration on Thursday sued California over its handling of voter fraud claims, asking a federal court to immediately bar the state from counting ballots from about 20,000 voters statewide — many in Los Angeles County — whom the administration alleges are “likely noncitizens.”
The lawsuit is highly unusual, particularly given that California voters have already begun voting in the Nov. 3 midterms via mail ballots, experts said.
It’s also “meritless,” highly inappropriate and based on questionable federal data that have proved wildly inaccurate in other states, state officials said.
“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X. “Courts have made clear the federal government has no role in running state elections. We will defend free and fair elections in the Golden State and call out every authoritarian attempt to undermine our democracy.”
“Every count, recount, hand count, lawsuit, and audit has found that there’s no widespread voter fraud in the U.S.,” California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta wrote on X. “The Trump Admin’s last-minute demands are meritless, and we look forward to making our case in court.”
U.S. Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche, in his own statement, defended the lawsuit.
“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” he said. “If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation’s representative system of government.”
The lawsuit states that “as part of an investigation into unlawful voting,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services conducted a “multiagency and multilevel review” of state voter and federal citizenship data and determined with “high confidence” that around 20,000 “likely noncitizens” are registered to vote in the state.
It then forwarded those names to Homeland Security Investigations, which conducted its own investigation and concluded the same, the lawsuit says.
Federal officials have given California election officials 48 hours to prove the citizenship of voters flagged as potential noncitizens, or withhold their ballots.
“This means that, consistent with state law, nearly 20,000 noncitizens in California have been sent a vote-by-mail ballot to participate in the federal election (or will receive one), with many addresses listed in Los Angeles County,” the lawsuit alleges.
The lawsuit comes two days after Acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter wrote to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office, giving them 48 hours to set aside the same ballots in order to investigate those voters’ citizenship status.
McCotter had said the Trump administration would be forced to file for emergency relief in the courts if Weber and Logan did not comply.
The lawsuit — which also names Weber and Logan as defendants — comes about three months after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote his own letter to Weber, alleging that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California.
The lawsuit makes no mention of that prior estimate, or why Homeland Security’s initial estimate was so much larger than its current estimate. It does say that USCIS identifying with “high confidence” that a voter is a likely noncitizen “means that the match between voter information on the voting roll and USCIS’ internal records is strong and consistent based on multiple identifiers that support a strong identity link.”
It also said, “The Federal Government notified California months ago that numerous noncitizens may be registered to vote in California. Despite knowing that California must send vote-by-mail ballots to every registered voter, the State made no serious attempt to work with the Federal Government to determine whether noncitizens are registered to vote.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for more information as to how the 190,000 figure dropped to 20,000.
In a letter back to McCotter, Weber noted both figures and accused the Trump administration of pushing forward to disenfranchise voters at the last minute before the midterms based on shoddy data work and no certainty that those voters are ineligible.
“Nowhere has the federal government clarified the basis for suspecting — not even confirming with any level of certainty — the listed individuals are non-citizens. And as one court recently noted, the federal government’s citizenship records are ‘known to be unreliable,’” Weber wrote, referring to a case brought against the Justice Department by the organization Common Cause. “To give just one example, in a similar incident in the State of Nevada, DHS initially alleged that Nevada’s voter roll included nearly 16,000 potential non-citizens. However, after working with the State of Nevada, DHS officials failed to establish that a single non-citizen was on the voter rolls.”
Weber called it “remarkable” that the Justice Department would demand that her office “review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours” despite providing no clear evidence that those individuals are wrongly registered.
“This is an emergency of the DOJ’s creation,” Weber wrote. “California’s election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands.”
Logan said Thursday that his office responded to McCotter’s letter by “outlining the legal and operational concerns” it had with his demands — including that the list of voters included people from throughout California, not just L.A. County — only to learn the Justice Department had filed its lawsuit without any acknowledgment of the county’s “timely response.”
Logan said the Justice Department “has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” and his office “cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations” — especially about people from outside the county.
First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, posted about the lawsuit on X, noting the 48-hour window given to Weber and Logan had lapsed and writing, “Time is up for California.”
“This is not political or controversial,” he wrote. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.”
The Trump administration’s lawsuit says that while the U.S. “actively investigates and prosecutes incidents of unlawful voting,” it “is not practicable or feasible for the United States to investigate before the 2026 election concludes thousands, let alone tens of thousands, of individuals that two federal investigative offices identified on the California voter roster as likely being sent vote-by-mail ballots.”
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time, challenging the growing practice of ICE agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near courthouses.
Because of that, it argues, “California is thus knowingly imposing an obstacle on the United States’ ability to enforce [federal election law] by facilitating unlawful voting rather than working with the Federal Government to prevent it,” and the state is therefore legally barred from sending mail ballots to the 20,000 voters Homeland Security has flagged.
It asks the federal court in the Central District of California to declare the state’s actions — including providing and counting ballots for those 20,000 people — to be barred by law and in violation of the Supremacy Clause, and to issue an injunction barring the state from counting those ballots in federal elections “until those individuals’ citizenship status can be verified.”
The Trump administration’s attempts to use immigration data to reach conclusions about California voter rolls and intervene in California’s election is already being challenged in a separate federal case in the district of Washington, D.C., brought by attorneys with the UCLA Voting Rights Project on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, and a California voter named Pedro Trujillo.
The UCLA attorneys filed their own emergency petition Thursday to preclude the Justice Department from moving forward with such actions against California, citing the letters McCotter sent to Weber and Logan.
A judge in that case ordered the parties to meet and file a status report with the court by Friday as to when each side would be able to brief the court on the issue.
Several Democratic senators with oversight of elections — including Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) — wrote Thursday to Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel to denounce a slate of election-related actions undertaken by the Justice Department recently, including the letters sent to Weber and Logan, as “laying the groundwork” for the Trump administration “to potentially challenge ballots ahead of Election Day.”
The senators wrote that the department’s 48-hour demands on California elections officials came “when state and local election officials should be focusing their time and resources on running a safe and secure election — and despite the Administration’s demonstrated track record of wrongly identifying eligible voters as non-citizens.”
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) also denounced the pressure campaign on California elections officials, calling it “another dangerous attempt to destabilize our safe and secure elections” in a post on X. “California will defend against this meddling and unwarranted intrusion on our constitutional rights,” he wrote. “Don’t poke the bear.”
Times staff writer Brittny Mejia contributed to this report.

A Journey Through Italian, African, and Postcolonial Literature in Cape Town
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:03:12 CEST
04:03:12 KST

As part of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, in collaboration with the Italian Consulate in Cape Town, the Italian Cultural Institute in Pretoria, and the Dante Alighieri Society, the Somali-Italian writer Ubah Cristina Ali Farah held a public discussion at the Cape Town Club alongside Dr. Mara Boccaccio, Senior Lecturer and Head of the Italian Studies Department at the University of Cape Town.
                                    
Ali Farah addressed complex and highly topical issues, explaining how coming to terms with her dual identity, her language, and her sense of belonging remains a daily and ongoing challenge. She spoke about what it means to be the daughter of an Italian mother and a Somali father, to have been born in Italy but raised in Mogadishu, where she attended both Italian and Somali schools. She also explained her decision to write in Italian with passages in Somali, incorporating words and narrative moments in her father’s language.
                                    
The author read evocative passages from two of her books, which have also been translated into English—*Madre piccola* (2007) and *Il comandante del fiume* (2014)—as well as an excerpt from the short story *La danza dell’orice* (2020), in memory of Sarah Baartman. She then enthusiastically answered a series of questions from the audience, which included many South African students studying Italian. She recounted that she wrote *Le stazioni della luna* (2021) while reading the “Corriere della Somalia” during the lockdown, while she was in Stellenbosch—about 40 kilometers from Cape Town—for a literary residency; however, she never managed to visit the city.
                                    
Ali Farah is deeply connected to the concept of individual and collective memory as a foundational element of her stories. She reflected on the meaning of surviving a civil war, on colonialism, and on what it meant for thousands of Somalis to find themselves in Italy, often facing significant challenges in integrating. She explained that she felt a duty to write about these refugees—who have often felt rejected by Italy—telling their stories in Italian to give voice to lives that must not be forgotten. Her writing has also grappled with the challenges of narratively representing violence and war.

Russia Moves to Ban Direct Crypto Trading, Forcing Citizens Into State-Regulated Exchanges by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:01:36 UTC
04:01:36 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Moves to Ban Direct Crypto Trading, Forcing Citizens Into State-Regulated Exchanges by 2027
Russia’s Central Bank plans to prohibit individuals from directly buying and selling cryptocurrency to each other starting July 1, 2027, according to The Moscow Times on October 15.
The Moscow Times reported that peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency transactions between individuals will remain permitted only until that date. Afterward, Russians will have to conduct such transactions through regulated intermediaries, including licensed brokers and registered cryptocurrency exchanges.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the outlet, the restrictions will also affect cryptocurrency transfers within Russia’s regulated financial infrastructure. The Central Bank will not permit transfers from regulated digital accounts to privately controlled cold wallets. Transfers between individuals using addresses administered by Russian digital depositories will also be subject to restrictions.
"Yes, but only until July 1, 2027," the Central Bank stated when asked whether individuals could continue trading cryptocurrency directly. The regulator clarified that Federal Law No. 282-FZ does not provide for direct P2P transactions between individuals after that date.
The Moscow Times noted that the restrictions are part of Russia’s broader overhaul of cryptocurrency regulation. The legislation, which largely took effect on September 1, 2026, establishes a regulated system of cryptocurrency brokers, exchanges, and digital depositories.
The changes will bring cryptocurrency trading and custody increasingly under the supervision of Russia’s Central Bank, limiting individuals’ ability to conduct transactions without regulated intermediaries.
The tightening of control over cryptocurrency comes as Russians increasingly seek alternative channels to move money beyond the domestic financial system. Russian households transferred about $7.2 billion to foreign brokerage accounts between June and December 2024, exceeding the total for the previous seven years combined.
Roughly 40% of those transfers amounted to direct capital flight, with foreign brokers effectively replacing conventional foreign-currency bank accounts as Western sanctions and banking scrutiny intensified.

Pope Leo has begun "working a little" after surgery to remove a tumor from his lung — the Vatican
Kyiv • UNN
The recovery of 71-year-old Pope Leo after the removal of part of his right lung is proceeding as planned. The pontiff is independently carrying out daily activities and undergoing physical therapy.
Pope Leo’s recovery after surgery for lung cancer is proceeding as planned, and the 71-year-old pontiff has already begun working little by little, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma — the most common form of lung cancer; on Tuesday afternoon, doctors performed surgery during which they removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
According to doctors, who provided an update on Thursday, the results of the pontiff’s routine examinations are within normal limits, while a chest X-ray indicates that the lung is recovering successfully.
The medics added that Leo is independently carrying out everyday tasks and undergoing physical therapy, performing movements with his full range of motion.
The diagnosis of “cancer” in the Pope, known for his relative youth and energy — and elected to the papacy only in May 2025 — came as a shock and raised questions about how his pontificate would develop amid his battle with the disease.
We add
The Vatican said that the surgery was successful and without complications. At present, no information has been provided about either the size of the tumor or whether the disease has spread to nearby lymph nodes — key factors in determining the prognosis.
All public events involving Leo have been canceled until next Tuesday. The results of the pathological examination, which will be crucial in determining further treatment, may not be ready for several days.
The Vatican’s medical bulletins on Leo’s health are signed by the pontiff’s chief surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone.
The Vatican, which had previously been reluctant to discuss the Popes’ health, has shown considerable openness in Leo’s case. This differs significantly from the approach of his predecessor, Francis: he usually did not announce his hospital visits in advance, which sometimes caused a genuine media frenzy surrounding his health.
On Sunday, the Pope himself told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square that a “localized nodule” had been found in his lung and that surgery was necessary. He also said that the disease had been detected at an early stage and that the growth had not spread beyond the affected area. He is being treated at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, known as the “Pope’s hospital.”

Dying in ICE custody: Inside one family’s story of heartbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:57:08 UTC
03:57:08 KST

Los Angeles, California – Saturdays marked a weekly pilgrimage for Lucia Uribe. Every weekend, she would travel to the edge of California's desert to visit her son, Ismael Ayala-Uribe, in detention.
Ismael was among the hundreds of thousands of people swept up in United States President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
Born in Mexico and brought to the US as a child, he was arrested on August 17 while working at a car wash. Ever since, he had been in the custody of immigration authorities, first at a local jail and later at a detention centre for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Adelanto, California.
But one Saturday was different. Lucia remembers that Ismael’s hands looked paler, his eyes were bloodshot, and the fever he had was rising.
“Mom, I’m not going to make it,” Lucia recalls Ismael telling her. There was little she could do but reassure him.
“I told him, ‘Oh, my son, just hang in there as long as you can,’” Lucia said. “When I said goodbye to him, I felt something in my chest, a tightness, and it made me want to cry.”
It was the last time she would see her son alive. Lucia’s fears were confirmed by a knock at her door two days later, when police told her that her son had died at 2:32am on September 22, 2025.
Ismael was one of more than 50 people to die in ICE custody during the first 500 days of Trump's second term.
A coroner's report from the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department in southern California found that his death was caused by complications from an abscess in his pelvic region.
Ismael's family, however, has argued that insufficient medical treatment in ICE facilities led a preventable infection to fester into a deadly condition.
For months, the Al Jazeera documentary series Fault Lines has spoken to people in ICE custody and the families of those who never made it out alive, to understand the conditions that could have led to deaths like Ismael's.
What it found was that 2025, the year Ismael died, was the deadliest year in history for those in ICE custody. But experts fear 2026 is on track to match or surpass that record.
'Not proportional'
The Trump administration has consistently denied reports that deaths in ICE custody are increasing.
In a social media post in June, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, claimed that the death rate has remained "consistent with data over the last decade".
"There has been NO spike in deaths," the department wrote, pointing to the percentage of deaths relative to the overall population of ICE detainees.
But experts and watchdog organisations warn that ICE's framing may be misleading.
“What has often been claimed is that the overall detained population is going up," said Nicholas Cuneo, an expert in immigrant health with Physicians for Human Rights, an advocacy organisation.
But he pointed to statistics that show the death rate has nearly tripled. “That clearly is not proportional to the detained population," Cuneo said.
In June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights published a joint report revealing that, since Trump returned to office, immigrants in ICE custody are dying at a rate roughly three times higher than under his predecessor Joe Biden.
The annualised mortality rate during Biden's four-year term was 2.24 for every 10,000 detainees. Since Trump began his second term, that proportion has risen to 6.38 deaths for every 10,000 people in custody.
In total, 33 people died in ICE custody last year, according to the agency's own statistics. So far in 2026, at least 26 people have died.
Reagan Williams, a human rights lawyer and researcher who worked on the June report, said that the increase in overall detentions does not explain the spike in deaths.
"The administration has incarcerated record numbers of immigrants," Williams said.
"And yet this rapid rise in detention does not fully account for the staggering increase in deaths. A higher percentage of detained immigrants are dying under this administration."
While overcrowding at ICE facilities is a factor, experts at Physicians for Human Rights also found a pattern of delayed emergency care, understaffing and failure to provide adequate medical treatment.
Those factors have raised concerns that many ICE deaths may have been preventable, including Ismael’s.
'A major failure'
A round-faced man with dark-rimmed glasses, a moustache and short-trimmed hair, Ismael came to the US when he was only five years old.
Southern California became his home, and as an adult, he qualified for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) programme, which offered temporary protection against deportation.
He lost his DACA status, however, in 2015 after a conviction for driving under the influence.
His family remembers him as a caring son and uncle, always willing to buy his niece and nephew new clothes or school supplies.
“Ismael was always looking after his siblings. He just had a big heart,” said his brother, Jose Miguel Ayala. “He was very protective of not just us, but my mum and dad too.”
He was 39 years old when he was brought to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
Two weeks after his arrival, Ismael told his family that he developed a high fever and a painful sore on his backside.
On September 18, 2025, workers at Adelanto initiated a Code Blue alert for Ismael, signalling a life-threatening medical emergency. Medical staff rushed him from his dorm to the infirmary in a wheelchair.
ICE documents show that Ismael was given pain medication, an ointment and a fibre supplement.
But according to Physicians for Human Rights' Cuneo, who reviewed the case, Ismael should have received a physical examination and antibiotics.
"That is a major failure," Cuneo said.
That weekend, hours after Lucia’s visit, Ismael’s condition worsened. Just after midnight on Sunday, ICE records say he was vomiting, shaking and sweating.
According to ICE documents, he was later sent to an intensive care unit, where he went into cardiac arrest within minutes of his arrival and subsequently died.
“I believe Ismael’s death could have fully been prevented by timely care,” Cuneo said. “It was a simple abscess that was not treated in a timely manner.”
Fault Lines obtained a coroner's investigation that reveals Ismael was critically ill when he first arrived at the hospital, a fact that was left out of ICE's public report on his death.
The coroner's report also contradicts ICE's timeline for Ismael's death. It indicates Ismael went into cardiac arrest early on September 21, nearly a full day before he passed away. Medical staff, however, managed to restore his heartbeat after intubating him.
That conflicts with ICE's report, which only notes his pulse stopping once: shortly before his death was announced on the morning of September 22. ICE described his condition on September 21 as "calm and cooperative", but it signalled no heart problems.
“If they had given him the medical care and what he needed, maybe he would be here with us,” Lucia said.
In a statement about Ismael’s death, ICE said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” throughout their time in custody.
But California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta told Fault Lines that his office found “the exact opposite" during its inspections of the state's detention centres.
“We've gone to these facilities. We've gone into Adelanto. We have done our own physical inspections," Bonta explained.
“If what the ICE spokesperson said was true, Mr Ayala-Uribe would be with us today.”
An internal mortality review committee also found that the care provided to Ismael at Adelanto "deviated beyond safe limits of practice", according to a document obtained by US media earlier this year.
It also suggests that medical staff delayed responding to calls about Ismael's declining health in the days leading up to his death.
'We want to go outside alive, not dead'
Fault Lines spoke to current detainees in the Adelanto detention centre who say they, too, fear the conditions could be harmful to their health.
Many described inadequate medical care, mouldy food and retaliation for protesting against the subpar conditions.
Some are part of a class-action lawsuit, filed in January, accusing the US government of "inhumane and illegal conditions" at Adelanto.
"They don't take things seriously," one detainee, Kurt Campbell, said of the Adelanto staff.
"They think everyone's a liar. So when you're going through something and you express what you're going through, they act like you're lying. We do want to go outside, but we want to go outside alive, not dead."
Four men have died in Adelanto between September 2025 and March 2026, including Ismael. Campbell, who is originally from Jamaica, said he knew one of the detainees who passed away.
"His last days were spent in confinement and in Adelanto instead of being with his family," Campbell said. "He didn't kill anyone. He didn't hurt anyone. His crime was coming over the border."
Guadalupe Moreno Cristin, another detainee in Adelanto, recalls experiencing rectal bleeding for more than a week, in addition to heart issues.
When he was taken to the infirmary, the only treatment he said he was given was Tylenol and a serum. His health has continued to deteriorate.
"I haven't had a bath for, like, eight days now because I can't lift my hands up," Cristin said. "I can't change myself on my own. I can't stand for long, and I can't walk much."
Detainee Jesus Jacobo Ortiz Ruiz estimated that, for every 320 people in ICE custody, there is only one doctor. "You've got to be literally dying in here for you to get sent to the hospital," Ruiz added.
Fault Lines spoke to US Representative Judy Chu, who represents a congressional district near Adelanto. For the past decade, she has been conducting oversight visits at the facility.
"I've seen firsthand for over a decade how they've cut corners, how they don't want to spend money on food, and most importantly, they don't want to spend money on medical care," Chu said.
To push for change, roughly 150 detainees signed a petition and went on hunger strike earlier this year to denounce the "unbearable and inhuman" conditions at Adelanto.
Campbell said he was placed into solitary confinement for 30 days for participating in the hunger strike. Other detainees reported receiving physical retaliation, including Ashraf Abujama.
"They just enjoy using force on me," Abujama said. "They want to just use me as an example to all the detainees, that '[this is] what we can do'."
'An emptiness that wasn't there before'
In recent weeks, changes have been under way at Adelanto.
The facility, formerly owned by the private prison firm Geo Group, has been sold to the Department of Homeland Security for $950m, as the federal government seeks to acquire more detention centres.
Critics, however, warn that the switch to federal ownership could make conditions inside Adelanto more opaque, limiting the ability of state and local authorities to exercise their oversight roles.
It is a change that concerns families of detainees like Ismael. Where once his mother Lucia visited him at Adelanto, she now spends her weekends with a new ritual: visiting his grave on Sundays.
Jose, Ismael’s brother, often joins her, along with his sister and her two kids.
Their father often stays behind. "My dad still has a hard time going," Jose explained.
More than a year has passed, but the entire family is still grappling with the loss.
"There's a time where I just feel like he's just going to walk in," Jose said. "There's just an emptiness that wasn't there before."

RIYADH, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Attacks on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh have killed 17 people and injured more than 330 others since Oct. 1, with the airport coming under 20 attacks during the two-week period, the Saudi-led coalition said Thursday, amid continued threats posed by Yemen's Houthi group against Saudi Arabia.
Speaking at a press conference in Riyadh, coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki presented statistics on Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia from March 26, 2016, to Oct. 15, 2026, saying the group had launched 1,104 ballistic missiles and 1,135 drones, and used 118 explosive-laden boats and 278 naval mines during the period.
Al-Maliki said the Houthis had acquired military technologies with the assistance of what he described as "regional parties," adding that the group had established weapons storage facilities in mountainous areas of Yemen's Sanaa, Saada and Amran provinces as launching points for attacks.
He said the coalition had destroyed 127 Houthi storage facilities in recent days, while insisting that Saudi air defense systems were effective in intercepting missiles and drones.
The coalition will continue its operations to counter Houthi military capabilities and threats to Saudi Arabia's security and maritime navigation in the southern Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, he added.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of attempting to target Islam's two holiest mosques in Mecca and Medina.
Earlier on Thursday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile in the Medina region. The Houthis soon rejected the allegation, saying the group had not carried out any attack toward Saudi territory during the day. ■

GWS player Tilly Lucas-Rodd says AFLW Pride Round is important to continue celebrating and championing while harmful attitudes towards queer people persist.
Lucas-Rodd, who is non-binary, said the joy and pride of the moment are an important counter to the discrimination queer people can still face in sport.
"I feel like we were getting to a place of more acceptance and now we're going backwards, and there's more discrimination, and more homophobia, and transphobia," Lucas-Rodd told ABC Sport.
They said this is particularly evident in online comment sections containing discriminatory rhetoric towards queer people, including, at times, AFLW posts on social media.
"People are coming out of the woodwork, and they're proud and happy to have these opinions, and they think it's okay, which is why I think it's so important that we still have Pride round, and show up and represent the community and challenge these dangerous beliefs with joy," they said.
"There's a time and place to be reflective on the harm and the negative parts in terms of, like, the discrimination we face and truly reflect on that and sit in that and be like 'this is not okay'.
"But there's also a time to use joy and pride and celebration as a form of resistance."
They have seen the impact representation can have on people's lives.
The top surgery was a procedure that involved the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.
They received many messages from people after the story came out, with people sharing it had opened up conversations with family members and given them a better understanding of the gender diverse and trans experience.
"A parent at my school that I taught at was like, 'You being so visible shows that for young trans (and) gender-diverse kids you can be successful, because they're often so hard on themselves and they don't see a future that's bright,'" they said.
"They see hardship, they see discrimination, they see transphobia as their future, but then they see someone being successful, being championed, being celebrated publicly, and they can see a way forward for themselves.
This year, what makes Pride Round even more special for Lucas-Rodd is it coincides with their 100th game.
Over the past 11 seasons, Lucas-Rodd has played for four different clubs, including Carlton (2017-2020), St Kilda (2020-2022), Hawthorn (2022-2025) and now GWS.
"It is so funny," Lucas-Rodd laughed, noting in particular the years at Carlton when they had shaved sides and bun. "There's been so many eras.
"I've changed completely as a person, and it was guided by AFLW. All I've ever known (as an adult) is AFLW, and all I've ever really been overly passionate about in my 20s is AFLW," they said.
The environments of the league helped shape them, which, they say, is why Pride Round is so important: the welcoming rooms they've been in aren't the same for everyone in sport.
They did a video with men's GWS player Tom Green earlier this week for the club's channel for Pride Round, during which he asked Lucas-Rodd if they ever struggle with using their platform.
It made them reflect on how they use their social media accounts — quite often championing trans and gender-diverse people playing sport and playing footy — and how it has created a two-way dialogue with more people in the community.
"When I speak to people or hear from people's actual lived experience in community sports, it's not safe," they said.
"And I was like, that's something I've only ever learned through more conversations around Pride Round."
Lucas-Rodd sometimes thinks, "Oh, this is probably getting old; people are probably bored of it", when they speak about their LGBTQ+ experience.
"But then I have someone message me being like, 'Oh, my parents read this, they heard this, they watched your video, and that made the conversation easy for me.'
"And it takes you back to why it's so important that we still have Pride Round.
"That's why it's so important that we have visibility and representation and keep talking about it over and over again because it helps make other people's lives easier out there in community."

Israeli firm weaponized digital ad network for spyware attacks, research shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:49:03 UTC
03:49:03 KST

Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech weaponized a vast commercial ad network to harvest personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant reported Thursday, Anadolu reports.
“The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting,” Confiant said in its investigative findings.
The coordinated operation enabled US-blacklisted Israeli spyware company Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos to exploit commercial ad inventory across major global platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia’s Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers termed “AdFection.”
Devices belonging to staff at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through the weaponized ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
– Global identity graph, data harvesting
Discover-Tech operated a specialized system called Controlium that converted routine commercial advertising auctions into an expansive surveillance apparatus. After analyzing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS in dozens of countries during a four-month period.
“Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies,” said Confiant.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens, and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations strictly barred processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also revealed that an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, utilized Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecom providers, matching digital advertising identities to physical phone numbers to deanonymize mobile subscribers en masse.
– Focus on Palestine, sensitive targets
Geographic telemetry revealed sharp traffic spikes pointing to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2% of all digital advertisements in the territory, peaking at roughly 10% on April 7, with one in every 36 Android ads originating from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also landed directly on sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister’s Office, international bodies, judicial agencies, universities and defense organizations.
Investigators detected surgical handoffs to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain, and others.
After the joint investigation was disclosed, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi severed Discover-Tech’s access to their digital advertising systems.

Panama removed from EU’s tax haven ‘blacklist’ a decade after the Panama Papers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:44:05 UTC
03:44:05 KST

PANAMA
Panama removed from EU’s tax haven ‘blacklist’ a decade after the Panama Papers
Ten years after ICIJ’s investigation exposed the country as a corporate haven, regulations and checks have been put in place to deal with the reputational damage.
The European Union has removed Panama from its tax haven “blacklist” in a move acknowledging corporate and tax transparency reforms made by a country infamously synonymous with offshore financial secrecy.
The update to the EU’s list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes was made by EU Finance Ministers last week, and comes a decade after Panama dealt with the fallout from the Panama Papers, an investigation led by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung into 11.5 million financial and legal records. The investigation exposed how a single Panama-based law firm registered 214,000 shell companies in over 200 countries, enabling companies and people to hide wealth and transactions.
“The Panama Papers revelations exposed weaknesses in the global financial system, with a particular focus on Panama and the lax regulations regarding transparency that were in place there at the time,” said Luis Moreno, an economist with the Global Alliance for Tax Justice and International Taxation Director at Latindadd.
“After the Panama Papers, Panama addressed various recommendations — including those from the OECD regarding tax transparency — which is precisely why it has now been removed from the ‘blacklist,'” Moreno added.
Following publication of ICIJ’s investigation in 2016, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development called Panama “the last major holdout that continues to allow funds to be hidden offshore from tax and law enforcement authorities.” An OECD review recommended that Panama adopt international tax reporting standards, join multilateral exchange agreements and improve company ownership records.
Panama was included on the EU’s first tax haven blacklist, which was implemented in December 2017 as a response to the Panama Papers investigation. But the Latin American country was removed just one month later, and instead put on a “grey” list, prompting backlash from transparency advocates.
In 2019, Panama voted to make tax evasion a crime. Still, in 2020, the EU put the country back on its blacklist, claiming the country had failed to implement promised transparency reforms. Shortly after, the Panama government created a registry of beneficial owners that requires disclosure of the people controlling every company.
More recently in May, Panama’s Congress approved a bill known as the Economic Substance Law, which applies to companies belonging to a multinational group. Such companies must show they have “substance” including staff, facilities and strategic decision-making in the country. Failure to show this results in a 15% tax rate on the company’s income.
The country celebrated last week’s announcement of its removal from the blacklist, with president José Raúl Mulino proclaiming in a social media post that the country was now “opening the door to new investments.”
But Carlos Barsallo, a lawyer and former president of Transparency International’s Panama chapter, flagged new challenges for regulating the financial industry and said Panama must be “careful not to end up back on the list.”
“What are the areas of concern that could lead to that? These are now global issues. Panama is not alone in this: virtual assets and everything related to the ‘crypto-economy,’” Barsallo said.
“Simply passing a law is not enough, there must be a mechanism in place to combat fraud involving these new virtual assets.”

IN BRIEF:
- Australia's unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent.
- An expert says if it rises people may be deterred from coming to Australia.
Australia needs a strong labour market to attract skilled migrants, an expert says, as the unemployment rate hovers above expectations and is expected to rise.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.
The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.
It's expected to rise over the next two years, as the government and Opposition have all sought to reduce net overseas migration (NOM).
The International Monetary Fund forecast unemployment in Australia would climb by 0.3 per cent, from 4.4 per cent on average this year to 4.7 per cent next year, at which point the number of Australians out of work would approach 800,000.

Economics and public policy commentator Abul Rizvi told SBS News a weak labour market would turn away not only migrants, but also Australian citizens.
"What you will see is an increase in departures and reduction in arrivals," he told SBS News.
But Rizvi said the unemployment rate in Australia would have to rise "much more significantly" for there to be the kind of "exodus" that was seen in previous years, including during the 1990-1991 recession.
Coalition migration approach 'illogical'
Rizvi has questioned the federal Coalition’s migration target, saying it doesn't take into account labour market factors.
The Coalition's migration plan, released last week, vowed to get NOM down to 100,000 — slashing temporary migrant visas, student visas and bridging visas, while increasing the number of skilled visas by 100,000.
Speaking on ABC's Insiders program on Sunday, Opposition leader Angus Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.
"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.
"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.
Rizvi said the Coalition's plan was "illogical" and avoided discussing the state of Australia's labour market.
"The Coalition wants to do two contradictory things at the same time," he said.
"They want to reduce the level of NOM, which requires a much weaker labour market. At the same time, they want to increase the level of skilled migration, which requires a strong labour market.
Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.
One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which it says will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.
A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy.
They generally arrive in the country after finishing their education, while the average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.
Motivations for coming to Australia
As debate continues over migration policy, analysis from libertarian think tank, the Centre for Independent Studies released this week, found that economic and job opportunities were the top reason first generation migrants self-reported for coming to Australia, and that their motivations differed greatly from what Australian-born citizens expected.
The next most common reason the report found was cultural factors, such as the Australian lifestyle, values and customs, while Australian-born citizens were much less likely to assume this as a motivation for migration.
The data on 3,552 voters across Australia found that new Australians were far less likely than Australian-born citizens to say that access to a strong social safety net or welfare was important to migrants’ decision to come.
It was a similar picture for the Australian environment, with 31 per cent of new Australians saying factors such as the weather and cleanliness were a reason for migrating, compared with what 11 per cent of Australian-born respondents thought.
Skill mismatch
Successive studies have found that even during times of economic strength, it was difficult for migrants, and especially refugees, to find appropriate work in Australia.
Research from public policy think tank the Committee for Economic Development of Australia, found nearly a quarter of permanent skilled migrants in Australia were working in a job beneath their skill level, or experiencing a "skill mismatch", which was at a substantially higher level among migrants on Family and Humanitarian visas.
It also found that, on average, recent migrants earned significantly less than the Australian-born population, across all temporary and permanent visa types.
In the Scanlan Foundation's 2026 Multiculturalism in Focus report, published in February, nearly half of interviewees reported that securing meaningful employment was their greatest challenge after arriving in Australia.
Common barriers included non-recognition of overseas qualifications and the disadvantage of lacking local work experience.
Migration’s boost for local workers
Migration has been found to reduce unemployment for domestic workers in international studies, including a 2025 study on OECD countries that found a "significant" negative relationship between net migration rate and the unemployment rate of Australian-born workers.
The report found that Australia demonstrated well-planned immigration approaches through active selection methods, accepting professionals with high qualifications while providing integration assistance to new residents.
Australia’s economy could absorb increasing numbers of migrants while still providing employment opportunities for both Australian-born workers and immigrants.
A series of OECD reports published from 2023 to 2024 also found that Australians of all ages and genders benefited from migration, which boosted the labour productivity and employment of Australian‑born workers.

More Than the Sum of Its Parts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:42:38 UTC
03:42:38 KST

Maya Valencia Goodall, Amelia Larson, and Miguel Cardona explain why structure, language, and literacy belong together
A midsized urban district serving many Multilingual Learners did something unique: looked hard at their data before the pandemic hit, not after. It would have been easy to let COVID take the blame for what they found, and that’s the story most people assume, but they didn’t reach for that explanation. Their scores had already started slipping in the years leading up to 2020, well before remote learning became a reality. When they pulled the numbers, without disaggregating by language or by school, one figure was impossible to look past: only about a third of their students were reading at or above proficiency. The other two-thirds were being let down by the approach itself, not by circumstance, and the district knew it.
They had spent years in balanced literacy, and between what the data was telling them and a new state law requiring evidence-based reading instruction, the direction was clear. What wasn’t easy was the timing. They rolled out new professional learning in structured literacy in the middle of COVID, over the same laptops their teachers were already using to hold remote classrooms together, because the data wasn’t going to wait for an easier moment.
That district’s experience wasn’t unique, even though the timeline was. Over 40 states now have some version of a reading law on the books (Schwartz, 2022/2026), and many of those laws landed on districts still sorting through years of what was often labeled the reading wars—the public debate that sometimes mistakenly framed evidence-based foundational instruction and multilingual or bilingual education as opposing positions. Instead, they need to inform one another: children need explicit instruction in how print works and opportunities to develop language, knowledge, comprehension, and literacy across the languages they use.
This is exactly the space the three of us set out to create together: a place where the distance between what the research already knows and what students actually experience stops being something districts manage around and starts being the actual work of implementation, turning what the research knows into what a classroom does, one lesson plan at a time. For a district, that means explicit, systematic instruction in the written code sitting in the same plan as oral language, comprehension, writing, and knowledge building, all of it drawing on the languages and experiences Multilingual Learners already bring, visible in the same lesson rather than scattered across separate initiatives.
Where the Research Has Already Converged
We know a great deal about how people learn to read, and for Multilingual Learners, that foundation does not change. What continues to develop is the nuance of implementation, how those same universal processes play out for a learner building literacy and language in two languages at once. The conversations continue because Multilingual Learners deserve instruction built around the full complexity of what they bring, not a simplified version designed for someone else and adjusted afterward. The components long treated as universal to reading, decoding, comprehension, and oral language are realized differently, and more richly, for a bilingual brain drawing on more than one language system. That means more oral language—more real speaking practice—has to be part of instruction from the start, not added once the other pieces are considered secure.
The Distance Between Legislation, Research, and Practice
Recently, we sat in on a panel conversation with state lawmakers and district leaders who shared their commitment to getting every student, including Multilingual Learners, the reading instruction the new laws are asking for. Across the conversation, the same thing came through clearly: the barriers are real, but so is the effort behind trying to solve them. Everyone at the table took the time to work through the nuances rather than reach for the easy answer, weighing what came next with real care. Funding is tight in places, and some state laws set timelines that assume a pace no district can actually move at. Others don’t name Multilingual Learners at all, leaving districts to figure out on their own what the law’s intent means for the students who need it most. Yet despite those barriers, we watched leaders turn them into opportunities, staying committed to making sure every student gets the instruction they’re owed.
None of that is a reason to stop, and none of the people in that room treated it as one. Every barrier named clearly is a barrier that’s closer to being solved, and what came through, over and over, was a field choosing to treat its barriers as design problems rather than dead ends.
From Convergence to Classroom Practice
At the classroom level, language and literacy don’t develop on separate timelines. They develop together, simultaneously and mutually reinforcing, not one paving the way for the other. Students should encounter worthwhile ideas through discussion, read-alouds, reading, and writing while they receive explicit instruction in the sound–spelling patterns they need. Their home languages, knowledge, and ways of expressing ideas are resources in that work. No student should have to demonstrate complete oral English proficiency before gaining access to substantive texts or writing about what they know.
In practice, a lesson can include explicit phonics instruction and purposeful discussion of content. When a student encounters an unfamiliar written word, the teacher directs attention to the letters and spelling patterns. Meaning can then help the student check a plausible pronunciation or understand a correctly decoded word. If the word is unfamiliar in English, a brief explanation, visual, discussion, or connection to a language the student knows can build understanding without asking the student to guess from context. Reading, speaking, listening, and writing reinforce one another throughout the lesson.
Integration over Isolation
The last piece of this is resisting the pull to let any single component of literacy carry the whole house on its own. Students need accurate word reading and opportunities to make meaning from text. Oral language, vocabulary, content knowledge, discussion, and writing develop alongside foundational skills. Teachers can examine whether a difficulty lies in decoding, unfamiliar English vocabulary, pronunciation variation, or comprehension, then respond with the support the student actually needs.
We use structured language and literacy to describe this intentional design: explicit, systematic instruction in the written code integrated with language development, knowledge building, meaningful reading, writing, and oracy. It is a way to plan and examine instruction, not a claim to have invented a new research framework or program.
Multilingual Learners are central to that design. They bring linguistic and cultural resources, and their literacy may develop across more than one language. Instruction can draw on cognates, morphology, cross-language comparisons, and students’ existing knowledge while teaching the English patterns they need. Their accents or developing English vocabulary should not automatically be mistaken for decoding problems. It is long overdue to consider the needs and strengths of Multilingual Learners as we plan core curricular and instructional design, not as an intervention post-core instruction.
That same principle extends beyond the classroom. Families carry language, knowledge, stories, culture, and literacy practices that schools can build on rather than work around. Strong literacy systems don’t ask families to set aside the language they know best so a child can learn English. They help families use that language to strengthen conversation, knowledge, and reading at home, which reinforces rather than competes with what’s happening at school.
Building a Cohesive Structure
Now we’ve established that the Science of Reading is broad enough to encompass methodologies that work for all students, including Multilingual Learners, we need to ensure that all educators have the tools, training, and support to give students the most appropriate instruction every day. Teachers across the curriculum should have the structure to be able to work cohesively using research-based instruction to achieve literacy goals.
The forward-thinking district we described earlier is still doing this work and its success at boosting literacy rates, including those of Multilingual Learners, still needs to be assessed. However, the decision to examine the data, strengthen foundational instruction, and plan language development alongside literacy offers a direction well worth studying in our pursuit of providing instruction that helps more children learn to read accurately in multiple languages, with depth of comprehension, while using their varied linguistic resources.
References
Schwartz, S. (2022; updated 2026). “Which States Have Passed ‘Science of Reading’ Laws? What’s in Them?” Education Week. www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/which-states-have-passed-science-of-reading-laws-whats-in-them/2022/07
Maya Valencia Goodall is chief impact officer at CORE Learning.
Amelia Larson is chief academic officer at Summit K12.
Dr. Miguel Cardona is president of Cardona Solutions and was the twelfth US secretary of education.

Fuel crisis compo clause could leave one state's taxpayers facing $80bn bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:41:58 UTC
03:41:58 KST

IN BRIEF
- Victoria considered overhauling decades-old fuel emergency laws amid fears of substantial legal liability.
- Proposed changes were never introduced, leaving any overhaul to the next parliament.
Victorian taxpayers could be on the hook for tens of billions of dollars in the event of a major fuel crisis under legislation that allows payment for those suffering economic loss.
The prospect of a budget black hole of up to $80 billion had forced the state government to consider updating its 1970s-era fuel emergency laws, which allow the preservation and allocation of fuel supplies during declared fuel emergencies.
The rethink came in June amid higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East and as the federal government extended fuel excise relief.
But the legislative amendments were ultimately not introduced before the end of the parliamentary sitting year, meaning any changes would now have to wait until the next parliament, with the state election due in late November.
Federal, state and territory governments can declare fuel emergencies, with the Victorian government initially appearing concerned over what liability it could be exposed to in the event it used powers under its laws.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Such declarations are made if any kind of fuel is likely to become unavailable, allowing compensation to be paid to those who suffer financial losses as a result of being forced to comply with ministerial directions.
The broad powers allow the minister to control, direct, restrict or prohibit the production, supply, distribution, sale, use or consumption of the fuel; or direct at what times and places services may be used.
The laws also allow people to be compensated for complying with the directions if they suffer losses or damages.
"Any sums required to be paid or provided for the purposes of this Act shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund," the law states, referring to the state's primary financial account into which all revenue is paid.
Declaring a state of emergency under the Fuel Emergency Act is rare. A 2020 parliamentary library research paper found the most recent declaration was in 2004, after a factory fire triggered a briquette shortage. The state government invoked the powers and secured the remaining briquette supply to keep hospital boilers running.
At the time, and still today, there was no indication of any immediate threat to Australia's or the state's liquid fuel supply.
Prices, however, have risen across the country following the end of temporary fuel excise relief, and against the backdrop of continued conflict in the Middle East and volatility in global oil markets.
The war has also sparked questions over Australia's energy security and how the nation might be impacted if there were severe disruptions or shortages.
In the case of Victoria, if it were to expose itself to compensation claims through the use of emergency powers, the state government could face a legal burden of up to $80 billion that would ultimately fall to taxpayers, according to a June draft government proposal seen by SBS News.
The potentially heavy cost was a key driver for the changes, the proposal states, as well as the inordinate amount of time and money it would take to manage claims and potential lawsuits.
The state government believed the current laws were out of step with other jurisdictions, where some fuel emergency regimes provide explicit immunity from certain legal claims, while compensation may be unavailable or subject to tighter thresholds.
A Victorian government spokesperson had previously told SBS News the Fuel Emergency Act would be updated to align it with other states and territories, ensuring a "consistent, modern approach" to managing fuel supply disruptions.
Asked last week why the government had not gone ahead with the amendments and whether it still believed the laws would expose it to substantial financial liability in the event of a state-declared fuel emergency, a spokesperson did not answer directly.
"The review of Victoria's Fuel Emergency Act was part of national contingency planning in response to global fuel supply risks," the spokesperson said.
"Victoria is now better prepared to respond to any fuel emergency, with stronger national coordination, better visibility of fuel supplies and clear arrangements to manage disruptions."
The spokesperson said the state's fuel supply "remains strong" and that the government was working with the federal government and industry to "prepare for any potential disruption".
The spokesperson did not address how the potential liability of up to $80 billion was calculated.
Earlier this year, Australia was gripped by concerns over fuel supply sparked by global oil shortages due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply flows.
The head of the International Energy Agency warned the global economy was facing a "major threat" to supply, describing the situation as worse than the two oil crises of the 1970s combined, as well as the crisis caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Political figures such as One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce had called for federal fuel rationing measures in the cities to mitigate the impact of shortages in the regions, calling on the federal government to enact a state of emergency over the situation.
The federal government had reportedly crisis-planned in the event of a national shortage, with measures including fuel rationing and limits on fuel purchase per vehicle, according to a report by Guardian Australia in May.

Google’s quantum Willow chip may be able to grow ‘magic states’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:39:34 UTC
03:39:34 KST

Quantum computers promise exponential computational power by processing many possibilities simultaneously. But the machines we have today are still far from this ideal. For one, their bits, called qubits, are prone to frequent errors, and as a result, quantum computers are limited for now. To overcome errors, the machines need to tap into so-called magic states—and scientists at Google Research think their quantum chip could help get them there. In a new study published today in Science, the researchers show how to supply magic states more cheaply using a gardening-inspired technique called cultivation.
Traditional computers build every calculation from a few simple logic gates, such as AND, OR and NOT. By contrast, “quantum computers have their own analogy of these operations called the Clifford gates,” explains Emma Rosenfeld, a researcher at Google Quantum AI and the study’s lead author. Clifford gates, however, can be imitated by a normal computer. “But there is one particular gate that unlocks the quantum computer’s power,” Rosenfeld says. “Physicists call it a non-Clifford gate, most often a T gate.” This extra gate is produced using a magic state.
A quibit in a magic state is prepared in a very specific blend of the states 0 and 1 (occupying a mixture of states is a specialty of quantum computers). Fed into a calculation, it is used up to perform the extra gate, and any flaw in the state becomes a flaw in the gate. “It has to be made very, very precisely,” Rosenfeld says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The standard recipe to make magic states is called distillation, and it creates fewer, more accurate quantum states from many imperfect ones. “You can have up to 95 percent of your quantum computer being spent just generating these high-fidelity magic states,” Rosenfeld says. To bypass this bottleneck, in 2024 her colleagues at Google Research proposed an alternative technique called cultivation, which works on a single state.
Using Google’s Willow chip, Rosenfeld’s team encoded a rough magic state in a few qubits and then measured it. Measuring a quantum state typically collapses it, forcing it into one of two possible answers. So instead of asking the question, “Are you 0 or 1?” which collapses the quantum state to either of those two options, the team asked, “Are you the right magic state: yes or no?”
States that pass this test are then spread across more qubits for stronger protection, hence the gardening name: the state starts small, gets checked and then grows. Without cultivation, about four attempts in 1,000 produced a faulty state. With it, errors fell by roughly 40-fold. The experiment used 54 physical qubits out of Willow’s 105.
“The Google experiment shows that cultivation works in practice,” says Kenneth Brown, director of the Duke Quantum Center at Duke University, who was not involved in the study. He notes, however, that the technique relies on a quality assurance step that rejects low-quality states, discarding 92 percent of attempts.
The result is still far from what practical applications demand. For example, using a quantum computer to break the current RSA-2048 encryption employed in website security, banking and electronic ID cards would require magic states that would fail only once in 10 billion tries. To simulate molecules, a use Rosenfeld says is more attainable, we would need such states with only one error in a million to one in 100 million. Right now the team stands at roughly one error in 10,000 attempts. Still, the new work represents a step in the right direction, she says.
“We’re more galvanized than ever to get to these near-term scientific applications,” Rosenfeld says.
