Israel was “very close” to creating conditions for regime change in Iran, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s foreign policy adviser Ophir Falk told The Jerusalem Post in a studio interview, while stressing that the Iranian people would have to determine their country’s future.
“I think we’re very close to creating those conditions,” Falk said when asked how close pressure on Tehran had brought the prospect of regime change. “Those conditions are being created as we speak right now.”
Speaking with Post Editor-in-Chief Zvika Klein and diplomatic correspondent Amichai Stein, Falk said Israel’s actions were creating conditions that would allow Iranians to challenge their rulers.
“Regime change in Iran is up to the Iranian people,” he said.
Falk described the US-led economic blockade as successful, while noting that economic pressure needed time to produce results. He argued that Iran and its regional proxies had been severely weakened by the war, citing strikes on senior figures, nuclear scientists, missiles, launchers and production capabilities.
Stein asked whether Israel and the US had done enough to provide the Iranian people with the means to challenge their rulers. Falk described Operations Rising Lion and Roaring Lion as “two of the most successful military operations in recent history,” saying their achievements had been “incredible” while acknowledging that no military operation could be perfect.
He also acknowledged the danger facing Iranians who took to the streets, citing the regime’s violent repression of protesters.
“I can appreciate the concerns of people,” he said when the discussion turned to their fear of demonstrating.
Falk did not offer a timetable for political change in Tehran or detail what further assistance might be provided to Iranians seeking it.
Gaza disarmament and the proposed two-week pause
Turning to Gaza, Falk said Hamas could disarm “in an afternoon” if it wanted to, and that Israel would not redeploy before the terrorist group was fully disarmed. Reconstruction, he said, would have to wait for demilitarization.
“If Hamas wanted to disarm, they could do that in an afternoon,” he said. “And that’s what we expect.”
Falk outlined three requirements for Gaza: disarming Hamas, demilitarizing the territory and deradicalizing its population. He presented those goals as consistent with US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan.
“That means zero weapons,” he said of demilitarization.
The Trump-led Board of Peace was established to oversee implementation of the plan, including Gaza’s reconstruction and transition to a new governing framework.
Stein pressed Falk on why Israel would not agree to a two-week pause in targeted killings and other military activity to allow an attempt at securing Hamas’s disarmament. The question followed Klein’s description of frustration among figures in the Trump administration over Israel’s approach to the board’s work.
Falk said he was unfamiliar with the 14-day proposal. He reiterated that Hamas and all other terrorist organizations in Gaza had to disarm, and that Israel would not redeploy before Hamas was fully disarmed throughout the territory.
“We’re not going to settle for anything less,” he said.
When Klein pointed out that changing attitudes among Gaza’s population could not be accomplished in an afternoon, Falk agreed that deradicalization would take time. He reiterated that Hamas could disarm in an afternoon if it wanted to.
‘We have not been as successful’ in information warfare
Falk’s assessment of Israel’s diplomatic position was consistently upbeat. He pointed to relations with the US, India, South American countries and European partners as evidence that Israel’s military strength had reinforced its international standing.
Klein challenged that assessment, asking about hostility toward Israel among Democrats and signs of erosion within the Republican Party. Stein raised statements marking October 7 in which US political figures devoted substantial attention to Palestinian suffering and criticism of Israel.
Falk acknowledged a problem in the public arena.
“We’ve been fighting a seven-front war, and on the eighth front, the information warfare, we have not been as successful as we have been on the battlefield,” he said. “And we will need to address that as well.”
He nevertheless maintained that the strategic relationship with Washington remained exceptionally close, citing joint military activity, planning and frequent conversations between Netanyahu and Trump.
Asked how many times the two leaders had spoken over the preceding week or two, Falk said they spoke often but could not recall the precise timing.
“I haven’t seen daylight between the president and the prime minister on the big issues,” he said when asked about differences over Iran.
Pressed on whether American requests had constrained Israeli military decisions, Falk said Netanyahu’s approach was to agree when possible and refuse when Israel’s security required it. He added that Netanyahu had said no on a number of occasions.
‘We’re going to get them all out’: Falk on the hostage negotiations
Falk said Netanyahu rejected an early working assumption held by some that Hamas would kill all the hostages and insisted that bringing every hostage home become a formal war objective.
“The prime minister did not accept that,” Falk said. “He said we’re going to get them all out, and we’re going to put it as a war objective to get them all out.”
Falk maintained that military pressure, diplomatic pressure and a united Israeli-American position were the combination that produced hostage releases. He said perceived differences between Jerusalem and Washington encouraged Hamas to retreat from negotiations.
Falk also credited Netanyahu with pressing then-president Joe Biden to increase pressure on Qatar to secure additional releases during the first agreement in November 2023.
One of the most pointed exchanges concerned whether Israel could have secured an additional hostage agreement between the November 2023 releases and the January 2025 deal.
Stein asked whether any agreement had been possible during that period, distinguishing between the availability of a deal and whether it would have been a good deal for Israel.
“No, there was no deal on the table,” Falk initially replied.
When pressed, he defined that answer in terms of the government’s war objectives: dismantling Hamas’s military and governing capabilities, freeing all the hostages and ensuring Gaza could no longer threaten Israel.
“There was no deal that could enable Israel to achieve its war objectives,” he said.
Falk argued that an arrangement requiring Israel to release large numbers of Palestinian prisoners, withdraw and leave the prewar threat intact would have contradicted the goals approved by the cabinet. He cited an Israeli proposal that then-US secretary of state Antony Blinken described in April 2024 as “extraordinarily generous,” saying Hamas had rejected it.
His account addressed a dispute that has resurfaced around former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk’s book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, and McGurk’s recent interview with the Post.
In a separate interview on Dan Senor’s Call Me Back podcast, McGurk called the suggestion that Hamas had been ready to release all the hostages in the days after October 7 “complete bullshit.” He said Hamas had demanded the release of all Palestinian prisoners, continued Hamas rule and a return to the prewar status quo.
Phil Gordon, who served as national security adviser to then-vice president Kamala Harris, challenged claims that McGurk’s account vindicated Netanyahu. Gordon alleged that Netanyahu introduced additional conditions in July 2024 after Hamas accepted the basic framework, delaying an agreement by six months.
Asked about McGurk’s impression that members of Israel’s negotiating team had sometimes gone beyond Netanyahu’s position, Falk declined to dispute the former US official’s personal assessment.
“I don’t want to argue with Brett’s feelings,” he said. He added that Netanyahu and the cabinet would not approve an agreement that jeopardized Israel or its war objectives.
Falk praised Trump’s approach, while declining to speculate about whether Israel would have reached the same position had Kamala Harris won the 2024 presidential election or Biden served another term.
He accused the Biden administration of imposing a “de facto embargo” on some weapons Israel needed before the Rafah operation. The Biden administration paused a shipment of heavy bombs in May 2024 over concerns about civilian casualties, while other US weapons continued to flow to Israel.
October 7: ‘It’s going to be a long war’
Falk also described his own morning on October 7, 2023, saying he was asleep when the attack began and was called shortly afterward to the Kirya, Israel’s military headquarters in Tel Aviv.
Before leaving, he woke his children, who were serving in the military, and told them to report to their units.
He described Netanyahu as focused while receiving updates on the unfolding attack.
“He told me it’s going to be a long war,” Falk recalled, saying the remark came on the way to an initial briefing from the security chiefs.
According to Falk, Netanyahu’s immediate instructions included reinforcing the northern front to deter Hezbollah from joining the fighting, enabling the military to concentrate on the south, preventing the terrorists who had entered Israel from returning to Gaza and calling up as many reservists as needed.
Falk said that, to the best of his recollection, French President Emmanuel Macron was the first foreign leader to call Netanyahu that day. He recalled Macron offering to mediate on the day of the massacre and Netanyahu rejecting the approach.
According to Falk, Netanyahu compared Hamas to ISIS and warned that Macron would face the group in Paris if Israel did not dismantle it in Gaza. Falk said Netanyahu also told Macron not to convey messages on his behalf, adding that Hamas would soon receive a message from Israel.
He also denied reports raised by Klein that UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had telephoned Netanyahu before October 7 to warn him of an impending attack.
“There was no such call,” Falk said.
Klein distinguished that allegation from possible communications between the countries’ intelligence agencies. Falk said he was unaware of any warning or caution, while reiterating his denial of a warning call between the leaders.
Abraham Accords and Saudi Arabia
On regional diplomacy, Falk praised the United Arab Emirates and said economic relations under the Abraham Accords, the US-brokered normalization agreements launched in 2020, had continued to develop through the war.
Asked why the UAE had publicly acknowledged Netanyahu’s visit, Falk said doing so served both countries’ national interests. He described the visit as “fantastic.”
He expressed support for normalization with Saudi Arabia but gave no details of negotiations or conditions for an agreement.
The discussion also touched on the flydubai passengers diverted to Saudi Arabia. Asked about the refusal to allow an Israeli civilian aircraft to collect them, Falk emphasized reports that they had been treated well and had reached Israel safely. He said a joint investigation into the incident was underway.
On the Houthis, the Iranian-backed movement in Yemen, Falk condemned attacks on civilians and said Israel would act to defend its security and national interests. He did not specify whether Israel was assisting Saudi Arabia against the group.
Asked what needed to happen for additional countries to establish relations with Israel, Falk initially said Israel had to win the war and then secure peace. When pressed on whether normalization would therefore have to wait, he said agreements could come whenever prospective partners were ready.
“I think that can happen and will happen much quicker than you think,” he said.

Years of civil war before the fall of longtime dictator Bashar Assad in late 2024 devastated Syria's oil, gas and electricity sectors, with the country becoming heavily reliant on imports to meet its needs.

Technical teams isolated the damaged section by closing valves at the plant and the Deir ez-Zor gas station in the al-Bughailiya area, while firefighting and safety crews headed to the site to secure the area, the statement said.
"Relevant authorities are monitoring the situation. The area has been cordoned off, the isolation valves on either side of the targeted section have been closed, and the surrounding area has been secured," the company said.
That incident at the Baniyas-Homs oil products pipeline caused a gasoline leak, the company said, adding that work was continuing to repair the damage and restore the line to service.
The state petroleum company said last week that an oil pipeline in the country's northeast was also damaged in a sabotage attack.
On Sept. 29, sabotage targeting a gas pipeline in eastern Syria caused an explosion, according to SANA.

The incidents come after demonstrations last month over rising fuel prices, which authorities linked to price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Palestine's deputy UN envoy told the Security Council on Thursday that Palestinians are being asked to prove their commitment to peace while enduring mass killing, displacement and annexation, declaring that "occupation must end."
Speaking at a council meeting on Palestine, Majed Bamya noted the aftermath of Oct. 7 events, saying he remembered condemnations for the attacks and demands for the release of hostages, as well as claims by some colleagues that Israel had to defend itself.
He said he searched his memory for any occasion when Palestinians were told, after a massacre, that they had the right to do whatever is necessary.
"Never. Not once before October 7, not once since, not when 10,000 Palestinians were killed, not when 20,000, not when 50,000, not when 70,000 Palestinians were killed," he said.
Bamya said Palestinians warned of the massacres to come, as well as forced displacement and annexation, and responded by seeking diplomacy.
"We sought protection, not justification of violence, whether legitimate or illegitimate. We sought justice, not vengeance," he said. "Yet, we are the ones asked to prove our commitment to peace."
He said "entire multi-generational" families had been wiped out in the Gaza Strip, while others were forced to keep running for their lives with no time to mourn, and that "92% of homes in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged.
Bamya said more than 1,000 Palestinians have been in the West Bank, including in East Jerusalem, in three years.
"Approximately 6,000 settler attacks have occurred since the beginning of this year," he said.
Bamya said Palestinians supported the ceasefire plan and the Security Council resolution endorsing it because they embodied principles including "no bloodshed, no occupation, no annexation, no forcible displacement."
"Yet Israel opposes every one of them," he said.
Noting that the Palestinian Authority has been undermined, with most of its employees unpaid for 15 months, Bamya asked council members which of their countries would still have a standing government under those conditions.
He said Israel "demands reforms while obstructing them, disarmament while its occupation forces continue killing, and while it continues arming settlers, security while denying ours."
"This is not peace; it is permanent subjugation," he said.
Rejecting security as a justification for annexation, he said, "Annexation cannot be justified by the need for security, not in Palestine, not in Lebanon, not in Syria, not anywhere, or borders would be meaningless, and wars would be permanent."
"We are either sovereign states, equal in rights and duties, sharing security and prosperity, or warring parties forever,” he said. "Occupation must end.”

Died more than 70,000 years ago – an unusual burial and the remains of a Neanderthal bearing signs of murder were discovered in Iraq
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:32:05 EEST
03:32:05 KST

Died more than 70,000 years ago – an unusual burial and the remains of a Neanderthal bearing signs of murder were discovered in Iraq
Kyiv • UNN
A Neanderthal shoulder blade more than 70,000 years old, with a hole made by a wooden spear, was found in Shanidar Cave. The blow may have been fatal, but the circumstances are unknown.
The evenly rounded hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal who died more than 70,000 years ago may be the oldest evidence to date that a human ancestor was killed by a wooden spear, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
Archaeologists discovered the distinctive injury while excavating the skeletal remains of an adult Neanderthal (along with the remains of other members of the species) in Shanidar Cave, in Iraqi Kurdistan. The remains lay beneath a layer of rock and sediment nearly 8 metres thick.
At this site — in a hollow behind a huge boulder near the cave entrance (no larger than a refrigerator) — at least five Neanderthals were buried over the course of several years. It appears that some bodies were placed on top of others that were still decomposing at the time.
"The fact that they returned to the same place to bury the dead over the course of several years or even decades is highly unusual for archaeological finds associated with Neanderthals," says Dr Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. "This indicates that placing the bodies at this site was a deliberate act."
In addition
Researchers were able to find only part of the skeleton of the injured Neanderthal — an adult approximately 45 years old. They discovered the left shoulder blade bearing traces of an injury, seven teeth, several ribs (and fragments of them), as well as an almost completely preserved right arm resting against a boulder.
A detailed examination of the shoulder blade revealed three fractures radiating from a 1.5-centimetre-diameter hole, as well as bone fragments that filled the wound. According to the scientists, these fragments were probably knocked out of the thin bone at the moment the spear struck.
The round shape of the hole and the nature of the bone damage provide compelling evidence that the wound was inflicted by a wooden spear that struck the body from the front. However, it is impossible to determine whether this was an accident during a hunt or a deliberate attack — perhaps a brutal blow delivered by an enemy.
According to Pomeroy, the location of the wound and the force needed for a spear to penetrate the chest (piercing the lung and probably severing arteries before exiting through the shoulder blade) indicate a "fatal blow" aimed at the heart. "It is unlikely that this could have happened by accident," she added. The spear wound was almost certainly fatal, but this individual was already in extremely poor condition before receiving the fatal blow. As noted in a publication in the journal Scientific Reports, an examination of the teeth revealed that one of the lower incisors had split vertically — only half of it remained in place, while the neighbouring teeth had turned inward. "To split a tooth and turn the others like that, a very powerful blow to the face would have been necessary," Pomeroy says. "This person probably needed assistance, as they must have been in terrible pain." A thick layer of hardened dental plaque had formed on the fractured tooth; it would have taken at least a year for so much to accumulate.
Chris Hunt, emeritus professor at Liverpool John Moores University and a co-author of the study, said that the Neanderthals at Shanidar mainly hunted ibexes and probably used wooden spears similar to modern sporting javelins for this purpose.
Because plant materials decompose quickly, very few wooden objects from the prehistoric era have survived to the present day. However, wooden spears around 200,000 years old were found in Germany, preserved because they lay in waterlogged soil. The oldest known find — more than 400,000 years old — is the sharpened end of a round wooden spear discovered in 1911 at Clacton-on-Sea.
Last week, scientists in Spain described hundreds of impressions of wooden objects and artifacts indicating that Neanderthals actively worked with wood: they made trays, plates, tripods, spears, and other items. However, finding evidence of deadly clashes in paleontological finds is much more difficult: we may never find out exactly how the injured Neanderthal from Shanidar died. “It is quite possible that it was an accident during a hunt,” Hunt notes. “However, the possibility that it was caused by deliberate violence between people cannot be ruled out.”

Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:25:37 UTC
03:25:37 KST

Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
Campus architects at Florida Southern College have updated the only planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as part of a decades-long restoration project at the school, which was masterplanned by Wright.
The restoration included interior and exterior updates of the building, known simply as the Planetarium. The structure, which sits at one end of the Polk County Science Building, has been largely closed since 2004, when the projection system stopped working.
The renovation was guided by Jeff Baker, resident campus architect and a principal at MCWB Architects. Baker has worked on Wright projects at Florida Southern College (FSC) for twenty years and said the Planetarium has long been a goal.
"Since the outset of these overall restoration efforts, the college was always looking for an opportunity to restore the Planetarium, knowing full well its potential to excite and inspire audiences of all ages as they get a glimpse into the heavens and the great genius of Frank Lloyd Wright," Baker told Dezeen.
Work on the exterior began in 2021. The team replaced the roof, flashings, failed stucco on upper portions of the facade and replaced over 280 hand-cast "textile" tiles that line the building's perimeter.
The team then moved inside starting in 2023, where "decades of interventions since Wright's death had dramatically altered the room", according to Baker.
The team updated the Planetarium's technology and audio, repainting the walls from a deep blue, and paring down or removing insertions such as a computer closet built in the 1980s.
It also included working with local craftsmen to restore the original Wright-designed seating made of plywood and colored vinyl upholstery, and repositioning it to its rightful orientation.
"The removal of the old computer closet retrieved the space as it was designed," said Baker. "This removal allowed us to restore and reinstate all the seating in its original circular form, which we learned is a very rare survival in planetariums throughout the country."
Other updates included reinstating the original paint and plaster, and restoring the floor in a "Cherokee Red" finish.
It is one of thirteen Wright buildings built between 1938 and 1958, which the university has been updating since 2007.
Previous restoration work included updating the Waterdome, Wright's largest built fountain, the Esplanades, monolithic covered walkways that traverse the campus and the towering Annie Pfieffer Chapel.
Baker said, like working on other buildings on campus, Wright's "elemental" architecture proved to be the most challenging aspect of the project, as there are "no 'poche' spaces to hide modern building systems".
"Frank Lloyd Wright spent his life conceiving architecture as a synthesis of art and structure," he said.
"At Florida Southern College, this is manifested in buildings that are elemental – the concrete floors are the ceilings for the rooms below, the concrete ceiling is also the roof above."
"We believe we were able to devise methods to insert these systems in sensitive ways that meet the needs of the college yet allowed us to retrieve Wright's vision for the space."
The team completed the ongoing work through grants from institutions such as the J Paul Getty Foundation, which supported the preparation of the original Campus Heritage Plan in 2007.
The college has used the plan as a guide to update Wright's buildings.
It is the only college Wright master-planned. FSC president Ludd Spivey commissioned the architect in 1938 and, deemed a National Historic Landmark in 2012, it is the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture in the world.
The Planetarium is now open to the campus and public for tours and screenings.
Dezeen recently rounded up six other Frank Lloyd Wright preservation projects across the US, including recent updates to the famed Falling Water house in Pennsylvania.
The photography is courtesy of Florida Southern College.

Poland launches security review of broadcaster takeover by Trump-linked US media giant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:23:18 UTC
03:23:18 KST

Jo Harper
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Poland has launched a formal national security review of the takeover of Polish commercial broadcaster TVN after Paramount Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery for $110 billion (€98 billion), Polish officials said Thursday.
The Ministry of State Assets (MAP) said it received formal notification of the change in TVN’s ownership late Tuesday and began administrative proceedings on Wednesday.
“The MAP will conduct proceedings in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 24 July 2015 on the control of certain investments,” said ministry communications director Przemyslaw Kuk, according to Polish media.
The European Commission approved the merger conditionally in July following an antitrust review. Polish media reported that the Commission examined competition concerns but did not assess the transaction’s possible effects on media pluralism.
At the end of 2024, Poland placed TVN, rival broadcaster Polsat, and several telecommunications and defense companies on a list of strategically protected firms. The government said the move was intended to protect public order, national security, and prevent potentially hostile takeovers. Prime Minister Donald Tusk at the time linked the decision to concerns about possible foreign interference, including Russian attempts to influence Poland’s media and political system.
Kuk said Thursday that the review would be carried out retrospectively because the global transaction has already been completed.
“The minister of state assets, acting as the supervisory authority, will be obliged to conduct administrative proceedings in this case in order to verify the impact of the completed transaction on security or public order in Poland,” he said.
The ministry has 90 days from receipt of the notification to issue its decision.
Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, forming a new media group known as Skydance. The combined company controls assets including CNN, CBS, HBO and TVN, one of Poland’s largest private broadcasters.
Under Polish law, the review can end either with approval of the existing ownership structure or with a finding that the shareholder may not exercise rights attached to its TVN shares.
“In such a case, the minister of state assets may order the sale of the shares of TVN within a specified deadline,” said Kuk.
TVN operates TVN24, one of Poland’s leading rolling-news channels, and has played a particularly prominent political role during the last decade.
Reporters Without Borders warned in July that the Paramount Skydance takeover posed a “direct risk” to TVN24’s editorial independence.
“TVN24 has spent years proving its independence in the face of political pressure at home,” said RSF, warning that those standards could be “quietly eroded by a corporate merger decided in Los Angeles.”
Skydance is led by David Ellison, son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who has maintained close relations with US President Donald Trump.
The company has faced wider scrutiny in the US for the political implications of its growing control of major news brands. Skydance said that when the Warner Bros. Discovery deal closed, the combined company would bring together CBS News and CNN alongside its broader entertainment assets.

Cornell faculty pressure president ahead of no-confidence vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:19:03 UTC
03:19:03 KST

Cornell faculty pressure president ahead of no-confidence vote
NEW YORK – Cornell University president Michael Kotlikoff is facing mounting pressure over the school’s handling of sexual assault allegations, after faculty peppered him with questions ahead of a no-confidence vote against the university’s leadership.
On Oct 14, members of the Cornell Faculty Senate questioned Kotlikoff over the safety of Greek life, the organisational structure of university leadership and how the Ivy League school has responded to the allegations.
Kotlikoff, who became interim president in 2024 and was named president the following year, also addressed concerns from current and former staff about how the sexual assault case has shaken trust in the school’s leaders.
“If this university feels that they will solve this problem by replacing a president, that, itself, is not good for Cornell’s reputation because I don’t think it’s the right way you address situations like this,” Kotlikoff responded to one question.
The meeting was closed to the media and accessible only to those with a school ID or log-in information, according to Cornell’s faculty dean.
A Cornell spokesperson declined to comment about the meeting.
The meeting comes as the faculty senate prepares to begin voting in October on a resolution expressing “no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault”. The body does not have the power to remove the president, but the resolution could be a barometer of support for Kotlikoff’s leadership.
Since September, protests have roiled the school in response to a former student’s allegations that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has drawn scrutiny beyond Cornell’s upstate New York campus over how the university and local authorities handled her allegations – which were laid out in a civil lawsuit – and why an earlier probe into the matter did not result in criminal charges.
During the meeting, several members of the faculty advocated reforms or the outright removal of Greek life. Andrew Moisey, an associate professor of art history and visual studies, said Cornell has been in an “abusive relationship with fraternities” dating back to a hazing death in 1873.
Fraternities “tell task forces that they’ll never do it again”, Moisey said. “A therapist or a good friend would advise us to say thanks for the memories, but it’s time to break up.”
Kotlikoff said the university should determine the overall safety of Greek life through data and study, not act on emotion.
“I just came from a town hall of alums who made the other point – that they felt that their sorority experience and fraternity experience was a very important part of their life at Cornell,” the president said. “We have to all take a step and carefully study this issue.”
Kotlikoff also said he was looking into whether Cornell’s public safety chief should continue to report to its top finance officer, an arrangement he described as “awkward”. Former faculty dean Charles Van Loan said the relationship could fuel suspicion that donor concerns influence prosecutions.
“I think you make an excellent point,” Kotlikoff told Van Loan.
At several points during the meeting, Kotlikoff said the university needed more data on sexual violence on campus. As is, the president said the university had a survey of students with a “very low participation rate”. “We do not have great data on this situation,” Kotlikoff said. “We need better data.”
Critics of the university’s handling of the case have grown to include New York Governor Kathy Hochul, an ex-officio Cornell trustee who said on Oct 13 that the university “failed that young woman”. But Kotlikoff said he was committed to making Cornell a leader in sexual violence response.
Throughout the meeting, faculty members suggested the university has responded to the former student’s allegations too late. Darlene Evans, a former lecturer, further questioned why Cornell would allow social gatherings at the fraternity on the night of the alleged assault after university police pursued a drug arrest at the location hours earlier.
After the alleged assault, the university conducted a Title IX investigation, assembled a task force on sexual assault, barred the fraternity from campus and sought punishments for the students involved. There have been no criminal charges in relation to the incident.
“This has been an issue on our campus and every college campus. It’s something I know people would like a president or provost to be able to immediately eliminate,” Kotlikoff said. “It’s something that we all have to work very hard to try and address.” BLOOMBERG

Ahead of US midterms, voters are frustrated with Trump, want change: Poll
Widespread voter disillusionment and pocketbook anxieties set a volatile stage for the GOP weeks before election night.
Voter sentiment across the United States is increasingly negative towards US President Donald Trump’s domestic and foreign policies, according to a new Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
In the closing weeks before the November 3 US congressional midterm elections, 80 percent of Americans polled said the country needs substantial change or “complete and total upheaval” in how it is run, according to the survey of over 1,100 US adults released on Thursday.
Democrats and independents are much more likely than Republicans to want a total overhaul of the country’s direction, the survey found, but even Republican voters are still looking for some change. Slightly fewer than half, 45 percent, want substantial change, while 13 percent are seeking upheaval.
The results point to a pervasive appetite for legislative realignment that poses a risk to the Republican Party’s power as it looks to keep control of both houses of the US Congress.
Fuelled by soaring living costs, everyday economics is driving a majority of the electorate, with 85 percent of respondents saying the economy is one of the most significant issues in weighing their vote in the upcoming election. About eight in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, and about three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.
Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a “very” or “somewhat” favourable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president.
More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
Immigration and crime rates are also top concerns for some voters, according to the survey results, with 45 percent of voters identifying them as top priorities, though the two issues are prioritised disproportionately by Republican voters who reference them more frequently than Democrats. Conversely, Democratic voters are more prone to name healthcare as their top priority.
Emerging cultural and technological concerns drew less immediate alarm across the board: 35 percent of voters ranked artificial intelligence as a substantial issue, while transgender issues sit significantly lower at 12 percent.
Healthcare is also considered a top issue for 69 percent of voters, while 64 percent cite the war on Iran as top-of-mind.
Despite their grievances, a majority of voters across both major American parties still value civic engagement.
About two-thirds of registered voters in the survey say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about two in 10 say it’s “very” important. Seventy-five percent of Democratic voters view it as “extremely” important, compared to roughly 60 percent of Republican respondents.

Why Data Centers Have Become Military Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:04 UTC
03:17:04 KST

When the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran earlier this year, Tehran responded by striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf. The result was a severe shock to global energy markets that continues to this day. Less publicized at the time were its strikes on another kind of infrastructure: data centers.
Similar attacks have since taken place in Russia and Ukraine, where both sides have been trading tit-for-tat strikes on data centers.
Experts say these attacks represent a new front in warfare, in which facilities powering the technology behind many critical industries have become military targets.
The AI boom has led to a surge in demand for computing power, data storage and cloud services, making the data centers that provide them a crucial part of modern infrastructure. A mass of data center construction is currently underway in the U.S., and tech companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to meet AI demand. Telecommunications companies, banks, hospitals and energy suppliers all rely on them.
“Data centers are now on the critical path for modern digital infrastructure,” Kirk Cameron, founding director of the Institute for Advanced Computing at Virginia Tech, tells TIME. “The loss of key data centers could collapse economies, disrupt public and private transportation with loss of GPS, and affect government essential services for health, emergency dispatch, and power grids.”
Military use of AI for targeting and information processing has made data centers crucial to fighting a war. Ukraine uses AI for an array of battlefield functions such as drone targeting, battle planning, and missile analyzing Russian missile attacks. U.S. tech companies such as Palantir now work closely with Ukraine’s military to develop new AI-powered weaponry, taking advantage of the ability to immediately test their technology on the battlefield. The U.S. military also uses Palantir’s Maven system to help identify targets for strikes.
“Data centers are competitive advantages in warfare,” Cameron says. “Knocking out capabilities means potentially crippling combat operations for an adversary. It’s also a form of economic warfare and could lead to longer-term competitive challenges for the target.”
Where have data centers been attacked?
The first wave of attacks on data centers was carried out in March this year by Iran, when it launched strikes on two Amazon facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and another in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby drone strike.
Those facilities have been mostly offline ever since; Amazon said on Sept. 15 that it had been “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in those two regions.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers in late September disrupted television broadcasts and internet access. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Ukraine’s response began on Oct. 8, and it has since carried out drone strikes on three data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, often called Russia’s version of Google. The first site hit, in Sasovo, houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to develop its AI models, Meduza reported, and the outage disrupted several companies relying on Yandex’s cloud services, including Russian Railways, MegaFon, T-Bank, and several media outlets.
Following the first strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the retaliation: "We always respond in kind. You all know that they are hitting and hitting our data centers; we responded to them.”
How have tech companies responded?
The spate of attacks over the last year has already caused tech companies to rethink how and where they build data centers.
The United Arab Emirates is reportedly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project following the Iranian strikes. The original plan envisioned a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, to be built in partnership with American tech companies like Oracle, Nvidia, and Cisco. Now the data centers will likely be spread out across the UAE, according to officials who spoke to Reuters.
Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, believes that data centers have become a new frontline in warfare—and that may require new strategies.
“If you’re Russia and you attack a Microsoft data center, is that an attack on Ukraine? Is that an attack on Microsoft? Is that an attack on a U.S. company and, by extension, the U.S.?” she asks.
The U.S. has largely followed a policy that attacks on American companies do not constitute an attack on the United States, but Harding says the government may need to decide on a new approach “that creates deterrence not just to protect life and health, but also data.”
And while the threat to data centers in the U.S. may be relatively low compared to the Gulf and Ukraine or Russia, tech companies will also have to think more about the security of their facilities when building, while trying to keep pace with massive demand.
“The knock-on effect is that the companies that own the data centers are realizing they can't protect them, and that kind of calls into question the cloud model in general,” Harding says. “They're having to make big adjustments. You could see a time in the future where Amazon starts losing business to Microsoft because Microsoft does a better job of hiding where their data centers are.”

"Thinkers Into Hinkers? Do AI Companies Want Philosophy, or Just Its Compliance?" An essay H. Mustafa Akyol (Keywords: AI Ethics; Governance;Institutions;Epistemic Independence;Public Philosophy)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:06:40 UTC
03:06:40 KST

"Thinkers Into Hinkers? Do AI Companies Want Philosophy, or Just Its Compliance?" An essay H. Mustafa Akyol (Keywords: AI Ethics; Governance;Institutions;Epistemic Independence;Public Philosophy)
If you enjoy reading this, please consider becoming a Patreon member or making a donation. The Philosopher is unfunded and your support is greatly appreciated.
The recent trend of AI companies hiring philosophers has largely been celebrated as a vindication for the discipline. The Economist recently reported that American philosophy graduates now find work at higher rates than their computer science peers, and that leading AI laboratories are recruiting philosophers into senior roles -– not merely to sharpen a model's chains of reasoning, but to draft the documents, such as Google's published 'AI Principles', that are meant to govern how a system behaves. Where criticism of this trend exists, it has tended to focus on familiar concerns: ethics washing, the risk of philosophy becoming a public-relations exercise, and the migration of talent away from universities that Luciano Floridi has called a 'haemorrhaging'. These concerns are real. But they may be missing a further, less visible risk, one that has nothing to do with where a philosopher's paycheck comes from.
Floridi's own diagnosis is more specific than the headlines suggest. In a recent essay, he argues that AI laboratories are not really buying philosophical knowledge but a temperament – the disposition Keats called negative capability, the ability to remain in uncertainty without an 'irritable reaching after fact and reason'. Philosophy departments cultivate this temperament unusually well, which is part of what makes their best graduates so easy to poach. His proposed remedy is structural: let philosophers hold two posts at once, one foot in the university and one in the laboratory, on condition that the university chair remains theirs to keep and their right to publish and dissent remains intact.
It is a generous and historically literate solution – he is right that Descartes was a soldier, that Leibniz was a diplomat and mining engineer, and that the philosopher confined to a single university post is a nineteenth-century invention rather than the discipline's natural state. But Floridi's remedy answers a question of institutional custody: who keeps the philosopher, and on what terms. It does not quite reach the question I want to raise, which is what happens to the practice of philosophy itself once it is put to work inside an organisation, regardless of who signs the contract. As AI ethics increasingly becomes a matter of compliance, auditing, and risk management – the very apparatus that produces documents like the 'AI Principles' The Economist describes – philosophy itself risks being transformed from a practice of questioning into a function of implementation. Even a philosopher with an unimpeachably independent university chair, free to publish and dissent, can find that the daily work reshapes what 'thinking' means long before anyone notices the shift.
A thinker asks whether a framework is justified. A hinker helps implement it more efficiently.
This is not a claim that compliance is worthless. Laws, safety standards, and ethical baselines matter, and few people would argue that AI systems should be exempt from them. The trouble starts when compliance is mistaken for ethics itself. Across contemporary AI governance, 'responsible AI' has increasingly come to mean audits, checklists, certification schemes, and risk registers. These mechanisms have real value; they create accountability and catch certain harms before they metastasise. But they also perform a quiet substitution. Questions become metrics. Values become key performance indicators. Moral reflection becomes process management. The resulting apparatus is very good at answering 'how do we comply with the ethical requirements we've been given?' and almost never asks 'why were these the requirements, and who decided that?'
It is worth being specific about the scale of this, since it is no longer a matter of a handful of isolated hires. Anthropic's philosophy contingent includes Amanda Askell, who leads the team responsible for Claude's 'constitution' – a document Anthropic has described as drawing on sources 'as diverse as Immanuel Kant, Apple's terms of service and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights', and which has been nicknamed, inside and outside the company, its 'soul doc' – alongside Joe Carlsmith, Ben Levinstein, and Jackson Kernion. Google DeepMind's roster includes Iason Gabriel, who leads the lab's AI morality work, together with Atoosa Kasirzadeh, Henry Shevlin, and others. OpenAI's Sam Altman has said the company consulted 'hundreds of moral philosophers' while drafting the principles behind ChatGPT. Several of these hires left tenured academic posts to take the roles, which may itself suggest how seriously the work is taken on both sides. None of this should be read as a claim about what any particular person is doing, still less as a judgement on them; taking a position at an AI lab is, as the historical examples above suggest, an entirely reasonable choice, and one this essay has no interest in second-guessing. The relevant point is only that a large share of what these roles are for – writing constitutions, drafting principles, building the documents that will govern how a system behaves – sits, by its own description, closer to the framework-building end of the spectrum this essay has been describing than to open-ended inquiry. Whether that reflects what these institutions most want from the philosophers they hire, or simply what they find easiest to reward, is the question the rest of this essay tries to answer.
It is worth pausing on what kind of claim this essay is making, and what kind it is not. This is not a description of what any of the philosophers named above are doing behind closed doors – none of us outside their teams can see that, and I have no wish to guess. It is not an accusation, and it is not a claim that the pattern described below is already the settled state of affairs. It is a risk assessment: an argument that a particular institutional pressure exists, that it would predictably push in one direction if left unchecked, and that a moment of rapid hiring is exactly the situation in which such a pressure is worth naming early, rather than only once it has already done its work.
***
Compliance concerns conformity to an existing framework. Philosophy concerns the examination of that framework. The two activities are related, but they are not the same, and institutions are structurally more likely to reward the first than the second.
A company would generally find it easier to fund research into how to operationalise a fairness metric than to fund a sustained argument that the system should not exist in its current form at all. It would tend to welcome help aligning a model with the organisation's stated goals more readily than a colleague who keeps asking whether those goals deserve to be pursued. This is the trap, and it rarely announces itself as one. Nobody sits a philosopher down and asks them to stop thinking. The transition, where it happens, tends to be gradual and almost administrative: a person hired to interrogate assumptions finds an increasing share of their week spent translating assumptions into governance procedure instead.
The trouble starts when compliance is mistaken for ethics itself... Questions become metrics. Values become key performance indicators. Moral reflection becomes process management.
There is a word for this in Turkish that I think names the phenomenon more precisely than any English term I know: hınk deyici, someone who reflexively agrees with authority and echoes the prevailing view rather than testing it. The nearest English cognate is 'yes-man', but that phrase carries a whiff of cowardice that misses what is actually happening here. Nobody involved need be spineless, or even particularly aware that anything has shifted. Borrowing the shape of the Turkish term, I want to propose a companion English one: a hinker. A thinker asks whether a framework is justified. A hinker helps implement it more efficiently. A thinker expands the space of reflection; a hinker accelerates execution within whatever space has already been agreed. It is worth being precise about which two forms of approval this covers, since they are easy to conflate: a hinker is not only someone who approves of the company, uncritically endorsing whatever it wants to build; a hinker can just as easily be someone who approves of compliance itself, uncritically accepting that 'alignment' and 'auditing' exhaust what ethical diligence requires. The second failure is quieter and, I suspect, more common among philosophers who would never think of themselves as corporate apologists. Most philosophers now working inside AI companies are, I want to be clear, neither cynical nor complicit – many are exactly as rigorous and independent as their academic training made them. The pressure that turns a thinker into a hinker is structural, not personal: it lies in what the institution is built to reward, not in any individual's failure of nerve.
Hannah Arendt gives this something closer to a proper name than anything borrowed so far. Reporting on Eichmann's trial, she was struck less by any demonic hatred in the man than by an almost total absence of reflection: he spoke in the fixed phrases of his office, and seemed unable to step far enough outside his role even to ask whether the role itself could be defended. She called this thoughtlessness, and she meant something quite specific by it – not stupidity, and not ignorance, but a professional habit so complete that it closes off the space in which a person might stop and ask what she is actually doing. One could object, fairly, that this is a strange comparison to reach for: thoughtlessness under totalitarian command is one thing, and a well-paid consultant drafting a fairness metric is a very different and much smaller thing, and the disanalogy is real. But the mechanism Arendt is describing does not need totalitarianism to run. It needs only an institution efficient enough that following its internal logic starts to feel like the whole of the job. Late in her life Arendt described the alternative as thinking without a banister – reasoning that refuses to lean on an inherited rule for support merely because the rule is already there, already signed off, already load-bearing. A hinker, in the sense this essay is using the word, is someone working with exactly such a banister permanently installed. The framework does the leaning on their behalf, and the daily habit of checking a system against it can quietly substitute for the harder work of asking whether the framework deserves the weight it has been given. Nobody need notice the substitution happening. That is rather the point.
Compliance concerns conformity to an existing framework. Philosophy concerns the examination of that framework.
It would be tempting to conclude from this that the safest place for a philosopher is as far from any institution as possible – that the banister only appears once someone accepts an office to lean on it in. But that conclusion does not survive much contact with the discipline's own history, and it is worth setting the temptation aside before it does any more work. Descartes served as a soldier before he became the author of the Meditations, and by his own account it was the itinerant years, not the stove-heated room, that first unsettled his certainties. Leibniz spent decades as a working diplomat and mining engineer, drafting political memoranda between treatises on monads. Hume was a librarian and, for a time, a civil servant under-secretary, and complained more than once that his administrative posts paid rather better than his philosophy did. The philosopher entangled in worldly institutions is arguably the historical norm rather than the exception; the mid-century image of philosophy as a cloistered, purely academic pursuit is itself the historical anomaly, and a fairly recent one. So the question was never whether philosophers should work inside powerful organisations, or whether doing so automatically hands them a banister to lean on. The question Arendt's diagnosis actually poses is narrower and harder to escape by staying clear of industry: whether a person inside such an organisation keeps enough distance from its internal logic to ask, periodically and seriously, whether that logic still deserves the trust it has been given.
With the term on the table, the question becomes empirical rather than definitional: are the philosophers now working at AI companies actually drifting toward hinker-work, or is the risk, so far, mostly theoretical?
***
An obvious objection is available, and it deserves more than a brief concession. Why assume that a company's interest in implementation crowds out its interest in genuine critique, rather than the two running together? There is a real economic case that they do run together. As the industry commentator Gerald Pallor has put it, a certification or audit process functions as a kind of bouncer at the door of enterprise sales – no certificate, no deal – and insurers are increasingly willing to offer better terms to firms that can document real oversight and bias testing, which means that documented rigour carries a cash value quite apart from whatever ethical good it does. On this view, a philosopher embedded in an AI company is not competing with the firm's commercial interest; she is serving it, and a company that wanted only the appearance of ethics could presumably get that more cheaply than by hiring philosophers with doctorates from Oxford and Berkeley.
This is a fair challenge, and the honest answer is that it relocates the risk rather than removing it. The claim here is not that firms lack a commercial interest in genuine philosophical rigour. It is that firms have a much easier time rewarding, measuring, and defending the parts of that work which yield a legible artefact – a certificate, a published constitution, a benchmark score – than the parts which yield only a harder question. This is a specific version of a general problem in organisations that assign people several kinds of work at once: when some of what an employee does is easy for others to observe and verify and some is not, incentives drift toward the observable part even when the organisation formally values both, because performance review, promotion, and resourcing all have to be justified in terms someone else can check. A philosopher who spends a quarter drafting a constitution has something to show for it. A philosopher who spends a quarter arguing that a product should not exist in its current form has, for the organisation's own bookkeeping, produced nothing any dashboard can register – even if the argument turns out, years later, to have been the most valuable thing anyone in the building said. Naming this risk does not require assuming AI companies are cynical about ethics. It requires only the weaker and much more defensible assumption that measurable work tends to crowd out unmeasurable work inside large organisations generally, whatever the people involved sincerely believe they value.
A society can build a perfectly auditable, thoroughly certified AI system and still have failed to ask whether it is heading in a direction worth going.
There is a small piece of evidence that speaks to where this boundary tends to fall in practice, even if it does not settle the matter. Joe Carlsmith writes, alongside his work on Claude's constitution, a long-running series of personal essays on philosophy of mind, AI moral status, and related questions – open-ended, unresolved work of exactly the kind this essay has been arguing philosophy should keep doing. Nearly all of them carry some version of the same disclaimer: 'I work at Anthropic, but I am here speaking only for myself and not for my employer.' The disclaimer is unremarkable as professional practice and implies nothing improper. But it marks, with more precision than most abstract argument could, exactly where this essay's distinction tends to fall: the constitution is the company's, drafted collectively and owned as an institutional document; the open questioning happens under a heading that keeps it from counting as the institution's own view. Whether that questioning ever finds its way back into the document it is formally kept apart from is not something an outside observer can verify, and outside observers are not always convinced that it does. Asked about the influence of in-house philosophers on product decisions, one AI industry engineer interviewed by the International Business Times put the doubt plainly: 'I'm not really confident whether they are actually taking philosophers into account at all, to be honest ... Primarily, all these companies, their main aim is revenue generation.' That is one person's impression, offered about the industry in general rather than any single lab, and it may undersell the people involved. But it names, from outside, roughly the same gap this essay has been trying to describe from within: the distance between a framework a philosopher helped write and the deeper interrogation that framework was always meant to follow.
There is now a considerably richer case study available than either of these, and it happens to cut both ways, which is exactly why it is worth dwelling on. A recent Guardian profile of Gabriel reports two things worth holding side by side. First, according to Rohin Shah, DeepMind's director for AGI alignment and safety, the framework Gabriel's team developed on the ethics of AI assistants 'has had real practical use' for technologists deciding what behaviour to train into systems like Gemini. Second, and more concretely: the same profile credits Gabriel's research on the risks of anthropomorphic AI with a specific design choice – Google's assistants, including the one launched this year as Gemini Spark, are trained not to imply they are people or to act like an 'interactive buddy'. Taken together, these are about as clean an instance as one is likely to find, outside the company itself, of philosophical critique shaping how a product actually behaves rather than merely accompanying it on the side.
Set against this, the same Guardian profile describes an episode in which commercial and geopolitical pressure appears to have simply overridden whatever deliberation preceded it. In April 2026, Google agreed to let the US military use its AI for 'any lawful government purpose', reversing a restriction the company had held since DeepMind's 2014 acquisition, and one that Anthropic had just refused at real commercial cost. Demis Hassabis, DeepMind's own chief executive, was unusually candid about what pressures of this kind do to the sort of deliberation his company's philosophers are paid to provide: this is not how he had hoped AI development would go, 'where we would be contemplating this philosophically and carefully considering each next step. We're not in that world'. That is not a claim this essay is making about the industry from outside. It is the head of one of its most consequential labs, describing from inside something close to the crowding-out this essay has been arguing is structural rather than incidental.
None of this settles which scenario predominates day to day inside any particular lab, and it would be dishonest to claim otherwise from outside. What can fairly be said is this: the institutional pressure described above is real and well documented in organisations generally; the philosophers currently doing this work are producing at least some artefacts, like the anthropomorphism research that shaped how Gemini Spark behaves, that show genuine critical input can register and change what gets shipped; and other evidence, like the disclaimer pattern, the engineer's doubt, and a chief executive's own admission that commercial pressure is crowding out philosophical deliberation, suggests it does not always do so, or does not do so where it matters most. The reasonable conclusion is not that philosophers in these roles have become hinkers. It is that the structural conditions under which they work make the drift toward hinker-work more likely than the institutions themselves would probably want, and that this is worth naming and watching for now, rather than either dismissing it because thoughtful individuals are involved or declaring it already settled on the strength of one troubling pattern.
A healthy institution needs someone able to say: perhaps we are asking the wrong question, perhaps the objective itself deserves scrutiny.
What philosophy has always contributed is not, primarily, the production of answers. Socrates is not remembered for having supplied Athens with a governance framework; he is remembered for refusing to let the city's unexamined assumptions pass as settled. Contemporary AI debates ask, reasonably, whether systems should be fair, transparent, accountable. Of course they should. But philosophy's distinctive move has always been to ask the question underneath that one: why is this system being built at all, what account of human flourishing is it quietly assuming, and which other accounts have been foreclosed without anyone noticing? These are not compliance questions. A society can build a perfectly auditable, thoroughly certified AI system and still have failed to ask whether it is heading in a direction worth going. Governance helps us navigate. Philosophy is what helps us ask whether we have the right destination, and confusing the two has a cost that compounds quietly, without ever showing up on a risk register.
A healthy institution needs someone able to say: perhaps we are asking the wrong question, perhaps the objective itself deserves scrutiny, perhaps the most affected people are not in this room. Such interventions rarely accelerate a product roadmap. They do not improve a quarterly earnings call. They are, nonetheless, close to the only thing that makes the rest of the apparatus worth trusting.
***
I have argued elsewhere, in my own work on deliberative AI governance, that legitimacy is not something a system acquires simply by complying with a set of pre-agreed principles. It comes from an ongoing public argument about what those principles should even be – from institutions that preserve structured disagreement rather than manufacture premature consensus. The same, I think, is true of philosophy's place inside the companies now hiring it. Its value was never in helping an organisation answer its ethical questions more efficiently. It was in making sure that the questions organisations, governments, and their own experts would prefer to treat as settled remain open enough to be asked again.
AI companies say they want philosophers for their capacity to question, and there is no reason to doubt that many of them mean it. The risk this essay has traced is narrower and more structural: that what an organisation can most easily recognise, reward, and act on is the capacity to answer, so that even sincerely wanted criticism finds it harder to register than an implemented framework does. Answering efficiently was never philosophy's contribution – identifying the question everyone else had already stopped asking was. There is no institutional design that could permanently remove this risk, and it would be a mistake to end by pretending otherwise. The point was never that philosophers should stay out of AI companies; the history rehearsed above suggests they never have stayed out of worldly institutions for long, and there is no obvious reason AI should be the exception. The point is to preserve the practice of philosophy inside them – to keep spaces where questioning is valued apart from what it implements, where dissent is treated as useful rather than merely tolerated, and where success is measured not only by the frameworks produced but by the quality of the questions those frameworks leave open.
Floridi may well be right that philosophers should keep one foot in the university. My argument has simply been that this cannot be sufficient on its own. The decisive question was never really where the philosopher works. It is whether the organisation around her preserves the conditions under which philosophy remains philosophy – and whether she, and the rest of us, keep noticing the difference between a thinker and a hinker for long enough that it continues to matter which one she is.
AI should not replace our reflection; rather, we should reflect more.
H. Mustafa Akyol is an independent researcher working at the intersection of artificial intelligence and philosophy. He holds separate bachelor's degrees in industrial engineering and philosophy, and has worked as an AI code reviewer and as a product manager. His writing addresses questions of responsibility, deliberation, and governance under increasingly capable AI systems; his chapter 'Deliberative AI Governance' is forthcoming in AI Regulation in Industry 5.0: Ethical Governance, Policy Frameworks, and Human-Centric Innovation (Springer Nature). He is currently at work on a book developing these arguments at greater length.

A senior UN official has warned that the situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank is dangerously fragile, saying a return to war must be avoided at all costs.
Briefing the UN Security Council on Palestine on Thursday, Ramiz Alakbarov, UN acting special coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, marked the anniversary of the October 7 events, saying Palestinians and Israelis need a political horizon.
"Palestinians and Israelis deserve more than short-term fixes. They deserve a credible path to peace and finally an end to this conflict," he said. "The international community must move beyond words and take concrete actions to ensure the future of security and dignity of the people. It is time to return to a genuine peace process.”
Turning to Gaza, Alakbarov noted that one year has passed since a ceasefire was completed. "While some progress has been made, the situation remains extremely fragile," he said.
He said Israeli military operations have continued, "causing some 1,500 fatalities, including more than 320 children."
Alakbarov described families in Gaza living in worn-out tents, overcrowded displacement sites and badly damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. "Most of Gaza still lives in darkness," he said.
"People in Gaza must not be forced to endure another winter without safe shelter and basic services," he stressed.
‘West Bank is also at a boiling point’
Highlighting the needs of children, he said, "Emergency assistance alone is not enough. Sustainable recovery and political progress must advance together."
On the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, Alakbarov said the situation continues to deteriorate amid Israeli military operations, movement restrictions, displacement and attacks on Palestinians. He said settler violence persists at "extremely high levels," with daily attacks on Palestinians.
Describing his assessment as "realistic," Alakbarov said he felt compelled to raise concerns before the council.
"Today, I feel obliged to sound the alarm. In Gaza, desperation is palpable," he said.
He warned that frustration among Gaza's population cannot continue to build indefinitely and described the risk of a return to war as extremely high. "This must be avoided at all costs," he said.
"The (occupied) West Bank is also at a boiling point," he added.

Lebanon's president says regional developments, Israeli elections slowed war talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:04:58 UTC
03:04:58 KST

Wassim Seifeddine, Lina Altawell
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Thursday that regional and international developments, along with Israeli elections, may have slowed negotiations to end Israel’s war against Lebanon, but stressed that the talks have not stopped, according to a statement from the Lebanese presidency.
Aoun made the remarks while receiving a delegation of third-year and master’s students in media studies from the Holy Spirit University of Kaslik at the Baabda presidential palace east of Beirut.
He said contacts led by Lebanon’s Ambassador to Washington, Nada Mouawad, and the US administration continued in an effort to move the negotiating process forward.
“There is no third option between war and negotiations,” he said. “If anyone has another option, let them tell me.”
“Wars usually end either with one side achieving an overwhelming victory that forces the other to surrender, or through negotiations,” said the president.
“The goal we are working toward is to stop the war, achieve an Israeli withdrawal, save and rebuild the south, secure the return of prisoners and displaced people, and prevent the war from expanding to all Lebanese territory,” Aoun added.
He argued that without negotiations, Israeli attacks would have reached Beirut and public facilities.
Direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel began April 14, with a US-sponsored meeting in Washington, with subsequent rounds addressing a ceasefire, withdrawal, borders, prisoners and missing persons.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored “framework formula” in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued. Israel remains in control of areas in the south, some occupied for decades and others seized during recent wars and military operations.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people, injured 12,413 and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
Separately, Aoun stressed the importance of accurate reporting and warned against using journalism to blackmail people or pursue personal and financial interests.
“The media is a weapon that can build or destroy,” he said, urging journalism students to uphold professional ethics and not use their work to serve private interests.
Aoun said he remained committed to freedom of expression and the press but added that “there is no absolute freedom, because then it turns into chaos,” saying national security sets the limits of freedom.
On domestic affairs, he urged placing the public interest above all other considerations, saying there is a Lebanese faction that represents the opposite of the state because its role would end once the state functions fully.
Aoun also cited achievements he said had not received sufficient media coverage, including Lebanon joining the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) ports network through the ports of Tripoli and Beirut, and demarcating the maritime border with Cyprus.
“Lebanon recorded 4% economic growth last year, while the Finance Ministry posted a $1.3 billion surplus and the central bank’s foreign currency holdings increased by $2 billion,” he said. “Growth had been projected at 6% this year, but the war prevented that.”
Addressing higher oil prices and their economic effect, Aoun attributed the increase to the war in the Gulf, whose effects he said are being felt worldwide, as well as what he described as “traders’ greed.”
“The state is working to ease the economic burden as much as possible,” said the president.
On Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran that killed thousands. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US sites in countries in the region.
A ceasefire was reached in April, but Washington later carried out further attacks on sites inside Iran amid stalled negotiations.
