French student protests make it clear: Neither Macron nor Le Pen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:00:56 UTC
03:00:56 KST

Breadcrumb
French student protests make it clear: Neither Macron nor Le Pen
On a rare holiday, on my first visit to Paris, I took the Metro from the modernist wonders of the 13th arrondissement to my next destination. Two stops before I was meant to get off to visit an art gallery, I saw an army of children with homemade placards and keffiyehs marching down the platform at Sully Morland. Instinctively inclined towards the idea that these rebellious kids could probably produce more creativity in one single protest than any art gallery could muster (a joke, kind of), I departed from my premeditated route and before I knew it, I was marching on the Bastille with tens of thousands of young working-class kids letting out their frustration and fury at an education system that was failing them and set only to worsen.
This crowd was a mosaic of multicultural France: white kids side-by-side with those from the Parisian banlieues whose roots trace right back across the Maghreb, Western and Central Africa, linking arms with teachers and trade unionists, making clear their opposition to the far-right National Rally (RN), current President Emmanuel Macron, and the ongoing acts of imperial violence in Palestine, Congo and Sudan.
More carnivalesque than a simple protest, this unleashed repressed energies from a generation of teenagers vilified by the press, forced into silos of demeaning desocialisation by social media platforms, and subjected to increasing impoverishment by a punishing austerity regime fronted by Macron.
The people have had enough
The ire of protesters’ antipathy: the French schooling system is in prolonged decay.
France has the highest class sizes in Europe; teachers are increasingly forced out of the profession by low pay, declining vacancies, and poor treatment, and the physical infrastructure that underpins French schooling is increasingly strained by dilapidation, infestation, and extreme weather conditions.
As William Bouchardon has noted in Jacobin, classes regularly miss teachers, there is a shortage of both school nurses and aides for children with disabilities and learning difficulties, and these realities are felt in racialised, working-class France. This is compounded by the reality that ministers contemplate further rounds of austerity as they defend, in the case of former National Education Minister Amélie Oudéa-Castér, sending their own children to private schools.
France, like so much of the world, is a country simmering with unease, class conflict and political polarisation. In Spain, the violent eviction and eventual death of Maricarmen Abascal was the catalyst for an unprecedented wave of militant national housing protests, sparking an early election initiated by Socialist Party Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
In Belgium, workers have fought and struck against exacerbating impoverishment and fiscal retrenchment. And in Brazil, millions have taken to the streets against the prospect of a far-right government led by Jair Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio. The world could be on the cusp of a sequence of global social revolt unseen in over a decade.
France Unbowed
One political project uniquely primed to take advantage of this radicalisation and polarisation is Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s France Unbowed Party (LFI). Founded ten years ago, the long product of a rupture from traditional French social democracy, LFI has become increasingly identified with the youth protests. Recently elected Mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko was subject to international acclaim, even compared to Spider-Man, for his brave defence of youths tear-gassed by the French riot police.
Bagayoko has also found himself under frequent attack by centrist and right-wing politicians and pundits, almost always with a deeply racist edge, such as the insults which saw him compared to a crack cocaine addict.
Similarly, Mélenchon faced political abuse since his resignation from François Mitterrand’s ambitious but eventually capitulating Socialist Party government in the 1980s. The LFI leader and long-time Presidential candidate was filmed sharing an intimate intergenerational moment with a student protester, made famous overnight for humiliating a journalist who tried to ask fellow protesters leading questions in the midst of the action.
Despite regular criticism of Mélenchon’s uninterrupted control of this start-up party, its rise to prominence is undeniable. As one keen observer of French politics noted to me, if you belonged to that generation of millennials increasingly radicalised by the 2008 financial crash and the attempts to manage it in the rich’s interests, in France, you’ve seen the Mélenchon project increase its influence, voter share and cultural resonance every single year since 2010.
In the 2022 presidential election, Mélenchon was a single point away from defeating far-right Marine Le Pen and making the second round against now-outgoing President Macron. In the 2024 legislative election, LFI was the largest component of the Nouveau Front Populaire, which won the contest and forced Macron to deny the democratic wishes of the French electorate by desperately appointing European technocrat Michel Barnier as Prime Minister.
Two years later, with Barnier lasting only months, centre-right politician Sébastian Lecornu now holds the role in alliance with the Macronists.
Mélenchon’s party has proven adept at exploiting the crisis of French neoliberalism, speaking to people’s anguish over the decimation of their living conditions, their increasing disenfranchisement, and a deep-seated feeling of alienation from the state, from nature, and from each other.
Anti-racism and Palestine
The party’s ‘A Shared Future’ (L’avenir en commun) programme which invokes the formation of a Sixth Republic which decentralises democratic control over society; guarantees the right to free energy and water in every household; and establishes ‘eco-regions’ geared towards protecting nature, agriculture and planetary life through ecological planning.
It is also a party which has undergone a profound set of ideological and moral changes since the turn of the decade. For example, in 2016, it would not have been a surprise to encounter Mélenchon and his coterie lauding the uniquely French brand of secularism, Laïcité. Whilst theoretically a paean to the history of French republicanism and the separation between church and state, in practice this state ideology has functioned as the basis for criminalising and defiling France’s large and diverse Muslim community.
A decade ago, LFI would have entertained this jamboree of racialised recrimination, entertaining Islamophobic policies such as the banning of the hijab. Today, Mélenchon’s populism has shifted, shaped by the rise of social movements in solidarity with Palestine, against racist state violence such as the police murder of Nahel Merzouk, and advocating a form of what the party describes as ‘creolisation’, the celebrated intermingling of cultures from across the world fundamentally changing the fabric of the French people themselves.
LFI has become a much more vigorously anti-racist and internationalist project. Among its senior cadre today, along with National Coordinator Manuel Bompard and President of elected representatives in the National Assembly Mathilde Panot, you encounter long-term anti-racist advocates such as the Gabonese-French representative of the Parisian 17th arrondissement Danièle Obono and Palestinian organiser and now LFI representative in the European Parliament, Rima Hassan.
This shift in policy and outlook also mediates a strategic recalculation. Partly because of the benefits of the French electoral system, LFI is actively geared towards building the core of its support base in the multicultural suburbs of France’s major cities. This is particularly the case among what party strategist Bompard has termed the ‘Fourth Bloc’ of young and racialised working-class voters who traditionally do not vote.
As the 2027 presidential election approaches, Mélenchon is consolidating his dominance over the left bloc in French society. With the Socialist Party now endorsing notorious centrist Raphael Glucksmann and the Ecologistes remaining divided over who they might break for, the LFI leader looks increasingly likely, according to polling, to be the principal challenger to Marine Le Pen’s violently toxic brand of far-right politics in the second round of next year’s election.
At last Wednesday’s protest, there were loud chants of ‘Mélenchon, Ballon D’or’ from the crowd of Paris’ youth demonstrators. A few days later, I spoke to a group of young men in their mid-twenties in La République. They were Mélenchon-sceptics but were clear they would vote for him to keep out Le Pen. For this historic figure of the French radical left, and this insurgent party of militants he has helped inaugurate as a model for left-wing politics globally, both dynamics will be essential to LFI defeating the far-right and implementing their programme when in power.
Jonas Marvin is the author of The Breaking of the English Working Class. He also cohosts Life of the Party podcast and blogs at Marx’s Dream Journal.

Machine learning uncovers early warning signs of depression in brain scans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:00:31 UTC
03:00:31 KST

A new computational model combined with brain imaging data reveals that relying too heavily on prior expectations when perceiving facial expressions can predict a person’s risk for developing depression. By analyzing how the human brain processes angry faces, researchers identified a mathematical pattern of visual distortion that appears up to four years before clinical symptoms emerge. The study was published in Science Advances.
Major depressive disorder affects millions of people worldwide and is often difficult to treat once established. Early detection remains a high priority for public health experts, but predicting who will develop the condition relies mostly on self-reported symptoms and environmental risk factors. Identifying biological markers that indicate an individual’s vulnerability before they feel ill could improve prevention efforts.
Mental health conditions are often characterized by altered emotional processing, such as a tendency to interpret ambiguous social cues as negative or threatening. Leading psychological theories propose that our brains construct emotional experiences by using abstract concepts stored in our memory to interpret raw sensory information, like the visual details of a face. In recent years, researchers have mapped out various brain regions associated with depression, but these descriptive patterns do not explain the exact mechanisms driving the illness.
Han Lu and Qiang Luo, researchers at Shenzhen University and Fudan University, respectively, sought to understand how this integration of sensory input and abstract memory might go wrong in people prone to depression. They hypothesized that the visual cortex, the brain region responsible for processing sight, might act as an early bottleneck where social threat signals become distorted. To test this idea, the researchers developed a mathematical simulation to replicate how the human brain learns to recognize emotional expressions.
The researchers first analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging brain scans from 1,332 nineteen-year-old participants in a population-based European study known as the IMAGEN cohort. This imaging technique measures blood flow in the brain to detect areas of neural activity. The scans tracked the adolescents’ brain activity while they viewed short video clips of faces transitioning from neutral expressions to angry ones.
Using a machine learning algorithm, the research team extracted a mathematical representation of how each participant’s visual cortex encoded the angry faces. They refer to this specific pattern of neural activity as a visual code. The team then grouped the participants based on the efficiency of these visual codes, separating them into one group with typical, highly efficient visual encoding and another with inefficient, noisy visual processing.
Adolescents in the less efficient group reported higher levels of emotional symptoms, such as anxiety and low mood, on clinical questionnaires. This relationship indicated that a degraded visual representation of angry faces was tied to emotional distress. The researchers determined that poor visual coding in the brain was directly related to the presence of emotional symptoms.
To understand the computational mechanism behind this degraded visual processing, the team built a deep neural network, which is an artificial intelligence model composed of interconnected algorithms modeled after the human brain. This specific model featured two distinct processing pathways. One pathway processed raw visual information from images, while the other pathway held abstract conceptual knowledge about different emotions.
In standard human perception, the brain uses abstract knowledge to guide and speed up the processing of visual information, allowing a person to recognize a facial expression quickly. The researchers programmed their artificial network to mimic this process, allowing the conceptual pathway to regulate the visual pathway as the model learned to identify facial expressions. When the researchers compared the artificial network’s internal mathematical code to the human brain scans, they found a strong alignment.
This similarity suggested the model successfully replicated the visual perception of angry faces. The team then conducted an experiment on the model by altering the strength of the conceptual pathway’s influence over the visual pathway. They systematically turned the regulation strength up and down to observe how the network would respond.
When the regulation was set to an intermediate level, the model achieved optimal emotion recognition. However, when the researchers forced the model to apply excessive conceptual regulation, it began to misclassify neutral faces as angry or sad. This overreliance on abstract concepts overrode the actual visual details, producing a computational negative bias.
The internal code of this overly regulated artificial model closely matched the inefficient, noisy brain patterns found in the adolescents with higher emotional symptoms. This suggests that overregularization, which is the act of letting preexisting beliefs overpower sensory reality, acts as a mechanism that drives negative emotional biases.
Building on this simulation, the researchers created a computational marker that quantified each human participant’s degree of visual overregularization based on their brain scans at age nineteen. They then followed up with 725 of these participants four years later. The goal was to see if the marker could forecast the onset of mental health issues.
Among the young adults who had no clinical symptoms at age nineteen, the mathematical marker successfully predicted which individuals would develop high levels of emotional symptoms by age twenty-three. This prediction model outperformed traditional baseline measures that rely only on demographics and basic brain activation levels. The finding suggests that the overregulation mechanism may precede the onset of emotional symptoms.
To determine if this computational mechanism was specific to depression, the team examined genetic data from the IMAGEN participants. They checked for associations between the overregulation marker and genetic variants tied to various psychiatric conditions. The analysis showed a link between the overregulated visual marker and a specific genetic variant associated with major depressive disorder, located on a gene involved in brain development.
The marker was also linked to the participants’ polygenic risk score for depression, which is a number that summarizes the estimated effect of many different genetic variants on a person’s risk for a disease. The visual marker did not show any links to the genetic risks for alcohol use disorder or eating disorders. This specificity supported the idea that the visual distortion mechanism is uniquely tied to depression.
Finally, the researchers tested their marker in a separate clinical dataset of young adults to see if it persisted in established illnesses. They analyzed brain scans from 134 patients diagnosed with major depressive disorder and 62 healthy control subjects. The patients with depression exhibited higher levels of the overregulation marker compared to the healthy controls.
The marker accurately classified whether a participant had depression or not. When applied to patients with alcohol use disorder, anorexia nervosa, and bulimia nervosa, the marker showed no group differences. The traditional brain activation measures were not statistically significant in distinguishing the depressed patients from the healthy controls.
The study participants from both the population-based and clinical cohorts were predominantly white individuals from middle-to-high socioeconomic backgrounds. Future research will need to examine whether these specific computational patterns apply equally to populations with different ethnic, racial, and socioeconomic demographics. The differences in emotional symptoms between the high-efficiency and low-efficiency visual processing groups in the general adolescent sample were also relatively small.
While expected in general population studies capturing subclinical distress, this small effect size means the visual clustering approach alone has limited diagnostic power for individual patients at this stage. Researchers must validate the broader clinical utility of this marker in independent patient groups. Tracking these computational markers in younger adolescents could reveal if the visual distortions appear even earlier in development.
Tracking patients over time will also help determine if the marker can predict long-term recovery versus chronic illness. Identifying whether the visual distortion is a permanent trait or a temporary state would assist in designing targeted therapies. Interventions that aim to retrain visual processing might one day help mitigate this depression risk.
The study, “Deep learning reveals a neurocomputational mechanism predicting depression risk in adolescents,” was authored by Han Lu, Xiaoqian Yan, Benjamin Becker, Andreas Heinz, Barbara J. Sahakian, Christelle Langley, Zhaoyu Zuo, Luolong Cao, Zuo Zhang, Lauren Robinson, Nilakshi Vaidya, Jeanne Winterer, Sinead King, Charlotte Walton, Tobias Banaschewski, Gareth J. Barker, Arun L.W. Bokde, Rüdiger Brühl, Herta Flor, Hugh Garavan, Penny Gowland, Antoine Grigis, Herve Lemaitre, Jean-Luc Martinot, Marie-Laure Paillère Martinot, Eric Artiges, Frauke Nees, Dimitri Papadopoulos Orfanos, Luise Poustka, Hedi Kebir, Ulrike Schmidt, Julia Sinclair, Michael N. Smolka, Sarah Hohmann, Nathalie Holz, Henrik Walter, Robert Whelan, Sylvane Desrivières, Gunter Schumann, Qiang Luo, STRATIFY/ESTRA Consortium, and IMAGEN Consortium.

Nuclear spending committee still due by end of year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:00:08 BST
03:00:08 KST

A new Commons committee to scrutinise spending and programmes across the Defence Nuclear Enterprise is still expected to be established before the end of the year, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Labour member for Clapham and Brixton Hill, asked what discussions the Defence Secretary had held with the Leader of the House on the timetable for tabling a motion to set the committee up.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The Secretary of State for Defence and the Leader of the House continue to work with the House of Commons to set up a new Committee, under the House’s Standing Orders, to scrutinise Defence Nuclear Enterprise expenditure and programmes. As set out in CP1668 (page 18), the intention is ‘to establish the new Committee by the end of the year’.”
Setting up a select committee requires a motion in the House to amend Standing Orders, which the government controls the timing of, and then an election of members. Ten weeks of the year remain.
The Defence Nuclear Enterprise is the collective name for everything that supports the deterrent and the nuclear-powered submarine fleet. It takes in warhead design and production at Aldermaston and Burghfield, submarine construction at Barrow, reactor plant from Rolls-Royce at Derby, the operating bases at Faslane and Coulport, deep maintenance at Devonport, and the people and infrastructure behind all of it. The Dreadnought class programme to replace the Vanguard boats and the SSN-AUKUS attack submarine programme both sit inside it.
Scrutiny of that spending has been a running argument in Parliament for years. The National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee have repeatedly reported cost growth and schedule slippage across the enterprise, while much of the detail is withheld on national security grounds, leaving members without the figures that would let them follow the money. A dedicated committee with the clearance to see classified material is the answer ministers have offered to that.
The Defence Nuclear Enterprise now accounts for a substantial share of the equipment budget, and the Defence Investment Plan set out spending across it alongside the commitment to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats.

Alleged Chinese spy posed as recruiter for 'retired Australian police'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Alleged Chinese spy posed as recruiter for 'retired Australian police'
In short:
A suspected Chinese spying network used a fictitious security firm, purportedly organised by three retired policemen, to target Australians and encourage them to share information.
ABC contacted the individuals in Shanghai whose phones had been used to target those Australians.
ASIO has openly warned about the threat of Chinese espionage online.
Towards the start of COVID-19 in May 2020, Australian lawyer Henry* received a casual offer on LinkedIn.
"We are looking for Security expert consultant employment from Australia and Canada (part-time)," wrote someone using the name "Sophy".
The account claimed to represent Data 31, a security consultancy "organised by three retired Australian police officers" based in Shanghai.
A US-qualified lawyer with extensive experience in China, Henry's practice had covered white-collar defence and investigations. He had also served in the Australian Army for nearly two decades, leaving with the rank of major.
But the consultancy pitch was part of something wider.
An ABC investigation has now identified that "Sophy" was one of several personas used by an alleged Chinese spying network that targeted thousands of people worldwide between 2016 and 2025, including for fictional companies like Data 31.
The LinkedIn accounts, allegedly operated by the Chinese intelligence service, were deregistered last year following an investigation by the Australian Federal Police into businessman Alexander Csergo.
Those approached by the alleged spies included government officials, former military personnel and security professionals linked to Australia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and New Zealand — the nations of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.
A persona targeting Australians
The account contacted at least seven Australians in 2020 under the Data 31 identity.
The contacts included people with Australian military backgrounds, a freelance writer and podcaster, a lawyer, a security executive and Australian trade department representatives.
Among those approached was an employee of an organisation belonging to Andrew Forrest, one of Australia's wealthiest and most influential businessmen. The mining magnate's success has been closely tied to China's demand for Australian iron ore.
In a message to an Australian security executive, the account claimed Data 31 was seeking consultants to conduct "active investigations" and write "security reports" to "assist banks, data companies and venture capital institutions in Shanghai".
The proposed reports covered international relations, economics and counterterrorism.
The ABC reached out to Henry for comment but received no response.
Mr Forrest was also contacted for comment but the ABC did not receive a direct response to its questions.
ABC has seen no evidence that any of the Australians had accepted the offers to write reports.
The accounts have a LinkedIn message history spanning eight years.
One persona, "Vera Su", featured in the Australian Federal Police investigation and subsequent prosecution of businessman Alexander Csergo, who in March became the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference under Australia's 2018 national security laws.
He is serving a three-and-a-half-year prison sentence.
The Chinese Embassy in Canberra rejected the AFP's claims as "entirely groundless".
Over the past few weeks, the ABC has reviewed thousands of messages from two LinkedIn accounts linked to the alleged Chinese spying operation.
One account was active as early as 2016. Over the following years, they connected with thousands of users, including Australians and people who had worked in Australia.
The accounts claimed a range of affiliations over time, including a Chinese government tourism project, an electronics company, an EV brand, Data 31 and two other fictitious Chinese think tanks. They also used several identities, including "Sophy Ding", "Hanna Lee" and "Vera Su".
Between April and July 2020, the account repeatedly messaged potential Australian targets on behalf of Data 31, which was said to be run by "three retired Australian policemen". The ABC could not identify a genuine organisation by that name.
The LinkedIn records do not show any of these contacts completing consultancy work, although some agreed to continue the conversation.
By March 2021, a second account linked to the first was using the name "Vera Su" and claiming to represent Nesa Consulting. It was through this persona that Csergo was approached.
Who is behind the accounts?
Between 2016 and 2025, the group targeted more than 60 Australians, including around 20 government officials.
They included a commander with the AFP, a former system analyst with the Royal Australian Air Force, a deputy CEO and senior commissioners of the Australian Trade and Investment Commission, and public servants from state governments around the country.
Other people approached came from a wide range of fields, including corporate law, business consulting, economic advice, research, academia, sales, marketing and senior management.
The ABC understands Australian authorities have contacted some of the individuals who were approached to assess whether any classified information was compromised.
Csergo's trial did not establish the real identities of those behind the accounts.
During the trial, an intelligence expert described how operatives concealed their identities through intermediaries known as "cut-outs" and commercial or academic cover.
Nesa Consulting had the hallmarks of such a front. Some of its marketing materials had been plagiarised from NERA Economic Consulting, a real firm, and the AFP could not locate a website or confirm an address for it.
The ABC has since obtained voice and text messages linked to the alleged agents. It has also investigated the addresses, emails and phone numbers connected to them, tracing them to one woman and a man based in Shanghai.
The same number is connected to a WeChat account, which she used to connect with her targets off LinkedIn. The account remains active and carries the same name — Ding Chenqi Sophy.
Chinese government records obtained by the ABC showed Ms Ding worked for Shanghai-based IT company Shanghai Geguan Internet while she was in contact with her targets, including Csergo. The ABC could not find any public record of the company.
The number used by "Ken" was linked to a man in his early 50s, Xu Gefeng, who was associated with another IT company, registered in 2005.
The ABC contacted Ms Ding by phone, but she did not answer. Mr Xu answered his phone but hung up after ABC journalists identified themselves. Mr Xu's phone could not be reached afterward.
ASIO warnings
The threat posed by Chinese intelligence has been a recurring theme for ASIO director-general Mike Burgess.
In ASIO's 2024 Annual Threat Assessment, the director-general described an espionage operation by the "A-Team", which adopted the name "Sophy" and others, and claimed to represent fictional companies such as Data 31.
In the organisation's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment, he revealed that a foreign spy had approached an Australian security clearance holder online, posing as a consultant.
"The spy paid the official to write two reports on Australia's relationship with our Pacific neighbours, and then, thinking he'd been hooked, offered money for inside information on AUKUS," Mr Burgess said.
The official grew suspicious and reported the contact to ASIO.
"My officers borrowed the phone from the official and rang the so-called consultant in her home country. Thinking it was her target, the spy picked up and got a very unwelcome surprise when she realised she was speaking to ASIO," he said.
"We demonstrated we knew exactly who she was, demanded she cease targeting Australian citizens.
"The spy hung up. Message received."
*Not his real name.

Private health rebate changes causing Labor 'a lot of pain in electorates'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor will need yet another backtrack to resurrect private health rebate cut
The ins and outs of some of the seemingly endless fights over the Albanese government's budget measures are often arcane or difficult for many people to easily understand.
That's the case, for example, with the legislation to crack down on trusts, introduced on Wednesday, which has been surrounded by a lot of heat.
But the tug of war over the government's plan to remove, from April next year, the age discrimination that favours older people taking out private health insurance is a very simple issue for voters to get their heads around, wherever they stand on the merits of the measure.
It's now a central battle for the government and it will be hard for it to rescue the measure without sacrificing big dollars — just when Treasurer Jim Chalmers needs to preserve the budget's savings.
In terms of personalities, there's a lot to watch too, with new Greens leader David Shoebridge and Health Minister Mark Butler as main players.
Both have something to prove in how this ends. It's Shoebridge's first big legislative test in his new role, and he flagged earlier the Greens would be more assertive under his leadership.
For Butler, seen as one of the frontrunners to eventually succeed Anthony Albanese, it will be another benchmark of his ability to land a deal — providing clues on how well he will handle the complexities ahead in his job of reforming the National Disability Insurance Scheme.
Ryan accuses government of hiding impact
Under present arrangements, people 65 and over who have private health insurance receive a bigger rebate than those who are younger. The amount is larger if they are 70 or older.
By removing the "top-ups", the government would save $3 billion over four years. It has said this would be put into aged care, which is much in need of money.
Its justification for the measure is equity — that it is unfair that people should be treated differently on the basis of age.
On Wednesday the opposition, Greens and other crossbenchers joined in the Senate to knock the legislation off the government's agenda.
The Greens say that, as the price of passage, they want pensioners removed from its ambit.
"You can't take a billion dollars from 1.2 million pensioners," Shoebridge says.
Butler on Thursday reintroduced the bill into the House of Representatives. Its future was unclear when parliament broke late on Thursday. The weeks ahead will see negotiations between the government and Greens.
There'll be plenty of time for the bill's critics to intensify their lobbying, which has already been full-on. One Labor backbencher, receiving a flood of emails, says the measure is causing a lot of pain in electorate offices. This MP thinks the government should at least remove pensioners from those hit, if not drop the bill entirely.
Teal independent Monique Ryan, a medical doctor, has been a strong critic, commissioning data from the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO).
Ryan said after the Senate vote: "It's unfair and unreasonable to strip support from older Australians who have worked for decades to retain their private health cover in retirement.
"The PBO analysis I commissioned found that half the $3 billion in savings the government had planned would have been taken from the pockets of the older Australians least able to afford them."
Ryan accuses the government of trying to hide the impact of the changes.
"It claimed that 44,000 older Australians might drop their cover because of these changes. The Health Department says it is closer to 80,000. That would shift the cost of their health care to public hospitals, and the government has refused to say how much that would cost the states."
For the government, and in particular the treasurer, the rejection of the health rebate bill capped off yet another fraught week, which saw Chalmers embarrassed when the prime minister seemed to be claiming all the ownership of last week's backflip over the Australian Taxation Office's credit card ban.
Loading
Budget update will be another test
This budget has such a long tail that it is running into the preparations for the mid-year update, due in December. Many concessions and corrections have had to be made.
At the macro level the news continues to be grim, with the latest International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook this week showing Australia expected to have continuing high inflation, in the top band of developed countries. Thursday's job figures showed unemployment at 4.7 per cent in September, a five-year high.
Expectations remain of another interest rate rise in this cycle, but Chalmers will fervently hope the Reserve Bank will press the pause button at its early November meeting, as is currently considered likely. Thursday's jobless numbers increase the prospect of a hold in November.
Chalmers finds himself under the most pressure that he has experienced in his time as treasurer, with no relief in sight and the budget update looming as yet another test.
Given his present problems and preoccupations, it was interesting that Chalmers this week delivered a major speech recognising the risks posed to Labor by One Nation and warning the progressive side of politics not to insult those attracted to voting for that party.
It was a timely reminder, as One Nation appears an increasing threat to Labor. A landmark test for the left side of politics will be next year's New South Wales election where, despite the Minns Labor government having a reasonable record (unlike Victorian Labor), One Nation appears to be gaining quite a strong foothold.
For the federal opposition, on the objective evidence, this week should have been a very good one, with the government seriously on the back foot.
Yet Angus Taylor and the Coalition still fail to present as a credible alternative, a message reinforced by implications in former treasurer Josh Frydenberg's autobiography, released this week.
Many in the current parliamentary Liberal party are highly critical of the former Liberal deputy leader producing the book now, or at all. But the point is, while people may dispute the solutions Frydenberg offers, he has held a mirror to the Liberals' problems and inadequacies.
The party has to fix what the mirror shows — it's no good just panning the man holding it.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

America's 'boomcession' and what it means for Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Economists are talking about a 'boomcession' in the US. Is it happening in Australia, too?
Australia's economy is growing, unemployment is relatively low and many of the headline numbers look healthy. So why do so many households feel worse off?
That's the paradox behind the term "boomcession", a combination of boom and recession, used to describe an economy that is performing well overall while many people feel like they're stuck in a downturn.
Coined by economics writer Matt Stoller, the phrase has gained traction in the US. But does it also describe what's happening in Australia? Here's what the experts say.
What is a 'boomcession'?
"Boomcession" describes a sharp disconnect between strong macro-level indicators and the widespread financial strain felt by everyday households.
By conventional measures, Australian economic conditions remain relatively strong: output has continued to expand (GDP), equity markets have benefited from enthusiasm around artificial intelligence, and unemployment remains low by historical standards.
Yet, many households feel like they're in a recession. But why?
- Inflation expectations/anxiety remain elevated.
- Interest rates are climbing.
- Housing affordability is stretched.
- Cost of everyday essentials continues to weigh on budgets.
Mr Stoller, a research director at the non-profit American Economic Liberties Project, said "traditionally" the US economy was performing well.
"But ordinary people are saying they're not," he said.
US consumer confidence fell to a preliminary reading of 46.3 this month, according to the University of Michigan's closely watched consumer sentiment index.
If the lower-than-expected reading were to hold, it would mark yet another historically weak reading for sentiment, just shy of May's record-low reading of 44.8.
Independent economist Nicki Hutley says there's a similar disconnect in Australia, though she prefers the term "vibecession" to describe the mood.
"On the surface, the economy looks OK, if not buoyant," she says, pointing to economic growth of about 2 per cent and unemployment that remains low by historical standards.
"However, you don't have to look too far beneath the surface to understand why the average Aussie is grumpy.
"The 2025 interest rate cuts have been taken back; inflation has remained just high enough to erode any wages growth and households are focusing on the 'bill shock' items."
According to Mr Stoller, his boomcession model is to raise awareness of the real financial struggles those outside of America's wealthiest social classes face.
Put simply, the economy may be expanding, but the gains aren't evenly distributed. And for those who don't own stocks or have large financial cushions, a booming market doesn't translate into day-to-day security.
Boomcession description 'no longer fits' Australia
William Buck chief economist Besa Deda said while Australia did display some of the characteristics of a boomcession earlier this year, that description no longer fit as well as it once did.
"Earlier in the cycle, many households felt like they were in a downturn while the broader economy, housing market and share market looked surprisingly resilient," Ms Deda said.
"Households were grappling with higher living costs, rising mortgage repayments and stretched budgets, yet economic growth remained resilient, unemployment was low, house prices were rising and the share market was hitting fresh highs."
However, Ms Deda says that resilience is starting to fade as the full effects of higher interest rates work their way through the economy.
Economic growth is slowing, the labour market is softening and asset markets are no longer providing the same support they once did.
Essentially, the gap between household experience and the headline economic data is narrowing.
Consumer sentiment remains subdued
While Australia may no longer fit the definition of a boomcession, households remain under pressure.
Consumer sentiment fell to 74.9 in October, its lowest level since mid-2024, reflecting ongoing cost-of-living pressures and concerns about the economic outlook.
The RBA has raised interest rates four times this year as underlying inflation has remained elevated, while higher fuel prices have also added to household budgets and flowed through to the cost of many goods and services.
Ms Deda says consumer sentiment is unlikely to recover meaningfully until households are convinced financial pressures are easing.
"That means greater confidence that interest rates have peaked and that relief is in sight through future rate cuts, alongside easing cost-of-living pressures and continued job security," she says.
Until then, the boomcession may be fading, but for many Australians, the feeling of living through one remains.

Carney campaigns for Canadian unity before Alberta secession vote
TORONTO, Canada - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned for national unity in Alberta on Oct 15, before the oil-rich province votes on whether it wants a binding independence referendum.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta’s roughly five million people want to break away from Canada, but Carney, who grew up in the western province, said “polls don’t vote.”
“We need people to show up and vote and stand up for Alberta, stand up for Canada,” he said during a television interview in Calgary.
Speaking later with local business leaders, Carney said he couldn’t think of a “worse time to have a referendum,” citing a “more dangerously divided world” and friction with the United States.
Alberta’s right-wing Premier Danielle Smith says she is against independence but called the non-binding vote on Oct 19 to settle a divisive issue.
If a majority votes for independence, she has committed to launching a legally binding separation process. If a majority votes to stay, Smith says she won’t approve another referendum.
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organisation, told AFP his side might “actually win this referendum.”
“I would be very surprised if we got less than 40 percent,” he said in an interview on Oct 13.
Oil in focus
Carney has put Alberta’s oil industry at the centre of his plans to solidify Canada’s economy and reduce dependence on the US, warning close economic ties have been permanently fractured by US President Donald Trump.
Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.
Carney has repeatedly cited the proposed pipeline to argue for Alberta’s future prosperity within a united Canada.
Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalised fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.
Smith told the CBC that Alberta separatists stepped up mobilisation because Trudeau, who left office last year, was “actively trying to kill” the oil industry.
Oil’s dominance in separatist discussion makes Alberta “mostly an outlier,” said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global secessionist groups.
Secessionist movements regularly have “economic motivations,” but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.
“There’s no magic line” dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta’s case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
American influence?
The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a “natural partner” for the US, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.
Earlier in October, Canada’s Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.
Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, US interests “don’t play any role” in Alberta “until we win and become government,” at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.
“There’s no animosity towards America here,” he said. “I can’t see why we wouldn’t want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world.”
Asked about alleged foreign interference on Oct 15, Carney said: “our expectation is – to be absolutely clear on foreign governments, United States included – we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves involved in our elections.” AFP

Trump ramps up third-country US deportations despite global rights outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:54:26 UTC
02:54:26 KST

Trump ramps up third-country US deportations despite global rights outcry
Official data shows tens of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers have been sent to countries they have no ties to.
United States immigration authorities have dramatically stepped up detentions and deportations since January 2025, when Donald Trump became president.
Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”. Officers with the Department of Homeland Security, the agency tasked with the crackdown, now make thousands of arrests a day across the country.
That includes people who are seeking asylum in the US, who are supposed to be given a chance to explain dangers they might face in their home country. And US law and international treaties, like the United Nations Convention Against Torture, prohibit authorities from deporting someone to any country in which they will be persecuted or tortured.
Many of those being detained in the US immigration crackdown say they are at risk of being hurt or killed if they return to their native countries, so the Trump administration has looked for alternative places to deport them, including places someone might have no cultural or legal ties to.
Third-country deportations, as the practice is known, have been criticised by the US as well as global rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, as well as the UN.
Critics of the practice say some of the countries taking in the deportees have a record of human rights abuses themselves, or are so dangerous that the US government tells its own citizens not to travel there. They also say there is little to ensure these third countries will give deportees a fair hearing on their cases for asylum, and in the end might send them back to their native countries to face persecution there.
Third-country deportations are not new, but rights groups say they were extremely rare before the Trump administration, and have never been used by the US at the scale they are now. Those being sent to other countries, rights groups say, would not have been deported without their consent. Some US courts have said the practice is illegal, but the US Supreme Court has allowed it to continue, including in a ruling in September.
Experts at the UN have said the practice was leading to a “cascade of human rights violations” across the globe, threatening to undo norms around how refugees and asylum seekers are treated.
A closer look at the third-country deportations
Rights groups have tried to tally forcible third-country deportations, and according to the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been subject to forcible third-country deportations so far, based on media reports and information from attorneys.
The Department of Homeland Security’s own data includes more than 16,000 cases of third-country deportations since Trump came into office in January 2025 and August 2026, the latest month for which data is available. The data, provided to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by Al Jazeera, is likely an undercount.
Deportations to these countries need the approval of authorities there, so the Trump administration has sought to make agreements, or reach informal understandings on how to send deportees to a growing list of countries.
Some countries have agreed to keep deportees in prisons, like El Salvador and Eswatini.
Others have agreed to hold deportees temporarily, with some signing Asylum Cooperative Agreements with the US, or “Safe Third Country Agreements”, which allow deportees to pursue asylum claims in a third country that has agreed to host them.
According to rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First, many of those deported have no idea where they are being sent, and end up finding themselves in countries where they do not speak the language and have little cultural understanding. Some don’t even have any documents like passports or identification cards, making it difficult to live there.
The list of countries people are being deported to has grown as the US offers financial aid, or business or visa concessions, in exchange for countries taking in third-country nationals the Trump administration wants to remove.
Liberia has agreed to take up to 1,200 deportees, for instance. The Trump administration at one point said it would extend the validity of certain visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months, and has committed $124m for the country’s health services.
In Cameroon, which agreed to take third-country nationals from the US in December 2025, the Trump administration has pledged to give $30m for the UN’s refugee work there, and $400m over the coming years for the country’s health services.

Fraud, property offenses drive rise in Swiss crime from 2022 to 2025: Study

2026-10-15
17:52:36 UTC

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Crime in Switzerland rose between 2022 and 2025, with fraud and property offenses among the main drivers, while residents reported feeling less safe, a study published by two Swiss universities found, according to Swissinfo.
“This means that the rise in recorded crime is not primarily attributable to a greater willingness to report offenses,” said Dirk Baier, a co-leader of the Crime Survey 2025 project and professor at the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW).
The survey found that 15.9% of respondents were victims of fraud in the previous year, up from 8.4% in 2022.
For almost all offenses examined, more respondents reported being victims of crime than in the previous survey, while reporting rates stayed largely unchanged.
Sexual offenses were an exception, with no increase in the victimization rate recorded.
The survey also found that 83.1% of respondents felt fairly or very safe in their neighborhood after dark, down from 87.6% in 2022.
Meanwhile, 37.9% considered police presence in public spaces insufficient, compared with 28.9% in 2022. Trust in the police nevertheless remained high.
The survey included 13,500 respondents aged 16 to 80 living in Switzerland.
Researchers said the decline in the sense of safety should be taken seriously without overstating its scale.
“Despite the decline in the sense of safety, the population continues to perceive Switzerland as a safe country,” said Nora Markwalder, co-director of the project and professor at the University of St. Gallen.
A supplementary report on domestic violence found no significant overall change compared with 2022 in the proportion of people who had experienced at least one form of domestic violence during a five-year period.
Women reported the experiences at a higher rate than men, at 5.4% compared with 2.2%.
The study also found a statistically significant increase in domestic hate crimes compared to 2022.

Israeli firm weaponized digital ad network for spyware attacks, research shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:47:42 UTC
02:47:42 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech weaponized a vast commercial ad network to harvest personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant reported Thursday.
"The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting," Confiant said in its investigative findings.
The coordinated operation enabled US-blacklisted Israeli spyware company Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos to exploit commercial ad inventory across major global platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia's Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers termed "AdFection."
Devices belonging to staff at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through the weaponized ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
Global identity graph, data harvesting
Discover-Tech operated a specialized system called Controlium that converted routine commercial advertising auctions into an expansive surveillance apparatus. After analyzing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS in dozens of countries during a four-month period.
"Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies," said Confiant.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens, and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations strictly barred processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also revealed that an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, utilized Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecom providers, matching digital advertising identities to physical phone numbers to deanonymize mobile subscribers en masse. 
Focus on Palestine, sensitive targets
Geographic telemetry revealed sharp traffic spikes pointing to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2% of all digital advertisements in the territory, peaking at roughly 10% on April 7, with one in every 36 Android ads originating from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also landed directly on sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister’s Office, international bodies, judicial agencies, universities and defense organizations.
Investigators detected surgical handoffs to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain, and others.
After the joint investigation was disclosed, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi severed Discover-Tech's access to their digital advertising systems.

PM Carney urges Canadian unity ahead of Alberta secession vote

2026-10-15
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a push for national unity in oil-rich Alberta on Thursday as the province prepared to vote on whether to pursue a binding referendum on independence from Canada.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada, but Carney, who grew up in the western province, said: "polls don't vote."
"We need people to show up and vote and stand up for Alberta, stand up for Canada," he said during a television interview in Calgary.
Speaking later with local business leaders, Carney said he couldn't think of a "worse time to have a referendum," citing a "more dangerously divided world" and friction with the United States.
Alberta's right-wing Premier Danielle Smith says she is against independence but called Monday's non-binding vote to settle a divisive issue.
If a majority votes for independence, she has committed to launching a legally binding separation process. If a majority votes to stay, Smith says she won't approve another referendum.
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP his side might "actually win this referendum."
"I would be very surprised if we got less than 40%," he said in an interview on Tuesday.
Carney has put Alberta's oil industry at the center of his plans to solidify Canada's economy and reduce dependence on the United States, warning close economic ties have been permanently fractured by President Donald Trump.
Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.
Carney has repeatedly cited the proposed pipeline to argue for Alberta's future prosperity within a united Canada.
Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalized fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.
Smith told the CBC that Alberta separatists stepped up mobilization because Trudeau, who left office last year, was "actively trying to kill" the oil industry.
Oil's dominance in separatist discussion makes Alberta "mostly an outlier," said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global secessionist groups.
Secessionist movements regularly have "economic motivations," but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.
"There's no magic line" dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta's case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.
Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, U.S. interests "don't play any role" in Alberta "until we win and become government," at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.
"There's no animosity towards America here," he said. "I can't see why we wouldn't want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world."
Asked about alleged foreign interference on Thursday, Carney said: "our expectation is – to be absolutely clear on foreign governments, United States included – we don't get ourselves involved in their elections, they don't get themselves involved in our elections."

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:43:01 UTC
02:43:01 KST

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
At Nasser Hospital, a kangaroo mother care pilot programme helps vulnerable newborns as Gaza’s healthcare system struggles with shortages.
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For 11 days after giving birth last month, Rania Fadel could not hold her newborn son.
The 24-year-old gave birth to twin boys, Ilyas and Yahya, on September 25.
While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.
Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.
Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.
“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”
As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.
It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.
“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.
During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.
“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”
For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.
“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”
Skin-to-skin
Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.
For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.
World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.
At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.
“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.
“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”
The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.
Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.
The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.
At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.
Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.
“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”
Shortage of neonatal equipment
The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.
By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.
Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.
In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.
The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.
“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.
Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.
Newborn in a tent
Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.
The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.
As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.
The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.
“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”
Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.
She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.
“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”
She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.
“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”

- California is challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
- State Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
- Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a ‘sobering milestone.’
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
“We’ve seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify,” Bonta said. “Our justice system cannot function this way.”
Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a “sobering milestone” and a reflection not of political interference on California’s part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump’s nearly unbridled lawlessness.
“It’s very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently,” Bonta said.
Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.
Federal officials have given California election officials 48 hours to prove the citizenship of voters flagged as potential noncitizens, or withhold their ballots.
Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump’s first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.
Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.
Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.
Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of “Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power,” said California’s raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration “doing more aggressive things right off the starting block” — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.
Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.
The White House has consistently derided Bonta’s litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about “filing frivolous lawsuits” and “focus on addressing problems in his own state.”
“The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions,” Bis said.
ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a “common sense” approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.
The 100th case
Bonta’s lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California’s rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its “core sovereign judicial and police functions,” Bonta’s office said.
His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump’s first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests “disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive.”
Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct “civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location.”
Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.
Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.
In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza’s advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.
“The victims are losing,” Barraza said. “Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing.”
In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE’s expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.
Three lawsuits filed Friday challenge the Trump administration’s rollback of vehicle mileage rules as illegal, including one led by California.
State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California’s protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.
Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that “no state law applies to them,” and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.
The wider legal battle
Bonta’s office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration’s biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.
Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California’s lawsuits have been “legally meritorious,” as there is a “whole lot of legal error” coming out of the Trump administration — with a “lot of the overreach” having been “facilitated by the lack of internal checks” from loyal Trump agency heads.
However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn’t “appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious,” because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.
Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump’s intentional effort to make that difficult.
“It was a shock and awe,” he said. “It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time.”
What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he’ll keep getting sued by California.

Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:38:56 UTC
02:38:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
A container ship and a dry bulk carrier sunk near the Strait of Hormuz inside 24 hours on Wednesday after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources.
"GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday.
In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organisation showed on Wednesday.
One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said.
Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment.
The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data.
"MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said.
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law."
GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment.
"The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday.
"The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage."
A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk.
The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.
(Reuters)
