Britain is providing Ukraine with a new batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:38:20 EEST
02:38:20 KST

Britain is providing Ukraine with a new batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles — media
Kyiv • UNN
London is providing Kyiv with additional Storm Shadows to counter Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure. The number of missiles has not been disclosed.
The United Kingdom is providing Ukraine with an additional batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles to help it disrupt Russian military operations targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter. People familiar with the situation said, reports UNN, citing Bloomberg.
According to sources who agreed to provide the information on condition of anonymity, the supply of these British-made cruise missiles was discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday. The weapons shipment had not previously been announced publicly.
The United Kingdom and other allies of Ukraine are stepping up support for the war-torn country. This is happening as U.S. President Donald Trump announced last week that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin on placing Russian diesel fuel on the global market. On Wednesday, in an interview on the program "Piers Morgan Uncensored," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by events in recent days — in particular, the diesel-fuel agreement, Trump’s announcement of an "energy ceasefire," as well as problems with Ukrainian troops’ access to SpaceX satellite technology.
The publication notes that the United Kingdom has been supplying Ukraine with Storm Shadow missiles since 2023, although their use was initially restricted to the combat zone within Ukrainian territory. At the end of 2024, Ukrainian forces expanded the geography of their use, striking military facilities on Russian territory with British cruise missiles for the first time.
According to the sources, the United Kingdom considers Ukraine’s use of long-range weapons against Russian facilities involved in attacks on civilians and infrastructure to be defensive actions. In recent weeks, Russia has increased production of jet-powered drones and missiles to intensify attacks on Ukraine, so it is important for Kyiv to have the ability to counter these actions, the sources said.
The Trump administration urged Kyiv to stop drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, but the strikes resumed on Thursday — in response to ongoing Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities. As evidence of differences between the positions of the British and U.S. governments, the sources said that, in London’s view, Ukraine should not stop striking Russia until Moscow itself abandons such actions.
The media outlet notes that the British government declined to comment. It does not disclose exactly how many Storm Shadow missiles have been supplied to Ukraine during the war and does not report on each individual delivery. Storm Shadow missiles, produced by MBDA, have proven highly effective at penetrating Russia’s air-defense system and striking military and industrial facilities. These highly precise air-launched missiles have a range of more than 250 kilometers (155 miles); they are difficult to defend against because they fly at high speed while following the contours of the terrain.
In August, Burnham announced that the United Kingdom would provide Kyiv with technical documentation for long-range missiles so that Ukraine could establish their production on its own territory, although implementing the project will likely take some time.
In addition, Britain is developing low-cost long-range strike systems for Ukraine that will not depend on the supply of components or data from the United States.

French Alpine region places 5th river basin under highest drought alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:35:49 UTC
02:35:49 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Authorities in France’s Haute-Savoie department placed a fifth river basin under the highest drought alert level Thursday as dry conditions persisted, according to the prefecture.
The middle Arve basin, known as Arve median, was moved to crisis level, the fourth and highest stage of the department’s drought alert system.
Authorities said the restrictions on water use already in effect across the department will remain in place until Oct. 30.
Five basins are now under crisis-level restrictions: the lower and middle Arve, the Dranses, the Cheran and the Usses.
The Fier and southwestern Lake Geneva basin remain under reinforced alert, while the Genevois and upper Arve basins are under alert.
Under crisis-level measures, only priority water uses are permitted, including drinking water supply, the survival of aquatic species, watering animals, civil protection and public health and sanitation needs.
The measures come amid persistent drought conditions in Haute-Savoie, where water levels have fallen significantly in several rivers, and some tributaries have dried up.

The Ministry of Defence has again said that it intends to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State to set out the number planned following the 2027 spending review.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, answered in one sentence: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, we intend to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.”

Australia is to build its own boats to the same design at Osborne in South Australia. The first British boat is expected to enter service in the late 2030s.

Netherlands opens nuclear deterrence talks with France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:26:45 UTC
02:26:45 KST

- The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, discussing European nuclear and conventional deterrence.
- The talks follow Macron’s March offer of a strategic dialogue, which the Dutch government says complements NATO deterrence instead of replacing it.
The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a new bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, opening high-level talks on how French nuclear forces and European conventional forces could work together to deter attacks on Europe, the Dutch Ministry of Defence said.
The ministry announced the meeting in a statement on Oct. 15, saying it was the first time the two countries had held talks on the subject at this level. Senior French government officials attended, while the Dutch delegation was drawn from the Ministry of General Affairs, which is the prime minister’s office, along with the defense and foreign ministries. The two sides discussed ways to strengthen the European dimension of nuclear and conventional deterrence, according to the statement, which did not describe any specific decisions.
The talks follow an offer French President Emmanuel Macron made in early March to a group of European countries, including the Netherlands. The Dutch government accepted the French offer in line with its coalition agreement.
Macron set out the plan in a speech on March 2 at the Île Longue base in Brittany, home to France’s ballistic missile submarines. He said France would increase the number of its nuclear warheads and adopt what he called advanced deterrence, under which elements of France’s nuclear-capable air forces could be temporarily deployed to allied countries, Defense News reported. He named Germany as a key partner alongside Poland, the Netherlands and several other European states, and said partners could contribute early warning, air defense and long-range strike capabilities while their territory would gain a clearer link to French deterrence.
The Dutch government said Russia’s war against Ukraine has fundamentally worsened European security and requires Europe to take more responsibility for its own defense, and that the French offer fits that goal. It stressed that cooperation with France is meant to add to NATO’s collective defense and deterrence, and does not replace it.
France is the only nuclear-armed member of the European Union. Its arsenal is kept under exclusive national control, with the president alone authorized to order its use, and Macron has said that will not change under the new arrangements.
The Netherlands already takes part in NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements, under which some allies provide aircraft and crews for the alliance’s nuclear mission while the United States retains control of the weapons.

Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the full scope of the project.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Project HALO SHIELD is an Army-led initiative examining how commercially available Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft System (C-UAS) technologies can improve the protection of UK military sites from the growing threat posed by uncrewed aircraft systems.”
Halo Shield sits alongside Project PRESAGIUM, the £240 million enhanced counter-drone system the department described in a separate answer, which it says will provide detection and defeat of emerging drone threats.
Drone activity over British bases has moved from an irritant to an operational concern over the past two years, with incursions reported over sites including RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall, and the Prime Minister this week attributing the September incident at RAF Fairford to direction by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Counter uncrewed aircraft systems generally pair radar, radio frequency and optical sensors to spot and identify a drone with a mix of jamming, spoofing, nets, guns and directed energy to bring it down.
Protecting a fixed site is awkward because commercial quadcopters return almost no radar signature, because anything shot down has to come down somewhere, and because jamming radio transmissions over British soil runs into civil aviation and telecommunications law.

Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly modified its weapons, changed its tactics for penetrating air defenses, and adjusted the scale of its attacks. Ukraine has responded by developing and improving its drone detection and interception capabilities.
For Israel, Ukraine's battlefield experience is particularly relevant because Iran and its allies use weapons based on similar technology. According to Ukrainian reports, the samples provided to Israel could help researchers better understand the modifications Russia has made to its drones and develop ways to counter them.
Ukraine, meanwhile, could also benefit from Israeli expertise. Israel has extensive operational, intelligence, and technological experience in confronting Iran, including its missile and drone capabilities and other military threats in the region.
Sharing intelligence, threat assessments, and lessons learned from military operations could benefit both countries and further strengthen their security cooperation.

After Oct. 7, Israel’s border communities need long-term philanthropy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:23:46 UTC
02:23:46 KST

In the months after the October 7 massacre, Jewish communities around the world responded with extraordinary generosity. Emergency funds were created almost overnight. Philanthropic foundations accelerated decisions that would normally take months.
Donors asked a simple question: What is needed now?
That response mattered enormously. It allowed organizations working in Israel’s border communities to act quickly, respond to changing needs, and build new initiatives in places facing evacuation, loss, and profound uncertainty.
Three years later, we are entering a very different stage.
The emergency is no longer new. Philanthropic institutions are understandably asking different questions. They are returning to strategic priorities, long-term planning, and more conventional funding cycles.
At the same time, Israel is approaching an election period, creating uncertainty around government commitments that many organizations assumed would help carry emergency initiatives into the next stage.
The problem is that communities do not recover according to either philanthropic or political calendars.
Across Israel’s border regions, projects launched during the emergency are only now reaching the point at which they can become sustainable. The danger is that the bridge between emergency response and long-term recovery may disappear precisely when communities are ready to cross it.
In one community along Israel’s border with Gaza, a compound is already waiting to become a new Kedma student village. The community has opened its doors. Students are ready to move in, become part of local life, and contribute to education and community rebuilding.
But the village has not opened.
Additional protective shelters are still required, and while we wait for the necessary arrangements, the emergency funding that allowed us to begin this process is running out.
On paper, this may look like a delayed project. In reality, much more is at stake.
Entering a community recovering from war takes time. An organization cannot simply arrive with a program. Local leaders and residents must first decide to trust it: to share what they need, to allow outsiders into a deeply disrupted community, and eventually to make room for a new group of young people within their daily lives.
That trust is built slowly.
The same dynamic can be seen elsewhere. In Menara, on the Lebanese border, where residents have endured evacuation and enormous destruction, rebuilding a student village is not simply about providing accommodation for young people. It is about helping restore a living community.
In Sufa and Urim, in the western Negev, programs bringing young adults and discharged soldiers to live, volunteer, and become part of local life similarly depend on relationships that cannot be created overnight.
These programs were born or expanded during an extraordinary period, when philanthropy understood that extraordinary measures were necessary. Government ministries also made commitments based on the assumption that the emergency phase would eventually be followed by sustained reconstruction.
But that handover is not automatic.
We need a transition period to sustain trust
An election year makes the problem more acute. Budgets can change. Priorities can shift. Decisions that appeared secure can be delayed or reconsidered. Organizations that expanded in response to national needs can suddenly find themselves caught between emergency philanthropic grants that are ending and government commitments that have not yet materialized.
The result is not primarily an organizational problem. It is a community problem.
If a program closes, staff positions can eventually be recreated. A new grant can finance new activities. But when an organization has spent months or years entering a traumatized community, listening to residents and earning their confidence, withdrawing has consequences that cannot be measured only in budget lines.
It tells a community that another partner has come and gone.
For communities that have already experienced evacuation, uncertainty, and the collapse of so many assumptions about their security and their future, that matters.
This is why the next phase of philanthropy in Israel should not be understood simply as a return from “emergency giving” to normal giving. The challenge now is to build a transition period between the two.
That does not mean every emergency initiative should continue indefinitely. Nor does it mean philanthropy should replace government responsibility. On the contrary: long-term recovery requires government, philanthropy, local authorities, and civil society to understand where each one’s responsibility begins and ends.
But transitions need time.
A responsible philanthropic strategy for the coming year should ask not only which new projects deserve support, but which successful emergency investments are currently standing at the edge of a funding gap. Which initiatives have already earned the communities’ trust? Which are waiting for government funding or infrastructure to catch up?
And where could one additional year of support make the difference between an emergency intervention that disappears and an institution that becomes locally sustainable?
The years since October 7 demonstrated the extraordinary capacity of Jewish philanthropy to respond quickly when Israel was in crisis. The next test may be less dramatic, but no less important: whether we can stay long enough for recovery to take root.
Because funding may return.
Trust is much harder to rebuild.
The writer is the president and founder of the Kedma pioneering social-Zionist organization.

He was just a plumber. Then he helped save a plane full of passengers - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:23:39 UTC
02:23:39 KST

JERUSALEM — He is a plumber by profession, a husband and father by nature, and a hero because of the decision he made when lives hung in the balance.
Yaniv Hayoun never boarded a plane expecting to become a hero. He was traveling home to Israel when violence erupted aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. When the captain was seriously injured and the aircraft began descending dangerously, Hayoun faced a choice that would test his courage: remain in his seat and hope someone else would act, or move toward the danger.
He chose to act.
Hayoun joined other passengers in confronting the attacker inside the cockpit. After helping restrain him, Hayoun returned to the cockpit and pulled back on the aircraft's controls in an effort to stabilize the plane until another pilot could take over. The aircraft was diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed safely. Everyone aboard survived.
Hayoun was not a commercial pilot. He was a plumber who suddenly found himself in a situation few people could imagine. Yet when lives were at stake, he refused to stand by. He acted alongside fellow passengers who were willing to risk their own safety to protect others.
His courage demonstrates a powerful truth: heroism does not depend on a title, a uniform, or professional training. Sometimes it begins with an ordinary person recognizing that others are in danger and refusing to look away.
A hero honored in Jerusalem
Just one week after the harrowing flight, Hayoun's story became part of a historic gathering in Jerusalem.
On October 7, 2026, the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, more than 2,100 Christian leaders gathered in Jerusalem for the Global Prayer Event, an international gathering of remembrance, prayer, and solidarity with the Jewish people. The event was part of a 24-hour global prayer broadcast, hosted by Friends of Zion, that united leaders across nations around a common message: Israel is not alone.
During the gathering, Hayoun received the Hineni Award, named for the Hebrew expression Hineni, meaning “Here I am.”
Throughout Scripture, Hineni expresses a willingness to answer a call and step forward, even when the outcome is uncertain, and the cost may be great.
Hayoun embodied that spirit aboard the aircraft. He could not have known how the confrontation would end or whether he would survive. But he moved toward those who needed help, putting his own safety at risk to protect the lives of others.
His recognition in Jerusalem was especially meaningful on a day devoted to remembering the victims of October 7, honoring survivors, and standing with families still carrying the pain of that terrible day.
Yet Hayoun was not the only person whose story of courage and survival was honored.
Honoring the survivors and former hostages of October 7
Among those who joined the Jerusalem gathering were four former hostages whose lives were forever changed by the October 7 attacks: Agam Berger, Sagui Dekel-Chen, Bar Kupershtein, and Evyatar David. Each represented a deeply personal story of captivity, survival, and the difficult journey of rebuilding life after unimaginable trauma.
Their presence gave the gathering a significance that extended beyond speeches and ceremonies. These were people whose lives had been directly affected by the attacks, whose families had endured extraordinary anguish, and whose survival carried a meaning that no statistic could fully convey.
Together with Hayoun, they represented different expressions of courage: the courage to intervene when lives are threatened, the courage to endure captivity, and the courage to begin again after profound suffering.
A message the world must never forget
The October 7, 2023, attacks claimed more than 1,200 lives and resulted in 251 people being taken hostage. The tragedy left families shattered, communities devastated, and survivors facing a long road toward healing.
Three years later, the pain remains. Remembering those who were murdered, listening to survivors, and honoring the former hostages are essential to preserving the truth of what happened and recognizing the humanity of those whose lives were changed forever.
For the organizers of the Global Prayer Event, bringing thousands together in Jerusalem was about more than marking an anniversary. It was a declaration that the Jewish people must never be abandoned to hatred or left to believe the world has forgotten their suffering.
The former hostages who joined the gathering offered a powerful reminder: survival is not the end of the story. Healing, rebuilding, and finding the strength to move forward can take years, and the support of others matters.
In honoring these men and women, Jerusalem became a place where courage, remembrance, and solidarity met. Their stories reminded those gathered that behind every headline are human beings whose lives deserve to be remembered and whose dignity must never be forgotten.
For Yaniv Hayoun, the journey from an ordinary day of travel to an extraordinary act of courage culminated in recognition in the very city where thousands had gathered to stand with Israel.
He did not act because he expected an award. He acted because people were in danger and someone needed to help.
That is what makes his story so powerful.
When lives are in danger, someone must be willing to say, “Here I am.”
Yaniv Hayoun answered that call. In Jerusalem, alongside survivors and former hostages whose courage continues to inspire, his story became part of a larger message to the world: even in the face of terror, courage can prevail, hope can endure, and no one should have to stand alone.
Dr. Mike Evans has written 120 books and is a #1 New York Times bestselling author. He is the founder of the Friends of Zion Museum in Jerusalem, the Ten Boom Museum in Holland, and Churches United with Israel, one of the largest Christian Zionist networks in America, with more than 30 million followers.

China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:21:00 UTC
02:21:00 KST

In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox.
By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension.
As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.
The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials.
That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.
That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security.
China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench.
Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power.
Rare earths may not define the South China Sea today, but they could help reshape how its strategic value is imagined tomorrow.

Despite the challenges, humanitarian partners have reached more than 152,000 people with emergency assistance, he added.
"We reiterate our call on all parties to respect international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and allow safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access that includes safe passage for supplies, patients, ambulances and medical teams," he stressed.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the national capital Sanaa, and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
The current escalation began in July, after a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022.

Lockheed adds 6,000 jobs to speed up missile production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:19:32 UTC
02:19:32 KST

- Lockheed Martin will invest $300 million to expand its Grand Prairie, Texas, missile parts plant as part of a plan to create 6,000 U.S. jobs.
- Hadrian will install a 24-machine automated cell at the plant in early 2027 to boost parts output for PAC-3 MSE, THAAD and other missiles.
Lockheed Martin plans to create 6,000 jobs across the United States, including 2,000 in Texas, as it expands munitions production. At the center of the plan is a $300 million expansion of its Grand Prairie missile parts plant, where defense manufacturing startup Hadrian will install an automated machining cell.
The company announced the plan on Oct. 14. The Grand Prairie expansion will grow the site to more than 68,000 square meters (735,000 square feet), including about 9,300 square meters (100,000 square feet) of new space and roughly 7,900 square meters (85,000 square feet) of former offices converted into production floor for automation, digital manufacturing and high-precision machining.
Grand Prairie, between Dallas and Fort Worth, is the headquarters of Lockheed’s Missiles and Fire Control business. It machines components for all of the unit’s programs, including the PAC-3 MSE interceptor fired by Patriot air defense batteries, the THAAD missile defense interceptor, the U.S. Army’s Precision Strike Missile and the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. Parts made there go to final assembly lines in Camden, Arkansas, and Troy, Alabama.
Nearly 800 production workers at the plant made 250,000 parts in 2025. Over the past few months, Lockheed has installed more than 30 additional high-precision machines in converted office space that now turn out thousands of components a week, and it expects to add nearly 100 new machines across the site by the end of 2026.
Hadrian’s cell will hold 24 machines and is expected to start running in early 2027, staffed by Lockheed’s own production workers. The Los Angeles-area startup builds highly automated factories driven by its own software and sells what it calls a factory-as-a-service model, and the two companies signed a seven-year agreement in 2025 for Hadrian to embed a machining and inspection cell at a Missiles and Fire Control site.
“The warfighter can’t wait on peacetime timelines,” said Chris Power, CEO of Hadrian.
Michael Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment, attended the event in Grand Prairie. Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed’s Missiles and Fire Control business, said in a LinkedIn post the next day that the company had marked the investment together with Hadrian, the plant’s workforce and GM Defense, which Lockheed recently brought in to apply automotive manufacturing methods to defense production.
“This expansion is more than just a new facility; it is a stronger supply chain and a more resilient industrial base,” said Duffey.
The investment is aimed at meeting production targets set under new long-term agreements with the U.S. Department of War. Under a seven-year deal, Lockheed is working to raise PAC-3 MSE output from roughly 600 interceptors in 2025 to about 2,000 a year, backed by a multiyear award now worth $58.62 billion. A separate framework signed in January calls for quadrupling THAAD production from 96 to 400 interceptors a year.
“By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale,” said Jim Taiclet, chairman, president and CEO of Lockheed Martin.
The Grand Prairie project is one piece of Lockheed’s plan to spend $8 billion to $9 billion through 2030 to expand munitions production and modernize or expand more than 20 facilities nationwide, with the Hadrian cell due to come online at the Texas plant in early 2027.

Britain funds Chornobyl repairs after Russian drone hit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:16:57 BST
02:16:57 KST

Britain is putting £17 million towards repairing the protective shelter over the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which was punctured by a Russian drone strike last year, according to the government.
The money forms part of an international programme coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development alongside the Ukrainian government and G7 donors, and will pay for work to restore the structure’s confinement and ventilation functions and protect its intended lifespan. Corrosion threatens to undermine decades of international investment and create longer term environmental and safety risks if the damage is left.
John Healey, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.”
Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, said: “Our message to Putin is clear, we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”
The structure in question is the New Safe Confinement, the arch built over the remains of reactor four and the Soviet-era sarcophagus around it, which was slid into position in 2016 and handed over in 2019 after an international effort costing around €1.5 billion. It was designed to hold for a century while the reactor underneath is dismantled, and its outer skin and ventilation system are what keep moisture out of the space where that work has to happen. A drone strike that breaches it turns a sealed structure into one that corrodes.
Attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have continued through the autumn at a heavy rate. Between 5 and 11 October Russia carried out more than two hundred strikes on electricity infrastructure and a further seventeen on oil and gas facilities, six of them after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. On 13 October Russia fired thirty-nine ballistic missiles at Ukraine in one of the largest such attacks of the war, much of it aimed at energy targets, leaving six hundred thousand civilians without power.
Britain has been involved in nuclear safety at the site for years. It was a founding donor to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account in 2020, when that account took over responsibility for safety in the exclusion zone, and has given €8 million to it, making it the third largest individual donor behind Norway and France.
The Foreign Secretary visited Kyiv last week for the first time since taking office and announced £54 million of winter support, including £20 million in energy funding. The Prime Minister hosted President Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, where he set out a further package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles built by Thales in Belfast.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

The United Kingdom will provide £17 million ($22.5 million) to restore the New Safe Confinement at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant after it was damaged by Russian attacks, Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy announced on October 15.
The funding, equivalent to more than €20 million ($22.4 million), will form part of an international restoration program coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development together with the Ukrainian government and G7 donor countries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia previously struck the New Safe Confinement at Chornobyl with a drone on February 14, 2025, damaging the structure covering Reactor No. 4 and triggering a fire. Radiation levels remained stable, but the attack compromised the shelter’s protective function.
The New Safe Confinement covers the destroyed Unit 4 reactor at the Chornobyl plant and is designed to contain radioactive material and enable the safe dismantling of unstable structures. Construction began in 2012, the arch was moved into position in 2016, and the facility was fully commissioned in 2019. The project cost about €1.5 billion ($1.68 billion), funded by more than 40 donor countries and institutions through the EBRD -managed Chornobyl Shelter Fund.
“We are grateful to the United Kingdom for its consistent support for Ukraine and its significant contribution to strengthening our nuclear and energy security,” First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal stated.
“This is an important contribution not only to restoring damaged infrastructure, but also to strengthening nuclear safety and protecting Europe from radiation threats,” he added.
Shmyhal emphasized that international cooperation remains particularly important as Ukraine works to repair nuclear infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks.
“In the current conditions, international solidarity and shared responsibility for nuclear safety are of particular importance,” he stated.
Ukraine has also been reinforcing the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone with trenches, checkpoints, firing positions, and anti-drone barriers amid concerns over another Russian advance from Belarus. Russian troops seized the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant on February 24, 2022, and occupied the area for several weeks during their failed push toward Kyiv.

How Israel's policies exposed Zionism's racist foundations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:12:17 UTC
02:12:17 KST

The UK's Green Party, whose leader Zack Polanski is Jewish, recently described Zionism as an ethnonationalist political project, triggering a fierce debate about the nature of Israel's founding ideology.
Zionism emerged in the late 19th century, shaped by European Jewish intellectuals like Moses Hess, Theodor Herzl and Nathan Birnbaum, partly in response to Western antisemitism.
Yet it has paradoxically embraced Jewish supremacy over Palestine’s native population, denying Palestinian self-determination and their national aspirations.
Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank since October 7, which some leading international bodies and political scientists have described as genocide, have led analysts to argue that Zionism has increasingly taken a racist turn.
This is a particularly stark accusation against a state that has drawn much of its historical legitimacy from the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany murdered millions of European Jews during World War II.
“In the aftermath of the Gaza genocide in response to the October 7 Hamas attack, the racist character of Israel has again surfaced,” seriously discrediting Zionism, according to Richard Falk, a prominent Jewish-American professor of international law.
Growing international criticism of Zionism has been reinforced by racist and genocidal statements from senior Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, since October 7.
Pro-Israel groups, meanwhile, have sought to equate criticism of Zionism with antisemitism, a move critics see as an attempt to shield Israel from international accountability.
From the British Green Party's characterisation of Zionism to the findings of the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese on the occupied Palestinian territories and the UN Human Rights Council's Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Navi Pillay, these developments “have deepened the perception of Zionism as an aggressive ideology,” Falk tells TRT World.
Zionism's growing aggressiveness has become “abhorrent to many countries in the world as testified to by the walkout of many delegations when it came time for Netanyahu to address the recent UN General Assembly,” he says.
The UK Green Party episode has also revived memories of the UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on November 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism. The resolution passed by 72 votes to 32, with 35 states abstaining.
It received overwhelming support from countries in the Global South, though Latin American nations were divided and Western countries largely opposed it.
“The resolution was withdrawn in response to Israel/US lobbying leverage in 1991, but without any language explaining the withdrawal, or exonerating Israel from the earlier charges,” Falk tells TRT World.
In a 2017 report commissioned by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA), Falk and Virginia Tilley, an American political scientist specialising in ethnic and racial conflict, concluded that Israel had established a system of racial discrimination against Palestinians.
“Despite Israel's strenuous objections to being labeled an apartheid state, it virtually acknowledged the allegation in the Knesset of a 2018 Basic Law which proclaimed Jewish preeminence in Israel, and vesting the right of self-determination exclusively in the Jewish people with Hebrew designated as the only official language,” Falk says.
Many see the Basic Law, enacted by the Netanyahu government, as the codification of Zionist principles within Israel's constitutional framework.
Has Zionism always been racist?
Beyond the developments since October 7, some Israeli historians argue that Zionism has been a racist ideology since Israel's establishment in 1948, rejecting the notion that different versions of Zionism have existed.
While a more recent narrative suggests that Israel's racist and discriminatory policies have emerged under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners, Israeli historian and political scientist Ilan Pappe argues that racism has always been central to the Jewish state's identity, describing “liberal Zionism” as an “illusion”.
In a recent interview, Pappe rejected this distinction, saying that “the problem is Zionism in its all varieties”, which was “behind the ethnic cleansing of 1948 and the military rule on Palestinians” as Israel's state ideology.
According to Pappe, the intimidation of Palestinians within Israel since 1948, as well as the tactics used against Palestinians and support for illegal settlers in territories occupied since 1967, have been “the results and the implementation of the Zionist ideology”.
British-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who identifies as an Arab Jew, argues that even if “liberal Zionism” once existed in Israel, it is now “dead” under Netanyahu, particularly following the adoption of far-right policies since October 7.
“This promise was never fulfilled. It was just one of many examples of the huge gap between the liberal Zionist rhetoric on universal values and the discriminatory, racist reality, a gap that was filled by Israel’s leaders with hypocrisy and humbug,” Shlaim wrote in an article last month.
“One of the very few things that can be said in favour of the present, far-right Israeli Government is that it has dispensed with the liberal rhetoric and exposed the ugly reality of contemporary Israeli society for all to see,” he added.
However, Alon Liel, a former director-general of Israel's foreign ministry, offers a different perspective, arguing that his country “had a different kind of Zionism” three decades ago.
“The comeback of equating Zionism as racism is definitely an outcome of the last war, especially because of the number of casualties and the destruction in Gaza,” Liel tells TRT World.
Over the years, Zionism, originally regarded as a secular ideology, “has become more nationalistic and messianic”, according to Liel.
He points to the growing influence of far-right groups in Israel, a development some analysts associate with the convergence of revisionist and messianic Zionism.
Zionism: settler colonialism
Western imperial powers ruled much of the world, from the Americas and Africa to Southeast Asia and the Middle East, drawing many of today's international borders. But colonial rule largely receded after World War II, as former colonies gained independence.
Despite this wave of decolonisation, Israel emerged as a settler-colonial state in Palestine, a land inhabited by its native population for centuries, following the armed campaigns of Zionist militant groups such as Haganah and Irgun.
Against this historical backdrop, experts argue that Zionism constitutes a settler-colonial project.
“Zionism is a self-avowed settler-colonial movement, and its principal political progeny – the State of Israel – is a settler-colonial state. The logic of settler-colonialism is the elimination of the natives in order to take over the land and its resources. Ethnic cleansing is the means by which this goal is achieved,” Shlaim viewed.
Zionist leaders also drew on European Orientalist attitudes and the continent's colonial history to gain support for their project, presenting themselves as representatives of Western civilisation in the Muslim-majority Middle East.
While Zionism was originally “a movement among Jews countering the racism embedded in European antisemitism”, it also “had its own racist outlook that can be associated with an Orientalist version of Western cultural superiority and a disregard for the rights of inferior non-Europeans, especially as embedded in Islamic majority countries of the MENA,” Falk says.
“In the aftermath of WW II, Orientalist attitudes combined with liberal guilt associated with allowing Hitler to get away with extreme forms of antisemitism eventuated in a Zionist settler colonial project to establish a state of their own within Palestine, pretending to accept partition as a solution but never giving up their vision of unified Israeli sovereignty over the whole of Palestine.”
Future of Zionism
If Zionism continues on its current aggressive path, what does the future hold for Israel?
The Netanyahu government, which has launched military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, appears confident in its approach, claiming it is changing “the face of the Middle East.”
But some historians argue that Israel's embrace of an increasingly aggressive form of Zionism, driven by ambitions pursued on a shorter timetable than those of earlier Zionist generations, could signal the ideology's final phase.
“Historically, I’m willing to say with some caution that this is the last phase of Zionism. Such developments in ideological movements, whether they are colonial or empires, it’s usually the final chapter [that is] the ruthless one, the most ambitious one. And then it’s too much and then they fall and collapse,” Pappe said in an interview last year.
Like Pappe, Gregory Simmons, an independent researcher and academic, sees a bleak future for Zionism beyond Israel and its Western supporters.
Simmons argues that Israel's actions in Gaza and its military campaigns across the Middle East have eroded public support and sympathy, even in Western countries, while alienating Jewish communities abroad and turning Zionism into “a globally toxic ideology”.
Liel, however, takes a more cautious view. The former Israeli diplomat says he wants to wait for the results of the October 27 election before assessing Zionism's future.
He considers the ideology “very solid” within Israel, while acknowledging that it has been “more rejected” internationally.
Nathan Birnbaum, the Austrian-Jewish writer and journalist credited with coining the term Zionism, offers a historical example of how attitudes towards the ideology can change.
Despite helping organise the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897 and serving as secretary-general of the Zionist Organisation, Birnbaum later became a staunch opponent of Zionism and the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine.

UK scraps three planned Boxer variants after budget cut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:10:07 UTC
02:10:07 KST

- The British Army has dropped armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch versions of Boxer, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told Parliament.
- Pollard said Boxer will not be used for armored cavalry and will form the spine of the mechanized infantry force.
The British Army has dropped plans for armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch versions of its Boxer wheeled armored vehicle, and has ruled out using Boxer in the armored cavalry role, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told Parliament.
Pollard, the minister for defence readiness and industry, gave the answers in response to written questions from Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member of Parliament for Huntingdon, the UK Defence Journal reported. Obese-Jecty asked what had been cut from the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme after the government’s major projects watchdog, the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority, recorded £1.86 billion ($2.47 billion) coming out of the programme in its annual report for 2025 to 2026.
“As part of reprioritisation within the Military Strategic Headquarters, the Armoured Mortar, Repair and Recovery and Mounted Close Combat Overwatch capabilities of the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme are no longer being pursued,” said Pollard.
He added that the Army is considering how the underlying capability requirements will be addressed, meaning the need for those three jobs remains even though the Boxer versions designed to fill them are gone.
Each of the cancelled variants was meant to cover a different gap in the British Army’s mechanized infantry brigades. The armored mortar would have given battlegroups their own 120 mm indirect fire that could move with the infantry, and Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land test-fired a mortar module on a Boxer on Salisbury Plain in 2022. The repair and recovery vehicle was intended to tow and fix damaged Boxers, which weigh well over 30 tonnes and need a purpose-built recovery vehicle to move once disabled. Mounted Close Combat Overwatch was the long-range anti-tank version, and Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land and MBDA had shown a Boxer concept carrying Brimstone missiles for the role.
Earlier Army planning had pointed to initial operating capability for the recovery vehicle in 2029, the armored mortar in 2030 and the overwatch variant in the early 2030s, EDR Magazine reported.
Asked how many Boxers would go to armored cavalry units and how many to mechanized infantry, Pollard said Boxer will not be used for armored cavalry at all.
“Boxer vehicles will not be used in the Armoured Cavalry role. Boxer will form the spine of the Mechanised Infantry force,” said Pollard.
Under current plans, he said, Boxer is being fielded in supporting roles across 3rd (UK) Division, including command and control, specialist troop carrier and medical vehicles, with detailed fielding plans and vehicle allocations still being refined. Armored cavalry, the British Army’s reconnaissance and screening role, is being equipped with the tracked Ajax family built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK, which carries a stabilized 40 mm cannon.
Britain rejoined the multinational Boxer program in 2018, 15 years after leaving it, and has ordered more than 600 of the 8×8 vehicles in infantry carrier, specialist carrier, command and ambulance versions. The vehicles are built under license in Britain by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and by KNDS UK, formerly WFEL, at Stockport, with the rest coming from German production lines.

Inside the fight to stop Israel-bound weapons at the East Coast’s biggest port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:08:19 UTC
02:08:19 KST

A line of trucks rounded the bend toward Port Newark-Elizabeth on October 3, 2025. Inside the trailers were combat boots and weapons components — including 61 tons of forging rings used for military jets — bound for Israel via a Maersk vessel departing that morning.
But before the truckers could enter the port and the Maersk Sentosa could be loaded, 100 activists organized under the banner “Port of Elizabeth Movement” (POEM) sprang into action.
“It was ass o’clock in the morning. The sun was far from up. It was pitch black. Everyone was tired. Someone yelled, ‘Go, go, go, go!'” said Danny Creamer, who was later arrested at the POEM action.
Port Newark-Elizabeth is the third-largest port in the U.S. and the largest on the East Coast. And it has become a recurring target for activists concerned with the weapons supply chain to Israel. About 900 tons of sea cargo — comprising 91% of all military cargo bound for Israel that does not pass through a military base — originates from a nearby warehouse and is transported through Port Newark-Elizabeth.
The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has jurisdiction over the port, with commissioners appointed by the governors of each state. Organizers claim that this power structure makes the organizing landscape less conducive to pressuring elected officials because of the Port Authority’s insulation from the local community.
“We don’t get into that kind of politics. If it’s local, if it was the city of Newark then maybe it would be worth a shot,” said Tova Fry, a long-time organizer with Port Workers and Communities for Palestine, a group focused on facilitating worker solidarity at ports across the U.S.
Instead of electoral or legislative strategies, the battle for Port Newark-Elizabeth is fought on different terrain: the dual threat of labor organizing by Port Workers and Communities for Palestine, and escalated direct actions by POEM. The two groups work autonomously and share the same goal — preventing vessels at Port Newark-Elizabeth from shipping U.S.-made weapons to assist Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
A poem for direct action
Back at the October 2025 action, Creamer and his fellow activists ran into the street, unfurled banners and laid 15 shrouds representing babies killed by Israel in Gaza. At one point somebody started playing the bagpipes. The activists blocked the road for about one hour with traffic cones and their bodies, obstructing the truckers’ entry and delaying the departure of the Maersk vessel. “It felt momentous, like ‘shit something’s happening here,’” said Creamer.
Eventually, the Port Authority Police responded with a dispersal order. Four people who refused to comply, including Creamer, were arrested and charged with disorderly conduct. Almost one year later, the four were found guilty of a violation (which Creamer compared to a traffic ticket) and sentenced to community service.
“We didn’t dismantle the U.S. imperialism shtick in one action, but we’ve at least inconvenienced it a little bit,” said Creamer. According to Creamer, this initial action demonstrated POEM’s animating principle. While large-scale rallies and marches show opposition and “serve as a threat, if we don’t follow through, then we can lose our leverage,” explained Creamer. “So we decided to try and stop the weapons shipments ourselves.”
At Port Newark-Elizabeth, this means using bill of lading data to track when Maersk and ZIM ships — the two major logistics companies that supply U.S.-made weapons to Israel — are set to depart and to coordinate timely escalations.
Difficult terrain for labor organizing
Maersk, an international Danish shipping company, is an integral player in this supply chain, and has been a target of the Palestine solidarity movement since the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM) launched the “Mask Off Maersk” campaign in June 2024. Recent research by Oxfam and PYM found that regular Maersk shipments out of Port Newark-Elizabeth include components for bullets, bombs, and mortars. Between October 2023 and July 2025, Maersk transported approximately 3,000 tons of weapons components to Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems.
ZIM, the other cargo carrier that transports weapons from Port Newark-Elizabeth to Israel, was founded in 1945 by the Jewish Agency and was Israeli-state owned until the company privatized in 2003. ZIM is one of Israel’s main weapons transporters, frequently chartered for emergency orders by the Israeli Ministry of Defense.
In 2014, Palestine solidarity organizers achieved a historic victory when West Coast dockworkers with the International Longshoremen’s Union (ILWU) refused to unload a ZIM ship at the Port of Oakland. ZIM has not returned since.
Tova Fry with Port Workers and Communities for Palestine was living on the West Coast and was involved in the 2014 movement against ZIM. But the labor landscape on the East Coast is different.
While the ILWU continues to express unprecedented solidarity with Palestine, “unfortunately there’s a different union here,” said Fry. Instead of the progressive ILWU, the International Longshareman’s Association (ILA) works the docks, manages the cranes, and ties the ships at Port Newark-Elizabeth. The ILA president expressed support for President Donald Trump in 2024. “I would say it’s one of the most right-wing unions in the country,” said Fry.
Port Workers and Communities for Palestine is taking an alternative route to labor organizing. The ILA has proven intractable thus far, “but who we do work with here, with much more success, is the [non-unionized] Port Truckers,” said Fry.
Port Truckers are independent contractors, often described as “sweatshops on wheels.” According to Fry, the truckers are a largely immigrant workforce who are aware of international politics. “Therefore, they tend to be supportive of Palestine,” said Fry. Some truckers even send pictures to notify the organizers when they spot military equipment on their ZIM trailers.
However, Port Workers and Communities for Palestine said that the truckers’ lack of union and reliance on ZIM and Maersk for work has proven a challenging organizing terrain.
The ILA has the power to stop shipping weapons to Israel, but not the will; the Port Truckers have the will, but not the power.
“It’s a constant strategy discussion about how to move forward and it’s a long term struggle. Unfortunately, as we see what’s happening, the genocide is not stopping,” said Fry.
For now, Port Workers and Communities for Palestine pursues two main tactics: pickets at the port and community outreach with truckers.
Organizers use publicly available data to plan pickets when ZIM or Maersk vessels are due to be loaded. During a recent picket on the morning of October 4, 2026, Mondoweiss joined activists at the Maher Terminal entrance, right as the ZIM Virginia arrived at the port.
On a strip of grass adjacent the dockworkers entrance, 35 people congregated to wave Palestinian flags and hand out flyers to workers. Umber, an organizer with Port Workers and Communities for Palestine using a pseudonym for security reasons, rallied the crowd with a speech.
“Today, the ZIM Virginia arrived at the Maher Terminal at 8:00 a.m. to load weapons for genocide. Some of the items that have been on this ship include ammunition shells, casing for ammunition… The reason we come out here every time this ZIM Virginia arrives, is to tell the ILA and to tell the truckers who might be carrying items for this shipment that this is not acceptable. This is a crime and it must be stopped.”
Passenger vehicles trickled in the terminal entrance, largely ignoring the protesters. One activist attempted to hand a flyer to a driver whose window was open; the driver threw it back. Fry later told Mondoweiss that these vehicles carried ILA workers tasked with loading the ship and preparing it for departure. The Port Truckers who were absent from the terminal had likely unloaded their cargo a day or two earlier.
At other pickets, Fry said the Port Truckers reacted by “honking and yelling and supporting us, sometimes holding up the line of truckers by slowing down… whereas the ILA workers, the last picket we had there, not a single one even slowed down to take a flyer,” said Fry.
In addition to pickets, Port Workers and Communities for Palestine conducts outreach work that includes flyering at places where Port Truckers congregate between shifts, hosting community picnics to support worker leadership, and passing out Palestinian flags to hang on their rearview mirrors. “We were invited to a mosque by some of the truckers a couple of times, where we made announcements about upcoming activities and handed out our flyers,” said Fry. “They’re eager to support in those kinds of ways. It’s just the major way of actually not carrying [weapons] that’s proving difficult,” said Fry.
The long term horizon for this work is to help the truckers organize themselves. “If they were able to unionize they could say ‘okay we’re not going to carry ZIM or we’re not going to carry weapons,” said Fry.
Climbing the escalation ladder
A few months earlier, and a few feet away from the site of the October 2026 ZIM Virginia picket, POEM executed its second direct action at the Port Newark-Elizabeth Maher Terminal on May 22, 2026.
Jonathan Nault, a South Jersey native who was compelled by the theory of direct action articulated by POEM, was in attendance. “Rather than continuing to march all the time I wanted to get involved in movements that address the problem at the supply chain level,” said Nault. “I honestly felt fortunate to be in a position where this is right in my backyard. I can actually do something about this.”
After the October 2025 action disrupting the Maersk Sentosa shipments, POEM saw an opportunity to turn up the pressure. “In October [2025], the police kicked the cones and shrouds out of the way. So we were thinking ‘what can we do to make ourselves un-pushable?’”
Gone were the traffic cones and bagpipes — this time POEM deployed an RV, a van and a boat to completely blockade the Maher terminal. Activists, including Nault and Creamer, who were chained together, locked themselves to pipes attached to the van, using a method called the “sleeping dragon.”
“There was a huge line of trucks that were completely blocked,” said Nault. “We blockaded the port for about three hours. In addition to buying time on the weapon shipment themselves… we may have elongated a Palestinian’s life because the ammunition didn’t get there in time.”
Ten activists including Nault and Creamer were arrested at the action and face ongoing misdemeanor disorderly person charges. But Nault said he wasn’t focused on the responding police officers, instead he was thinking, “this is the direction I hope the broader pro-Palestine movement will go. Prioritizing addressing the problem directly over symbolic marches and rallies.”
While Nault believes that mass mobilizations should also continue, he maintains it is time for a movement-wide paradigm shift. “The horrors that Israel has been inflicting on the Palestinians have been evolving. Our mode of pushback has to grow and evolve too. We have to take our struggle to the supply chain level en masse.”
Port Workers and Communities for Palestine continues the long-term struggle of labor organizing at the port, and Nault said that POEM is focused on “introducing people to the escalation ladder of protest. Our long-term goal is to set precedents about the level of risk the movement will take.”

Ukraine will no longer abide by US President Donald Trump’s demands to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, amid a deepening rift over a US-Russia diesel deal.
“The block (on attacking refineries) is out,” Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published on Thursday. “We’re done.”
Relations between Kiev and Washington have soured since Trump eased sanctions on Russia last week in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Zelenskyy called the agreement a “weak decision” that would encourage Russia to prolong the war, while several European allies also criticised it.
Trump blamed Ukrainian refinery attacks for rising diesel prices and said on Saturday that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president”. He later announced a surprise “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, which Zelenskyy said he knew nothing about.
In an interview with British journalist Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy agreed that he felt “betrayed” by the diesel deal.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “I think his advisors are wrong. This is not (the) right side of history.”
Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian energy infrastructure, causing power and heating shortages. Ukraine has targeted Russian refineries it says help fund the war.
Zelenskyy in Brussels
After meeting Zelenskyy in Brussels on Thursday, NATO chief Mark Rutte said they discussed “implementing an energy ceasefire as well as NATO allies’ continuous support for Ukraine”.
Zelenskyy made no mention of a ceasefire in his account of the meeting on X.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov accused Ukraine of undermining US peace efforts after Russian authorities reported a drone attack that set a refinery south of Moscow ablaze.
Satellite row
Restrictions on the US-controlled Starshield satellite system, which Ukraine uses to detect Russian attacks and coordinate battlefield operations, have fuelled anger in Kiev.
Defence officials confirmed that the US had threatened to withdraw intelligence-sharing if Ukraine continued long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries. Officials also reported slower Starshield speeds on Wednesday, affecting connectivity.
Ballistic missiles struck Kiev and the surrounding region on Tuesday and Wednesday night before air raid sirens could warn residents to take cover.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk denied his company was responsible for disruptions.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.

Saab rolls out Sweden’s first GlobalEye radar jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:05:31 UTC
02:05:31 KST

- Saab presented the first of three GlobalEye early warning aircraft ordered by Sweden, which will now enter testing ahead of its first flight.
- The jets replace the two Saab 340-based ASC 890 radar planes Sweden gave to Ukraine, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027.
Saab has presented the first GlobalEye airborne early warning and control aircraft built for the Swedish Air Force, a business jet-based radar plane that will replace the two older surveillance aircraft Sweden gave to Ukraine.
The company unveiled the aircraft on Oct. 15. The jet will now go through a phase of testing and verification before its first flight and delivery to Sweden’s Defence Materiel Administration, known as FMV. Deliveries of the Swedish GlobalEyes are scheduled to begin in 2027.
“The presentation of Sweden’s first GlobalEye marks an important milestone for both Saab and the Swedish Armed Forces,” said Micael Johansson, president and CEO of Saab.
Sweden has ordered three of the aircraft, which it designates S 106. FMV signed for the first two in June 2022 with an option for more, and in June 2024 it exercised that option for a third aircraft worth about 2.6 billion Swedish kronor, roughly $246 million at the time.
GlobalEye is built on Bombardier’s Global 6000 long-range business jet, with Saab’s Erieye ER radar mounted in a roughly 10-meter (33-foot) fairing on top of the fuselage. Saab says the radar can detect targets up to about 550 km (342 miles) away when the aircraft flies at 35,000 feet, a 70% gain in range over earlier Erieye versions thanks in part to gallium nitride electronics. The aircraft can stay airborne for more than 11 hours.
The Swedish version carries a maritime surveillance radar, an electro-optical and infrared camera, electronic intelligence sensors and Link 16 data links alongside the main radar, letting crews track aircraft, ships and ground vehicles from one platform and share the picture with fighters, ships and ground units.
The order grew after Sweden decided in May 2024 to send Ukraine its two Saab 340-based ASC 890 early warning aircraft, the Swedish Air Force’s only airborne radar planes at the time. Stockholm said then that it would make up for the loss by buying a third GlobalEye and speeding up deliveries of the first two. In Swedish service, the GlobalEyes will be based at Ärna Air Base near Uppsala.
The United Arab Emirates became GlobalEye’s first operator in 2020. France placed a firm order on Dec. 30, 2025, for two aircraft worth 12.3 billion kronor, with options for two more and deliveries planned from 2029 to 2032, to replace its aging E-3F Sentry AWACS fleet.
Sweden also holds an option for a fourth GlobalEye, and the first Swedish aircraft now moves into ground and flight testing ahead of its 2027 delivery.

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Was an Affiliate Marketer for a Fitness MLM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:05:19 UTC
02:05:19 KST

Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.
A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online résumé shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”
Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications adviser at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.
Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top-tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.
On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, had been identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)
WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online and created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.
Zacharia says she was, rather, an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, following her 2013 return from China. She recalls being brought in by a friend and promoting its Shakeology product, which is promoted as a “superfood nutrition shake.” She stopped using and promoting the product, she says, because of its vitamin A content, which she didn’t feel was good for her while pregnant.
Beachbody, now known as BODi, confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was among its 300,000 “independent Team Beachbody distributors” in 2013. A spokesperson added that they believed it would be “misrepresentation” to conflate Zacharia’s time at Beachbody with “BODi’s current business and operations.”
Perhaps unsurprisingly for a company that relied on a multilevel marketing scheme for decades, the company has run into a number of legal issues over the years. It's been accused of falsely advertising a revolutionary anti-aging treatment (the suit was voluntarily dismissed) and making false or misleading income promises to contractors. It got into a copyright battle with a company called Orderlegalsteroids.com, accusing it of stealing an image of Israeli bodybuilder Sagi Kalev from promotional materials for its “BODY BEAST” Program. (Beachbody won a default judgment.)
In 2017, Beachbody, without admitting any wrongdoing, settled a $3.6 million consumer protection lawsuit with the city attorney in Santa Monica, California. Prosecutors alleged that Beachbody made health-related claims about its products, including Shakeology, that were “false, misleading, and not backed by scientific evidence.” They also claimed in filings that Beachbody had been automatically charging customers credit cards for renewals of their products without their consent. As part of its settlement, Beachbody was ordered to pay $1 million to nonprofits that promote health and nutrition.
And in 2023, Beachbody was hit with a class action lawsuit accusing it of scamming its coaches. The lead plaintiff was a schoolteacher who alleged she joined Beachbody with the hope of making a supplementary income but ended up paying $20,000 in personal funds to cover expenses related to her coaching role—all while making about $50 per month for about 50 hours of work. The following year, the company dropped its multilevel marketing program in favor of a “single-level affiliate” one. In 2025, it reached a settlement in the class action suit that resulted in the dismissal of all claims, and the lawsuit was later formally dismissed.
In a statement to WIRED, BODi says, “Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network” and that the company “helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in-home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology.”
This particular notch on Zacharia’s résumé puts her in good company with other high-profile Trumpworld personnel, a cadre of professionals who have a great fondness for supplement-related business opportunities. FBI chief Kash Patel previously promoted supplements that promised to help people “detox” from the Covid-19 vaccine. Nicole Saphier, Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, reported receiving nearly $300,000 in business income from her own company that owns a supplement line. And President Trump himself once oversaw a multilevel marketing company, The Trump Network, which sold an array of vitamins, home urine tests claiming to test for vitamin deficiency, and children’s snacks.

Trump and Netanyahu unlikely to strike Iran before elections, but Israel fears surprise attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:04:29 UTC
02:04:29 KST

Israel's political and security establishment widely believes that neither Israel nor the United States will launch an attack on Iran before their respective elections, with just 12 days remaining until Israelis vote and less than three weeks until the U.S. midterms. However, Israeli officials remain concerned that an Iranian provocation, an attack by Tehran's regional proxies or a military miscalculation could trigger a confrontation despite efforts to avoid one.
The prevailing assessment is that President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are unwilling to risk a new military campaign ahead of the elections. Netanyahu is particularly concerned that renewed fighting with Iran could damage Likud's chances of remaining in power in the October 27 vote.
The possibility of an attack was discussed during a conversation between Netanyahu and Trump last week. Although Israeli officials generally consider a preelection strike unlikely, they still regard the possibility as significant.
One concern is that Iran or the Houthi rebels in Yemen could provoke an Israeli response through a limited operation or an attack carried out by one of Tehran's regional proxies.
Another is the possibility of a miscalculation, with each side interpreting the other's military preparations as evidence of an imminent attack and deciding to strike first.
Israel has conveyed a warning to Washington that if Iran makes such a move, it will face an exceptionally severe response, potentially unprecedented in scale, even after the thousands of Iranian targets struck by Israel and the United States during the war.
Israeli security forces are therefore maintaining a high state of alert and preparing for possible surprise attacks by Iran, Hezbollah or the Houthis.
Security officials have emphasized that any Israeli decision to attack Iran ultimately depends on Trump. Without the American president's approval, they say, Israel would be unable to carry out such an operation.
Trump does not appear to have reached a final decision and is continuing to weigh his options. Officials familiar with the matter said he blocked at least two planned Israeli strikes during the summer, both based on Israeli intelligence indicating that Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program.
Earlier Thursday, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir conducted a situation assessment and operational briefing at Central Command, warning commanders that the danger of escalation had increased.
"Given the numerous warnings across all fronts and the sensitivity of the current period, the potential for escalation has increased," Zamir said.
The military chief also recently warned senior American government and military officials that renewed hostilities with Iran could lead to the postponement of Israel's parliamentary election.
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, issued a similar warning Thursday ahead of a Security Council meeting, saying he had delivered a direct message to Iran and Hezbollah.
"Do not try to exploit Israel's election period. Anyone who dares attack us will suffer a devastating blow," Danon said.
An Israeli security official assessed Wednesday that another military campaign resembling previous operations would be unlikely to produce a fundamentally different outcome without an American ground operation.
"There is an understanding that without a ground operation by the Americans, there is no chance of achieving something different and new," the official said, adding that repeating previous military actions before the U.S. elections would be a political disaster for Trump.
