Trump cannot figure out peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

US President Donald Trump’s deal to purchase diesel fuel from Russia is a moral outrage: It rewards an aggressor that is terrorizing Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles, while punishing the victim for fighting back. Its economic benefits for the US would be modest at best. Above all, the deal is sadly indicative of a deeper failing in Trump’s Ukraine policy. The president genuinely desires peace in that country, but his strategic blinders and indiscipline keep making that task harder.
The details of the deal are dispiriting. The US has agreed to temporarily lift sanctions so Russia can bring about 2 million barrels of diesel to market immediately (with about 13 million barrels committed in total), in hopes of driving down prices at the pump in the US before the midterm elections next month. The deal follows growing US frustration with Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, which have added to stress on global markets. It is not clear if the agreement would ease that pressure, given that the volumes involved are relatively small and the real problem in global energy markets is the president’s war with Iran.
However, the deal would have a strategic impact, by weakening the push to cut Western purchases of Russian energy. It threatens to undo a year’s worth of European efforts to convince Trump that Russia, not Ukraine, is the primary obstacle to peace. And it creates a perverse scenario in which Trump fills the coffers of a neo-fascist autocracy while penalizing Ukraine for targeting Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war economy in self-defense.
Illustration: Mountain People
A bipartisan group of senators has already condemned the deal. Trump has defended it and announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia — a breakthrough more imagined than real.
Whatever comes of this episode, it illustrates how election-year incentives and economic blowback from the Iran war are affecting US foreign policy in theaters far beyond the Middle East. It is also a window into the frustrations of Trump’s bid to end the war in Ukraine.
Trump seems genuinely appalled by the killing. He has strong strategic incentives to seek a peace deal, amid a potential forever-war in the Persian Gulf and a rising Chinese threat in the Pacific — but his approach to peacemaking has done more harm than good.
To be fair, a realistic strategy would have included some of Trump’s initiatives, such as pushing the Europeans to take primary responsibility for aiding Ukraine. It would also involve quietly urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s government to accept that it would not recapture all the territory it has lost to Russia or become a member of NATO.
Yet the other half of this strategy would have involved a concerted effort to ratchet up sanctions pressure on Russia, consistent support for Ukraine’s punishing deep-strike campaign, and strong measures to convince Putin that he cannot simply outlast US support for Ukraine or wait for the Western coalition to fracture. Here, the record is bleak.
Since his Oval Office showdown with Zelenskiy in February last year, Trump has repeatedly feuded with the Ukrainian leader in public and threatened to withdraw US intelligence and military support. He has brawled with European allies not just in good causes (burden sharing), but also in bad ones (acquiring Greenland). His administration has sometimes taken Russia’s side in seeking to influence European elections; it might withdraw significant US forces from the continent just as Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign intensifies. Trump and his aides also convey the strong impression that they want to get back to business with Moscow, once the pesky war in Ukraine is cleared away.
All this has surely encouraged Putin to think he can divide the US from Ukraine and from Europe if he shows enough bloody-minded patience. It gives him confidence he can win the war in Washington even if he cannot win it on the battlefield in Donetsk. Even when the administration seeks peace by offering up major Ukrainian concessions — as Trump did at his summit with Putin in Alaska last year — these efforts cannot satiate Moscow’s sweeping demands.
Trump’s Ukraine peacemaking has been a self-defeating experience that reflects two of his worst strategic flaws.
First, he has consistently misdiagnosed the source of the deadlock. He often seems more frustrated with Ukraine’s insistence on surviving as an independent nation than with Russia’s obsessive drive to snuff that independence out. He insists, against all evidence to the contrary, that Putin wants peace more than Zelenskiy.
That view might reflect Trump’s spheres-of-influence mentality, which holds that smaller powers must accommodate larger powers, but it blinds him to the fact that Putin seeks Ukrainian surrender as part of his larger geopolitical assault on the West. The Russian leader would only quit when the price of persistence becomes too high.
Second, a president who prioritizes quick fixes fails at the hard work of strategy. Peacemaking in Ukraine was never going to be easy. It demands deftly mixing pressure and diplomacy with Moscow; it requires sustaining Western solidarity while moving toward unsatisfying compromises.
However, Trump lacks the patience for careful, coordinated statecraft; he disdains consultation with allies. So he has repeatedly launched ill-considered peace initiatives that panic Kyiv and Europe, but fail to move Putin.
Now, Trump has struck a diesel deal that would have scant economic benefits and serious strategic costs. He is, reportedly, threatening to abandon Ukraine unless it drops its deep-strike campaign against Russian energy targets — that is, its best tool for making the price of Putin’s war prohibitive.
In the process, Trump is depleting US leverage, by encouraging Putin to continue his onslaught, and squandering US influence in Kyiv. Peace in Ukraine is a worthy destination. Alas, Trump has no idea how to get there.

GlobalFoundries gets US$21bn for plants in US-Japan deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

GlobalFoundries Inc plans to build two new chip plants with the backing of as much as US$21 billion from the Japanese government, part of an arrangement that also includes the US taking a 4 percent stake in the company.
Under an agreement announced on Wednesday, GlobalFoundries will operate factories at its site in upstate New York that are jointly owned by the US and Japan. The facilities will be funded with money from Japan’s pledge to invest US$550 billion in the US.
The factories will make so-called essential chips, the vital yet less sophisticated semiconductors used in vehicles, industrial equipment and communications gear.
Photo: John Carl D’Annibale, The Albany Times Union via AP
The GlobalFoundries agreement is meant to boost American production of essential chips and reduce dependence on East Asian suppliers — addressing a national security concern for the US.
Under a broader arrangement with GlobalFoundries, the US Department of Commerce will take a roughly 4 percent equity stake in the company, “further enabling the American public to share in GF’s growth.”
GlobalFoundries will get to redirect funds from a previous US CHIPS and Science Act grant to invest in honing its manufacturing abilities. That includes advancing its work in fields such as silicon photonics, chip packaging and silicon germanium.
In a separate statement, the US Department of Commerce said it was reallocating US$955 million in CHIPS Act incentives to go toward GlobalFoundries’ factory expansion and modernization. As part of the agreement, the company will devote US$5 billion to capital investments at its plants in New York and Vermont.
The new Japan-linked factories will be operated in the same way that GlobalFoundries runs its current facilities, which serve customers such as Apple Inc and Japanese firms including Renesas Electronics Corp.
Profits will be divided among the owners and GlobalFoundries, following an approach laid out in last year’s US trade deal with Japan. US President Donald Trump touted the accord on his Truth Social site, saying it would help revitalize America’s industrial base and create jobs.
For GlobalFoundries, the arrangement will help the company meet surging demand for its products, chief executive officer Tim Breen said in an interview.
“We need to respond to what our customers need,” he said. “Right now, the whole industry is in short supply.”
The company has already begun work on the first plant, located by GlobalFoundries’ home base in Malta, New York. It expects to have the factory up and running in 2029. The second will go ahead as quickly as possible after the initial plant is completed. But that will depend in part on future demand, Breen said.
“Of course, it will be market-dependent,” he said. “We’re not going to do it if the market isn’t there, but every indicator I see today is flashing green around market demand.”
GlobalFoundries has taken a more conservative approach to spending on its factory network. That’s made it profitable but often resulted in anemic top-line growth.
Its annual budget for new plants and equipment was less than US$1 billion last year. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), the biggest chip foundry, spent more than US$40 billion.
The US-Japan deal gives GlobalFoundries a chance to expand in a smart way, Breen said.
“It’s actually a pretty exciting win-win in terms of the economics of it,” he said.

Ministry passes bamboo forest carbon sink project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

The first carbon sink project for bamboo forest management has passed review by the Ministry of Environment, marking a milestone in the development of Taiwan’s natural carbon sink policy, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency said yesterday.
The environmental, social and governance (ESG) project by Chunghwa Telecom Co covers 34 hectares of makino bamboo grove in Taoyuan’s Fusing District (復興), the agency said.
The project was matched with Chunghwa Telecom through the agency’s Hsinchu branch two years ago and would run through the end of 2034, it said.
Photo courtesy of Chunghwa Telecom
Chunghwa Telecom prepared documents according to the bamboo forest management methodology and applied for the plan to be accredited as a voluntary emission reduction project, the agency said.
The project passed the review on Oct. 2 and became the first validated carbon sink project for bamboo forest management nationwide, it said.
That showed that Taiwan has not only established a calculation methodology for bamboo forest carbon sink, but has also put it into practice, marking a milestone in natural carbon sink development, the agency said.
Bamboo forest diebacks could occur if the plants are left unattended, it said, adding that proper management and human intervention are the key to maintaining bamboo forests’ carbon sequestration potential.
Bamboo forests renew about every four years and bamboo aged four years or older should be removed via selective cutting to create growing space for young bamboo, the agency said.
The agency set up the carbon sink and biodiversity ESG project matching platform in April 2024 to help match corporate investments with natural habitats or forests in need of conservation, it said.
Such projects can assist companies in acquiring carbon sinks or carbon credits while creating job opportunities for locals, the agency said.
For example, Chunghwa Telecom is to cooperate with an Atayal village as part of the project, it said.
Bamboo management requires substantial manual labor, the agency said, adding that the felled bamboo would be processed into products.
More bamboo forest-based ESG projects could be launched on the platform in the future, it said.
So far, the platform’s ESG projects are open only to companies or foundations that have registered and incorporated in Taiwan, it added.
The agency expects Chunghwa Telecom’s experience to encourage more companies to take on natural carbon sink projects via the platform based on their core technology and sustainability targets, the agency said.

Taiwanese highly support sustainable waste management
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

Taiwanese highly supported convenience stores’ efforts to reduce single-use items, but only 26.1 percent knew the significance of “refuse” in the “5R” sustainable living principle, a Taiwan Re-Think Environmental Education Association survey showed.
Results showed that people’s environmental knowledge and attitude have continued to improve over the years, association chief brand officer Sandra Wang (王滋鮮) said.
However, more than 70 percent did not know that refusing single-use items or unnecessary plastics is the first step of the 5R principle: “refuse, reduce, reuse, repair and recycle,” Wang said.
Photo: Lin Cheng-hung, Taipei Times
Only 26.1 percent knew the significance of “refuse” in the 5R principle, of whom more than 80 percent still ask for single-use items, she said.
This year, about 93.9 percent of respondents knew that paper coffee cups are recyclable, up from 84.6 percent last year, while people with knowledge of recycling plastics increased from 68.4 percent last year to 70.6 percent this year.
However, the percentage of people answering correctly to questions about kitchen waste recycling declined from 88.1 percent last year to 77.44 percent this year, likely because the rules were revised this year, the results showed.
The Ministry of the Environment also collaborated with the association and Taiwan FamilyMart Co on an environmental exhibition at Huashan 1914 Creative Park in Taipei.
The exhibition runs from today to Oct. 26, featuring a glass wall with more than 17,000 discarded cigarette butts, as well as thought-provoking environmental issues in daily life.
At a news conference yesterday, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) thanked the association for helping promote environmental education with innovative ideas.
He also thanked FamilyMart for collaborating with the ministry on resource circulation, including a coffee grounds recycling program, which won a grand award in the Presidential Hackathon last year, he said.
As kitchen waste disposal fees surged due to the ban on feeding swill to pigs, proper management of kitchen waste has become a key issue, Peng said.
While kitchen waste disposal involves downstream management, reducing upstream waste is also important, he said.
The ministry has initiated communications with 20 major chain restaurants on the issue, Peng said, adding that the ministry has discussed food waste reduction with department stores and hotels, which produce kitchen waste mainly through food courts and buffets.
The ministry would establish an alliance to promote the “clean plate” campaign by the end of this year and launch a “cherish food Wednesday” campaign, Peng said.

Executive Yuan skeptical of Songshan plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:56 UTC
01:42:56 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) yesterday attended a Cabinet meeting to discuss his proposal to relocate Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport), a week after his re-election campaign unveiled the proposition.
Chiang and the Executive Yuan offered differing accounts of the meeting, with the former emphasizing progress in exploring the proposal and the latter expressing skepticism about the “significant reversal” in the city’s urban development policy.
Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport’s first and second terminals have a combined capacity of 48 million people a year, which is projected to expand to 70 million with the opening of the third terminal, Chiang said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
This increase is more than enough to replace Songshan airport, whose capacity is 5.6 million people, he said.
Asked why he did not make this policy request earlier during his term as mayor, Chiang said that he had filed a recommendation for the removal of Songshan airport to the central government in August last year.
Chiang declined to respond to questions about replacing the airport’s role as a logistics hub for Taiwan’s outlying islands and medical patients requiring air transport.
Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said that this was the first time Chiang discussed relocating the airport with the central government.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) strongly hopes that Chiang would explain the significant developmental reversal and provide documentation on the city’s internal discussions to help assist with the project, she added.
Songshan airport is used for accessing the outlying islands, transporting medical patients by air, and international flights, a reserve for Taoyuan airport and doubles as a military airbase for the capital’s defense, she said.
Without Songshan airport, there would be a critical capability gap that is immensely challenging to fill, especially due to its role as the sole airport capable of accommodating E and F type aircraft, she said.
Taoyuan airport’s third terminal is not expected to be completed before 2030, or reach its full operational potential in less than 10 years, she said.
The Executive Yuan would defer to Chiang’s plans for replacing Songshan airport’s vital capabilities, she said.
Separately, Civil Aviation Administration Deputy Director Yang Kuo-feng (楊國?) said that Chiang had previously agreed to the government’s Songshan airport 2040 plan.
Under the plan, approved by the Cabinet in 2023, the airport would become Taiwan’s primary hub for business jets, focusing on flights connecting to regional capitals and cross-strait business hubs, while still providing reliable transport to outlying islands.

Better conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

Labor groups yesterday accused a Taiwanese offshore wind equipment manufacturer of exploiting Indonesian technical workers whose monthly salary contracts were allegedly replaced with lower-paying hourly agreements, and urged a review of the system used to bring them to Taiwan.
At a protest outside the Ministry of Labor in Taipei, groups including the Taiwan International Workers' Association (TIWA) said five workers, representing a larger group, had complained about pay and working conditions on offshore wind projects involving Century Energy Co, Ltd, a major Taiwanese manufacturer of offshore wind subsea foundations.
Photo: CNA
TIWA coordinator Betty Chen (陳容柔) said the workers — qualified welders and fitters — were brought to Taiwan by Singapore-based Sheffield Green and Indonesia's PT Kepodang Makmur Sejahtera under a "contract performance" system that allows overseas companies to send personnel to work on contracted projects.
Some had initially signed contracts promising NT$48,000 (US$1,477) a month, but were later paid about NT$100 to NT$143 per hour, Chen said.
In a statement issued later yesterday, Century Energy said the foreign technical workers had been brought to Taiwan under arrangements approved by Taiwanese authorities, and denied evading any legal responsibilities.
It also disputed the allegations about the workers' wages, saying they "did not match the facts," but did not provide further details or wage figures.
The company said employment terms were governed by agreements between the workers and overseas contractors, making it "inappropriate" for it to intervene directly.
However, it pledged to continue monitoring the workers' welfare and to cooperate with government inspections.
Eko, a pseudonym for an Indonesian fitter who said he had worked on the projects for five years, said he earned about NT$100 an hour despite holding professional qualifications.
He also trained Philippine and Vietnamese blue-collar migrant workers who, he said, lacked comparable technical qualifications.
"Why am I paid less than blue-collar migrant workers?" he asked, adding that he worked about 260 hours a month and had no labor or occupational accident insurance.
Another Indonesian worker, speaking under the pseudonym Yat, said he signed an agreement promising NT$48,000 a month, but was given a lower-paying hourly contract just days before leaving Indonesia.
Chen said workers had raised concerns with the company, but were told: "If you don't want to work, go home."
Taiwan's minimum wage is currently NT$29,500 per month, or NT$196 per hour, for covered workers. Based on an illustrative calculation of 26 workdays a month plus 14 hours of overtime, Chen estimated that a worker earning NT$100 an hour would receive NT$28,362 a month, including bonuses and overtime pay.
Citing Century Energy's sustainability report from last year, the groups said the company had 508 contract performance personnel that year, assigned to facilities in New Taipei City's Bali District (八里) and Taichung.
They estimated that the company could save more than NT$14 million a month in wages and employment-related contributions if similar arrangements applied to about 500 workers.
The protesters called for investigations into suspected disguised employment, reviews of workers' contracts, compensation for the workers, continued employment under terms applicable to foreign technical workers and a system to help and shelter workers seeking redress.
The ministry replied in general terms, saying foreign workers dispatched to Taiwan under commercial contracts must receive the protections for employment terms and occupational injury compensation provided under applicable Taiwanese laws, such as the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) where it applies.
The ministry said it would step up inspections of high-risk cases and "deal strictly under the law" with companies found using contract performance arrangements to "circumvent employment and labor regulations."

HPA touts e-cigarette collection rate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

E-cigarettes collected at anonymous disposal points had reached 633kg since the scheme began on Sept. 8, equivalent to about 12,660 devices based on an average weight of 50g each, the Health Promotion Agency (HPA) said yesterday.
The six special municipalities accounted for about 70 percent of the total, while northern and central Taiwan combined accounted for 80 percent, the agency said.
On Sept. 8, the HPA set up 431 e-cigarette collection spots nationwide for people to anonymously dispose of e-cigarettes.
Photo: CNA
It added one more the following day.
The Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) prohibits the manufacture, import, sale, supply, display, advertisement and use of e-cigarettes.
The disposal boxes are positioned mainly at local health departments, health bureaus and public health centers.
The agency’s proposal to add “possession” to the list of e-cigarette prohibitions was passed by the Executive Yuan on June 25 and has been sent to the legislature for review, HPA Tobacco Control Division Director Lo Su-ying (羅素英) said.
Once it takes effect, there would be a one-month grace period in which the devices would be confiscated, but no fines would be issued. After the grace period, people found with the devices would face a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$100,000, as well as confiscation of the device, the HPA said.
Public support for the collection scheme was evident, HPA Deputy Director-General Lin Li-ju (林莉茹) said, adding that it would continue to provide the service and encourage people to properly dispose of their devices.
The program is expected to continue until one month after the revisions to the act take effect, with additional locations to be considered based on local demand, Lin said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

Seven years after COVID-19 put the brakes on Indonesia’s new women’s soccer league, Zahra Naqiyyah would finally return to the field with “high hopes” for the women’s game in the country.
Sunday’s matches in the Indonesia Women’s League (IWL) would be the first since 2019 and a new chapter for women’s soccer in the Muslim-majority country of 290 million people.
“I really believe that if Indonesia’s women’s football is properly managed we can become a powerhouse in Asia,” Zahra said at a training session in Bekasi, east of Jakarta.
Photo: AFP
“I have high hopes for women’s football in Indonesia,” she added, wearing a black hijab and the turquoise jersey of her club, Garudayaksa Women.
Indonesia has long been an outlier among soccer nations, including much smaller Asian ones, in not having a permanent league for women. That was until 2019, when the IWL was launched and Zahra, only 15 at the time, helped her team to victory and celebrated with a hero’s parade in her home city of Bandung — fulfilling a dream.
However, the league managed only one season because of the pandemic and subsequent financial problems, and has been on hold ever since.
Now, the Football Association of Indonesia has allocated 24 billion rupiah (US$1.34 million) to restart the league and pay salaries, albeit small ones, to players.
There would be six clubs to start in the five-year trial period, said association chairman Erick Thohir, former owner of Inter.
At 22, Zahra is still young enough to make a career of it. Others were not so lucky.
“Many of my friends ended up quitting because what else could they do? There is no league, and if they want to become coaches, who are they supposed to coach?” Zahra said.
While she learned to be a coach, others tried their luck with clubs abroad.
Nastasia Suci Ramadhani played last year in the Maldives.
The 20-year-old returned to Indonesia in January to play alongside Zahra.
Unsure about the league’s staying power, Nastasia is studying management and has also considered becoming a police officer or soldier.
“For men there’s a league every year, but for women there isn’t,” she said.
Garudayaksa coach Yopie Riwoe said the going will be tough if Indonesia wants to compete with top Asian nations.
Japan won the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2011 and are the current Asian champions, while China and South Korea also boast women’s leagues and are competitive at international level.
“All this time they haven’t done continuous training like daily sessions with high intensity, so it’s been a bit difficult,” Yopie said of Indonesia’s women. “We’re trying to go slowly.”
Indonesia’s women have never been to the World Cup and failed to qualify for the Asian Cup last year, although they did reach the continental showpiece in 2022, losing all three games.
However, they won the regional ASEAN Football Federation Women’s Cup in 2024 and again this year.
They are currently ranked No. 105 in the world.
Hoping to join the national side one day, Azra Zifa Kayla is playing in the IWL for Persita Women, based west of Jakarta.
The 22-year-old would juggle afternoon practice with mornings teaching physical education to elementary-school students, afraid to stake everything, including a regular salary, on her passion for soccer.
“I am an athlete first,” she said on a soccer pitch in Tangerang, near the capital. “But to be an athlete — especially as a woman in Indonesia — can be limiting.”
“I should also focus on education because that’s the guarantee of my future,” said Azra, who studied health and sport science.
The IWL returns with about 200 players from clubs all from Greater Jakarta.
IWL boss Teddy Tjahjono said the long-term goal was to create a sustainable women’s soccer industry.
“If the industry is strong, then financially it will be good for the clubs, for the players and for the entire support system around women’s football, which will also continue to improve,” he said.

Montenegro changes temporary protection rules for Ukrainian men liable for military service
Kyiv • UNN
New male applicants need a document confirming completion of or discharge from military service. The rule does not apply to those who already have protection.
The Government of Montenegro is changing the rules for temporary protection for Ukrainian men liable for military service in the country. From now on, to obtain protection, they must provide a document confirming completion of or exemption from military service. The restriction does not apply to Ukrainians who already have temporary protection status, the Government of Montenegro reports, according to UNN.
At its 142nd meeting, the Government adopted a decision amending the decision approving temporary protection for persons from Ukraine
The Government said that the decision complies with the provisions of Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1912 of July 30, 2026.
The decision states that "temporary protection until March 4, 2027, is granted to Ukrainian citizens who, before arriving in Montenegro, actually resided in Ukraine and who have fulfilled their military duty in Ukraine or are exempt from military duty in Ukraine, subject to the submission of supporting documents, and who cannot return to Ukraine, which they were forced to leave because of the armed conflict".
The aforementioned restriction will not apply to persons from Ukraine who already enjoy temporary protection in Montenegro.
It will be recalled
On October 8, the period of temporary protection for Ukrainian refugees in Germany was extended until March 2028.

Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:41:30 UTC

Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread
Prime Minister Edi Rama condemns ‘chaos’ as protests continue for a third day in the capital and spread to other cities.
Albania’s prime minister has dismissed calls for his resignation as thousands of protesters clash with riot police in the capital for the third day in a row, leaving government buildings damaged.
“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Prime Minister Edi Rama said in a written statement to the Reuters news agency, following protester demands for him to resign.
“The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership,” Rama added on Thursday.
This comes as riot police used water cannons and tear gas against crowds of protesters in the capital, Tirana. Demonstrators have accused officials of corruption and neglecting education, expressing anger about the sale of parts of Albania’s southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Tirana’s streets were littered with burnt-out rubbish bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights. In the capital’s central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on.
Thursday’s protests also spread to several smaller cities as students joined university boycotts.
Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
“Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future,” Rama said in his statement to Reuters.
‘Everyone will certainly pay’
Rama earlier posted a video on his Facebook page showing him touring the burnt-out remains of an office at a university campus in Tirana.
“Until yesterday, this was the office of the College of Europe, the school of a united Europe,” he said in the video, his first public comments since the protests began.
“Everyone is responsible before the law, and everyone who has had a hand in this chaos will certainly pay.”
The prime minister was due to meet his party’s parliamentary group early on Thursday, when protesters circulated an “ultimatum” demanding his resignation by 1pm (11:00 GMT).
But even before the deadline passed, protesters had already begun clashing with police, building makeshift barriers and setting fire to bins.
‘Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption’
A student who gave her name as Kiara told Reuters the cost of living, poor job prospects and alleged corruption were the main issues for protesters.
“Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy,” she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday.
The protesters demanded Rama’s resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the luxury resort development linked to Kushner.
Police said 65 people were arrested during Wednesday’s protests, suspected of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.
The Health Ministry said in a statement that hospitals in Tirana treated 89 people on Wednesday, including 61 police officers.
Four officers and two protesters remained hospitalised, with a demonstrator and two officers expected to undergo surgery.
“Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students,” Rama said.

Trump Cancels Livestream of Fort Hood Firing Squad Execution Amid Bipartisan Pushback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

President Donald Trump on Thursday called off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan following a wave of fierce bipartisan backlash.
In a post on Truth Social, the President said he thought streaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM,” but that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die.”
The families of victims may view the execution “if they so choose,” Trump added.
The execution remains scheduled for Dec. 3 and marks the first U.S. military firing squad execution since World War II.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Oct. 8 that the execution of Hasan would be livestreamed, sparking fierce backlash from both sides of the aisle.
Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the livestream. He also said that he would not watch the livestream if it took place.
House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he would not watch the execution. In an interview with CBS News earlier this month, he said he had colleagues "who have concerns,” over the livestream, one of them being “that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists."
In addition to many Democrats in Congress, several Republican lawmakers also expressed their disapproval over the plans..
“I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do,” said Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, in a post on X. “America is better than that.”
Republican Rep. John Curtis of Utah said that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” in a post on X in which he urged Hegseth to “reconsider” his decision. “Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite.”
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, an outspoken GOP critic against Hegseth, called the livestream “beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
Trump had reconsidered livestreaming Hasan’s execution this week after learning that he is paralyzed from the waist down, according to sources familiar with the matter who spoke to CNN.
Polling shows a majority of Americans disapprove of livestreamed executions
A majority of Americans also opposed the livestream of Hasan’s execution. According to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, eight in ten Americans said the execution should not be livestreamed.
Majorities across party lines opposed the livestream, with 91% of Democrats, 83% of Independents, and 64% of Republicans, according to the poll.
Another YouGov poll found that 69% of respondents opposed broadcasting executions to the public, including 52% of Republicans, 67% of independents, and 87% of Democrats.
Among those who supported the death penalty, 55% opposed livestreaming executions.
In general, support for the death penalty has declined in the U.S. According to a Gallup poll, 52% of Americans supported capital punishment for convicted murderers in 2025, down from around 80% in 1994.
What was Hasan convicted of?
Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
He opened fire inside a processing center where soldiers were preparing for deployments overseas, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian employee. Pvt. Francheska Velez, 21, was three months pregnant when she was shot and killed by Hasan.
Hasan said that he was motivated by opposition to U.S. operations in Afghanistan and support for the Taliban.
“I was on the wrong side but I switched sides,” Hasan said in 2013.

Trump scraps plan to livestream execution after global condemnation
The firing squad execution of a convicted military base shooter will not be livestreamed, US President Donald Trump announced Thursday, canceling a contentious plan by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The move to livestream Nidal Hasan's execution was widely opposed at home and abroad, prompting outrage from both US Democratic and Republican politicians, the Catholic Church and the United Nations.
The cancellation is a blow to Hegseth, who is already under fire over the stalemated Iran war and its fallout, which are weighing on Trump's Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections.
Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.
The US president indicated he did not personally oppose the streaming plan, saying it "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die," Trump said, adding that the execution could still be viewed in person by immediate family of the victims if they wanted to do so.
Hasan's execution - scheduled for 3 December at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 - is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945.
Hegseth said last week that "we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," later confirming that the plan was to livestream the execution.
"People need to understand that...there's serious consequence for these types of things," he said.
Most Americans opposed
Backlash to the plan quickly grew following Hegseth's announcement.
The United Nations said streaming the execution would amount to "torture," while the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops said it was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death," and both Australia and Britain's prime ministers described it as "abhorrent."
Vice President JD Vance, who recently released a memoir on his Catholic faith, said he would not watch the execution if the plan went forward.
A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Thursday found that eight in 10 Americans opposed the livestreaming of the execution.
Lawmakers from both main US parties have said they are against it, including top House Republican Mike Johnson, who said it could be a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."
Dozens of retired US military officers also warned in an open letter against broadcasting the execution.
It "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," and "will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers," said the officers, including more than 40 generals and admirals.
The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
The Death Penalty Information Center says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916.
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 - six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.
He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

Syria announces arrest of Assad-era paramilitary leader
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Syria announces arrest of Assad-era paramilitary leader
Syrian authorities on Thursday announced the arrest of a paramilitary leader who backed ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad during the country's civil war, and who is accused of being the main culprit in a massacre of nearly 250 civilians.
"The intelligence services have arrested Ali Kayali, who also went by the name Mihrac Ural, the main suspect in the Banias massacre of 2013, while he was attempting to flee across the border," state news agency SANA said.
It did not specify which country the man was trying to flee to.
In May 2013, government and forces and their allies killed at least 248 people in mass executions in the predominantly Sunni Muslim towns of Bayda and Banias, located in the coastal province of Tartus, according to Human Rights Watch.
The monitor had at the time described the killings as "one of the deadliest instances of mass executions in Syria's increasingly bloody conflict".
The arrest "sends a clear message: there is no room in Syria for impunity for criminals; the rights of victims will not be lost, no matter how much time passes," Syrian Justice Minister Mazhar Alwais wrote on X.
Syria's war began with pro-democracy protests in 2011 that were violently suppressed by the government, and quickly morphed into a complex armed conflict that drew in paramilitary forces, jihadists and foreign powers.
In a multiconfessional country, the war took on a sectarian nature, with the killings in Banias and Bayda often seen as a starting point of that shift.
It ended with the ousting of Assad in 2024 in a lightning offensive led by an Islamist rebel group that subsequently took power.
According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor, the death tolls in Banias and Bayda came to around 400.
Kayali fled from jail in 1982 in his home country of Turkey, before moving to Syria where he would end up founding a paramilitary force allied with Assad's government.
The new authorities in Syria have arrested dozens of former security officials. Their trials began in April.
President Ahmed al-Sharaa's media adviser Ahmed Zeydan welcomed Kayali's arrest, describing him as "a criminal... who committed massacres during the Syrian war, including those in Bayda and Banias. Every murderous criminal will be hunted down".

According to the SSU, the suspect was conscripted into the army of the aggressor state in late July of this year. This occurred after he served eight years in prison for the intentional infliction of severe bodily harm and theft."
Details: He fought against Ukraine in the Chuhuiv district of Kharkiv Oblast.
The SSU found that on 5-6 October, Ryzhikov came under fire from the Ukrainian Armed Forces in the village of Starytsia.
Armed with an AK-74 assault rifle, he fled the area and began walking towards the city of Kharkiv, hiding in forested areas.
Along the way, he burgled an abandoned house, stealing civilian clothes from it.
Quote: "On 13 October, near the village of Mykhailivka in the Kharkiv district, Ryzhikov unprovokedly shot dead a 60-year-old peaceful local resident, who was fishing at a pond, using his assault rifle. After killing the elderly man, he pushed his body into the water.
That same day, Yula broke into a private property in the village of Momotove, where five Ukrainian Armed Forces servicemen were temporarily staying. At the time, they were not taking part in hostilities, were unarmed and were dressed in civilian clothes, making them civilians under the Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War.
With no need to do so, Ryzhikov ruthlessly shot these people, some of whom were simply sleeping."
Details: Law enforcement officers report that Ryzhikov hid the assault rifle and headed towards Kharkiv.
On 14 October, SSU officers, together with the National Police and the National Guard, detained him in the Saltivskyi district.
Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office has published a video showing the suspect being questioned.
Based on the gathered evidence, Security Service investigators have served the detained Russian serviceman with a notice of suspicion under Article 438.2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes resulting in death).
He faces life imprisonment.
Background:
- On 13 October, an unknown assailant shot and killed five soldiers from the 72nd Separate Mechanised Brigade inside a residential building in the Kharkiv district. It was reported that the attacker was wanted.
- Law enforcement officers have detained a Russian serviceman on suspicion of murdering five Ukrainian soldiers and one civilian.

UK Green member behind anti-Zionism motion ‘receives death threats’

UK Green member behind anti-Zionism motion ‘receives death threats’
Lubna Speitan, who has Palestinian roots, believes messages and emails are part of an effort to intimidate her.
London, United Kingdom – The British-Palestinian woman behind the Zionism is racism motion, passed by the Green Party of England and Wales earlier this month, says she has received death and rape threats since the vote.
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, Green member Lubna Speitan, an artist and activist, said she has received dozens of ominous social media messages and emails, which she has reported to the police.
“These threats were anticipated,” said Speitan, who believes they are a form of “intimidation” from pro-Israel agitators.
While “no one wants to be on the receiving end of death threats”, she said it is “necessary to confront these evils”.
The Greens passed the motion by 1,022 votes to 813 at their party conference in Brighton, but it has been criticised by virtually all other British political parties and has brought turmoil to the Greens.
Several of its left-wing MPs have criticised the move, and on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out partnering with the party, calling the motion “wrong” and “anti-Semitic”.
The motion defines Zionism, the belief that Jews have a historic claim to Palestine, as a form of racism, predicated on the dispossession and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Palestinians made up more than 90 percent of the population in 1917, when Britain declared its support for a Jewish state in the country.
The motion supports Palestinians’ right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state in historic Palestine for Muslims and Jews. It also says that anti-Zionism should not be equated with anti-Semitism.
‘Personally smeared’
Fifty-six members of Speitan’s family have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.
“Zionism is defined clearly as an ethnonationalist settler-colonial project. The motion also recognises, correctly, that not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews,” she said. “It targets an ideology: Zionism.”
She added that she has been “personally smeared” by media outlets.
Recent headlines in the British press have claimed she was “friends” with an “al-Qaeda terrorist”, as she reportedly offered to testify in defence of Minh Quang Pham, a UK citizen who had planned an attack at Heathrow Airport.
“This tactic of guilt by association will not be dignified with a response,” Speitan said of the reports.
The Green Party of England and Wales told Al Jazeera that Speitan holds no party positions “other than being a member”.
“The Green Party takes all allegations of this nature seriously. Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party’s values, we have internal processes to investigate, and an investigation is under way,” it said.
Media watchdog NewsCord, which reviewed coverage of the motion, concluded that opponents of the resolution received 10 times more coverage than its supporters.
The Green Party is not the first Western political institution to classify Zionism as a form of racism. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly passed a resolution declaring that Zionism was a racist ideology. Seventy-two countries voted in favour of the motion, while 35 opposed it and 32 abstained. The resolution was later repealed in 1991.

A senior UN official warned on Thursday that the situation in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank is dangerously fragile, saying a return to war must be avoided at all costs.
Briefing the UN Security Council on Palestine, Ramiz Alakbarov, UN acting special coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, marked the anniversary of the Oct. 7 events, saying Palestinians and Israelis need a political horizon.
"Palestinians and Israelis deserve more than short-term fixes. They deserve a credible path to peace and finally an end to this conflict," he said. "The international community must move beyond words and take concrete actions to ensure the future of security and dignity of the people. It is time to return to a genuine peace process.”

He said Israeli military operations have continued, "causing some 1,500 fatalities, including more than 320 children."
Alakbarov described families in Gaza living in worn-out tents, overcrowded displacement sites and badly damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. "Most of Gaza still lives in darkness," he said.

On the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Alakbarov said the situation continues to deteriorate amid Israeli military operations, movement restrictions, displacement and Palestinian attacks. He said settler violence persists at "extremely high levels," with daily attacks on Palestinians.
Describing his assessment as "realistic," Alakbarov said he felt compelled to raise concerns before the council.
"Today, I feel obliged to sound the alarm. In Gaza, desperation is palpable," he said.
He warned that frustration among Gaza's population cannot continue to build indefinitely and described the risk of a return to war as extremely high. "This must be avoided at all costs," he said.
"The West Bank is also at a boiling point," he added.

Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:35:00 UTC
01:35:00 KST

The RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 has been awarded to Lion Green Road, a housing development in Coulsdon, South London, designed by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS for Croydon Council. Comprising 157 homes across five residential blocks, the project combines privately owned and socially rented housing on a former car park. Presented annually by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), the Stirling Prize recognizes a building considered to make a significant contribution to the evolution of architecture and the built environment. The 2026 winner was announced at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London on October 15, marking the prize's 30th anniversary.
Replacing a car park on a sloping site with an eight-meter difference in elevation, Lion Green Road reconsiders how higher-density housing can respond to suburban contexts. Rather than leveling the terrain or organizing the development around conventional residential streets, the architects used the site's topography to shape the arrangement of the buildings and their relationship to the surrounding landscape. The five blocks are positioned and rotated to respond to changes in level and take advantage of different views, including views toward a surviving fragment of the Surrey Iron Railway, recognized as the world's first fully independent public railway. The buildings form what the architects describe as a "living landscape," accommodating 635 residents while establishing a connection between Lion Green Road and the parkland beyond.
The five blocks share the same construction specification but vary subtly in height, orientation, and brickwork patterns. A palette of three brown brick tones relates the buildings to the surrounding greenery, while differences in brickwork give each block an individual identity. The development is organized around shared outdoor spaces, with a new public pathway connecting the street to the parkland. Children's play areas, a sensory trail, and residents' allotments provide spaces for recreation and everyday interaction, extending the landscape's use beyond the residential buildings and creating opportunities for engagement between residents and their neighbors.
Related Article
RIBA Reveals the Shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize
Within the apartments, dual-aspect layouts bring daylight into each home and provide views in more than one direction. Balconies are positioned to limit direct overlooking between neighboring homes, allowing the blocks to sit relatively close together without sacrificing privacy or access to outdoor space. This arrangement supports the project's approach to density, in which the positioning of buildings and the planning of individual homes are used to balance housing provision with daylight, views, and private outdoor areas. The project also incorporates measures to reduce its environmental impact, including efficient construction methods, simple finishes, and a streamlined building process intended to reduce carbon emissions. The landscape strategy further supports existing wildlife and biodiversity.
The 2026 Stirling Prize shortlist also included A House at Fairmead in Epping Forest by Sergison Bates, BEAM in Hertfordshire by Bennetts Associates, Paddington Square in London by Renzo Piano Building Workshop with Adamson Associates, Pembroke, Mill Lane by Haworth Tompkins, and River Wing at Clare College by Witherford Watson Mann Architects. Previous winners of the prize include Appleby Blue Almshouse by Witherford Watson Mann Architects (2025), The Elizabeth Line by Grimshaw, Maynard, Equation, and AtkinsRéalis (2024), The John Morden Centre by Mæ (2023), and The New Library at Magdalene College by Níall McLaughlin Architects (2022).

Israeli ad-tech firm helped place spyware on Al Jazeera devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:32:03 UTC
01:32:03 KST

Israeli ad-tech firm helped place spyware on Al Jazeera devices
Citizen Lab investigation says dozens of Al Jazeera devices were infected by malware planted through advertisements.
Israeli advertising technology company Discover-Tech helped place spyware on dozens of devices used by Al Jazeera and other companies.
Al Jazeera Media Network on Thursday said it “condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff” and pledged to continue to “protect its employees and systems”.
The network said targeting journalists is an “assault on press freedom” and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
A Citizen Lab investigation, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, has confirmed that spyware from Candiru, an Israeli spyware firm blacklisted by the United States government in 2021 for its malicious cyber activities, was planted on these devices, using the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising.
The nature of installing this spyware means that once an infected advertisement appears on a device, that device, too, is infected – spying on, and feeding, all the data and information available on that platform to those stealing it.
The malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms.
To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
The particular tool used is understood to have cost several million dollars.
The incident highlights the sophisticated nature of threats posed by groups like Candiru, and their customers, who use techniques to bypass modern security defences.
The Citizen Lab, a research unit at the University of Toronto, concluded in its report that Discover-Tech purchased the advertisements with built-in spyware. It then directed devices to Candiru’s malware through these advertisements.
Al Jazeera journalists were among the millions whose devices were targeted – including several who reported on sensitive subjects.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. The pattern continued into 2025. Al Jazeera reached out to Citizen Lab for a more detailed investigation into its suspicions that spyware was responsible for the activity.
“Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed,” the University of Toronto-based team said in its report published Thursday.
Al Jazeera said that the cooperation “helped verify and publicly document these attacks”.
Meanwhile, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said in a separate report that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
Candiru’s spyware has previously been used to carry out surveillance on at least 100 journalists, dissidents and others in several countries.

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:28:44 UTC
01:28:44 KST

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
They allege ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, coaching its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others.
Eight US states have filed the most significant coordinated state action against tech giant OpenAI, adding to a wave of legal challenges that the firm is facing as it prepares for a public listing.
Recent legal and regulatory challenges have highlighted concerns about how AI chatbots and social media platforms are used and triggered discussions on policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.
Calls have been growing for AI companies to be held accountable for the impact of their digital platforms on users, specifically children, who are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.
What is this legal action about?
Florida filed the first lawsuit in June, alleging that the platform has harmed children by enabling information to be gathered by school shooters, providing access to guidance on self-harm and using addictive algorithms to keep young users hooked.
It cited a shooting at Florida State University in Tallahassee in April 2025, when a 20-year-old gunman shot dead two adults and wounded five others. According to the lawsuit, gunman Phoenix Ikner consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT programme about what type of weapon and ammunition to use and at what time campus would be busiest.
On Wednesday, attorneys general from eight states – Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia – said they had also sued OpenAI in courts across the country.
They all claim ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement that OpenAI was “hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans.”
“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend,” she said.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for sensitive conversations involving suicide, school shootings and self-harm. “We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said.
What are the allegations?
The legal action alleges that ChatGPT has been designed to be “agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users”. In doing so, it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.
Additionally, the suits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of their AI tool, which in fact poses a danger to the health of the states’ residents.
The states are seeking orders forcing OpenAI to make substantial changes to how ChatGPT works, as well as measures barring the company from developing AI models that can improve themselves until it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the lawsuit “simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company”.
How has OpenAI responded?
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri gave a statement to the media, saying that the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.
“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri said.
“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”
What other lawsuits is the tech giant facing?
OpenAI is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence.
A mother, whose two children use the chatbot, alleged in a proposed class action lawsuit filed on Tuesday in San Francisco federal court that OpenAI illegally profits from the personal information and data that minors share with ChatGPT.
The lawsuit claims the chatbot is designed to collect data and information from minors, which is then used to train OpenAI’s AI models. Minors can’t consent to the use of their data under California law.
In July, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, claiming ChatGPT’s inaccurate medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for recurrent dizzy spells, leading him to suffer a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.
OpenAI is also facing a series of lawsuits over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on ChatGPT in advance of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history.
The province of British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in a California court in September, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge, including his mother and half-brother, before dying by suicide.
The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI had failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT, accusing the company of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting”.
Victims of that shooting and their families filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.
OpenAI said it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months before the shooting, and deactivated it, but did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.

He served in the 2nd Battalion of the 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment of the 68th Motorized Rifle Division of the 6th Combined Arms Army of the Russian armed forces and had the call sign "Yula."
According to the SBU, the suspect was mobilized into the army of the aggressor state at the end of July this year. This occurred after he had served eight years in prison for intentionally causing grievous bodily harm and theft.
After his mobilization, "Yula" was sent to fight against Ukraine in the temporarily occupied territory of the Chuhuiv district of the Kharkiv region.
The SBU established that on October 5–6, while at the positions of Russian occupation forces near the village of Starytsia in the Chuhuiv district, Ryzhikov came under fire from the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Armed with an AK-74 assault rifle, he fled the area and began walking toward the city of Kharkiv, hiding in tree belts.
While moving, he robbed an abandoned private house, stealing civilian clothing from it.
On October 13, near the village of Mykhailivka in the Kharkiv district, Ryzhikov shot dead, without any reason, a 60-year-old local civilian who was fishing in a pond. After killing the elderly man, he pushed his body into the water.
On the same day, "Yula" entered a private household in the village of Momotove, where five servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine were temporarily staying. At that time, they were not participating in hostilities, had no weapons with them, and were dressed in civilian clothing, meaning that they were civilians within the meaning of the Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War.
Without any necessity, Ryzhikov mercilessly shot these people, some of whom were simply sleeping. Afterward, he hid his assault rifle in one of the properties of a dacha-and-garden association located nearby and, hiding in forest belts, headed toward Kharkiv
SBU officers, together with the National Police and the National Guard, detained the Russian serviceman on October 14, 2026, in the Saltivskyi district of Kharkiv, where he was hiding after committing the crimes.
Law enforcement officers also found and seized the weapon used to commit the crime – an AK-74 Kalashnikov assault rifle that belonged to Ryzhikov.
Based on the evidence collected, investigators of the Security Service notified the detained Russian serviceman of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes resulting in the death of people).
He faces life imprisonment.
The issue of imposing a preventive measure in the form of detention in custody is being considered.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing.
Reminder
In a residential building in the Kharkiv region, five servicemen of the 72nd Brigade were shot dead. The prosecutor's office is investigating the intentional murder; Russian citizens are suspected among those involved.

Egypt becomes first country to retain WHO gold-tier Hep C status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:23:16 UTC
01:23:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt becomes world's first to retain WHO hepatitis C elimination status
Egypt has become the first country in the world to receive certification for maintaining the World Health Organization’s gold-tier status in its efforts to eliminate hepatitis C, following a review of its achievements in combating the virus between 2023 and 2025.
Until the 2010s, Egypt had the highest prevalence of Hep C globally, affecting roughly 10% of the population, largely due to historical public health campaigns involving unsterilised medical needles in the 20th century.
But on Wednesday, the country received the certificate from the WHO after the organisation confirmed that it had met the requirements for retaining the status, which it first obtained in October 2023.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus presented the certificate to Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar during a news conference in Cairo, held on the sidelines of the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean.
The WHO said the recognition reflected Egypt’s continued progress in tackling Hep C. The review of the country’s efforts between 2023 and 2025 confirmed that it had fulfilled the requirements for maintaining the gold-tier status.
The decision had previously been approved in July 2026 by the WHO Regional Committee for the Validation of the Elimination of HIV, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections.
Egypt's Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the country’s achievements were built on the 100 Million Health campaign, launched in 2018. The campaign screened 68 million Egyptians and provided free treatment to around 4.5 million people living with the virus, using locally produced medicines.
In a statement, the WHO said Egypt had moved away from large-scale screening campaigns towards a sustainable and integrated approach to combating Hep C during the period in which it maintained its gold-tier status.
The approach includes strengthening routine screening, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance and prevention, while expanding access to services for people living with the virus.
The organisation highlighted Egypt’s expansion of screening, diagnosis and treatment services, as well as efforts to strengthen governance and oversight between 2025 and 2030.
Other measures include drawing up a national plan to sustain the elimination of Hep C and continuing to integrate hepatitis services into primary healthcare and the country’s comprehensive health insurance system.
Egypt has also worked to improve laboratory quality and disease surveillance systems, while maintaining high standards for blood and injection safety, according to the WHO.
The WHO first awarded Egypt gold-tier status in October 2023, making it the first country in the world to receive the recognition for its progress towards eliminating Hep C.
Over roughly a decade, Egypt, a country of more than 120 million people today, reduced the prevalence of the virus from 10% to 0.38%.
During that period, the country diagnosed 87% of people living with the virus and provided treatment to 93% of those diagnosed.
These figures exceeded the WHO’s gold-tier benchmarks, which require countries to diagnose at least 80% of people living with Hep C and treat at least 70% of those diagnosed.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Santa Ana Winds Trigger Wildfire Warnings in Southern California. Here's What To Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:22:13 UTC
01:22:13 KST

Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season are set to arrive.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening follows a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California. Only 300,000 acres have burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Why are Santa Ana winds so dangerous?
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong, according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS has warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
What areas of Southern California are under fire warnings?
The NWS has issued a red flag warning for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
Southern California Edison is considering shutting off power to some 250,000 customers. Areas in Northern and Central California, including parts of Alameda county, Fresno County, and Napa County could also face power outages. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
Recent rain means that San Diego and Orange County will face less of a fire risk, though the areas should still expect to see strong winds.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or improperly discarding cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

Russia’s New Drone Base Could Launch Over 100 Jet-Powered Drones Daily, Expert Warns
Russia has nearly completed a major new base for launching jet-powered attack drones near Ukraine after just six weeks of construction, according to Reuters on October 15.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs and Airbus, reviewed by Reuters, shows the facility in Russia’s Rostov region expanding from an empty field on August 31 into a complex covering approximately 0.9 square kilometers, equivalent to roughly 126 soccer fields.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Reuters investigation, DroneSec founder Mike Monnik assessed that the facility could launch Russia’s newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones.
Satellite images reveal eight launch platforms on the western side, with rails installed on two and construction continuing on others. Monnik estimated that the base could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones within 24 hours, depending on operational requirements and available weapons.
“The speed of construction … demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” Monnik stated, as quoted by Reuters. He assessed that the facility could become fully operational within weeks, if not sooner.
The installation is located approximately 3.5 kilometers from Russia’s Millerovo air base, which hosts the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment. DroneSec assessed that the new facility likely benefits from the air defense systems protecting the military airfield, potentially complicating Ukrainian efforts to strike it, Reuters reported.
Russia increased its deployment of jet-powered drones roughly sixfold during a three-month period this summer, according to Ukrainian military data previously examined by Reuters. These drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, making them substantially harder for Ukrainian interceptor drones to engage.
Drone infrastructure around Millerovo has already drawn repeated Ukrainian strikes.
On August 30, Ukrainian forces hit a facility in the area used to store, prepare and launch Russian attack drones, roughly 170 kilometers from the front line.
The overnight strike sparked a fire and coincided with an attack on the Yeysk military airfield in Krasnodar Krai. Earlier, Ukrainian drones targeted a Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo airfield, a site used to launch Shahed drones and other UAVs against Ukraine.

School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:15:06 BST
01:15:06 KST

School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
- Published
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
