Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:21:32 BST
00:21:32 KST

Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
- Published
A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.
Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport.
They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase.
They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks.
"My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office.
Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul.
The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance.
He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul.
As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany.
"Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said.
Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport.
They were destined for private buyers in Germany.

Rosatom says UN atomic agency-mediated ceasefire implemented near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:20:27 UTC
00:20:27 KST

Burç Eruygur
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The head of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said Thursday that a local ceasefire is being implemented near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to allow repairs at the facility under Moscow’s control.
Alexey Likhachev told reporters in Moscow that power supply to the ZNPP via the 330kV Ferosplavnaya-1 backup external power line is “extremely unstable and fraught with risks,” noting a “very high probability” of recurring loss of a stable power supply to the plant due to the “semi-destroyed state” of the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP).
Likhachev said Russia began efforts to arrange a localized ceasefire days ago to facilitate repairs at the ZTPP, and that the plant’s switchgear is essential for ensuring safety and power supply, including for the ZNPP.
“By engaging the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) and coordinating with our relevant ministries … we have successfully established a ‘regime of silence’ at the ZTPP today,” Likhachev was quoted by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass.
He went on to say that Rosatom specialists are heading to the site to begin repairing technical equipment, which he said will help strengthen power supply to the ZNPP.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns about a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kyiv frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility in southeastern Ukraine.
Since Sept. 1, 2022, IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant, which Russia has controlled since March 2022.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced earlier this month that he was negotiating a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow repairs at the ZTPP.

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:19:18 UTC
00:19:18 KST

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence
Court rulings concern violence and killings during March 2025 uprising by pro-Assad forces, and retaliatory attacks.
A court in Syria has sentenced to death two supporters of the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime for inciting an uprising last year, and handed hefty sentences to members of the current government’s security forces for the killing of hundreds of civilians from the Alawite religious minority.
The Military Criminal Court at the Justice Palace in the northern city of Aleppo gave death sentences to Al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali, according to state media.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported that the pair were convicted of seeking to incite civil war and sectarian fighting and for leading armed gangs with the intent to attack public forces.
A third defendant, Maher Othman, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, the court also announced on Thursday without immediately specifying the charges on which he was convicted.
In separate rulings, the court sentenced Mohammed Bakour, a member of the Defence Ministry’s 82nd Division in the new government, to 20 years in prison after convicting him of intentional homicide.
It also sentenced Ammar Abdul Aal to three years for torture and acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammed Zarzouri, SANA said.
The rulings concern investigations carried out by a government committee into attacks in March last year. At least 1,426 people, mostly civilians, were killed in several days of sectarian violence in the predominantly Alawite areas of Syria’s coastal regions.
The defendants included loyalists to the former al-Assad regime and members of the new government’s security forces. It is the first time government-linked personnel have been put on trial for acts of violence.
The government committee said it had identified 298 suspects implicated in serious violations during the violence in the Alawite heartland.
The committee’s investigation documented “serious violations against civilians on March 7, 8 and 9 [2025], including murder, premeditated murder, looting, destruction and burning of homes, torture and sectarian insults”.
The committee said 238 members of the army and security forces were killed by pro-Assad fighters in the attacks in the provinces of Tartous, Latakia and Hama.
About 200,000 pro-government military reinforcements then converged on the area, carrying out alleged revenge killings.
Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the Syrian capital, Damascus, said the uprising was started by individuals still loyal to the regime of al-Assad, who himself is from the Alawite religious minority.
“After the Assad regime fell and its leadership fled the country at the end of 2024, supporters including loyal soldiers from the ousted regime as well as militia members fled to the mountains from where they launched an uprising in March 2025 against the new government”, Pett said.
She added that forces loyal to the new government are accused of killing civilians from the Alawite minority group in revenge attacks.
“These trials are for seven men who took part in the initial pro-Assad uprising, and also seven members of the new government’s security forces who were subsequently deployed into the area and are accused of carrying out revenge attacks,” she said.
SANA reported that on September 17, the court issued verdicts in cases involving four other defendants accused of violations during the events in the coastal region last March. One was sentenced to death, one to life imprisonment and one to 20 years in prison; the fourth was acquitted.

Interview: Chinese desertification control expert calls for global unity to protect planet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:19:11 CST
00:19:11 KST

ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A leading Chinese expert on desertification control has called for global unity to protect food security and the environment.
Yin Yuzhen, who has spent more than four decades restoring the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that she hopes to share her experience and inspire collective efforts to safeguard the future of the planet.
Yin was named one of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' (FAO) 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development on Thursday.
Speaking to Xinhua in Rome, she said desertification control has not only transformed the local environment but also created new opportunities for rural residents to improve their livelihoods.
"I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin said.
Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) -- an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches -- of sandy land. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth.
For Yin, combating desertification is closely linked to food security. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said, stressing that protecting the land is essential to producing quality agricultural products and ensuring that ecological restoration benefits local communities.
"The Maowusu Sandy Land has turned green, and now it is becoming a land of gold," she said, describing the transformation as an example of the Chinese concept that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets.
Yin's work has also fostered a friendship that transcends national borders. In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, an American teaching in China at the time, saw a television report on Yin's tree-planting efforts and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her work.
Like the trees, their friendship has grown and endured.
"Although we come from two different countries and speak different languages, our hearts are connected," Yin said.
She sees their friendship as a reflection of the need for international cooperation in environmental protection.
"It is like the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity proposed by China. Although we come from different countries, we live on the same planet," she said. "We must unite to cherish nature and protect our planet."
Yin hopes to share her experience with communities facing land degradation, drought and desertification. Although conditions vary across regions, she believes that determination, and locally adapted approaches can help restore degraded land and improve people's lives.
The year 2026 has been designated by the United Nations as the International Year of the Woman Farmer. Yin said women play an important role in families and society and deserve greater support and opportunities in agriculture and rural development.
"They need not only equal status, but also more opportunities to put their abilities to use," she said. "Give them a little sunshine, and they will flourish."
Being named one of the FAO's 100 Women Heroes is both a recognition of Yin's past efforts, and an encouragement to continue her work, which shows that perseverance and cooperation can transform barren land into a fertile landscape.
"Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination," she said. ■

====================================================================================================

ACC Mulls Commercial Counter-Drone Services for Air Base Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:15:36 UTC
00:15:36 KST

Air Combat Command is looking for defense firms capable of providing a private counter-drone service, complete with the personnel to operate it, for defending air bases across the Air Force.
ACC, which oversees the service’s Point Defense Task Force, is conducting a market survey to identify companies specializing in counter-small unmanned aerial systems defense technology that can provide “C-sUAS as a Service,” according to an Oct. 13 solicitation.
According to the solicitation, the intent of the service model is to:
- Provide organic, resilient, sustainable, and agile Point Defense capabilities across Department of the Air Force installations
- Implement a flexible, scalable architecture allowing installations to scale operational capacity up or down based on dynamic threat levels
- Leverage mature, commercially available or rapidly adaptable systems rather than initiating high-risk developmental programs
The market survey comes as the Air Force races to develop an arsenal of capabilities to defend its installations against drone threat.
“The Government envisions an initial prototype deployment at two designated Continental United States Air Force installations, with option mechanisms to scale across additional ACC installations upon proven performance,” the document states.
Interested firms have until Oct. 31 to respond to the solicitation. ACC is interested in companies that can provide technology for detecting, tracking, and identifying drones—ranging from small quadcopters to larger, Group 3 systems like the Iranian Shahed one-way attack drones that weight up to 1,320 pounds—at distances of up to five miles from a base perimeter, the document states.
Firms should also be capable of incorporating “government-approved kinetic and/or nonkinetic” effectors that range from radio frequency jamming to directed-energy such as lasers and high-powered microwave systems, the document states. Interested defense firms would also have to show they would continuously refresh software and hardware “within a multiyear service contract without frequent contract modifications,” according to the document.
ACC would also want a commercial capability to have the built-in logistical support to be self-sufficient for up to 96 hours, the document states.
The concept would require the contractor to “provide a complete, integrated, turn-key service solution covering materiel, personnel, training, sustainment, and ongoing modernization,” the solicitation states.
It’s unclear how this commercial service would align with the service’s intent to create a new point defense career field for enlisted Airmen, training and equipping them to defend air bases from drone and missile attack. The Air Force is slated to start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. As a short-term fix, the service has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Currently, the Air Force is equipping installations with the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
The service is also acquiring additional counter-drone systems through the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. In the future, counter-drone technology will fall under the “point defense weapon system,” a classification to manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and non-kinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.

Ukraine has exhausted its stockpiles of missiles for the American Patriot air defense system, making it more vulnerable to attacks by Russian ballistic missiles
As noted, for several months, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of American Patriot interceptor missiles, which are one of the few types of defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.

It should be recalled

Is the AI mathocalypse coming for encryption next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:11:15 UTC
00:11:15 KST

Last week OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, dropped 722 mathematical manuscripts online in one go, every one of them penned by an artificial intelligence model unavailable to the public. The output was far from perfect: OpenAI withdrew three of the papers within a day, and mathematicians are still poring over the rest. But the scale of the research, and the incisiveness of its insights, has some worried.
Math powers cryptography. Every text you send and every bank log-in you submit is protected by a math problem that’s supposedly impossible to crack. The system rests on the assumption that no one will figure out how. And AI just showed it’s pretty good at math.
That worries Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University. In a social media post a few days after OpenAI’s massive math release, he suggested there was a 15 percent chance that we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms—which allow computers to establish secure connections and verify digital identities without first exchanging a shared secret key.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
That confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to break those algorithms. Take elliptic curve cryptography, used across the Internet and by cryptocurrencies. Its security relies on the belief that there’s no efficient algorithm capable of reversing the mathematical operations at its core. But if AI can spot shortcuts that humans have missed, that belief could be proven wrong.
Humans have found such shortcuts before, Green says. An algorithm called the number field sieve made it far easier to crack RSA, another widely used public-key system, when it relied on 512-bit keys. Cryptographers responded by lengthening the keys, and 2,048 bits is now considered the minimum. Another advance on that scale “could potentially seriously reduce the security level of the schemes that we standardize,” he says.
Govind Pimpale, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, thinks AI could make the next one more likely. Public-key cryptography depends on relatively few mathematical problems, he says, each studied by a comparatively small community. Machines could throw vastly more effort at them and find flaws or faster algorithms that would let attackers work out secret keys from public ones. “Public-key cryptography is necessary for essentially all online commerce and secure messaging, so its loss would have dire consequences,” he says.
Plenty of others disagree that AI will break modern encryption. Yehuda Lindell, a professor at Bar-Ilan University in Israel and head of cryptography at Coinbase, wrote on X that there is “no evidence whatsoever” of a breakthrough against the mathematical problems underlying those systems. Nor does a single one of OpenAI’s 722 papers deal with cryptography, which Dan Boneh, a professor of computer science at Stanford University, calls “a little striking.”
Still, Green’s worry is not entirely hypothetical. In a recent preprint, Florian Tramèr, a computer scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich, and his colleagues—three of them at the AI company Anthropic—pitted leading AI models against 191 code-breaking challenges. “It’s pretty clear that models’ ability in cryptanalysis is growing extremely rapidly,” Tramèr says. In summer 2025 the researchers weren’t even sure AI could reproduce relatively simple attacks. Months later, the models were turning up weaknesses no one had spotted before. Anthropic has also reported that its Claude model found a substantially improved attack on HAWK, a proposed digital signature scheme designed to withstand quantum computers.
But there’s a huge gulf between finding weaknesses in experimental cryptography and breaking the systems that secure large parts of our digital lives. “Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes. The bigger concern is a shortcut that cracks an entire family of mathematical problems at once, and with it every system built on them.
Public-key cryptography secures the connection between your browser and the sites you visit, and it produces the digital signatures that certify a software update or a cryptocurrency transaction. Crack it, and attackers could pose as your bank or listen in on your messages. Anyone who has stockpiled encrypted traffic could go back and read it years after the senders assumed it was safe.
Even then, it wouldn’t necessarily signal disaster. Bart Preneel, a cryptography professor at the Catholic University of Leuven (KU Leuven) in Belgium, says the consequences would depend on the scale of any breakthrough. A modest mathematical advance might dent the protection offered by existing systems but not break it. Even making an attack a billion times faster might still leave it requiring more computing power than anyone could realistically muster, AI or no AI. “I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
Even a modest advance would necessitate a defense upgrade, and Green thinks that that could do damage of its own. “The upgrade process itself is going to be a bit of a catastrophe,” he says. “We screw up the upgrade, and we end up with something insecure accidentally.”
Eyal Ronen, a researcher at Tel Aviv University, who co-authored the cryptanalysis study, is, like Preneel, cautious. AI is already very good at finding software vulnerabilities, he says, which presents a much more immediate threat than the hypothetical disappearance of encryption. And any hacker is more likely to take the easier route, such as hacking someone’s computer to steal their encryption keys, than to try breaking the mathematics protecting them.
Efforts to prepare for quantum computers, another potential threat, are already forcing governments and companies to rethink their encryption. Boneh says those efforts could help if AI discovers something unexpected, although the two threats aren’t identical. HAWK, after all, was built for the quantum era, yet AI found a way to weaken it.
For now, Boneh wants something relatively straightforward from AI companies: greater transparency about what their models have tried and how often they’ve succeeded. Green agrees. “We’re getting no signal whatsoever,” he says. If the labs have pointed their models at the mathematical problems underpinning cryptography, saying so would help reassure the people responsible for securing the Internet. “Please tell us what you have discovered when you tried some cryptography questions,” Boneh says. Until someone does, nobody can say whether AI has exposed something fundamental about the mathematics we rely on—or whether it’s simply getting better at solving problems that were always solvable.

What was going on at Shanidar? Another Neanderthal reported with fatal wound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:10:04 UTC
00:10:04 KST

About 75,000 years ago, a Neanderthal was stabbed in the chest, almost certainly by somebody who meant it. He was about 45 when he died and was buried in Shanidar Cave in northern Iraq, and he wasn't even the first victim of possible hominin-on-hominin violence reported from Shanidar, he was the second.
Whether the implement of aggression against this Neanderthal, dubbed Shanidar A, was a sharpened wooden stick or a stone-tipped spear isn't clear. What can be said is that it slammed into his chest from the front, passed through a lung on a slightly upward trajectory and punched a round hole in his left shoulder blade, Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge and colleagues reported in Nature on Thursday.
Nor was it Shanidar A's first rodeo. He had previously suffered facial injuries so severe that one of his front teeth had shattered and part of it had fallen out of his mouth. That painful mangling had been healing for about a year before he took the blow to the chest that killed him, according to the team's deductions.
But was poor Shanidar A merely unfortunate – could he have been the victim of a hunting accident by some myopic peer who mistook him for a gazelle or rabbit, and threw a spear? Or was this murder most foul, and if so, by what species exactly?
The find somewhat weakens hypotheses about the benignity of hominin hunter-gatherers, who wouldn't need to engage in snarling conflict with their peers but could move away, and here we have two victims of mayhem in Shanidar, albeit at a vast distance in time.
The first was a Neanderthal male dubbed Shanidar 3 who also died in his 40s following a fatal injury to the ribs around 50,000 years ago. The theory was posited that Shanidar 3 was murdered by a modern human, Homo sapiens, throwing a stone-tipped spear.
The common thinking was that Neanderthals used spears to thrust, but but didn't throw projectiles. Pomeroy clarifies that is no longer the thinking. Now it is that Neanderthals could throw a mean wooden spear just as well as we could. So there's no reason, really, to pick on our species.
We add that Shanidar 3 wasn't in the pink of health when he died either – he had a degenerative disorder of the foot that must have made ambulation painful.
What have we so far? Two dead Neanderthals buried in the cave around 25,000 years apart, who both survived injuries and illnesses that strongly indicate they were cared for by their peers; yet both died violently at the hands of their peers, and while our species Homo sapiens and Neanderthals were apparently both running around in the region both 75,000 and 50,000 years ago (including in Israel!), there's no particular reason to think we did it.
Home not alone
Shanidar is famed for being a "Neanderthal cemetery," a term that Pomeroy explains is all wrong. But the new research shores up the impression that Neanderthals engaged in mortuary rituals.
Shanidar is famed for being a "Neanderthal cemetery," a term that that Pomeroy explains is all wrong. But the new research shores up the growing impression that Neanderthals engaged in mortuary rituals.
Neanderthals definitely buried at least some of their dead in the cave, in two main phases; at least five in one cluster between 75,000 to 70,000 years ago; and a different group with three bodies around 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. Shanidar A and Shanidar 3 belong to the older cluster.
Regarding Shanidar 4, a romantic "flower burial" theory proposed in 1975 by the archaeologist Ralph Solecki, sadly turned out to be inaccurate. High concentrations of fossil pollen identified around the skeleton were suggested as meaning the body had been laid to rest on a bed of flowers. Later work favored burrowing bees transporting clusters of pollen, burrowing rodents disrupting the archaeological layers, and pollen blowing in with the wind.
The Neanderthals in the cluster were placed over years, though not over that much time, with evidence of new ones being put in before the body beneath had fully decayed, Pomeroy explains. But the living also used the cave for other things, not just to visit the dead like we do in today's cemeteries, she explains. So it isn't a cemetery per se.
Note that burying the dead inside the home isn't as weird as one might think. We did it too. Around 10,000 to 9,000 years ago, modern humans in the Neolithic Levant and Turkey would bury their dead under the floor of the home. In any case the Neanderthals seem to have used the cave sporadically, not for constant occupation. Among other things, the cave is in the Zagros Mountains where it gets snowy in winter.
Anyway, sequential burial at one spot suggests they attached meaning to the site as opposed to obeying pure practicality, the team says.
Further evidence of mortuary practices in Neanderthals is reported at sites in Europe, such as La Ferrassie, Le Regourdou and others in France. In Krapina, Croatia, archaeologists detected Neanderthal cannibalism, which could have been due to starvation, or maybe those Neanderthals ritually ate their dead. Some people do. "Recent populations do it as a kind of dominance over others – maybe they did that too," Pomeroy posits.
Murder Og wrote
The bottom line is that the evidence of caring for each other (or eating each other) doesn't actually contradict the implied evidence of interpersonal loathing, Pomeroy points out. Don't we humans evince the same two-facedness, or at least changeability? We do.
The brutal facial injuries Shanidar A survived show that somebody cared for him, and the manner of his death suggests not everyone felt the love. His scapula was preserved whole but for that telltale 1.5-centimeter-wide exactly round hole in it.
That hole could have been made by exactly the sort of Neanderthal spears found in the swamps of Schöningen in Germany, from 200,000 years ago. (The spears had been initially assessed at about 400,000 years ago, then 300,000 and now are believed to be 200,000 years old).
We assume the Schöningen spears were used to hunt animals, of which plenty were found, notably megafauna in the form of horses. There are no smoking spears in Shanidar but the shape of the scapular lesion is indicative of sharpened wooden spear. If the spear had a stone tip, the lesion would have been shaped like a lozenge but it's "extremely round," Pomeroy explains.
The team also deduced that the hole in his scapula couldn't have been made by a tree root or burrowing insects. In addition, remarkably similar lesions have been observed in the fossil skeletons of animals, from giants to small ones, at prehistoric sites.
What have we? Evidence that the guy went down like a hunted deer, presumably gnashing his healed teeth.
It's true that physical trauma was common among prehistoric humans and hominins, who hunted dangerous animals and maybe each other too. That is a suggestion that archaeologists tend to resist. But here we are.
"Neanderthals lived a precarious life so we do find healed fractures and bangs on the head but severe injury to the face is quite unusual," Pomeroy points out in respect to Shanidar's A smashed mouth, which healed over about a year. That kind of oral injury was atypical.
Is there any reason to connect the posited violence against Shanidar A and 3? Not over a time span of 25,000 years. Maybe it was coincidence. Or, early human lives were more violent than we thought, she answers and notes the case reported by archaeologists in Israel in July: of an early Homo sapiens in Qafzeh Cave who was smashed in the face with a rock about 100,000 years ago but was cared for, and survived.
"I think we have to see the same complexity in Neanderthals that we see in people today. Some are violent, some care," Pomeroy sums up. "We have contrasting stereotypes about hunter-gatherers – one where they are at one with nature, the other that life was nasty, brutish and short. But the story is more complex than that." And in Shanidar, the preponderance of the evidence is that they had deeply mixed feelings about each other.

‘One Day at a Time’: Inside an IDP Camp in Myanmar, Survival Is a Daily Challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:08:00 UTC
00:08:00 KST

Sam Sam burst into tears when asked to narrate the circumstances that compelled her to become an internally displaced person (IDP). She pointed to clothes and utensils in her single-room thatched hut, the only things she could carry while fleeing her village. Then, she pulled out a tattered photograph from a bag.
“This was our home,” she said, pointing to the sprawling house in the photograph. “I never imagined that we would end up at a refugee camp someday.”
On February 6, 2024, the Myanmar military torched Kyar Ma Thout village in Sittwe township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. It has burned down several other settlements in the area in order to deprive the Arakan Army (AA) of a base in the city’s suburbs.
Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State and a military hub that houses the Regional Operations Command (ROC), is among three of 17 townships in the state that remain under the military’s control. By emptying its suburbs, the military is hoping to secure its control of the city and surrounding areas.
When Kyar Ma Thout was burnt by the military, most of its 650 residents, including Sam Sam, her husband, and two children, fled for safety in the areas under the control of the AA. About a third of the village’s residents, including a sizable number of elderly and disabled people, settled in monasteries in Sittwe city.
Sam Sam and ten other families from Kyar Ma Thout landed at the Old Kran Khun IDP Camp in Ponnagyun township about 80 kilometers to the north of Sittwe. The township was captured by the AA in mid-March of 2024 after weeks of fierce fighting with the military.
Their journey to the camp was perilous and involved travelling on the Kaladan River as well. With the arrival of IDPs from Sittwe, the camp’s population swelled to 1,643.
Old Kran Khun camp is one of 93 IDP camps scattered across AA-held areas. An estimated 100,000 people live in these camps, as per data compiled by the AA’s political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA). Another 100,000 are sheltering in monasteries and in the homes of their relatives. Those numbers could not be confirmed independently.
On February 8 this year, I visited the Old Kran Khun camp located 150 meters north of the highway between Ponnagyun and Kyauktaw. The mood there was heavy with sorrow and quiet desperation. There were around 400 huts in the camp. These were cramped and identical shelters built of straw, bamboo, and tarpaulin. The IDPs staying here are struggling to cope with myriad problems, including the loss of their traditional livelihoods, neighborhood networks, and support systems.
Riches to Rags
Maung Tin Hla is an affluent businessman from Ma Jay Mying (Ward No. 3) in Sittwe city. He owned five acres of land on the city’s outskirts, which was cultivated throughout the year and provided him with additional income.
Since the military’s offensives were directed at villages surrounding Sittwe, Ma Jay Mying had little reason to believe that the gun would be pointed at households like his own that were inside the city. But everything changed on March 16, 2024, when the military began targeting some localities and burning houses inside Sittwe.
Several people were arrested on suspicion of being AA functionaries. “We heard that the Arakan Liberation Party, which has joined hands with the military, had provided the military with information about some households. And I got the feeling that my name was also on the list,” Maung Tin Hla recalled.
On March 17, Maung Tin Hla began frenzied preparations to leave the village around midnight after a young man in his mid-20s was killed by the military near his residence. He hit the escape trail to the AA’s area of control with his wife and son and seven bags containing gold ornaments, money, clothes, and utensils.
After a grueling 90-km journey that lasted five days, the family reached the IDP camp in Ponnagyun township. Maung Tin Hla then purchased materials needed to build a thatched hut to shelter his family. He then arranged for food and water in the camp.
“I had around 1 million kyats (around U.S. $476), but this lasted just for a month. Then we began selling the gold ornaments. Almost half of the total amount I brought from home has been exhausted,” Maung Tin Hla said. “We can last for another year by selling whatever is left.”
Fishermen among the IDPs have been catching fish from the nearby Kaladan River and selling them for a livelihood. Others gather firewood, bamboo, and vegetables from the hills, which they consume themselves or sell in the camp and neighboring villages. But Maung Tin Hla is neither a fisherman nor is he adept at climbing the hills to gather food and firewood. His wife is busy all day with household chores and takes care of their 7-year-old son, who is enrolled in Grade 1 at a school about 2 km from the camp.
“So far, I have not been able to identify any source of income that will sustain my family,” Maung Tin Hla said. He is keeping his “fingers crossed and is hopeful of returning home soon.”
There are many like Maung Tin Hla in the Old Kran Khun camp, who have similar riches-to-rags stories to share. Their houses were either burnt by the military or destroyed by shelling. Forced to flee their villages, they are now sheltering in the IDP camp and are foraging forests and hills for food and firewood.
Hills Emerge as a Savior
The daily itinerary in the IDP camp is dictated by scarcity. Long before sunrise, residents begin preparations to search for food and livelihood. Many embark on an 8-km trek to the hills that lie to the west of the camp. They return by noon with whatever vegetables and firewood they could lay their hands on.
For Maung Aye Tun and his 14-year-old son, going to the hills has been a daily routine ever since they arrived at the camp from Mrit Nar village in Sittwe township two years ago, after it was burned by the military. “The hills are getting depleted owing to the unrestrained scavenging by camp inmates over the past three years,” he lamented.
“Now more effort is required to gather vegetables and firewood compared to the situation two years ago. We have to go deeper into the hills every day. And there is no certainty that the same quantity of food and firewood can be fetched daily,” Maung Aye Tun said. Alarmed over the rapid deforestation of the hills, the ULA imposed restrictions five months ago on logging.
The daily expenditure on food alone for Maung Aye Tun’s family of four, including his wife and two children, is around 60,000 kyats. But his daily income from selling vegetables and firewood sometimes does not exceed 10,000 kyats. Whatever is earned is mostly spent on buying foodgrains.
During the rainy season, which extends from April to September, the availability of food in the hills drops, and there is excess firewood in the camp but not enough buyers in the rest of the year. Almost every third hut in the camp has bundles of chopped logs placed at the entrance waiting to be sold.
Larger households are able to send some of their family members to markets in the neighboring villages, where the scope of selling commodities at a higher price is brighter. But there have been times when the markets remain shut for days on end after airstrikes or shelling in neighboring areas. This has eaten into the income and reduced food consumption for every household.
One Meal a Day
During my stay at the Old Kran Khun IDP camp, I came across three households for whom two square meals per day or being able to add vegetables to rice was a luxury.
Oo Tin Nyunt (75) is a widow without children, who was displaced from Kran Daw village in Sittwe township when it was bulldozed and then torched by the military in August 2025. She reached the IDP camp with the assistance of her neighbors who were also headed to the same camp. Except for 80,000 kyats, Oo Tin Nyunt had nothing else that could have helped sustain her in the camp. She survived on donations from two NGOs and the ULA till the end of last year.
She is currently dependent on assistance from other households in the camp. She is too frail to gather food from the hills. Neither can she work as a daily wager.
When I asked her about her plans, Oo Tin Nyunt stared for a few seconds and then, with a smile, said: “It’s one day at a time for me. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow.”
The uncertainty looming over the IDP camps is also due to the reduced supply of foodgrains by NGOs and the ULA.
“There are more than 50 NGOs that offered assistance to the IDP camps in the liberated zone. But support has never matched the requirements. Funding from global organizations has decreased drastically over the past year owing to many factors, including the crackdown on the networks that remitted funds,” said Hla Nwe, an official with the Humanitarian and Development Coordination Office (HDCO) under the ULA.
Wong Myint, who heads an NGO, confirmed that funding from global organizations has diminished substantially.
The difficult situation has prompted some camp inmates hailing from Ponnagyun township to return to their fields for cultivation.
Owing to continuous shelling by the military, Nyein Nyein Tun and her family of five were forced to leave Kyay Thoe village in late 2024. Her husband could not work as a daily wager or trek to the hills for firewood and vegetables as he was injured from the shelling.
For almost the whole of last year, the family subsisted on one meal a day and was entirely dependent on assistance from other organizations. Last year, after recovering from his injury, Nyein Nyein Tun’s husband decided to follow others from Ponnagyun township who had returned to cultivating foodgrains in their fields. This required him to live in the fields about 50 km north of the camp for two months, and to return again for the harvest five months later.
However, the harvest last year was not very encouraging for these farmers, Nyein Nyein Tun said. “We are hopeful of a better situation this year if the selling price of foodgrains does not drop sharply. And then we can afford two meals every day.”
Struggle for Water
All the IDP camps in Ponnagyun township suffer from a shortage of water. The groundwater level in the township is lower than in the adjoining regions. Water levels in the wells dug in the camp and the two ponds nearby fall sharply during the winter months.
According to a ULA functionary, water in the area around the camp is available at a depth of 600 feet. To dig functional wells, mechanical equipment is needed, but this is not easily available.
Between December and April each year, every household in the camp has to fetch water from the Kaladan River, located 500 meters away. This is difficult for the elderly, especially those who do not have younger relatives to assist them. Therefore, they must manage with small amounts of water every day.
Last year, with the assistance of the ULA, an NGO installed five large-sized water storage tanks at the camp. Previously, trucks were used to ferry water from the river, but their services came to a halt early this year when funds from global organizations shrank.
In addition to the water shortage, IDP camps have to make do with water that has a tinge of turbidity, whether it is from the river or from wells and water bodies. NGO activists claimed that facilities for filtration of water have been provided in a few IDP camps, but the demand is far too high. More funds and equipment are needed to cover more camps.
Myo Aung, who recovered five months ago from skin ailments due to contaminated water, said that while some households boil the water for drinking, “many do not.” “Water is the source of most diseases in the camp,” he said. Besides skin diseases, inmates suffer from diarrhea and malaria during the rainy season. There were two deaths in the camp due to illnesses over the past three years.
A doctor at a health unit run by the ULA in a village about a kilometer from the IDP camp diagnoses patients and prescribes medicines. But medicines are not always readily available as they are imported from different sources, including India and Bangladesh.
An Exception With the Handloom
The battle for survival in the IDP camps has prompted some residents to devise ingenious means to earn a steady income. Ma Mya Oo journeyed from her home in Padetha village in Ponnagyun township with her family of six members sometime in the middle of last year. The village was evacuated after it was shelled, resulting in the death of one and injuries to four others.
Ma Mya Oo was an established weaver of traditional shawls and skirts, which she sold at shops in Ponnagyun and Kyauktaw. During the relocation from her village located 60 km east of the camp, the family could carry only necessities, like clothes and utensils. The raw materials for her handloom products were left behind in the village. Thankfully, these were not destroyed in the shelling.
“Three months after arriving in the camp, I decided to install the loom at our hut in the camp. This was necessary for additional income as my husband’s earnings as a daily wager were erratic,” Ma Mya Oo said. She then made two trips to her village and transported the materials for the handloom back to the camp. “Only the foot pedals for the loom had to be chiseled from wood in the camp,” she said.
The work soon began, and the first shawl woven in the IDP camp rolled out in November last year. Five more followed in the next couple of months. “This is much less than what was produced at home,” Ma Mya Oo said. Besides, the quality of the shawls fell, as did their price.
Subsequently, Ma Mya Oo helped another woman from Kyaukhyu, who was also a weaver, install a handloom in the camp. However, since not all the materials were easily available, production proved challenging.
Similar to Ma Mya Oo’s case was that of an artisan from Sittwe, who carves figurines out of materials like wood. Small pieces of chopped logs were stacked outside his thatched hut in the camp. He had finished carving three figurines depicting a boat and elephants.
A Third of All Children Have Opted Out of School
Anxiety and sorrow are writ large among the inmates in the Kyar Ma Thout camp over an uncertain future. This is most discernible among the parents of children who do not go to school. They would like their children to study, but difficult circumstances force parents to send children to work. Around a fourth of all inmates in the camp are children, and one-third of them have opted out of school.
As I strolled around the camp, I met some teenagers engaged in fetching water, slicing logs, and selling vegetables and firewood. Many of these youngsters belong to smaller households with fewer members, where their contribution to family income is vital.
Instead of being in classrooms, their daily curriculum is shaped by the exigencies of survival in a hostile environment. As a middle-aged father of a 15-year-old hailing from Sittwe said, “We cannot afford to send our son to school. That could change only with better sources of livelihood.”
The ULA has slashed the fees in schools it runs to enable impoverished parents to educate their children. Last year, several NGOs worked on persuading parents to send their children, but the results were hardly encouraging. Only four families reportedly agreed to admit their children to a school; the rest remained unconvinced.
Besides financial reasons, at least 20 children have dropped out of school for fear of airstrikes. They are mostly from villages in Ponnagyun and Sittwe townships that were devastated by airstrikes and shelling. The trauma of being nearly killed and uprooted from their homes is deeply etched in their memories. It has impacted many facets of the lives of children.
Sitting Ducks for Airstrikes
On October 4-5 this year, at least eight IDPs were killed and 13 others injured during airstrikes on two separate IDP camps in Ponnagyun Township. There have been several such military’s attacks on IDP camps in the region. The ULA has claimed that 16 IDPs were killed and more than 40 injured over the last couple of years across Rakhine in aerial attacks before the recent airstrikes in Ponnagyun. The figures could not be independently verified.
Many IDPs in the region, therefore, suffer from trauma and phobia about aerial attacks. Khin Maung, who was displaced from Che Lay Than village in Sittwe in the middle of last year, said that such fears among IDPs have been compounded by the lack of trenches in the camp. “The fear is so high that some IDPs rush out of their huts with their children whenever a rumble is heard,” he said. He recalled a “stampede-like situation” at the camp on the evening of January 19 when the sound of fighter jets was heard. Fearing that the IDP camp would be targeted, people rushed out of the camp and stayed outside for the whole night.
There is no space to dig trenches in the Old Kran Khun camp. I saw only three small trenches in the entire camp in the narrow spaces between the thatched huts. Usually, children are made to take cover in them whenever there is apprehension of aerial attacks. Two families had dug trenches inside their huts, and these were covered with wooden planks.
Many dwellings in the camp have long bamboo poles with hooks that are attached to the huts. I was told that in the event of an airstrike, these poles would be quickly used to pull down a burning chunk of thatch to prevent the whole hut from being incinerated.
Last year, the Old Kran Khun camp committee proposed to dig trenches in the vicinity of the settlement. However, accommodating 1,643 people required a large number of trenches. Digging them would involve a huge amount of time and labor. Consequently, the proposal has remained unimplemented so far.
As Sam Sam noted, “Survival in an IDP camp hinges on luck ultimately. Many things have to work out correctly all the time for the inmates to survive.”

Many were surprised by the announcement that the execution would be broadcast live. It is known that no other country broadcasts judicial executions on television or live.

Yemeni rights network says Houthis killed 7 civilians, detained 26 in Taiz over 2 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:06:58 UTC
00:06:58 KST

Mohammed Sameai, Ikram Kouachi
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
 A Yemeni human rights group said Thursday that Houthi fire killed seven civilians and the group detained 26 others in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen during a 48-hour period.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms, a nongovernmental organization, said in a report that it documented “219 crimes and violations committed by the Houthis” in Taiz in the last 48 hours.
It said the violations included killings, injuries, abductions, enforced disappearances, raids and searches of homes, looting, indiscriminate shelling of residential neighborhoods and a tightening of the siege on the city.
The group said its field team documented the deaths of seven civilians and injuries to nine others of varying severity in incidents involving shelling of homes, a landmine explosion and a civilian being run over by a Houthi military vehicle.
It added that “the Houthi militias raided, searched and looted more than 130 homes” in the areas of Al-Turbah, Al-Shamayatayn and Jabal Habashi in Taiz province.
The Houthis also abducted and forcibly disappeared 26 people, including children, the elderly and sick individuals, and transferred them to the provinces of Ibb and Dhamar, it said.
The network said the Houthis fired around 377 projectiles at Taiz city, damaging 29 homes and 18 privately owned vehicles, with some sustaining partial damage and others being destroyed.
Yemeni human rights and humanitarian organizations said the Houthis have closed most roads leading to areas under government control in Taiz province.
The organizations accuse the Houthis of besieging Taiz city since 2015 and preventing relief convoys from reaching residents and those affected by the war. The Houthis deny the allegations.
The fighting comes amid the Dawn of Yemen military operation launched by Yemen’s internationally recognized government earlier this month to retake Houthi-held areas, including the national capital, Sanaa.
The offensive, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, has intensified fighting on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, where government forces and the Houthis have battled for control of strategic positions and supply routes.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognized government from the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in support of the government in 2015.

Jaguar Trafficking in Latin America Persists Through Bone Paste and Pet Smuggling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

Reported by
Skins in markets, fangs turned into jewelry, and bones processed into paste: the illegal trade in jaguars persists in Latin America. An investigation spanning seven countries points to a primarily local, small-scale business, with evidence of international trafficking in Peru and Suriname.
Between 2023 and 2025, the Wildlife Justice Commission (WJC) investigated the trade of these big cats in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Panama, Peru, and Suriname. Its findings—shared with OCCRP—describe a market that often relies on sporadic sales opportunities, though the investigation also identified a network trafficking multiple species.
The latest WJC report "The Illegal Jaguar Trade in Latin America: An Updated Picture," published Thursday, found that a significant portion of the demand stems from local buyers, including members of Asian communities residing in the region. These results add nuance to alarms raised in the early 2010s regarding a new international market for jaguar parts targeting China, while not ruling out the continued existence of those connections.
Wildlife Justice Commission Executive Director Olivia Swaak-Goldman told OCCRP that the investigation identified two main types of trade: a local market for handicrafts and jaguar parts, observed in Colombia and Bolivia, and a higher-priced market linked to international demand, including for jaguar bone paste, observed in Suriname.
There, operatives identified suppliers of jaguar bone paste and retailers selling jewelry made from jaguar fangs in the capital, Paramaribo.
Swaak-Goldman said Suriname remained a high-risk country because of its proximity to large jaguar populations and porous borders that facilitate smuggling with neighboring countries, including Brazil and Guyana. She also pointed to demand from certain foreign nationals and the difficulties local authorities face in detecting international trafficking networks.
“Even so, the trade we observed was relatively low-volume and discreet. What made Suriname particularly important was the evidence of links between local wildlife products and international demand.”
The founder of Probios—an environmental organization based in Paramaribo—Erlan Sleur, also described the production of jaguar bone paste. “They make a black paste from it that is sold at an exorbitant price in China,” Sleur confirmed to OCCRP.
Sleur has raised awareness regarding the illegal hunting of jaguars in Suriname’s forested interior—animals targeted for years for use in Asian medicine and luxury goods. When OCCRP visited Sleur in Paramaribo in 2022, he displayed a cage he planned to use to capture jaguars that had accidentally wandered into agricultural fields, hoping to save them from poachers. “Those jaguars—those animals are simply shot,” he said.
According to the WJC report, transactions appeared infrequent, were carried out on demand, and provided supplementary income for the sellers. Records compiled by the organization included the seizure of at least 29 fangs and 16 kilograms of jaguar bone paste in Suriname between 2019 and 2025. At least four suspects were arrested, with two receiving prison sentences.
In Peru, the WJC identified a network of Peruvian citizens and individuals of Chinese origin operating between Lima and Iquitos. Its members offered jaguar parts and trafficked in other wildlife and marine species.
In Bolivia, investigators found vendors selling small quantities of skins, paws, claws, fangs, and handicrafts in La Paz, Santa Cruz, and Trinidad. “Temporary Chinese migrants working as independent contractors on large infrastructure projects are present in some sectors of the illegal trade in Bolivia. Specifically in Trinidad, some local traders stated that there were now fewer buyers of jaguar products, and [noted] that prices had dropped since the completion of a major road construction project, as foreign workers had moved to projects underway in other areas,” the report details.
The WJC found indications that law enforcement pressure had pushed some traders to operate more covertly or abandon the business entirely. However, it also noted gaps in information regarding subsequent judicial proceedings, the demand for live animals, and the ultimate destination of the products in Asia.
Meanwhile, a supplementary review of seizures between 2019 and 2025 revealed a dynamic that field investigations had barely captured: live jaguars were the most frequently seized category, accounting for 38 percent of the records. The majority of these seizures took place in Mexico.
Swaak-Goldman described Mexico as both a source and a destination market for the illegal pet trade in jaguars. She noted that jaguars are harder to breed in captivity than other big cats, such as tigers, and that their rarity makes them prestige animals in that market.
“So we know there is a signal in the seizure data, but we still need to understand how this market operates and what is driving the demand.”
For Swaak-Goldman, the findings offer grounds for cautious optimism.
“The report is not a reason for complacency, but it does provide an encouraging lesson: sustained, targeted enforcement can change the behaviour of traffickers and make an illegal market harder and less profitable to operate.”

IEA to expedite 100M-barrel oil release as supply concerns persist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:03:12 UTC
00:03:12 KST

International Energy Agency (IEA) members have agreed to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as soon as possible amid continued tightness in global energy markets.
The agency's Governing Board said on Thursday its latest assessments pointed to persistent tightness in oil markets, particularly diesel, following a meeting on energy markets and security.
Approximately 330 million barrels have already been released under the collective action launched in March in response to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
Total releases will exceed the original commitment of 400 million barrels, as some members have released more than initially pledged and others intend to do so, the board said.
Members agreed to take all necessary steps to complete the remaining releases promptly, consistent with national circumstances, with specific acceleration plans already in place.
The board also encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supplies of crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and emphasised the importance of the free flow of energy trade.
Reaffirming their commitment to international energy security, members expressed willingness to take further action to address global energy market challenges, building on the G7 statement of October 2.
The IEA Secretariat will monitor progress and inform G7 leaders and the Governing Board of further action needed, drawing on an updated oil market assessment focused on diesel.

Veterans organisations have been specifically invited to respond to a government consultation on reforming fireworks legislation, which ministers say has prompted ongoing engagement across departments, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Susan Murray, the Liberal Democrat member for Mid Dunbartonshire, asked what discussions had taken place with the Business Secretary on the impact of the proposals on veterans living with post-traumatic stress disorder, referring to the consultation on fireworks and pyrotechnics published on 16 July.

Campaigners including veterans’ charities have pressed for tighter noise limits and for sales to be restricted to organised displays, arguing that unannounced explosions through October and November are the problem for people with post-traumatic stress disorder.
Op COURAGE was launched by NHS England in 2021, bringing three separate veteran mental health services into a single referral pathway covering assessment, treatment for complex cases and support with housing, employment and substance misuse.

More than two hundred Ajax vehicles now accepted
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:00:14 BST
00:00:14 KST

The Ministry of Defence had accepted 227 Ajax Capability Drop 3 vehicles as of 15 September, including 41 taken on since 17 April, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the overall total of each variant now held, mapped against the current production schedule, following an answer of 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, gave the headline figure but declined the breakdown. “The Department does not routinely disclose fleet holdings by variant, nor provide variant-level delivery information against production schedules,” he said. “Such information is directly linked to military readiness and operational capability, and its disclosure could prejudice operational effectiveness by enabling assessments to be made about the availability, preparedness and deployment of capability.”
He added: “The Ajax programme remains on track to deliver all 589 vehicles as contracted.”
Forty one vehicles accepted in five months gives a run rate of roughly eight a month. At that pace the remaining 362 vehicles would take around three and a half years, though the answer gives no delivery profile and no completion date.
Ajax is a family of tracked armoured vehicles built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK, with hulls from Spain and final assembly at Merthyr Tydfil. The reconnaissance variant carries a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon, and the family covers six variants in all. The programme was contracted for 589 vehicles at a firm price of £5.5 billion, and trials were suspended for a period after crews reported hearing damage and joint injuries linked to noise and vibration.

A telling hole in a Neandertal bone hints at a bitter end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A telling hole in a Neandertal bone hints at a bitter end
But a shattered tooth suggests a more nuanced tale of life
A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.
The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.
These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.
Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.
During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.
At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.
The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.
Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.
The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.
The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.
The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.
“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

The Gulf needs a security order that Washington cannot switch off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:58:44 UTC
23:58:44 KST

The Gulf has spent decades buying security from the world’s most powerful military. American bases dot the region, advanced weapons fill its arsenals, and defence agreements bind its rulers to Washington. Yet the war involving Iran has exposed a troubling paradox. The Gulf’s security arrangements may help deter adversaries, but they cannot guarantee that the region will escape a conflict shaped by decisions made elsewhere.
The consequences are no longer confined to military installations or oil terminals. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz threatens energy exports and maritime commerce, while attacks on critical infrastructure jeopardise the economic transformation programmes on which Gulf governments have staked their futures. Wealth can finance reconstruction, but it cannot restore lost confidence overnight.
The problem is not that the United States has become irrelevant. Its intelligence, airpower, naval capabilities and logistical reach remain difficult to replace. Nor does greater independence mean that Iran’s regional ambitions should be ignored. Rather, the Gulf faces a structural dilemma: the states most exposed to escalation do not necessarily possess the greatest influence over the decisions that produce it.
That dilemma demands a different ambition.
The Gulf does not need a security order without Washington. It needs one that can survive Washington’s changing priorities. The objective should be to turn external protection into one pillar of regional security, rather than the foundation on which everything else depends.
The limits of an American security umbrella
For decades, American military power has underwritten the security of the Gulf monarchies. The US Fifth Fleet operates from Bahrain, while Qatar hosts Al Udeid Air Base, a major centre for American air operations. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have invested heavily in American aircraft, missile defence and other advanced systems. These arrangements provide capabilities that would be costly and difficult to reproduce independently.
But military protection is not the same as strategic control. Washington ultimately decides how to deploy its forces, which threats deserve priority and when military action serves American interests. Gulf governments can influence these calculations through diplomacy and cooperation, but they cannot assume that their preferences will prevail.
The distinction becomes critical when Washington’s objectives collide with the region’s exposure to retaliation. An American operation may be designed to weaken an adversary or restore deterrence, yet its consequences can fall disproportionately on neighbouring states whose ports, airports, energy facilities and shipping routes become vulnerable. The presence of American forces can strengthen deterrence without eliminating the risks associated with escalation.
Recent events have also exposed the limits of military expenditure as a measure of security.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Saudi Arabia spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the Middle East’s largest military spender. Nevertheless, sophisticated arsenals cannot automatically prevent attacks by adversaries using drones, missiles and other asymmetric capabilities.
The lesson is not that American protection has failed or that Gulf governments should abandon their alliances. It is that a security model built around external military superiority leaves too much dependent on decisions that regional governments cannot control. A durable system must preserve the benefits of American power while reducing the consequences of its possible absence, inconsistency or strategic redirection.
READ: Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
Why the Gulf cannot secure itself alone
Reducing dependence on Washington, however, is easier said than done. The Gulf Cooperation Council has existed since 1981, yet its members have struggled to translate shared vulnerabilities into a fully integrated security system. They differ in their perceptions of Iran, their relationships with outside powers and their preferred responses to regional crises. Their rulers also remain reluctant to surrender sovereign authority over national defence.
These divisions matter more than the number of weapons purchased. A regional security order requires compatible warning systems, reliable intelligence-sharing, coordinated responses and clear procedures for consultation when a crisis erupts. Without these mechanisms, neighbouring states may possess formidable individual capabilities while remaining collectively vulnerable.
Nor would replacing American dependence with a collection of new foreign partnerships solve the problem. Saudi Arabia’s expanding defence relationship with Pakistan and Turkey illustrates the search for additional strategic options.
Their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement promises closer military cooperation, including coordination among their armed forces. Such arrangements can broaden the Gulf’s choices, but their value will ultimately depend on operational coordination, credible commitments and the ability to respond effectively under pressure.
The danger is that diversification becomes an exercise in accumulating partners rather than building regional capacity. Multiple alliances can offer useful insurance, but they can also create competing expectations and overlapping commitments. A state that depends on several external powers without developing its own mechanisms for crisis management may remain exposed to the same underlying problem.
Iran must also be part of the equation. No credible Gulf security order can simply assume away Tehran’s military capabilities, its regional relationships or its ability to threaten maritime commerce. Yet treating Iran exclusively as a target to be deterred leaves little room for managing incidents before they become wars. Deterrence and diplomacy are not alternatives; each is more effective when the other exists.
The challenge, therefore, is political as much as military. Gulf governments must recognise that national security cannot be secured through bilateral relationships alone when threats cross borders and the consequences of conflict spread across the entire region.
Building an order Washington cannot switch off
A more resilient security order should begin with practical cooperation rather than grand declarations. The GCC needs stronger mechanisms for sharing intelligence, coordinating early warning and integrating air and missile defence. Common operating procedures would help governments identify threats, distinguish deliberate attacks from accidents and coordinate responses before confusion escalates into confrontation.
Second, the region needs institutionalised crisis diplomacy. Direct communication channels, maritime incident protocols and regular consultations involving Gulf states and Iran could reduce the danger of miscalculation. Such arrangements would not resolve every dispute or eliminate the need for deterrence. Their purpose would be narrower but essential: to prevent individual incidents from triggering a regional conflict that no government can easily contain.
Third, economic resilience must become part of security planning. The International Monetary Fund has highlighted the potential benefits of completing the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects, which could reduce economic losses during a closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative energy routes, diversified shipping arrangements and stronger regional logistics would likewise give governments more options when maritime traffic is disrupted. Infrastructure should be assessed not only by its commercial return, but also by the strategic flexibility it provides.
Finally, Gulf governments must define more clearly what collective security means in practice. Which threats require immediate consultation? How should members coordinate assistance after an attack? What commitments can each state credibly make, and how can those commitments be implemented without undermining national sovereignty? Answering these questions will be more valuable than announcing another ambitious pact whose operational foundations remain uncertain.
None of this requires the United States to withdraw. Washington can remain an indispensable partner, providing capabilities that regional states cannot quickly replicate. But a stronger regional framework would also make that partnership more sustainable by giving Gulf governments greater agency, reducing the risk of unilateral escalation and ensuring that essential security functions do not depend entirely on decisions made abroad.
The ultimate test of Gulf power is not how much its governments spend on weapons or how many foreign partners they can attract. It is whether they can shape the conditions under which their people, economies and infrastructure remain secure.
The Gulf cannot dictate Washington’s choices, any more than it can eliminate rivalry with Iran. It can, however, build institutions, capabilities and diplomatic channels that make those choices less decisive for its future. That is the difference between being protected by a powerful ally and possessing a security order of its own.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:54:16 UTC
23:54:16 KST

Israel has continued to close the Rafah land crossing for a second week, preventing patients from leaving the Gaza Strip for treatment abroad and causing a “dangerous buildup” of critical cases, the Gaza Health Ministry said Thursday.
In a statement, the ministry warned that the continued closure had led to a “dangerous and rapidly growing accumulation of critical cases,” with waiting lists for treatment abroad increasing by the day.
It said the number of people awaiting evacuation far exceeds the capacity of Gaza’s deteriorating and besieged hospitals to accommodate them or provide even the minimum level of treatment.
The ministry described the continued closure as a “grave violation of international humanitarian law and a deliberate deprivation of patients and wounded people of their right to treatment.”
It called on relevant parties to “exert serious and urgent pressure on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing and all other crossings and facilitate the departure of critically ill patients for treatment abroad.”
The continued closure comes as more than 20,000 patients and wounded people in Gaza await evacuation for treatment abroad, amid severe shortages of medicines, medical equipment, and specialized medical services following Israel’s destruction of the healthcare system during its genocidal war on the enclave.
More than 1,344 patients have died while waiting for treatment since the ceasefire agreement took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
On Feb. 2, 2026, Israel reopened the crossing on a limited basis, allowing small numbers of patients and wounded people to leave under tight restrictions.
READ: Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
According to Health Ministry statistics, a total of 2,480 patients and wounded people left Gaza through the crossing between Feb. 2 and Sept. 2.
This amounts to an average of about 12 patients and wounded people per day, compared with the agreed arrangement of 50 patients and 50 companions daily.
According to Health Ministry figures from October 2025, Israel’s war destroyed or rendered inoperable 25 of Gaza’s 38 hospitals, leaving 13 operating partially under difficult conditions.
The Israeli army also destroyed 103 of the enclave’s 157 primary healthcare centers during the genocide, while the remaining 54 continued to operate partially.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire had killed 1,501 Palestinians and injured 5,323 others as of Monday, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocide, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
