‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:22:13 UTC
23:22:13 KST

‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Experts say Albania’s protests reflect ignored student grievances and growing frustration.
Student protests against poor conditions in Albania’s education system have continued for a third day in the capital, Tirana, as Prime Minister Edi Rama insists he will not resign.
Demonstrators have called on Rama to quit in often violent protests since Tuesday. They have set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
Dozens of police officers and protesters have been injured amid attempts to disperse the crowds using water cannon and tear gas.
“What you are seeing is the boiling point of months of suppressed grievances,” Albanian journalist Arlis Alikaj told Al Jazeera.
Students have complained for months about the high cost of education and their limited employment prospects after graduation.
Afrim Krasniqi, a professor and researcher at the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana, told Al Jazeera that students and young people protested peacefully for nearly three months, “yet their demands were largely ignored, while the government often responded with discrediting campaigns rather than genuine dialogue”.
He added that the current escalation reflects “frustration not only with the government itself, but also with the lack of institutional accountability and responsiveness.”
The protests represent one of the most serious waves of public discontent directed at Rama, who won a fourth term last May but has since faced public anger over corruption allegations involving senior officials.
The unrest in Tirana coincides with a broader wave of student protests across Europe. In France, secondary school students have spent weeks protesting and blockading schools, demanding more teachers and better learning facilities. They have warned that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining the quality of education.
Protests against Rama’s government began a few months ago, fuelled by plans to build a luxury resort along Albania’s largely unspoilt southern coast. Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son in law, is involved in the project.
Local media reported that the protests spread from Tirana to universities in Elbasan and Shkoder on Wednesday.
Albania is among the economies of the Western Balkans seeking to catch up with European living standards. However, the gap with the European Union average remains evident in purchasing power, wages, productivity and the quality of public services. Despite economic progress, the country continues to face challenges including emigration, regional inequalities and the need for stronger institutions and the rule of law.
After Montenegro, Albania stands out as one of the countries that has made the most progress towards full EU membership. However, behind the optimistic political rhetoric, frustration is growing among citizens over the slow pace of European integration and the lack of tangible improvements in their daily lives.
While opposition groups seek to support the demonstrators and capitalise on the moment to strengthen their own position, Alikaj said the protests are being driven by young people and students demanding systemic change.
On Thursday, Rama – who has been PM since 2013 – told Reuters, “As for calls for my resignation, governments change through democratic elections. Last year, we had elections, not a revolution.”
Sokol Lleshi, a lecturer at the University of New York Tirana specialising in political science, said social change is more likely to emerge from a broader coalition of different social groups, rather than mass mobilisation limited to university and secondary school students.
“Elite defection from the current ruling political elite could enable the institutional means to channel societal dissatisfaction or resentment into political and policy changes. Yet, the current student protest does not seem to replicate the December 2018 mass movement of university students and its effects”, Lleshi said.
The student protests that shook Albania in December 2018 began over rising education costs and forced Rama to dismiss eight ministers as part of a cabinet reshuffle and announce a package of measures known as the “Pact for the University”.
But some of the students’ demands remained unmet.
Lleshi drew some more positive conclusions from Albania’s past experience of social unrest.
Albanian society is polarised and unequal, “with hollowed intermediary political institutions”, he said, but the legacy of unrest and political confrontation will serve as a “warning to avoid destabilisation”, he said.

====================================================================================================

Johns Hopkins lab gets up to $500M for DARPA research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:22:04 UTC
23:22:04 KST

- DARPA awarded Johns Hopkins APL a sole-source contract worth up to $499.8 million for engineering, development and research work through October 2031.
- The award continues a DARPA-APL arrangement that began with a $225 million contract in 2021 and later grew to about $1.1 billion.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s advanced research arm, has awarded the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory a contract worth up to $499.8 million to keep the lab working on DARPA engineering, development and research projects through October 2031.
The U.S. Department of War announced the award on Oct. 14. Under the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, DARPA will place individual task orders with the Laurel, Maryland, laboratory as work is needed, paying costs plus a fixed fee, up to the $499.8 million ceiling. No money was obligated at signing, and the minimum guaranteed amount will be funded with the first task order.
The contract covers what the Pentagon describes as an essential capability for engineering and developmental work that puts scientific and technical findings into practical use. DARPA awarded it on a sole-source basis, without a competition, which is standard for work assigned to a university affiliated research center.
APL is one of the Pentagon’s university affiliated research centers, a small group of nonprofit laboratories tied to universities that the U.S. Department of War keeps on long-term contracts for engineering work it considers too important to compete for each time. Based in Laurel, between Washington and Baltimore, the lab works for several defense customers, including the U.S. Navy, which holds a separate APL contract for fiscal 2023 through 2032 with a potential value of up to $10.6 billion.
The new award continues a long-running arrangement between DARPA and APL. DARPA gave the lab a $225 million sole-source contract in November 2021 for the same kind of engineering and development support, then raised its value to $740 million with a $515 million modification in May 2024. A later $388.8 million modification lifted the total to about $1.1 billion, with task orders running into November 2027, ExecutiveGov reported.
Under the earlier contract, DARPA issued task orders for support services on programs it often identifies only by code names. Two such orders placed in April 2026, labeled Ibiza and Bratislava, were worth about $6.1 million and $5.3 million, according to federal contracting data.
DARPA runs research programs across areas ranging from hypersonics and space to biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and relies on outside laboratories such as APL for engineering analysis, prototyping and technical support as those projects move from research toward practical systems.
Work under the new contract will be performed primarily in Laurel, and DARPA can place orders under it until October 2031.

====================================================================================================

Israel ended Iran war with more interceptors than it started with, Rafael CEO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:21:16 UTC
23:21:16 KST

WASHINGTON - Rafael Advanced Defense Systems emerged from Israel’s recent wars with Iran with more Tamir interceptors in stock than it had when the fighting began, despite thousands of interceptors being fired to defend the country against missiles, rockets, and drones, according to CEO Yoav Tourgeman.
"We ended the war with more Tamir interceptors than before," Tourgeman told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post in an exclusive interview at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, DC.
For decades, air-defense development focused primarily on improving the performance of individual systems with greater range, better accuracy, and higher interception rates. But recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed a significant challenge where even the most advanced interceptor is of limited value if a defending country cannot produce enough of them to sustain operations through a prolonged campaign.
For Rafael, the Israeli defense company behind the famous Iron Dome and David’s Sling, industrial capacity is becoming inseparable from operational effectiveness.
The challenge is building an architecture that can handle them all, including simultaneous attacks designed to overwhelm defenses through sheer volume. The company’s answer is a layered approach to air defense, matching different systems to different threats, from inexpensive drones and rockets to ballistic missiles and emerging hypersonic weapons.
No single interceptor can economically or effectively address every threat, Tourgeman argued, adding that “we are building the right solution for the right threat.”
The Israeli company's combat credentials remain central to that argument. According to Tourgeman, Iron Dome and David's Sling have intercepted more than 11,000 threats together since becoming operational.
“There would have been a lot more blood in the streets without the Iron Dome,” he said. “These systems have proven themselves in situations we once thought impossible.”
1,000 interceptors a year
But intercepting incoming weapons is only part of the equation. Replenishing inventories during a sustained conflict requires manufacturing capacity, reliable supply chains, skilled workers, and the ability to expand output without compromising quality.
That has been driving Rafael’s international expansion across 48 different countries, and with governments increasingly looking not only for advanced technology but also for confidence that suppliers can deliver when demand surges, Rafael has subsidiaries worldwide.
Rafael has also increased automation across its manufacturing operations and is expanding production partnerships overseas. Its new facility in Arkansas is expected to have the capacity to produce roughly 1,000 interceptors annually for both the United States and Israel. It will also provide a US-based manufacturing source as Washington and its allies seek to rebuild munitions stockpiles and strengthen domestic defense production.
Tourgeman also told D&T that Rafael is willing to transfer intellectual property and deepen cooperation with American industry. And for end-users, that appeal extends beyond delivery timelines because domestic production can reduce dependence on overseas supply chains and give governments greater control over critical defense capabilities during a crisis.
As European governments confront a more threatening security environment and the prospect of sustained high-intensity warfare, the continent is another major market. Germany, in particular, has been rebuilding its long-term air and missile-defense requirements.
In September, the German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, and Aurelius Capital signed a letter of intent to purchase Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, allowing the Israeli defense company to establish the production of Iron Dome components in Germany.
That, Tourgeman confirmed, was the first step towards Berlin acquiring the Iron Dome.
“What we’re doing in Germany is bringing confidence and safety to the population,” he said.
He also suggested that civilian industrial sectors, particularly automotive manufacturing, could play a larger role in defense production. Car plants already possess expertise in high-volume manufacturing, quality control, and supply-chain management, which could help governments rapidly scale weapons production during periods of crisis.
Staying ahead of the next generation of threats
Beyond today's missile threats, Rafael is preparing for the next generation of challenges.
At AUSA the company showcased a full-size model of Sky Sonic, its interceptor designed to counter hypersonic missiles. The interceptor was first announced over three years and Tourgeman dismissed the idea that hypersonic weapons represent an entirely new category of threat, arguing that many of the technologies needed to defeat advanced missiles already exist within Rafael's portfolio.
More pressing, he suggested, is the rise of coordinated attacks involving large numbers of inexpensive drones operating alongside traditional missiles.
Such attacks can expose critical infrastructure and create a difficult economic and operational problem for defenders, and the West has already seen how using costly interceptors against cheap drones can quickly strain inventories.
Countering the threat will require systems that can coordinate sensors, weapons, and decision-making across a network rather than operate as isolated platforms.
At AUSA, the company showcased solutions designed to operate within networked defense architectures and is advancing concepts such as Hunter Eagle, which Tourgeman described as a platform capable of functioning within a mesh network against drone swarms, both offensively and defensively.
That approach reflects a broader change in the economics of air warfare. The side launching an attack can increasingly draw on large numbers of relatively cheap, expendable weapons. The defender, meanwhile, must preserve enough interceptors and other capabilities to protect cities, military assets, and critical infrastructure over days, weeks, or longer.
For Rafael, the next contest in air defense will therefore be measured not only by interception rates or technological sophistication, but also by production lines, supply chains, and the ability to replenish stocks while fighting continues.
In a prolonged war, the decisive advantage may belong not simply to the country with the best interceptor, but to the one that can keep producing it at scale.

J&amp;K HC restricts motorboat operations on Dal Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:20:01 UTC
23:20:01 KST

The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has ordered a ban on fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake.
The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has prohibited the operation of fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake until further orders.A division bench comprising chief justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri passed the directive on Wednesday while hearing a petition filed by Mohammad Rafiq Mir.The court directed the authorities, including the lakes conservation and management authority (LCMA), the tourism department and the police, to ensure strict implementation of the ban.“In the larger interest of justice, taking a comprehensive view of the submissions made, it is directed that the respondent authorities LCMA, tourism, and police shall ensure that no motor boat, whether it be a shikara motorboat or Jet Ski which operates by fuel, is operated in the Dal Lake until further orders,” the bench said.The court also warned that any violation of its directive would amount to contempt of court, instructing the concerned officials to strictly prohibit such operations, according to the new agency PTI.
Court stresses need to protect Dal Lake from pollution
The bench observed that protecting lake ecosystems has become increasingly important, making it necessary to restrict activities that contribute to pollution.It also emphasised that the policy governing motorised boats should strike a reasonable balance between tourism-related activities, environmental protection and ensuring uniform rules for all operators.
The judges suggested that solar-powered and electric boats could provide a viable alternative, allowing tourism operators to continue their activities while safeguarding the lake's ecological health.
Solar-powered boats suggested as an alternative
The court asked the government to examine whether conventional motorisation could be replaced with solar-powered systems or electric engines.
Senior additional advocate general Mohsin Qadri was asked to explore the possibility of replacing existing motorised boats with solar-powered electric engines and present the findings before the court.The government had earlier been directed to submit a comprehensive policy on the operation of motorised boats.However, the court clarified that the prohibition would not apply to boats used for emergency services, law and order, disaster management and safety-related operations.The matter has been listed for the next hearing on October 30.

Lagarde may leave her post as President of the European Central Bank early — what she will do

Lagarde may leave her post as President of the European Central Bank early — what she will do
Kyiv • UNN
Christine Lagarde could be elected head of the WEF as early as November, which would lead to an early change in the ECB leadership. No final decision has yet been made.
The World Economic Forum (WEF) may appoint Christine Lagarde as its next chair as early as next month. Four people close to the organization told Reuters, reports UNN.
The publication notes that this would mean Lagarde leaving her post as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) ahead of schedule, which, in turn, would trigger broader personnel changes in the ECB’s leadership.
Lagarde’s term at the ECB expires in October 2027. An early departure would give European Union leaders the opportunity to choose a new ECB president before France’s spring presidential election — which, according to polls, could be won by the far right — and would also pave the way for agreements on two other senior positions at the ECB.
According to people close to the organization (who wished to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the matter), the WEF Board of Trustees, which includes Lagarde herself, will meet on November 2. At that meeting, she may be elected chair of the forum.
No final decision has been made yet, they said.
Two sources said the board could use the meeting to set a date for the vote. This would allow Lagarde to officially take up the post of WEF chair before the start of the forum’s annual meeting in Davos, which will take place in January. Davos traditionally brings together political and business leaders to discuss global economic and financial issues.
They noted that Lagarde’s election is not yet guaranteed, but added that the 70-year-old former French finance minister has broad support among board members (according to information on the website, the board has a total of 27 members).
The ECB declined to comment.
It should be added
The publication notes that any of the possible schedules would leave sufficient time for the new ECB president to complete all the formal procedures required for appointments within EU institutions — and this would take place well before Emmanuel Macron’s presidential term ends in May.
According to a fifth source, one factor influencing the timing was Lagarde’s desire to give Macron an opportunity to influence the choice of her successor. There are concerns in European political circles that negotiations over who will replace Lagarde could become significantly more complicated if far-right leader Marine Le Pen wins France’s presidential election. The World Economic Forum (WEF) Board, based in Geneva, currently has two co-chairs: BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Roche Vice Chairman André Hoffmann. The latter took up the position after forum founder Klaus Schwab stepped down last year.
The board also includes public-sector representatives — in particular, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and Queen Rania of Jordan — as well as leading business figures, including Salesforce’s Marc Benioff and Siemens’ Jim Hagemann Snabe.
Lagarde, who is attending the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok this week, said she would remain at the ECB until next year, but did not make a clear commitment to serve until the official end of her term in October.
If she leaves, a second vacancy will arise on the ECB’s six-member Executive Board — following the resignation of Isabel Schnabel last month. Meanwhile, Chief Economist Philip Lane is due to leave his post in May.
According to EU officials, appointments to these three positions could be agreed as part of a package deal among the member states.
Former central bank chiefs of the Netherlands and Spain — Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos — are considered the leading candidates for the ECB presidency, while France is reportedly seeking the chief economist position.
Germany plans to nominate a candidate to replace Schnabel, who oversees the ECB’s market operations, sources said.

London Protest to Oppose Hijab Restrictions in Azerbaijani Schools This Friday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:18:27 UTC
23:18:27 KST

The student organisation ASAP in Britain and its partners are preparing to hold a protest outside the Azerbaijani Embassy in London on Friday 16 October, in opposition to restrictions on the wearing of hijab in Azerbaijani schools and in solidarity with Muslim pupils and teachers who face measures preventing them from attending school or continuing their work because they wear the hijab.
The demonstration is scheduled to take place from 4pm to 6pm outside the Azerbaijani Embassy at 66 Holland Park, London, W11 3SJ, near Holland Park station. It will be held under the slogan “Hands Off My Hijab”.
The protest comes amid renewed opposition to restrictions in Azerbaijan, where school uniform rules have sparked widespread controversy following reports that hijab-wearing pupils have been prevented from entering classrooms. The developments have brought questions surrounding the hijab, the right to education and freedom of religious belief back into the spotlight.
Call for Solidarity and a Strong Turnout
The organisers are hoping for a substantial turnout that reflects the level of solidarity with women and girls affected by the restrictions and sends a clear message against making access to education conditional on adhering to a uniform policy that excludes the hijab.
Participants have been asked to bring handmade solidarity placards, featuring messages in support of pupils and teachers in Azerbaijan. The signs are intended to reinforce the message that women and girls should have the right to education without discrimination on the grounds of religious belief or appearance.
The demonstration is expected to highlight the principle that education is a fundamental right and that preventing pupils from attending school because they wear the hijab raises serious questions about religious freedom, equality and equal access to educational opportunities.
The protest will also provide an opportunity to call for a review of restrictions that have reportedly resulted in some pupils being barred from entering their schools.
Background: Hijab Restrictions in Azerbaijani Schools
The controversy surrounding the hijab in Azerbaijani schools dates back to December 2010, when the then education minister, Misir Mardanov, announced on 9 December that the wearing of hijab would be prohibited in primary and secondary schools, citing school uniform requirements and the country’s secular education system.
READ: An estimated quarter of a million join London march marking three years of Gaza genocide
Although no explicit law banning the hijab was enacted at the time, the implementation of school uniform rules effectively imposed restrictions on its wearing.
The decision prompted a series of protests. On 10 December 2010, hundreds of people reportedly demonstrated outside the Ministry of Education in the capital, Baku, while further gatherings took place in other parts of the country. In May 2011, police dispersed another protest in Baku and arrested several participants, according to media and human rights reports.
The issue resurfaced in September 2026, following reports that Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers approved amendments to school uniform regulations on 21 September. The changes reportedly included restrictions on clothing considered inconsistent with uniform requirements or the principle of secular education.
Although the amendments did not explicitly mention a ban on the hijab, recent reports indicate that some schools have prevented hijab-wearing pupils from entering classrooms. Objections have also emerged from pupils, parents and teachers over the implementation of the new rules.
The current opposition therefore extends beyond a debate about school uniforms. It raises broader questions about how education regulations can be reconciled with freedom of religion and how pupils can be protected from being denied an education because they wear the hijab.
As opposition continues and solidarity campaigns emerge both within Azerbaijan and abroad, the planned demonstration outside the Azerbaijani Embassy in London forms part of wider efforts to challenge the restrictions, highlight their educational and social consequences, and call for women and girls to be able to study and work without discrimination.
Protest Details
Date: Friday 16 October 2026
Time: 4pm–6pm
Venue: Embassy of Azerbaijan, 66 Holland Park, London, W11 3SJ
Organisers: ASAP student organisation in Britain and its partners
Slogan: “Hands Off My Hijab”
What to bring: Handmade placards expressing solidarity with Muslim women and girls and supporting their right to education.
The demonstration is intended to bring together members of the Muslim and wider community, students, human rights campaigners and others who support freedom of religion and equal access to education.

Unknown Publisher

14:16:40 UTC
23:16:40 KST

A Syrian military court has handed down sentences ranging from two months in prison to the death penalty against several defendants, including defence ministry personnel, over violations committed during deadly violence along the country’s coast in March 2025.
The Military Criminal Court in Aleppo sentenced al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali to death at a hearing at the city’s Justice Palace on Thursday, state-run Alikhbaria TV reported.
The court convicted both men of acts intended to “provoke civil war and sectarian fighting” and of leading armed groups to attack government forces, the broadcaster quoted the presiding judge as saying.
A third defendant, Maher Othman, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, though the court did not immediately specify the charges on which he was convicted.
In rulings involving defence ministry personnel, Mohammed Bakour, a member of the ministry’s 82nd Division, received a 20-year prison sentence for intentional homicide.
Captain Mustafa Shannan and Khaled Muhaimeed, both from the 54th Division, were each sentenced to two years in prison for involvement in torture. Another ministry member, Mahmoud Shaheen, received a two-month sentence for causing bodily harm.
The court acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakr Jan and Mohammed Louay Zarzouri, members of the 50th and 54th divisions respectively, of intentional homicide charges “due to insufficient evidence”.
Widespread abuses against civilians
The rulings are part of proceedings against former regime members and personnel serving under Syria’s current defence ministry accused of violations during the coastal violence.
The violence erupted in March 2025 after armed groups loyal to ousted president Bashar al Assad attacked government security forces in the coastal provinces of Latakia and Tartus, triggering clashes and widespread abuses against civilians.
The violence killed hundreds of civilians and security forces personnel.
Public trials began at Aleppo’s Justice Palace in November 2025, with defendants facing charges including incitement to sectarian strife, homicide, theft and attacks on security forces.
On September 17, the same court sentenced one defendant to death, another to life in prison and a third to 20 years, while acquitting a fourth.

Gaza’s child amputees are growing faster than their prosthetics allow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:13:03 UTC
23:13:03 KST

Abdul-Rahman al-Nashash, 11, holds onto the edge of a chair and pushes his left leg into a plastic prosthetic that doesn’t fit him anymore. The bone that was cut two years ago has kept growing inside, and it presses painfully against his skin.
His doctors told him to stop wearing it. He wears it anyway, every morning, pulling the straps tight and rolling his pants down so no one sees the plastic before he takes his first step. He bites his lip when it hurts and holds his shoulders straight so no one can tell he is limping.
“He forces himself to wear it,” his mother said, “just so no one knows he has a disability.”
Before the genocide, al-Nashash played for a local soccer club, and he would chase the ball across a dirt field until the sun went down. He is the eldest son in his family, and he was the one his mother leaned on at home. When she needed water, he was the one who ran to carry the heavy gallon of water, and he never got tired. Now, he is not able.
When he finally takes the prosthetic off, he sits curled up. He is waiting for his third surgery, and his mother said he will need one every year.
As a child grows, the bone in the amputated leg grows too, but the prosthetic doesn’t. At some point it stops fitting, and sometimes the child needs another operation before he can get a new one. In Gaza, that often means starting over with surgery, then rehabilitation, then a new limb if one can be made at all, because Israel restricts the parts and materials needed to make and repair them. Some children in Gaza have outgrown their limbs and are waiting for new ones. Others never received one, because there are none in Gaza that fit them.
Al-Nashash’s family was forced to evacuate from al-Bureij refugee camp in Central Gaza in 2023 and took shelter in UNRWA schools. His father stayed behind. Two days after they left, on October 20, the house was struck, and his father was killed along with several relatives. The three-wheeled motorcycle that had been the family’s only source of income was parked in the storeroom and was destroyed in the same strike.
From there, the family moved from school to school and tent to tent. They spent about three months in Rafah, then moved to schools in Nuseirat. With no money coming in, his mother opened a small stall with her brother-in-law, selling a variety of canned beans.
Around noon on July 16, 2024, her sister asked her to come light a fire and cook, so she left her son to mind the stall in her place. An Israeli airstrike hit the tents in the middle of al-Razi school, a UNRWA shelter in Nuseirat camp, killing 23 people, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. A piece of shrapnel struck his leg directly. His mother said his injured left foot was split in two, the bones of his toes exposed, and she kept screaming that her son had been killed.
At first, she said, she was told doctors hoped to fix the leg with metal plates rather than amputate. At Al-Aqsa Hospital, one doctor told her the leg would have to be amputated, and she asked them to cut off her own leg and give it to him, because he was the one who took care of her. He was then taken by an ambulance to a hospital by the sea in Deir al-Balah where a foreign medical team was working. There they told her nothing more could be done. The amputation needed her consent. She signed, because there was no other choice.
When al-Nashash woke from the anesthesia, he kept staring at himself as if he were losing his mind. It was only after counselors came and he began to see other children like him that he slowly started to adjust.
After the amputation, therapists from local rehabilitation programs came to work with him regularly. But his natural childhood growth worked against his recovery. “My son grows fast,” his mother said. By March 2025, just eight months after he lost his leg, the bone had already grown too long.
They traveled to Jordan, where surgeons cut the bone back and fitted him with his first prosthetic, the one he still wears today. The trip lasted five months. When al-Nashash returned to Gaza, the boy who used to sprint on the soccer field had to start physical therapy from scratch, learning how to balance and walk all over again.
Today, that same cycle is about to restart. Once he manages to get his next surgery, he will face three more months of physical therapy before he can even begin training to walk again. His mother has applied for a medical evacuation out of Gaza, hoping he can be treated abroad. “I wish I could see my son walk like other children,” she told Mondoweiss.
Until that approval comes, al-Nashash also uses a pair of forearm crutches that are are breaking down. The soft material on the hand grips has completely worn away, leaving his hands to rub against the hard surface. “There are no spare parts for the grips,” his mother said.
The indefinite wait for prosthetics
Mahmoud al-Darbali, 10, lost his right leg up to the hip when he was nine, and over a year later, he is still waiting to receive his first prosthetic.
Al-Darbali’s family home near the Zeitoun car market was bombed a week after they evacuated. After being displaced south more than ten times, the family returned north, squeezing into a single room in his grandmother’s house on Kishko Street, in the Zeitoun neighborhood of Gaza City. “We were happy,” his mother told Mondoweiss.
On July 5, 2025, three shells struck the house. The blast killed several relatives, including al-Darbali’s 14-year-old sister. “I didn’t get to say goodbye. She died hungry,” his mother said. The explosion severed Mahmoud’s right leg instantly and burned his left thigh. Shrapnel hit his seven-year-old brother’s lung and struck his mother’s knee. His 16-year-old brother still has shrapnel near his spine, and he cannot sleep without painkillers.
They spent over two months at Al-Ahli Arab Baptist Hospital, where al-Darbali was taken to the operating room daily just to change his bandages. The mother and her five surviving children shared a single hospital bed. In July 2025, the same month Mahmoud was injured, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said injured patients at its clinics in Gaza were asking for food instead of medicine, because their wounds were not healing without enough protein.
After leaving the hospital, the family managed on the street. Al-Darbali relies on crutches and a wheelchair, yet he cannot walk more than a hundred meters on the crutches. Without electricity, he often loses his balance in the dark. “Many times I wake up to his terrified voice as he hits the ground,” his mother says.
He still feels the missing leg. “Mom, my heel hurts,” he tells her, his mother said. His brother holds the empty space where Mahmoud’s leg used to be and presses on it. “I feel better,” Mahmoud says. He receives no psychological support. When he is given paper, he draws tanks, missiles and blood.
Because the amputation reaches his pelvis, leaving only a tiny fraction of the thigh bone, the family has been told no prosthetic in Gaza can fit him. He has been referred for medical evacuation abroad, but no country has accepted his case yet. “The situation is hard,” his mother said, “and there is no food.”
A shortage by design
Dr. Mohammed Abu Mansi, a physical therapy and rehabilitation specialist at Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al Thani Hospital for Rehabilitation and Prosthetics in Gaza City, explained that while not every child requires annual revision surgeries, bone overgrowth causes complications in some children. For patients like al-Nashash, the growing bone creates a protrusion. “When the child puts weight on the prosthetic, this spot becomes very painful,” he said. “The pressure inside the prosthetic becomes unbearable.”
Revision surgeries can be done in Gaza, he said, but only within what is available in operating rooms, anesthesia and follow-up care. Complicated cases need to travel abroad.
For hip-level amputations like al-Darbali’s, the problem is the materials. “We used to fit this type of prosthetic inside Gaza before the war,” Dr. Abu Mansi told Mondoweiss. “But now the materials needed to make a prosthetic for an amputation up to the hip are not available.” Before the war, he said, prosthetic parts and materials came in regularly, and the hospital could provide steady care to amputees.
Children like al-Darbali, left without a prosthetic, he said, develop muscle weakness, muscle contractures, limited movement and changes in the shape of the amputated limb as their bodies continue to grow. Relying on crutches and wheelchairs for a long time also causes other complications.
Al-Nashash and al-Darbali are among thousands of amputees. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 5,000 people in Gaza have lost limbs since October 2023, and that one in five of them is a child. Of 2,277 amputees the WHO evaluated between September 2024 and May 2026, only 502 had been fitted with a prosthetic. Eighteen percent were children, and 32 percent had above-knee amputations. 225 needed revision surgery on what remained of their limb, and only eight prosthetists were working in the entire Strip.
According to the same report, no rehabilitation equipment entered Gaza between May 2024 and April 14, 2026. By that date, 18 shipments, including prosthetic limbs and children’s wheelchairs, were still waiting for clearance, for 136 days on average and 526 days in the longest case. In the six months before that, four shipments were rejected. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that Israeli authorities had denied prosthetic hand, knee and ankle joints, silicone liners and medical shoes, despite repeated requests.
Treatment abroad is not guaranteed either. A medical referral is only the first step. A host country has to select the patient, and the list then goes to Israeli authorities for clearance. By mid-September, 13,555 patients had been evacuated since October 2023, including 6,326 children. Before the war, 50 to 100 patients left Gaza every day for treatment. In January, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said more than 18,500 patients, including 4,000 children, still needed urgent medical evacuation. Citing Gaza’s Ministry of Health, he said 1,092 patients had died while waiting between July 2024 and November 2025.
Al-Darbali turned 10 in July. His mother is still waiting for a call from the officials handling his referral to tell her that his evacuation has been approved. “Every second, I pray my phone will ring, and they’ll tell me to get ready,” she said.
Now, when al-Darbali is taken to the hospital, he refuses to be put to sleep. His left leg, the only one he has left, is scarred from the burns.
“I don’t want to sleep,” Mahmoud said. “They’ll cut off my other leg.”

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The Israeli government is set to vote Thursday on extending the state of emergency on the home front until Nov. 3, past the Oct. 27 elections, citing “uncertainty over the situation,” particularly on the Iran and Lebanon fronts.  
The state of emergency was imposed when the Israeli-US war on Iran began Feb. 28. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.  
Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that ministers will vote on extending the declaration of a “special state of emergency” beyond the Oct. 27 general elections.  
It added that a document submitted by the cabinet secretary cited “uncertainty over the situation, particularly regarding the fronts in Iran and Lebanon.”  
The document, according to the broadcaster, stated that “according to security officials’ assessments, there remains a high likelihood of an attack” against Israel.  
Since October 2023, Israel has been committing genocide in the Gaza Strip and carrying out attacks in the occupied West Bank. It has also waged two wars against Lebanon and Iran, in addition to launching airstrikes on Yemen and Qatar and conducting daily ground incursions into Syria.
Since March 2, Israel has been waging an offensive against Lebanon, killing more than 4,300 people, wounding 12,400 and displacing more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.  
KAN said a legal opinion attached to the document referred to security establishment assessments regarding the possibility of an attack on Israel.  
The opinion concluded that “the circumstances justify approving the proposal to extend the declaration of a special state of emergency on the home front until Nov. 3.”  
The broadcaster noted that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned two weeks ago that Israel could face an attack in the coming weeks.  
The opposition says Netanyahu is engaging in election propaganda by repeatedly making claims about security threats ahead of the vote.  
Netanyahu has headed the government since December 2022, leading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.  
He also faces charges of corruption, bribery, and breach of trust in three cases.   
In addition to the domestic corruption trial, Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2024 for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza, where more than 74,000 victims have been killed in the genocidal war since October 2023.

Burç Eruygur

Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day halt due to an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy expressed support for his US counterpart's proposed energy ceasefire, but claimed Russian strikes continued despite Kyiv’s halt.
“That's it. Block is out,” Zelenskyy said, responding to a question about how much longer Ukraine will maintain a halt to energy strikes.
On reports that the US suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Zelenskyy said that over the course of Ukraine’s three-day halt to strikes in Russia, his country was subject to ballistic missile attacks and did not receive any early warning alerts.
He said Washington had earlier warned Kyiv about the blocking of intelligence if it did not stop strikes on Russian energy sites.
“This is, I think, the problem. And when it goes together with Starlink's decision, which is 100% the decision of American side … I think that (it is) not (about) military people. I think it's about SpaceX. So together it makes huge problems,” Zelenskyy added.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump that Ukraine will "destroy" Russia's ballistic missile launchers if Starlink opens on Russian territory.
He argued that if a diesel deal, such as the one announced over the weekend, forces Ukraine to be silent on the battlefield, then questions will arise concerning "when the next deal will be," which would "definitely" concern Russian gas.
The Ukraine leader said he does not want to interfere in "diesel deals," but Ukraine will respond to Russian strikes.
"The question (is): can you give me missiles for Patriot (systems), because when I will not attack them because you asked me not attack them, they will attack me. It's fair if you will give me with what to defend.
"It's the minimum what I ask. No? I think yes. And when I'm asking this, your answer is blocking Starlink," he added.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a freelance adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said on Wednesday that speed restrictions were implemented on Starlink satellites in Ukraine, limiting their speed to 100 mph (161 kph).
"Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," Beskrestnov added.
US billionaire Elon Musk said Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government," and decisions on speed or usage restrictions are made by the US military and ultimately the president.
Separately, Zelenskyy told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt "betrayed" over the diesel agreement between Russia and the US.
He said he is "sure that they knew what they did," commenting on a question on whether the speed restrictions on Starlink satellites were implemented deliberately.

Brent fell amid US consideration of easing sanctions on Russia’s &quot;shadow fleet&quot;

Brent fell amid US consideration of easing sanctions on Russia’s "shadow fleet"
Kyiv • UNN
Brent fell by nearly 1% following U.S. signals of a possible easing of sanctions on Russian tankers. WTI rose amid the anticipated decline in inventories.
Brent crude prices fell by approximately 1% on Thursday, October 15. This came as potential U.S. moves to ease restrictions on tankers from Russia's "shadow fleet" "calmed concerns about high prices." UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
The international Brent benchmark fell by $1.03, or 0.97%, to $105.03 per barrel by 13:26 GMT (16:26 Kyiv time).
Futures for U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose by $1.04, or 1.09%, to $96.13 per barrel, driven by expectations of a significant reduction in U.S. inventories for the week.
Oil prices fell after a U.S. official said on Wednesday that the U.S. administration was considering easing sanctions on some unregulated Russian tankers, which could help lower freight rates and increase flexibility in diesel fuel supply, said PVM Oil analyst John Evans.
The discussions are taking place several days after U.S. President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel "to mitigate rising prices worldwide," the publication writes. According to the U.S. official, the new talks are focused on whether Washington could potentially allow the transportation of "legal oil" on vessels that had previously been sanctioned.
However, prices are still supported by the escalation of the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthis, as well as by the resumption of attacks on vessels in the region.
A container ship and a bulk carrier sank near the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, shipping officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have increased over the past 10 days, and Iran said it was intensifying strikes in response to the U.S. blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.
"The ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis maintains a geopolitical premium in oil markets, but energy infrastructure has not come under attack in recent days," MUFG analysts said in a note.
At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT about the lifting of the ban on strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Release of diesel reserves
Spain will release 4.4 million barrels from its strategic reserves in October, an Energy Ministry representative said on Thursday, as the International Energy Agency began a meeting expected to clarify details of the release of 100 million barrels of oil reserves, including diesel fuel, with a focus on the timing and scale of the move.
U.S. crude oil and distillate inventories fell last week, while gasoline inventories rose, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.
Crude oil inventories fell by 11.1 million barrels in the week ending October 9, the sources said. This was far more than analysts polled by Reuters had expected.

Frederiksen rejects EU budget proposal; demands major spending cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

Denmark faces an estimated increase of 12.7 billion DKK in annual contributions to the European Union under Ireland’s latest proposal, raising concerns about the impact on domestic spending.
Speaking Thursday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the proposed budget unacceptable, arguing that it was too large and failed to reflect Europe’s changing priorities.
“The proposal on the table from the Irish is unacceptable. That applies both in terms of level, it is too large an EU budget being proposed, but it also applies to the distribution,” Frederiksen said.
She argued that too much funding remained directed toward agricultural subsidies and regional development rather than defense and economic competitiveness.
Frederiksen, who leads Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said the overall budget needed to be reduced significantly but did not specify an amount.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson expressed similar concerns, declaring that Sweden “is not the EU’s ATM”.
Denmark and Sweden have joined Germany, the Netherlands, Finland and Austria in opposing the proposed spending increases.
All six countries contribute more to the EU budget than they receive and are seeking reductions to the overall proposal.
Several southern European countries, however, favor maintaining or increasing EU spending, making an agreement difficult.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has also warned against substantial cuts.
“I want to warn against major cuts. That would entail a risk of cutting deeply into the important priorities that we all have agreed on,” she said earlier this month, according to AFP.
EU leaders remain divided over the budget’s size and spending priorities, with negotiations continuing in Brussels.

German court sentences two for plotting to kill leader of German Jewish community for Iran
FRANKFURT, Oct 15 - A German court on Thursday handed two men prison sentences of up to 8-1/2 years for planning to kill the leader of a Jewish organisation in Germany, saying one man had been steered by Iran's intelligence service.
One man, previously identified as Danish national Ali S., was sentenced to eight years and six months for preparing an assassination and aggravated arson, judges ruled.
"The court is convinced that the defendant, S., was recruited by the Iranian secret service and integrated into it to carry out state-sponsored terrorist activities in Germany under Iran’s direction," the court in the northern city of Hamburg said in a statement.
The Iranian Embassy in Germany did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Another man, previously named as Afghan national Tawab M., was sentenced to four years and six months for his role in the plot.
The verdicts, which can be appealed, come as a war with Iran launched by the United States and Israel in February has spilled over into an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
German federal prosecutors brought criminal charges against the two men in May.
The court said that in early 2025, S. was tasked with gathering information on the President of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and the Chairman of the German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck.
He was also instructed to spy on two Jewish grocers in Berlin, they added. REUTERS

Too Good To Go to sell surplus household and personal care products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

The Danish-founded app is introducing five new product categories, allowing customers to buy discounted goods ranging from pet accessories to flowers and dietary supplements.
Too Good To Go announced Thursday that its platform will now offer surplus personal care products, pet accessories, flowers and plants, nutrition and dietary supplements, and household goods.
The expansion marks a shift for the company, which has focused on reducing food waste since its launch in 2016.
“Too Good To Go started with food because we saw how absurd it was that something so valuable could end up as waste. Ten years later, it is clear that the same principle applies outside the world of food,” CEO Mette Lykke said.
According to the company, more than 8,500 stores will offer products across the new categories.
Approximately one-third of those retailers already work with Too Good To Go to sell surplus food.
The app currently operates in 20 countries, with 150 million registered users and 200,000 active business partners.
Through its existing model, retailers sell unsold food in discounted surprise bags, with Too Good To Go receiving a percentage of each transaction.
The company says its expansion will help businesses recover value from unsold merchandise while giving customers access to a wider selection of discounted products.
“Our partners are increasingly approaching us with challenges regarding surplus goods that extend beyond food and asking if we can help. Surplus exists in all parts of the store,” Lykke said.
Surplus stock can include seasonal products, discontinued items, outdated packaging and gift sets that are no longer in demand.

Crown Prince Christian receives Denmark’s highest Dannebrog honor
King Frederik has marked his eldest son’s 21st birthday with a royal decoration and the release of new official portraits, while celebrations remain private.
Crown Prince Christian was awarded the Grand Commander Cross of the Order of the Dannebrog on Thursday, according to a statement from the Danish Royal House.
The decoration is the highest rank within the Order of the Dannebrog and is reserved for members of royalty who already hold the Order of the Elephant.
Christian received the Order of the Elephant on his 18th birthday, making him eligible for the distinction.
With his appointment, Denmark now has seven Grand Commanders of the Order of the Dannebrog.
The cross currently bears the monogram of King Frederik IX, who last awarded it. It will be updated with King Frederik’s monogram during restoration.
The Royal House also released portraits showing Christian wearing the Royal Life Guards’ red ceremonial uniform.
The photographs were taken several weeks earlier at Christian VII’s Palace at Amalienborg.
Christian currently serves as a second lieutenant and platoon commander with the Royal Life Guards at Høvelte Barracks.
He completed his compulsory military service in August 2025 before beginning officer training and is expected to remain in service until summer 2027.
The crown prince receives neither a military training salary nor a royal allowance.
His father also trained as a lieutenant, later qualifying as a naval frogman and serving four months with Greenland’s Sirius Patrol in 2000.
In a recent interview with Politiken, Christian said he would consider deployment after completing his lieutenant training.
The Nordic region’s largest bank reported third-quarter earnings broadly in line with analysts’ expectations, but uncertainty surrounding regulatory assessments weighed on investor confidence Thursday.
Nordea shares fell 7.3 percent by 12:50 p.m., making the bank the worst performer in Denmark’s C25 stock index.
The decline followed the publication of Nordea’s quarterly financial results, which showed a profit of 1,181 billion euros and total income of 2,968 billion euros.
Both figures were broadly consistent with analysts’ forecasts.
However, the bank announced it would suspend a planned share buyback program while awaiting clarification from the European Central Bank (ECB) regarding its risk assessments.
The regulatory process is not expected to conclude until 2027.
Share buybacks allow companies to return money to shareholders by purchasing their own shares, often reducing the number available and potentially increasing the value of those remaining.
According to Danish financial newspaper Børsen, Nordea had planned to repurchase approximately 500 million euros worth of shares.
Martin Munk, senior equity adviser at Jyske Bank, said the market reaction reflected regulatory uncertainty rather than disappointing financial performance.
“It is not the financial statements that are creating noise. Rather, it is the uncertainty about where they land with the ECB,” Munk told MarketWire.
Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen acknowledged that the regulatory review was taking longer than anticipated.
“It has proven to be a long process,” he told Børsen.
Vang-Jensen said the bank considered pausing repurchases appropriate while uncertainty remained over its future risk-weighted assets, a measure used to determine how much capital banks must hold against potential losses.
Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Free public transport for young people will have limited value without reliable bus and train connections, according to Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance.

Auto group charged with exploiting 18 foreign mechanics in Denmark
A criminal case involving workers from India, Sri Lanka and other countries will be heard at the Court in Hillerød, following allegations of unpaid overtime, threats and restrictions on trade union membership.
According to TV 2 Kosmopol, prosecutors have brought charges against two men and two companies connected to a car group in North Zealand.
North Zealand Police allege that 18 foreign mechanics were subjected to human exploitation over a four-year period.
The indictment states that the workers were required to work overtime and weekends without additional pay.
They were also allegedly prohibited from joining a trade union, limiting their ability to seek collective representation over their employment conditions.
Prosecutors further allege that the mechanics were threatened with dismissal and deportation to their home countries if they complained about their working or living conditions.
TV 2 Kosmopol reported that although the mechanics’ stated monthly salaries were 38,000 DKK, they received only 7,517 DKK after tax.
The case will now be considered by the Court in Hillerød, which must determine whether the defendants are guilty of the charges.
The court will also decide whether approximately 4.1 million DKK should be confiscated from the defendants in connection with the alleged exploitation.
Denmark introduced a specific provision on human exploitation into its criminal code in June 2022.
The provision was designed to address serious cases of labor exploitation that do not meet the legal definition of human trafficking.
The charges in the North Zealand case have been brought under that provision, with the defendants’ criminal responsibility yet to be established.

The Danish government is preparing for difficult negotiations in Brussels over the European Union’s next budget, with disagreements emerging over spending priorities and national contributions.
According to estimates from Denmark’s Finance Ministry, a proposal presented by Ireland’s EU presidency could increase Denmark’s annual contribution by approximately 12.7 billion DKK compared with the current budget period.

For comparison, its plan to eliminate VAT on fruit and vegetables and halve VAT on other food products would cost approximately 17.4 billion DKK annually.

Denmark has joined Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Finland and Austria in calling for tighter EU spending.
The six countries want greater emphasis on defense and economic competitiveness rather than agricultural subsidies and regional development funding.
France has also expressed opposition to higher national contributions, citing financial pressures.
However, several other EU members want to preserve existing agricultural and regional support programs.
Despite disagreements, no member state has rejected Ireland’s proposal as the basis for negotiations.
European Council President António Costa will oversee the discussions, with a possible agreement expected at December’s EU summit.
Border checks between Denmark and Germany extended for another six months
Travelers entering the country may continue to face inspections until May 17, 2027, as authorities maintain that security threats remain serious.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, informed the European Commission of the decision Wednesday, according to a statement from the Justice Ministry.
The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Reports of AI-generated child abuse material rise sharply in Denmark
Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.
Denmark restricts land registry searches after 17 million queries in days
An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.
The system provides limited public information about properties, cooperative housing and vehicles.
Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said he had informed the Danish Parliament about the incident.
Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.

A proposed one-year suspension of permits for new conventional pig farms and expansions of existing facilities has raised questions about the government’s legal authority and potential compensation claims.

“I am completely at ease. I do not make an amendment to an executive order without an assessment of the legal basis having been carried out,” he said in September.

A signal fault near Kildebrønde in eastern Zealand is disrupting train services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
On Wednesday morning, DSB said passengers should expect longer travel times until 1 p.m. But about an hour before that deadline, the railway operator announced that disruptions would continue until 7 p.m., according to its website.
Banedanmark, which operates and maintains Denmark’s state-owned railway network, told DSB that repair work would not take place until Wednesday night, leading into Thursday.
However, a solution has been found that will allow trains to run normally on the affected section after 7 p.m., even though the fault will not yet have been repaired.
Some trains that usually run via Køge Nord are being diverted through Roskilde instead. These services will not stop between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.

Meanwhile, fewer trains are running between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, according to DSB. The date is provisional, and services could return to normal earlier or later than expected.
All regional trains on the route have been replaced by buses since Friday, following a fire in a railway relay hut near Aarup in western Funen.
International trains, as well as InterCityLyn and InterCity services, are running as normal, but at reduced speeds on some sections of the route.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Government party proposes mandatory helmets for e-bike riders
Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

Greenland moves closer to restoring former time zone and ending daylight saving time
Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago.
The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq.
The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year.
“We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said.
In 2022, Greenland’s parliament approved a move from UTC-3 to UTC-2 to balance the time difference with Europe and the United States. The change took effect in March 2023.
However, the decision has remained controversial, with 4,142 residents signing a petition calling for the previous time zone to return.
Opposition parties Naleraq and Siumut proposed reversing the change in May. The government initially opposed the move but supported ending daylight saving time.
Despite the government’s changed position, Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit, the Democrats party, warned about potential consequences.
He said the change would increase the time difference with Europe by one hour in winter and two hours in summer.
Nielsen argued that reduced overlap with Danish medical specialists could lead to longer patient waiting times.
He also warned of higher costs for businesses, weaker flight connections with Europe and financial expenses associated with changing the time zone.
The proposal is scheduled for a final parliamentary vote October 21.
