AI generated
LONDON/PARIS – French supermarkets are facing millions of euros in losses after a cyberattack forced them to throw away food, in a crisis that is not typically covered by cyber insurance policies but could still lead to higher premiums in future, insurers told Reuters.
Hackers – whose identity remains unknown – took control of cooling units at around 350 French supermarkets on the night of Oct 11, raising the temperature of internet-connected fridges and freezers to 50 deg C.
The attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, Thierry Cotillard, president of Intermarche owner Les Mousquetaires, estimated on Oct 12, saying that supermarkets will begin a legal battle over who is responsible for the losses.
Cyber insurance typically does not cover physical losses from attacks and supermarkets’ claims could be affected if they lacked the latest software updates, four insurance brokers told Reuters.
If a state actor turns out to be behind the hack, it could complicate supermarkets’ insurance claims because cyber policies typically do not cover acts of war, according to a cyber underwriter, who requested anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly.
As companies have embraced the so-called Internet of Things, the growing connectivity of once largely mechanical equipment has exposed them to new security threats compounded by technological advancements including AI.
Between 2020 and 2025, cyberattacks in France, Germany, Italy and Spain cost over €300 billion (S$431 billion) in economic losses, insurance broker Howden estimates.
David Molony, head of cyber and financial sponsors at insurance broker Aon, said he recommended for companies in some sectors, including retail and pharmaceuticals, specific cover for perishable goods that need to be stored in tightly controlled physical conditions.
“Given the increasing digitisation of operational technology and connected systems, this is an area that businesses should review carefully,” he said.
Cyberattack, physical losses
Supermarkets’ cyber insurance policies may cover some costs, such as investigating internally or hiring PR advisors, but typically exclude physical losses.
Intermarche told AFP on Oct 12 that its insurance did not cover this type of incident. Asked by Reuters, Les Mousquetaires did not disclose its insurance arrangements. Carrefour, Monoprix, Cooperative U and E.Leclerc did not respond to requests for comment.
The hack affected fridges using software supplied by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell, France’s cybersecurity agency said. Danfoss said many of the appliances were using out-of-date software or had “reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates”.
Whether failing to update the software could affect the insurance depends on the details of the contract, insurers said.
Typically a company taking out a cyber insurance policy would declare its policy on software updates, for example committing to critical updates within a particular time period, said Emma Pleut, head of cyber for France at WTW.
Paul Gooch, deputy departmental head at Tokio Marine Kiln, said outdated software is not usually in itself a reason to reject a claim.
Higher premiums, new products
Retailers are increasingly seeking cyber insurance which covers physical damage, Aon’s Molony said. Such policies are already used in the energy, marine cargo, and defence sectors.
Aon has advised large retailers and other clients to get insurance that extends to “perishable stock”, and has recently arranged “high-value towers” – policies with large maximum payouts – in the London market with such cover included, Molony said.
Recent cyberattacks on retailers in Britain and France could also lead to higher premiums, underwriters said.
Asked whether European retailers could face higher insurance prices following cyberattacks, Sydonie Williams, head of international cyber risks at Beazley, said: “I absolutely think that could happen.”
TMK’s Gooch said that he expected greater focus on insurance products that specifically address physical losses from attacks.
“The recent cyberattack impacting refrigeration systems across France should act as a wake-up call to those who underestimate the potential physical consequences of cyber incidents,” he said. REUTERS

EU is negotiating Ukraine’s association with its satellite communications system amid disruptions to Starlink

The European Commission is aware of reports regarding Starlink restrictions for Ukraine. The EU is discussing Ukraine’s full association with the Govsatcom programme.
The European Commission is aware of reports about restrictions on Starlink for Ukraine and stated what it is offering on its side: it is negotiating with Ukraine on Ukraine’s "full association" with the EU’s GOVSATCOM satellite communications programme. European Commission spokespersons Paula Pinho and Thomas Regnier said this during a briefing on 15 October, UNN reports.
Details
"Regarding reports of disruptions to Starlink, we are aware of these reports, and we cannot comment further until we receive more information. It is also important to say that we have no indication that intelligence sharing has ceased, so it is also important to flag this," European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said.
At the same time, Pinho noted that "we are doing a lot of work, of course, to increase our own satellite assistance."
"The war in Ukraine clearly shows that our security also depends on space, and we are doing quite a lot here, and we are certainly ready to support Ukraine wherever we can," Thomas Regnier stressed.
He pointed to "two things that we already have."
"First, there is Govsatcom, which is the pooling and shared use of the existing satellite capabilities of the member states. The good news here is that the platform was created and set up in January this year, and is operating together with our member states," he said.
We are now trying to find a way, and we are currently negotiating with Ukraine on Ukraine’s full association with Govsatcom
According to him, "the second phase will take place in January or at the beginning of next year."
"We could add commercial capacities to Govsatcom, and this would allow us to bridge the gap until 2029, when our constellation of more than 300 satellites under Iris² will be fully operational," he stressed.
Asked how this satellite system could provide Ukraine with the same services that Starshield provides, Pinho stressed: "We are not making any comparison here between what is being offered and the areas on which we are working."
"We are fully aware of the importance of this satellite service, especially in the current context," Pinho also said.
Recall
The liberal political group in the European Parliament Renew Europe called on the European Commission and the Council of the EU to purchase satellite communications services from European providers for Ukraine after new restrictions on Starlink reportedly disrupted Ukrainian military operations. In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa, the liberal group called for temporary access to the EU’s GOVSATCOM programme and procurement from Eutelsat, Hispasat and SES.

Who Are the Houthis and Why Are They Attacking Saudi Arabia’s Airports?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:43:41 UTC
22:43:41 KST

The European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council on Thursday announced the postponement of a joint summit set to take place in Saudi Arabia next week, amid safety concerns prompted by Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
Citing the “continued attempts by the terrorist Houthi militia to target the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its civilian infrastructure, which threatens the security and safety of innocent civilians,” the council said the Gulf-European Summit will be rescheduled.
The postponement comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday vowed to forge ahead with the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities, just hours after striking oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters.
“Operations toward Saudi depths will continue in the coming days,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, describing the locations as “legitimate targets” and framing their attacks as a direct response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. Saudi-led forces said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday and local journalists reported hearing “loud blasts” in the Saudi capital.
The escalation follows weeks of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The conflict reignited amid the widespread fallout of the U.S.-Iran war, bringing further instability to the Gulf region. In September, the Houthis said they had captured the strategic Perim Island that sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint. They also seized other islands in a bid to tighten their grip on the Red Sea coastline. Amid fears that a stronger Houthi position along the coast could further constrain global energy supplies, Saudi-backed forces recaptured key areas around the strait in early October. The Houthis have since ramped up their focus on Saudi Arabia’s airports and energy infrastructure.
Tuesday night’s attack on Aramco’s executive offices in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a limited fire, Saudi’s Ministry of Energy confirmed. No injuries were reported. TIME has reached out to Aramco and the Saudi government’s media office for further information. Saudi authorities said several missiles and drones had been intercepted elsewhere, and that falling debris injured four people in the capital of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia launched strikes on an oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sanaa on Tuesday, as the tit-for-tat attacks escalated.
The Saudi strike on the oil depot appeared to be in response to the Houthis’ attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left over 300 injured. A projectile hit that same airport on Sunday, killing one person, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed. The week before, an attack on Abha International Airport killed two people and wounded 28, said GACA.
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. However, it is struggling to defend itself against the Houthis, who are positioned to strike deep into the kingdom. The Saudis are currently investigating how their defense systems failed to stop the deadly attacks. Experts cite the vast mass of Saudi land as one reason why defensive measures may have failed. The Saudi border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles. “Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” said Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, in an online post.
Operations at King Khalid remain suspended in the wake of the attacks. Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Philippine Airlines are among the carriers to announce a suspension of flights to Riyadh.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans in the country of “potential flight cancelations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” stipulating that U.S. government employees now require “special authorization” to use any airport in the country.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the Houthis “are behaving very badly.” In a Truth Social post, he continued, “I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the hell out of them and, at their request, stopped,” seemingly referencing the U.S. strikes between March and May last year, which came in response to the Houthis attacking vessels in the Red Sea and disrupting global trade. Weeks after the strikes began, a cease-fire between the U.S. and the Houthis was reached via Omani mediations.
On Saturday, Trump suggested that the U.S. may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Asked about the possibility of U.S. strikes, a senior U.S. official told TIME that Washington is “in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability and we will always fulfill our commitments to our partners.”
As tensions in the region continue to escalate, here’s what to know about the Houthis, their history with Saudi Arabia, and why they are attacking airports.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis are a political and armed group in Yemen that first emerged in the 1990s and have been fighting the country’s internationally recognized government for around two decades. The group is a revivalist movement for Zaidism, a branch of Shi‘ite Islam. The Zaidi muslim population in the country represents around 35% of the Yemeni population.
The Houthi movement was largely born from a transformation of the Believing Youth Forum (BYF), according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The group became known as the Houthis in honor of their founder and leader, Hussein al-Houthi. Before he was killed by Yemeni forces in 2004, al-Houthi had developed the group into a more militarized movement. The group is now led by his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi.
Civil war broke out in 2014 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden. Since then, the group has been engaged in fighting against a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government. The Houthis currently have control of most of the country’s west, including Sanaa.
Experts compare the Houthis to authoritarian regimes on account of the social restrictions imposed in areas under the group’s control and alleged human rights abuses.
“The Houthis are dominated with very ideological and radical ideas, like a Zaidi ISIS. They have similarities also with the Taliban in terms of social control," says Mahmoud Shehrah, a Yemeni political analyst at London-based think tank Chatham House.
How are the Houthi rebels linked to Iran?
The Houthis hold strong ties to Iran, often taking action in line with Tehran’s objectives.
“Since 2009, Iran [has] started to speed up weapons supplies, training, but also a lot of funding to the Houthis,” says Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemeni research fellow at Chatham House, noting that links between the two began as early as the 1990s.
The Houthis are often considered part of Iran’s proxy network, known as the “Axis of Resistance,” which also includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Islamic Resistance network in Iraq, and previously the Assad regime in Syria, until its collapse in December 2024.
In response to the Israel-Hamas war, the Yemeni militia launched several strikes on shipping vessels in the Red Sea, disrupting global trade in late 2023 and the early months of 2024. The U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024 for a series of strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen in retaliation for the attacks on unarmed vessels. The U.S. carried out an additional campaign against Houthi targets later that year.
The Houthis entered the Iran war in March by firing a barrage of ballistic missiles at southern Israel. In the months since, the group’s advances along the Red Sea are widely considered to serve the interests of Iran. A Houthi blockade in the region against Saudi Arabia was declared in July, and several vessels have been attacked. The threat that the Houthis could bring another critical maritime chokepoint to a standstill, much like Iran has done with the Strait of Hormuz, could give Tehran significant leverage in its negotiations with Washington.
However, experts say it’s not entirely accurate to call the Houthis a direct proxy.
"The Houthis are one of the more independent regional allies of Iran in the Middle East. They have their own independent interests, even though their interests converge regionally and globally,” says Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
Even so, the Houthis have become increasingly vital for Iran. “With the fall of Assad, with the weakening of Hezbollah, the Houthis became the most important regional ally Iran has,” says Al Muslimi, pointing specifically toward the Houthis' ability to disrupt trade in the Red Sea.
What do the Houthis want?
The group’s goals have changed over time, as regional developments have unfolded, experts note.
“The Houthi's ultimate goal is to be a regional power,” says Al-Muslimi. With regard to the reignited civil war, the Houthis ultimately want an end to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory.
“The Houthis want to have the skies and the ports of the country open for trade, for goods and services,” says Gerges. “They want money to flow into the coffers of the Houthis.”
The civil war has had a disastrous effect on Yemen, with nearly half of the population in government-controlled areas facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the United Nations. “The current situation is very dire for the Yemeni population, but also for the ability of the Houthis to rule Yemen effectively,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis want to consolidate rule and regime. They want to be recognized as the legitimate government in Sanaa, as opposed to being considered a non-state actor,” he adds.
When did the Houthis and Saudi Arabia begin fighting again?
A cease-fire brokered by the United Nations in April 2022 largely held for over four years, before collapsing in July. The Houthis claimed Saudi Arabia had launched strikes on Sanaa Airport, targeting a Houthi delegation returning from Iran. In a move they framed as retaliatory, the Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia.
“The Houthis saw this as a golden opportunity to change the balance of power against Saudi Arabia and Yemen itself and launch a lightning offensive,” says Gerges.
Following further strikes on Houthi targets later that month, the militia group began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, belonging to the state-owned petroleum company Aramco.
In September, strikes on oil refineries and other related facilities ramped up, and Saudi Arabia’s airports became a target.
Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports?
Prior to the 2022 cease-fire, attacks on airports were largely considered a signature move of the Houthis.
In a highly-publicized attack, the group struck Abha International Airport in June 2019, injuring at least 26 people, Saudi authorities said. The strike earned international condemnation and was deemed a possible war crime by Human Rights Watch.
Now, after fatal strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the Houthis have threatened to keep targeting airports. The main motivation behind these attacks is the economic and geopolitical pressure they apply to Saudi Arabia, experts say.
“The Houthis want to put severe pressure on the Saudi Arabia economy, airport infrastructure, and security,” says Shehrah. “They want to squeeze Saudi Arabia's arms to push them to a political settlement.”
The unrest threatens to have a strong economic and political impact on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman's governance. The disruption is “costly” to him, says Al-Muslimi, who notes that Bin Salman is eager for Saudi Arabia to be seen as a “safe harbor.”
The financial and reputational damage of these strikes has also put the Saudi public on the frontline of the conflict. It’s a “shock, because it's the first time in years that such major attacks have targeted deep inside Saudi Arabia,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis are trying to exert tremendous pressure on the leaders of Saudi Arabia to force them to accept conditions for lifting the blockade on Yemen and recognizing their legitimacy,” he continues. “Although, I doubt that the Saudi leadership will concede to Houthi demands… this would be seen as a surrender and humiliation."

Thursday saw a timely withdrawal of the Summer Monsoon (Photo: PTI).
NEW DELHI: The southwest (summer) monsoon withdrew from the entire country on Thursday, exactly on the date of its normal withdrawal, while the northeast (winter) monsoon rainfall activity simultaneously commenced over part of south Peninsular India, IMD said.Summer monsoon normally starts withdrawing from west Rajasthan on Sept 17 and its withdrawal process ends on Oct 15. This year, the withdrawal started on Sept 19. Last year, the complete monsoon withdrawal happened by Oct 16.
A diagrammatic representation of the Southwest Monsoon withdrawal.
“With the onset of the northeast Monsoon, a wet spell with isolated heavy falls is likely over many parts of south Peninsular India till Oct 21,” said the Met department. The parts of south India that witnessed winter rainfall showers on Thursday include Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, south interior Karnataka and Kerala.IMD has already predicted a ‘normal’ winter monsoon in south Peninsular India during the Oct-Dec period. Overall, south Peninsular India receives about 30% of its annual rainfall during the northeast monsoon season (Oct to Dec). Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal receive approximately 48% of their annual rainfall during the season.
Normal winter monsoon rainfall this year may bring some relief to the region, which received the fourth-lowest summer monsoon rainfall since 1901 and the second-lowest since 2001.
Though the country as a whole recorded a deficit of nearly 13% during the June-Sept summer monsoon period — the fourth-lowest season since 2001 and 13th lowest since 1901 — the deficit in Karnataka was as high as 30% followed by 28% in Kerala, 25% in Andhra Pradesh and 20% in Tamil Nadu.

Germany's trade deficit with China set to hit record as automotive surplus collapses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Germany's trade deficit with China is expected to exceed €100 billion ($112 billion) for the first time this year, driven by widening imbalances in key industrial sectors, the German Economic Institute (IW) said Thursday.
The deficit would be more than seven times its 2019 level of €14.1 billion if trade trends from the first half of 2026 continue through the rest of the year, the institute said.
Germany imported almost 2.5 times as much from China as it exported to the country in the first six months. The projected annual deficit would surpass the previous record of about €90 billion in 2025.
German goods exports to China are projected to be roughly 25% below their 2019 level, while imports from China are expected to be about 62% higher.
Core industrial sectors under pressure
The automotive industry accounts for almost 24% of the projected increase in the deficit since 2019, making it the largest individual contributor.
Germany's automotive trade surplus with China is expected to shrink from more than €23 billion in 2019 to about €1 billion this year. Automotive exports to China are projected to fall 54% over that period, while imports of Chinese vehicles and parts are expected to rise more than 475%.
The trade deficit in electrical equipment is forecast to exceed €24 billion, compared with €4.8 billion in 2019.
Machinery manufacturing is also expected to record its first trade deficit with China, at slightly more than €1 billion, reversing a surplus of nearly €10 billion in 2019.
Energy-intensive industries, including chemicals, paper, glass and metals, account for only around €4 billion of the widening gap, IW said, arguing that higher energy costs explain only a small part of the deterioration.
The institute attributed the shift to China's technological advances and what it described as competitive distortions, including substantial subsidies and a sharply undervalued currency.
IW foreign trade expert Jurgen Matthes called for domestic reforms and broad countervailing tariffs that could be implemented quickly.
He urged the European Council to ask the European Commission to develop a new trade instrument, arguing that such measures would restore fair competition.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence has received 389 applications from foreign manufacturers of military equipment and weapons seeking to register on TrophyLab, a unified web portal for research into Russian equipment.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Details: More than 650 applications have been submitted in total. Ukrainian manufacturers, military units and government institutions can also register on the portal.
The Defence Ministry said TrophyLab contains data on captured Russian weapons that engineers, scientists and defence technology manufacturers in Ukraine and partner countries can use.
The database is populated by units of Ukraine's defence forces, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Security Service of Ukraine and specialised research institutions.
"Every registered researcher can request a sample or a fragment of it for independent study," the ministry said.
Users can access research findings online or request weapon samples for offline analysis.
To gain access to TrophyLab, applicants must complete a form on the platform's website. The Defence Ministry explained that applicants are screened for links to Russia, Ukrainian or international sanctions, and compliance with other mandatory criteria.
Once they pass the checks, users gain access to the catalogue of Russian weapons and the findings of research into them.
The Defence Ministry said that access to TrophyLab enables faster and safer exchanges of information on Russian weapons, helping accelerate the development of effective countermeasures for Ukraine's defence forces. It also contributes to international security and strengthens the defence capabilities of partner countries.
Background:
- As of late August, more than 130 Ukrainian weapons manufacturers and over 300 foreign companies had applied for access to TrophyLab.
- The platform was launched in June 2026 to facilitate research into Russian weapons.

Can pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers get vaccinated against influenza: a doctor&apos;s answer
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:38:49 EEST
22:38:49 KST

Can pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers get vaccinated against influenza: a doctor's answer
Kyiv • UNN
The WHO recommends that pregnant women receive an inactivated influenza vaccine in any trimester. The vaccine also protects the infant after birth.
Autumn is the period when the incidence of acute respiratory infections begins to rise. Changes in weather conditions and shorter daylight hours, people spending more time indoors, and inadequate ventilation of homes due to the drop in air temperature—all of this creates favorable conditions for viruses to circulate and contributes to weakened local immunity (drying of the mucous membranes of the nose and throat). As a result, they perform their protective function less effectively, allowing viruses to enter the body more easily and cause seasonal infectious diseases, one of the most dangerous of which is influenza, writes UNN.
The best time to get vaccinated against influenza is before the peak incidence of acute respiratory viral infections.
Usually, the influenza vaccination period begins in September–October. However, if patients did not manage to get vaccinated within the aforementioned period, they can still do so later, throughout the entire period of virus circulation. Revaccination is carried out once a year because the influenza virus constantly mutates, and the composition of vaccines is updated annually in accordance with the projected strains.
Particular attention should be paid to influenza prevention among pregnant women and women who have recently given birth and are breastfeeding. A number of physiological changes that occur in a pregnant woman’s body make them more vulnerable to severe disease and increase the risk of complications
Do pregnant women need to be vaccinated against influenza?
"Absolutely yes!" the doctor says.
According to WHO recommendations, pregnant women belong to the priority groups for influenza vaccination. According to a study by the CDC (the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), influenza vaccination during pregnancy reduced the risk of hospitalization due to influenza by an average of 40%.
Vaccination is safe for both the expectant mother and the child
Vaccination during pregnancy is completely safe because only inactivated vaccines, which do not contain live virus, are used. Such vaccines may be administered during any trimester of pregnancy, even at a very early stage
In addition, according to the doctor, special attention should be paid to the fact that vaccination during pregnancy protects not only the woman but also the future newborn child.
After vaccination, antibodies are formed in the mother’s blood, protecting her body from developing the disease. These same antibodies enter the child’s body through the placenta via the bloodstream and continue circulating in the infant’s body after birth, providing passive immune protection during the first months of life. And since children can be vaccinated against influenza from the age of 6 months, your baby will be protected until then
Mothers who are breastfeeding can also get vaccinated against influenza
Yes! Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination. It is safe for both the mother and the infant, again because an inactivated vaccine that does not contain live virus is administered. Vaccination does not negatively affect the quality of breast milk and does not require a temporary interruption of breastfeeding or expressing milk in advance of vaccination. Antibodies produced in the mother’s body after vaccination partially pass into breast milk and provide additional immune protection for the child
The influenza virus poses significant risks to the health of the woman and the fetus
Influenza during pregnancy poses a significant threat, the doctor explains, because the immune, respiratory, and cardiovascular systems operate under increased strain.
A pregnant woman becomes significantly more vulnerable to a severe course of the disease, with a considerably higher risk of complications. After entering the human body, the virus rapidly spreads throughout the body, the protective barrier of the respiratory tract’s mucous membranes breaks down, creating favorable conditions for the subsequent attachment of bacterial pathogens—pneumococcus, staphylococcus, etc. Speaking about the risks directly for a pregnant woman, these may include complications such as pneumonia and respiratory failure, as well as exacerbation of existing chronic diseases, such as asthma or cardiovascular disease
According to her, the high fever and intoxication that most often accompany influenza cause dehydration, which negatively affects the woman’s general condition and disrupts placental blood flow.
There is a threat of impaired placental function and, as a consequence, this may cause oxygen deprivation in the fetus (hypoxia), intrauterine growth restriction, and the risk of premature birth. Infection with the influenza virus is especially dangerous during the first trimester, before 12 weeks of pregnancy
This is explained by the fact that it is during this stage of pregnancy that the main process of laying down all the organs and systems in the fetus takes place.
High fever and intoxication can negatively affect these processes and cause the development of congenital defects in the fetus (neural tube defects, anterior abdominal wall defects, heart defects, etc.) or even lead to spontaneous miscarriage
The doctor emphasized the dangers of self-medication, since, while trying to reduce their fever or treat other flu symptoms on their own, pregnant women often begin using vasoconstrictor drops or anti-inflammatory medications. These drugs increase the risk of fetal abdominal wall defects during the first trimester.
The best decision is to immediately contact the obstetrician-gynecologist with whom you are registered, or a family doctor/therapist, at the first symptoms of a cold so that appropriate treatment can be prescribed based on your stage of pregnancy and clinical presentation

Turkish army gets three more E-ZPT electric armored carriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:38:48 UTC
22:38:48 KST

- MKE delivered three more E-ZPT electric armored personnel carriers, rebuilt from M113s, to the Turkish Land Forces Command on Oct. 15.
- The E-ZPT carries seven people, travels about 150 km on battery power and up to 650 km with its onboard generator.
Türkiye’s state-owned defense company MKE has delivered three more E-ZPT electric armored personnel carriers to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a small fleet of rebuilt M113s that run on battery power instead of a diesel engine alone.
MKE announced the handover in a post on X on Oct. 15, describing the E-ZPT as Türkiye’s first electric armored personnel carrier. The company said the vehicle’s all-electric drive gives it lower acoustic and thermal signatures, making it harder for enemy troops and sensors to hear or spot, and that maintenance and repair costs are lower than for conventional vehicles.
The E-ZPT is a modernized version of the M113, the tracked American-designed troop carrier that has served in the Turkish military for decades. MKE kept the original armored hull and replaced the powertrain with electric motors fed by battery packs mounted on both sides of the vehicle, an approach that lets the army reuse existing hulls.
On battery power alone, the vehicle can travel about 150 km (93 miles), Turdef reported, and an onboard diesel generator that recharges the batteries on the move stretches total range to 650 km (404 miles). MKE said fast charging takes the batteries from 20% to 80% in 1.5 hours. The E-ZPT carries seven people, including a driver, a commander, a gunner and four more crew members, and is armed with a 12.7 mm remote-controlled weapon station.
The vehicle has a combat weight of around 15 tonnes and can carry 2.5 tonnes of payload. Before acceptance, MKE put it through a qualification program that began in October 2024 and covered about 3,000 km (1,860 miles) of driving on asphalt and off-road terrain, along with climbs on 60% gradients, 30% side slopes, trench crossings and testing in hot and cold weather.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defense announced the delivery of the first serial-production E-ZPT in January 2026, and MKE handed over its first batch of three vehicles to the Land Forces in July. The program calls for 50 E-ZPTs in total, C Savunma reported, and MKE has also developed an armed version of the electric M113 called the E-ZMA.
With the latest handover, MKE has now delivered two batches of three E-ZPTs to the Turkish Land Forces this year, as it works toward the planned fleet of 50 electric carriers.

European Parliament chief says proposed EU budget cuts 'don't fly' amid growing challenges
Unknown

2026-10-15

Melike Pala
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola on Thursday criticized proposed cuts in the EU's next long-term budget, saying reductions in funding for civil protection, research and strategic infrastructure, and defense were incompatible with the bloc's growing challenges.
Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, Metsola warned that the proposed cuts risk undermining the balance between new priorities and traditional EU policies.
"We cannot agree on Europe's ambitions and then cut the means to achieve them," she said.
Metsola highlighted a proposed 35% cut to civil protection funding, a 10% cut to the Horizon research programme, and a 14% cut to funding for strategic infrastructure and defense.
"This, in our opinion, doesn't fly for us," she said.
Her remarks came amid an ongoing dispute between member states and the European Parliament on the bloc's next multiannual financial framework (MFF), with disagreements about funding priorities and how to finance the union's growing ambitions.
The EU aims to reach a political agreement on the 2028-2034 MFF by the end of 2026, allowing the necessary legislative acts to be adopted in 2027 and ensuring the new budget takes effect Jan. 1, 2028.
Deep divisions among member states and disagreements with parliament, however, could complicate the timeline.
Metsola said parliament was ready to work with EU leaders to reach a compromise but stressed that lawmakers would not simply endorse an agreement reached by member states.
"The parliament is not a rubber stamp and never will be," she said, adding that securing the necessary majority in the assembly would be challenging.
She noted that approving the next long-term budget would require 361 votes in parliament, stressing that any agreement must have the support of directly elected representatives.
Metsola also urged the introduction of new EU resources to help finance the next budget, saying it would ease pressure on national budgets and prevent the financial burden from being passed on to future generations.

Why Azerbaijan, Bahrain's Baku meetings with President Herzog are important - analysis

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog met in Baku on Wednesday with Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani during his attendance at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
These meetings, of importance for Israel, come amid a number of diplomatic and other recent successes, such as Colombia inaugurating its embassy in Jerusalem. Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar came to Israel for the event. Additionally, on October 8, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with Paraguay's Vice President, Pedro Alliana, in Jerusalem.
These are historic days for the Jewish state. Three years after the October 7 attacks, Israel is increasing its engagement with several countries. This comes as the media discusses whether fighting will resume against the Islamic Republic. In this context, the meetings between Herzog and the president of Azerbaijan, as well as Bahrain’s foreign minister, are important. Azerbaijan is a rising power in the Caucasus, with influence that extends to Europe, Central Asia, and beyond. It also borders Iran.
Bahrain is an important Gulf country. It joined the Abraham Accords in 2020. About the Wednesday meeting between Herzog and Aliyev, the President’s Office, in a statement distributed by Israel’s Government press Office, noted that Herzog had attended the summit “at the invitation of President Aliyev” and that he “thanked President Aliyev for the warm welcome and noted that Azerbaijan is a model of stability and an important and respected voice in the international community.”
Azerbaijan is an important country for many reasons
The leaders looked at “ways to deepen the strategic relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan, which is rooted in mutual respect, shared interests, and the deep historical ties between the two peoples. They also discussed recent regional developments and their countries’ shared commitment to stability and security in the region.”
Azerbaijan is strategically important: It has been reaching out to Syria recently, and it is a close friend of Turkey’s. Turkey has tended to be critical of Israel; and Israel has concerns about Turkey’s role in Syria. Baku can potentially play an important role in reducing tensions between the two.
Herzog’s office noted that “President Aliyev thanked President Herzog for his words of appreciation regarding Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of CICA, and emphasized that his country continues to work to strengthen mutual trust among CICA member states and to advance practical cooperation between them.”
Herzog said, “Israel and Azerbaijan share a unique relationship, one that has been developed over many years and has proven its importance in complex times as well. I thank President Ilham Aliyev for our partnership and for the open dialogue between us, and I believe we have much more to achieve together: strengthening the ties between our peoples, expanding our cooperation, and creating new opportunities for generations to come.”
In the meeting with Bahrain, Herzog also brought up the importance of strengthening the Abraham Accords. The October 7 massacre and the ensuing Israel-Hamas War created a backdrop against which it was difficult for expansion of the accords to take place. Currently, though, there are many opportunities.
“President Herzog emphasized the great importance Israel attaches to its relations with the Kingdom of Bahrain and commended the courageous leadership of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and the Government of Bahrain. The President conveyed his warmest wishes to His Majesty the King and the Bahraini people,” Herzog’s office said.
The important relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan
It is worth recalling the important relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan that has developed over the last decades. They established diplomatic relations in April 1992, shortly after Azerbaijan gained independence, following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The relationship expanded over the years: Energy trade and defense sales have been important building blocks. Azerbaijan has become a modern military power and has showcased Israeli defense technology during events in the past. In 2023, Azerbaijan opened an embassy in Israel. George Deek played a key role as ambassador to Azerbaijan from 2018 to 2025.
Bahrain-Israel ties are also important, though less in the spotlight than Israel-UAE ties or even Israel-Morocco ties. However, Bahrain is an important part of the Abraham Accords. It is a cautious country, and this caution means it is not often in the spotlight in the Gulf. However, it has also suffered from threats during the recent Iran conflict. Israel opened an embassy in Manama in 2021, following the signing of the Abraham Accords. Its first ambassador, Eitan Na’eh, was a former ambassador to Azerbaijan and Turkey – as well as Israel’s first envoy to the United Arab Emirates in 2021. (He died of a heart attack in January.)
There has been cooperation between Israel and Bahrain in recent years.
The meetings in Baku are important in terms of the larger regional context. Israeli defense companies also had a major role at the Marrakesh Air Show this week in Morocco. As such, there is a growing perception that Israeli ties with various Muslim countries are now improving and have become more public than they were in the past several years.

Israelis and Diaspora Jews are donating more since Oct. 7, says JGive founder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:47 UTC
22:37:47 KST

Charitable giving to and within Israel has not fallen since the surge that followed October 7, but has kept rising, JGive founder and CEO Ori Ben-Shlomo said on The Deep Dive this week.
Ben-Shlomo said the platform expects to finish this year at more than four times its pre-war volume, with over 250,000 Israeli and Diaspora donors giving about NIS 500 million.
"It changed society," he said. He added that Israelis now see civil society organizations as a "must-have" rather than a nice extra. Ben-Shlomo, a lawyer who was general counsel at a major Israeli media group, founded JGive after serving in Gaza as a reservist during Operation Protective Edge in 2014. There, he said, he saw how much donated goodwill was lost to poor coordination.
On October 7, as calls came in from New York, Los Angeles and London, JGive helped thousands of charities raise emergency funds. It also set up a national emergency fund whose leadership included a former Israel Air Force commander and a former Supreme Court justice. The fund began with basic needs, such as food, clothing and medication for evacuees from the kibbutzim, including Holocaust survivors, before moving on to education and rehabilitation.
The way Diaspora Jews give has also changed, Ben-Shlomo said. Their grandparents' generation wrote checks to large institutions. Younger donors want to give "without the middleman," to specific causes they have researched themselves, and increasingly alongside Israelis rather than simply to them. "Israel is not a young state," he noted. "We're close to 80." He said young people are now among JGive's top donors, the same group that major charities had once told him they could not reach.
Israeli elections two weeks away
With Israel's elections two weeks away, the conversation turned to Diaspora Jews who feel tied to the country's future but cannot vote. Ben-Shlomo argued that giving is "the best way" for them to have a say, and said it does more to shape the country than politics does. "Politics divides people, and giving connects people," he said. He also addressed the strain that rising antisemitism has placed on Jewish communities abroad, which must fund their own security while still supporting Israel. He said those donors have shifted the balance toward their own communities without stopping their support for Israel, and argued that the Israeli government and Israeli donors should now help Diaspora communities in return.
Ben-Shlomo described working with Israel's Tax Authority to introduce donor-advised funds, a tool familiar in the US, and to allow donations of stocks and other assets, which he called "a game changer." He said further reform is still needed, including ceilings on tax benefits for major donors. He framed the larger task as building what he called Israel's "fourth power." After defense, the economy and technology, he said, the country now needs the strength of a society "that makes sure no one is left behind," built from the ground up, much like the start-up nation.
Asked whether he is optimistic about the next generation, he answered with the story of a reserve officer badly wounded in Lebanon who, while still in rehabilitation, organized a campaign for a fellow patient.

Europe distinguishes Iranians from Iran. Why not Israelis from Israel? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:40 UTC
22:37:40 KST

Europe knows how to condemn a government without condemning everyone it governs.
When Iranians take to the streets, European leaders do not tell them they are responsible for the Islamic Republic. They condemn the regime and express solidarity with the protesters. Europe sanctions North Korea while speaking of North Koreans as victims of repression. It condemns Hezbollah without pretending that Lebanon and Hezbollah are the same thing.
The distinction has been particularly clear in the Palestinian case. After the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led massacres in Israel, the European Union (EU) repeatedly separated Hamas, the Palestinian Authority, and the Palestinian people. Josep Borrell, then the EU’s foreign policy chief, warned against collective punishment and reminded Europeans that “not all the Palestinian people are terrorists.”
Russia complicates the picture. Even before the invasion of Ukraine, the European Parliament distinguished “between the Russian people and President Putin’s regime.” After the invasion, ordinary Russians faced visa restrictions and exclusions from sports and culture. Still, European leaders continued to talk about Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war and Putin’s regime.
None of these comparisons is exact. Iran, Russia, and North Korea are authoritarian states. Hezbollah is a terrorist organization whose weapons answer to no electorate. Hamas won Palestinian elections in 2006 and has not faced voters in two decades.
Israel is different. It is a democracy. Israelis choose their governments.
And this is where things get uncomfortable
Across parts of Europe, Israeli universities are treated as extensions of the state. Israeli artists and cultural institutions face calls for exclusion. Broadcasters withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest because Israel’s public broadcaster, KAN, was taking part. There is growing pressure to keep Israeli athletes out of international competitions.
Official Europe is more careful. When European Council President António Costa supported proposed measures against Israel in September 2025, he stressed that they were “not aimed at the Israeli people,” but were a response to the government’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Outside Brussels, that distinction is less secure. In debates over universities, culture, broadcasting, and sports, the categories slide into one another. The Israeli government becomes Israel. Israel becomes its institutions. Its institutions become its citizens.
Why? The obvious answer is democracy.
ISRAELIS VOTE, pay taxes, and elect the politicians who govern them. Many serve in the military. Perhaps Europeans are, therefore, entitled to hold Israelis responsible in a way they would hesitate to hold Iranians responsible for the ayatollahs.
There is something to that argument. Israelis cannot have democracy both ways. We cannot celebrate democratic choice when it produces governments we like, and then pretend that governments we dislike have nothing to do with the society that elected them. The death, displacement, and destruction in Gaza resulted from decisions made by an elected Israeli government. European anger at Israel did not come from nowhere.
But there is a long distance between political responsibility and collective guilt.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested against the judicial overhaul. Israelis have demonstrated for the hostages and demanded accountability for October 7. Israel’s research universities went on strike against the judicial overhaul in 2023. Supporting a war does not mean supporting everything done in its course.
And what about the roughly one-fifth of Israeli citizens who are Arab, many among the government’s strongest critics? If responsibility follows automatically from an Israeli passport, where do they fit?
Citizens in a democracy have a relationship with state power. But they are not the state.
Still, democracy is not the whole explanation. Israel occupies a peculiar place in the European imagination. It is not European, but neither does it feel entirely foreign.
Much of its early political leadership came from Europe. Its universities, political parties, trade unions, legal traditions, and public culture were deeply influenced by European ideas. The Holocaust sits at the heart of both Israeli political memory and Europe’s understanding of its postwar self. Israel participates extensively in European research, culture, trade, and sports.
That closeness does not always work in Israel’s favor.
When many Europeans look at Israel’s rule over Palestinians, they see things they recognize from their own history: a powerful state ruling another people, settlements, contested land, and a profound imbalance of power. Much of the language now used to describe Israel comes from Europe’s arguments about its past: colonialism, occupation, settler colonialism.
Europe spent centuries ruling other peoples, building settlements, drawing borders, and calling domination civilization. Much of postwar Europe was built around the determination not to be that Europe anymore.
Israel, therefore, does something unusual. It does not confront Europe only with the Middle East. It confronts Europe with Europe.
Perhaps that is part of what makes Israel so difficult for Europeans to discuss. It is familiar enough to be judged by European standards, yet different enough to carry meanings beyond the country itself. Arguments about Israel become arguments about colonialism, nationalism, war, memory, and Europe’s own past.
The settler-colonial argument takes this further. If the problem is understood not as the policy of one government but as something built into Israeli society itself, the Israeli citizen becomes part of the structure being condemned. The distinction between government and people begins to disappear.
THIS DID NOT begin with Gaza. Before October 7, an EU Agency for Fundamental Rights survey found that 75% of Jewish respondents felt people held them responsible for the Israeli government’s actions because they were Jewish. The war did not invent this tendency. It intensified it.
Government becomes country. Country becomes citizens. Citizens become Jews.
Yet democracy should push us in the opposite direction. Elections create responsibility, but they also reveal disagreement. A democracy contains those who voted for the government and those who voted against it, majorities and minorities, supporters and protesters.
None of this means Israel should be shielded from criticism. Israeli governments should answer for their decisions. Israeli institutions should be judged for what they do. Israelis who commit crimes should be held responsible.
But responsibility should be attached to conduct.
That should also guide European decisions about “Horizon Europe,” cultural programs, universities, and artists. If an Israeli institution is complicit in wrongdoing, make the case and act accordingly. If an individual has done something that warrants exclusion, demonstrate it. Nationality itself should not become the evidence.
And Israelis cannot demand this distinction only for themselves.
Palestinians are not Hamas. Criticism of Israeli policy is not necessarily hostility toward Israel. Hostility toward Israel is not automatically antisemitism. If we insist that Europeans distinguish between Israel and Israelis, we must be equally serious about distinguishing between Palestinians and those who claim to act in their name.
Otherwise, this is not a principle. It is simply an argument we use when it suits us.
Europe knows how to make these distinctions, imperfectly but deliberately.
It should be able to make them with Israel too.
The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

‘Hope is still mandatory’: Israel’s resilience three years after October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:39 UTC
22:37:39 KST

Over two years into my second term as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, I have heard countless speeches and witnessed countless moments. But some words stay with you.
“Hope is still mandatory.”
Those words were spoken by Rachel Goldberg-Polin, the mother of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was murdered in Hamas captivity. A few months ago, we invited Rachel to address an international gathering of counterterrorism agency heads from UN member states in New York, making her the first Israeli to address the conference in years.
I remember listening to her and asking myself: After everything she has endured, how can she still hold on to hope? The answer became clear: resilience.
Resilience: The secret to holding onto hope after October 7
Three years ago, on October 7, Hamas invaded Israel and tried to destroy the Jewish state.
It murdered families in their homes, burned people alive in safe rooms, slaughtered young people at a music festival, and fired thousands of rockets at Israeli communities. It dragged 251 men, women, and children into Gaza and subjected them to unimaginable cruelty.
October 7 changed Israel forever. It wounded us. It left scars that will never fully disappear. But it did not break us.
Three years later, the defining story of October 7 is not only what Hamas did to us. It is the resilience we showed afterward. We chose to rebuild.
Resilience is part of our DNA. Our history has taught us that resilience is more than surviving tragedy. It is the strength to rise from it, rebuild, and choose life.
We have seen that resilience throughout our history. We saw it in the generations that survived persecution and exile. We saw it in Holocaust survivors who, after losing everything, dedicated themselves to rebuilding Jewish life and building the State of Israel.
On October 7, we saw that same resilience. Parents protected their children. Soldiers rushed into battle. Ordinary citizens became heroes, saving strangers and carrying the wounded to safety.
While Israel fought against its enemies, its people refused to leave its hostages behind. That determination showed who we are: a nation that leaves nobody behind. A nation that couldn’t move forward until all our loved ones came home.
Eliya Cohen and Ziv Abud exemplified that resilience better than most. On October 7, the couple was at the Nova music festival when Hamas terrorists attacked. They fled to a bomb shelter, where they faced grenades and gunfire. Abud survived by hiding among the bodies of those who had been murdered. Cohen was taken hostage and spent 505 days in captivity.
For months, Abud advocated relentlessly for Cohen’s return. When Cohen finally came home, their ordeal was not over. They had to begin the difficult process of rebuilding lives that were shattered by an experience neither of them should ever have endured.
And yet, they chose to build. On August 19, they celebrated their wedding and the future they had fought so hard to reach. Their marriage was not a denial of their pain or an attempt to leave October 7 behind. It was a declaration that what happened to them would not determine the rest of their lives. They chose each other. They chose a future. They chose life.
This year, I invited Abud and Cohen to speak together for the first time as a married couple at the United Nations. I wanted their resilience to be heard.
Their story is also the story of thousands of Israelis carrying invisible wounds. It is the families who spent sleepless nights with their children in bomb shelters, and the parents who still flinch when they hear a siren. It is the soldiers who lost lifelong friends and returned from battle with life-altering injuries. It is the families who lost sons and daughters and nevertheless found the strength to keep raising their children and moving forward.
Their sacrifices were not in vain. Three years after October 7, Israel is stronger than it was on that terrible morning. We have confronted threats from Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran, and other forces determined to destroy us. We have strengthened our alliances and expanded our circle of peace.
Despite these accomplishments, Israel still faces challenges. Hamas and Hezbollah must be disarmed. Iran continues to seek Israel’s destruction.
At the United Nations, the campaign to demonize Israel continues. The country that suffered one of the worst terrorist attacks of the 21st century now faces accusations of genocide, war crimes, and starvation. Those who should be defending the truth have instead turned the victim into the accused.
Today, we have one message: Israel is still here. We are raising our children, building our communities, developing our hi-tech sector, strengthening our alliances, and expanding our circle of peace.
After everything we have endured, we continue to choose life.
Three years later, we remember the victims. We honor the survivors. We stand with the families who continue to carry unimaginable pain because hope is still mandatory.
We do what the Jewish people have always done. We rise. We rebuild. And we choose life.
The writer is the Israeli ambassador to the United Nations.

Saudi Arabia could help unlock the next phase of Trump's Gaza plan - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:30 UTC
22:37:30 KST

In September 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the 20-point Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, which established a framework for ending the war, returning the remaining hostages, providing humanitarian assistance, establishing transitional governance, and ultimately demilitarizing Gaza and facilitating its reconstruction.
On November 17, 2025, the UN Security Council adopted this plan through Resolution 2803, which also welcomed the establishment of the Board of Peace.
However, nearly one year after the ceasefire, the UN reported in September 2026 that Hamas and other armed groups had not disarmed, the transitional governance arrangements had not yet become operational in Gaza, and the International Stabilization Force had not deployed.
The main obstacle has been disagreement over the sequencing and implementation of the second phase.
While the US and Israel insist on dismantling Hamas as an initial step according to the plan, and before a complete withdrawal of the IDF, leaders of Arab states maintain that the second phase must include immediate delivery of humanitarian assistance, rehabilitation of critical infrastructure, and a clear path to the two-state solution.
These gaps have created a significant financing problem, as the failure to establish the security and governance conditions has prevented reconstruction from proceeding.
On February 19, 2026, Saudi Arabia joined eight other founding donors in signing the Declaration of the Founding Donors to the Board of Peace.
Riyadh committed to providing core financial support to implement the plan and pledged $1 billion toward peace and reconstruction.
However, it has since withheld these funds, making full delivery of humanitarian aid and a clear path to a two-state solution preconditions for its support.
The impasse therefore threatens to prolong humanitarian suffering, delay reconstruction, and perpetuate the broader regional instability that emerged from the Gaza war.
Saudi Arabia is the country best placed to break the diplomatic deadlock and restore US credibility in the region. Saudi Arabia has agreed that proceeding to phase two won’t happen as long as Hamas holds military capabilities. Additionally, strengthening Saudi security serves a core US interest in regional stability, which is why the two countries signed the Strategic Defense Agreement in November 2025.
Houthis pose a threat to Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia faces an increasingly serious security challenge from the Houthis in Yemen. By September, the Houthis escalated attacks on Riyadh. While Pakistan and Turkey remained cautious about the extent of their involvement under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, Saudi Arabia may seek alternatives.
Since the US has already considered a military campaign against the Houthis, Washington should now go further and turn that readiness into a more strategic course of action that serves long-term US interests. It should offer Riyadh security guarantees that are stronger than the 2025 agreement and more credible than the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
In exchange, Riyadh would recommit to implementing phase two of the 20-point plan without further preconditions.
The subsequent escalation of Houthi activity and the abstention of Pakistan and Turkey from taking an active part in the defense alliance have exposed the limits of relying exclusively on regional partners.
Israel and Saudi Arabia have already shown an intention to collaborate and share intelligence against the Houthis. The US could exploit Pakistan’s and Turkey’s hesitancy by offering Saudi Arabia an alternative: a US-Saudi joint defense agreement that commits US forces to direct action against the Houthis while deepening the US-mediated channel for Israeli-Saudi security cooperation.
This course of action would demonstrate that the US remains the only credible security guarantor capable of assisting Saudi Arabia’s national security. A joint defense treaty with the US would give the Saudis the ultimate strategic “carrot.” This would give Riyadh the political cover to translate its commitment into concrete action on phase two of the 20-point Comprehensive Plan.
Bringing the US and Saudi Arabia into direct ties through a joint defense agreement could lead to the most desirable outcome in aggregate terms.
Sharing responsibilities with Israel, which has a strong incentive to eliminate the Houthi threat, the US could create a framework for gradual engagement, allowing Israel to serve as their frontliner in the Middle East. In other words, the US could devise a plan of escalating measures, providing an initial, indirect response through intelligence, weaponry, and advanced defense systems, while intervening actively only when necessary.
This framework could also strengthen Saudi-Israeli ties and improve the prospects for normalization, which Washington has declared a US national security interest.
Finally, by giving Saudi Arabia incentives to reengage with the 20-point plan, the US could restore the plan’s credibility, encourage other members of the Board of Peace to follow suit, and strengthen regional stability.
This course of action reflects the understanding that a two-state pathway is a possible outcome that should be discussed simultaneously through diplomatic means, but not as a precondition for implementing the plan. It depends on both sides implementing the plan in good faith, which would create the conditions for Palestinian self-determination.
The writer is an Israeli attorney and an MA candidate in international relations at Johns Hopkins University, School of Advanced International Studies, specializing in International economics and finance. The writer has a comprehensive security background, with about eight years of service as an officer and combatant commander in the IDF.

Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:35:46 UTC
22:35:46 KST

Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film
An Al Jazeera data investigation raises questions about claims that an Israeli counter-documentary to NAZA got 40mn views.
An Al Jazeera investigation has exposed holes in claims that an Israeli counter-film to the acclaimed documentary NAZA achieved more than 44 million views. By examining domain registries, web archives, source code, and three independent traffic tools, the investigation exposed the fabricated numbers adopted by official Israeli entities to promote the film.
The original award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers, accusing the army of using artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems to kill numerous civilians in Gaza. The documentary takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes. After winning the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the film was scheduled to screen in 56 countries.
Official backlash
The success of the original documentary triggered a political storm in Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants and prosecute them for information security violations.
The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, were accused of treason, and Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.
Network of domains
To counter the film’s global resonance, opponents created a counter-film. On September 16, just days after NAZA premiered, the domain nazadocumentary.com was registered via Cloudflare, with the owner’s details hidden.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine revealed the site initially disguised itself as the official NAZA website, listing the directors’ names and information on screenings and press. However, it described the film as exposing the systems behind the calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza. By September 30, this deceptive page vanished, replaced by a new title, “NAZA: The Real Story”.
The individuals behind the 49-minute counter-film are Ariel Averbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman, who claimed the work was self-funded. Later, two more domains, whatisnaza.com and watchnaza.com, were registered to redirect users to the counter-film.
The fake counter
By the morning of October 14, the nazadocumentary.com website’s counter displayed 43,758,421 views, without disclosing the source of the number or how it was calculated.
Public platforms told a drastically different story. The full 49-minute version of the film on its official YouTube channel had not exceeded 130,000 views by the same date. This means the website’s counter displayed roughly 336 times the actual viewership. The YouTube channel had fewer than 2,000 subscribers, and the film’s account on X had only 170 followers.
Independent traffic analysis platforms confirmed the discrepancy. The US-based platform Semrush estimated the site’s total visits by October 8 at about half a million. Israeli-founded Similarweb estimated only 326 visits for September. Furthermore, the film’s domains were absent from the Tranco list of the world’s top one million visited domains.
Discrepancies and code
An examination of the page’s source code revealed that the element displaying the huge number was internally tagged as “visitors” but displayed to users as “views”. The number is delivered directly from the site’s server, making its calculation method invisible from the outside. Upon opening the page, the counter begins at 97 percent of its value and counts up for three seconds, creating the illusion of a live counter.
Additionally, the site collects actual viewing data without publishing it, sending a “watch-tracker” file after about 25 seconds of video playback to identify the viewing session and parts watched, leaving it unknown whether the counter is based on this data.
State promotion
Despite the seemingly fabricated metrics, official Israeli accounts spearheaded the promotion of the counter-film. The Israeli Embassy in Washington promoted it on October 3 on social media.
Tzipi Hotovely, head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, awarded the three creators certificates of recognition for countering the original film. Hotovely said the film had garnered tens of millions of views, transforming an unsupported, fabricated number into an official talking point.
This elaborate digital campaign unfolds against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Since the conflict started, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen has been named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
The honorees were celebrated at a ceremony on Thursday at the FAO headquarters in Rome as part of this year's World Food Forum.
Yin has spent more than four decades combating desertification in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. After decades of persistent tree planting, she and her family have transformed stretches of the once-barren landscape into a green expanse, overcoming harsh conditions and shifting sands.
Her story also forged an enduring friendship with retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who raised 5,000 U.S. dollars decades ago to support her afforestation work.
Yin told Xinhua that the recognition had strengthened her resolve to continue her work. "Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination, doing my work well and giving back to nature," she said.
Sitting in the audience at the ceremony, Sakolsky applauded Yin's achievement. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," he told Xinhua.
Launched by the FAO to mark the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026, the global initiative recognizes 100 women for their outstanding contributions to agriculture, food systems and rural development. ■

World Insights: Black Sea drone attacks add to global energy, shipping strains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:34:07 CST
22:34:07 KST

SOFIA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A fresh wave of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, an alternative shipping route to the disrupted Strait of Hormuz, is deepening insecurity along the European Union's (EU's) eastern flank and compounding pressures on an already stretched global shipping network.
A San Marino-flagged vessel caught fire in the Black Sea early Thursday morning, with eight of its 12 crew members still missing, according to Romanian maritime authorities. The incident came just hours after a suspected drone strike on a Comoros-flagged tanker in Romanian waters on Wednesday.
Despite reports about drones detected in the area overnight, Romania's Ministry of National Defense has not confirmed the two vessels were struck by drones. However, over the past week, drones have struck multiple vessels off Bulgaria's coast, leaving 11 crew missing and 10 presumed dead. Both Russia and Ukraine have denied involvement in the recent attacks.
DIPLOMATIC FALLOUT
The strikes have triggered a diplomatic row. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has summoned Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova, saying that although there was "no conclusive evidence," "the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation."
Mitrofanova denied knowledge of the strikes and suggested a "provocation by a third party." Moscow rejected a limited naval ceasefire proposal brokered by Türkiye and the UN, saying it lacked guarantees against arms shipments to Ukraine by sea, and blaming Kyiv for refusing comprehensive agreements.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told British media that Kyiv would resume strikes on Russia's oil refineries, citing Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as violations against the U.S.-announced "energy ceasefire."
In response, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would "adjust our deterrence and defense posture as needed." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the Black Sea "another front of escalation" of the Russia-Ukraine war, which is "unacceptable." France and Germany also urged a halt to attacks on commercial vessels.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova and Romanian President Nicusor Dan have agreed to jointly push for an emergency item on the Black Sea at the European Council. On Thursday afternoon, the Bulgarian prime minister and the Romanian president met with Mark Rutte in Brussels for regional security discussions. The three NATO littoral states -- Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye -- have also agreed to boost surveillance and intelligence-sharing.
FROM ONE CHOKEPOINT TO ANOTHER
The attacks are compounding a crisis that began thousands of miles away. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil and gas supplies, has faced repeated attacks on tankers since late February. This has pushed some energy and grain cargoes toward alternative routes -- including the Black Sea corridor, now itself in jeopardy.
The Black Sea handles roughly 25 to 30 percent of global wheat exports, over 10 percent of corn and two-thirds of sunflower oil. Russia and Ukraine together normally supply about 27 percent of the world's wheat, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. Their combined wheat shipments from July to September were 6.5 million tons below the same period a year earlier, according to estimates from the International Food Policy Research Institute and the Agricultural Market Information System. Separately, Barva Invest has warned that up to 38 million tons of wheat and corn exports could be at risk in 2026/27 if deep-sea port restrictions persist.
"We see three concerning chokepoints right now that are driving up food prices across the world," said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the UN World Food Programme, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab Al Mandeb strait and the Black Sea. "All those three are causing disruptions to maritime trade, which is pushing up the price of energy and of food." Countries dependent on Black Sea grain, including Egypt, Türkiye and other parts of the Middle East, face the sharpest impact.
Insurance costs reflect the escalation of the conflict. War-risk premiums for Black Sea voyages have jumped from about 200,000 U.S. dollars to 2.5 million dollars per vessel, according to Lukoil's commercial manager in Bulgaria. Meanwhile, London-based insurance body Joint War Committee has expanded its high-risk zone to cover almost the entire basin.
"The Black Sea didn't become more expensive; it became just harder to access," Alexey Zavarskiy, a ship operator at Angara Denizcilik, said at an industry conference held on Sept. 22. He estimated that around 90 percent of shipowners had suspended calls at affected ports.
Washington's decision on Oct. 9 to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports illustrates the dilemma. On paper, it appears to be a release valve for a tight global diesel market: U.S. diesel prices are up 70 percent since February. However, the relief depends on a route that is itself under attack -- Russian diesel loads primarily at Black Sea ports such as Novorossiysk, the same waters where drones are now striking commercial vessels.
The first tranche of about 2.25 million barrels is less than a single day of U.S. diesel demand, and analysts from Quilter Cheviot to Wood Mackenzie have dismissed it as too small and too exposed to make a difference.
CALL FOR NEW FRAMEWORK
Military analysts warn the Black Sea has become one of the world's most dangerous shipping routes, with drone attacks having overtaken sea mines as the primary risk.
Retired Romanian Navy commander Sandu Valentin Mateiu told local media that the density of incidents pointed to a deliberate hybrid campaign. Mateiu said Romania should prepare a serious case for diplomatic protest, potentially raising the issue even at the level of NATO's Article 4. Poland took this step in September 2025 after drones violated its airspace, leading to emergency consultations and the deployment of allied fighter jets and air defense systems to the alliance's eastern flank under the "Eastern Sentry" mission.
Murat Ersavci, director of the International Studies Center at the Economic Policy Research Foundation of Türkiye, said the changing nature of the conflict is reshaping the Black Sea into a "multilayered security environment," with the boundary between trade and security becoming increasingly blurred.
Ersavci called for a comprehensive maritime security arrangement to ensure safe, predictable commercial navigation, distinguish civilian vessels from military targets, and coordinate efforts among littoral states to protect energy and food shipments.
Canan Tercan, a foreign policy expert at Istanbul Aydin University, warned that the Black Sea risked mirroring the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, and that navigational safety "must be secured through an international non-combat agreement, not through naval forces." ■
