Chinese medical team brings care to South Sudan communities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:52 CST
22:33:52 KST

JUBA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 14th batch of the Chinese medical team in South Sudan delivered healthcare services to communities at the latest weekly clinical outreach session on Wednesday.
Conducted at the University of Juba clinic in the capital city, the session benefited not only enrolled students but also vulnerable people from surrounding communities.
Sonia Laku, 25, a medical student at the University of Juba, returned to the outreach clinic for follow-up care two months after her first visit.
Laku sought pain-relief plasters for her knee. Although the plasters she sought were temporarily unavailable, doctors prescribed alternative pain medication.
"Whenever I come here, I find not only students but also people from neighboring communities. The Chinese medical team has been providing great services to vulnerable people who are unable to access proper medical care due to the prevailing economic hardship," she said.
Chinese medicated pain plasters are widely utilized to provide temporary relief for minor muscle aches, joint stiffness, backaches, sprains, and bruises.
Margret Tabu Tereza, an engineering student who sought treatment for a severe headache, said Chinese doctors reassessed an elderly woman who had previously been diagnosed with diabetes at a private clinic.
"It was my first time visiting the clinic, and I saw Chinese doctors helping our people. I met an elderly woman who had been wrongly diagnosed with diabetes. The Chinese doctors noticed the anomaly and rectified this grave mistake," Tabu said.
The medical team's evaluation found that the woman did not have diabetes, and doctors prescribed medication for her actual condition.
Alfred Angwet Gai, a waste management supervisor at the University of Juba, returned to the campus clinic for a follow-up visit after receiving treatment for severe chest pain in the last session.
"I came here last week with terrible chest pain. The Chinese doctors examined me and gave me medicine that relieved the pain," Angwet said.
He said the team's outreach efforts also extend beyond the university, bringing health care services to communities in other parts of the country.
Li Zheng, a gynecologist in the 14th batch of the Chinese medical team, said that many patients arrive with advanced or deteriorated conditions primarily due to delays in receiving timely medical intervention.
Individuals seeking care at the outreach clinics frequently present with a wide range of ailments, including chronic abdominal discomfort, joint and musculoskeletal pain, hypertension, and diabetes, Li added.
"We not only treat the patients but also provide them with medical advice on healthy living such as good eating habits and adequate rest," Li said. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Long March legacy takes root in greener landscapes of revolutionary heartlands
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:31 CST
22:33:31 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Perched on a hillside in Changting County of southern China, visitors soak in lush scenery stretching beside the glistening Tingjiang River.
But things weren't always so picturesque.
Changting, an old revolutionary base area in Fujian Province, was among the counties hardest hit by soil erosion in China's red-soil region, which threatened local people's livelihoods and left the landscape degraded.
Efforts to improve the local environment began nearly a century ago.
In November 1931, the Communist Party of China (CPC) established the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province, where the CPC put its revolutionary ideals into governance experimentation. The following year, it launched a tree-planting campaign to protect farmland from floods and droughts, reclaim barren hills and benefit local people.
During this campaign, CPC-led Red Army soldiers in Changting, which neighbors Ruijin, taught residents how to plant trees. In turn, residents brought food and seedlings to the soldiers and joined the planting campaign voluntarily.
"Even amid the turmoil of war, the Party still called for tree planting with great vigor," said Chen Liping, a researcher of CPC history and local chronicles in the county. "It reflects the Party's commitment to putting people's interests first and laying the foundations for future development."
As the war intensified, however, the tree-planting campaign had to be halted. The Red Army then embarked on the Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) forces. With some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers, the arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
As one of the starting points of the Long March, Changting has carried forward the Red Army's legacy in its decades-long efforts to combat soil erosion.
Tree planting, as the Red Army had practiced earlier, remained an effective method to tackle the problem. However, in severely eroded areas, ground temperatures can soar above 70 degrees Celsius, making it difficult for trees to survive.
Through experimentation, the county developed a phased approach suited to its natural conditions: first planting grass, then shrubs, and next trees, bringing the barren hills back to life step by step.
"Grass helps lower ground temperatures and create favorable conditions for other vegetation, allowing a mix of tree species to take root," said Shangguan Yuanbin, deputy head of the county's soil and water conservation station.
Over the years, local people adapted to changing conditions and met emerging problems with determination, patience and ingenuity.
Years of effort have paid off. To date, Changting has reduced the area affected by soil erosion by about 1.17 million mu (about 78,000 hectares), while its soil erosion rate fell from 31.47 percent to 6.31 percent, according to local authorities.
"Had we given up at any point over these decades, we would not have achieved such results today," said Shangguan. "We've applied the fearless Long March spirit to soil and water conservation."
Changting's transformation epitomizes a broader greening trend in China, which marks a national tree-planting day annually. Official data showed that between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation, while its forest and grass coverage rate exceeded 56 percent in 2025.
China's greening endeavor has gained international recognition. In 2021, Changting's comprehensive soil erosion control and ecological restoration practices were selected as a model case at the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP15).
But restoring the land is not the end of the story. The next challenge is to turn environmental recovery into lasting economic opportunities for local communities.
One of these places is Xikuangshan, an old mining area in central China's Hunan Province. During the Long March, about 1,500 well-disciplined Red Army soldiers were stationed there for a week. Through their words and deeds, they gained the trust of locals, who went from hiding from the Red Army to following it.
Dubbed the "World's Capital of Antimony," Xikuangshan has witnessed decades of intensive underground mining dating back to 1897, which led to vegetation loss, air and water pollution, and ground subsidence. Some even joked that "a white bird flying across Xikuangshan could turn black."
In 2004, local people mounted an all-out campaign for ecological restoration. Inspired by the perseverance shown by the Red Army, a research team conducted countless experiments and finally achieved a breakthrough in the treatment of harmful residue generated during antimony refining, a challenge that has long confronted the industry worldwide.
The once-scarred mining landscape gradually regained its vitality. The improved environment, together with its revolutionary history and mining culture, helped Xikuangshan to develop into a well-known tourist destination with around 300 million yuan (about 44.6 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue annually.
Yang Lijun is among those who have benefited. After more than a decade, he decided to return home in 2021 upon seeing his hometown's blue skies and clear waters. He rented an abandoned rural house and opened a tourist restaurant featuring local specialties, which now generates an annual income of more than 100,000 yuan.
"In the past, many residents, myself included, left home because of worsening environmental conditions," he recalled. "Now, with the environment improving, more tourists are coming, bringing new opportunities for a better life."
For places like Changting and Xikuangshan, ecological restoration is therefore not simply about bringing back greenery, but also about higher-quality lives and new development paths for former revolutionary base areas.
Earlier this year, China issued guidelines on accelerating the development of such areas, with measures to support systematic environmental protection and encourage eco-tourism.
For Yue Hui, director of the soil and water conservation center in Changting, the changes are encouraging, but the work is far from over.
"Combating soil erosion requires sustained effort. We will continue our march toward a greener future," Yue said. ■

TAIYUAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Congress of Chinese Archaeology opened on Thursday in Yuncheng, north China's Shanxi Province, under the theme of "Archaeology: The Past and the Future."
Scheduled to run through Saturday, the congress draws hundreds of archaeologists from home and abroad, featuring keynote speeches and 28 parallel sessions, with more than 570 academic presentations and 22 public lectures.
Yuncheng, the host city, is where the Xiyin site in Xia County was excavated 100 years ago. The site dates back to the Neolithic Age. The excavation unearthed thousands of pottery fragments and other artifacts associated with the Yangshao culture, which originated around the middle reaches of the Yellow River and dates back 4,700 to 7,000 years.
Led by Chinese archaeologist Li Ji and geologist Yuan Fuli, it was the first modern scientific archaeological excavation independently conducted by Chinese scholars, ushering in a new era for Chinese archaeology and becoming a landmark in modern Chinese archaeology.
Marie Louise Stig Sørensen, professor of Prehistoric Europe and Heritage Studies at the University of Cambridge's Department of Archaeology and a guest at the congress, said she became interested in archaeology related to the Yangshao Culture after working with some young scholars about the importance of the culture.
"It is such a fascinating part of our world history, and at the same time, its archaeology is so similar in some way to what I do in Europe," she said.
Established in 2016, the Congress of Chinese Archaeology aims to showcase the current state and achievements of Chinese archaeology, promote greater openness and international academic exchanges, and advance the overall development of Chinese archaeology. ■

According to a report from the Bed Management Office of Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, 53 patients were brought to the hospital, including 33 who died and three who remained under observation. Seventeen others were discharged after observation.
The hospital list included children aged 4 to 14, as well as a 25-year-old woman.

Cyber hit on a defence prime would cost capacity, warns MP
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:59 BST
22:32:59 KST

A cyber attack on the scale of the one that stopped Jaguar Land Rover would, if it struck a defence prime or a munitions supplier, take British industrial capacity out of the fight as well as money out of the economy, the Labour MP Graeme Downie has told the UK Defence Journal.
Downie, the member for Dunfermline and Dollar, was asked what an attack of that size against a defence manufacturer would mean for the country.
“I think the implications are the same, but with the added that you’ve probably taken down or reduced direct UK industrial capacity,” he said. “That obviously has a short-term impact, but also then huge knock-on effects to supply chain, availability of skills, raw materials, and lots of other things. So it would be a more direct attack, but it would nonetheless still have a huge economic impact, and then possibly knock on down to our industrial capacity.”
The comparison he was working from is the attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which his report identifies as the costliest cyber attack in British history. Downie said its effects travelled a long way past the company’s own balance sheet.
“What was striking is not only did that meaningfully affect UK GDP, reducing it by I think it was 0.1 per cent, in an economy that’s only growing by you know 1 per cent a year, that’s a significant number,” he said. “It’s noteworthy that it also affected Bank of England interest rate decisions and could have delayed an interest rate cut because of the performance of the economy. So not only was it costly to a large British company and all of the knock-on to supply chain and everything else, but that actually hit British mortgage payers potentially and cost them money.”
Asked what defence firms themselves could do about the risk while government works out how to measure it, Downie said the burden does not sit with them.
“I don’t think there’s anything defence firms can do in the meantime. I think at the moment this is something that really is on government to start publishing the cost of attacks,” he said. “I think there’s probably things government can do with businesses to not compel them to publish the cost of a cyber attack, for example, because that is difficult. But I think you can probably compel them much faster to have in place the right protections against cyber attack, and I think government just needs to be much quicker and more proactive.”
His prescription for the National Cyber Security Centre is that it should arrive without being asked, and leave with a number. “NCSC and other parts of government need to be much stronger at not only being there to assist when asked, but actually going in and assisting, not only to fix the problem as they did with JLR, for example, but also, while we’re here, we are going to find out how much this has cost your business, and then find a way to publish that.”
Downie’s report puts the cost of Russian hostile activity to the British economy at between £2 billion and £2.5 billion, a figure that excludes the additional defence spending the Russian threat has driven. He said the exclusions were deliberate and the real number is a good deal larger.
“What we did with all the figures was we took very conservative estimates because I wanted to make sure these figures were credible and were only what we could absolutely find,” he said. “I’m hoping that we will have more information out in the coming weeks and months as other information becomes available to us. I think it will be significantly bigger. But as I say, what’s important is that we don’t start spreading misinformation and unattributed sources. I think we’ve got to be really careful as we’re introducing this concept to the British public about how much Russian activity costs us.”
The Jaguar Land Rover attack halted production for weeks from the end of August last year and has been estimated by the Cyber Monitoring Centre at around £1.9 billion, the largest figure it has put on a single cyber event in the United Kingdom. Britain’s defence manufacturers sit on the same kind of integrated production systems, with the added exposure of long single-source supply chains for forgings, energetics and specialist components, where the loss of one plant for a few weeks cannot be made up elsewhere.
One of the four recommendations in The Putin Tax, published this month, asks the Ministry of Defence to begin costing physical attacks on British interests.

Kuwait drone shield to cover the sea as well as the air
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:41 BST
22:32:41 KST

The counter-drone system Kuwait is buying from the British firm MARSS will defend against seaborne drones along the coast as well as airborne ones, using sonar alongside radar and electro-optical sensors feeding a network of command centres, according to the company.
MARSS, an EOS company, will act as prime contractor and systems integrator on the £370 million contract, installing sensors across a network of sites that report into central command centres. Its NiDAR command and control platform fuses that data into threat assessments and provides what the company describes as hemispherical coverage against airborne and coastal seaborne drones. The contract also covers an initial supply of hard-kill interceptors and soft-kill jammers.
Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system. It is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Over the coming 24 months, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Doctor Andreas Schwer, chief executive of EOS, said: “Air defence is being redefined by the drone. Nations can no longer afford to answer low-cost threats with high-cost interceptors, and they need integrated systems that can respond faster than the threat. MARSS’ NiDAR is the intelligence layer in EOS’ counter-drone strategy, connecting sensors and effectors into a single, scalable architecture. Kuwait’s decision to deploy this capability nationwide shows where the market is heading, and it positions EOS as a leading provider of integrated counter-drone defence.”
Having both soft-kill and hard-kill effectors run through the same command system gives operators layered defeat options and a choice of response for each engagement, the company said, with NiDAR using AI to classify threats automatically and recommend an engagement, shortening the time between detection and defeat.
MARSS said the contract builds on NiDAR systems it has already fielded in the Gulf, which it said have been in operational use throughout the recent crisis in the region, and extends that approach to a national scale.
Delivery will be phased over 24 months and followed by a multi-year integrated logistic support programme. A training package running over several months will put MARSS personnel on the ground to train Kuwaiti operators across the sensors, the effectors and NiDAR itself, and a team will deploy to Kuwait for the duration, with recruitment already under way.
The commercial side of the deal was announced by the Ministry of Defence earlier, including the £370 million value, the roughly one hundred jobs expected across MARSS and its British supply chain, production proposed for Bristol, and the contract’s place within Taskforce Sabre, the government and industry effort to help Gulf states buy what they need quickly. Britain has already supplied Kuwait with the Rapid Sentry ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country.
NiDAR itself covers air, surface, sub-surface and land, detecting, tracking and classifying threats and recommending responses, and MARSS says it has more than sixty deployments worldwide. The company has been working on AI-enabled command and control for around twenty years, including research with the European Union, NATO and defence agencies.
EOS is an Australian group listed on the ASX with divisions covering defence and space. Its defence products include remote weapon stations, high energy laser weapons and drone interceptors, and NiDAR sits inside that portfolio as the command layer. MARSS is exhibiting NiDAR at SOFEX in Jordan from 27 to 29 October, where it will be shown integrated onto vehicle platforms alongside EOS remote weapon stations.

What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:32:16 UTC
22:32:16 KST

What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service, to fight Russia.
Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service.
The Reuters news agency, quoting a source, reported that Kyiv is still seeking clarifications from Starshield’s parent company, SpaceX, as to why its service was disrupted between Tuesday and Wednesday.
Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has denied the company’s involvement and suggested only the US government could have disrupted it, despite President Donald Trump’s insistence that Washington is still sharing intelligence with Kyiv.
Here’s what we know:
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, an array of 11,000 satellites placed by SpaceX into Earth’s low orbit to provide high-speed internet connectivity even in remote areas.
Starshield, launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.
What happened to Ukraine’s access to Starshield?
On Tuesday, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian strikes, which hit the country with more than 100 drones and five ballistic missiles, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X. “Regarding this strike, unfortunately, there was no warning from partners.”
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (160km/h).
That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.
Officials said the restrictions also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.
Who controls Starshield?
On Wednesday, Musk denied any involvement in the incident, insisting that the service is “controlled by the US government”.
Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.
Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.
Last year, Starlink cut off access for Russian troops who were covertly using the service on the battlefront in Ukraine.
Is Musk supportive of Ukraine?
The SpaceX boss has shown an active interest in the Russia-Ukraine war since it began, but has not been particularly favourable towards Kyiv. In 2022 – just after Russia invaded Ukraine – he proposed a “peace plan” under which Kyiv would end its claim to Russia-occupied Crimea and would drop hopes for joining NATO. Zelenskyy criticised Musk’s comments, and tensions between the two have remained.
On Sunday, the billionaire, who is also the CEO of Tesla and owns X, said Zelenskyy “has gone too far”, in a response to Trump’s comments that the Ukrainian president should leave office.
On Wednesday, Musk appeared to blame Zelenskyy for deaths in the war. “And so the slaughter continues,” he wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”
Does Ukraine blame the US for restricting intelligence?
Ukrainian officials have complained that the country received no warning in advance of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday. Usually, the US provides crucial early-warning alerts that allow Kyiv to issue evacuation orders.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.
The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.
Why might the US restrict intelligence from Ukraine?
Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Trump took office last year over a host of issues, including weapons transfers and the US’s increasing closeness to Russia.
In recent weeks, Washington has pressured Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries to allow more oil into global markets. In particular, Trump has sought to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel facilities for the rising price of the fuel globally ahead of November midterm elections.
Trump said last week he had agreed to a deal with President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel stocks into the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions on Russian oil.
Zelenskyy criticised the move and said it would embolden Putin.
Over the weekend, Trump unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, apparently without consulting Zelenskyy, who told reporters the deal was “news to me”. Russia also did not confirm it. Angered, Trump called for Ukraine to replace its president and blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for global energy disruptions.
Ukraine said it had, in fact, refrained from attacking Russian refineries and would continue to do so if Russia did the same. However, Russian strikes have continued. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure had caused blackouts affecting 600,000 people.
“We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in the FT interview, confirming that Kyiv had subsequently resumed attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure.

Ex-IAS Divya Mittal launches own party: 10 civil servants who quit service to enter politics

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:31:31 UTC
22:31:31 KST

Mittal launched her party, the Jan Neeti Bharat Party.
NEW DELHI: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal on Thursday launched the Jan Neeti Bharat party and announced that it would contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. Her announcement comes nearly a month after she took voluntary retirement from the civil services, ending a 13-year administrative career to pursue politics independently.In a video message on X, Mittal said the party will focus on making people central to policymaking and ensuring that the government remains accountable to them throughout its five-year term, rather than only on election day."Politics rules over you. In Jan Neeti, you will be the ones who rule," she said, announcing the party's name and its decision to contest the state polls due early next year.
Her decision to launch a party of her own places her among a group of civil servants who left government service before their scheduled retirement to enter politics.Here are 10 former civil servants who made the transition from bureaucracy to politics before completing their service.
1. Yashwant Sinha
Yashwant Sinha resigned from the Indian Administrative Service in 1984 to enter active politics. He joined the Janata Party and subsequently became associated with the Janata Dal before joining the BJP.Sinha first served as Union finance minister in the Chandra Shekhar government in 1990-91.
Under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, he returned to the finance ministry in 1998 and held the portfolio until 2002, when he became external affairs minister.His political career also included membership of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Sinha later distanced himself from the BJP and joined the Trinamool Congress in 2021, before contesting the 2022 presidential election as the opposition's joint candidate.
2. Ajit Jogi
Ajit Jogi left the IAS in 1986 to enter politics and joined the Congress. He had served as a district collector before moving into political life and was subsequently elected to the Rajya Sabha.Jogi's biggest political breakthrough came in 2000, when Chhattisgarh was carved out of Madhya Pradesh. He became the newly created state's first chief minister, holding office until 2003.After years in the Congress, Jogi broke away from the party in 2016 and founded the Janata Congress Chhattisgarh, seeking to establish an independent regional political platform.His career stands out as an example of a former administrator moving from district-level governance to the leadership of a newly formed state and later attempting to build a party of his own.
3. Mani Shankar Aiyar
Mani Shankar Aiyar resigned from the Indian Foreign Service in 1989 to enter politics. He had served as a diplomat for more than two decades and spent part of his career on deputation to the Prime Minister's Office under Rajiv Gandhi.Aiyar joined the Congress and won the Mayiladuthurai Lok Sabha seat in Tamil Nadu in 1991. He went on to become a prominent party leader and served as Union minister for petroleum and natural gas during the UPA government.He also held the panchayati raj portfolio and was involved in efforts to strengthen local self-government institutions.
4. Arvind Kejriwal
Arvind Kejriwal resigned from the Indian Revenue Service in 2006 after working in the income tax department. He had become involved in the Right to Information movement and founded the non-governmental organisation Parivartan to address citizens' grievances.His political journey gathered momentum during the Ana Hazare-led India Against Corruption movement, which campaigned for a stronger anti-corruption law. In 2012, Kejriwal founded the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), choosing to build a political organisation rather than join an established party.AAP made its electoral debut in the 2013 Delhi assembly elections, when Kejriwal defeated then chief minister Sheila Dikshit. He became Delhi chief minister in December 2013 and returned to the post after the party's victories in 2015 and 2020.
5. KJ Alphons
KJ Alphons took voluntary retirement from the IAS in 2006 and entered electoral politics in Kerala. He contested the Kanjirappally assembly seat in Kerala as an independent candidate supported by the Left Democratic Front and won.Alphons later founded the Jana Shakti platform before joining the BJP in 2011. His political journey subsequently took him to Parliament, when he became a Rajya Sabha member.In 2017, he was inducted into the Narendra Modi government as Union minister of state for tourism, with independent charge, and also handled electronics and information technology.His transition from a civil servant known for urban development initiatives to a state-level politician and Union minister is an example of an officer moving across political formations during his career.
6. Satyapal Singh
Satyapal Singh, a 1980-batch IPS officer of the Maharashtra cadre, opted for voluntary retirement in January 2014 while serving as Mumbai police commissioner, ahead of the Lok Sabha elections.He joined the BJP and contested the Baghpat Lok Sabha seat in Uttar Pradesh in 2014, defeating Rashtriya Lok Dal chief Ajit Singh. He retained the constituency in the 2019 general election.Singh served as Union minister of state for human resource development and water resources during the Modi government's first term. Before entering politics, he had served in several police leadership roles and was known for his work in law enforcement.
7. OP Choudhary
OP Choudhary, a 2005-batch IAS officer, resigned from the service in 2018 while serving as Raipur collector to enter politics. He joined the BJP and contested the Kharsia assembly constituency in Chhattisgarh in the same year.Choudhary lost that election but returned to the electoral contest in 2023, this time winning the Raipur City South seat. He was subsequently inducted into the Chhattisgarh government as a minister.His career highlights the uncertain transition from administration to politics. Unlike officers who win their first election, Choudhary's initial defeat did not end his political ambitions. He returned five years later and secured a place in the state Cabinet.
8. Aparajita Sarangi
Aparajita Sarangi, a 1994-batch IAS officer of the Odisha cadre, took voluntary retirement in 2018 while serving as joint secretary in the Union rural development ministry.She joined the BJP in November that year and contested the 2019 Lok Sabha election from Bhubaneswar. Sarangi won the seat, defeating Biju Janata Dal candidate Arup Patnaik.She retained the constituency in the 2024 general election, establishing herself as a BJP leader in Odisha.Sarangi's transition was particularly swift: she moved from a senior central government position to an electoral contest within months of leaving the service and subsequently secured two consecutive Lok Sabha victories.
9. AK Sharma
AK Sharma, a 1988-batch IAS officer of the Gujarat cadre, took voluntary retirement in January 2021, around 18 months before his scheduled superannuation.Sharma had spent a substantial part of his career working in the Prime Minister's Office and was associated with Narendra Modi's administration during his tenure as Gujarat chief minister and later as prime minister.After leaving the service, Sharma joined the BJP and was elected to the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council. He subsequently became a minister in the Yogi Adityanath government, handling portfolios including urban development and energy.His move demonstrated how a senior bureaucrat with experience in the central administration could enter state politics and secure a position in the Cabinet without first contesting a direct assembly election.
10. Asim Arun
Asim Arun, a 1994-batch IPS officer, took voluntary retirement in January 2022 while serving as Kanpur police commissioner. He joined the BJP soon afterwards, ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.Arun contested the Kannauj assembly seat and won, entering a constituency associated with the Samajwadi Party. He was subsequently inducted into the Yogi Adityanath government.His political entry came within weeks of his voluntary retirement, making him one of the clearest recent examples of a serving police officer moving directly into electoral politics before the end of his career.
Bonus: K Annamalai
K Annamalai, a 2011-batch IPS officer of the Karnataka cadre, resigned from the police service in September 2019, before completing his tenure. He had served as superintendent of police in Udupi and Chikkamagaluru districts before leaving the force.
He joined the BJP in August 2020 and rose rapidly through the party's ranks. In July 2021, he was appointed the BJP's Tamil Nadu president, becoming one of the party's most prominent faces in the state.Annamalai contested the 2021 Tamil Nadu assembly election from Aravakurichi but lost to the DMK's R Elango. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, he contested from Coimbatore but lost to DMK candidate Ganapathi P Rajkumar.In June 2026, Annamalai quit the BJP following differences with the party leadership over its political strategy in Tamil Nadu and launched a new political movement, 'We The Leaders'. He said the movement would focus on "common man politics", challenge what he described as "cult and dynastic politics", and eventually evolve into a political party. He has outlined plans to contest the 2031 Tamil Nadu assembly elections.

How the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:31:02 UTC
22:31:02 KST

How the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point
DUBAI, Oct 15 - The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.
By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions, they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran's economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources.
The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia's prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb in the Red Sea.
Iran, under mounting economic and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington's strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage.
“The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability.
The Houthis have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends.
But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognised government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen.
A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks would continue unless Saudi restrictions were lifted.
The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that could undermine his transformation agenda, but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030.
The Saudi government media office and Iran's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran's behest, saying its demands were centred on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants' salaries from Yemen's own resources.
"Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else," he said.
FLAGSHIP CONFERENCES DISRUPTED
Saudi Arabia has faced a widening wave of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a strike on Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors.
The attacks have disrupted Riyadh's flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives to withdraw, and forced organisers to offer remote participation at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum.
The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire.
However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. "They reached a point of NO negotiations," he said. "They have no other choice except military action."
The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. "What the Houthis are asking now is a victor's peace," he said.
The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington's reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome.
SAUDIS HAVE MORE TO LOSE
At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS asked Trump for help to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while appearing to defer any response until after the US midterm elections.
The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defences, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favour them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group's advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake.
"Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure," he said. "They have so much less to lose than the Saudis."
Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis' campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula.
At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unravelling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran.
"We're heading towards the worst outcome imaginable," al-Muslimi said. "A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies."
He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. "The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone," he said. "They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war." REUTERS

Turkish army buys CAKIR ground-launched cruise missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:30:23 UTC
22:30:23 KST

- Türkiye signed a contract with Roketsan for land-based ÇAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, defense industry chief Haluk Görgün said.
- ÇAKIR is a jet-powered cruise missile with a range of more than 150 km and a 70 kg warhead.
Türkiye has signed a supply contract with missile maker Roketsan for land-based CAKIR cruise missile systems for the Turkish Land Forces, Haluk Görgün, head of the country’s Presidency of Defense Industries, announced on Oct. 15.
Görgün said in a post on X that the contract is meant to strengthen the army’s long-range strike capability, and that more than 200 subcontractors took part in the project, including nearly 20 large and medium-sized companies.
“We have signed the ÇAKIR Project Supply Contract for land-based systems to enhance the strategic strike capabilities of our Land Forces,” Görgün said, in a statement translated from Turkish.
Roketsan’s ÇAKIR is a compact, jet-powered subsonic cruise missile that can be fired from aircraft, armed drones, ships and uncrewed surface vessels, as well as tactical wheeled vehicles. According to the company’s specifications, the missile weighs up to 275 kg (606 pounds) on its own and up to 330 kg (728 pounds) with the solid-fuel booster used for ground and ship launches. It carries a 70 kg (154-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 150 km (93 miles).
The missile is powered by the KTJ-1750 turbojet engine developed by Turkish firm Kale R&D. Its guidance combines inertial navigation with jam-resistant satellite navigation and a radar altimeter, so it can keep flying on course under heavy electronic jamming. Roketsan says ÇAKIR can fly very low over water or follow terrain to stay below enemy radar, and that its airframe uses radar-absorbing materials. The family includes land-attack, anti-ship and electronic warfare versions with different seekers.
Roketsan carried out the first publicly announced ground launches of ÇAKIR in August, when two missiles fired from a mobile launcher hit separate land and sea targets, Naval News reported. Indonesia’s ambassador to Türkiye said the same month that his country had bought ÇAKIR missiles, and the missile has been linked to Qatari fast attack craft projects.
Görgün placed the deal alongside Türkiye’s other surface-to-surface missiles, saying deliveries of the BORA and TAYFUN ballistic missiles to the army are continuing while ÇAKIR and the land-based KARA ATMACA cruise missile add to the country’s deterrent. Roketsan made its first delivery of KARA ATMACA, a ground-launched version of the Atmaca anti-ship missile, to the Turkish Land Forces in April 2026.
He said Türkiye is expanding serial production of missile and air defense systems to meet demand from its own army and from friendly and allied countries, as part of a wider push to make the Turkish defense industry fully independent.
The contract brings a ground-launched cruise missile with a 150-km reach into Turkish army service alongside the longer-range KARA ATMACA and Roketsan’s ballistic missiles, with more than 200 Turkish subcontractors involved in its production.

US Ambassador Mike Huckabee held a secret meeting with an Israeli opposition leader just weeks before this month’s hard-fought Knesset elections, Israel’s public broadcaster reported Thursday.

Neither the US ambassador nor Eisenkot’s office issued an official announcement about the meeting, while the Yashar party declined to comment, according to the broadcaster.

Netanyahu also faces charges of corruption, bribery and breach of trust in three cases.

Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”
Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.
The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.
Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”
“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.
We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”
Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.
Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”
Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.
When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.
“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

Netflix to cut roughly 1,000 jobs, or 6% of workforce: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:29:48 UTC
22:29:48 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Netflix plans to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, representing about 6% of its workforce, as part of organizational changes primarily affecting its product, technology, legal and human resources teams.
Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters announced the reductions in an internal memo sent to employees Wednesday and obtained by CNBC.
The executives said the company needed to prioritize its staff and resources to support its entertainment ambitions, while maintaining that its business remained strong and growing.
Netflix remains on track to meet its full-year forecast and will continue investing in areas expected to improve its service and support growth and innovation, according to the memo.
Sarandos and Peters said supporting departing employees was the immediate priority, adding that notification procedures would vary by country and that managers would contact affected staff.
A Netflix spokesperson said the company had no further comment beyond the memo.
Netflix employed about 16,000 full-time workers at the end of 2025. The company is scheduled to release its third-quarter financial results on Oct. 20.

Polish seizure leaves UK out of pocket by over one million
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:27:11 BST
22:27:11 KST

Assets bought by the Ministry of Defence under a short-term contract were seized by the Polish authorities during an investigation into the supplier and could not be recovered, producing a fruitless payment of £1.039 million, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what the specific nature of the payment was, referring to the losses section of the department’s annual report and accounts for 2025 to 2026.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The fruitless payment of £1.039 million related to assets procured under a short-term contract let in line with existing normal processes. This included a due diligence visit to verify manufacturing capabilities, supply chain and deliverability of the requirement. The procurement formed part of a project involving multiple government stakeholders, which increased its complexity. The assets were subsequently seized by the Polish authorities as part of an independent investigation into the supplier which was unrelated to the Ministry of Defence’s procurement activity. As a result, the assets could not be recovered or returned to the Department.”
A second loss in the same accounts was also put to the minister, asked about the nature of the fruitless payment recorded against Project SERAPH, Mr Pollard said: “A fruitless payment of £1.354 million was made to Deloitte following the termination for convenience of the Project SERAPH contract. The payment was made in accordance with the contractual terms and was negotiated by the Department.”
Termination for convenience is the clause that lets a customer end a contract without the supplier being at fault, and the payment is what the department owed Deloitte for doing so. No explanation was given for why the contract was cancelled.

Accelerating US inflation fuels hawkish Fed expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:26:28 UTC
22:26:28 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gökkoyun, Dilara Zengin Okay
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
US inflation accelerated faster than expected and further cemented expectations that the Federal Reserve will hold rates this month before a 25-basis-point hike in December.
US monthly inflation rose 0.6% in September, and annual inflation hit a four-month high of 3.7%, according to the Labor Department’s data.
Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, exceeded expectations by rising 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% on an annual basis.
The Fed’s Beige Book released Wednesday showed price pressures remained and intensified in some regions of the country.
The US 10-Year Treasury bond yield rose 11 basis points to 5.33% and the 30-year yield hit 5.63% following the data release.
The US dollar gained 0.7% and reached 102.94, its highest of the year, due to the expectations of a tighter monetary policy environment.
Analysts believe the Fed may keep its monetary policy tight for longer to ensure price stability before hiking rates once more this year. But some said it is uncertain whether the bank will wait until December for the next rate hike.
While a weaker-than-expected jobs report showing 29,000 new nonfarm payrolls and a 4.2% unemployment rate fueled expectations that the Fed may pause rate hikes, the hotter consumer price index (CPI) data drove CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange) Group futures indicating a 67% possibility that the bank will maintain rates this month, alongside a 33% probability of an immediate rate hike.
The July and August nonfarm payrolls were downwardly revised by 60,000.
Market pricing suggests the Fed may hike rates by 25 basis points at its final meeting of the year in December.
Padhraic Garvey, head of regional research for the Americas at ING, told Anadolu that rising housing costs confirmed the upward risks to core inflation. But the overall economic outlook is not strong enough to prompt the Fed to hike rates in October, expecting a rate hike by at least December.
Garvey added that the sharp rise in gas prices was the driver of headline inflation, noting that food prices remained unchanged and price movements in health care, education and communications were more limited.
Steven Kamin, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, stated that consecutive monthly increases in core inflation showed that mounting energy costs spilled over into other sectors, and that geopolitical tensions could lead the disinflationary process to take a longer time to take effect.
Kamin noted that inflation is likely to ease once energy prices fall, adding that while Fed officials previously took a rate hike possibility in October off the table, the recent data may have brought it back.

The Africa Pivot: India and Japan’s Quest for Critical Mineral Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

A new axis is emerging in the global race for resources, and the Indian Ocean serves as a bridge. It is emerging as a critical corridor linking Africa’s mineral wealth to Asia’s industrial ambitions. Africa sits at one end of a strategic corridor, and its minerals are becoming the new terrain of strategic competition.
The continent is home to critical minerals essential for the global energy transition, including 55 percent of the world’s cobalt, 47.65 percent of its manganese, 21.6 percent of its graphite, 5.9 percent of its copper, and 0.6 percent of its iron ore. Africa is already emerging as a priority in ongoing India-Japan discussions on economic security and supply chains and, as the India-Japan leaders’ recent summit and the subsequent India-Japan Joint Declaration on Economic Security Cooperation confirmed, it now sits squarely within the partnership’s formal architecture. Backed by the India-Japan Joint Economic Forum, a new JETRO strategic report, and renewed focus on the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), India and Japan are positioning themselves to deepen cooperation in critical minerals, digital infrastructure, healthcare, green energy, and resilient supply chains across the Global South, seeing it as an opportunity for the next phase of investment. At the heart of this push is Africa, where the race for critical minerals is reshaping economic partnerships into long-term strategic leverage.
Forging a Trilateral Partnership for Africa’s Critical Mineral Future
India and Japan recognize the world’s growing dependency on China for critical minerals. China controls roughly 90 percent of global rare-earth refining and has also achieved a monopolistic advantage in development aid programs in Africa. This realization comes at a time when the new Trump administration, through an executive order in January 2025, titled “Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid” has suspended all U.S. foreign development aid, putting several welfare projects for African nations at risk. Given this situation, African nations are eager to diversify their partnerships.
In this context, India and Japan can step up to support Africa’s development in a sustainable manner. Institutional cooperation on Africa predates both the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) and the AAGC. In October 2010, India and Japan held their first Dialogue on Africa in Tokyo, launched after the Japanese foreign minister’s visit to India earlier that year. The dialogue sought to coordinate the two countries’ approaches to Africa amid China’s expanding presence, highlighting Japan’s financial resources and India’s capacity-building model.
However, a significant triangular relationship is reflected in an MoU signed in June 2025 between Pensana Plc and Toyota Tsusho for rare earth offtake. Toyota Tsusho, the trading arm of Japan’s Toyota Group, committed to offtaking up to 20,000 tonnes per year of mixed rare-earth carbonate from London-listed Pensana’s Longonjo mine in Angola, with processing at Toyotsu Rare Earths India (TREI) in Visakhapatnam before final delivery to Japanese magnet manufacturers. This represents a significant step in developing a global rare earth supply chain and strengthening and diversifying the broader rare earth value chain.
Similarly, the Mozambique LNG project, worth roughly $20 billion and led by France’s TotalEnergies, includes two onshore trains capable of producing about 13 million tonnes per annum. Within the Mozambique LNG project, Indian companies, along with Japan’s Mitsui, are already working in tandem on a major energy project in Africa. Indian state-owned firms ONGC Videsh, Bharat Petroleum, and Oil India together hold a combined 30 percent of Mozambique LNG, while Japan’s Mitsui holds 20 percent. This model could also be replicated in mineral projects across East and Southern Africa. While Japan has financed the expansion of Kenya’s largest port in Mombasa, Indian companies have contributed to related logistics and trade facilitation. India and Japan are also working together to enhance road and rail connectivity in countries like Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique.
The principle underlining all of these engagements is that India provides ecosystem know-how, implementation capability, and processing capabilities, and Japan provides patient capital, technology, and industry standards. Above all, producers in Africa are the core of the resource base.
In February 2026, Japan hosted the Japan-India-Africa Business Forum in Tokyo, organized by the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI) along with Nikkei. It drew over 2,000 participants from 46 countries and regions. The forum was held to discuss collaborative efforts between the public and private sectors of Japan, India, and Africa. At the forum, Japan launched the Japan-India Cooperation Initiative for Sustainable Economic Development in Africa. The initiative aims to encourage Japanese companies to concentrate their industrial presence in India to boost trade with Africa. It also focuses on expanding private investment, job creation, technology transfer, and human resource development in Africa. Through the initiative, Japan and India aim to strengthen supply chains by integrating the growth markets of India and Africa into Japan’s economic activities, with a particular emphasis on value addition in key sectors such as critical minerals.
In July 2026, the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit was held in New Delhi during Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s visit to India. The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) and the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) convened the India-Japan Joint Economic Forum, which brought together more than 150 Japanese and 80 Indian companies. The forum was notable for the explicit place it accorded to Africa within the India-Japan bilateral architecture, signaling an intent to move the relationship into effective third-country cooperation. Through these and other engagements – including the August 2025 Modi-Ishiba summit in Tokyo and the January 2026 18th India-Japan Strategic Dialogue in New Delhi – these two Indo-Pacific democracies have begun assembling a parallel, intersecting architecture for engaging Africa’s mineral economy.
India has been in talks with several African countries to acquire critical mineral blocks on a government-to-government basis. In August 2026, India resumed talks with Zambia to explore investment opportunities in copper and other critical minerals, as New Delhi looks increasingly overseas for raw materials to meet rising demand from its rapidly growing economy. In Africa, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia in particular can play an important role in meeting India’s growing requirements for copper and cobalt.
Africa has become a crucial partner given India’s need to diversify energy supply sources to achieve its renewable energy and electric vehicle (EV) goals and the government’s “mines-to-magnets” industrial push. With demand expected to rise nearly fourfold by 2030, and near-total import dependency on lithium and high-purity rare earths, securing diversified offshore supply has become a national-security calculation. India’s mission to build a sustainable future depends heavily on critical minerals. New Delhi’s approach is not built on “extractive models” but rather on long-term capacity building, skill development, and technology transfer to ensure that African countries develop a self-sustaining growth ecosystem.
India’s historical ties, along with its experience in trade and project implementation in Africa, combined with Japan’s strengths in finance and quality infrastructure, can provide an alternative development model in Africa. Tokyo has also been working since the 2010 Chinese rare-earth embargo to engineer its way out of single-source dependency. Hence, this will be a model in which India serves as the industrial concentration and logistics hub for trade with Africa while Japan brings capital, standards, and processing technology.
From Architecture to Action: Making the India-Japan-Africa Partnership Work
The architecture of this partnership reflects solid progress, but design alone does not translate into delivery. While India wants to keep mineral processing at home, Africa, through the African Union’s Green Minerals Strategy and national plans, wants to keep it on the continent. Japan needs access to resources in both cases.
The ultimate test of an India-Japan-Africa trilateral partnership will be its capacity to turn agreements into tangible projects while accommodating the distinct and sometimes competing priorities of all three partners. A Joint Working Group could help bridge ambition and delivery. With no formal group yet established, however, its ability to do so remains untested.
Whether the existing efforts translate into concrete outcomes will depend on execution. This includes whether Japan’s commitment of 10 trillion yen ($68 billion) over a decade through the India-Japan Strategic Investment Pact of 2025, and the critical-mineral, green-ammonia, and pharmaceuticals priorities, convert into bankable third-country projects rather than another shared vision document. There is a deliberate attempt to re-anchor the India-Japan-Africa relationship in a more coherent institutional frame, routing this effort through FOIP rather than presenting Africa as a standalone strategy. In this framework, FOIP has become the umbrella vision under which Tokyo and New Delhi organize their joint external economic diplomacy, from Northeast India to the Indian Ocean to the African continent.
Japanese capital, India’s industrial and digital capabilities, and Africa’s demographic and market potential are increasingly complementary rather than separate strengths. The strategic question is whether these strengths can be integrated into durable investment and supply-chain partnerships. The real opportunity is to turn that complementarity into an economic architecture, one that moves India-Japan ties beyond diplomatic alignment and toward strategic co-investment. Africa is emerging as the arena where India-Japan diplomatic convergence could acquire real commercial weight.

EC announces Special Summary Revision of voters' list in 17 states amid SIR row

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) has informed the states that it would be conducting a Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls in 17 states, including the poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa.In a letter to the chief electoral officers of the states and Union territories concerned, including Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa, the Election Commission said January 1, 2027, would be the qualifying date for the exercise.The Special Summary Revision (SSR) is intended to add eligible voters, especially young people and first-time electors, rectify errors in existing entries and ensure electoral rolls are accurate and up to date.The current term of the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly ends on May 22 next year. The tenures of the assemblies in Manipur, Goa, Punjab and Uttarakhand, which have 60, 40, 117 and 70 seats, respectively, are due to end on different dates in March 2027.Under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission is permitted to conduct elections "earlier than six months before the term expires".
Notice by EC
ECI's notice to states.
How's Special Revision different from SIR
While a Summary Revision focuses on new eligibles and routine corrections, SIR goes far deeper, involving statewide house-to-house verification, detailed scrutiny of entries, and large-scale data audits.
For instance, under a Summary Revision, a voter who has shifted homes must file a form to update their address. Under SIR, the Booth Level Officer visits that address, confirms whether the voter still lives there, checks if anyone new has become eligible, and updates the roll based on physical verification rather than waiting for the voter to initiate the change.The SIR of electoral rolls has triggered a political controversy, with opposition parties raising concerns over the deletion of voters' names and the possibility of eligible citizens being left out of electoral lists.The poll panel has maintained that the exercise is aimed at cleaning up electoral rolls by removing duplicate and ineligible entries, including those belonging to deceased voters, while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included.
ALSO READ: ‘Anarchic, immature’: BJP targets Rahul over anti-CEC protests; claims misconduct with women copHowever, opposition parties have questioned the process, alleging that the exercise could lead to genuine voters losing their right to vote. They have also raised concerns over documentation requirements, verification procedures and the possibility of disproportionate effects on vulnerable groups, including migrant workers, the elderly and economically disadvantaged people.One of the main concerns surrounding SIR is the potential deletion of eligible voters' names during the verification process.The dispute has also reached the Supreme Court, with petitions raising concerns about the manner in which the revision is being conducted. The legal debate centres on the Election Commission's authority to revise electoral rolls and the safeguards available to voters who challenge their exclusion.

Houthi attacks threaten to strain Pakistan-Iran relations: Analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:21:22 UTC
22:21:22 KST

Escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are testing Pakistan’s ability to defend a longstanding security partner without damaging relations with neighboring Iran, with experts warning that deeper military involvement could carry consequences at home and across its borders.
Islamabad’s dilemma brings together two relationships it has strong reasons to preserve – a defense and financial partnership with Riyadh, and cooperation with Tehran on border security, trade, energy and regional diplomacy.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Aug. 7, treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all three. This month, the countries agreed to implement their collective defense commitments amid attacks on Saudi territory.
“Pakistan cannot stay idle as it has committed itself to Saudi Arabia's defense,” Umer Karim, a doctoral researcher at the University of Birmingham, told Anadolu.
But defending the kingdom against the Iran-backed Houthis could undermine Islamabad’s efforts to deepen ties with Tehran and facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States, he added.
Saudi Arabia’s importance to Pakistan extends beyond military cooperation. Riyadh has provided financial support to help Islamabad manage pressure on its external finances, including a pledge in April of an additional $3 billion finacial assistance alongside an extension of an existing $5 billion deposit.
Iran’s importance rests partly on geography. The countries share a 909-kilometer (565-mile) border, making cooperation over militancy, smuggling and cross-border movement a practical security concern.
Relations combine cooperation with recurring mistrust. In January 2024, the countries exchanged cross-border strikes against militant targets.
Both have nevertheless sought closer economic ties. In August, they agreed to expand trade, improve customs coordination, energy cooperation and activate joint border markets, pursuing a $10 billion annual trade target and a free trade agreement.
Christoph Bluth, professor of international relations and security at the University of Bradford, described Pakistan’s approach to Iran as pragmatic cooperation combined with strategic caution.
Tehran was an important neighbor, he said, but not a strategic ally on the same level as Saudi Arabia or China. The defense agreement could create friction without necessarily causing a breakdown in relations.
“The decisive question is implementation,” he told Anadolu. “If it develops into what is perceived as an operational anti-Iran or anti-Houthi coalition, it would seriously damage Islamabad-Tehran relations.”
Iranian lawmakers have criticized Pakistan’s growing military alignment with Saudi Arabia.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei expressed concern this month over reports of a possible large-scale Pakistani troop deployment, adding that he hoped it was only a "rumor."
Bluth described Tehran’s response as divided. Some lawmakers had warned of retaliation if Iran were attacked from pact members’ territory, while the Foreign Ministry had indicated it did not presently regard the agreement as directed against Iran.
Pakistan’s leaders have sought to offer reassurance. President Asif Ali Zardari said Tuesday that the pact was “purely defensive and not directed against any country.” Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security the following day.
Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry has also said its forces would defend Saudi territory rather than cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis. On Friday, it said that Pakistan has deployed a “substantial” number of military forces and resources in Saudi Arabia.
Bluth considered participation in a ground war unlikely, with involvement instead potentially focused on air and missile defense, intelligence, training and protecting Saudi territory.
“Pakistan has agreed to provide rapidly deployable forces, but their numbers and precise mission remain undisclosed,” he said.
“A defensive role would cause tension with Iran but could remain manageable,” he added. “If it comes to direct operations against the Houthis, that would risk a major diplomatic crisis.”
Karim said Pakistan’s existing military presence in Saudi Arabia demonstrated its commitment to Riyadh.
“Pakistan's military is already on the ground within Saudi Arabia, which signifies Pakistan's resolve to stand by its Saudi ally,” he said. "It's only a matter of time that it will become whether directly or indirectly involved against Houthis," he said.
According to him, the Iranian side clearly does not view this positively and "is likely to express its disappointment mainly through unofficial channels and also by mobilizing pro-Iran constituencies within Pakistan."
Arhama Siddiqa, a research fellow at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad, emphasized the distinction between defensive cooperation and offensive operations.
“Pakistan has clarified that the agreement is defensive and does not envisage cross-border operations against the Houthis in Yemen,” she told Anadolu.
Instead, Islamabad has an interest in encouraging restraint and a negotiated settlement to prevent wider conflict and preserve constructive relations with Iran, she added.
The experts differed over how deteriorating relations with Tehran would affect Pakistan.
Karim argued that security conditions had already worsened on both sides, limiting the additional impact of a diplomatic downturn. He also expected relatively limited consequences for energy cooperation because economic links remained weak.
Bluth, however, warned that strained relations could weaken intelligence-sharing and border management, giving armed groups greater room to operate across the frontier between Pakistan’s Balochistan and Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan provinces.
“It could also aggravate sectarian tensions inside Pakistan,” he said.
Border commerce, local livelihoods and Iranian electricity supplies could suffer, alongside prospects for the Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline and wider energy cooperation.
The principal danger, Bluth said, was not conventional war but “a more unstable border, intensified insurgency and increased security risks for Pakistan.”
Siddiqa similarly warned that weaker cooperation could allow non-state actors to exploit vulnerabilities, while disrupting trade, border markets, connectivity and energy projects.
“The two neighbours face common challenges relating to cross-border terrorism, militancy, smuggling and border management, making sustained security coordination indispensable,” she said.
Neither country would benefit from further border instability, she added, stressing the importance of maintaining diplomatic and institutional contacts.
Pakistan’s role in brokering talks between Tehran and Washington, which led to the Islamabad Memorandum in June, gives it another reason to preserve relations with Iran.
Islamabad has served as an intermediary between the two sides, and Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said Iran reaffirmed its trust in Islamabad’s mediation during President Masoud Pezeshkian’s June visit.
But Karim said those diplomatic efforts were increasingly in conflict with the security demands arising from Houthi attacks and renewed fighting in Yemen.
Bluth argued that mediation did not require complete neutrality. Iran’s continued willingness to exchange messages through intermediaries, including Pakistan, suggested that trust had not entirely collapsed.
“Pakistan must keep its Saudi commitment restricted to defensive measures, maintain direct consultation with Tehran and support political engagement with the Houthis,” he said.
“If Pakistani forces participate in direct offensive operations against the Houthis or Iran, it is unlikely it can sustain its role as mediator,” he added.
Siddiqa said the defense cooperation did not inherently contradict Pakistan’s role as a facilitator. Effective mediation, however, depended on maintaining trust, credibility and open communication.
Karim was more pessimistic that Pakistan could act as a mediator while also engaging in the Yemen conflict.
“It will be extremely difficult, and eventually Pakistan will have to choose one side,” he said.
