Kallas: Understandable why Ukraine targets Russia's oil revenues
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas made the remarks ahead of a European Council meeting in Brussels, Ukrinform reports.
"The majority of Russia's funding for the war comes from oil revenue. So clearly, Ukraine wants this war to stop, and that is why cutting off the funding for the war is the way to do it," Kallas said.
She expressed her conviction that the West should "put pressure on Russia" rather than force Ukraine to surrender in order to end the war, adding that the EU was "very committed."
As Ukrinform reported, a two-day meeting of the European Council began today. Support for Ukraine is scheduled to be discussed tomorrow.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is due to address the leaders of EU member states tomorrow morning.

Representatives of several countries, including Türkiye, left the gathering hall as Israel’s president began his speech at an Asian security summit in Baku, Azerbaijan's capital.
As Isaac Herzog began his speech around noon on Thursday at the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) summit, representatives of more than 10 countries, including Türkiye, walked out of the gathering hall.
Türkiye’s delegation, led by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, along with representatives of 10 other countries, walked out of the room while the Israeli president was addressing the CICA summit in Baku, TRT World reported.
A similar walkout was seen at September’s UN General Assembly high-level week in New York during a speech by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister.
Thursday’s one-day summit, hosted by Azerbaijan as the current CICA chair, is bringing together representatives of member states, observer countries, and partner international organisations.
Discussions will focus on regional cooperation, connectivity, digitalisation, and sustainable development under Azerbaijan's chairmanship.
The summit is expected to adopt a Baku declaration and a statement on cooperation in occupational safety and health, as well as announce Laos' accession as a new member.
Fidan later said that Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) member states must take a firm stance in supporting the rights of Palestine, which is among the group’s members, as well as in opposing ongoing oppression and grave violations.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 wounded in Gaza in Israel’s genocide, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli raids and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property have also intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since then.

2nd week of Rafah crossing closure worsens crisis for patients: Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:16:21 UTC
22:16:21 KST

Jomaa Younis, kram Kouachi
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Israel has continued to close the Rafah land crossing for a second week, preventing patients from leaving the Gaza Strip for treatment abroad and causing a “dangerous buildup” of critical cases, the Gaza Health Ministry said Thursday.
In a statement, the ministry warned that the continued closure had led to a “dangerous and rapidly growing accumulation of critical cases,” with waiting lists for treatment abroad increasing by the day.
It said the number of people awaiting evacuation far exceeds the capacity of Gaza’s deteriorating and besieged hospitals to accommodate them or provide even the minimum level of treatment.
The ministry described the continued closure as a “grave violation of international humanitarian law and a deliberate deprivation of patients and wounded people of their right to treatment.”
It called on relevant parties to “exert serious and urgent pressure on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing and all other crossings and facilitate the departure of critically ill patients for treatment abroad.”
The continued closure comes as more than 20,000 patients and wounded people in Gaza await evacuation for treatment abroad, amid severe shortages of medicines, medical equipment, and specialized medical services following Israel’s destruction of the healthcare system during its genocidal war on the enclave.
More than 1,344 patients have died while waiting for treatment since the ceasefire agreement took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
On Feb. 2, 2026, Israel reopened the crossing on a limited basis, allowing small numbers of patients and wounded people to leave under tight restrictions.
According to Health Ministry statistics, a total of 2,480 patients and wounded people left Gaza through the crossing between Feb. 2 and Sept. 2.
This amounts to an average of about 12 patients and wounded people per day, compared with the agreed arrangement of 50 patients and 50 companions daily.
According to Health Ministry figures from October 2025, Israel’s war destroyed or rendered inoperable 25 of Gaza’s 38 hospitals, leaving 13 operating partially under difficult conditions.
The Israeli army also destroyed 103 of the enclave’s 157 primary healthcare centers during the genocide, while the remaining 54 continued to operate partially.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire had killed 1,501 Palestinians and injured 5,323 others as of Monday, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocide, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

How Chinese Clean Tech Is Reshaping Ukraine’s Wartime Energy Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine has shown that energy security is no longer just about access to fuels, pipelines, and large power stations. It also depends on solar panels, batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that can keep homes, businesses, and critical services operating when the electricity grid is under attack.
Ironically, most of the equipment helping Ukraine keep the lights on comes from China.
Beijing has maintained close strategic ties with Russia. Yet through trade and global supply chains, Chinese-made clean energy technologies are helping Ukraine reduce the vulnerability created by Russian attacks on its energy system.
Russia’s attacks exposed the vulnerability of Ukraine’s highly centralized power system. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that around half of Ukraine’s generation capacity was occupied, damaged or destroyed during 2022-23, while around half of its large network substations were damaged by missiles and drones. After another wave of attacks in spring 2024, Ukraine lost a further 9 GW of generation capacity, leaving it with only around one-third of its pre-war capacity. On January 20, 2026, another major Russian attack on energy infrastructure left almost half of Kyiv without heat and power.
Such attacks turned Ukraine’s large, fixed energy assets into major points of vulnerability, making energy decentralization an increasingly important source of resilience. Consequently, there has been a resurgence of solar power in Ukraine.
The country was already a significant solar market before Russia’s full-scale invasion, ranking ninth globally for new solar capacity addition in 2019. But deployment and trade collapsed after February 2022. Chinese module exports to Ukraine fell from 83.9 MW in February 2022 to just 7.5 MW in March, and totaled only 15.8 MW in 2023.
Since then, the market has recovered. The Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that around 800 MW of solar was installed in 2024 and 1.5 GW in 2025. Businesses and households have been installing solar power to reduce their dependence on the grid. Distributed solar PV, often combined with battery storage, has therefore become an important part of Ukraine’s wartime energy security.
International organizations, such as the IEA and the Center for Strategic and International Studies, have recently examined Ukraine’s energy reconstruction, covering aspects such as decentralization, solar power, battery storage, financing, and electricity-market reform. However, these reports tell us remarkably little about the sources of the equipment needed for this transition.
In particular, the role of Chinese-made equipment in this shift has received much less attention. According to the IEA, China accounts for around 85 percent of global solar supply-chain production capacity and around 80 percent of lithium-ion battery production capacity. Its share in some specific segments is even higher – for example, China supplies around 95 percent of global PV wafer capacity.
Currently there is no authoritative estimate on the specific share of Chinese-made equipment in Ukraine’s solar and battery markets, not least because some products reach Ukraine through third countries, international procurement channels, and aid programs. Still, given China’s dominance of these supply chains, Chinese-made equipment is likely to have played an important role in Ukraine’s decentralized energy expansion and will probably continue to do so.
This raises an intriguing question. Does China’s position in these supply chains give Beijing significant leverage over Ukraine? Could China, particularly given its close relations with Russia, use access to clean energy equipment as a coercive geopolitical tool?
Supply chain concentration undoubtedly creates structural influence. But as I argued in an article in September 2025 in The Diplomat, it does not translate automatically into the kind of coercive power historically associated with oil and gas.
In Ukraine’s case, three factors are particularly relevant.
First, clean energy equipment moves through complex international commercial networks. A substantial volume of Chinese products can reach Ukraine indirectly through third countries, distributors, international procurement, and aid programs. This makes it difficult for Beijing to control the ultimate destination or end user. Blocking such flows would require much wider restrictions and would be commercially and politically difficult.
Second, weaponizing clean-energy supply would impose considerable costs on China’s own industries. It could expose Chinese companies to greater regulatory and compliance risks while strengthening Western arguments for supply chain diversification, domestic manufacturing, and “friend-shoring.” In the long run, that could accelerate precisely the reduction in dependence that Chinese manufacturers would prefer to avoid.
Third, such restrictions would contradict Beijing’s stated approach to the Russia-Ukraine war. China has repeatedly called for promoting peace talks while maintaining civilian trade. Deliberately restricting technologies important to civilian electricity supply would be difficult to reconcile with that position and could carry diplomatic and reputational costs.
When it comes to clean energy, China’s industrial dominance does not necessarily translate into the ability to exercise political control. Global commercial networks can significantly constrain a government’s ability to determine where clean technologies ultimately go and how they are used.
A further question is how the Chinese government and Chinese companies might participate constructively in Ukraine’s ongoing energy transformation and eventual reconstruction.
The potential market is substantial. The IEA estimates that Ukraine would need to add around 4 GW of distributed solar PV each year through 2030 to build a more decentralized and secure electricity system while meeting its national energy and climate objectives. It would also require an additional 5.6 GW of battery energy capacity by 2030.
For Chinese companies, the opportunities extend beyond exporting more solar modules and batteries. There is considerable scope for cooperation in system integration, energy management, technology transfer, joint project development, local assembly and production, and operations and maintenance.
But such involvement would not be straightforward. Chinese firms would have to navigate wartime risks, technical standards, financing constraints, supply chain security screening, and an increasingly complex geopolitical environment. Companies seeking to participate will therefore need to create value locally, build trusted partnerships, and adapt to an institutional and regulatory environment, particularly as Ukraine becomes more deeply integrated into European energy markets.
Ukraine’s experience offers a broader lesson about the geopolitics of clean energy. Countries still need secure fuel supplies and reliable power grids, but they also need access to the equipment used to produce and store electricity locally. China’s lead in manufacturing gives it considerable influence, though not complete control. Once solar panels and batteries enter global trading networks, they can contribute to energy security in ways that go beyond the intentions or expectations of their country of origin.

US weekly jobless claims rise to 199,000, matching expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:15:12 UTC
22:15:12 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The number of Americans filing first-time claims for unemployment benefits rose by 1,000 to 199,000 last week, matching market expectations, according to Labor Department data released Thursday.
The previous week’s figure was revised up by 1,000 to 198,000 from 197,000.
The four-week moving average, which smooths out weekly fluctuations, increased by 250 to 198,500 in the week ending Oct. 10. The previous week’s average was revised up by 250 to 198,250.
Continuing claims, which measure the number of people already receiving unemployment benefits, fell by 4,000 to 1.71 million in the week ending Oct. 3.
The previous week’s continuing claims figure was revised down by 2,000 to 1.714 million.
The four-week moving average of continuing claims declined by 1,750 to 1,708,750.
The seasonally adjusted insured unemployment rate remained unchanged at 1.1% for the week ending Oct. 3.
In September, the US economy added just 29,000 nonfarm jobs, well below forecasts of 90,000, according to an earlier Bureau of Labor Statistics report.
The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.

Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:14:50 UTC
22:14:50 KST

Nearly a year after the UN Security Council endorsed the Board of Peace to oversee Gaza’s transition, questions over who controls it, and in whose interest, have not gone away. For Anouar El Gharbi, president of the Geneva Centre for Democracy and Human Rights (GCDHR), the problem begins with the Board’s origin. It was not born of an independent international process grounded in the freely expressed will of the Palestinian people, he told MEMO in an interview, but of a political initiative led by the US. That origin, he argues, shapes everything that follows: the scope of the Board’s mandate, the powers it holds and the people it answers to.
The Board emerged from the “Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict” advanced by US President Donald Trump. The Security Council endorsed the plan on 17 November 2025 through Resolution 2803, adopted by 13 votes with Russia and China abstaining. The resolution recognised the Board as a transitional administration with international legal personality and authorised a set of operational arrangements on the ground.
El Gharbi rejects any suggestion that this grants the Board permission to place itself above the law. Its work, he insists, “must respect the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, the prohibition on acquiring territory by force and the obligations of international humanitarian law”.
Asked whether the backing of the Security Council settles the question of legitimacy, he points to the sequence of events in the formation of the board. “Washington designed the initiative and shaped the framework under which the Board operates, and the Council’s endorsement came afterwards.” This, he says, “raises serious questions about the Board’s independence, about how far Palestinians take part in its decisions and about whether there is adequate international oversight to hold it to account”.
El Gharbi draws a clear distinction. A temporary international framework to support reconstruction, humanitarian aid and transitional administration is one thing; a political trusteeship over Gaza is another. The right to self-determination, he says, belongs to Palestinians, and no outside power can exercise it on their behalf.
READ: Trump’s Gaza board accused of creating legal black hole to protect officials and contractors
International law, El Gharbi explains, gives no state or international body an unrestricted right to impose permanent political arrangements on a people under occupation. “Transitional arrangements must stay within their mandate, be subject to effective oversight and must not displace legitimate Palestinian institutions or weaken the ability of Palestinians to exercise their political rights,” he says.
Accountability is a recurring concern. Although Resolution 2803 gives the Board an international legal framework, the Board is not a subsidiary organ of the UN. That, El Gharbi says, makes it crucial to spell out who is responsible for what among the Board, the participating states, the operational bodies and the international institutions involved. Legal personality, he stresses, does not exempt an entity from its obligations under international law, nor does it grant unlimited immunity from the courts.
“The scope of any privileges and immunities must be determined by the relevant legal instruments,” El Gharbi says. “They cannot simply be presumed to extend to every act or every official associated with the transitional arrangements.” He warns that Palestinians would pay the price if this is not resolved. “Excessively broad immunities, inadequate accountability, or decisions about public resources and property taken without proper legal safeguards could seriously endanger the rights of Gaza’s population, including their access to justice and to effective remedies.”
On the role of Palestinians themselves, El Gharbi is unequivocal. The Palestinian people, he says, remain the holders of the right to decide their political future and how their territory is governed. Resolution 2803 does provide for a Palestinian technocratic committee to run day-to-day administration, but in his view meaningful participation must go well beyond administrative tasks. It must shape the decisions that determine Gaza’s governance, its reconstruction and its long-term political future. “Shutting Palestinians out of real decision-making,” he argues, “would undermine the political legitimacy of the whole arrangement and raise serious doubts about whether it is consistent with the right to self-determination.”
READ: From Count Bernadotte to the ‘Gaza Board of Peace’
Nor, in El Gharbi’s view, does the new arrangement relieve Israel of its responsibilities as the occupying power. “Setting up an international transitional mechanism or a local administrative committee does not, by itself, end Israel’s obligations under international law towards the occupied Palestinian territory,” he says. “The obligations arising from the law of occupation must be judged against the relevant legal criteria and the facts on the ground, and new governance arrangements cannot wipe out existing responsibilities or absolve any party of accountability for violations it has committed.”
El Gharbi also points out that international humanitarian law requires the protection of civilians and the delivery of essential aid. Access to food, medicine, shelter and basic services, he says, must not be made subject to unlawful political conditions that put civilian lives and dignity at risk.
El Gharbi is concerned, too, that continuing violence and obstacles to reconstruction raise questions about the practical effectiveness of the transitional framework, and whether it can protect civilians, support humanitarian recovery and ensure compliance with international law.
This is not, he insists, an argument against international help for Gaza. The danger, he says, is that a mechanism of this kind could reduce the Palestinian question to a humanitarian and security matter and sideline the core legal and political issues of occupation, self-determination and national rights.
READ: Why the recent UNSC Resolution 2803 “Board of Peace” violates the UN Charter
“Transitional powers must not become a way of entrenching prolonged external rule over Gaza, or of cementing its separation from the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory,” he stresses. “Resolution 2803 grants only a time-limited authorisation, subject to further action by the Security Council, and this time limit must be respected in practice. It cannot be used to justify open-ended foreign control without the meaningful participation and consent of Palestinians.”
The resolution itself, El Gharbi maintains, must be read and implemented in line with the UN Charter and international law, including peremptory norms and the right of Palestinians to self-determination. It cannot reasonably be treated as a blank cheque for any state or body to decide the permanent political future of Palestinian territory regardless of the rights of its people.
El Gharbi calls for clear and effective international oversight of the Board, greater transparency in how it takes decisions and a precise definition of the powers and responsibilities of everybody involved, and of how each will be held to account. He also urges human rights organisations, legal institutions and independent monitors to scrutinise how the arrangements are carried out, particularly where they affect Palestinian rights, public property, humanitarian access, access to justice and the ability of Palestinians to run their own affairs.
In the end, El Gharbi returns to the point where he began. No political initiative led by the US, he says, can take the place of the freely expressed will of the Palestinian people. A Security Council resolution is not enough on its own to make an international arrangement legitimate; that arrangement must also comply with international law and respect fundamental rights. A lasting peace, he argues, requires three things: respect for international law, the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and a lawful end to the occupation. Without them, he warns, any transitional arrangement will remain fragile, no matter how many powerful states stand behind it.

EU leaders divided over bloc’s next long-term budget ahead of summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:12:41 UTC
22:12:41 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
European leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the economy, competitiveness, support for Ukraine, and the situation in the Middle East, while expressing differing views on the EU’s long-term budget for 2028-2034.
Several leaders voiced opposing positions on the bloc’s proposed multiannual financial framework as they arrived for a European Council meeting, with disagreements centering on the budget’s size, spending priorities, and contributions from member states.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten called on European countries to increase their financial and military support for Ukraine, saying some member states were lagging behind.
“A lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine. So let's step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war,” Jetten said.
On the EU’s long-term budget, Jetten said the proposal put forward by the Irish presidency was "not good enough," arguing that it should be reduced in size and modernized to prioritize competitiveness, security, and future welfare.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also rejected the proposed budget, saying it would increase Sweden’s net contribution by around 60%.
"A 60% increase of the Swedish contribution is simply not acceptable. It's a no-go zone," he said, adding that Sweden would not accept a further increase in its contributions.
Kristersson said the negotiations would be tense and questioned whether an agreement could be reached before the end of the year, stressing the need for a budget that balances modernization, support for Ukraine, and traditional spending priorities.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, meanwhile, welcomed the Irish presidency’s proposal, describing it as well-balanced, but expressed concern over cuts to the Connecting Europe Facility, particularly military mobility, and the competitiveness fund.
He stressed that an ambitious budget with sufficient funding was necessary to implement the bloc’s priorities, adding that reaching a consensus by the end of the year would be difficult.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said security, connectivity and competitiveness were among his country’s main priorities, particularly given its location on the EU’s eastern border.
He also called for reducing bureaucracy to help the bloc compete with China and the US, while saying he did not expect major compromises during the summit.
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin defended the proposal, saying the presidency had sought to facilitate negotiations by balancing the positions of member states.
He said the proposal preserved cohesion funding and maintained key elements of the competitiveness fund, while acknowledging that issues remained to be resolved before the end of the year.
"My view all along has been a larger budget is required for Europe to attain its objectives," Martin added.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs stressed the importance of agreeing on the next seven-year budget, noting that "strong economy can only bring a strong defense."
He said eastern European countries needed additional economic support to keep the bloc’s eastern borders safe.
He also called for further measures to help Ukraine export its agricultural products and implement sanctions against Russia.
Kulbergs described the coming winter as critical for Ukraine, saying the country’s ability to remain resilient was closely linked to Europe’s own security.
"We should think a little bit less about the comfort, a little bit less about ourselves and think further what is best for Europe in general," he added.
"It is one beer less for a European a year. We can afford that, but Ukraine needs it now. That one beer is just the cost. There it's the cost of life," Kulbergs further said.

US producer inflation hits 6.3% in September, exceeding expectations of 5.3%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:12:29 UTC
22:12:29 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
US annual producer inflation reached 6.3% in September, exceeding expectations of 5.3%, as surging energy costs drove a sharp increase in prices, according to data released Thursday.
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 1.3% from the previous month, the largest monthly increase since March 2022, said the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The increase followed gains of 0.5% in August and 0.2% in July.
Prices for final demand goods climbed 2.6% in September, while services prices advanced 0.8%.
Energy prices jumped 10.8%, accounting for more than 80% of the monthly increase in goods prices. Gasoline prices surged 20.3%, contributing half of the overall rise in goods prices.
Diesel fuel, jet fuel, residential electricity, and crude petroleum prices also rose.
Food prices climbed 1.2%, while goods prices excluding food and energy increased 0.3%. Prices for chicken eggs, however, plunged 39.7%.
Services prices also accelerate
The 0.8% increase in services prices was the largest since April, with nearly half of the gain attributable to a 1.4% rise in trade services margins, which measure the difference between wholesalers’ and retailers’ selling and purchase prices.
Transportation and warehousing services prices climbed 3.4%, while services excluding trade, transportation, and warehousing rose 0.3%.
Margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling increased 3.9%, accounting for more than one-fifth of the rise in services prices.
Meanwhile, producer prices excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% in September, following a 0.3% gain in August.
That metric rose 5% over the 12 months through September.

Hong Kong suffered a record net loss of 40 kindergartens this year amid a shrinking student population and as the median age of women giving birth to their first child rose to its highest yet, according to official figures.
In its overview of preschools released on Thursday, the Education Bureau revealed that 930 kindergartens were currently operating in Hong Kong, down from roughly 970 in the previous school year.
While some new kindergartens were launched, the net decrease stood at 40, the highest on record. Each of the past four academic years witnessed a net decrease of about 20 preschools.

Türkiye's Fidan urges CICA members to stand firm against Israel's oppression of Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:10:42 UTC
22:10:42 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) member states must take a firm stance in supporting the rights of Palestine, which is among the group’s members, as well as in opposing ongoing oppression and grave violations.
Addressing the 7th CICA Summit in Azerbaijan’s capital Baku on Thursday, Fidan said: “We cannot uphold this commitment while Israel, a CICA member, violates the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people through a systematic policy of oppression.”
“A lasting solution requires the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital,” he stressed.
Stronger CICA essential for Asia’s security, prosperity
Fidan stressed that a stronger CICA is essential to ensuring peace and prosperity at a time when Asia’s rise is shaping the global landscape.
“Türkiye is committed to strengthening CICA as Asia’s most inclusive security forum,” he said.
“We must enhance economic security and improve connectivity by expanding transport links and diversifying energy corridors,” he said.
Fidan highlighted the importance of the Middle Corridor project, saying it would significantly boost the effectiveness of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
“This will not only facilitate trade between Asia and Europe but also help us build new bridges for people-to-people contacts,” he said.
On the Development Road project from Iraq’s Grand Faw Port through Türkiye, Fidan said: “This project will connect the Gulf to Europe through Iraq and Türkiye while also supporting stability and prosperity in the region and beyond.”
Improving coordination
Fidan also highlighted the importance of enhancing synergies among different regional cooperation mechanisms in Asia.
“Improving coordination among CICA, the Organization of Turkic States, the Economic Cooperation Organization, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization will undoubtedly strengthen connectivity across the continent,” he said.
Noting that connectivity also extends to the digital world, Fidan said cooperation in science, technology, and innovation should be deepened under CICA to ensure that artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies benefit people not only in Asia but around the world.
The Turkish foreign minister also said sustainable development requires action to address environmental challenges, noting that Türkiye continues to play a leading role in tackling the effects of climate change.

Akhilesh’s anti-BJP formula for UP: PDA, Muslim-Yadav votes and Gen Z
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:10:18 UTC
22:10:18 KST

Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav addresses a press conference at the party headquarters in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. He defended the right to peaceful demonstrations and questioned why people in civilian clothes who allegedly attacked protesters during a demonstration in Delhi had not been arrested.
NEW DELHI: With the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections on the horizon, Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav is looking to expand his party’s anti-BJP coalition. His game plan for the UP elections includes bringing together backward classes, Dalits, minorities, its traditional Muslim-Yadav vote base and discontented young voters.On Friday, Yadav said the combination of PDA, Muslim-Yadav votes and growing anger among Gen Z would ensure the BJP’s defeat in the state.“If the Muslim-Yadav (M-Y) votes are intact and the PDA is brought together, with the anger growing among Gen Z, the BJP's wipeout is certain,” he said.PDA stands for “Picchda, Dalit, Alpasankhyak”, meaning backward classes, Dalits and minorities. The SP leader coined the term to expand the party’s social base and present a broader political alternative to the BJP.Over the past few years, Akhilesh has largely avoided foregrounding the M-Y formula in his public messaging, focusing instead on the PDA coalition.The BJP has repeatedly targeted the Samajwadi Party’s Muslim-Yadav support base. During the 2022 assembly election campaign, BJP leaders recast M-Y as “Modi-Yogi”, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath. The party also used the acronym to mean “Mahila” (women) and “Yuva” (youth).
Akhilesh backs peaceful protests
Commenting on recent protests against the Election Commission, Akhilesh Yadav defended the right to peaceful demonstrations and questioned why people in civilian clothes who allegedly attacked protesters during a demonstration in Delhi had not been arrested.“In a democracy, people have the right to march, stage a sit-in and peacefully express their views,” he said.“From what we are seeing and hearing, and from what the pictures indicate, the BJP has not arrested them because they are associated with the same ideology,” he alleged.Drawing a comparison with Nazi Germany, Yadav accused the BJP of using political workers against ordinary people.“This is what Hitler used to do. During Hitler's time, political workers were dressed in police uniforms, while others in civilian clothes also took action against the public. They have learnt this from Hitler,” he said.
He also blamed the BJP for the problems faced by public institutions. “The BJP is the crisis. Remove the crisis, and then your institutions will improve.”
Akhilesh attacks Centre’s foreign policy
Akhilesh also criticised the BJP-led Centre’s foreign policy amid the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel. He accused the government of failing to protect Indian citizens working abroad.“I have not seen a government so weak on its foreign policy,” he said.Taking a swipe at the BJP’s claims of making India a Vishwaguru, Yadav invoked the principle of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam. He said such claims rang hollow if the government could not protect the lives of Indians living and working overseas.

Ukraine passes key laws to help unlock billions in aid from EU, IMF
KYIV, Oct 15 - Ukraine's parliament passed a package of legislation on Thursday to advance the implementation of key demands from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund to unlock billions in foreign aid.
As the war with Russia is in its fifth year, Ukraine faces a budget crisis driven by a huge military funding deficit, stalled economic growth, and domestic revenue shortfalls due to intensified Russian strikes on businesses and infrastructure.
Lawmakers approved bills to raise taxes on foreign parcels, increase e-commerce transparency, and amend financial monitoring rules for politicians.
"The laws approved today establish a modern model for the taxation of e-commerce, which is in line with the European Union’s approach and is fair to domestic businesses," said Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko.
"The reform is also part of the cooperation programme with the IMF and a condition for macro-financial support from the EU."
As the war gets more expensive and demand for weapons, drones and ammunition continues to grow, Ukraine is struggling to cover its defence spending with domestic revenue and crucially depends on financial aid from its Western allies.
Last month, the government was forced to delay some of the budget spending – like reconstruction work and preparations for winter – due to a budget liquidity crisis. Domestic tax revenue fell by 32 billion hryvnias ($711 million) in August and September as Russia intensified its strikes on the Ukrainian infrastructure, logistics and businesses.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said that the results of this week's parliamentary work gave the government cause for optimism, but there was still a lot of work to do to meet all the requirements of the country's lenders.
For the remainder of this year, Ukraine has around $29 billion available in EU financial support waiting for continued disbursement.
The finance ministry said that the new rules for foreign parcels, introducing a 20% value-added tax, would take effect no earlier than July 2027. It was expected to generate an additional 20-30 billion hryvnias in budget revenue, lawmakers estimated. REUTERS

Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
The technology could get those with ALS, Parkinson’s disease and brain injuries “talking” again
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.
I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.
Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
“There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.
In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.
Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.
The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.
But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.
Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”
The voice inside
On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?
Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.
“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”
Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.
The Deep End podcast explores what makes your voice yours
What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.
By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.
From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.
A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”
Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”
Looking for a cheetah
Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.
Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.
But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.
After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.
When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”
Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.
Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”
Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.
Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”
Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”
But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.
The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.
“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”
Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”
From thoughts to words
Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them into
words. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.
Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.
But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.
For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.
“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”
Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”
More than words
Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.
The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neurosurgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.
Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.
Paradromics’ priority is to test whether the implant is safe. If so, scientists can turn to the goal of restoring speech in real time. “The moment that you’re thinking the words, you don’t have to wait for the sentence to complete,” says Willsey, who, like Brandman, is a site investigator for the Paradromics clinical trial. “You can let the words kind of flow out as they would in a normal conversation.”
Scientists also want to decode more than words. Qualities of voice, such as pitch, are important for marking questions, says Vikash Gilja, a Paradromics neuroscientist. Speakers can also alter or pace their conversation to show sarcasm or concern. These sounds are all made by moving muscles, Gilja says, and can therefore be decoded from the brain.
“Our near-term goal right now is just to restore speech,” says Paradromics neurosurgeon Stephen Ryu. “But eventually, we’re hoping that we can actually restore someone’s ability to be fully involved in a conversation, to basically decode things like their timing, their emotions, their personality.”
Other researchers are trying to incorporate the gestures that many of us use to communicate.
“Some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up,” says bioengineer Samantha Brosler of the University of California, San Fransico. Gestures can also change the meaning of words; a “maybe” with a head nod is close to a yes, for instance. “I think of gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech,” Brosler says.
In a new study, Brosler and colleagues enabled two people with paralysis who had lost their speaking ability to instead use their brain signals to control both the words and gestures of digital avatars. The advance, reported in September in Nature Neuroscience, adds to the repertoire of signals that could be decoded and turned into action.
And as all this is happening, scientists are creating smaller, more stable types of electrodes to embed in the brain; more powerful computational algorithms to handle larger amounts of data; and better models of how those signals relate to sounds, words and gestures, Gilja says. “We can see all the pieces coming together.”
There are many reasons to be optimistic about the future, says Brandman, who is an investigator for the clinical trial led by Paradromics. “I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation,” he says. “‘Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate.’”
That conversation is tantalizing. But there are no guarantees that these systems will work as hoped, or that they will be widely available. Such implants would probably come with hefty price tags, invasive brain surgeries and perhaps more demand than the few capable clinicians and technologists could meet.
And there are underlying questions about the brain itself. One concern is that changes to the brain over time might render neural signals unreliable, especially as diseases progress. If that happens, a person’s interface might produce a scrambled message — or be left without enough neural data to decode.
“These are real challenges, and the field is working on them,” Stavisky says. “But they’re not solved yet.”
Despite these hurdles, the push for voice-restoring technology can’t come soon enough for people who have lost theirs. In September, researchers reported that the woman with the Paradromics implant had a message for them. “OK,” she used her brain-computer interface to tell researchers. “I have a lot to say.” With her system, she was able to call her grandchildren on the telephone.
And Harrell is now living a life that looks very different from the one he might have imagined six years ago. Although his disease keeps him close to home, he can now share his thoughts with the world — and his family — instead of locking them away inside.
“The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress, the ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear,” Harrell says. “These are the things that life is all about, and when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now.”
But he too has a vision, a day when these devices are commonplace, “when I am one of many, instead of being one of one.”
For more about the human voice and to hear from Casey Harrell himself, listen to The Deep End podcast Season Two, called Talk to Me. It’s free wherever you get your podcasts.

Taiwan's ITRI and eJoule improve drone battery manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

TAIPEI (TAIPEI NEWS) – Hsinchu-based Industrial Technology Research Institute said Thursday that it has partnered with local battery maker eJoule to make high-capacity batteries for drones and electric vehicles.
Medium-and high-lithium ternary batteries use nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Higher lithium content means greater storage capacity, making them suitable for drones, robotics, and electric vehicles.
According to a press release, drones and EVs are driving demand for lighter, longer-lasting batteries. Although ternary batteries are valued for their capacity, there are lifecycle and safety bottlenecks that need to be addressed before commercialization.
ITRI and eJoule co-developed a solution using single-crystal structures, electrode fabrication, and power cell certification to speed commercialization for drones, robotics, and storage applications. The project also aims to achieve production and supply chain self-reliance.
Electrode fabrication combines raw materials with metal foils to create the positive and negative charges required for batteries to function. The common method involves mixing the materials with additives and solvents such as water for coating onto the foils, which are then vacuumed and pressed into batteries.
ITRI Material and Chemical Research Laboratories Director Chiu Kuo-chan (邱國展) said eJoule provided the material while ITRI designed battery specifications and conducted performance tests. He noted that the material proved stable after extensive, repetitive cycles of charging and discharging, making it a suitable candidate comparable to lithium iron phosphate batteries in terms of lifespan as well as safer than traditional ternary materials.
ITRI said eJoule’s patented dynamic crystallization process yields simple, high-performing structures without using toxic precursors. eJoule Vice President Liu Min-tuan (劉敏端) said the initiative would combine ITRI's battery expertise to speed material applications from laboratory settings to commercially viable products.

Cheng said global electrification stands at about 21%, compared with 30% in Taiwan, and electricity demand will continue rising as transportation, industry, and data centers expand. He projected that EV power consumption could increase fivefold over the next decade, while data center electricity use could triple from last year’s level by 2030.
Citing estimates, Cheng said US data centers are expected to add 44 GW of electricity demand by 2028, while the power grid is projected to add only 25 GW in supply capacity, leaving a 19 GW gap. He attributed the infrastructure lag partly to regulations, equipment lifespans, and investment returns.
Cheng said improving energy efficiency is essential to stable power supplies. He noted that Delta has invested in solid oxide fuel cells, which generate electricity using hydrogen or natural gas and can achieve overall efficiency of up to 85%, per Anue.
Cheng said the company is also developing solid-state transformers that convert medium-voltage alternating current directly into 800-volt direct current, reducing conversion losses in data centers. He added that the company’s new prefabricated power solution can cut on-site deployment time by 50%.

Euro area industrial output unexpectedly falls 0.5% in August

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Industrial production in the euro area fell 0.5% month-on-month in August, against expectations of stagnation, according to Eurostat data released Thursday.
The decline followed a 0.3% contraction in July and a 0.1% drop in June, marking the third consecutive monthly fall.
Across the EU, seasonally adjusted industrial output decreased 0.3% in August, following a 0.4% drop in July.
Euro area production of non-durable consumer goods saw the sharpest monthly decline among the main industrial groupings, down 2.7%. Intermediate goods output decreased 0.8%, while energy production slipped 0.6%.
Capital goods production, however, rose 0.4%, and durable consumer goods output climbed 0.2%.
Across the EU, non-durable consumer goods production fell 2.3%, energy output declined 0.5%, and intermediate goods production dropped 0.3%. Capital goods output rose 0.7%, while durable consumer goods production remained unchanged.
Among member states, Belgium saw the largest monthly decline at 5.1%, followed by Ireland at 3.1% and Portugal at 2%.
Sweden posted the strongest increase at 6.5%, followed by Estonia at 4.3% and the Netherlands at 2.6%.
Among the bloc’s largest economies, industrial output rose 0.4% in Germany but fell 0.3% in France, 1.3% in Italy, and 0.8% in Spain.
On an annual basis, industrial production declined 1.1% in the euro area and 0.2% across the EU.
Euro area non-durable consumer goods output dropped 9.1% from August 2025, while intermediate goods production fell 0.4%. Energy, capital goods, and durable consumer goods output climbed 3.1%, 3%, and 0.4%, respectively.
Ireland saw the steepest annual contraction at 15%, followed by Belgium at 7.1% and Bulgaria at 5.4%. The Netherlands saw the largest jump at 9.8%, ahead of Hungary at 8.8% and Denmark at 8.3%.

Former US President Barack Obama has criticized Israel’s handling of the Middle East conflict, warning that military strength cannot guarantee lasting security and that refusing concessions to Palestinians risks undermining its moral standing.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay at Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should “pain everybody”, describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
“That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
“If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
“That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
“I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
“It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

Photos: China and North Korea open new border bridge amid deepening ties
The New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong, China, and Sinuiju, North Korea, enhancing regional trade and collaboration.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said a launch ceremony was held on Thursday for the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju.

More than 70 percent of official trade between the two countries currently goes through that crossing, according to Chinese data. The South Korean government has counted at least 17 active road and rail links along the 1,400km (870-mile) North Korea-China border.

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:52:05 UTC
21:52:05 KST

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- Baylor College of Medicine
- Summary:
- Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.
- Share:
Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.
Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.
"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them."
Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia
To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.
These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories.
The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.
According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.
The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.
Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.
This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.
The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words
The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.
They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.
The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.
But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.
The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.
"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.
This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.
Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.
"This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.
What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?
The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.
Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.
This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.
The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.
One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.
Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.
A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence
The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).
Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.
The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.
Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.
The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.
One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.
If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.
"Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.
Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain
Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.
The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.
It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.
Another important limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.
Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.
Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.
"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," said Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand."
