Pope Leo's cancer operation already reshaping papacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:41:51 UTC
21:41:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Pope Leo XIV's cancer operation already reshaping papacy
With Pope Leo XIV recovering in hospital on Thursday following his lung cancer operation, questions are swirling about how the illness could change his papacy, less than two years after his election.
The 71-year-old leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics had a part of his lung removed on Tuesday and is undergoing further tests to determine if he is cancer-free or needs further treatment.
In the meantime, the Chicago-born pontiff is expected to spend at least a few days recovering at the Gemelli Hospital in Rome.
In a note published by the Vatican, his doctors on Thursday said a chest X-ray "showed a good recovery of the operated lung".
"The post-operative course is progressing as expected," they said.
A Vatican source said the pope has not had any visitors aside from a few members of his entourage, and has been able to do some work in hospital.
But experts said the unexpected diagnosis will fundamentally change the papacy in some ways.
"Illness acts as a crossroads in a pontificate—it either accelerates its momentum or diminishes its power," Vatican watcher Giacomo Galeazzi wrote in La Stampa daily on Thursday.
Mikael Corre, Vatican correspondent for France's La Croix newspaper, told AFP the way Leo is perceived has shifted.
"No-one expected to be waiting for medical bulletins again so soon—certainly not with this particular pope, who was 69 at the time of the conclave" in which he was elected, he said.
When Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, spent more than five weeks in hospital in early 2025, the Vatican began issuing regular medical bulletins detailing the pope's medical treatment and the critical episodes when his life was in danger.
In May 2025, tennis-mad Leo—a keen gym-goer— became the youngest man chosen to lead the Church since John Paul II almost 40 years earlier.
"He was the 'athletic pope' who also proved to be a great traveller," Corre said. "He may remain both but he will now also be a pope whose health is constantly scrutinised."
'Prudent'
Leo has cancelled all his audiences until 20 October and his near-term travel plans are uncertain, including a demanding scheduled trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November.
He is expected initially to have a scaled-back schedule, with fewer public engagements.
"I think he is going to want to jump right back into things as much as he can. I think he'll push himself," said US Vatican expert Elise Ann Allen, who has written a biography of the pope.
"But he's also very prudent. Leo understands his limitations and he'll listen to them," she told AFP.
The world's first American pope has gradually imprinted his style on the Church leadership, speaking out on some of the world's most pressing issues, from conflicts to artificial intelligence.
He has also proved unafraid to criticise world leaders or defend himself against US President Donald Trump's attacks.
"We're not going to see him change his style," Allen said.
"Scares like this have a way of crystallising things for you, of what's important," she said. "He will be even more determined, I think."
'Shift priorities'
Some Vatican insiders think Leo's illness might "shift his priorities", meaning fewer trips and more appointments, Corre said.
Several appointments are expected soon, in any case.
Leo has yet to create any cardinals, the red-hatted Princes of the Church who will vote in the conclave to elect his successor.
Five heads of dicasteries—Vatican departments—have also reached retirement age but have yet to be replaced.
Leo inherited a divided Church, with liberal and conservative factions that bickered under his predecessor Francis.
While he has been tasked with overcoming such polarisation, there are those inside the Vatican who hope Leo's illness will spur him into replacing close allies of Francis in key dicasteries with more conservative figures, Corre said.
Others expect him to forge ahead instead with diplomatic efforts, which have already "brought great stability", Allen said.
"I think this health crisis has eased those frictions even further," she said.
"It's brought the Catholic Church together in support around Pope Leo in a very strong way," she said.

Russian diesel fuel may reach the US before the midterm elections — NYP
Kyiv • UNN
The US may receive significant volumes of Russian diesel fuel before the November 3 elections. The deal could bring Moscow up to $4 billion.
Russian diesel fuel could reach the U.S. market before the November 3 midterm elections after Donald Trump suspended sanctions on its exports and Vladimir Putin lifted the corresponding ban. The New York Post reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to one of the publication’s American sources, Russia has agreed to supply a "fairly substantial" volume of fuel. However, the sources did not disclose specific plans for its delivery to the United States.
Trump previously said the agreement should help ease pressure on global fuel prices. On Tuesday, he told reporters that the diesel was intended for the global market, which had been hit by high prices.
Trump reached the agreement on diesel fuel supplies with Putin after expressing dissatisfaction with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. According to The New York Post, the United States repeatedly asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to refrain from such strikes, arguing that they affected American consumers.
Zelenskyy criticized the agreement on Russian fuel, calling it a "weak" decision that would provide Russia with funds to continue its war against Ukraine. At the same time, he later agreed to Trump’s demand not to attack oil refineries.
Experts estimate that the deal could bring Moscow an additional $4 billion in revenue.
On Sunday, Trump announced a limited "energy truce" between Russia and Ukraine. According to a U.S. official, Russia agreed not to attack Ukrainian oil refineries and gas stations on the condition that Ukraine halt drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
At the same time, the agreement does not provide for an end to Russian strikes on other targets in Ukraine, including the energy system. Ukraine currently has no operating oil refineries, although it could theoretically resume their operation during a pause in hostilities.
Diesel fuel prices in the United States
According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of diesel fuel in the United States is $6.30 per gallon. This is nearly twice as much as a year ago, when fuel cost $3.66 per gallon.
At the end of September, the price reached a record level of $6.53 per gallon.
Despite other measures by the Trump administration to contain fuel costs, including expanding the ability to purchase tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, prices remain high.
Rising fuel costs are affecting consumers. In September, annual inflation in the United States accelerated again, reaching 3.7%.
High fuel prices remain one of the economic challenges for the Trump administration ahead of the November 3 midterm elections for Congress. According to the publication, prices have risen significantly over the past year, in particular because of the nearly eight-month war between the United States and Iran, which has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Hezbollah says it owned confiscated explosives, meant to attack Israel
BEIRUT, Oct 15 - A Hezbollah lawmaker said on Thursday that hundreds of kilograms of explosives seized last week by Lebanese security forces belonged to his group, as tensions persist over the government's push to disarm the Iran-backed movement.
Lebanese authorities stopped the explosives-laden vehicle at a checkpoint in the eastern Bekaa region last week and arrested two people in the car.
At the time, authorities did not say who the vehicle belonged to, prompting widespread worry in Lebanon that the explosives were intended for car bomb assassinations or other destabilising attacks inside the country.
Speaking to reporters at the Lebanese parliament on Thursday, lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said Hezbollah had intended to use the explosives against Israel, whose troops are occupying swathes of Lebanese territory seized in this year's war.
PRESIDENT CALLS FOR ISRAELI COMPLIANCE
A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters that the explosives seized in the car last week were intended to be used in explosive drones targeting Israeli troops.
Fadlallah said Hezbollah had immediately contacted security agencies to clarify that it owned the vehicle and the cargo, and to demand the materials be returned and those detained be released.
Fadlallah's acknowledgment reflects Hezbollah's efforts to continue transporting weapons across Lebanon despite the government's vow to bring all arms in the country under state control.
On March 2, the government specifically banned Hezbollah's military activities, hours after the movement launched rockets at Israel to back up Tehran, pulling Lebanon into the regional war begun by US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
The government decision was an attempt to reverse the relative freedom Hezbollah had enjoyed for years in transporting military equipment across Lebanon.
The group's main arms supply route through Syria was severed when its ally, then-president Bashar al-Assad, was ousted in late 2024. The new Syrian authorities have regularly announced seizures of weapons along their border with Lebanon that they say are intended for Hezbollah.
Throughout 2025, Lebanese troops seized and destroyed Hezbollah weapons depots in southern Lebanon in line with the government's plan to exert state control over all weapons, but that roadmap was put on pause when the new war erupted.
President Joseph Aoun told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a telephone call on Thursday that the Lebanese army and security forces were fully carrying out decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the presidency said.
Aoun said recent measures taken by the security services fell within that effort, and said judicial authorities would pursue all cases referred to them, with no leniency for offenders.
Under a deal reached through US-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel this year, Beirut has vowed to disarm Hezbollah, which would in turn lead to Israeli troops gradually withdrawing from Lebanon.
But Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain on Lebanese land and Israel has continued carrying out strikes across southern Lebanon. Israel says its actions in the area are aimed against Hezbollah.
Aoun asked Rubio to pressure Israel to halt what the presidency described as attacks on southern Lebanese towns and villages, comply with the framework agreement, stop bulldozing work and allow farmers to reach their land without being targeted, the presidency said. REUTERS

The International Monetary Fund should check its own forecasting record before criticizing U.S. fiscal policy, David Zervos, newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary, said on Thursday.
"When we see pieces on the IMF, it's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," Zervos said in emailed comments to CNBC.
The former Wall Street economist was responding to the IMF's Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, who cautioned during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday that strong U.S. economic growth would not be sufficient to put mounting federal debt on a sustainable course.
Georgieva was herself responding to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in August that the U.S. could "grow our way out" of a rising debt-to-GDP ratio, after government debt surpassed $40 trillion.
Zervos, formerly chief market strategist at Jefferies, said Thursday: "In 2008, [the IMF's World Economic Outlook] had world growth at 3% and we had the first global contraction in post-world history a year later. We saw them positive on Southeast Asia in 1997 before the collapse."
"We saw them very negative on Russia in 2022, and Russia actually barely saw a blip down in growth before it started growing strongly. We saw them very positive on Argentina after their big bailout of $57 billion. And by 2020, Argentina was basically in default again. And the history books go on and on, whether it's Greece, whether it was the transitory call on inflation in the U.S."
"So take it all with a grain of salt," he added.
Many economists warn that mounting U.S. interest payments and a high deficit have raised the risk of an unsustainable debt spiral. However, they are divided on whether the U.S. could be pushed into a true fiscal crisis.
The IMF's Georgieva has issued similar warnings to other big economies over the need for fiscal consolidation, telling CNBC on Oct. 7 that her message to France was: "Get your house in order."
Other economic institutions are also sounding the alarm over the rising cost of servicing global debt, which topped $365 trillion in the first half of the year. The Institute of International Finance argued in a September report that a "vicious cycle between elections and short-term quick fixes" to debt challenges was reducing the ability to spend money on public services.

Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:40:44 UTC
21:40:44 KST

Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, with satellite records revealing that the region's remaining ice is becoming thinner, younger, and more vulnerable to melting. Despite a recent slowdown in summer losses, scientists warn that the Arctic could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050.
- Share:
Nearly five decades of satellite observations reveal a troubling transformation in the Arctic, where sea ice is shrinking in both summer and winter, and much of the remaining ice is becoming younger and thinner.
The Arctic Ocean is covered by a vast expanse of frozen seawater that expands and contracts with the seasons. Ice typically builds up throughout the long, dark winter, reaching its greatest extent in March before retreating during the warmer months to a September minimum. This seasonal cycle has continued for thousands of years, but satellite measurements reveal that the amount of ice covering the ocean has declined substantially at both ends of the cycle.
In 2026, Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum extent on September 12 (above), covering approximately 4.6 million square kilometers (1.78 million square miles). According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), this tied the minimums recorded in 2008, 2010, and 2025 for the 10th-lowest level since satellite monitoring began.
The maps below illustrate how Arctic sea ice has changed over time, comparing September conditions since 1990 (left), when ice coverage is typically at its lowest, with the following March (right), when it approaches its annual peak. The sequence continues through March 2026.
Decades of Arctic Sea Ice Loss
Satellites have continuously tracked the seasonal expansion and retreat of Arctic sea ice since late 1978, providing scientists with nearly five decades of observations. Those measurements reveal a long-term decline that accelerated during the 2000s, leading to a succession of exceptionally low ice levels.
One particularly striking pattern is that every summer from 2007 through 2026 ranks among the 20 lowest September sea ice extents in the satellite record. The smallest extent ever observed occurred in September 2012.
However, the rate of summer ice loss has not been consistent. During the past decade, September sea ice coverage has remained comparatively stable rather than continuing its earlier rapid decline. Scientists emphasize that short-term weather conditions can strongly influence how much ice disappears in any given summer.
For instance, increased cloud cover over the Arctic during recent years has reduced the amount of sunlight reaching the ice, helping to limit additional melting. NASA researchers have identified this as one factor contributing to the recent slowdown. Even with that temporary stabilization, however, September ice coverage remains far below its historical average.
The Arctic Is Losing Its Oldest, Thickest Ice
The changes extend beyond the shrinking area covered by sea ice. Scientists have also documented a major shift in the ice itself, which is becoming increasingly young and thin.
Historically, much of the Arctic contained multiyear ice, which survives at least one summer melting season. Because this ice can persist and accumulate over multiple years, it generally becomes thicker and more resilient than ice that forms during a single winter.
Satellite observations now show that multiyear ice has declined significantly. As a result, the Arctic is increasingly covered by thinner first-year ice, which forms during the cold months but is more susceptible to melting when summer returns.
The decline is also evident during winter, when Arctic sea ice normally reaches its greatest coverage. In March 2026, the annual maximum statistically tied the March 2025 maximum for the lowest winter peak in the satellite record.
Could the Arctic Become Nearly Ice-Free?
Natural climate patterns influence Arctic sea ice from year to year. One example is the Arctic Oscillation, a pattern of atmospheric circulation that affects temperatures, winds, and ice conditions across the region.
However, natural fluctuations cannot fully account for the persistent decline recorded by satellites since 1978. Rising global temperatures, together with natural climate variability, have contributed to the growing loss of Arctic sea ice.
Looking ahead, scientists project that the Arctic Ocean could become essentially free of sea ice during the summer at least once before the middle of the 21st century. Such an event would mark a profound change in a region that has maintained extensive seasonal ice cover for millennia.
How Satellites Track Arctic Ice Through Clouds
Scientists measure Arctic sea ice coverage using satellites equipped with passive microwave sensors. These instruments detect microwave energy naturally emitted by Earth's surface, allowing researchers to distinguish frozen seawater from the surrounding open ocean.
Sea ice emits more microwave energy than liquid water, producing a recognizable contrast in satellite observations. Unlike visible-light imaging, microwave measurements can penetrate cloud cover, making it possible to monitor the Arctic consistently even when storms or persistent clouds obscure the surface.
The continuous satellite record began in 1978 with NASA's Nimbus-7 spacecraft. Additional observations came from the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), beginning in 1987, and NASA's Aqua satellite, which provided measurements between 2002 and 2011.
In 2025, researchers began incorporating observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's GCOM-W satellite, continuing the long-running effort to measure changes in the planet's polar ice.
The satellite maps also contain a white circular region at the North Pole known as the "pole hole." This represents an area beyond the historical coverage of the satellite sensors, where direct measurements were unavailable. When calculating total sea ice extent, scientists assume this region is covered by ice.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using data from the National Snow and Ice Data Center.
Story Source:

KABUL, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Afghan authorities on Thursday declared the central province of Bamiyan free of landmines and explosive remnants left over from past conflicts, making it the first province in the country to achieve this milestone.
Nearly 85 million square meters of land have been cleared of landmines and unexploded ordnance in Bamiyan over the past 36 years, according to Hafiz Mohammad Yusuf Hammad, spokesman for the authority.
Approximately 262 incidents involving landmines and unexploded ordnance were recorded in the province during this period, resulting in 330 people killed or injured, Hammad said, noting that children accounted for the majority of the casualties.
Afghanistan remains one of the world's most heavily landmine-contaminated countries. More than four decades of conflict have left a deadly legacy of explosive remnants that continue to kill or maim dozens of people every month. ■

Column: A new grammar of major-country relations: from warm welcome to strategic stability
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:39:55 CST
21:39:55 KST

by Francisco Jose Leandro
As a scholar of international relations, I have long argued that the true significance of diplomatic summits can be seen in the political signals embedded in official communiques or carefully choreographed ceremonies. President Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States should be understood through precisely this lens. Beyond the symbolism of state dinners, military honors and public displays of cordiality, the visit reflects deeper transformations in the structure of contemporary international relations.
The first and perhaps most visible signal is the growing recognition that relations between China and the United States have entered a new phase, with both sides agreeing to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. The scale of the welcome extended to President Xi was not merely an exercise in diplomatic protocol. It conveyed a clear recognition that the stability of the international system increasingly depends on constructive engagement between the two countries. Whether one speaks of economic influence, technological innovation, geopolitical reach or normative leadership, both countries possess a level of agency that renders them indispensable actors in the management of global affairs.
A second and more substantive outcome lies in the emphasis placed on strategic stability. In my view, this constitutes the most important dimension of the visit. Strategic stability should not be interpreted as the absence of competition. Competition will remain a defining feature of China-U.S. relations for the foreseeable future. Rather, it signifies a mutual recognition that competition must be of a healthy sort governed by rules, communication mechanisms and a degree of strategic restraint. Great powers do not threaten international order because they compete; they threaten it when they cease to communicate.
Particularly encouraging is the growing attention devoted to emerging technologies and artificial intelligence governance. As technological breakthroughs increasingly shape both prosperity and security, the establishment of mechanisms capable of reducing misunderstandings and preventing unintended escalation represents a prudent and necessary step. China's recent efforts to promote international cooperation through the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization suggest that both national and multilateral approaches will be required to address challenges that no state can manage alone.
The visit also serves as an important prelude to the forthcoming G20 Summit. At a time when the international community faces simultaneous economic, technological, environmental and security challenges, effective leadership from major countries remains essential.
Naturally, profound differences remain. Yet the significance of this visit lies not in the expectation of immediate consensus, but in the willingness to sustain dialogue despite disagreement. That, in itself, is a valuable achievement in an increasingly fragmented world.
History teaches us that lasting peace is not achieved when states agree on everything. It is built when they learn how to disagree without abandoning cooperation. Strategic stability begins when dialogue becomes stronger than distrust.
Ultimately, what emerged from this visit was more than a diplomatic encounter between two heads of state. It reflected the gradual emergence of what may be called a new grammar of major-country relations, one that seeks to move beyond the binary logic of dominance and containment towards a more sophisticated balance between competition and cooperation.
In an increasingly interconnected world, where challenges such as technological disruption, energy security, geopolitical instability and climate change transcend national borders, neither China nor the United States can secure prosperity or stability in isolation. The true test of leadership in the 21st century will not be determined by which country prevails over the other, but by whether both possess the wisdom to transform competition into responsible stewardship of the international system.
If the spirit of this visit can be translated into sustained dialogue, strategic restraint and practical cooperation, it may mark the beginning of a more stable era in global affairs. After all, a new grammar of major-country relations is created when nations recognize that managing competition is not a sign of weakness, but the highest expression of strategic maturity. The future will belong not to those who can dominate the international system, but to those who can stabilize it.
Editor's note: The author is an associate professor at the University of Macau.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

China Focus: New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:39:31 CST
21:39:31 KST

An opening ceremony is held for a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Yulong)
SHENYANG, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on Thursday, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery.
The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between the city of Dandong in northeast China's Liaoning Province and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan Province of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).
The double-pylon and double-cable-plane bridge features a 28.5-meter-wide deck designed with four lanes for two-way traffic, while its water navigation clearance is designed for vessels of up to the 3,000-tonne class.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed the bridge as a new landmark of China-DPRK friendship. "The bridge is bound to become a new landmark symbolizing the traditional friendship between China and the DPRK," Li said in a video speech at the opening ceremony.
In his remarks, Li called on China and the DPRK to take the opening of the new bridge as an opportunity to continuously optimize port clearance, enhance connectivity, tap the potential for cooperation in border areas, and improve the well-being of the two peoples.
China is willing to work with the DPRK to continue making efforts to implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and countries, strengthen strategic communication, consolidate political mutual trust, expand practical cooperation, and enhance multilateral coordination, so as to continuously deepen the development of China-DPRK relations and bring more benefits to the two peoples, Li said.
The new bridge will further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday.
China and the DPRK are friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, and the new bridge is an important facility for connectivity between the two countries, Mao told a regular press briefing.
Dandong boasts China's largest border trade port with the DPRK. Before the new road bridge, the Yalu River Bridge, also known as the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge, served as a combined road-rail bridge. The old one, however, could only accommodate trucks weighing no more than 20 tonnes for one-way road traffic.
China and the DPRK agreed in 2010 to build a new road bridge downstream from the old one. ■

China Spied on Taiwanese President’s Son – in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

News broke earlier this month that the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had arrested real estate agent Wanying “Heather” Zhang for spying on Lai Ting-yu, the eldest child of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te. Zhang lived in Irvine, California, where she worked as a real estate agent. She was originally from Changsha, China, before emigrating to the United States and naturalizing.
Lai Ting-yu is not a political figure – members of the Lai family tend to keep a low profile. Lai Ching-te’s wife, First Lady Wu Mei-ju, does not often make public appearances with her husband. Arguably, the most famous members of the Lai family outside of Lai Ching-te himself are the family dogs, Murphy, Banban, and Luke, though Luke has since passed away. Banban in particular is best known as a dog that had lost a leg to a wild boar trap before being adopted by the Lai family.
Lai Ting-yu, who holds a doctorate in bioengineering from the University of Washington, works for electronics company Philips and lives in Seattle with his wife and son.
The FBI alleged that Lai was being surveilled by Zhang, along with other accomplices, in September 2025. It is unclear what Zhang was attempting to accomplish, given Lai Ting-yu’s lack of a political background.
There could be a domestic political angle. Lai Ching-te has long been criticized by members of the pan-Blue camp over allegations that his son lives in the United States. The suggestion is that Lai is hypocritical in calling for Taiwan to increase defense spending to ward off Chinese threats, even as his own children live abroad.
Alternatively, China may have sought to project its reach, or possibly to threaten Lai Ting-yu in order to have leverage over Taiwan’s president. Indeed, the idea that China might seek to kidnap the children of influential government officials in the course of an invasion, so as to blackmail political leaders during the turmoil of armed conflict, has occasionally been raised. This sort of political kidnapping is a plot thread that comes up in several episodes of “Zero Day Attack,” the hit 2025 television show dramatizing a Chinese invasion.
Whatever the motive, according to the FBI, Zhang was working in coordination with Chinese handlers and demonstrated signs of tradecraft to cover her tracks, such as renting vehicles for several hours then returning them, or booking short-range flights with little notice. It is unclear how evidence of her activities was detected, but Zhang was arrested in October 2026 while attempting to board a flight to Shanghai.
The FBI did not comment on when Zhang was recruited, or her motivations, seeing as she lived in a $6 million home and handled real estate transactions that were in the millions. Though there have been reports of China increasingly recruiting “disposable” agents that are used temporarily and then cast aside, tradecraft by Zhang may indicate professional training.
The Taiwanese government has criticized such actions as Chinese transnational repression. This is not the first case occurring in the United States. Individuals allegedly working for China’s government were arrested for surveilling Taiwan’s then-President Tsai Ing-wen’s travels in California in 2023. Reports indicate that Taiwanese government officials such as Joseph Wu were surveilled during past trips to Europe.
Most famously, news broke in June 2025 of an attempt by the Chinese military attaché in Prague to ram a vehicle into the motorcade of Taiwan’s then-vice president-elect Hsiao Bi-khim. Allegations of Chinese espionage against visiting Taiwanese government officials are fairly common; reports of China attempting direct kinetic action – what could be construed as either an attempt at intimidation or an assassination attempt – are rare. The timing of the car crash attempt raised some questions domestically in Taiwan, as this took place in a similar timeframe to the Kuomintang (KMT) introducing a bill that would require a new set of presidential elections to be held if the vice president-elect died.
China has repeatedly sanctioned senior government officials with the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), preventing them or their family members from doing business in China. Such sanctions have disproportionately honed in on figures involved in civil defense efforts, such as UMC founder Robert Tsao, former Sunflower Movement student leader Lin Fei-fan, or DPP legislator Puma Shen.
Shen in particular has often been targeted, He is the founder of the disinformation research organization Doublethink Lab and the civil defense organization Kuma Academy. Sanctions have honed in on his father, a businessman who sells auto parts in China. Likewise, Shen has reported threats directed at his children, as well as cases of attempted impersonation while attending conferences abroad.
DPP senior political figures and their families likely know better than to travel to China at this point. That being said, according to the Mainland Affairs Council in June, the number of Taiwanese who have been detained in China is on the rise. While most have been detained due to fraud or criminal charges, 23 were detained for religious reasons, and one was detained on a national security charge. Past precedent shows that when Taiwanese are detained in China on national security charges, they are usually prevented from returning to Taiwan even after being released at the end of their sentences.
China’s surveillance of the relatives of Taiwanese government officials abroad also raises the possibility of surveillance or acts of repression within Taiwan. In particular, some analysts have raised the possibility of fifth-column groups becoming active in the event of an invasion. Such groups could be constituted out of pro-China organized crime groups, such as those linked to the Bamboo Union. A number of recent espionage arrests in Taiwan in the past two years have also alleged the existence of paramilitary cells that would become active in wartime.
That being said, it has been more common to see acts of vandalism rather than outright violence in Taiwan. An attack in late September on a comedy club in Taipei saw the club’s entrance smeared with a mixture of white paint and feces. The vandalism was carried out by a 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo, who was reportedly paid NT$50,000 by a 33-year-old man surnamed Liu for the attack. It is thought that the attack occurred because of past mockery of Chinese President Xi Jinping by one of the comedians performing at the club in a clip that went viral online.
Nevertheless, acts of violence do occur. In July, political commentator Akio Yaita was attacked at a hotel in Taichung, where Yaita was giving a speech. The accused was a Chinese man who traveled using a Hong Kong passport.
There have also been reports in the past month of individuals attempting to impersonate the distributors of the documentary “State Organs,” which details allegations of China conducting organ harvesting on members of the Falun Gong religious group. There have also been threats directed against screenings of “State Organs.”
The highly partisan political environment in Taiwan is likely to stymie efforts to strengthen legal measures against transnational repression or surveillance, especially ahead of November’s local elections. In the past, the opposition KMT accused the ruling DPP of attempting a power grab when the DPP proposed the reintroduction of military courts for espionage cases.

‘We Have Stitched Our Hearts to Hope’: The Unseen Resistance of Afghan Women Under Taliban Rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

“Life in Afghanistan has become… exactly like a dark grave.”
These words, spoken by a woman in Sar-e Pol province of Afghanistan, are not hyperbole. They are an accurate description of daily existence in the country ranked worst in the world for women.
Since August 2021, when the Taliban regime retook power, Afghan women have been subjected to unprecedented levels of gender-based oppression that they describe as akin to imprisonment. Many recall the pride of attending school or contributing to their communities through work. That pride has been replaced by feelings of isolation and frustration as doors remain closed.
“Families are now afraid to have daughters because they see them only as a burden in the home,” said Zulaikha from Parwan, one of 165 testimonies of Afghan women recently collected by the Organization for Policy Research and Development Studies (DROPS).
In rural areas, women are completely excluded from employment and education and must rely on male relatives for any public activity. They face extreme barriers to accessing health care with a severe shortage of female health workers. In urban areas, women face morality police in all spaces, bans on makeup and mobile phones, and constant surveillance and harassment for their clothing or any “unapproved” behavior such as speaking loudly or laughing.
These are not just policy setbacks, but personal blows to women’s dignity and future. As Zulaikha explained, “If you need even the smallest thing, you must ask a man for money and then face many questions: Why do you want it? What do you need?”
Unsurprisingly, this has led to a widespread mental health and fatigue crisis. Trapped inside homes with compounding trauma and fear, several testimonials detailed severe depression, exhaustion, anxiety, and rising suicide rates, often following incidents of sexual violence.
These accounts offer a glimpse into the unprecedented horror and heartbreak Afghan women navigate. However, while the world may only see them as victims, their reality is far more complex. Despite deep frustration, fear, and grief, many Afghan women have doubled down on their efforts to lead a better life.
As Behnaz from Herat put it: “What I see from [women in Afghanistan] every day is effort, creativity, and resistance in order to carry on living.”
In urban areas, many Afghan women report focusing on home-based economic activities such as tailoring, handicrafts, and food production in order to generate income. They also use online platforms for education and work, including teaching, translation, design, social media management, and networks that provide information, resources, and emotional support.
Women in rural areas have turned to agriculture, livestock, and cooperative solutions for skill development, and also rely on family and community support.
Afghan women emphasized that they respond to Taliban oppression in vastly different ways depending on their social, cultural, and personal contexts. While many practice active defiance such as teaching secretly, for others, survival strategies may mean more pragmatic adaptations, such as economic marriage or acceptance of restrictions. Women emphasized that recognizing this spectrum of responses is essential, as it highlights individual agency and varied realities without diminishing the systemic harm Taliban policies inflict on all women and girls.
“…Everyone finds a way according to the resources available to them,” Farida from Jawzjan said.
Resistance is not successful only when there is policy change. As many women articulated, any resistance in the face of such insurmountable odds is a success.
“It is women’s resistance that has at least prevented all schools from being closed and kept some fields of work open to women, though under severe restrictions,” Zohal from Baghlan explained.
This dual reality of an unprecedented human rights catastrophe alongside an indefatigable spirit of defiance was reinforced by a survey of 500 Afghan women peacebuilders conducted by DROPS and the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace and Security (GIWPS). Afghan women who work across multiple sectors reported greater negative consequences (including from aid cuts) and fewer personal benefits from their efforts compared to women globally. And yet, the majority of Afghan women said they will continue their efforts.
These reports from Afghan women underscore why their perspectives are essential in charting the international community’s response to Afghanistan. Only they can accurately describe the impact of restrictions. Without their input, policies risk perpetuating harm and failing to address half the population’s needs. Afghan women insist on meaningful inclusion in peacebuilding, humanitarian response, and political decision-making processes.
The GIWPS-DROPS report includes a more comprehensive list of key demands of Afghan women, including pressuring Taliban authorities to urgently restore education and employment opportunities, as well as directing flexible funding to local organizations and setting up mentorship networks.
Afghan women have demonstrated unrivalled courage in unimaginably difficult circumstances and at great costs; the world must honor their persistence and begin by ensuring they have a seat at the table.
“Nevertheless, Afghan women still try to remain strong and build their lives and futures. We live in hope of a bright future. As the poet says, ‘We have stitched our hearts to hope,’” said Samana from Sar-e Pol.

Sachin Pilot keeps door open on Amarinder Singh’s Congress return
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sachin Pilot has said “anything is possible in politics” when asked about speculation that former Punjab chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh could return to the Congress, while stressing that he has not spoken to Singh about his political plans.In an exclusive interview with news agency PTI, Pilot, the Congress’ in-charge of Punjab, described Singh as someone who had served the state “well” and was “a man of a very tall stature”.However, he said he had not discussed with the former chief minister the possibility of joining or leaving any political party.“As far as Captain sahab is concerned, I've known him personally since I was very young. And I've worked closely with him. Personally, I've not had any interaction with him on this particular issue. But like they say, politics mein 'kuch bhi ho sakta hai' (Anything is possible in politics)?” Pilot said.
“I mean, who knows? I think he's actually, just like me, part of the armed forces. He's served Punjab well. And he's a man of a very tall stature, certainly. How the BJP has taken to him, I'm not sure,” he added.Pilot said he had seen Singh's recent critical remarks about the BJP but had not spoken to him personally about his future plans.
Asked whether Singh might expect a prominent position if he returned to the Congress, Pilot said he could not comment on what the former chief minister was thinking.“I don't know what he's (Captain) thinking. I've not spoken to him or had any communication on that front. Time will tell what happens. I can't say anything right now,” Pilot said.
Amarinder Singh’s discontent with BJP
The speculation about Singh's possible return to the Congress has gathered attention amid his recent expressions of dissatisfaction with the BJP. Last month, Singh said the party had not consulted him on Punjab. He maintained that it was his duty to convey his views on the state to the BJP and that doing so did not mean he was quitting the party.Singh also said he was going through “difficult times” but did not elaborate.Speculation about his political future had begun in August, when Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, the leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha, named Singh as his favourite politician from the BJP during an ‘Ask me’ session on Instagram.Responding to Rahul's remarks, Singh said his personal relationship with the Gandhi family would always remain but his political commitment was to the BJP.
Singh’s journey from Congress to BJP
Singh was among the Congress’ prominent regional leaders in Punjab and led the party to a landslide victory in the 117-member state Assembly in 2017, becoming chief minister for a second time.He served as chief minister from 2002 to 2007 and again from 2017 to 2021. He resigned from the post and left the Congress in 2021 following infighting within the party's Punjab unit.Singh subsequently formed the Punjab Lok Congress (PLC), which failed to win any seats in the 2022 Punjab Assembly elections. The party was later merged with the BJP.His wife and former MP Preneet Kaur, son Raninder Singh and daughter Jai Inder Kaur are also with the BJP.Singh has served as a Punjab MLA, a Lok Sabha MP and president of the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee on three occasions.
Pilot to undertake five-day Punjab yatra
Separately, Pilot is scheduled to undertake a five-day yatra across Punjab from October 16 to 20 to meet families who have lost relatives to gangster violence and alleged failures in law and order.The Congress said the yatra would cover Moga, Bathinda, Mansa, Ludhiana, Jalandhar, Kapurthala, Hoshiarpur, Pathankot, Gurdaspur, Tarn Taran and Amritsar.
During the visits, Pilot will meet bereaved families, offer condolences and hear their accounts of the crimes and the responses they have received from the police and the state government, the party said.The Congress said several families had waited months, and in some cases years, for arrests, chargesheets or a fair trial in cases involving killings claimed by or linked to organised gangs.The party said the yatra aimed to bring the families' demands for justice to the public and the state government and, where necessary, to the courts.It also said Pilot would highlight what it described as a deterioration in law and order under the Aam Aadmi Party government in Punjab.

Black mould, bugs found at Chinese plants making GLP-1 compounding agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:35:00 UTC
21:35:00 KST

Black mould, bugs found at Chinese plants making GLP-1 compounding agents
US inspectors documented egregious conditions at two Chinese factories making key components for compounded GLP-1 drugs popular in America, including black mould on equipment and “gross contamination” on floors at one plant.
The inspectors caught employees trying to hide paperwork and furtively pouring out product samples at that plant and evidence of bogus documentation at the other, according to reports obtained under a Freedom of Information Act request.
The two companies manufactured semaglutide and tirzepatide – the active ingredients in weight-loss blockbusters from Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly – for custom-made versions that are not approved for sale by regulators nor reviewed for safety or effectiveness.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) put the companies on its import-alert list, meaning their products can be prevented from entering the US.
So-called drug compounders have flooded the market with relatively cheap copies of hugely popular weight-loss medications, with China a major supplier of the active ingredients.
The inspection findings “suggest a serious accident waiting to happen,” said Michael Rogers, a principal at Canal Row Advisors and a former associate commissioner for inspections and investigations at the FDA.
One of the manufacturers, Chengdu Shengnuo Biopharm, is a subsidiary of Chengdu Shengnuo Biotec. It said in a regulatory filing in China that it has been “diligently implementing effective measures” to rectify the issues.
‘Insect activity’
When FDA inspectors arrived at Chengdu Shengnuo in south-west China in August, they caught quality control staff running with documents from their lab to a room across the hall, where they stuffed the papers into lockers, according to the report.
The inspectors said they were not able to recover all the documents and that they also saw personnel pouring product samples into sinks “in a seemingly coordinated effort”.
In addition to the mould and filthy floors, inspectors noticed “significant insect activity” in ceilings.
At Nanjing Chengong Pharmaceutical on China’s east coast, inspectors discovered in September that workers had been buying active ingredients made by other factories and slapping Nanjing Chengong’s seal of approval on them, according to a second report.
Nanjing Chengong’s staff did not review the other factories’ testing information to confirm the products were safe, according to the report.
Drug and active-ingredient makers that sell to the US market are supposed to test samples and retain supporting documentation for FDA inspectors.
The companies did not respond to email requests for comment.
Amphastar Pharmaceuticals, a speciality-drug company based in Rancho Cucamonga, California, holds an 11.5% minority ownership in Nanjing Hanxin Pharmaceutical Technology, said Dan Dischner, a spokesperson. Nanjing Chengong is a subsidiary of Nanjing Hanxin. Amphastar neither controls nor is actively involved in Nanjing Hanxin’s or its subsidiaries’ operations, Dischner said.
Shortage over
While brand-name and generic drugs receive FDA review and approval, compounded drugs do not.
Inspectors make spot checks of suppliers of compounding facilities, which are required to purchase ingredients from FDA-registered manufacturers. Nanjing Chengong was last inspected in March 2025 and Chengdu Shengnuo in September 2023, according to agency records.
Compounders are allowed to offer alternatives to patients who cannot tolerate brand-name medications, tweaking a formula by, say, removing inactive ingredients people are allergic to or creating different dosage forms.
And if a drug falls into short supply – as semaglutide and tirzepatide did in 2022 – the compounding industry may step in.
But they are no longer in shortage, and not all compounders have scaled down. Some operate under the theory that US law allows the sale of copycats if at least one additive is thrown in, such as vitamin B12.
Compounding came under intense scrutiny almost 15 years ago when the New England Compounding Pharmacy sold contaminated drugs, including steroid shots for pain, that infected more than 700 people with meningitis, killing 64.
The deaths prompted a congressional investigation and gave the FDA increased oversight of compounders. But the agency has struggled to maintain the resources to keep up with the task.
A significant proportion of active ingredients in compounded GLP-1s come from China, according to an analysis from the Brookings Institution, a think-tank in Washington. Its 2025 report said Nanjing Hanxin, Nanjing Chengong’s parent company, was a large supplier.
Plants in that country have often fallen short of US pharmaceutical-manufacturing standards, even as China has increasingly become an integral part of the generic market, providing active ingredients and raw materials to companies that finish and sell the lower-cost, FDA-approved versions of treatments. Modi’s Friday ‘sermon’: The language of oppression in India-administered Kashmir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:34:59 UTC
21:34:59 KST

This week, the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board proposed standardising Friday sermons across the mosques and shrines it manages in India-administered Kashmir.
The Board is chaired by Syed Darakhshan Andrabi, a senior leader of the ruling Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), while its core members were nominated by the party.
The proposal drew condemnation from individuals and organisations across the valley, who described it as "interference in the religious affairs of Kashmiri Muslims".
That criticism is important but incomplete. The proposal should not be viewed as an isolated overreach.
It is part of a broader effort by the Indian state to determine how Kashmiri Muslims practise their faith and to cultivate a form of Islam that aligns with its own interests.
Seen this way, the uniform-sermon proposal is the latest in a series of interventions, some openly repressive, others more subtle and administrative.
The methods have changed over time, but the aim has remained largely the same: to prevent religious spaces from becoming platforms for ideas, expressions or activities the state considers problematic.
This matters particularly in Kashmir, where resistance has long drawn on religious spaces and the language of faith.
The mosque has long served as both a place of prayer and a platform for public speech, something the state has understood for decades.
What it permits, then, is a faith that either lends legitimacy to its rule or, at the very least, remains silent about the oppression of everyday life. A faith that only says yes, and never no.
The struggle of oppressed
Consider a 2023 directive that barred Friday sermons from mentioning Palestine and required that any spoken prayers for Palestine be made only in Arabic, not Kashmiri.
Why should the language of a prayer matter? Most Kashmiris can recite Arabic but do not understand it.
Kashmiris have long seen Palestine as a reflection of their own condition, and the state's concern was that a prayer for Palestine, heard and understood, could become a statement about Kashmir. Here, prayer and protest are close.
The Muharram procession in Srinagar tells a similar story.
It was banned in 1989 on "law and order" grounds and allowed to resume only in 2023. Behind the ban was the government's fear that Muharram processions could turn into anti-occupation demonstrations.
What is revealing, however, are the conditions imposed on its return. Participants were barred from expressing anything deemed "anti-national" or "provocative", or displaying symbols of "banned organisations" or "terrorists".
These are the state's euphemisms for the people, ideas and organisations associated with the Kashmiri struggle for self-determination.
In earlier years, the procession had featured photographs of young men who resisted Indian rule and those killed by Indian forces.
Muharram commemorates Karbala, which, for many Muslims, represents the struggle of the oppressed against the oppressor. Kashmiris had long seen their own condition reflected in it. The procession was allowed to resume only on the condition that they stop doing so.
The state's management of Islam in Kashmir also works through endorsement.
In 2023, the same BJP-led Waqf Board invited Hashim Gilani, described as a descendant of Shaykh Abdul Qadir Gilani, the Hanbali jurist, preacher and Sufi master.
Kashmiris revere Shaykh Abdul Qadir Gilani as Dastgeer Sahib, and his shrine in Srinagar's Khanyar neighbourhood is among the valley's most visited.
In one of his addresses, Hashim Gilani said he had heard Kashmir described in terms of violence and conflict but had found only "peace" and "development".
Borrowed spiritual authority was put to work to reinforce the state's narrative of normalcy, a normalcy made possible by the abnormality of our lives: the militarisation of daily life, our loved ones held in prisons, homes demolished and property seized, and families denied the bodies of their dead.
Gilani was not the first. Visiting preachers from India, sponsored directly or indirectly, have used the minbar in Kashmir to make arguments the state could not make as convincingly itself.
Some have argued that geography is determined by God and cannot be altered by humans, meaning Kashmir's place within India must be accepted as fate. Others have called Kashmir the crown of India, asking who would willingly give up a crown.
Still others have described Kashmir as the land of peaceful Sufi saints, where violence has no place. By this, they mean the resistance of Kashmiris, never the violence of the state.
Scholars who preach this kind of Islam are promoted, while those who do not are jailed or lose their pulpits.
Repression in plain form
The Board itself is the product of gradual centralisation. It began under Dogra rule as the Muslim Auqaf Trust, established by Sheikh Abdullah's movement to manage religious endowments, and later became, in effect, an asset of his National Conference party.
In 2003, the PDP-Congress government took control of the Board and made the chief minister its chairman.
In 2019, the Reorganisation Act replaced Kashmir's Waqf law with the central law, while leaving the laws governing Hindu and Sikh shrines intact.
In less than a century, Kashmir's shrines had passed from a community trust to a political party, then to the local government and finally to New Delhi.
The Board's reach also extends to the economy of devotion.
In August 2022, it banned what it called "unethical practices" at shrines. Board officials, accompanied by police, removed donation boxes maintained by hereditary custodians.
The Board presented the move as a matter of transparency. In effect, it marked another step in the centralisation of power.
Then there is repression in its plainest form, such as the repeated closure of Jamia Masjid, one of Srinagar's most important mosques. Its gates are locked, and worshippers are turned away.
This kind of control is easy to see and oppose. A uniform sermon is harder to resist because it leaves the minbar functioning while controlling what is said from it.
But the closure of Jamia Masjid and the uniform-sermon proposal are expressions of the same power. One is justified in the name of "order", the other in the name of "harmony" and "unity". Both seek to define the limits of what Kashmiri Muslims may say and do in relation to their faith.
BJP rule has transformed much in Kashmir, but it has also inherited a great deal.
This is worth emphasising because popular discourse often treats Modi's rise to power or the abrogation of Kashmir's nominal autonomy in 2019 as the point where history begins.
Both brought significant changes. However, India's anxiety about the faith of Kashmiri Muslims is older and systemic.
Decades ago, a preacher invited to speak about the life of the Prophet on state-run Radio Kashmir was told to leave out the Battle of Badr, in which the early Muslim community defeated the Quraysh of Mecca.
The officers seem to have feared that a story of beleaguered Muslims prevailing over a stronger adversary would be understood in Kashmir as something more than history.
In some ways, the uniform-sermon proposal is a newer version of the same instruction.

The German chemicals firm Covestro plans to cut 309 of the 976 jobs at its Antwerp site. The news means that 260 people will be made redundant. The company intends to reorganise the site given global overcapacity. Staff were informed this morning. “The staff have reacted with surprise and dismay; this affects 25 per cent of the workforce,” says Patrik Collier of the Christian ACV union.
Chemicals giant Covestro to axe 309 jobs in the Port of Antwerp
According to trade union representative Collier, the management is closing a BPA plant and five of the six production lines at the Makrolon plant. As a result, only the Aniline plant and the Polyether plant will remain. Management cities 2027 as the deadline. “When you have 970 employees and they’re talking about 260 redundancies, which amounts to 25 per cent of the workforce – and, above all, the families who depend on them,” says Collier.
Covestro produces polycarbonate plastic pellets at the Makrolon plant. This material is used in items such as car headlights. The management points to global overcapacity in the market and that new sites have been established in Asia.
According to the management, this is putting pressure on prices and means that the grades produced in Antwerp are no longer profitable. In Europe, the company only intends to produce profitable polycarbonate grades in future.
The remaining plants form part of the MDI chain. Collier says there is certainly potential for future growth and profit here. However, capacity utilisation at the polyether plant has fallen in recent years. “So, the question is what will remain and how viable that is,” he says. The industry uses polyether and aniline for foams in mattresses, sofas and cars.
Structural crisis in the chemicals sector
The company points to a structural crisis in the European chemicals sector. “It is becoming increasingly difficult for Covestro to sell materials produced in Europe competitively and profitably, particularly in the segment of lower-cost standard polycarbonates. Failing to take action today would undermine the long-term economic viability of our Antwerp site,” Susanne Buchholz, managing director at Covestro, said.

It added that the affidavits subsequently provided detailed particulars to establish that the actions taken by the government and the police were in accordance with the law and that no case of contempt was made out against them.Mohan, in his affidavit filed late on Wednesday night, said the suspension of cellular internet services within a four-kilometre radius of Raisina Hills from 10 pm on October 9 to 10 pm on October 10 was necessary to prevent a disturbance of public order and maintain peace.
He said the Delhi Police's request for the suspension “was found to be a proportionate measure, having regard to the magnitude of the situation and the need to prevent any disturbance of public order in the national capital.”The Supreme Court had issued contempt notices to Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson on October 11 over the alleged violation of its earlier order. The court had directed that “internet facilities should function unhindered”.
Mohan said the suspension was limited to cellular internet services and did not cover Wi-Fi, broadband or other non-cellular internet services. He argued that suspending internet services for a limited period and within a defined geographical area, subject to statutory safeguards, was a recognised measure to maintain public order in appropriate circumstances.The home secretary also requested the Supreme Court to modify its October 11 order “to the extent necessary to permit the suspension of internet services in situations of necessity, strictly in accordance with law and subject to applicable statutory requirements and safeguards”.

The Navy destroyed four Su-34 aircraft, with two more hit — what is known about the carrier of guided aerial bombs used to terrorize Ukraine

The Navy destroyed four Su-34 aircraft, with two more hit — what is known about the carrier of guided aerial bombs used to terrorize Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Navy struck the Borisoglebsk airfield in Voronezh Oblast with a Neptune missile. Four Su-34s were destroyed and two more damaged.
The Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine destroyed 4 Russian Su-34 bombers, and two more were damaged on the territory of the "Borisoglebsk" airport. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic Su-34 frontline bomber, which russia began producing serially in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, this aircraft is the main carrier of KAB guided aerial bombs and precision-guided missiles with which the enemy attacks Ukraine’s frontline regions, UNN writes.
Details
On the morning of Thursday, October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the destruction of 6 Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers during the night of October 15.
During the night of October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the "Borisoglebsk" military airfield in russia’s Voronezh region using a Neptune coastal missile system. Six Su-34Ms destroyed by Neptune strike at Russian airfield - Navy15.10.26, 11:00 • 32607 views
Later, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had struck the airfield. Four Su-34 aircraft were destroyed, and two Su-34 aircraft were hit.
The Russians used them to terrorize our people. These were precisely the aircraft that were ready for new strikes against Ukraine and were armed with aerial bombs. What is known about the Su-34M
The Su-34 (under NATO codification: Fullback (Крайній захисник) is a Soviet/Russian all-weather, two-seat fighter-bomber developed by the Sukhoi Design Bureau.
The Su-34 was designed to carry out precise missile and bomb strikes against enemy ground targets at operational and tactical depths, as well as to engage enemy air targets. It can reach speeds of up to 1,900 km/h at altitudes of up to 14.6 km.
The Su-34 prototype made its first flight in 1990. The aircraft was designed through extensive modernization of the Su-27 fighter.
The Su-34M (also known as "Sych" or Su-34 NVO - Navigation and External Equipment) is a deeply modernized version of the basic Russian Su-34 frontline bomber. The contract for its serial production and delivery to the armed forces was signed in 2020, after which it completely replaced the basic modification on the production line.
Following modernization, the Su-34M received more advanced navigation equipment, powerful reconnaissance systems, and a targeting system with a target-designation system. This expands the range of weapons used, increases the crew’s ability to detect targets, and improves firing accuracy.
For the Su-34 NVO version, three variants of unified suspended reconnaissance pods were developed: electro-optical, electronic intelligence, and radar.
With their help, the aircraft will be able to independently detect ground, sea, and air targets in any weather at a greater distance than before.
The bombers received new radar, targeting, and communications systems, and their missile and bomb armament was expanded. Onboard radio-electronic equipment and electronic warfare systems were improved.
The Su-34M gained the ability to use the latest range of precision-guided munitions (air-to-surface missiles, new guided aerial bombs, and so on), which increased the range and effectiveness of engaging targets without entering the zone of dense enemy air defenses.
In particular, the bomber has 12 hardpoints and can carry up to 8,000 kg of various weapons. At the same time, the aircraft is the main carrier of aerial bombs equipped with UМПК modules (Universal Planning and Correction Module), which turn conventional free-fall bombs into precision-guided glide weapons with a release range of 40–80 km.
What is a guided aerial bomb: range, speed, and countermeasures23.09.26, 07:10 • 58107 views
These are the very aircraft that are "terrorizing" Ukraine's frontline regions. The bomber can be equipped with high-explosive bombs of various calibers — FAB-250, FAB-500, FAB-1500, FAB-3000 with UMPK, as well as KAB-500 and KAB-1500.
It can also be equipped with air-to-surface missiles such as the Kh-38, Kh-29, Kh-59MK2 and Kh-69, as well as anti-radiation missiles: Kh-31P / Kh-31PD, and anti-ship missiles: Kh-31A and Kh-35U.
In addition, the bomber can be equipped with missiles "for self-defense," that is, air-to-air missiles, including medium-/long-range missiles with active radar homing, the R-77, and short-range missiles with infrared homing heads for close-range maneuvering combat, the R-73.
It is not known exactly how many of these aircraft the Russian Federation may have. However, as reported by Russian media, since 2012 the Russian Ministry of Defense has received more than 120 Su-34 aircraft. By 2027, the military agency planned to receive at least 76 upgraded Su-34M aircraft. In 2021, the first six aircraft entered service with the Russian Aerospace Forces.
Russian Federation losses
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Russia has lost 443 aircraft since the beginning of the war. It has been visually confirmed that the Russian Federation lost only one Su-34M aircraft. This occurred in July 2022. The bomber was shot down near Alchevsk, Luhansk region, and it was the Russians themselves who did so as a result of "friendly fire."
Overall, Ukraine has destroyed 43 Su-34 aircraft.

12:11:15 UTC
21:11:15 KST

Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory.
Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future.
The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years.
Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed 123 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through Wednesday's close, when the 10-year traded at 5.19%.
Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market.
If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields.
But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term.
There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The Treasury Department will in the next few days give official results for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September. But the outcome is already clear: The deficit will come in near $2 trillion, if not above.
That is likely to put the deficit in the range of 6.0-6.2% of gross domestic product for the year, based on the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of a $1.993 trillion deficit and a projection of third-quarter GDP.
Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits.
The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.3% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years.
"My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.
AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets.
GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy.
Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.
In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker, wants to reverse the $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package.
And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties.
The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much further out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.
For now, though higher yields are also attracting investors to U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

Armenia PM hopes for Azerbaijan peace treaty within 5 years

Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (L), and President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev (R), shake hands during a Board of Peace meeting at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026, in Washington.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on Oct. 15 he hoped to sign and ratify a peace treaty with Azerbaijan before 2031, as the arch-foes pursue normalization after decades of territorial conflict.
The Caucasus neighbors fought two wars over Azerbaijan’s Armenian-populated Karabakh region, which Baku recaptured in a lightning offensive in 2023, prompting the exodus of its entire ethnic Armenian population.
A lasting settlement could reopen transport routes across the strategic region, where Russia, Türkiye and Iran compete for influence.
“Signing a peace treaty with Azerbaijan is one of the most important issues for the government and for me personally,” Pashinyan told a televised cabinet meeting.
“I have set myself a task, a specific timetable, to resolve the issue before 2031,” he said.
“I see such a possibility. Otherwise, I would not raise this issue.”
The countries initialed a peace agreement at a White House summit hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump in August 2025 but the treaty has yet to be formally signed and ratified.
Azerbaijan has demanded changes to Armenia’s constitution before signing, saying its reference to a declaration of independence calling for unification with Karabakh amounts to a territorial claim.
The constitutional changes sought by Baku would require approval in a national referendum.
Yerevan rejects that interpretation, arguing that the agreed treaty text addresses concerns about territorial claims.
The draft commits both countries to respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, renounce territorial claims and establish diplomatic relations.

Quick hits: Walsh vomits after try, Ponga shines then suffers in epic duel
