2026-10-15
12:09:07 UTC
21:09:07 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Reece Walsh vomits against Kiwis, Kalyn Ponga injured as Jack Bostock shines
Australia and New Zealand have set a high standard for the 17th edition of the Rugby League World Cup, opening the 2026 tournament with an all-time classic.
Young Kiwi Casey McLean defied gravity and debutant Aussie Jack Bostock won the match for the Kangaroos.
Meanwhile, a vomiting Reece Walsh and a broken-armed Kalyn Ponga produced one of the great fullback duels.
Here are the quick hits from the opening match.
1. McLean defies gravity in all-time finish
Casey McLean is Kiwi superman.
After a towering bomb from Jahrome Hughes was batted back by Ronaldo Mulitalo, Isaiah Papali'i threw what could best be described as a one-handed chuck, collected by McLean on the blind side.
With no space to work in, and Kangaroos halfback Mitchell Moses smothering him while directing him towards touch, McLean went airborne.
Somehow, seemingly in slow motion, as his body hovered horizontally over the sideline, McLean grounded the ball in the corner.
ABC Sport expert commentator Luke Lewis described it as "one of the best finishes you will see in this game".
And just four minutes into this World Cup, a contender for try of the tournament was born.
2. Long-range intercepts put Kangaroos on top
The Kiwis dominated the first half at the Sydney Football Stadium.
The New Zealanders had 59 per cent of the ball, made 300 more metres running, and had 66 fewer tackles.
But they went into the break level after the Kangaroos scored two 90-metre intercept tries.
The first Kangaroos score came from debutant Jack Bostock, who rushed out of the defensive line to grab a looping pass by Kiwi halfback Jahrome Hughes.
If that ball got over his head, it would have been a try for the Kiwis. But the Australian winger took the ball cleanly, broke the grasp of a Kiwi, and ran for the goal line.
Incredibly, an almost identical play happened for Australia's other winger, Tom Trbojevic, on the other side of the field.
Kiwi centre Casey McLean gave a pass meant for his unmarked winger, but Trbojevic stuck his arm in the way and caught the footy.
Trbojevic then showed the speed he was known for at the start of his career, beating the cover tackle attempt of Kodi Nikorima and streaking away.
3. After first-half denial, Ponga breathes fire
The duel of the opposing fullbacks was one of the most hyped heading into this game, featuring two of the most electric talents in the game.
And it produced everything fans could hope for.
Kiwi custodian Kalyn Ponga came into the tournament off the back of a breathtaking season for the Knights, while Kangaroos number one Reece Walsh was considered a somewhat controversial selection, preferred over the Roosters' Clive Churchill medallist, James Tedesco.
After being kept relatively quiet for most of the first half, Ponga burst to life on the left, dancing, darting and taunting the Kangaroos.
He slipped past Staggs and tried to sidestep Walsh, who produced a scintillating try-saver, bundling Ponga into touch.
It was one for the purists, in shades of Scott Sattler's tackle on Toddy Byrne in the 2003 NRL grand final.
Ponga shook it off after the break, and the Kiwis' debutant was on the end of some slick passing from the Kiwis for a straightforward finish for his first try.
His second was better, a 40-metre vintage Ponga effort.
With his shorts pulled halfway down his legs, he still managed to power past Walsh with a classic step, sending the sizeable Kiwi contingent in Sydney into delirium.
4. Walsh plunders then chunders, Ponga goes off
The Kangaroos were staring down a rare defeat to their arch-rivals in this arena, when Walsh responded to his opposite number's heroics and left the Kiwis in his dust.
Deep in their own half and trailing by six, Bostock slipped a clever flick pass behind his back, and the Broncos superstar swooped.
He swerved past defenders, running 60 metres to go over in the corner.
But he gave everything in the effort, and as he prepared to take the conversion, he was interrupted by his exhaustion.
He threw up and was unable to take the kick, with Lattrell Mitchell stepping up instead.
Walsh continued to dry retch and looked completely spent. But he managed to keep it together (and inside) to stay on the field and see out the game.
But it was a horrible end to the game for Ponga; his night ended early with a suspected broken arm — a huge blow for the Kiwis' title hopes.
Ponga had nursed his left arm after a tackle on Cam Munster early in the second half.
He stayed out there, but appeared to hit his arm again in a collision with teammate Hughes in an attempt to tackle Walsh.
5. Bostock hat trick
Jack Bostock had already made his mark on international rugby league with his 90-metre intercept try in the first half.
But he was not done scoring and it proved a match-winning performance.
His second try came in the 57th minute, with the Aussies trailing by six points.
Kangaroos five-eighth Cam Munster put up a pinpoint kick for Bostock to chase.
The Australian went up against his Dolphins teammate Jamayne Isaako, beat him in the air, and scored a fantastic try to help level the scores.
But Bostock had an even better effort to win the game.
Down by two with less than four minutes to play, it was Munster again who put up a high kick for Bostock to chase.
Isaako was in a much better position this time, and appeared to have caught the footy.
But Bostock ripped the ball out of the Kiwi's arms, in turn, ripping the game away from New Zealand.

OPCON Transition: Now It Is Time for the Commanders-in-Chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:09:00 UTC
21:09:00 KST

The debate over wartime operational control (OPCON) transition once again stands at the threshold of decision. At the 57th Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) in 2025, South Korea and the United States agreed to pursue verification of the full operational capability (FOC) of the Future Combined Forces Command headquarters in 2026, and the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy (NDS) assessed that South Korea is capable of taking primary responsibility for deterring North Korea with “critical but more limited” U.S. support.
More than 20 years have passed since the allies formalized OPCON transition, and more than a decade of preparation and verification has accumulated since they adopted the conditions-based transition plan. Meanwhile, South Korea has grown into an ally with military and economic capabilities entirely different from those it had when this arrangement was created some 70 years ago.
With the next SCM approaching, the question must change. Until now, the debate has centered on asking: have the military conditions been met? The purpose of a conditions-based approach was not to avoid a decision, but to make a responsible decision possible. Military preparation always carries residual risk, and from the moment one judges what level of risk is acceptable, the question moves beyond military assessment into the realm of political responsibility.
Whose Decision Is It?
The wartime OPCON exercised by the commander of the ROK-U.S. Combined Forces Command derives from two sources. For U.S. forces, this authority is delegated through the chain of command from the U.S. president, through the secretary of defense, to the combatant commander. For South Korean forces, it is delegated under the South Korean president’s authority as commander-in-chief. OPCON transition, then, is neither a one-directional “return” of operational control nor simply a change in military structure. It is a political decision by the two commanders-in-chief to delegate their respective authorities to a new structure.
This distinction matters. If transition is seen as South Korea’s demand alone, the United States becomes the examiner and South Korea the examinee. If it is seen as a joint decision of the two commanders-in-chief, both sides have things they must do to make the decision possible. What OPCON transition needs, therefore, is not only the military authorities’ assessment of conditions, but a responsible decision by the supreme commanders, the presidents of South Korea and the United States.
The political tasks for transition can be sorted into four lines of effort. They are tasks the two countries’ political leaders must carry out, and at the same time political criteria for agreeing on transition at the summit level.
1: Understand and Address Military Concerns
The vulnerability of a transition period cannot be denied. Viewed from a purely military perspective, OPCON transition can only be postponed indefinitely, for a perfectly prepared military does not exist. Yet denying it only deepens distrust within the alliance. What is needed is for the two countries’ political leaders to jointly acknowledge this vulnerability, and to offset and manage it with alliance-level political-strategic means alongside military compensating measures.
The starting point is understanding that the two sides’ concerns differ. South Korea’s concerns converge on the credibility of extended deterrence, the deployment of reinforcements in a contingency, and a command gap during transition. On the U.S. side, the main concerns are possible degradation of the combined defense posture, the institutional and political problems of U.S. forces operating under a South Korean general, and the risk perceptions of the Combined Forces Command and parts of Congress.
The South Korean president must demonstrate, through exercises and verification, that South Korea has a working crisis decision-making structure to lead theater operations, running from the president to the Ministry of National Defense, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Future Combined Forces Command. The U.S. president must reaffirm the defense commitment and extended deterrence at the summit level and continue institutionalization through the Nuclear Consultative Group. The scope and procedures of the bridging and enduring capabilities the United States will provide should be codified in the relevant agreements and strategic directives. The NDS’s reference to “critical but more limited support” needs to be fleshed out with specifics.
There are also things the two countries must do together. Whether to accept or limit escalation in a crisis, and under what conditions to begin and to end a war, are matters for the commanders-in-chief to judge. The two leaders must therefore identify and align, in peacetime, their perceptions of war aims, escalation thresholds, and war termination conditions. The allies should also adopt a “No Surprise” principle: changes in posture, command reorganization, and the movement of forces in and out must be consulted in advance.
2: Commit Resources and Assets Continuously
A decision not backed by the necessary resources is no more than a political declaration. The investment South Korea must bear is considerable, but what is needed is not money alone. It also includes the commitment of national capacity for the employment and posture of military forces. Both sides need multiyear, bipartisan commitments that can survive changes of government.
South Korea must link its roadmap for core military capabilities to the Mid-Term Defense Plan and secure its sustainability through the National Assembly. Recent defense spending increases should be explained not as burden-sharing, but as part of the national goal of transition and independent capability.
The United States must back the assets, posture, and budget needed to provide bridging and enduring capabilities, such as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), space, strategic asset deployment, and reinforcement plans. A responsible answer by the administration to the National Defense Authorization Act provision concerning transition-related funding and certification is also part of this effort.
South Korea’s commitment of resources becomes the basis for a capability-based voice within the alliance. The U.S. commitment of assets ensures that “limited support” is never read as “uncertain support.” OPCON transition is not a single event, but part of a process of completing a future-oriented combined command structure – one that the legislatures and executive branches of both countries must resource together.
3: Develop a Future-Oriented Alliance Architecture
Security and alliance issues must not be treated as transactions, like trade negotiations. If OPCON transition is transactionally linked to other issues, it becomes something obtained by paying a price. This can fuel political backlash against transition in both countries and damage trust in the alliance. Defense cost-sharing, reductions in U.S. Forces Korea, and the Northeast Asia Command concept could all become subjects of such transactional linkage. These issues are not entirely unrelated to OPCON transition, but they must be handled on separate tracks and must not become terms of exchange.
For the U.S. president, policy alignment within the administration is needed above all. Within Washington, OPCON transition can be viewed through the White House’s alliance policy and negotiations, the defense establishment’s burden-sharing, and the combatant command’s command relationships. Aligning these into a single strategic direction is a task only the commander-in-chief can perform.
The South Korean president, for his part, should not make out-of-area contributions a term of exchange for progress on transition. Leading the defense of the Korean Peninsula and making selective contributions in the Indo-Pacific are separate matters, each under its own principles. At home, OPCON should not be consumed merely as a symbol of sovereignty. The two countries can begin by describing these issues separately in official documents such as the SCM joint communiqué.
Of course, not every link can be cut. Command relationships among the Future Combined Forces Command, the United Nations Command, and U.S. Forces Korea, access to United Nations Command rear bases in a contingency, and the alliance’s regional role cannot be thought of apart from transition. Transactional linkage and structural linkage must therefore be clearly distinguished. Structural linkage should not be hidden or postponed, but discussed transparently and established together in designing the transition.
4: Take Responsibility for and Explain the Political Decision
If OPCON transition is not made by military judgment alone, responsibility for the decision should not rest on the military alone either. The military assessment that “the military is ready” and the political judgment that “the two governments have decided” must be kept distinct. Otherwise, when problems arise, responsibility shifts to commanders, and political leaders hide behind military outcomes.
The U.S. Congress is already involved through the National Defense Authorization Act, overseeing whether conditions are met, the Future Combined Forces Command’s national command reporting chain, the relationship with the United Nations Command, the impact on nuclear proliferation, and military risk. If the administration does not answer these questions systematically, caution in Congress and in the field will delay the decision at the working level.
The South Korean National Assembly, by contrast, has no equivalent procedure. As the body that must provide the budget and institutional arrangements, it should be involved through regular reporting and verification, and the executive branch must explain why transition needs to happen now, what changes and what does not, and what is required.
Political accountability also includes the management of trust. South Korea must not treat transition only as a political timetable and neglect military preparation, nor give that impression. The United States should refrain from messages suggesting that the Combined Forces Command could be dissolved if conditions are not met. That, too, is part of the responsibility for completing an agreement the two countries have pursued together for 20 years across administrations.
The Politics of Decision and Responsibility
In the end, the last gateway of OPCON transition is not military assessment alone but the responsible political judgment of the two commanders-in-chief. For 20 years, military assessments have often provided grounds for deferring political decisions. What is needed now is not to keep asking whether the conditions have been met, but for the commanders-in-chief to decide and to take responsibility for that decision.
That means four lines of effort: identifying and managing the military risks of transition; continuously providing the resources and assets to support it; designing the future alliance’ command structure together rather than treating transition as a transaction; and explaining the decision to the public and the legislature and taking responsibility for its results.
These are not South Korea’s homework alone. If only one side carries out these steps, transition remains one side’s demand or a one-sided transfer of burden. Only when carried out together do they work as political criteria and as a driving force. OPCON transition is not an event that settles the past, but a process of jointly designing the alliance’s future command structure – and completing that design is, in the end, the commanders-in-chief’s responsibility.

Latvian PM urges Europeans to give up one beer a year to help Ukraine
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told journalists in Brussels on Thursday 15 October that helping Ukraine would require each EU resident to donate only the equivalent of the cost of one beer a year.
Source: European Pravda, citing Delfi

Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
- Published
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.
Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".
Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.
They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.
Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.
In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.
- Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast 
  - Published11 hours ago
The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.
But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".
"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."
He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."
Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".
Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".
Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.
There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.
Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.
Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.
Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.
He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."
Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.
But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.
Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.
At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.
"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

Psychologists identify three distinct profiles of support for free speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:28 UTC
21:00:28 KST

People who express the most permissive attitudes toward free speech often harbor stronger beliefs in conspiracy theories and lower trust in societal institutions. These patterns suggest that advocating for unrestricted expression is not always driven by a commitment to democratic values, but might also stem from a deep skepticism toward official narratives. The research was published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Psychologists have traditionally measured support for freedom of speech as a single, overarching attitude. This approach assumes that a person who defends the right to speak freely will do so evenly across all situations. In recent years, researchers have proposed that this support is actually broken down into different categories, depending on the type of speech involved. A person might tolerate everyday disagreements but draw the line at speech that is deeply offensive or threatens social order.
To capture these nuances, researchers have recently defined free speech support across four specific dimensions. The first is tolerance for offensive speech, which involves accepting language that challenges deeply held moral frameworks or sacred values. The second is tolerance for disagreement, or allowing others to express contradictory beliefs that might cause interpersonal tension.
The third dimension is tolerance for heterodox speech. This involves an openness to non-mainstream or unconventional ideas, even those that seem irrational. The final dimension is tolerance for socially divisive speech, which reflects support for public advocacy or protests that could be seen as threatening societal cohesion.
Researchers also suspected that attitudes about free speech might relate to how people view information and authority. People who distrust dominant institutions, such as the government or the news media, might favor completely unrestricted expression as a way to bypass what they perceive as informational control. Nejc Plohl, a psychologist at the University of Maribor in Slovenia, led a research team to investigate how these different dimensions of free speech support combine within individuals. Plohl and his colleagues, Dean Korošak and Boris Podobnik, wanted to see if specific types of people share distinct patterns of tolerance for controversial speech.
The researchers surveyed 563 European adults online. The participants completed a 24-item questionnaire designed to measure their tolerance for the four specific types of speech mentioned above. Participants rated how much they agreed with statements assessing their willingness to allow offensive, disagreeing, heterodox, and socially divisive speech.
Alongside the free speech questionnaire, the participants answered questions about their political ideology, their level of education, and their gender. They also completed measures to gauge their belief in conspiracy theories and their trust in three major societal institutions. To assess institutional trust, participants estimated the percentage of journalists, politicians, and scientists who prioritize truth and public well-being over other interests. To measure conspiracy ideation, participants rated how strongly they believed that official accounts of events are frequently designed to hide the truth.
The researchers first used a statistical technique called confirmatory factor analysis to see if the participants’ answers naturally grouped into the four proposed categories of speech. This method tests whether a set of survey items accurately measures the distinct concepts they were designed to evaluate. The analysis showed that people do indeed view offensive, disagreeing, heterodox, and socially divisive speech as distinct concepts. The researchers found no statistical support for a single, general attitude covering all forms of free expression.
Next, the team used a method called latent profile analysis to sort the participants into groups based on their shared response patterns. This technique identifies hidden subgroups within a larger population by finding people who answer questions in very similar ways. The analysis revealed three distinct profiles of free speech support.
The majority of the participants, making up about 57 percent of the group, fell into a “conditional tolerance” profile. These individuals showed average tolerance for offensive speech and disagreement, but were slightly less tolerant of heterodox and socially divisive speech. This suggests they hold a moderate, context-sensitive view of free expression.
About 20 percent of the participants formed a “low tolerance” profile. These individuals consistently reported the lowest acceptance of controversial or norm-challenging speech across all four categories. They were especially intolerant of offensive speech and basic disagreement.
The remaining 23 percent of the sample fell into a “broad tolerance” profile. These participants expressed highly permissive attitudes toward all forms of speech, including ideas that most people would find offensive or socially destructive.
When the researchers looked at how these profiles aligned with other personal characteristics, several patterns emerged. Men and highly educated individuals were heavily overrepresented in the broad tolerance group. Women were more prevalent in the low tolerance group. Age differences between the profiles were not statistically significant.
In terms of politics, the low tolerance profile leaned slightly more conservative than the other groups. The broad tolerance profile leaned more liberal, with the conditional tolerance profile falling in the middle. The most pronounced differences, however, appeared in how the groups viewed institutions and information.
Participants in the broad tolerance group reported the highest levels of belief in conspiracy theories and the lowest levels of trust in science, politics, and journalism. Conversely, the conditional tolerance group exhibited the highest trust in these institutions and the lowest endorsement of conspiracy theories. The researchers concluded that a blanket endorsement of free speech often co-occurs with an underlying distrust of official authorities.
The study relied on an abstract questionnaire that asked participants how they felt about hypothetical types of speech. People often respond differently when confronted with specific, real-world examples of controversial statements. Because the survey did not present concrete scenarios, the findings represent how people think about free speech in theory rather than how they might react in practice. The researchers noted that individuals might support free speech in principle but oppose it when faced with specific topics or targets.
The research relied on data collected at a single point in time, meaning it cannot determine the direction of the relationship between free speech attitudes and institutional trust. It is unknown whether a deep skepticism of institutions causes people to support unrestricted speech, or if holding permissive views on speech naturally leads to greater distrust of authority. It is also possible that an unmeasured factor drives both of these attitudes simultaneously.
The researchers measured political ideology and conspiracy beliefs using very brief questionnaires to reduce the time burden on participants. While these shorter surveys are common in psychological research, they cannot capture the full depth of a person’s political worldview or their specific conspiratorial beliefs. Future studies will need to use more comprehensive assessments to fully understand how these complex traits relate to free speech attitudes.
The study, “Distinct profiles of free speech support and their demographic, ideological, and epistemic characteristics,” was authored by Nejc Plohl, Dean Korošak, and Boris Podobnik.

What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US could use against Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

Breadcrumb
What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US is considering to use against Iran?
The United States is considering using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iran as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes, raising questions about its devastating impact and whether it could penetrate Tehran's heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
According to a CNN report on Thursday, US military planners have drawn up options involving the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs" or MOAB, to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The plans reportedly include possible strikes on Pickaxe Mountain, an underground facility near Natanz where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The reported plans come as Trump faces mounting pressure to end the war with Iran, with negotiations stalled and the US president seeking a way to bring the conflict to a close without appearing to concede defeat.
No decision to deploy the bomb has been announced, and the White House has said Trump is keeping all options available.
Here is what to know about the weapon, its destructive capabilities and why the US is considering using it against Iran.
What is the 'mother of all bombs'?
The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) is the most powerful conventional bomb in the US military's arsenal.
Weighing approximately 9,800 kilograms (21,600 pounds) and measuring more than nine metres in length, the GPS-guided weapon was developed by the US Air Force in 2003 ahead of the American invasion of Iraq.
Unlike conventional bombs designed to penetrate fortified underground structures, the MOAB is an air-blast weapon that detonates above the ground, generating an enormous explosion across a wide area.
During testing in March 2003, the explosion produced a mushroom cloud visible from approximately 20 miles away.
The weapon was originally designed to destroy large concentrations of troops, military equipment and above-ground fortifications, although its potential targets later expanded to include caves and tunnels.
How destructive is the bomb?
The MOAB is capable of devastating large areas through an immense blast wave that can destroy buildings, military installations and other structures.
The weapon can devastate an area equivalent to approximately nine city blocks, according to the CNN report, although the actual extent of destruction depends on the terrain, surrounding structures and other conditions.
Despite its enormous size, the MOAB is not a nuclear weapon and does not produce the radioactive fallout associated with a nuclear explosion.
The bomb is GPS-guided and is delivered from a military transport aircraft rather than a conventional fighter jet. During its first combat deployment, it was dropped from an American MC-130 aircraft.
Its enormous size and destructive capabilities have also made it a tool of psychological warfare, with US military officials originally hoping that the threat of its use would intimidate enemy forces into surrendering.
Has the 'mother of all bombs' been used before?
Yes. The United States first deployed the MOAB in combat in April 2017, during Trump's first presidential term.
The bomb was dropped on a network of tunnels used by Islamic State (IS) militants in Afghanistan's eastern Nangarhar province, near the border with Pakistan.
The US military said the strike targeted underground tunnels and caves used by IS fighters to move between positions and launch attacks against Afghan and US forces.
Afghan officials reported that 36 IS fighters were killed and three underground tunnels destroyed, along with weapons and ammunition.
US and Afghan officials said at the time that no civilians were killed, although the strike attracted criticism over the use of such an enormous weapon.
Former Afghan President Hamid Karzai condemned the bombing, accusing Washington of using Afghanistan as a testing ground for destructive weapons.
Trump praised the operation at the time, describing it as "another successful job".
The 2017 strike remains the only publicly acknowledged combat use of the MOAB.
Why is Trump considering using it against Iran?
The reported plans come amid uncertainty over how Washington intends to end the conflict after more than six months of US military operations against Iran.
According to CNN, some Trump administration officials have discussed launching a final round of strikes before withdrawing American forces from the region, potentially allowing the president to present the operation as a military victory.
One source familiar with the plans said the proposed attacks could take place before a US military withdrawal from the region covered by Central Command.
The MOAB's psychological impact could also be a factor, with officials suggesting that its deployment could demonstrate overwhelming American military power and increase pressure on Tehran.
However, sources familiar with the discussions have questioned whether such an operation would achieve Washington's strategic objectives or bring the conflict any closer to an end.
Trump has publicly suggested he would refrain from additional military action before November's US midterm elections, although advisers reportedly remain uncertain whether he will maintain that position.
Could the bomb destroy Iran's underground nuclear facilities?
Military officials have expressed serious doubts about whether the MOAB could destroy Iran's most heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
Unlike specialised bunker-busting weapons, the MOAB is designed to unleash a massive explosion across the surface rather than penetrate deeply underground.
Pickaxe Mountain, for example, is believed to be protected by substantial layers of granite, potentially shielding its underground facilities from the bomb's effects.
The US possesses another weapon specifically designed for such targets: the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP), which can penetrate hardened underground structures before detonating.
American B-2 bombers deployed 14 of these penetrator bombs during US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, according to a US Department of Defense report.
The difference highlights a central question surrounding the reported plans: whether deploying the MOAB would inflict meaningful damage on Iran's nuclear programme or primarily serve as a show of force.
What would be the consequences of using it against Iran?
Deploying the MOAB against Iran would represent a significant escalation in the conflict, particularly if the weapon were used against energy infrastructure or facilities near populated areas.
Its enormous blast could cause widespread destruction, while damage to electricity supplies, industrial installations and other essential infrastructure could have consequences far beyond the immediate target.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has warned that explosive weapons with wide-area effects are particularly dangerous in populated areas because their impact can extend beyond intended military targets.
Such attacks can kill and injure civilians, destroy homes and disrupt services essential for survival, including water, electricity and healthcare.
The US military's use of the MOAB would also raise serious questions under international humanitarian law, which requires attacks to distinguish between military objectives and civilians, prohibits disproportionate civilian harm and obliges forces to take feasible precautions to protect civilians.

Can the Public See DOGE’s Records? The Supreme Court Takes Up a Key Fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The U.S. Supreme Court said Tuesday that it will take up a case to decide whether a watchdog organization can obtain information to help establish whether the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) is subject to a federal public records law.
It’s the latest update on a lawsuit filed by a nonprofit called Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) that argues DOGE, the initiative that was spearheaded by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).
The Trump Administration has argued that FOIA does not apply to DOGE because it was not a federal agency—it was a presidential advisory body.
Signed into law in 1966 by President Lyndon B. Johnson, FOIA grants “the public the right to request access to records from any federal agency,” according to the federal government’s website. Johnson said at the time that he hoped the government would, in upholding the law, weigh national security, individual privacy, confidential government deliberations, and the benefit of a well-informed constituency.
“The founding principle of FOIA is that it’s crucial in a democracy to have an informed citizenry,” says Sara Creighton, an associate professor at Georgetown Law and the former Deputy Chief Counsel at American Oversight, a government transparency nonprofit. “The whole idea is that we need an informed voting public.”
Justices have agreed to hear arguments over whether, and to what extent, discovery can proceed for CREW v. DOGE Service. This phase of the legal process allows opposing parties to collect information, including records and depositions, with which to make their cases.
Experts say this decision will not only affect the pending lawsuit, but may also have ramifications for the future of government transparency.
How did the DOGE records case reach the Supreme Court?
CREW filed an FOIA request seeking expedited processing for information about DOGE on Jan. 24, 2025, seeking insights about its structure and communications with other agencies. When it didn’t receive the documents it requested, the organization sued.
“The law is clear about how government records should be preserved so that, when the public requests them, they are easily and readily accessible. If the administration valued transparency, following records laws would be a priority,” CREW President Noah Bookbinder said in a statement announcing the lawsuit on Feb. 20, 2025. “Instead, US DOGE Service and OMB are acting as though the law does not apply to them. It does.”
“The fight ultimately in the DOGE case, and what CREW was hoping to test with its litigation, was whether DOGE [is] subject to FOIA,” says Ryan Mulvey, a senior policy counsel at the Americans for Prosperity Foundation.
On April 15, 2025, Judge Christopher Cooper ruled on behalf of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia that the case could proceed to discovery. The Department of Justice, however, filed an emergency appeal in May 2025 asking the Supreme Court to intervene. The Supreme Court paused the discovery orders on May 23, 2025. On June 6, 2025, it directed the appeals court to narrow the requests, finding that those concerning DOGE’s recommendations and whether agencies followed them were “not appropriately tailored.”
CREW then pared back its requests for discovery, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld them. The Trump Administration again filed a request to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower court was not adhering to the previous ruling by granting “wide-ranging and intrusive discovery.”
In response, the Supreme Court agreed this week to take up the question of whether the case can proceed to discovery. It’s unclear at this point when oral arguments would begin, but a ruling is expected by the end of term in late June or early July 2027.
What could the Supreme Court’s DOGE ruling mean for public access?
The Supreme Court’s ruling will determine if CREW can access the information that could help it make its case that DOGE acted as a federal authority that is subject to FOIA, according to Creighton. If not, the nonprofit may have difficulty pursuing its argument.
“Because so much about how DOGE operated … was not publicly explained, discovery is the only way to unearth key facts about DOGE’s operations and exercises of authority,” says Margaret Kwoka, the Frank R. Strong Chair in Law at Ohio State University’s Moritz College of Law, who joined a brief supporting CREW as an outside legal expert. “Those details will illuminate whether it is in fact exercising independent authority or whether it is acting as an advisor to the President.”
The outcome of the case could have implications beyond the current Administration, Creighton says.
“Whether an entity is subject to FOIA really determines how much information the public gets to know about it, and whether [entities] have any obligation to disclose their documents to the public,” Creighton says.
The current issue before the Supreme Court pertains to discovery, but Creighton warns that if the Supreme Court ultimately rules that DOGE is not subject to FOIA, that could potentially “open the door for future presidents to create entities inside the Executive Office of the President that do significant work—even potentially work relating to the work of agencies who are usually subject to FOIA—but allow that work to be outside the scope of FOIA.”
CREW did not respond to TIME’s request for comment, but it has previously said that government transparency is at stake.
“The lower courts have uniformly ruled that CREW is entitled to discovery in this case to help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to FOIA,” CREW’s chief counsel, Nikhel Sus, told POLITICO in a statement on Tuesday. “We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government.”
Solicitor General D. John Sauer, meanwhile, argued in his filing to the Supreme Court that the appeals court ruling “intrudes into the autonomy and confidentiality of presidential advisors and augurs time-consuming and burdensome discovery litigation.”
He further claimed that the lower court decision “threatens to burden future presidential administrations” with similar legal cases.
The White House referred TIME to the Department of Justice, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
What other records lawsuits has the Trump Administration faced?
The DOGE dispute is among several legal battles over access to, and preservation of, government records under the Trump Administration.
In 2025, American Oversight filed a lawsuit asking the court to order multiple national security officials to preserve official communications that were exchanged on the encrypted messaging app Signal. The request was filed after it came to light that the officials were exchanging messages regarding planned military strikes in Yemen. The case is still ongoing.
In April, the same group, along with the American Historical Association, sued the Trump Administration over a legal opinion released by the Department of Justice that claimed the Presidential Records Act—which stipulates that presidential records be preserved and transferred to the National Archives when the President leaves office—is unconstitutional. That case is also ongoing.
While those cases remain ongoing, American Oversight has secured a win in another records dispute. In August, a federal judge struck down an Energy Department policy that would have permitted it to close pending FOIA requests filed earlier than Oct. 1, 2024, unless requesters reaffirmed their interest within 30 days. The court sided with the watchdog group.

Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.

Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.
The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.
Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.

Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware. Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets, while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.

Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace.
Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.

With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.
The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said.
An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.

World losing ground in ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.
“Biodiversity underpins life on Earth,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people.”
Trailing behind
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline, the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
Glass half full
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.
Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
The road ahead
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”

Points deduction, relegation or stripped titles: What could happen to Manchester City?

20:59:24 KST

Findings of financial misconduct against Manchester City have set the stage for a potentially landmark case that could reshape both the club’s future and the way English football polices its richest clubs.
The independent commission’s conclusions span nine seasons and open the door to sanctions that could reach far beyond a conventional financial penalty.
Sports law expert Jan Zglinski said the scale of the case is unlike anything previously seen, with possible consequences ranging from a heavy points deduction and compensation claims to questions over titles won during the period under scrutiny.
“I really hope this case will in a few years’ time be seen as a turning point, because this is a breach of unprecedented scale,” Zglinski, an associate professor of law at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), told Anadolu.
“It’s been systematic, and the financial volume of it is something we haven’t seen yet in English football or in world football,” he added.
The Premier League announced in late September that an independent commission had found City guilty of serious financial rule breaches spanning nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, following charges brought against the club in February 2023.
The commission found that City used “sham” contracts with commercial partners as part of schemes that artificially inflated revenue and reduced reported costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion), concealing the true state of the club's finances from auditors and football regulators.
It also found that City had significantly breached Premier League and UEFA spending limits and failed to cooperate fully with the league's investigation.
The Premier League confirmed City's appeal on Oct. 2, with the club rejecting the commission's findings and maintaining its innocence.
“The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case,” City said in a statement.
Potential sanctions have yet to be determined.
Zglinski said approximately £830 million of the nearly £950 million in sponsorship revenue recorded by City had been funded by the club's ownership rather than the sponsors themselves, describing the scale as “quite shocking.”
He explained that sponsors paid only a fraction of the amounts recorded as revenue, with the club's owners covering the remainder.
“And this is how we get to the situation where there was on the books a really large sum of money that was coming into the club. But in reality, very little of that was paid by the sponsors themselves. Most of it was footed by the club ownership,” he said.
Zglinski said the distinction between funding provided by the club's ownership and money originating from the UAE government would not change the Premier League's findings on sponsorship revenue.
“Now, one way in which I don't think it's going to matter is that the Premier League's financial rules clearly stipulate that the club itself must be earning the sponsorship rights,” he said.
However, he said the origin of the money could become relevant in potential proceedings involving individuals in City's leadership, particularly where questions of state immunity arise.
“So the origin of that money indeed will have a consequence,” he said. “They shouldn't, though, impact the Premier League's findings in this matter.”
Asked how City could challenge the findings, Zglinski pointed to the club's previous legal proceedings against UEFA, suggesting it could again question whether the evidence met the required standard.
“Back then, the basis of the appeal was that Manchester City thought the standards of evidence hadn't been met,” he said. “It said that UEFA didn’t have quite the right information to justify a sanction. I am sure that in this case, they will try that as well.”
Unlike City's previous UEFA case, which reached the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), the Premier League proceedings follow a separate appeals process.
“Here we're now going to have the appeal by the Premier League Appeal Board,” Zglinski said.
“From that, there might be a further step to the High Court here in England, but that allows an appeal only on quite narrow grounds,” he added.
Zglinski warned that City could face a substantial points deduction, potentially accompanied by a fine.
“Realistically, I think we’re looking at the very least at a very heavy points deduction, possibly combined with the fine,” he said.
Zglinski said a sufficiently heavy points deduction could effectively relegate City, while a separate decision to force the club out of the Premier League would create practical difficulties because the English Football League (EFL) would need to accommodate it.
“The EFL would need to accept Manchester City as part of these clubs,” he said.
He explained that accommodating City could require another EFL club to drop out or the league to temporarily expand, an option he believed the EFL would be reluctant to consider.
Previous points deductions imposed on Everton and Nottingham Forest offered some guidance on how the Premier League applies its financial rules, but Zglinski cautioned that City's case involved breaches on a far greater financial scale.
“These are, of course, in some ways valuable precedents because they show how the Premier League's handbook is applied,” he said.
“However, they, of course, concern a completely different order of magnitude,” he added.
The possibility of stripping City of titles won during the period covered by the findings was another issue.
“There’s a strong argument to be made that Manchester City should not in the history books carry on the honor of having won the Premier League or the FA Cup in a period where they systematically and significantly breached the financial rules of this country,” Zglinski said.
However, he said awarding those titles to rival clubs would be more complicated.
“Whether that means that other clubs will be reinstated in their position, whether Liverpool finally gets to lift that trophy, I don’t think is quite as straightforward,” he added.
Beyond potential sporting sanctions, Zglinski said rival clubs that believed they had suffered financial or sporting harm could pursue compensation claims against Manchester City.
He cited the dispute between Burnley and Everton, in which an independent Premier League commission ordered Everton in June to pay Burnley £26 million ($35 million) in damages, plus £9.1 million in interest, over financial-rule breaches linked to the 2021/22 season.
The commission found that Everton's breaches had given the club a sporting advantage that contributed to Burnley's relegation that season. Everton appealed the compensation ruling, arguing that the decision was flawed in law and fact.
However, Zglinski warned that the unprecedented scale of City's case could make it difficult to establish a workable compensation framework.
“Because of the unprecedented scale, we don’t really know how that will practically happen,” he said.
As for possible consequences beyond English football, Zglinski considered further action by UEFA unlikely. He noted that CAS overturned City's two-season European competition ban in 2020, with some of UEFA's claims in those proceedings found to be time-barred.
“I would not be expecting, in the first place, UEFA to take action now,” he said.
He added that FIFA had no official role in the Premier League investigation and was not in a position to impose sanctions at that stage.
Beyond the potential sanctions, Zglinski criticized the length of the Premier League's investigation, saying football authorities needed to respond more quickly to financial misconduct.
“It also needs remembering that this investigation took very, very long,” he said, referring to the years that had passed since City's early successes during the period covered by the breaches.
“That’s way too long and that cannot be the way forward,” he added.
Zglinski urged the Premier League to review its procedures to prevent similar delays in future cases.
“So I'm very much hoping that the Premier League will take a hard look in the mirror and try to find ways of making the system more effective,” he said.
“Because one thing that no one wants, not the clubs, not the fans, is to discuss titles and championships a decade later in the courtroom instead of on the pitch,” he said.

Belarus Modernizes Infrastructure for Russian Aggression Near NATO Borders by 2027
Belarus could be ready for full-scale participation in a wider Russian war by spring or mid-2027 as military infrastructure and arms production expand toward NATO borders, Centrum Europy reported on October 14.
The report, prepared by the Belarusian democratic forces’ analytical center BELPOL together with the underground Association of Belarusian Railway Workers, was presented in Warsaw. Centrum Europy noted that its authors relied on open sources, leaked documents, and information they claimed was obtained after “bribing Russian generals.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Centrum Europy, BELPOL identified a secure military communications network being built across Belarus from east to west, rather than radiating outward from Minsk. The group argued that its layout is designed to support the movement of Russian forces from the Russian border toward Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Ukraine.
“This network is being built from east to west, along Belarus’s largest roads and highways,” BELPOL representative Maćwiej Kuprejczyk told Centrum Europy. “The center of this system is not in Belarus.”
Centrum Europy also detailed Russian-funded railway modernization connecting Belarus with Ukraine and NATO states, including stronger tracks, new unloading ramps, sidings to ammunition depots, and infrastructure for underground fuel storage.
BELPOL assessed that these upgrades could allow Russian divisions and heavy equipment to move rapidly toward NATO borders without first concentrating forces in eastern Belarus.
Particular attention was given to routes leading toward the Suwałki Gap, the narrow area connecting Poland and Lithuania that links the Baltic states with the rest of NATO.
Centrum Europy reported that BELPOL representatives claimed Russian commanders had described the infrastructure as potentially useful for an operation aimed at seizing the corridor and cutting Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia off from Poland.
BELPOL also identified around 120 Belarusian companies producing or preparing to produce for the Russian Armed Forces. The report described new defense plants and civilian factories being converted for military output, including a facility expected to assemble 122 mm rockets for BM-21 Grad launchers.
“The preliminary date when everything will be ready is the beginning or middle of 2027,” Kuprejczyk stated.
He added that most facilities were expected to reach maximum production capacity by March 2027, with the remainder reaching full capacity by midyear.
Asked by Centrum Europy whether that meant Belarus could be ready for war by spring 2027, Kuprejczyk answered affirmatively.
BELPOL maintained that the buildup could support Russian operations not only against Ukraine but potentially against NATO’s Baltic members.
Centrum Europy noted that BELPOL had already warned in 2024 that Belarus under Alexander Lukashenko was preparing for deeper involvement in Russia’s war and potentially for operations against NATO states. The group now argues that the continuing expansion of railways, communications networks, and military production has made that scenario more concrete.
Days earlier, masked individuals crossing from Belarus damaged Latvian border surveillance equipment and stole cameras before retreating back across the frontier.
Latvian authorities also reported that armed masked individuals had accompanied migrants toward the border, describing the episode as part of continued provocations and hybrid activity targeting Latvia and NATO’s eastern flank.

What to know about Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused Starlink service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:43 UTC
20:54:43 KST

Uncertainty over who controls SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention, as restrictions on the technology hinder Ukraine's defenses.
Ukraine has accused SpaceX-owned Starlink of restricting its military-grade services, known as Starshield, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv.
Officials in Kyiv said SpaceX had imposed restrictions on Starshield without advance notice, disrupting military operations and hampering efforts to protect civilians amid intense Russian attacks this week.
In response, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk appeared to shift responsibility for any changes to Starshield's use in Ukraine to the U.S. government and President Donald Trump. He said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by Washington, with the U.S. military and ultimately the president determining any limits on their use. The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately reply to CNBC's request for comment.
Here's what to know about Starshield, and how it differs from Starlink.
What is Starshield and how does it work?
Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology developed for Starlink. On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials reported that their Starlink communication systems were no longer working for terminals moving at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or about 160 kilometers per hour.
Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats. Ukraine's military also uses the commercial Starlink technology, according to media reports, but it is not clear which of its terminals operate under the commercial arm versus those provided through Starshield.
Speaking to Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy lamented that "Starlink was switched off."
He said connectivity in the middle of the night, disrupting Ukrainian drones used to intercept Russian attacks, and that restrictions had prevented Ukraine from intercepting some Russian drones, contributing to civilian deaths. He also criticized the lack of advance warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
"Often when we destroy jet shaheeds, we use drones with Starlinks," he said.
"It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work."
"They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said, referring to SpaceX and the U.S. and describing the Starlink restrictions as particularly troubling given Ukraine's reliance on the U.S. as a strategic partner.
Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently Ukraine's defense minister, said Wednesday that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."
According to SpaceX, Starshield currently focuses on Earth observation, secure global communications for government users, and so-called "hosted payloads," which refers to hosting specialized equipment aboard satellites for customers.
Unlike Starlink, which serves consumers and businesses, Starshield offers enhanced security features, including high-assurance cryptographic capability designed to handle classified information. It says its satellites can handle a range of equipment and connect with other satellites through laser communications technology.
SpaceX was awarded over $6 billion in multi-year U.S. government contracts for Starshield, primarily from two major Space Force contracts for low Earth orbit-based communications and sensing constellations, SpaceX said in its latest earnings report.
Musk on Wednesday distinguished Starshield from SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, which he said was restricted to civilian and defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations.
How does Starshield differ from Starlink?
Although Starshield serves a different purpose from Starlink's commercial internet service, which provides high-speed connectivity to regular people, the two are closely connected.
Starlink is SpaceX's general satellite internet service, sold for consumer, civilian, and defense purposes, and offers internet access in remote areas where it has traditionally been limited.
Starshield uses stronger encryption and specialized terminals for secure communications, but relies on Starlink's extensive satellite network to operate.
According to SpaceX, Starlink operates in more than 160 countries, territories and other markets, offering residential plans starting at $55 per month. The company says its service can deliver download speeds exceeding 400 megabits per second in most locations.
Why does Starshield matter to Ukraine?
On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials reported that their Starlink communication systems were no longer working for terminals moving at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or about 160 kilometers per hour.
Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats. Ukraine's military also uses the commercial Starlink technology, according to media reports, but it is not clear which of its terminals operate under the commercial arm versus those provided through Starshield.
Speaking to Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy lamented that "Starlink was switched off."
He said connectivity was cut off in the middle of the night, disrupting Ukrainian drones used to intercept Russian attacks. Those restrictions prevented Ukraine from intercepting some Russian drones, contributing to civilian deaths. He also criticized the lack of advance warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
"Often when we destroy jet Shaheds, we use drones with Starlinks," he explained.
"It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work."
"They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said, referring to SpaceX and the U.S. and describing the Starlink restrictions as particularly troubling given Ukraine's reliance on the U.S. as a strategic partner.
Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently Ukraine's defense minister, said Wednesday that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."

Anthropic thinks your fridge could one day hide a rogue AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:42 UTC
20:54:42 KST

Everything is a computer these days. Fridges, washing machines, televisions, and more are now outfitted with computer chips to give them new capabilities, and manufacturers called them “smart” even before ChatGPT came out. Now, though, researchers have strung 15 cheap TV boxes together to run an artificial intelligence model, raising the possibility that the computers inside these everyday gadgets could someday help spread autonomous, AI-powered malware.
On Monday Anthropic released a blog post exploring this sort of attack. Researchers at the company tested how AI models might act as computer worms, programs that move between devices and leave copies of themselves behind, among everyday household gadgets. A worm that runs on smart devices instead of relying on a data center could prove difficult to shut down. Anthropic’s experiments suggest how that might happen—though they stop short of demonstrating the full threat.
Typically, large language models (LLMs) are trained and run in data centers, which can contain hundreds of thousands of specialized chips called graphics processing units, or GPUs. “Just because you don’t have a big GPU doesn’t mean that you can’t be a host to one of these models,” says Jeffrey Ladish, founder and executive director of Palisade Research, a California-based AI safety nonprofit that studies the risk of AI systems slipping beyond human control, past malware to rogue behavior.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In recent months, researchers have experimented with various types of computer worms, stapling AI models onto them to make them adaptive and harder to kill. Here, though, the researchers explored whether an AI model itself could be distributed as the worm, spreading its weights to new devices and running across even weak chips.
"Anybody with an open-weight model, with the right prompts and by brute-force luck, can find these worms," says computer scientist Vyas Sekar.
Specifically, researchers working on Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team showed two key capabilities. First, they were able to split up a relatively small model—one from Google DeepMind’s open-weight Gemma line—across 15 TV boxes they had bought and networked themselves so that they could run the entire model by chaining these boxes together. Each individual box was too weak to run the model on its own. But LLMs can be split into layers, an arrangement in which each layer manipulates the data it receives and passes that revised data to the next layer. By giving each box the job of handling just a couple of these layers, the team was able to run Gemma entirely and get responses back from just the weak chips in these boxes.
After that, the researchers tested how an AI worm might spread across devices in a virtual sandbox. A larger model—from the Chinese start-up Z.ai—managed to get a smaller model—one of Meta’s Llama models—running on the targets. But the larger model was too large to run on those weak devices itself, and it still relied on a separate server. This means the team did not show an AI worm capable of spreading and running itself on such devices. Anthropic argues that as small models become more capable, one could eventually use both methods.
The research also raises the prospect of adaptation and improvement by suggesting that AI models could subsist on low-power devices and drift through the Internet, getting better at spreading as they go. Anthropic makes this clear in its blog post about the work, concluding that AI systems could soon be “passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves.”
Ladish believes the main lesson from the research is in how AI models could divvy up work across computers of all shapes and sizes. “Basically, compute is a resource that these models can use,” he says, pointing to everything from Apple MacBooks to data centers to everyday objects like smart TVs as possible sources of computing power if attackers can hack them.
Not everyone thinks that the experiments amount to a new kind of threat, however. “I think there’s some caution that’s needed here to make sure we talk about what capabilities are new and transformative,” says Michael Bailey, a professor studying computer systems security at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He emphasizes avoiding “fearmongering” with the lessons taken away from this kind of work. Researchers already know how insecure devices like TV boxes can be. “We already had self-replicating malware,” says Bailey. “We had botnets.”
“All of these are classical computer security threats,” adds Vyas Sekar, a professor of computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. According to Sekar, the bigger problem is that more people might be able to launch such attacks—a “democratization of being evil,” as he calls it. Sekar thinks this makes monitoring and restricting data flow between smart devices even more important.
Even the risk of hijacking raw computing power on chips is not new. Hackers have long taken over other people’s computers to mine cryptocurrency. So while smart devices could face new attacks of the kind Anthropic describes, the underlying weakness is an old one: plenty of our gadgets are already easy to commandeer.
