Security costs at Netanyahu's residences top $41 million, quaduple previous prime ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:27:31 UTC
20:27:31 KST

Israel's Prime Minister's Office paid 127,432,277 (about $41 million) shekels for security and protection projects at prime ministerial residences between 2023 and October 2026, during Benjamin Netanyahu's current term, more than four times the approximately 29 million shekels (about $9.4 million) paid in the preceding three years, according to newly disclosed government figures.
The figures, released Wednesday by the Prime Minister's Office Freedom of Information Unit following a petition filed by the Givat Mordechai Community Association with the Jerusalem District Court, reveal a sharp increase in security spending at properties under the office's responsibility.
The properties include the official prime ministerial residence on Balfour Street in Jerusalem, Netanyahu's private residence on Gaza Street in Jerusalem, which was designated an alternative official residence, and his private home in Caesarea.
However, the Prime Minister's Office stressed that the figures cover all residences under its responsibility, including official and private properties belonging to serving and former prime ministers. The disclosure does not specify how much was spent at each property.
According to the figures, 10.9 million shekels (about $3.5 million) was paid in 2023, rising to 27.8 million (nearly $9 million) in 2024. Spending then surged to 72.5 million (about $23.4) shekels in 2025, approximately six times the amount paid in 2022. A further 16.2 million shekels (about $5.2 million) was paid between January and October 2026.
By comparison, approximately 29 million shekels was paid during 2020–2022. The two totals cover periods of different lengths, with the latest figures spanning nearly four years and the earlier figures covering three.
The Prime Minister's Office attributed much of the increase since 2024 to changes in the security threat level that required substantial investment in protecting the official residence. The explanation appears to refer, at least in part, to the threat posed by explosive drones following the October 2024 drone strike on Netanyahu's private residence in Caesarea.
The attack highlighted the vulnerability of highly secured locations to aerial threats and prompted renewed scrutiny of security arrangements around the prime minister and his family. Despite releasing the overall figures, the Prime Minister's Office has refused to disclose how much was spent at individual residences, arguing that such information could compromise national security.
The disclosure has renewed scrutiny of Netanyahu's previous criticism of his predecessor, Naftali Bennett, over spending on security arrangements at Bennett's private residence in Ra'anana.
In 2022, Netanyahu shared a television report and accused Bennett of using public funds to renovate his home at a cost of 50 million shekels (about $16 million). "At the expense of Israeli citizens: Bennett renovated his private home in Ra'anana for 50 million shekels. Watch Ayala Hasson's investigation," Netanyahu wrote at the time.
However, the latest government disclosure comes alongside official figures showing that the cost of security and protection work at Bennett's home was approximately half the amount Netanyahu had publicized. According to the State Comptroller, the cost of security work at Bennett's Ra'anana residence totaled approximately 24.9 million shekels (about $8 million). 
During 2021 and 2022, when Bennett and Yair Lapid served as prime ministers for most of the period, approximately 22.7 million shekels ($7.3 million) was paid for security projects across all prime ministerial residences combined. The figures do not necessarily represent the full costs incurred during those years, as some payments for projects undertaken at the time may have been made in subsequent years.
Kobi Eisen, chairman of the Givat Mordechai Community Association, which filed the petition, told the court that the earlier report concerning Bennett had been false and argued that Netanyahu had amplified its claims. "That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," Eisen said.
Government: Spending figures could expose security weaknesses
The Security Division of the Prime Minister's Office opposed releasing a breakdown of expenses by property, saying the information could help hostile actors identify vulnerabilities and assess the level of protection at different residences.
"Publishing security expenditures for the prime minister's residences and offices could reveal the extent of the security investment allocated to them and make it possible to draw conclusions about the level of protection and security priorities," the division argued.
It warned that publishing expenses for individual properties could create security risks. According to the division, hostile actors routinely collect publicly available information, including photographs, intelligence obtained through agents and drones, and other sources.
Such information, it argued, could be combined with spending figures to identify preferred targets, potential weaknesses and possible methods of attack. The division stressed that Israel is currently facing a security threat level that is among the highest since the establishment of the state, if not the highest. Under those circumstances, it said, the requested detailed disclosure could not be permitted.
Alon Halva, the Prime Minister's Office deputy director general for security, emergency preparedness, information and cyber affairs, who is considered close to Netanyahu and his wife, also opposed releasing the figures.
Speaking during the court hearing, Halva argued that even the amount allocated to each property could provide valuable intelligence.
An adversary examining the figures alongside information gathered from other sources, he said, could compare the sums invested at residences associated with Lapid, Bennett and Netanyahu and use them to assess their respective levels of protection.
‘A number that reveals nothing’
Eisen rejected the government's arguments, maintaining that disclosing spending totals would not expose actual security arrangements or technical details. "Disclosing quantitative information does not harm security," he told the court. "There is no problem showing how much money was invested in the building on Balfour Street. The information does not allow a third party to know what the money was spent on, only how much was spent."
He argued that the figures were important primarily because they would enable voters to assess the use of public funds. "It is a number that reveals nothing, other than allowing voters to know how much was invested," Eisen said.
He again referred to Netanyahu's earlier criticism of Bennett, arguing that transparency was particularly important given the public controversy surrounding the former prime minister's residence. "The prime minister amplified the false report about Naftali Bennett concerning investments in Bennett's home. That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," he said.
Eisen emphasized that his association wanted the information released before the October 27 election. "We want the information to reach voters before voters reach the ballot box," he said. "There is a kind of limbo here. They say the voters should decide, but they are not giving voters the information they need."
Jerusalem District Court Deputy President Judge Arnon Darel ordered the Prime Minister's Office to provide an additional breakdown by Thursday, distinguishing between private and public residences and separating the figures according to periods or governments.
The order represents a further step in the legal dispute over how much information the public should receive about security expenditures at properties used by Israeli prime ministers. The court's next hearing is scheduled for Sunday, October 18, when it is expected to decide whether the more detailed figures should be made public.

Don&#8217;t let Britain shelve Sally Rooney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:25:47 UTC
20:25:47 KST

This week, something happened in Britain that should worry every reader, every writer and everyone who believes in free speech.
Faber, the publisher of the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, announced that it will no longer supply her books in the United Kingdom, in any format. Her novels, Normal People, Conversations with Friends, Beautiful World, Where Are You and Intermezzo, will slowly disappear from British bookshops.
Faber said that current UK law means it cannot pass on UK earnings to the author. It said that selling a writer’s work without paying her is not acceptable for any publisher. It will continue to sell her books in every other country.
Think about that for a moment. A British publisher can sell its own author’s books all over the world, but not in Britain.
How did we reach this point? In July 2025, the government banned the direct-action group Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act. A month later, Rooney wrote openly in The Irish Times about her position and said she would direct the proceeds of her work accordingly. The group is not banned in Ireland, where she lives. In Britain, however, she says that fulfilling her publishing contracts could now be a serious criminal offence.
She warned the High Court last year that this could happen. She also won the Sky Arts Award for literature for Intermezzo, but she could not come to London to receive it because she feared arrest.
This week, she said she had tried to be honest with the public about her beliefs, and that she was ready to accept the consequences. Many public figures hide their views to protect their careers. Rooney did the opposite. She told the truth and accepted the price.
It is fair to state the government’s position too. In June, the Court of Appeal ruled that the ban is lawful. Ministers say people can always oppose the ban by lawful means. The case is not finished, and it is expected to go to the Supreme Court. The courts will decide what is legal. But what is legal is not always what is wise.
No court has convicted Sally Rooney of any crime. No jury has heard her case. Yet the result is clear: a novelist is being separated from her readers in a democratic country because of a view she expressed. When this happens in other countries, Britain is quick to criticise it. We should hold ourselves to the same standard.
Since the ban began, thousands of people have been arrested across Britain, most of them for holding signs. Many were older people, teachers, faith leaders and former soldiers. Now the effect of the law has moved from the streets into the bookshops. Jeremy Corbyn described the decision as more proof that the ban is absurd. The band Kneecap expressed their solidarity.
Many writers and readers are now asking a simple question: if this can happen to one of the most famous writers of her generation, what is happening quietly to the writers, artists and academics we never hear about?
READ: UK removes signage from East Jerusalem consulate as Israeli closure deadline expires
For me, as a Palestinian, this is personal. My father was born in Majdal Sadiq, near Ramla. In 1948, he left with my grandfather and never returned. Our story as Palestinians has often been told by others, cut by others, or kept off the shelf completely. So when a writer with Sally Rooney’s voice refuses to stay silent, it means a great deal to us.
This is not the first time she has paid a price. In 2021, she refused to sell the Hebrew translation rights of her third novel to an Israeli publisher that would not distance itself from apartheid. Two major Israeli bookshop chains removed her books. At the same time, a Palestinian bookshop in occupied East Jerusalem ordered more copies, because readers were asking for them. Today, her books are leaving the shelves of another country.
So what can we do? We can do a lot, and all of it within the law.
First, buy the copies that are still in shops. Waterstones has confirmed that its existing stock can still be sold. Ask for her books at your local bookshop while they are still there.
Second, look for second-hand copies. Charity shops, Oxfam’s online shop, World of Books and AbeBooks all have copies already in circulation.
Third, use your public library. Borrow her novels, reserve them, and ask your library to keep them on the shelves. Librarians notice what readers ask for.
Fourth, read her and share her. Choose one of her novels for your book club. Lend your copy to a friend. A book only truly disappears when people stop reading it.
Fifth, write to your MP. Ask a simple question: why is Britain the only country where her own publisher cannot sell her books? Ask whether a law made to stop violence should end up removing novels from bookshops.
You do not have to agree with every view Sally Rooney holds to stand with her. You only need to believe in something Britain has always said it values: that writers should not lose their readers because of what they believe and say.
Her novels are about ordinary people trying to speak honestly to each other. It would be very sad if the country that made her famous became the one place where her honesty cost her a voice.
Britain can still change course. Until then, the least we can do is keep her books in our hands, and keep her voice on our shelves.

Türkiye expects the US to lift CAATSA sanctions and "all direct or indirect restrictions" on its defense industry, the Turkish National Defense Ministry said Thursday, as talks continue with the US over the delivery of six F-35 fighter jets produced for Türkiye.
“As we have said before, our expectation is the lifting of CAATSA sanctions, which are incompatible with the spirit of alliance, and all direct or indirect restrictions on our defense industry,” ministry spokesperson Zeki Akturk said in a statement responding to reporters’ questions following its weekly press briefing, referring to the US law known as the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA).
The ministry said contacts with US officials continue, expressing hope that the process will conclude positively in line with the two countries’ alliance ties and mutual interests.
 
Türkiye’s potential military contribution to Saudi Arabia
Akturk said any Turkish military contribution to Saudi Arabia under the new Mecca Defense Alliance would be determined in accordance with the Turkish Constitution and relevant legislation.
It said the agreement – signed this August between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan – must be approved by the Turkish parliament and the necessary authorization procedures for deploying Turkish Armed Forces personnel abroad must be completed.
The scope of any contributions will be determined based on Saudi Arabia’s needs and requests, developments on the ground, and operational requirements, following assessments by relevant authorities and an agreement between the parties, he said.
 
Türkiye set to receive first two C-130J aircraft from UK in December
The ministry said 12 C-130J aircraft procured from the UK would strengthen the Turkish Armed Forces’ air transport capabilities.
Maintenance and modification work is being carried out by the manufacturer in the UK under the supervision of authorized Turkish Air Force personnel, it said.

“Flight, maintenance and repair activities will be carried out with our own means and capabilities,” the ministry said.
 
Türkiye hands over NATO-led KFOR command to Italy
Türkiye continues to contribute to peace and stability across a wide region through the Turkish Armed Forces’ international missions and bilateral engagements, Akturk said.
Akturk added that Türkiye on Thursday handed over command of the NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR) to Italy, following its second turn at the helm, which began last October.

'International community must take a more determined stance against Israel'
Israel continues to carry out attacks and make provocative statements that threaten regional security and stability, Akturk said, calling on the international community to take a firmer stance against Israel.
“We once again stress that the international community must take a more determined stance against Israel” to end its attacks and prevent further suffering among Palestinians, he said.
Akturk also condemned Houthi attacks targeting the main airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which killed and injured people, saying attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international humanitarian law and risk further escalating regional tensions.

IISc, Samsung open quantum lab to advance research in next-gen technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:22:16 UTC
20:22:16 KST

BENGALURU: The Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Samsung Semiconductor India Research (SSIR) on Thursday inaugurated a Quantum Research Lab at IISc, aiming to strengthen India's research capabilities in quantum technologies and advanced semiconductors.Supported by Samsung's corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, the lab supports research into quantum devices, cryogenic electronics (electronics operating at extremely low temperatures), and materials that could help develop future technologies.Quantum technologies exploit the unusual behaviour of matter at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. Unlike conventional computers, which use bits representing zero or one, quantum computers use quantum bits (qubits), which harness quantum effects to perform certain calculations in fundamentally different ways. Building reliable qubits and the systems to control them remains a major challenge.The new facility will focus on qubit characterisation, cryogenic electronics, quantum-device reliability, and single-photon sources and detectors. Single photons are individual particles of light that can carry quantum information, making them important for quantum communication and other applications.Researchers will also investigate two-dimensional (2D) materials, which are extremely thin and can have properties different from their bulk counterparts.
The work includes exploring 2D-material-based quantum devices under cryogenic conditions.A key objective of the collaboration is to make specialised research infrastructure accessible to students and researchers beyond IISc. Such equipment can be expensive to acquire and operate, limiting opportunities for institutions without dedicated facilities. The lab aims to address this gap through structured training and research exposure.The partnership will also connect quantum research with semiconductor skills development through the India Semiconductor Workforce Development Program (ISWDP), which addresses gaps in device physics, process development, modelling, simulation, characterisation and reliability. Selected modules will cover quantum materials and devices, cryogenic electronics and qubit technologies.Prof Mayank Shrivastava, chair of IISc's Department of Electronic Systems Engineering and lead for the two initiatives, said the aim was to build capabilities spanning semiconductor education and advanced research. He said the workforce programme was giving thousands of learners practical exposure to semiconductor workflows, while the new lab was advancing research into 2D-material-based quantum devices, including qubits and single-photon detectors.
Samsung Semiconductor India Research managing director Rajesh Krishnan said semiconductors and quantum were poised to be the next wave of innovation, making talent critical to India's technology ambitions, and industry-academia collaboration could create lasting impact through infrastructure, education and access.IISc director Prof Govindan Rangarajan said Samsung's support had enabled IISc to strengthen frontier quantum research and semiconductor workforce development, complementing its larger role in advancing national capabilities in quantum computing and next-generation semiconductor technologies.The initiative comes as India seeks to expand domestic expertise in semiconductors and quantum technologies. By combining specialised facilities with wider access to training, the collaboration aims to strengthen research while developing talent for these emerging fields.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Switzerland plans tougher social media rules to protect minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:21:50 UTC
20:21:50 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Switzerland plans to introduce stricter rules for major communication platforms and search engines to strengthen the protection of minors online, the Federal Council said Wednesday.
Under the proposed legislation, major platforms and search engines, including those powered by artificial intelligence, would be required to assess the risks their services pose to minors and take measures to mitigate them.
Providers would also be prohibited from displaying advertisements to minors based on profiling, which involves analyzing users’ online behavior and personal characteristics.
The Federal Council said the draft legislation had received broad support during the consultation, including from a majority of political parties represented in the Federal Assembly, cantons and national associations.
The proposed bill aims to strengthen users’ rights and increase transparency among major communication platforms and search engines, as “people increasingly rely on” them to access information.
It would also require communication platform providers to establish procedures allowing users to easily report content they suspect is illegal.
The legislation would apply to very large communication platforms and search engines, while smaller services would remain outside its scope.
The Federal Council also said it would consider whether additional measures to protect minors should be included in the legislation.

Voting in Israeli elections begins at diplomatic missions abroad

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Voting in Israel’s general elections began Thursday at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad, nearly two weeks ahead of the nationwide vote scheduled for Oct. 27.
The Times of Israel reported that the first votes in Israel’s 2026 elections were cast overnight as polling began at Israeli diplomatic missions around the world.
It said voting for diplomatic mission employees abroad and their family members would last about 30 hours, with each embassy opening its polling station during daytime hours according to the local time of its host country.
According to the daily, 101 polling stations will operate across 99 diplomatic missions, allowing approximately 4,800 eligible voters to cast their ballots.
It noted that overseas voting is restricted to diplomatic envoys, diplomatic staff and their family members.
The Israeli Embassy in Wellington, New Zealand, was the first mission to open for voting, with polling beginning at 9 am local time, corresponding to 11 pm (2000GMT) Wednesday in Israel.
Staff at the Israeli Embassy in Fiji followed, with its polling station opening an hour after voting began in New Zealand.
The last missions scheduled to hold voting are the consulates in San Francisco and Los Angeles in the US, where polling will close at 8 pm local time, corresponding to 6 am (0300GMT) Friday in Israel.
After voting concludes, the ballots will be flown to Israel and then sent to the Knesset, the parliament, for counting, according to the daily.
Opinion polls show that neither the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor the Jewish opposition bloc can independently reach the 61 seats, out of 120, required to form a government.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, leading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu also faces charges of corruption, bribery and breach of trust in three cases.
In addition to the domestic corruption trial, Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s genocidal war since October 2023.

Syrian authorities arrest main suspect in 2013 Baniyas mass killings
Syrian officials apprehended Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, as he tried to cross the border, SANA reports.
Syrian authorities have arrested a suspect accused of involvement in the mass killing of civilians in the coastal city of Baniyas in 2013, according to state media.
Intelligence officials apprehended Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, “while he was attempting to flee across the border”, state news agency SANA reported on Thursday. It did not say which country he was trying to flee to.
Kayali has long been suspected of playing a leading role in the killing of mostly Sunni civilians in the villages of Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa in the Baniyas region of western Syria in 2013.
At the time, he led an armed group loyal to then-President Bashar al-Assad.
At least 264 civilians, including 36 children and 28 women, were killed in the massacre at Bayda, whereas 195 people, including 56 children, were killed in Ras al-Nabaa by Kayali’s militia, according to figures from the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), quoted by SANA.
Human Rights Watch in 2013 described the killings as “one of the deadliest instances of mass executions in Syria’s increasingly bloody conflict”.
Militias affiliated with Kayali are also accused of committing massacres in the Latakia, Aleppo and Idlib countrysides, leaving hundreds of people dead or wounded.
Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu news agency reported that Kayali is also the main suspect in the 2013 twin bombings in the Turkish border town of Reyhanli, in which at least 52 people were killed.
Named Mihrac Ural at birth in 1956 in Hatay, Turkiye, Kayali fled to Syria in 1982. SANA said he is married to Malak al-Fadel from the country’s Alawite community, a religious minority to which former leader al-Assad belongs.
Earlier this month, Kayali’s deputy Jamal Tarabulsi was arrested by Syrian security forces, as authorities intensify efforts to capture former regime officials and militia commanders accused of crimes against civilians during the country’s civil war.
Syria’s war began with pro-democracy protests in 2011, and quickly morphed into a complex armed conflict that drew in paramilitary forces, armed groups and foreign powers.
In a multiconfessional country, the war took on a sectarian nature, with the killings in Baniyas and Bayda often seen as a starting point of that shift.
It ended with the ousting of al-Assad in 2024 by a rebel group that took power in a lightning offensive.

Espionage novels portray the spy as a person in a trench coat carrying stolen documents and disappearing into a dark alley. Israeli spy, Jonathan Pollard, certainly fit that picture. A Navy analyst who stole American secrets including the complete ten-volume manual of the National Security Agency exposing how the US gathers its signal intelligence and the names of thousands of foreign individuals who worked for US spy agencies. Intelligence officials believe Israel shared stolen documents with the Soviet Union. According to several intelligence assessments, Pollard was one of the most damaging spies in US history.

Pollard was neither the first nor the last Israeli asset. Lawrence Franklin, a Pentagon analyst, pleaded guilty in 2005 to passing classified information to an Israeli embassy official and two AIPAC staffers. Ben-Ami Kadish, a former Army engineer, pleaded guilty in 2008 to passing secret documents to an Israeli consulate official, and served no prison time. Stewart Nozette from NASA was charged with attempted espionage following an FBI sting operation. In 1970, Richard Perle was caught in an FBI wiretap discussing classified information with an Israeli embassy official.
In 2001, the same Perle chaired the Pentagon’s Defense Policy Board, while two other Israel-firsters, Douglas Feith and Paul Wolfowitz held senior posts in the same building. Franklin had worked in Feith’s policy office when he was indicted for espionage. In 1996, a study group led by Perle, and Feith, prepared a policy paper for incoming Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu titled “A Clean Break.” It urged Israel to abandon the Oslo Accords and the peace process with the Palestinians, and it proposed removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq as part of a broader Israeli strategy to reshape the region. Five years later, as leaders in the Pentagon, they delivered America’s first made-for-Israel war in Iraq.
The above is in no way intended to insinuate or allege that anyone, least of all these Zionist Americans, has dual loyalties. No. It is so profound, there is only one way to describe it: Israel-first loyalty.

No Kings protest across the US aims to get voters to the polls for midterms
The upcoming No Kings mass demonstrations this weekend aim to mobilise voter turn-out for the upcoming 3 November US midterm elections.
On Saturday 17 October, cities across the US will be holding demonstrations to get Americans to the polls ahead of the 2026 midterm elections–what many see as key to preserving the country's democracy.
"No Kings Vote Early is the next step in reclaiming our power after a year of mass mobilisations," reads a statement on the No Kings website.
"It's a day of non-partisan voter participation, being in community with each other, and making sure every eligible voter has a plan, knows their options and is ready to make their voice count," the statement continues.
The midterms will take place on 3 November. Early voting has already started in multiple states, and many advocates are urging for people to cast their ballots as soon as possible to ensure their vote is secured.
According to polls, Democrats are expected to bring in a blue wave by reclaiming the House and possibly the Senate. US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused the Democrats of rigging the elections, has said that he will be sending election monitors to polling sites. The last several months have seen internal debates among protest organisers over whether or not they should continue holding mass demonstrations or focus on voter turnout. This event is brings together both camps.

To date, three No Kings protests have taken place across the US, each having its own theme. The first one, in June 2025, was to compete with Trump’s America 250 concert that was also a celebration of his birthday. The demonstrations were a response to the suggestion that Trump was ruling as a king.

EXPLAINER - Why higher oil prices cannot shield Gulf economies from Hormuz shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:03:41 UTC
20:03:41 KST

- Saudi Arabia, UAE also expected to shrink as production and export disruptions outweigh gains from higher prices
- IMF forecasts point to a strong rebound in 2027, but recovery depends on restored production and trade
Gulf economies are expected to shrink sharply this year as long-term disruptions to energy production and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz outweigh the benefits of higher oil and gas prices, according to the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts.
The October World Economic Outlook points to particularly severe declines in economies most exposed to interruptions in hydrocarbon output and transport, with Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain facing double-digit contractions.
The deterioration highlights a central feature of the regional shock: higher global energy prices offer limited protection when producers cannot maintain production or deliver exports to customers.
The damage also extends beyond hydrocarbons, as weaker trade, higher costs and uncertainty weigh on business activity and complicate efforts to diversify Gulf economies.
Smaller Gulf producers face steepest declines
The IMF projects Kuwait's economy will contract 16.7% in 2026, while Qatar is expected to shrink 15.6% and Bahrain 11.3%, according to published accounts of the October report.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also forecast to contract, although by smaller margins, reflecting differences in economic structure and exposure to disrupted export routes.
Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to shrink 3.3% this year, a sharp reversal from the 1.7% growth forecast in July. The change represents a five-percentage-point downgrade in just three months.
The IMF expects Saudi growth to rebound to 7.9% in 2027, compared with its previous projection of 5.5%, indicating that part of the activity lost this year could return as conditions improve.
The UAE is forecast to contract 3.9% in 2026 before expanding 7.7% next year. Outside the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, Iraq faces a projected 16% contraction, underlining the broader exposure of regional energy exporters to the disruption.
These figures are projections for annual real economic output, rather than confirmed full-year outcomes, and remain sensitive to the course of the conflict and the restoration of trade.
Outlook deteriorates as disruption persists
The new forecasts mark a substantial deterioration from the IMF's spring assessment.
In April, the fund still projected 2% growth for the Gulf Cooperation Council as a whole in 2026. Its country forecasts included contractions of 8.6% for Qatar, 0.6% for Kuwait and 0.5% for Bahrain.
That earlier outlook assumed a relatively short-lived conflict, with trade resuming and production normalizing by the middle of the year.
The persistence of disruption has therefore undermined a central assumption behind the earlier projections, leaving economies exposed to a longer period of reduced output and impaired logistics.
The geographical differences are important. In its April regional briefing, the IMF highlighted that Oman faced a more limited downgrade because its access to the sea lies outside the Strait of Hormuz.
That distinction illustrates why the availability of alternative export routes can influence economic outcomes alongside the size of financial reserves or the level of global oil prices.
Higher prices cannot replace lost production
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned Gulf finance ministers and central bank governors on Oct. 1 that the regional economy was expected to contract as hydrocarbon production fell sharply and growth outside the sector slowed.
She identified the near closure of Hormuz, disruption in the Red Sea and damage to energy facilities as constraints on exports and production capacity.
Reduced trade, weaker business confidence and rising prices for essential goods were also restricting non-hydrocarbon activity, she said.
For energy producers, the distinction between prices and volumes is critical. A higher price per barrel can support receipts from the oil that is sold, but it does not restore barrels that cannot be produced or shipped.
Real GDP measures production after accounting for price changes. Consequently, an increase in export prices does not automatically prevent an economy from contracting when physical output falls.
This also helps explain why an energy shock can simultaneously raise import costs elsewhere and reduce economic activity in the countries supplying those commodities.
Strong rebound would not erase every loss
The IMF's projections envisage substantial recoveries in several of the hardest-hit economies next year as production, exports and logistics normalize.
Qatar is forecast to grow 18.8% in 2027, Kuwait 17.1% and Bahrain 13.9%. The broader Middle East and Central Asia region is projected to expand 6.3% after contracting 0.3% this year.
However, large percentage rebounds partly reflect the lower starting point created by this year's contractions.
Applying the projected annual changes illustrates the distinction. Kuwait's output would fall from an index of 100 in 2025 to 83.3 in 2026, then recover to approximately 97.5 in 2027. It would therefore remain about 2.5% below its 2025 level despite double-digit growth.
Qatar's projected contraction and rebound would bring output approximately back to its 2025 level. Neither calculation captures the additional production that might have occurred had the disruption never happened.
Financial buffers and logistics shape resilience
Georgieva said government measures and investment in energy and logistics infrastructure had helped contain the wider fallout, including through rerouting supplies and supporting firms and banks.
She nevertheless stressed that financial buffers cannot substitute for physical resilience to trade shocks.
The IMF has highlighted the potential for the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects to reduce losses from a Hormuz closure by improving alternative transport connections.
Its policy advice calls for temporary, targeted support where needed, while avoiding broad stimulus when the principal constraint is disrupted supply.
As conditions normalize, the fund recommends rebuilding financial buffers and maintaining investment in diversification and economic security.

Honeybees deemphasize potential ‘misinformation’ in their waggle dances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:01:38 UTC
20:01:38 KST

When a bee wants to tell its hive mates how to find a scrumptious field of flowers, it wiggles its rear end. A complicated combination of figure eight–like movements known as a waggle dance tells nearby bees what direction to fly in and how far to go. But what happens if a waggling bee is unsure of its directions?
A study published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology earlier this year shows that bees amplify their communication based on how certain they are that their information is true. It seems the more confident a bee is in what it’s conveying, the more emphatically it communicates with the hive, says study lead author Karmi Oxman, a behavioral ecologist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Confidence is sort of a human-y word, but it’s useful in this context,” Oxman says. Confidence reflects the communicator’s belief in a message’s relevance or reliability, “and the dance is a self-report of the situation in the field.” This extra information also prevents the bee from accidentally misleading the hive.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The experiment started with one bee flying to a specialized feeder. This first bee, also known as the focal bee, was always met with a sugar solution. The researchers then manipulated the scenario by changing what happened after the focal bee returned to the hive and gave directions to the feeder. In the “honest” scenario, the feeder remained full, and all the bees following the directions got a sugary treat. In the “liar” scenario, the feeder was found empty. And in the “unverified” scenario, all the bees were caught before they could return to the hive and report what happened.
When given the chance to communicate the feeder’s location to the hive again in a later experimental stage, the focal bee in the honest scenario tried harder to convince its fellows to visit the sugar source by performing more waggle dance circuits—suggesting the bee could assess the reliability of its own signal. Unverified and “liar” bees did not show that same increase; in fact, unverified bees decreased their recruitment efforts.
“For me, the big takeaway is that bees are not little robots,” says James C. Nieh, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study. “They’re getting information from their environment, and that [information] also includes how successful they are in communicating to their nest mates.”
Both Oxman and Nieh say they wonder what other types of communication beyond what we can see—such as chemical signals or vibrations—could be playing a role in waggle dances. Further research into how bees communicate can help with efforts to “maintain the world in a way that they can still thrive,” Nieh says.

Israel has arrested more than 2,000 Palestinian children since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza, with at least 350 still in detention under harsh conditions, the Palestinian Prisoners Society said in a report on Wednesday.
The non-governmental organisation added that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and Al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.
The organisation’s monitoring and documentation indicated that “more than 2,000 children have been arrested since the start of the genocide in October 2023, while at least 350 remain in detention under harsh conditions,” it said.
The group warned of an escalation in the targeting of Palestinian children through practices including intimidation, arrest, torture, starvation, isolation and denial of health care.
It added that information on the number of children detained from Gaza since the start of the war remains incomplete, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of “enforced disappearance.”
The group said Israel’s administrative detention policy, under which Palestinian detainees are held without charge or a clear timeframe for release, leaves children facing an uncertain future and deprives them of family life and educational stability.
It also said Israeli courts contribute to the continuation of violations against children amid the absence of effective accountability.
Detention conditions
The Palestinian Prisoners Society cited the case of child Walid Khaled Ahmad, who “died in Megiddo Prison in March 2025, amid medical findings at the time indicating severe emaciation and signs of malnutrition and dehydration.”
The group raised questions about accountability for his death, noting that the investigation into the case had been closed.
It also highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who it said developed scabies while detained in Ofer Prison, leading to a deterioration in his health and serious infections affecting vital organs.
Hamid underwent heart surgeries and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition before one of his legs was later amputated, the group said.
It added that Hamid has continued receiving treatment for about three months since Israeli authorities released him following the deterioration of his health, a move the group described as “an evasion of responsibility for his medical care.”
The group called for international action to secure the release of children held arbitrarily, end administrative detention and coercive interrogations, and stop torture, starvation and the denial of medical treatment.
It stressed the need to move beyond documentation and condemnation towards concrete measures that end the violations and bring impunity to an end, saying that “protecting Palestinian children requires firm international intervention to ensure respect for their rights, lives and dignity.”
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocidal war, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli army raids and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property have also intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since then.

====================================================================================================

Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.
Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.
Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads and doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.
The company’s cofounder and chief product officer, Tanyella Leta, tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”
Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”
Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet, and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.
It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps child development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.
AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.
Michael Robb, head of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb believes YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”
A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.
According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.
Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.
Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on Academy of Pediatrics’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”
In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”
A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.
For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.
Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”
“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric: minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”
One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”
The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.
“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”
Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.
Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”
Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers, who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”
“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

World Insights: Xi's principles on settling Africa's hotspot issues resonate across continent
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:54:29 CST
19:54:29 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The four principles proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping for resolving Africa's hotspot issues have resonated across the continent, with diplomats, scholars and media professionals hailing them as timely and practical guidance for promoting peace and development in Africa.
The four principles -- adhering to the principle of "Africa-led," upholding fairness and justice, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace, and addressing both symptoms and root causes -- were put forward on Tuesday in Beijing during Xi's meeting with Faure Essozimna Gnassingbe, president of the Council of Ministers of Togo, who is on an official visit to China.
Noting that the proposal comes at a time when conflicts across the continent are compounded by external interference and intensifying geopolitical rivalries, African experts said they support its emphasis on building lasting security through African ownership, international fairness, peaceful dialogue and sustainable development.
AFRICAN OWNERSHIP
At the heart of the four principles is the "Africa-led" approach, under which the African people are the true masters of Africa, and should play a central role in regional affairs.
Claudio Rabenja, a Malagasy economist and international affairs expert, said the principle is "relevant and particularly important in the current geopolitical context," as crises in Africa stem from complex local factors that outside actors often fail to understand.
"Solutions imported from or imposed by external actors do not always provide lasting answers," he said, adding that Xi's approach responds to Africa's aspiration to stop being a battleground for major-power rivalry and is consistent with China's tradition of non-interference.
Similarly, Etienne Bankuwiha, a Burundian sinologist, said Xi's proposal "consolidates the fundamental principle of African solutions to African problems," affirming that African countries are entitled to choose their own partners and development paths while rejecting externally imposed governance agendas.
Emmanuel Yenshu Vubo, dean of the Faculty of Social and Management Sciences at the University of Buea in Cameroon, said Africa "is not and cannot be reduced to mere spheres of influence or former colonial units that have only nominal independence ... Africa should be its own master."
FAIRNESS AND JUSTICE
The principle of upholding fairness and justice calls on all parties to abide by the principles of the UN Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned.
Rabenja said respect for sovereignty and the UN Charter helps safeguard territorial integrity, curb destabilizing interventions and promote the peaceful settlement of disputes.
"It is essential that African countries be able to resolve their disputes without being subjected to pressure that runs counter to their national interests," he said, noting that China's consistent stance gives African governments greater freedom to make their own choices.
Gerard Njoya, editor-in-chief of Actu Chine Cameroon, said the principle reinforces the African Union (AU)'s Agenda 2063 by opposing unilateral sanctions and arbitrary interventions, addressing the long-standing demand for "an end to interference and double standards."
Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, said the principle's call for consistent application of international law underscores the need to treat African countries fairly and with dignity.
PEACE THROUGH DIALOGUE
Noting that wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts, experts said the principle of promoting peace through a cessation of hostilities calls for mutual respect, extensive consultations, seeking common ground while setting aside differences, and fostering mutual understanding and accommodation.
Moutlakgola Masire, a journalist at Radio Botswana, said multi-stakeholder consultations and ceasefire commitments can prevent further civilian suffering and open the way for sustainable settlements.
Rabenja said military confrontation without a credible political process often fails to eliminate the root causes of violence.
"Mutual concessions do not mean abandoning fundamental principles," he said. "They recognize that lasting peace often requires arrangements acceptable to all parties."
China's diplomatic experience and relations with African countries can help support mediation, complementing the efforts of the AU, subregional organizations and the United Nations, he said.
Njoya said ending hostilities through dialogue aligns with the AU's Silencing the Guns initiative, offering an approach to conflict resolution rooted in African values.
SECURITY AND DEVELOPMENT
As the principle of addressing both symptoms and root causes calls for tackling immediate security threats while pursuing long-term development, experts said China can help Africa address its challenges, citing its contributions to infrastructure construction, scholarships and vocational training across the continent.
Rabenja called security and development "two inseparable dimensions of stability."
Beyond protecting civilians in the short term, he said, the underlying causes of conflict -- poverty, youth unemployment, inequality and weak institutions -- must be addressed through investment in education, agriculture, energy, infrastructure and industrialization.
"Security creates the conditions necessary for investment, while development reduces some of the vulnerabilities that can fuel conflict," he said.
Njoya said addressing root causes is essential to achieving the goals of Agenda 2063, adding that the principle "endorses the AU's integrated approach, which seeks to tackle poverty, youth unemployment and inequality -- the underlying causes of instability."
Bankuwiha said China-Africa cooperation in agriculture, industrialization, poverty alleviation, green transition and infrastructure provides the economic empowerment needed to address the structural drivers of conflict in regions such as the Horn of Africa and the Lake Chad Basin.
Observers said the four principles forge "a new framework of equal partnership" that respects Africa's independent choices.
"Taken together, these four principles can serve as a practical reference guide for settling past, present and future hotspot issues in Africa," Demissie said. ■

The article says that the fight against corruption must be pursued with greater sobriety and resolve. It describes the anti-corruption campaign as a high-stakes struggle that cannot be lost, requiring an unswerving high-pressure posture to be maintained.
It further demands the timely detection, accurate identification and effective resolution of all forms of corruption, with refined anti-corruption mechanisms that align oversight actions across all sectors. ■

Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:52:12 UTC
19:52:12 KST

Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Houthis attempt to raise the cost of the Yemen war for Saudi Arabia as attacks, fighting intensify.
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.

leda papaconstantinou’s spetses players turned the greek island into a stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:50:07 UTC
19:50:07 KST

leda papaconstantinou’s spetses players turned the greek island into a stage
led by the greek avant-garde performance artist, the spetses players developed an experimental form of performance rooted in the island’s landscape, local community, and changing social realities.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
in the 70s, a performance group took shape on Spetses
In the early 1970s, Leda Papaconstantinou returned to Greece during the military junta after studying and working in England. She settled on Spetses, where her parents had moved from Athens, together with her then-husband, the British artist and teacher David Hughes. She had already been working with performance in England and wanted to continue. The first step was to find people with whom she could work.
The Spetses Players began to take shape around 1972, bringing together artists, teachers, professors, students, musicians and people connected to literature and philosophy. Many of them were from outside Greece. At the time, Spetses attracted people from the US, UK, Germany, France, Sweden, Italy, Denmark and elsewhere, many of whom travelled for long periods rather than the short holidays associated with tourism today.
‘It wasn’t theatre,’ Papaconstantinou recalls during our discussion, because there was no fixed written story that was performed repeatedly. Instead, the collaborators had to decide together what they wanted to talk about and how to turn it into a performance.
the making of the Spetses Players
The group’s approach had parallels with the work of Italian playwright and performer Dario Fo, who Leda Papaconstantinou describes as someone who would look at the local newspaper, identify an issue affecting a particular community, and develop a performance around it. The Greek artist also saw a connection with Karagiozis, the Greek shadow-theatre character who could change according to the story and circumstances around him. The Spetses Players began with subjects connected to the place and then had to find a form through which to tell them. Papaconstantinou was the only member who spoke Greek, while the others brought different languages and backgrounds to the group. Some were artists, while others were teachers, professors or students taking time away from their studies.
Among the recurring characters in Papaconstantinou’s performances was Bouboulitsa, a fictional little girl named after Laskarina Bouboulina, the legendary figure of Spetses. The choice connected the performances to one of the island’s best-known stories while giving the group a new character through which to explore its own ideas. Bouboulitsa was born behind the screen of a Karagiozis shadow theatre, appearing as a gift to an old fisherman and his wife. Around her were sea creatures including jellyfish, sea urchins, red mullet and sardines. Leda Papaconstantinou herself appeared as an angel-mermaid, while other performers became marine creatures or, in another scene, ‘motorcycle monsters.’ Costumes were closely tied to movement. In one performance, a performer dressed as a chicken wore feathers that changed the way the body moved, making the character’s actions resemble those of a chicken. The visual language developed alongside the stories rather than being added afterwards.
stories about life on the island
The Bouboulitsa performances addressed the changes taking place around them. Tourism was becoming increasingly important to the economy of Spetses, while houses were being sold to wealthy foreign buyers and local residents struggled to find homes they could afford. In one story, a property agent sells houses at prices beyond the reach of local people. Bouboulitsa and the other characters eventually make him change his mind, building a house from milk cartons. Bouboulitsa and the Terrible Dragon, performed in 1977, dealt with water, including shortages and the rising cost of the resource. Another performance addressed waste and the lack of medical care.
These subjects were part of the reality the performers and their audience were living through. The local community was an important part of the work. Performances were often full, and the group was primarily interested in reaching the people who lived on Spetses rather than the visitors who arrived during the summer. The connection continued beyond the performances. Years later, Papaconstantinou found that people on the island still associated her with Bouboulitsa. That recognition became important when she later worked with filmmaker Carole Roussopoulos on a documentary about Bouboulina. Because local women already knew the Greek artist through the Bouboulitsa performances, they were more willing to open their homes, share their stories and participate in the project.
performing across Spetses
In 1977, the group organized the first and only international Spetses Festival. The program brought together the Spetses Players and visiting artists, with works by Timberlake Wertenbaker, Clement Biddle Wood and Simon Carr. Most of the festival took place around the old harbor, using the island’s existing spaces for the performances, including the chambers of the iconic Figaro discotheque and a house designed by the Greek architect Aris Konstantinidis. The series continued until Bouboulitsa’s Dream in 1979. Each performance dealt with different aspects of life on the island, but they all ended with the same song, inviting people to return to Spetses and take care of it. By the end, the audience would get up, dance and sing along.
when the images began circulating again
Almost fifty years later, photographs from the performances have started circulating again. In 2026, color photographs of the costumes and characters have appeared on social media, often reaching people who know little about the original stories. Leda Papaconstantinou sees this renewed attention partly through the work’s aesthetics. She describes herself as ‘a component of the visual language’ and suggests that the images can activate the viewer in a different way, prompting them to ask what they are looking at before they know where it came from.
There is also a reversal in the way the work can now be encountered. Originally, words, literature and stories were what generated the images. Today, the artist suggests, the process can work in the opposite direction. ‘The image can create the references to the words.’ She wants to return to the stories behind each Bouboulitsa performance with the collaborators who are still alive and remember the work. For her, understanding how literature and language produced the images is still an unfinished part of the history.
The photographs also create an unexpected distance between the time when the work was made and the way it is seen now. Papaconstantinou points to the colors, fabrics and costumes, which can appear surprisingly contemporary to viewers encountering them online today. There is a certain admiration in seeing what was being made in the 1970s, but also a more difficult question: if these ideas were already present then, why do many of the issues still feel familiar?
preserving the work
In 2013, on the occasion of AGORA, the 4th Athens Biennale, she contacted surviving collaborators and gathered their memories and material from the period, creating an archive rather than reproducing the performances. ‘I never reproduce performances,’ she comments. What remains instead is a collection of photographs, memories, texts and stories that can be revisited from different directions. Leda Papaconstantinou has since transferred her archive to EMST, the National Museum of Contemporary Art Athens.
The archive now sits alongside the photographs circulating online, giving the Spetses Players another life through images. For those discovering the work today, the photograph may come before the story. The costumes and characters catch the eye first, with the words, literature and ideas behind them emerging afterwards.
project info:
name: The Spetses Players
artist: Leda Papaconstantinou
