Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:05:24 UTC
19:05:24 KST

Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- Penn Medicine
- Summary:
- A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.
- Share:
An unusually detailed examination of an Alzheimer's patient's brain has revealed striking differences between regions where treatment successfully removed harmful amyloid plaques and areas where those plaques remained. The regions cleared of amyloid showed little or no buildup of tau tangles, another protein abnormality strongly associated with brain cell damage and declining memory. Nearby areas that still contained amyloid, however, showed much higher levels of tau and evidence of continued neurodegeneration.
The discovery offers rare evidence from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques may provide protection against other damaging processes involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The results also suggest that clearing amyloid thoroughly, particularly early in the disease, could help limit tau accumulation and slow the progression of brain damage.
Researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania presented the findings at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference. The study was also published in JAMA.
"Seeing both disease patterns side-by-side in the same brain gave us a rare opportunity to understand how amyloid removal affects other proteins that contribute to Alzheimer's disease," said co-senior author David Wolk, MD, co-director of the Penn Memory Center and director of the Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. "The findings provide some of the clearest human evidence to date that anti-amyloid therapies may limit the accumulation of tau and slow the brain changes that lead to memory loss and cognitive decline."
How Amyloid and Tau Contribute to Alzheimer's Disease
Two proteins play major roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease. Beta-amyloid collects outside nerve cells, forming sticky deposits known as plaques. Tau, meanwhile, accumulates inside neurons and forms abnormal tangles. Both are associated with the progressive damage to brain cells that contributes to memory problems, changes in personality, and difficulties with thinking.
Treatments designed to eliminate amyloid plaques have significantly changed how Alzheimer's is managed in recent years. Aducanumab became the first drug of this type to receive accelerated approval from the FDA, although it is no longer sold. Since then, newer and more effective medications that target amyloid through a similar approach, donanemab (Kisunla) and lecanemab (Leqembi), have received full FDA approval.
Researchers have long believed that amyloid buildup helps create the conditions in which harmful tau tangles develop. What has been much harder to establish is whether eliminating amyloid can also limit tau accumulation in the human brain.
Direct evidence has been scarce because relatively few people who received amyloid-clearing drugs have undergone brain examinations after death.
A Rare Brain Examination Reveals a Striking Pattern
The researchers were able to investigate this question using brain tissue donated by a former Alzheimer's clinical trial participant.
The man was in his fifties when he was diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment caused by Alzheimer's disease. He subsequently joined a clinical trial testing aducanumab and received 30 doses of the medication over four and a half years.
He died approximately four years after his last dose, more than a decade after his first symptoms appeared. Before his death, he expressed a wish to donate his brain to scientific research. The tissue was provided to the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine.
When specialists examined the donated brain, they discovered an unusual pattern in which neighboring regions showed dramatically different amounts of Alzheimer's-related damage.
The raised ridges of the brain's folded surface, known as gyri, had lost most of their amyloid plaques and contained very little accumulated tau. In contrast, the neighboring grooves between these ridges, called sulci, still contained considerable amyloid buildup. These regions also exhibited substantially more tau tangles, inflammation, and degeneration of brain tissue.
This patchwork distribution was consistent with scans taken while the patient was alive, which had already indicated that amyloid removal varied considerably across different parts of his brain.
"Many previous reports have shown either extensive amyloid clearance or limited clearance," said co-senior author Edward B. Lee, MD, PhD, the John Q. Trojanowski, MD, PhD Professor for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in Pathology and Laboratory Medicine. "This case represented a unique 'Goldilocks' scenario in which some regions cleared amyloid and others did not. It allowed us to directly compare what happened next in neighboring brain regions and better understand the relationship between amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration."
Could Alzheimer's Treatments Protect the Brain for Years?
The findings could have important implications for the latest generation of Alzheimer's medications, which remove amyloid using mechanisms similar to the therapy received by this patient.
Although the investigation involved only one individual, the contrast between different brain regions suggests that substantial amyloid removal may influence other disease processes long after treatment has stopped.
The results also raise an important question about how the benefits of Alzheimer's drugs are measured. Clinical trials commonly evaluate patients over approximately 18 months, but some protective effects might take considerably longer to become apparent.
However, the study cannot establish how much amyloid must be removed to achieve lasting protection or prove that plaque clearance was directly responsible for the differences in tau accumulation and brain damage.
Researchers now hope to understand why certain parts of the brain respond more effectively to amyloid-clearing treatments than others. Identifying and potentially strengthening the biological mechanisms responsible for plaque removal could lead to better therapies.
Another major question is whether beginning treatment before extensive tau tangles develop could substantially delay Alzheimer's or even prevent the disease from emerging.
Why Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment Could Matter
Because amyloid can accumulate silently in the brain for many years before memory problems begin, researchers are increasingly interested in treating people during the earliest stages of the disease, potentially before noticeable symptoms appear.
"Patients may accumulate amyloid for years before symptoms appear," said first author Christopher A. Brown, MD, PhD, an assistant professor of Neurology. "This case suggests that removing amyloid early may help limit the changes that ultimately damage brain cells. Ongoing trials will help determine whether starting treatment before symptoms begin can provide even greater benefit."
This research received support from the National Institutes of Health (P30-AG072979, RF1-AG069474, R01-AG056014, R01-AG055005, R01-AG072796, R01-AG065341, P01-AG084497).

Journal Reference:
- Christopher A. Brown, John L. Robinson, Sandhitsu R. Das, Emily McGrew, EunRan Suh, Viviana M. Van Deerlin, David J. Irwin, Ilya M. Nasrallah, Dawn Mechanic-Hamilton, Paul A. Yushkevich, David A. Wolk, Edward B. Lee. Clinicopathologic Evaluation of Amyloid Clearance in Alzheimer Disease. JAMA, 2026; DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.13058

Zelenskyy earlier told the British newspaper the Financial Times that strikes on Russian oil refineries would resume, and accused the US of weakening Ukraine’s position on the battlefield by allegedly withdrawing crucial intelligence sharing.
Trump on Sunday unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was not publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukraine said it suspended attacks on Russian energy sites for several days after Trump’s announcement.
The US has pressured Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian refineries, claiming that a suspension of attacks and a deal for Russia to export 1.8 million tonnes of diesel would help reduce soaring fuel prices.
“This politically is not simple [in America], because everybody will want to ask how it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying – and you make … business with the guys with such aggression,” Zelenskyy told the FT.
Zelenskyy also alleged that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s satellite internet service was restricted, potentially leaving it more vulnerable to Russian attacks. The Ukrainian armed forces use SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield system for offensive and defensive operations.

In a separate post, he called for Zelenskyy to “go” as Ukraine’s leader.
“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote in a separate post on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”
‘Pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender’

Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
On Thursday, Zelenskyy also arrived in Brussels to meet with European leaders as he pushes for tougher sanctions on Moscow and faster delivery of support from the European Union.
Asked by reporters in Brussels whether the European Union still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: “We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender.”
She said: “Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has called on EU leaders to “step up” their game to ensure Ukraine wins the war against Russia.
The EU has already pledged $50bn in support for Ukraine next year. However, the sum falls far short of the $175bn Kyiv plans to spend on its defences next year.
Trump has denied that the US has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

According to the Istanbul Governor's Office, a 14-year-old boy was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle in the Balat neighborhood of Fatih district. In a separate incident in Sariyer district, a 34-year-old pedestrian was killed after slipping in floodwaters while crossing a street.

Rewilding could help tiny islands withstand rising seas: study

19:01:45 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Protecting seabirds and restoring native vegetation could help low-lying tropical atoll islands withstand rising sea levels by boosting coral reef growth and reducing erosion, a new study has found.
An international team analyzed ecological data from 28 atoll islands in the Indian and Pacific oceans to examine how nutrients from seabirds affect the islands and surrounding coral reefs, influencing their ability to adapt to climate change-driven sea-level rise, according to a statement from the University of Auckland released Thursday.
By looking at seabird census data, the researchers estimated the amount of "energy" seabirds bring from the open ocean back to each of the small atoll islands and how the nutrients, deposited in seabirds' droppings, influence the islands and surrounding marine ecosystems, according to the study published in Science Advances.
The study found that reefs in lagoons around islands free of invasive rats, which support abundant seabird populations, grew 1.8 times faster than reefs around rat-infested islands. Ocean-facing reefs grew 2.5 times faster around rat-free islands.
Seabird droppings transfer nutrients from the open ocean to islands and surrounding ecosystems, boosting coral growth and sediment production that helps build or maintain islands and reduce erosion as sea levels rise, the study found.
The researchers said that replacing abandoned coconut plantations with natural vegetation and restoring seabird populations by eradicating invasive rats could be key to the survival of low-lying islands. ■

Nepal explores disaster financing mechanism in wake of devastating floods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:01:30 CST
19:01:30 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Nepal and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the lending arm of the World Bank Group, signed a mandate agreement to explore the development of a catastrophe bond to help Nepal access funds quickly in case of a major earthquake, the global development financier said on Thursday.
"The agreement marks the beginning of a collaboration to assess how capital markets can support Nepal's broader disaster risk management strategy," said the World Bank in a statement.
This initiative is part of the World Bank Group's established catastrophe bond program, which helps countries access international capital markets to transfer disaster risk and secure financial protection against natural hazards.
Payouts rely on objective physical triggers, such as an earthquake's magnitude or a storm's wind speed within a designated geographical grid, rather than lengthy post-disaster damage assessments. This ensures rapid liquidity for emergency relief.
As one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, Nepal is working to better prepare for, withstand, and recover from future natural disasters through a combination of risk reduction, preparedness, and financial protection measures.
The two sides signed the agreement in the wake of devastating mudslides and floods on Aug. 26 that have so far claimed nearly 1,500 lives while over 5,000 are unaccounted for. The disaster also swept away communities, houses, hydropower facilities, bridges, roads and other infrastructure.
The estimated physical damage was 1.66 billion U.S. dollars, according to the World Bank's Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation report. ■

Responding to a question from Komeito party lawmaker Shinichi Isa at a House of Representatives Budget Committee session, Takaichi said the Japanese government is still upholding the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, but added that, as work on revising the three security documents is under way, there is "still room for discussion" regarding the specific wording on the principles.

Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles refer to not possessing, not producing, and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country.
The National Security Strategy, one of the three security documents, states clearly that "Japan will adhere to the basic policy of observing the Three Non-Nuclear Principles."
According to the report, Takaichi had long advocated revising the principle of not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons before becoming prime minister.
In June this year, the Japan Innovation Party, the junior coalition partner of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, also called for making a "realistic review" of the principle in its proposal on revising the three key security documents.
Meanwhile, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has repeatedly said in public since July that nuclear weapons-related policies should be discussed "without taboo." This series of developments has fueled growing concerns in Japan over a possible shift in the Takaichi government's nuclear policy. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Ancient, modern canals connect and create opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:01:21 CST
19:01:21 KST

NANNING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- From a viewing platform above the ship lock at the Madao Junction in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, foreign delegates watched as water filled one of the world's largest inland lock chambers.
The structure is designed to raise or lower vessels to overcome a maximum water-level difference of 29.6 meters. It is part of the newly opened Pinglu Canal, a 134.2-km waterway linking the Xijiang River system in southern China with the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
For many of the delegates attending the World Canals Conference 2026 that concludes Thursday, the scale was simply striking.
Edith Bronder, an expert on China's canals who has studied waterways in China and overseas, said she had encountered no comparable project elsewhere. Sharon Leighton, president of Inland Waterways International (IWI), called the canal "history in the making."
Their visit on Monday is part of the conference agenda. The four-day gathering has brought together representatives from canal cities, universities, research institutions and waterway organizations in more than 20 countries and regions.
Themed "Innovation and Perseverance: A Crucial Choice," the event places two Guangxi waterways at the center of its discussions: the 2,200-year-old Lingqu Canal and the Pinglu Canal, which opened to shipping last month.
"Canals are not simply artifacts of the past," Leighton said at the opening ceremony of the conference. "They are living infrastructure, living landscapes and influential heritage assets."
Weng Xiaobing, an official with the Water Transport Bureau of China's Ministry of Transport, said the country's water transport sector is at a critical point in its shift from large-scale infrastructure construction toward a greater focus on quality, efficiency, integration and innovation.
That transition is visible in Guangxi, where a waterway built over 2,200 years ago now shares the conference agenda with the country's newest river-to-sea canal.
Completed in 214 B.C. under Emperor Qinshihuang, the Lingqu Canal was originally built to carry provisions for the Qin army during its military campaign in southern China. By linking the Xiangjiang and Lijiang rivers, the 36.4-km canal opened a navigable route between the Yangtze and Pearl River systems.
Though roads and railways replaced the canal as a major freight route, Lingqu still supports irrigation, local water supplies and tourism. Restoration work has repaired historic structures, improved sewage collection and helped secure dry-season water supplies.
The Lingqu scenic area received more than 1 million tourist visits in 2025, according to local authorities.
The Pinglu Canal tackles a longstanding challenge: getting cargo from inland production centers to the coast despite mountains and winding river routes.
Built at an estimated cost of 72.7 billion yuan (10.8 billion U.S. dollars), the canal provides parts of southwestern China with a more direct route to domestic and overseas markets. It shortens the journey to the sea by more than 560 km compared with routes through neighboring Guangdong, and official estimates suggest logistics costs could be slashed by 18 to 30 percent.
Last month, Nanning Port, previously an inland river port with no direct waterway link to the Beibu Gulf, handled 668,400 tonnes of cargo, up 145 percent year on year, as shipments began using the new canal, port authorities said.
Other supporting infrastructure is also expanding. A railway spur serving the industrial complex near Nanning Port is under construction. Designed to handle 3.2 million tonnes of cargo annually, it is scheduled for completion in August 2027, according to Beibu Gulf Port Group.
"The Pinglu Canal introduces a new chapter in the long story of populations using waterways to connect and create opportunity," said Leighton, the IWI president. "It incorporates the engineering, knowledge and technology of our era and is carefully designed to ensure tangible benefits for generations to come." ■

A criminal case involving workers from India, Sri Lanka and other countries will be heard at the Court in Hillerød, following allegations of unpaid overtime, threats and restrictions on trade union membership.
According to TV 2 Kosmopol, prosecutors have brought charges against two men and two companies connected to a car group in North Zealand.
North Zealand Police allege that 18 foreign mechanics were subjected to human exploitation over a four-year period.
The indictment states that the workers were required to work overtime and weekends without additional pay.
They were also allegedly prohibited from joining a trade union, limiting their ability to seek collective representation over their employment conditions.
Prosecutors further allege that the mechanics were threatened with dismissal and deportation to their home countries if they complained about their working or living conditions.

The case will now be considered by the Court in Hillerød, which must determine whether the defendants are guilty of the charges.
The court will also decide whether approximately 4.1 million DKK should be confiscated from the defendants in connection with the alleged exploitation.
Denmark introduced a specific provision on human exploitation into its criminal code in June 2022.
The provision was designed to address serious cases of labor exploitation that do not meet the legal definition of human trafficking.
The charges in the North Zealand case have been brought under that provision, with the defendants’ criminal responsibility yet to be established.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Travelers entering the country may continue to face inspections until May 17, 2027, as authorities maintain that security threats remain serious.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, informed the European Commission of the decision Wednesday, according to a statement from the Justice Ministry.
The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Reports of AI-generated child abuse material rise sharply in Denmark
Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.

An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.

Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.

Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.

“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.

A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.

Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.

The number of people under age 40 receiving disability pensions in Denmark has fallen for the first time in more than six years, according to figures from the Jobindsats.dk employment database.
In September, 43,229 people in the age group received disability pensions, 98 fewer than in August. It was the first monthly decline since early 2020.
Jesper Brask Fischer, head of welfare at pension company PFA, said it was too early to celebrate.

Denmark had 261,418 disability pension recipients in September, down 487 from August.
Fischer said further consecutive declines could indicate that fewer people are entering the disability pension system. For now, however, he described the figures as only a cautious positive sign after years of significant growth.
Renovating all public concrete shelters could cost up to 3 billion DKK
Renovating Denmark’s 1,694 public concrete trench shelters and preparing them for use could cost between 2 billion and 3 billion DKK.
Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of the Socialist People’s Party provided the estimate in a response to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, according to construction trade publication Licitationen.
The estimate remains highly uncertain and requires further assessment.
Renovating only the 831 shelters that already meet basic requirements and could be opened during an immediate emergency would cost between 500 million and 1 billion DKK.
Most of the shelters require treatment for mold and pests because they have not been used for many years, the parliamentary response said.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness began inspecting Denmark’s shelter capacity and condition in May 2025. The review of concrete trench shelters is complete, while inspections of reinforced shelters are expected to continue until 2027.
Concrete trench shelters are public facilities intended for people away from home, including road users and residents of buildings without shelters.
Most Danish shelter spaces are in reinforced rooms inside residential and other buildings. Denmark also has supplementary shelters that offer some protection but do not meet full shelter requirements.
A 2024 inventory found about 3.4 million shelter spaces nationwide. Concrete trench shelters accounted for 113,018 of them.

Danish inflation rises to 2.2 percent as fuel prices increase
Denmark’s annual inflation rate rose to 2.2 percent in September, up 0.2 percentage points from August, Statistics Denmark reported Monday.
Higher fuel costs were the main reason for the increase, with transportation prices contributing significantly to inflation between August and September.
Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organization representing managers and executives, said similar developments were visible in neighboring countries.
“But in fact, the rising energy prices do not become quite as visible in Danish inflation because the electricity tax has largely been removed this year and next year,” she wrote in a commentary.
Lower prices for holiday home rentals, package holidays and food helped offset the increase.
Larsen said there was no reason for serious concern because inflation remained close to the two percent level generally associated with stable prices. She added that there were no signs that higher energy costs were spreading throughout the economy.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, reached a similar conclusion.
However, he said the reduced electricity tax was concealing a significant rise in underlying inflation during recent months.
“In fact, in recent quarters there has been a decline in purchasing power for the Danes because precisely during that period prices have run faster than wages,” Kristensen wrote.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 raises researcher fears the Chinese model can fake AI safety tests
Researchers say the model’s apparent awareness of how it and successor versions are trained could undermine safety evaluations
The model, launched in August, showed an ability to consider how its behaviour during safety evaluations might influence how future versions of itself would be trained, according to AI safety organisation Apollo Research.
This phenomenon, referred to as “update-aware reasoning” by researchers Axel Hojmark and Ezra Newman, was unprompted and could lead to “alignment faking”, a scenario where the AI systems comply during training to hide their true objectives until deployment, they said.
“These reasoning patterns should make us more wary about RSI,” Hojmark told the South China Morning Post, referring to “recursive self-improvement”, the prospect of AI systems progressively improving through successive rounds of development with no human involvement.

“It is not the financial statements that are creating noise. Rather, it is the uncertainty about where they land with the ECB,” Munk told MarketWire.
Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen acknowledged that the regulatory review was taking longer than anticipated.
“It has proven to be a long process,” he told Børsen.
Vang-Jensen said the bank considered pausing repurchases appropriate while uncertainty remained over its future risk-weighted assets, a measure used to determine how much capital banks must hold against potential losses.
Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.

Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Psilocybin appears to strengthen this optical illusion, but LSD microdoses do not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

New research indicates that very low doses of LSD can make the world look blurrier, more colorful, and more dynamic to participants, even without causing full hallucinogenic trips. However, the drug did not appear to change how strongly people experienced a visual illusion that depends on the surrounding scene. The findings were published in Neuroscience of Consciousness.
To make sense of what we see, the visual cortex, the brain region at the back of the head that processes sight, takes the surrounding scene into account. One result is an illusion called contrast surround suppression: a striped pattern looks fainter, or lower in contrast, when it is surrounded by a bold, high-contrast pattern. Scientists think this happens partly because activity in brain cells responding to the surround dampens the response of cells responding to the center.
Classic psychedelics such as LSD and psilocybin produce their effects mainly by activating a type of serotonin receptor, a chemical docking site on brain cells. A study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which analyzed more than 6,000 written accounts of psychedelic trips, linked descriptions of altered sensory perception to areas of the visual cortex rich in serotonin receptors.
Previous experiments suggest that psychedelics can change how strongly the brain relies on visual context. For example, a 2019 study of mice showed that a psychedelic drug reduced surround suppression in the visual cortex.
In humans, however, the effect might go the other direction. A small 2024 pilot study of six volunteers found that a high dose of psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, made a similar contrast illusion stronger, and that people with more intense visual effects showed bigger changes.
Adding to this evidence, a 2025 study found that low to moderate doses of psilocybin made people more susceptible to the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which a circle looks larger or smaller depending on the size of the circles around it. Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin can change how the human brain uses surrounding visual context.
Some people take very small amounts of psychedelics, known as microdoses, in hopes of boosting their mood or creativity. However, a second study covered by PsyPost in 2022 found that repeated LSD microdoses did not reliably improve mood or cognitive performance compared with a placebo, though the higher dose produced small increases in feelings of vigor. The new study tests whether these very low doses might still objectively alter basic visual perception.
The research, led by Lucca Jaeckel, a doctoral student at the Translational Psychiatry Lab at the University of Basel’s Department of Psychiatry, aimed to test whether a low dose of a different psychedelic, LSD, would produce changes like those seen with psilocybin. “There are different theories about how psychedelic drugs cause altered visual perception,” Jaeckel told PsyPost.
“A few studies, two of which investigated psilocybin in humans, have shown alterations in a neural phenomenon called surround suppression, where brain responses to a stimulus at some location in the visual field are suppressed by stimulation in the surrounding area,” he explained. “One way to study surround suppression is through studying visual illusions. The previous studies showed that psilocybin could enhance the illusory amplification of perceived stimulus size and the illusory suppression of stimulus contrast, which are both linked with these surround suppression mechanisms.”
“We wanted to see if LSD microdoses (10 and 20 μg) affect these processes in the same way as psilocybin, using a contrast discrimination task in healthy human participants,” Jaeckel said.
The researchers conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, analyzing data from 31 healthy adults who completed at least two sessions. Each participant was scheduled for three testing sessions at least a week apart, receiving a placebo in one, 10 micrograms of LSD in another, and 20 micrograms in the third. Neither the participants nor the researchers knew which substance was given on which day until the study concluded. The participants averaged 28 years old, and about half had used psychedelics before.
Four hours after taking the dose, the participants completed a visual contrast task on a computer. On each of 100 trials, they saw two circular patches of drifting light and dark stripes for one second. One patch sat in the center of the screen inside a ring of high-contrast stripes, while the other appeared off to the side with no ring.
The participants pressed a key to indicate which patch looked higher in contrast. Because the surrounding ring creates a suppressing illusion, people typically underestimate the contrast of the center patch.
Throughout the testing days, participants also filled out detailed questionnaires about their subjective experiences. They rated how they felt on sliding scales, answering questions about whether their vision seemed sharper or blurrier, brighter or darker, more or less saturated with color, and static or dynamic. They also rated broader psychological feelings, such as whether they felt a sense of boundary dissolution or visionary changes.
These subjective measures were examined in exploratory analyses, meaning they were not part of the plan the researchers registered in advance. On a 100-point scale, ratings of “any drug effect” rose by about 17 points at 20 micrograms and about 5 points at 10 micrograms. The 20-microgram dose also produced a mildly altered state of consciousness, with higher scores for visionary changes, oceanic boundlessness (pleasant feelings such as bliss and insightfulness), and reduced alertness. These increases were small, amounting to roughly 2 to 5 percent of each scale’s maximum.
Visually, participants reported that 20 micrograms made colors look more saturated, made the world seem more dynamic, as if things were in motion, and made their vision blurrier. Even the 10-microgram dose made vision slightly blurrier than placebo, while brightness ratings did not change. These shifts were modest, between about 3 and 7 points on a scale running 50 points in either direction from “normal.”
At the end of each session, participants guessed which treatment they had received. They identified the placebo and the 20-microgram dose at better-than-chance rates, but not the 10-microgram dose.
“There is considerable disagreement as to what dose of a psychedelic constitutes a microdose,” Jaeckel noted. “We used doses of 10 and 20 μg which are often considered microdoses.”
“Some people would argue a microdose is a dose that does not noticeably affect conscious state,” he explained. “Interestingly, our 10 μg dose was not identified as an active dose beyond chance level, yet we could show a small effect of that low dose on subjective visual perception.”
Despite these subjective changes in how the world looked, the objective task results told a different story. Of the 93 completed sessions, 68 sessions from 24 participants met the researchers’ quality criteria; most of the rest were excluded because the responses suggested participants had misunderstood or could not perform the task. In the remaining data, the task reliably produced the illusion, but LSD did not measurably change its strength. A statistical analysis designed to weigh evidence for and against an effect strongly favored no effect of the drug.
The researchers also checked whether participants who reported the biggest changes in their visual perception at 20 micrograms showed bigger changes on the task. They found no correlation, unlike the 2024 psilocybin pilot study, which had linked more intense visual effects to stronger suppression. This suggests that, at these doses, the conscious feeling of altered vision can occur without changes in the brain’s early, automatic filtering of visual contrast.
“Unlike psilocybin, LSD did not affect spatial context-related contrast perception as would be expected from altered surround suppression. At the same time, we did find subjective alterations to visual perception,” Jaeckel said. “This indicates that alterations in surround suppression are not necessary for the perceptual alterations induced by LSD. Nevertheless, it may be that psychedelics affect surround suppression at higher doses where this may affect visual perception.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because participants could often tell when they had received the 20-microgram dose or the placebo, expectations may have inflated their subjective ratings. The authors argue that expectations alone are unlikely to explain the visual effects, noting that some sources describe low-dose psychedelics as making vision sharper, the opposite of the blurriness participants reported.
The authors suggest the most likely reason for the lack of an objective effect is the low dose. Based on a direct comparison study, 20 micrograms of LSD is roughly equivalent to 4 milligrams of psilocybin, far below the 25-milligram dose used in the 2024 contrast study and slightly below the 5-milligram dose that affected the size illusion in the 2025 study.
Low doses of LSD may change conscious perception without being strong enough to shift early visual processing. LSD also acts on dopamine receptors in ways psilocybin does not, and the authors speculate that these effects, which may emerge later in the drug’s time course, could have counteracted any change in surround suppression.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the study design. The contrast task was administered four hours after the participants took the drug, past the absolute peak of the drug’s effects. Additionally, participants were asked to avoid caffeine before and during sessions, because caffeine can itself influence brain activity measures and surround suppression. For regular caffeine users, withdrawal or fatigue four hours into the session may have made it harder to maintain focus.
Future studies could build on these findings by testing higher doses of LSD to see if the contrast illusion eventually shifts, or by testing participants earlier in the drug’s timeline. For now, the evidence indicates that while low doses of LSD can make the world seem more colorful, blurry, and dynamic, they did not measurably change how the brain handles this contrast illusion.
“This is the first publication from a larger study investigating how LSD affects how different kinds of context are used toward making choices about perceptual stimuli,” Jaeckel told PsyPost. “So there’ll be more data coming out soon.”
One of the study’s co-authors, Matthias Liechti, serves as a consultant for Mind Medicine, a company developing LSD-based treatments, and Lykos Therapeutics.
The study, “Low-dose lysergic acid diethylamide alters subjective visual perception but not visual contrast surround suppression,” was authored by Lucca F. Jaeckel, Deborah Logvinski, Mika Kanana, Felix Müller, Nicolai Rohner, Anna M. Becker, Matthias E. Liechti, and Philipp Sterzer.

Demining coalition hands Ukraine new Inguar armored vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

- Ukraine’s Support Forces received a new batch of equipment from the Lithuania- and Iceland-led Demining Capability Coalition, including Ukrainian-made Inguar-3 armored vehicles.
- The Inguar-3 is a Kyiv-built MRAP rated to withstand 7.62 mm armor-piercing rounds, 155 mm shell fragments and an 8 kg mine blast.
Ukraine’s Support Forces, the branch that runs the military’s engineering and demining units, have received another batch of equipment from the international Demining Capability Coalition led by Lithuania and Iceland, including Ukrainian-built Inguar-3 mine-resistant armored vehicles.
The Support Forces Command announced the handover on Oct. 15 but did not list the full contents of the delivery or the number of vehicles. Maj. Gen. Dmytro Herega, the command’s commander, thanked partners for their steady support and said engineering units need reliable equipment to carry out both combat and humanitarian demining.
The Inguar-3 is a mine-resistant ambush protected vehicle, or MRAP, designed and built by Kyiv-based Inguar Defence on its own chassis rather than an adapted commercial truck. The manufacturer rates its steel and aluminum armor to STANAG 4569 Level 3, the NATO standard covering protection against 7.62 mm armor-piercing rounds, fragments from a 155 mm shell bursting 60 meters (about 200 feet) away, and an 8 kg (18-pound) mine blast under the hull. A 356-horsepower Deutz diesel and an Allison automatic gearbox drive the vehicle, which also has central tire inflation and run-flat inserts so crews can keep moving after a puncture.
Before entering service, the Inguar-3 covered about 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of trials, including combat testing with the National Guard’s Azov brigade in the Serebryansky Forest, and won its first orders from Ukrainian military customers in early 2025, The Defense Post reported. Inguar Defence later took the vehicle to the Eurosatory 2026 exhibition in Paris.
For deminers, a vehicle with that level of protection matters because sapper teams often work close to the front line, where they face mines along routes as well as artillery and drone strikes while moving between clearance sites.
Lithuania launched the Demining Capability Coalition in 2023 and invited Iceland to co-lead it, and the group now includes 23 member countries along with observers and partner organizations. Member states paid about 150 million euros ($168 million) into the coalition fund in 2024–2026, and the coalition used that money to buy and send Ukraine 89 million euros ($100 million) worth of equipment, the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence said in June. Separately, Ukraine has received 608 million euros ($681 million) in donated demining equipment from countries including Germany, Lithuania, Finland and Denmark.
The coalition’s purchases have ranged from mine detectors and explosive ordnance disposal kits to trucks, ambulances, mine rollers and electronic warfare systems. At its June meeting in Lviv, the group handed over trucks, MRAP armored vehicles and minibuses bought with the fund.
Lithuanian officials describe Ukraine as the most heavily mine-contaminated country in the world, and the coalition plans to spend at least 165 million euros ($185 million) in 2026 on equipment, machinery and specialist training for Ukrainian demining units.
