Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:17:00 EEST
18:17:00 KST

Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Just two weeks ago, relations between Ukraine and South Korea seemed almost trouble-free. Russia and North Korea were deepening their military cooperation, North Korean soldiers were fighting against Ukraine, and Kyiv and Seoul appeared to have an increasing number of shared security interests.
On 23 September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in New York. They discussed strengthening political dialogue, trade, investment, Ukraine's reconstruction, and the common threats posed by military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The meeting was a continuation of an eventful year in bilateral relations. In July, Volodymyr Zelenskyy met South Korean President Lee Jae-myung for the first time. Seoul announced an additional US$100 million in non-military assistance to Ukraine. Economic cooperation also held considerable potential: a framework agreement between the two countries provided for up to US$2.1 billion in preferential South Korean loans for Ukraine's reconstruction by 2029.
But on that very same day, 23 September, relations between the two countries began to deteriorate rapidly.
During his address to the UN General Assembly, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Both soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025.
On the face of it, this should have been seen as an example of successful cooperation between Kyiv and Seoul. After all, South Korea had previously advocated the transfer of prisoners to its territory, where they could live in safety.
Instead, on 24 September, President Lee Jae-myung publicly accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. According to Seoul, the transfer was supposed to remain undisclosed to protect the prisoners themselves and their families still living in North Korea. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed.
South Korea demanded an official explanation and an apology. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the situation as a diplomatic misunderstanding. His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun, later confirmed that he had received a letter of apology but said it fell short of Seoul's expectations.
On 2 October, Lee Jae-myung threatened Ukraine with further measures unless Kyiv acknowledged its breach of the agreement and issued a public apology. He also criticised Ukrainian statements about the threat of a military conflict between North and South Korea, accusing Kyiv of using rhetoric that could push the Korean Peninsula towards war.
On 8 October, the diplomatic crisis escalated to the recall of an ambassador: South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced its decision to bring its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, back to Seoul.
Ukrainian–South Korean relations had thus entered one of their most serious political crises since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
All this is happening as President Lee Jae-myung seeks to ease tensions with North Korea and restore inter-Korean dialogue. Pyongyang, however, has shown little interest in reciprocating.
Quite the opposite. On 7 October, Kim Jong Un sent Vladimir Putin a birthday message in which he called the Russian president his "dearest friend", reaffirmed his commitment to developing the strategic alliance with Moscow, and once again expressed support for Russia's "sacred war".
While Seoul is looking for ways to reconcile with Pyongyang, North Korean troops are gaining combat experience in Russia's war against Ukraine, and Moscow is helping North Korea develop its military technologies.
Why did the transfer of two prisoners of war provoke such a strong reaction from South Korea? Does Seoul's policy of reconciliation with Pyongyang stand any chance of success? What is North Korea gaining from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, and how could this change the balance of power on the Korean Peninsula?
Ukrainska Pravda spoke about these issues with Sangmin Shim, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Foreign Policy and National Security at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, who specialises in international law and security affairs. His analytical articles and commentary on security and environmental issues in East Asia have appeared in international publications, including the American magazine The National Interest, as well as leading South Korean newspapers such as Chosun Ilbo and JoongAng Ilbo.
Although Shim is critical of certain policies and approaches pursued by the current South Korean administration, he is not a political opposition figure. His perspective is primarily that of an independent policy expert, shaped by his background in international law, diplomacy and national security. He previously taught international law at the Korea National Diplomatic Academy and has advised the government on legal and foreign policy issues.
The crisis in Ukrainian-South Korean relations
Ukrainian-South Korean relations are experiencing their first political crisis since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. South Korea recently even recalled its ambassador from Ukraine. Why has the issue of the two North Korean prisoners become so sensitive for President Lee Jae-Myung's administration?
Well, this is my personal take, but I believe the South Korean government is so pro-Russian that anything potentially sensitive for bilateral relations between North Korea and the Russian Federation is largely discounted. That is what we are seeing today. Even though Ukraine has graciously sent those North Korean prisoners to South Korea, the South Korean government is not really appreciative of it. South Korea is so preoccupied with normalising relations with the Russian Federation that the many gestures the Ukrainian government approaches us with do not really count from the South Korean perspective. This is a truly sad matter, in my view.
Did the situation with those two North Korean prisoners create any domestic debate in South Korea?
In the general public's view, it is great that these prisoners have been transferred to South Korean territory to live in a free state. But the current South Korean government is extremely worried about the consequences of having these North Korean prisoners on its territory.
They fear the possible negative effects of holding them in South Korean custody, which makes them highly sensitive about their presence. This is completely irrational from my perspective. South Korea has always strongly argued for the transfer of Korean prisoners of war to its territory, as the government deems these POWs to be its own citizens.
There is a total inconsistency in logic between the South Korean government's general policy and what they are doing in this specific situation.
Inter-Korean tensions
What we see in the news now is that the South Korean president wants to ease tensions and restore inter-Korean relations and dialogue. But how realistic is this when there appears to be very little interest in dialogue from North Korea?
This might be my personal judgement, but looking at the South Korean government's attempts to ease tensions with North Korea, I don't think it is going to happen. The North Korean government is completely focused on differentiating the two regimes. Pyongyang believes that any ties it might have with South Korea will not bring any real benefit to the prosperity of the North Korean regime. Therefore, the North Korean regime has decided to totally sever ties with South Korea, and that is exactly what they are doing. Unfortunately, the South Korean government is not ready to give up its hope for reconciliation with North Korea. This is where the real tragedy begins.
We also see that North Korea has physically reinforced the separation. They are building barriers, laying mines, and fortifying the border with South Korea. From your point of view, is this just another period of rising tension, or has Kim's "two hostile states" policy changed these relations?
From what I can see, North Korea is highly focused on differentiating between the South Korean and North Korean regimes. They started by laying mines to prevent South Korean troops from crossing into North Korean territory. This is extremely unfortunate, and as you know, it has led to unnecessary casualties among South Korean soldiers. I do not know how this issue can be resolved between the governments of South Korea and North Korea, but I really hope it will be smoothed over. I hope we can find common ground to talk to each other, with the understanding that this issue should not destroy us. There are still many factors that can influence a hopeful outcome in the future.
President Lee's opponents accuse him of being overly cautious about provoking North Korea. How strong is this criticism inside South Korea, and does it explain the unusually sharp reaction to Ukraine?
There is a deep political divide between the progressive and conservative fronts. The conservative front argues that any engagement with North Korea is basically a concession. Meanwhile, the progressive front believes it is a necessary step toward reconciliation. So, there is a huge divide regarding how they want to move forward in the current situation.
President Lee also criticised Ukraine's statement regarding a possible future conflict between North and South Korea, saying such rhetoric could push the peninsula towards war. Why is this topic particularly sensitive for him?
This is anyone's guess, but as I perceive it, a high-ranking official from the Ukrainian Presidential Office stated that ignoring the ties between North Korea and the rest of the world would have a ripple effect on South Korea's security. But is South Korea ready to accept that?
They believe that through peaceful inter-Korean relations, we will have better relations with every country south of the Korean peninsula. But this is unproven. So we will continue to have contentious relations with both the Ukrainian and North Korean governments.
The role of the North Korean military in the war in Ukraine
North Korea has already sent roughly 15,000 troops to Russia, and thousands of them have reportedly been killed or wounded. Before this, North Korea lacked military experience in such a large-scale war. How different is the North Korean army today because of its experience in Ukraine?
After sending their forces to defend or take over the Kursk region, those North Korean troops have gained valuable battlefield experience in modern warfare — particularly combining drone warfare with conventional warfare. From a South Korean perspective, this is not something we can easily discount. South Korea now needs to prepare for potential provocations from North Korea. However, the current government is not taking this seriously. Because this administration leans pro-Russia, pro-China, and pro-North Korea, they do not see these signs of provocation as something to truly worry about. I am sorry to criticise my government, but this appears to be the reality.
And have you already seen evidence that the lessons learned by North Korean soldiers have been incorporated into North Korean training or doctrine at home?
What I can see from the collaboration between North Korean and Russian forces is that the Russians have been sharing technical advice to further develop North Korea's military expertise — particularly in military tactics and drone warfare. Because of this, North Korean forces are in a better position. I do not know how else to put it, but those North Korean forces are now superior to South Korean forces in terms of dealing with drone warfare and other non-conventional forces involvement.
So, could you say that soldiers returning from Russia will eventually form a new, combat-experienced elite within the North Korean military?
First of all, the initial group sent to Russian territory consisted of combat troops from their special operations forces. They sent about 10,000 of their best elite troops, and the results speak for themselves. The involvement of these forces has genuinely contributed to retaking territories crucial to the Russians from Ukrainian control. This has had a major effect. I do not know if this trend can continue, because the North Korean government will also face difficulties with the continuous mobilisation of its armed forces. We do not know how the next stage will play out.
Let us look at the evidence the North Korean government is presenting. They are doing everything they can not to reveal the presence of their personnel on the battlefield. They want to limit their manpower to factories and other workforces – helping Russian forces and industries build stronger weapon systems. So, from what I perceive, North Korean personnel are not going to be seen anywhere near the front lines. But what I really want to emphasise in this case is that North Korea is collaborating with the Russian government and military to build up Russian stockpiles, ensuring the Russian military is prepared for incoming attacks from Ukraine or other countries.
We have a fairly good picture of what is moving from North Korea to Russia: soldiers, ammunition, and missiles. But we know much less about what is moving in the opposite direction and so from your point of view, what's North Korea actually getting in return from Russia?
I mean, what North Korea really hopes to gain from the collaboration with the Russian regime is that they will get military expertise in terms of ballistic missiles development and other top-notch military development. And in turn those current regimes will provide war forces in the form of manual labour and everything to provide the help necessary for the Russian Federation to rebuild their drone systems. So, then they will be able to compete with Ukraine in terms of non-conventional forces engagement.
The Russian government is seeing that the Ukrainian government will not be able to provide all the necessary supplies for all the necessary equipment for forever. And then this is going to be a kind of a war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine in which both will be subject to having to pay the highest consequences from this military conflict. This is so sad but this is also a fact.
If North Korea is developing the capacity to mass produce Shahed-type drones with Russian assistance, how would that change the threat facing South Korea and is South Korea prepared for the kind of mass drone warfare we have seen in Ukraine?
I mean, we have heard the most recent report from the National Security Advisor of the Korean Republic that if North Korea has been engaging too much in this Russia-Ukraine conflict, this would be the best opportunity for Korea to start taking over the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and making the whole Korean Peninsula as a unified nation. But this is not going to be the case that I have been seeing because this is not going to involve the political discussions between the major powers and basically the military aspect will not resolve the matters as we see it.
So what I perceive to be the case is that whatever happens in the territories between Ukraine and Russia will not have any consequences for the inter-Korean relations.
Inter-Korean relations will have to be dealt with by their own dynamics. Meaning that Russia, the United States, Japan, Korea and both North and South Korea will have to be sitting at the same table to negotiate away the differences. This is not going to be a short-term matter but it has to include the case of negotiations.
How Ukraine іs perceived in North Korea
Maybe you know how North Korean propaganda explains Ukraine to its own population? What have North Koreans been told about why their soldiers are fighting and dying thousands of kilometres from home?
I mean the North Korean government is ready to just decorate their lost lives as their national heroes. But this is not going to be the case if the loss of the lives and casualties continues to accrue for the North Korean regime. We have a report that records those current casualties at around 3,000 soldiers who have lost their lives and then another 33,000 soldiers who have basically lost their capability to re-engage in the world.
But with the intensification of the war and tensions within Russia and Ukraine, this will lead to more casualties for North Koreans. And I don't know if the North Korean government will be able to continue to persuade their general public with this loss of life as an unavoidable matter.
I don't know, but the North Korean government is not a democratic nation but they will not be subject to national approval or to answering the questions of the people but they will still feel the pressure from the North Korean populace about the loss of life that has been the consequence of the involvement of North Korean troops in the Ukrainian military conflict.
Is Ukraine portrayed as an enemy in its own right or is it simply as part of a larger confrontation with the United States and the West?
This is a really interesting question. Between the US and Ukraine, they don't seem to have much differences. But by just looking at the recent episode between the Ukraine and Republic of Korea, they seem to have some impending conditions to be dealt with between these two nations.
But from my perspective, these would be only diplomatic matters and if these matters were to be entrusted with both countries' foreign ministers, these differences will be easily negotiated away. What matters to Korea for now is that the current president of the administration. He's so active in voicing criticism about the Ukrainian government. This is not going to be helpful for settling the battle between Ukraine and South Korea. I really hope that the South Korean president will stay silent for at least for the next two weeks for the two ministers to be able to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement.
And from your point of view, how much do the average North Koreans actually know about the scale of their country's involvement in Russia's war?
From the conservative people's point of view, this government is so pro-North Korea and they suspect that North Korea has a huge influence over the matters of the South Korean government, but I don't believe this. But whatever is the case with the North Korean and the South Korean government, I suspect that the South Korean government needs to be in a better position to fight away the incoming threats from North Korea.
Basically in terms of cybersecurity and maritime security. But without those concerns, we have to see that the South Korean government is going to live their lives as if nothing has happened. This is not going to be a very positive case for the South Korean population.
And what happened with thousands of soldiers who return home with direct experience of Russia, of modern warfare, of modern technologies which are most likely not represented in North Korea?
I mean, these North Korean soldiers who have been sent back to the North Korean territories have returned with better experience with drone warfare and better experience with modern warfare. So they may have something to say to their military leadership. But what are considered to be the barricades with these North Koreans, they have been so exhausted with the too-stressful battlefield conditions. So, they may be the key. I mean, this is my hopeful suggestion, but these people will be the driving forces for asking for more changes regarding the South Korea and North Korea territories. And then, if the current administration fails to address these questions then there will be more political decisions, moving forward.
And could these people potentially be a problem for the regime now?
This is another matter that we don't really know the answer to. Military and civilian society have been in co-existence for a long time. But what I perceive in that case is that the military, they are taking the upper hand with the civilian structures. So whatever situation may arrive, it's going to be down to the hands of the military that will take the final decisions.
How South Korea іs helping Russia and what the consequences could be
What we see in the recent investigation by Reuters is that South Korean petroleum product experts have reportedly helped Russia with fuel shortages caused partly by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. How is this issue perceived in South Korea or is it even discussed there?
There are two different opinions about this matter. For conservative people, this is a really serious matter because it seems to be the case that the South Korean government is basically just looking away in the case of helping the Russian economy by support with petrochemical fuels.
But at the same time, from a purely technical perspective, the South Korean government is not prohibited from providing petrochemical products to the Russian Federation because this is not going to be subject to any country's sanctions regimes. So this is kind of revealing a kind of difference between many different countries' sanctions regimes.
From my perspective, it should be right to tighten the grip upon the differences in the different countries' sanction regimes. But at the same time, we have to hold our countries to settle out the differences between many unlike-minded nations to achieve the core missions of these sanctions which is to weaken the fighting ability of the Russian Federation in terms of the battlefield between the Russian Federation and Ukraine.
From the Ukrainian perspective this trade could be the next major source of tension between Seoul and Kyiv. From your perspective, how could these South Korean-Ukrainian relations be mended?
I mean, we have current issues between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea, but I strongly believe that this case will be settled away between the diplomatic negotiations between these countries.
What I perceive to be the more worrisome outcome is if the South Korean president Lee Jae-myung continues to press hard on the relations between Ukraine and the Korean Republic. And if that would be the case, then there's not going to be a case for these two bilateral regimes to be reconciled pretty much soon. Because as long as the president's mandate is not going to be met, there's not much that the South Korean foreign minister will do proactively to settle the differences. So all it might come down to is the president changing his position between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea.
In a way, the revealing of the identity of the prisoners, those North Korean soldiers, would not be so much to disrupt the bilateral relations between these countries. It's really important that the South Korean government is so aware of this importance and also about the importance of not being too far away from these two government's positions.

Norway’s Kongsberg to Make Anti-Drone Cannon Turrets in Poland From 2028
Norwegian defense manufacturer Kongsberg is preparing to build a production facility for anti-drone hardware in Poland to support the domestic SAN air defense network.
The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of the year, with construction starting immediately afterward, Defense Express reported on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The total financial commitment stands at 200 million Polish zlotys ($51 million), equivalent to €45 million ($50.2 million), with operations expected to launch in 2028.
Integrating production facilities within Poland aims to streamline supply chains for the country's national defense architecture. The plant will produce Kongsberg PROTECTOR weapon stations equipped with 30mm cannons, which serve as core modules for the SAN counter-drone system.
Establishing localized manufacturing addresses prior concerns regarding reliance on external components, helping to ensure greater domestic control over military hardware while creating economic value within the country.
The SAN air defense network relies on a combination of defensive platforms. Alongside 30mm cannon turrets, the network incorporates 12.7mm machine gun mounts, self-propelled 35mm SA-35 anti-aircraft systems, electronic warfare units, APKWS precision rockets, and Merops interceptor drones. These capabilities are configured onto Legwan all-terrain vehicles and Jelcz heavy trucks, as reported by Defense Express.
Polish armed forces have ordered 18 batteries of the system, comprising 18 command platoons and 52 firing platoons to expand protection against unmanned aerial threats. Neighboring Slovakia has also indicated interest in the platform through regional defense cooperation frameworks.
Cannon and machine gun turrets offer a cost-effective countermeasure compared to traditional surface-to-air missiles, despite functional constraints regarding operational ceiling and maximum engagement range.
Previously, Poland signed a major defense contract valued at approximately $4.2 billion with a consortium of PGZ and Kongsberg to acquire the SAN anti-drone system.
The contract, which was scheduled for delivery between 2026 and 2028, included 18 batteries, 18 command platoons, and 52 fire platoons capable of autonomously detecting, classifying, and neutralizing drones.

Herzog flies over Turkey despite ban on Israeli state planes, joins summit alongside Iranian representative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:16:06 UTC
18:16:06 KST

Israeli President Isaac Herzog arrived in Azerbaijan for an international summit attended by representatives of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel, including Iran, after taking an unusual flight through Turkish airspace despite Ankara's ban on Israeli government aircraft.
Among those attending were the emir of Qatar, Kuwait's deputy foreign minister, the ambassadors to Azerbaijan of Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Malaysia and Indonesia, Bangladesh's acting foreign minister and Iran's deputy foreign minister. When Herzog addressed the summit, the representatives of Iran, Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan and the Palestinian Authority left the hall. The emir of Qatar remained, as did representatives of Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Central Asian countries.
Herzog landed in Baku on Wednesday aboard a commercial Azerbaijan Airlines flight, allowing him to reach the Azerbaijani capital without taking a longer route over the Black Sea, which his team considered potentially dangerous because of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
The flight also provided an unexpected workaround to Turkey's restrictions on Israeli official aircraft, which have previously disrupted visits by senior Israeli leaders to Azerbaijan.
Herzog arrived for a day-and-a-half visit to participate in the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), an international forum dedicated to strengthening cooperation and relations among Asian countries.
Alongside the Israeli president, the summit includes representatives from several countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, including Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Indonesia. An Iranian representative is also attending.
According to a report by Middle East Eye, flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 and footage from Herzog's welcoming ceremony in Baku indicate that the Israeli president traveled on Azerbaijan Airlines flight J222. The flight departed Ben-Gurion Airport at 11:35 a.m. Wednesday, crossed Turkish airspace and landed in Baku at 3:40 p.m. local time.
Images from the welcoming ceremony showed Herzog arriving on an Azerbaijan Airlines Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, matching the aircraft type recorded for the flight.
The president's team reportedly chose the commercial flight rather than a longer alternative route through Greece, Bulgaria and the Black Sea. The alternative raised security concerns because of continuing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine war.
Turkey has barred Israeli government aircraft from using its airspace, but commercial flights operated by Israeli and foreign airlines are still permitted to pass through the country on routes to and from Israel.
According to Middle East Eye, an official familiar with the matter said Azerbaijan had not informed Ankara that Herzog was aboard the flight.
"Naturally, Turkey cannot get the passenger manifest for every airliner just passing through the airspace," the Turkish official said. The official added that Israel had stopped submitting requests to use Turkish airspace because it was already familiar with Ankara's position.
Turkey's restrictions have previously interfered with Israeli diplomatic travel. In May 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu postponed a planned visit to Baku, with reports at the time citing Ankara's refusal to allow Israel's official Wing of Zion aircraft to pass through Turkish airspace. Netanyahu's office cited developments in Gaza and Syria and a demanding political and security schedule.
Herzog himself canceled a planned visit to the COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan in November 2024, amid reports that Turkey had refused permission for the Israeli state aircraft to cross its territory. This time, Wing of Zion was unavailable because of maintenance work, and Herzog traveled aboard the Azerbaijani aircraft instead. The President's Office declined to comment on the flight details.
The unusual journey also attracted attention because of the name of the aircraft carrying Herzog. Social media users identified the Azerbaijani plane as "Shusha," a name associated with the Shusha Declaration, a 2021 agreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey strengthening their strategic and defense cooperation following the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.
Some commentators interpreted the choice of aircraft as a further symbolic jab by Baku at Ankara, although there has been no confirmation that the aircraft was selected for that reason.
The diplomatic symbolism extended to the summit itself. Herzog met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev ahead of the gathering, which brings together countries with sharply differing positions on Israel and the wider Middle East.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan did not attend the summit, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan representing Ankara instead. Some reports suggested Erdogan's absence may have been connected to Herzog's participation, although this has not been officially confirmed. The meeting comes at a sensitive moment in relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan, two close regional allies.
Azerbaijan's recent school dress-code restrictions, which have prevented some students and teachers wearing Islamic headscarves from entering classrooms, have triggered protests and a public dispute involving political figures in both countries.
The restrictions have become another source of friction between Ankara and Baku, adding a further dimension to Herzog's appearance at the international gathering. On Thursday morning, as voting opened at Israeli diplomatic missions around the world ahead of the October 27 election, Herzog visited the Israeli Embassy in Baku alongside Israel's ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ronen Krausz.
"This is a very important moment during my state visit here to Azerbaijan," Herzog said. "I have the opportunity to see how the election process begins and how voting is actually conducted at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad, here at the embassy in Baku."
The president encouraged Israelis to participate in the democratic process and emphasized the importance of the upcoming election after a difficult period for the country.
"These elections are a celebration of democracy in Israel and at its embassies abroad," he said. "I call on all Israeli citizens to exercise their right to vote and, of course, to influence Israel's future."
Herzog also appealed for restraint amid political tensions surrounding the election campaign. "These are very important elections after a difficult period for the State of Israel, and the main thing I want to say to every Israeli citizen is that elections are not a civil war," he said.
"On the contrary, they are the genuine democratic process through which we influence our lives and determine the direction our country takes."

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Routine vaccinations are free of charge and available at healthcare facilities.
50,000 doses of the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine have arrived in Ukraine for free vaccination of children in accordance with the Immunization Schedule. This was reported by the Public Health Center of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Ukraine receives these vaccines as part of cooperation between the Ministry of Health and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (Gavi). The partnership agreement between the Global Alliance and Ukraine was signed at the end of 2024. Under the agreement, Gavi finances part of the vaccines supporting the national immunization program, in accordance with the national Immunization Development Strategy through 2030
According to the available information, במסגרת this partnership, UNICEF procures and delivers the vaccines to the country, while the Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine coordinates their distribution to regional disease control and prevention centers (DCCs). The vaccines have now reached healthcare facilities, which will ensure the continuity of routine immunization for children.
Where a child can be vaccinated
To vaccinate a child, you should contact your family doctor, pediatrician or the nearest healthcare facility. The Public Health Center emphasizes that vaccination under the National Immunization Schedule is free of charge.
If a child has missed any routine vaccinations, you should contact a doctor as soon as possible; the doctor will draw up an individual catch-up schedule
Why these infections are dangerous
Measles is a contagious infectious disease that can lead to serious complications, from pneumonia to encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and even death. In pregnant women, measles can cause premature labor or miscarriage.
Mumps is one of the most common and contagious infections in the world, and can cause a number of severe complications, such as orchitis in men (inflammation of the testicle, which can lead to infertility), acute pancreatitis, meningitis and deafness.
Rubella is an infectious viral disease that can lead to miscarriage or congenital malformations in the child in pregnant women.
Vaccination is the most effective protection against these diseases.

Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.
Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.
In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?
BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.
Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?
The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.
One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.
You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?
If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.
We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.
We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.
From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.
When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?
I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.
The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.
There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.
There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.
Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Zelenskyy: 850 Shaheds came as Starlink limits hit defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:11:10 UTC
18:11:10 KST

- Zelenskyy said Russia launched over 850 Shaheds between Oct. 14 and 9 a.m. Oct. 15, during a SpaceX speed cap on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals.
- The 160 km/h Starshield limit, imposed overnight Oct. 13–14, cripples interceptor drones needed against Russian jet-powered Shaheds flying up to 600 km/h.
Russia launched more than 850 Shahed attack drones at Ukraine in roughly a day and a half, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 15, an onslaught that came as a new speed cap on SpaceX’s Starlink network curtailed the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to shoot them down.
Zelenskyy said the count covered the period from the start of Oct. 14 until 9 a.m. on Oct. 15. He said attacks came in constant waves and that Ukrainian airspace was not free of drones for a single hour. Russian strikes killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three more in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian media reported.
“From the start of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there have already been more than 850 Shaheds, and this is precisely at a time of an artificial speed restriction on our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelenskyy said, in remarks translated from Ukrainian.
The restriction he referred to took effect overnight on Oct. 13–14, when SpaceX capped Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s armed forces, at 160 km/h (about 100 mph) for terminals in motion. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said SpaceX imposed the limit unilaterally and without warning, and that any terminal moving faster than that loses its connection, disrupting interceptor and mid-range drone missions as well as frontline reconnaissance, logistics and signal relays.
Under the cap, the restriction falls most heavily on Ukraine’s air defense. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), so interceptors that must chase them down need far more speed than 160 km/h. Starlink has been blocked over Russian territory since February 2026 under a whitelist of approved terminals, and Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian targets rely on other communications. The capped terminals instead serve tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles operating over Ukraine and the occupied territories, which means the limit cuts into Ukraine’s defense.
Service was later restored below the 160 km/h threshold, and Mykhailo Fedorov said attack and interceptor drones should be able to fly again, while adding that Ukraine now needs the Starshield speed limit removed altogether.
Elon Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the U.S. president, the Associated Press reported, while the White House told Kyiv it does not control SpaceX, according to Axios. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times on Oct. 15 that the restriction was a deliberate decision on the American side rather than a technical fault, though he said he did not know whether SpaceX or the U.S. government made the call.
Zelenskyy also accused Moscow of escalating its strikes after seeing sanctions eased and attempts to pressure Kyiv, and urged Americans to side with Ukraine’s defense instead of the aggressor.
The Defense Ministry said it is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners and is setting up backup communication channels, but neither SpaceX nor the U.S. Department of War has said whether or when the 160 km/h cap will be lifted.

Arriving for a summit in Brussels, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Thursday that European leaders remain widely divided on the European Union’s next long-term budget.
“We are facing difficult negotiations,” Merz told reporters at the summit venue, adding that leaders would hold intensive and constructive talks but that an agreement was unlikely to be reached in the coming days.
“I wish that we can reach a result on the multiannual financial framework by the end of the year, although the ideas within the European Union are very far apart today,” he said.
“We face difficult negotiations, but I enter these negotiations with the firm will to bring them to a good result. Because Europe must remain capable of acting and become sovereign,” he added.
Merz criticized Ireland’s latest compromise proposal for the EU budget, saying that the planned reductions fall far short of what is needed for a deal.
“We must significantly reduce the common budget compared with the (European) Commission’s proposals. No member state in the European Union can afford to pay contributions to the European Union on this scale,” he said.
Merz noted that the current proposal lies 50% above the funding level of the ongoing multiannual financial framework and insisted that defense and the EU’s competitiveness should be priorities in the next budget.
Asked about the EU’s aid pledges to Ukraine, the German chancellor said Europeans need to boost funding to ensure that support for Ukraine remains sustainable in the long term.
“It remains my firm conviction that we are not only defending the territorial integrity of Ukraine, but we are defending the political order of Europe, which is being challenged by Russia in every respect,” he said.
Asked about placing Russian assets frozen in the EU under US control, Merz rejected the idea.
“These are assets that are frozen in Europe. They should remain frozen in Europe. This is our matter, and we decide on it,” he said.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday, citing insiders, that the United States had proposed to European states that part of the frozen Russian assets be released and transferred to a financial vehicle controlled by Washington to revive peace talks with Moscow.
The plan was presented by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, but was rejected by European representatives, the newspaper said.

Australian study explores blood test for cervical cancer detection

Led by the University of Queensland (UQ), the CLARITY cervical cancer study at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital will investigate the potential of blood biomarkers in the screening, monitoring and management of cervical cancer, according to a UQ statement released recently.
"The project has the potential to improve early detection, treatment responses and post-treatment surveillance, as well as support more personalized treatment approaches for women with cervical cancer," said Andreas Obermair, chief investigator at UQ's Queensland Center for Gynecological Cancer Research.
Despite advances in prevention and treatment, including the Gardasil vaccine, cervical cancer continues to impose significant physical, emotional and financial burdens on women worldwide, Obermair noted.
A reliable, non-invasive test could offer "a more accessible and acceptable alternative" to current cervical screening methods, particularly for women facing cultural, systemic or personal barriers to screening, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and culturally diverse communities, he said. ■

Pakistan school roof collapses in Peshawar, killing almost 30 young students and a teacher
Islamabad — Almost 30 students and a teacher were killed Thursday when the roof of a private school collapsed in the Pakistani city of Peshawar, local officials said.
The bodies of 17 children were brought to Lady Reading Hospital in the city following the incident, in addition to the body of a female teacher, Mohammad Asim, a spokesperson for the hospital told CBS News, adding that some survivors were also admitted in critical condition.
At least 29 people were killed in total after the collapse at the Al-Khair Education Center in Peshawar's southwest Dir district, according to Asim and other local officials.
The cause of the disaster remained unconfirmed, but a witness told CBS News the building appeared "not suitable" for use as a school, and a local police official said there was ongoing construction on the roof that could have overweighted the structure.
"We have taken out at least 45 children," district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan said, according to the Reuters news agency.
Mahwish Zaman, a teacher who was injured in the collapse, told the Associated Press after regaining consciousness in her hospital bed that the school had about 1,200 students enrolled, and she was in her class when the roof collapsed. She described it as feeling as if the sky had fallen.
Zahir Hussain, who lives a couple of blocks from the school, told CBS News he was walking to work when he saw people running out onto the street.
"I rushed to the spot and the school with others to see what had happened," he said. "Apparently first-period classes had just started … The building was overcrowded. The lesson had barely begun" when the collapse occurred.
He said the school was in a relatively small residential building on a narrow street, and that it catered mainly to children from low-income families. Signage on the outside of the building indicated that there were classes for both boys and girls.
"The parents and families were in unbearable pain. The street was extremely narrow, which made it difficult for rescue teams to reach the site quickly," he told CBS News.
"The building was not suitable for use as a school at all. It is a very tragic incident, seeing dead innocent children's bodies left me silent, and it was extremely painful," Hussain said, calling it a "heavy tragedy for parents and the entire Dir colony."
"It was a weak building structure," Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said, according to Reuters. "Its roof was overweight with construction on a weak structure that caused the collapse."

Türkiye’s electric car fleet nears 500,000

The number of electric cars registered in Türkiye rose to 486,359 as of the end of September 2026, up from just 80,043 in 2023 and 14,552 in 2022, according to motor vehicle data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 15.
At the same time, hybrid vehicle ownership climbed to 915,892, highlighting the country’s accelerating shift toward alternative-fuel vehicles.
The data showed a sharp increase in EV and hybrid cars over recent years, while the share of diesel and LPG-powered vehicles continued to decline. EVs accounted for 2.7 percent of all registered cars in September, compared with 0.5 percent in 2023 and just 0.1 percent in 2022. Hybrid cars represented 5.1 percent of the fleet, up from 1.5 percent three years earlier.
Diesel cars, once the dominant fuel type, made up 32 percent of all registered automobiles at the end of September, down from a peak of 38.3 percent in 2020. At the same time, gasoline-powered vehicles increased their share of the fleet to 31 percent, while remaining below the levels seen in the mid-2000s, when they accounted for more than two-thirds of all passenger cars.
According to TÜİK, 18.12 million automobiles were registered in traffic as of the end of September.
The total number of registered motor vehicles in Türkiye increased 6.2 percent year-on-year in September to 35.07 million.
Automobiles accounted for 51.7 percent of all registered vehicles, followed by motorcycles at 21.9 percent, pickup trucks at 14.2 percent, tractors at 6.7 percent, trucks at 3 percent, minibuses at 1.6 percent and buses at 0.6 percent.
Among passenger cars newly registered in September, Renault held the largest share at 16.1 percent. TOGG ranked second with 9.8 percent, followed by Hyundai with 8.6 percent, Volkswagen with 7.1 percent and Toyota with 6.8 percent.
Other major brands included Mercedes-Benz with 5.3 percent, Skoda with 5 percent, Kia with 4.5 percent, Peugeot with 3.7 percent, Nissan with 3.3 percent, Opel, Fiat and Tesla with 2.7 percent each.
In the January-September period, the number of newly registered vehicles fell 14.5 percent year-on-year to 1.5 million, said TÜİK.

====================================================================================================

Unions Are the Key to America’s Cost of Living Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

Ask an everyday working American, and they’ll likely tell you there’s something fundamentally wrong with our economy. Across industries, big cities, and small towns, working people are struggling. Their paychecks aren’t stretching far enough. They stress over every expense and struggle to cover rent and electric bills, let alone take their families to dinner once in a while. Meanwhile, our research shows that top CEOs gave themselves massive raises in 2025 and now make well over 300 times what typical workers are paid.
As everything gets more and more expensive, we believe there is a powerful solution: unions.
Union contracts raise pay for workers. A new report from the Economic Policy Institute shows that tripling union membership in this country would deliver a 14.5% raise to the median worker—more than $7,700 a year or the equivalent of 7.5 extra weeks of pay annually. This adds up to nearly $270,000 over a 35-year career. Unions can also be powerful tools for combating racial pay discrimination; the new report shows tripling union membership would narrow the racial wage gap by more than a third.
Tripling union density wouldn’t only benefit union members. Nonunion workers would also see large raises, because strong unions lift standards across the economy. All told, EPI estimates that tripling union membership would shift $1.2 trillion of wealth in the economy to working people every year, reversing a third of the rise in inequality since 1979. And because union workers can win better benefits like health insurance, tripling union membership would also provide health care to 6.8 million more Americans. It’s what the labor movement calls the union difference: higher wages, access to health care, retirement security, paid time off and sick leave, and dignity on the job.
An economy where 30% of workers are union members isn’t a pipe dreamーit’s part of our own history. After New Deal policies of the 1930s and 40s secured workers’ legal rights, union membership soared. In the 1950s, union membership was above 30%, and working people saw huge gains. Wages grew, and racial wage gaps shrank.
A fundamental promise of a union is that the workers will share in the profit they create—and as soon as wealthy executives and shareholders saw their bottom lines under threat, they went to work attacking that progress.
Anti-union court rulings and so-called “right-to-work” state laws have broken the labor law that once protected workers. Relentless and retaliatory union-busting has created significant risks for unionizing, with corporations spending more than $1.5 billion a year to stop workers from exercising their fundamental right to organize. And the Trump Administration has weakened worker protections at the Department of Labor and prevented the government agency charged with protecting workers’ rights to organize and bargain collectively from operating for nearly all of 2025, closing off workers’ avenue for justice.
But workers are fighting back, and seeing real results. There is more organizing happening on the ground than at any point in our lifetimes. Workers are organizing at manufacturing plants, in newsrooms, in technology, in hospitals, on college campuses, and construction sites. They’re changing the game with historic contracts in women’s sports. They’re organizing in “right-to-work” states in the South and are being led by women, communities of color, and young workers.
The results are in the numbers. Nearly half a million workers unionized in 2025 alone, and the number of workers in unions is at a 16-year high. Public-sector employees increased their unionization rates to 36.4% in 2025, and the number of private-sector workers covered by union contracts increased by close to a quarter million, including in industries such as health care, retail, construction, and education. Union representation among federal workers actually grew in the last year, reaching 31.1%, despite the Trump Administration stripping union rights from more than one million of those workers.
The recent spike in worker organizing coincides with a sharp rise in public approval of unions, and there are millions of nonunion workers in the United States who say they would join a union tomorrow if given the opportunity.
Still, we know that union membership remains well below the level needed to unlock the full potential of worker power and raise pay standards across the economy. Even as we make essential progress, we’re still at about one-third of that 1950s high. The reality is that organizing alone can’t fix a system stacked against us.
It’s clear to us that we must use this momentum to win key legislation that makes it easier for Americans to organize—and we have a roadmap in Congress to get there. We believe the Protecting the Right to Organize Act would restore worker protections eroded by legal loopholes and impose real penalties on companies that violate labor laws. Part of the legislation passed the House earlier this summer with bipartisan support. Another bill, the Public Service Freedom to Negotiate Act, would guarantee for the first time that every public-sector worker in the country has the right to bargain collectively.
Alongside these necessary labor law reforms, Congress can pursue bold new proposals, like requiring collective bargaining at companies where CEOs are paid at least 100 times more than typical workers, or guaranteeing newly unionized workers a cost-of-living raise.
These are big fights. But they are fights we can win. That means ensuring our elected leaders will stand with workers, not billionaires, and pass pro-worker legislation. It means continuing to organize, even when the bosses and billionaires try to stand in the way. Together, we can build a better economy for working people by strengthening workers’ rights to organize and bargain collectively. Because the research proves what workers have always known: It's better in a union.

====================================================================================================

Over $600 Million in Polymarket Election Trades Took Place After Races Ended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.
Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.
This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.
Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.
Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.
When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.
The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”
Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening.
Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option.
It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says.
Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform.
Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn't always wash trading,” says Sethi.
MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.
This type of behavior has been observed before in the cryptocurrency industry. “These are textbook examples on how market participants farm a potential airdrop,” says Andre Guettler, the director of Ulm University’s Institute of Strategic Management and Finance, who researches the structure of prediction markets.
When MSR Decode analyzed the Ethiopian election market, it found that it was highly unlikely that the trading volume could be attributed to sophisticated traders using algorithms to eke out profits. It analyzed over 38,000 “trade loops” that took place after the election (instances where individual wallets bought and sold to each other in quick succession) and found that over 98 percent resulted in neither side losing or gaining money. The median time that the accounts held onto the contracts they purchased before selling them again was nine seconds.
These types of unusual trading patterns are not a new phenomenon on Polymarket. Earlier this year, Barron’s reported that much of the activity on markets predicting the 2028 US presidential election centered on unlikely candidates such as Elon Musk and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of whom is eligible to run because they were born outside of the country.
Both Polymarket and its chief rival, Kalshi, have been publicly scrutinized for unusual market activity in recent months. Furor over suspicious activity on its recently launched perpetual futures market for cryptocurrency grew so intense on X that Kalshi published a blog post denying allegations of wash trading on it. (Sethi agrees with Kalshi that the allegations were unfounded. He argues that the unusual volume could instead be explained by Kalshi’s incentives for market makers, which create opportunities for other traders to profit from small price discrepancies.)
Polymarket recently raised an over $1 billion round of funding led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The company is now valued at an estimated $21 billion, and earlier this summer, it announced that its annualized revenue was now over $1 billion. Polymarket’s explosive growth is often measured in volume traded, since it’s a metric that can point to how active users are.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the United States, declined to comment on whether it is looking into these election trades. The CFTC previously investigated a number of suspected instances of market manipulation on Polymarket, including several exclusively reported by WIRED, but they usually involved potential insider trading rather than wash trading or other suspicious activity.
In the past, the agency has issued hefty fines for wash trading in other sectors. “It seems to me that the CFTC would want to know about weird activity in a very large market,” a former CFTC employee tells WIRED.

- MSI Defense Solutions says its Self-Loading Equipment Deck appeared on several partners’ displays at AUSA 2026, including General Dynamics Land Systems.
- The U.S. Army has asked industry for a self-loading deck air defense package for light infantry vehicles, targeting fielding in 2027 to 2029.
Mooresville, North Carolina-based MSI Defense Solutions says its Self-Loading Equipment Deck, a removable mission pallet that can carry weapons and sensors on and off vehicles, appeared on several partner companies’ displays at this week’s Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington, including one built by General Dynamics Land Systems.
In a series of LinkedIn posts during the show, MSI described the SLED as part of its Common Deck family, a modular base meant to let partners integrate mission systems faster across different vehicles. The company did not say which General Dynamics Land Systems capability was mounted on its deck, how many other partners used it at the show, or whether any of the configurations are under contract.
“Our SLED (Self-Loading Equipment Deck), part of the Common Deck family, provides a modular foundation for integrating mission systems across different platforms and requirements,” MSI Defense Solutions said.
The idea behind a self-loading deck is that a small crew can lift a complete weapon or sensor package off one vehicle and onto another, or onto the ground, without a forklift or crane. Partner company 3SL, which showed an air defense version called the EAGLS SLED at the AUSA Global Force symposium in Huntsville in March, said that design lets three or four soldiers swap mission payloads in the field.
In a March 2026 request for information for Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense Increment 4, the U.S. Army said it wants an air defense package for light infantry built on a self-loading equipment deck that can ride on vehicles such as the Infantry Squad Vehicle and the uncrewed Robotic Combat Vehicle. The service specified that the deck must keep working independently once removed and that the carrier vehicle must return to full functionality without it, with fielding targeted for 2027 to 2029.
MSI, which moved from motorsports engineering into defense work in 2008, already sells an air defense system that fits that requirement’s description. Its EAGLS package uses laser-guided 70 mm rockets fitted with BAE Systems’ APKWS guidance kits to shoot down drones, and the company says on its website that it has delivered six EAGLS systems and fielded APKWS-equipped platforms to UK special operations forces and Ukrainian marines.
During the same week, MSI said in a separate post that it held talks with representatives from Kosovo about how its modular platforms and weapons integration work could support that country’s emerging defense requirements, though it did not describe any specific proposal.

Can Europe step in as Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:56:31 UTC
17:56:31 KST

Can Europe step in as Ukraine struggles with Starlink and US satellite data?
- Ukraine faced Starlink and US warning gaps as Russian missile threats continued. Zelensky said partners gave no alert for a second night.
- Europe has no quick replacement for Starlink or US missile warning systems. Experts said OneWeb is not suited to frontline use and terminals would need replacing.
- Officials warned Europe is too dependent on American space power. The EU plans IRIS², but it is years away, so countries want their own capabilities.
AI generated
KYIV – As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives.
Ukrainian officials said on Oct 14 the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defence.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, for the second night running, Ukraine had received no warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed another souring of relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Trump said on Oct 13 that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, said the US government controlled that system’s speeds.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on the social media platform X, using the acronym for president of the United States.
Musk has been a close political ally of Trump.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelensky.
But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
“That is fairly unique and… what basically that can detect is the heat generated by missiles as they’re launched,” said Marc DeVore, an associate fellow at think tank Chatham House. “There is nothing equivalent in Europe.”
No simple Starlink swop for Ukraine, Europe
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Oct 14 following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
But Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, said Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to wartime use.
“Its current constellation remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” he said.
“Capacity and performance constraints, combined with the cost, weight, bulk and power consumption of its user terminals, limit its suitability for frontline applications.”
A spokesperson for Eutelsat told Reuters that the company continued to provide connectivity services in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit networks with its partners.
It declined to comment further “given the sensitive nature of the situation”.
Von der Ropp also said switching networks would require replacing thousands of terminals, as Starlink and Starshield terminals use proprietary technology and could not simply connect to OneWeb.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defence technology startup Buntar Aerospace, said the sudden interruption to Starshield services “highlights to almost every end user both in Ukraine and abroad you can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off”.
“You need to have some kind of sovereign capabilities,” he added, so that “you are not subject to somebody’s mood today”.
Fears of over-reliance on US defence technology have grown in Europe in recent years, as Trump has threatened to quit the NATO military alliance just as European leaders see Russia posing the greatest threat to the continent in decades.
European Defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a conference hosted by Politico in Brussels on Oct 14 that the continent was “quite dependent on American space capabilities”.
“The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities,” he added, mentioning the European Union’s planned satellite constellation IRIS² and urging European countries to work together.
But that project is years from becoming operational even if everything goes according to plan, causing frustration among European government officials. Germany is developing its own military satellite constellation. REUTERS
