Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:56:25 UTC
17:56:25 KST

Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show
- Russia has nearly finished a new jet-drone base in Rostov in six weeks, showing a rapid expansion of its attack power near Ukraine.
- Satellite images show the site could launch Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones, with eight launch platforms and a possible capacity of 100 drones in 24 hours.
- Experts say the faster drones are harder for Ukraine and NATO to stop, creating a strategic risk as Russia plans more winter attacks.
AI generated
LONDON – Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defence experts and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.
The site in what was an empty field in Russia’s south-western Rostov region on Aug 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Oct 14, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed.
The construction coincides with a surge in the use of Russian jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, which is struggling to intercept the faster weapons that can travel at speeds of up to 600km.
With the full-scale war well into its fifth year, Kyiv expects Russia to further escalate jet drone and missile attacks this winter.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, Russia’s newest types of jet-powered drone.
He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine.
“The speed of construction... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” Monnik said.
The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be “probably a matter of weeks before (it is) fully operational, if not earlier.”
A challenge for NATO
The construction of the facility coincides with worsening relations between Russia and the NATO military alliance.
European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyber attacks against them, while Russia warned in September it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave.
Monnik said the combination of industrial production of jet-powered drones, their increasing sophistication and the relative lack of comprehensive counter-drone defences in many NATO countries were a challenge for the West.
“This ability to rapidly field an ability to launch large-scale attacks using UAS (unmanned aerial systems) poses a strategic vulnerability for NATO countries,” he said.
Monnik said the facility may have the potential to fire 100 jet-powered drones or more in 24 hours, although Russia normally fires them in small numbers throughout the day.
It would also depend on factors like available supplies and objectives.
Rob Jordan, programme director at the London-based RUSI think-tank, said the concrete pads and two possible takeoff rails shown in the imagery looked consistent with launch tracks for Russian Geran drones.
“This level of construction in this short a time is impressive,” he said. “This shows the relative faith Russia is putting in its deep strike capability – possibly to the detriment of its conventional land forces.”
Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the facility and on its jet-powered drone programme more broadly.
Use of jet drones surges
Military analysts say Russia has shifted its drone production capabilities to jet-powered models as Ukraine has struggled to counter them.
Russia increased its use of jet-powered drones roughly six-fold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data reported by Reuters in September.
Kyiv and the surrounding region were targeted most heavily, the data showed.
The jet drones pose a problem because they are too fast for the interceptor drones designed by Ukraine to cheaply intercept their slower, piston-powered predecessors.
Kyiv is now scrambling to devise a solution.
Overhead imagery of the new facility taken on Aug 31 pictured a few vehicles in a field but no sign of construction.
Imagery taken the following morning showed that work had begun.
The site, which occupies an area of around 0.9sq km, lies about 3.5km from Russia’s Millerovo air base, home to the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
According to DroneSec, the new launch site likely sits within the air defence “bubble” provided by systems at the airbase, making Ukrainian attempts to target the new facility more difficult.
Of the eight launch platforms, two already had rails on them, a Reuters analysis showed.
Rails were being constructed on two other pads as well, while other construction work was visible from space over the course of three days this week. REUTERS

A United States federal judge temporarily blocked US President Donald Trump's administration from sanctioning two US-based human rights organizations on Tuesday for working with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in its investigations into alleged Israeli war crimes in the Gaza Strip.
In his order, US Judge Jesse M. Furman cited a 2025 case in which two law professors filed a lawsuit challenging Trump's executive order imposing sanctions on the ICC.
Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) sued the Trump administration in July over these ICC sanctions. At the time, they argued that the order "unconstitutionally restrict [s] Americans from seeking justice on Palestine at the ICC and working with human rights defenders designated solely for calling on the ICC to investigate Israeli and American nationals."
Furman said that DAWN and TAAG raised a similar challenge in their lawsuit against the two law professors, in which the court had decided that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny."
However, Furman rejected the plaintiffs' request to declare the 2025 executive order as "facially unconstitutional."
US State Department says ICC poses 'intolerable threat' to US sovereignty
A US State Department spokesperson told The Guardian that, while they could not comment on pending litigation, “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Omar Shakir, DAWN's executive director, celebrated the courtroom victory, saying that the court had "put the brakes" on the Trump administration's efforts to "shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.
"The court ruling makes clear that the law does not permit barring Americans from advocating for justice at the ICC or working with human rights defenders that this administration sanctioned solely for calling for justice for US and Israeli war crimes," Shakir added.
TAAG's Anna Marie Stenberg also responded to the court decision, saying that the judge had "affirmed important First Amendment protections," and that it was a "significant victory, but our work is far from over."
Trump administration sanctions ICC after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the ICC on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.

Iranian People's Fighters Front claims responsibility for six attacks
Attacks targeting members of the IRGC and other security forces in the province appear to have increased in recent weeks. The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported earlier this week that at least 94 people were killed and 33 wounded in 63 armed incidents across southeastern Iran between March 31 and October 10.
The People’s Fighters Front has claimed responsibility for only six of the incidents HRANA documented. The groups responsible for the remaining incidents remain unknown.
Security expert Roger Macmillan told The Jerusalem Post that anti-regime attacks have increased since the Sunni group Jaish al-Adl merged with the PFF. He said there had been significant anger toward the IRGC over its “systematic arrest and torture of their people, many of whom don’t even speak Farsi, and were forced into signing false documents, which have seen them convicted of alleged terrorist attacks, and then executed.”
He argued that, with the brutal repression of Iranians across the country, the assassinations will continue to worsen.
In one of the most notable incidents last week, Tasnim reported that Lieutenant-Colonel Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for cultural and social affairs of the Law Enforcement Command in the province, was killed in what the agency described as a “terrorist attack.”
Earlier this week, Haalvsh, an independent human rights organization and news outlet that documents human rights violations and security incidents in Sistan and Baluchestan, also reported that more than 20 members of the Fatemiyoun terrorist group were killed or wounded in an hours-long clash on Tuesday. The Iran-backed Shia group is composed primarily of Afghan Hazara refugees and migrants, and is both funded and trained by the IRGC.
Iranian regime seeking to project strength, public support for Basij
The attacks come as the regime seeks to project an image of strength, cohesion, and public support for the Basij. The Islamic Republic has released numerous images from its Janfada (self-sacrifice) training exercises, prominently featuring women training with guns and drones. Janfada spokesperson Sasan Zare claimed that more than 500,000 women registered within 100 minutes of registration opening for the “National Resistance” battalions, filling the first 1,000 units.
Despite the alleged masses who have registered for the self-sacrifice training, the Iran Human Rights Monitor has reported the regime is using violent criminals to fill its ranks, offering conditional release to those willing to suppress protests and signs of dissent.
Basing its report on testimonies received from inmates, their families, informed sources within prisons, and field reports from human rights groups, criminals convicted of general, violent, or drug offenses were offered repentance forms in August and September and granted bail after they registered with the Basij.
Although reports of personnel shortages in the Basij and IRGC predate the recent attacks, Macmillan suggested that financial desperation could drive people to enlist despite the risk of assassination.

Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:52:20 UTC
17:52:20 KST

Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?
Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.
There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Why are Saudi defenses struggling?
Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom’s first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.
Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.
A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.
A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis’ growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh’s airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.
The kingdom has faced similar problems before.
After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.
The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.
The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.
Saudi Arabia’s geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.
Israel’s much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.
Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain’s Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.
Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.
Which Israeli systems could help?
Israel’s air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.
Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.
Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom’s territory.
David’s Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.
Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.
Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.
Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.
Rafael’s mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.
Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia’s existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom’s command and radar networks.
Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.
The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.
Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.
Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.
Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.
How has Israel helped defend the UAE?
The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.
After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael’s SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.
The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.
Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.
On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.
The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.
Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee’s remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.
There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.
Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.
Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?
Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.
Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.
Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.
Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.
In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.
Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.
The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.
Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.
“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.
Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.
Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.
Germany’s purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington’s consent.
Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.
Would Israeli technology solve the problem?
Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.
Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom’s existing Patriot and THAAD systems.
Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.
Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.
For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.
A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

EXPLAINER - Argentina’s Milei faces fresh congressional battle over economic deregulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:51 UTC
17:40:51 KST

Argentina’s President Javier Milei faces a renewed showdown with Congress over his sweeping economic deregulation decree as opposition lawmakers seek to overturn the measure following a Supreme Court ruling that temporarily reinstated restrictions on foreign ownership of rural land.
The dispute centers on Decree of Necessity and Urgency 70/2023, known as DNU 70/2023, which Milei signed shortly after taking office in December 2023. The measure introduced extensive changes to Argentina’s legal and economic framework, including the repeal of a law restricting foreign ownership of rural land.
The latest judicial decision has complicated the parliamentary debate ahead of a special session called by opposition lawmakers for Thursday.
The governing party has scheduled a separate session for Oct. 21 as both sides pursue different approaches to land ownership rules and the broader decree.
Milei signed DNU 70/2023, titled “Bases for the Reconstruction of the Argentine Economy,” on Dec. 20, 2023. It was published in Argentina’s Official Gazette the following day.
The decree’s preamble describes Argentina as facing a severe economic and social crisis and argues that urgent structural reforms are needed. It identifies excessive regulation and state intervention as obstacles to economic activity and investment.
Article 2 states that the government will promote an economic system based on free decisions, competition, private property and the constitutional principles of the free movement of goods, services and labor.
The decree changes or repeals provisions across numerous sectors, including foreign trade, agriculture, labor relations, health care, housing rentals and commercial activity. The government presented it as part of a broader effort to reduce state intervention, deregulate the economy and encourage private investment.
One of its most controversial provisions is Article 154, which repeals Law 26,737, known as the Rural Land Law. Enacted in 2011, the law established limits on foreign ownership of rural property.
The government argued that these restrictions constrained property rights and investment in agriculture. Opponents questioned whether such a significant change should have been introduced through an emergency decree rather than ordinary legislation.
Argentina’s Constitution allows presidents to issue decrees of necessity and urgency under exceptional circumstances, subject to specific restrictions and congressional review.
The breadth of DNU 70/2023 has raised questions about the extent to which the executive can modify existing laws without ordinary legislative approval.
Argentina’s Rural Land Law established restrictions on foreign ownership to limit land concentration and protect national interests linked to territory and natural resources.
The law set a general ceiling of 15% for foreign ownership of rural land at the national, provincial and departmental levels.
It also stipulated that no single foreign nationality could account for more than 30% of the permitted foreign-owned share.
In addition, the legislation limited a single foreign owner to 1,000 hectares in Argentina’s core agricultural zone, or an equivalent area elsewhere, depending on the location. It also restricted foreign ownership of certain properties involving significant bodies of water and areas near international borders.
Supporters of the law argue that these safeguards protect Argentina’s territorial interests, agricultural resources and control over strategically important areas.
They also warn about land concentration and the potential consequences for local communities and access to natural resources.
The government and supporters of deregulation argue that removing the restrictions could attract foreign capital, facilitate agricultural investment and expand productive activity.
The debate therefore concerns not only who can purchase farmland but also how Argentina balances investment opportunities with safeguards involving land, water resources and border areas.
The issue had already become contentious during congressional discussions over a separate bill concerning private property.
According to Argentine fact-checking organization Chequeado, the government later proposed allowing foreign ownership of up to 25% of rural land at the provincial level rather than eliminating all restrictions.
The proposal retained a provincial ceiling while allowing greater room for foreign ownership within individual departments or municipalities.
The government ultimately withdrew the chapter concerning land restrictions after failing to secure sufficient support, highlighting the political difficulties of changing the rules through ordinary legislation.
The legal battle over the repeal took a new turn with two Supreme Court decisions on Sept. 29 and Oct. 9.
Although both concerned challenges to the repeal, they involved separate proceedings and different legal arguments.
On Sept. 29, the Supreme Court overturned an earlier ruling by the Federal Court of Appeals in La Plata that had declared the repeal unconstitutional. The case had been brought by the Center for Malvinas Islands War Veterans, known as CECIM.
The Supreme Court rejected the claim because it found that CECIM lacked the legal standing required to bring the case.
The ruling did not determine whether Milei could constitutionally repeal the Rural Land Law through an emergency decree.
The decision removed that particular judicial obstacle, leaving the repeal in effect at that stage.
The situation changed on Oct. 9, when the Supreme Court temporarily suspended the effects of Article 154 in a separate proceeding involving the environmental organization Arbol de Pie and other claimants, including former senator and Río Negro provincial legislator María Magdalena Odarda.
The claimants raised different legal arguments, including concerns related to environmental protection.
The court sent the case back to the Federal Court in Bariloche, where a judge must determine whether the claimants have legal standing and consider their request for precautionary relief.
In the meantime, the Supreme Court provisionally suspended the repeal provision to prevent potential irreparable harm while the proceedings continue. The measure temporarily restored the Rural Land Law’s restrictions but did not resolve whether repealing the law through DNU 70/2023 was constitutional.
The decision was not unanimous. Justice Carlos Rosenkrantz opposed the interim suspension, arguing that the Supreme Court lacked the authority to issue such a measure before the lower court had ruled on the request.
The distinction between the two rulings is central to the dispute. The September decision concerned the legal standing of one claimant, while the October ruling provided interim relief in a separate case. Neither constituted a final decision on the constitutionality of repealing the law through the decree.
Opposition lawmakers have called a special session of the Chamber of Deputies for Oct. 15 to seek rejection of DNU 70/2023. Their initiative extends beyond the Rural Land Law, targeting the entire decree and its changes across numerous sectors of Argentina’s economy.
The Senate rejected the decree in March 2024, but the Chamber of Deputies has not voted on it. A rejection by the lower house would complete the parliamentary process required to overturn the measure under Argentina’s current legal framework.
Under Law 26,122, Congress reviews decrees of necessity and urgency through a specific procedure.
The Permanent Bicameral Committee examines each decree and submits its conclusions to both chambers.
Lawmakers cannot amend individual articles through this review mechanism. Each chamber must accept or reject the decree as a whole. Its formal rejection by both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate results in its repeal while preserving rights acquired during its validity.
This creates a political dilemma for lawmakers who oppose the repeal of the Rural Land Law but support other provisions of DNU 70/2023. Rejecting the decree would also reverse its other reforms, making the vote a broader judgment on Milei’s economic program.
The opposition must secure sufficient support to open the session and then obtain the votes needed to reject the decree.
Negotiations with provincial and centrist blocs are particularly important, as some lawmakers may oppose the removal of foreign land ownership restrictions while remaining reluctant to reverse the government’s wider economic reforms.
The Supreme Court’s temporary suspension of Article 154 adds another consideration to those negotiations. However, the court has not ruled on the broader legal status of the decree or the scope of presidential emergency powers.
The governing party has called a separate session for Oct. 21, with proposals concerning private property and other policy issues on the agenda. The government can also seek changes to land ownership rules through ordinary legislation, subject to congressional debate and voting.
The confrontation highlights competing views on foreign investment, national control of rural land and the limits of presidential emergency powers.
For Milei’s government, deregulation is a central component of its economic program intended to reduce state intervention and encourage investment. Opponents argue that restrictions on foreign land ownership protect national interests, natural resources and strategically important territory.
The dispute also underscores the role of Argentina’s legislative and judicial branches in checking executive power. The Supreme Court’s interim measure has temporarily restored the land restrictions without settling the constitutional challenge, while Congress faces a separate decision on the decree as a whole.
The Oct. 15 and Oct. 21 sessions will provide the next opportunities for lawmakers to advance their competing strategies. Their outcomes remain uncertain as of Oct. 13.
Ultimately, the dispute will test the reach of Milei’s deregulation agenda and Congress’s ability to scrutinize presidential decrees. The future of the Rural Land Law will depend on the ongoing judicial proceedings and decisions by lawmakers.

The case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors: how prolonging the trial could help the accused avoid responsibility
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:40:25 EEST
17:40:25 KST

The case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors: how prolonging the trial could help the accused avoid responsibility
Kyiv • UNN
In the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, five consecutive court hearings have been postponed. Against the backdrop of systematic delays in considering the case, the risk of the statute of limitations expiring is growing. Lawyer Rostyslav Kravets explained how the court can counteract the delaying of proceedings and what consequences deliberate evasion could have for the accused.
The criminal case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors is once again on hold: the court was forced to postpone five hearings in a row. Each such postponement brings the case closer to the expiration of the statute of limitations, after which the defendants may avoid criminal liability. UNN looked into whether the court has mechanisms to counteract the delaying of proceedings.
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa continues hearing the criminal case against private Odrex clinic doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who are accused of improper performance of their professional duties while treating businessman Adnan Kivan at the clinic. However, instead of conducting a consistent examination of the evidence, the trial is being interrupted with increasing frequency by motions from the defense.
In the past two weeks alone, the court postponed five hearings in a row. Thus, the hearings scheduled for October 9 and 13 did not take place because of a motion by the lawyer for the accused, Maryna Bielotserkovska. Subsequently, the court postponed three hearings at once, scheduled for October 14, 15, and 16. This time, the reason was a motion by the accused, Vitalii Rusakov, who, according to UNN sources, is on sick leave.
The situation with the postponements became more acute back in September. At that time, the court scheduled 13 hearings, expecting to expedite consideration of the criminal case. However, only six took place. More than half did not take place because of motions from the defense.
Such delays may have serious legal consequences. The doctors are accused under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, which provides for up to two years of imprisonment. Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, the statute of limitations for such an offense is three years. Adnan Kivan died in October 2024, so in the absence of circumstances that suspend or interrupt the running of the limitation period, the issue of its expiration may arise as early as 2027. This means that, under certain conditions, the accused may be released from criminal liability. Even if the court finds the doctors guilty, the expiration of the limitation period may serve as grounds for releasing them from the sentence imposed.
Can the court stop the case from being delayed?
As lawyer Rostyslav Kravets explained in a comment to UNN , criminal procedural legislation provides mechanisms for responding to systematic failures by defense lawyers to appear. In particular, the court may initiate a disciplinary review of the lawyers’ actions and, where there are legal grounds, apply other procedural measures.
If we are talking about cases in which a lawyer systematically fails to appear at court hearings, the court has several mechanisms for responding. First, it may send a relevant referral to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar concerning the possible bringing of the lawyer to disciplinary liability. Second, where the grounds provided by law exist, the court may impose a monetary penalty on the lawyer. In addition, in cases stipulated by law, the court may appoint a defense lawyer through the system of free legal aid to participate in a specific procedural action. At the same time, such replacement must take into account the accused’s right to defense and must not create risks for his procedural interests
In the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors, presiding judge Viktor Chaplytskyi has already used one of these mechanisms. He found the reasons for the accused’s lawyers’ failures to appear unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. The commission must now assess whether the defense lawyers’ actions contain signs of a disciplinary offense.
At the same time, contacting the disciplinary commission in itself does not guarantee that subsequent hearings will take place without delays. The court must ensure a balance between the accused’s right to adequate defense and the need to hear the criminal case within a reasonable time.
Changing lawyers as another possible way to delay the proceedings
According to Rostyslav Kravets, the abuse of the right to change defense attorneys poses a particular danger. This concerns situations in which defendants may systematically engage new lawyers so that they can submit motions to adjourn hearings to review the case materials.
Another problem is the systematic replacement of defense attorneys by defendants. Such changes may lead to repeated motions requesting time to review the case materials, adjournments of hearings, and other procedural delays. As a result, court proceedings may last for years while the statutes of limitations expire
According to the lawyer, establishing the real reasons for the procedural actions of the defense is of fundamental importance in such situations.
In such cases, it is crucial to establish whether there were objective reasons for changing defense attorneys and adjourning hearings, or whether the relevant motions were submitted formally and systematically, despite the court having already expressed its position on them
The expiration of the statute of limitations is not an acquittal
At the same time, exemption from criminal liability due to the expiration of the statute of limitations does not mean that the defendants have been acquitted. Closing a case on this ground is not a rehabilitating decision and does not establish innocence.
If Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska are confident of their innocence and want to prove it in court, the law allows them to object to the dismissal of the case due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. In that case, the trial must continue under the general procedure. This will give the defendants an opportunity to defend their names and professional reputations and obtain a final court decision concerning the charges brought against them.
Reminder
According to the investigation, the improper performance of professional duties by medical personnel while treating businessman Adnan Kivan could have led to postoperative complications and sepsis, which, against the backdrop of his oncological illness, could have caused his death. The court must provide the final assessment of the evidence and the question of their culpability.

Taiwan chip equipment suppliers eye gains as ASML weighs 2028 expansion

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese semiconductor equipment suppliers could benefit from growing industry demand as Dutch firm ASML considers expanding production capacity in 2028, CTEE reported Thursday.
ASML develops and manufactures photolithography machines, which chipmakers use to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. CEO Christophe Fouquet said customers had raised their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts.
Some customers are also interested in placing orders for 2029 and beyond, pointing to sustained demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Taiwanese suppliers including Foxsemicon Integrated Technology Inc., Gudeng Precision Industrial Co., and Marketech International Corp. could benefit from the broader industry outlook.
Foxsemicon specializes in precision components, equipment module assembly, and system integration. Its contract manufacturing business, which accounts for about 87% of total revenue, is best known for producing etching and thin-film deposition equipment, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Strong industry demand has extended Foxsemicon’s order visibility from three to six months to six to nine months. Foxsemicon has also entered the optical inspection equipment market this year, with the product line becoming the fastest-growing segment of its contract manufacturing business.
Gudeng specializes in photomask and carrier solutions used to protect, transport, and store materials during front-end semiconductor manufacturing. Its extreme ultraviolet (EUV) pods protect 6-inch photomasks as they move between processing stations, according to Gudeng and DigiTimes.
Photomasks transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. As chipmakers adopt EUV lithography to manufacture 2-nanometer and more advanced chips, demand for protective pods and related handling and storage equipment is expected to grow.
Marketech provides semiconductor equipment agency services, system integration, and fab engineering services. Its major engineering projects include TSMC facilities in Taiwan and the US, with order visibility extending through 2028, according to FTV.
Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting said Marketech’s outstanding orders totaled NT$134.7 billion (US$4.2 billion) as of August, a record high. About 80% came from fab engineering projects, while equipment contract manufacturing and agency services accounted for the remaining 20%, supporting further revenue growth over the next two years.
Semiconductor equipment plays a critical role in the development of smart devices, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence. From wafer fabrication to final packaging, these machines perform the precise operations needed to manufacture chips, according to Sinotrade.
Front-end equipment is used to form nanoscale transistors on silicon wafers and build multiple layers of interconnects that carry electrical signals. Key tools include lithography systems and thin-film deposition equipment, which must operate reliably under demanding conditions, including high temperatures and vacuum environments, to maintain high manufacturing yields.
Back-end equipment focuses on wafer dicing, chip bonding, packaging, and testing. Automated systems, including probe cards and burn-in testers, help identify defects and verify that chips operate reliably.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tropical Depression TD33 strengthened into Typhoon Champi at 2 p.m. Thursday east of Guam and was moving west-northwest, according to the Central Weather Administration (CWA).
CWA forecaster Hsieh Pei-yun (謝佩芸) said the storm was still more than 4,200 kilometers from Taiwan. It was expected to remain far away even five days later, and forecasters needed more time to determine whether it could approach Taiwan’s coast, UDN reported.
Meteorologist Wu Der-rong (吳德榮) said the storm had the potential to strengthen into a severe typhoon. European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts model simulations indicated a track mainly over water south of Japan, followed by a pronounced turn to the northeast. Other models showed widely divergent paths, highlighting considerable uncertainty.
WeatherRisk meteorologist Wu Sheng-yu (吳聖宇) forecast that Champi would generally move northwest along the edge of a high-pressure system while gradually strengthening and expanding. He said the storm could reach severe typhoon strength by Monday or Tuesday, with its radius potentially growing to 280 kilometers or more, per UDN.
Wu said the typhoon could continue moving northwest toward waters southeast of Taiwan before slowing and turning north as a Pacific high-pressure system retreats. The storm could then pass near the Ryukyu Islands before continuing toward Japan, although its turning point and distance from Taiwan remain uncertain.
Wu assessed the likelihood of a direct hit on Taiwan as low. However, if the storm turns north closer to Taiwan, its outer circulation could affect weather and sea conditions around the island from next Thursday through Saturday.
People planning outdoor activities or travel over the long holiday weekend should monitor weather updates and take precautions, he said.

Trump Says Leakers ‘Should Be Shot’ and Rails Against Media at Rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:40:04 UTC
17:40:04 KST

President Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that people who leak sensitive information about the government to the media “should be shot,” calling them the “scum of the earth.”
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said Wednesday during a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump’s remark came as he described a planned raid on Iran that he said had to be delayed after somebody “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to Operation Midnight Hammer in June last year, when the U.S., in a surprise attack, struck three of Iran’s most critical nuclear sites as Tehran was in a 12-day war with Israel.
In the wake of the June attack, a leaked Defense Intelligence Agency preliminary report found that Iran’s nuclear sites had not been as damaged as the Trump Administration first claimed them to be and that Iran could still enrich uranium. Reports also said Iran may have also moved enriched material from the facilities before the attack.
“Somebody leaked—some sleazebag,” the President said. “They ought to go to jail and be shot. For the rest of their life, They should be in jail. But they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in the New York Times, CNN.”
Moments later, Trump pointed to the journalists covering his rally and said they were “almost as bad” as leakers. “They leak false information,” the President said. “That makes them a leaker, right?”
Trump’s long-held view that leakers are bad—most of the time
Leakers have incensed Trump even before he was President. In a 2010 clip previewing the radio show of Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade, Trump assailed WikiLeaks, which, at the time, had just released hundreds of thousands of classified U.S. military and diplomatic documents provided by Army private Chelsea Manning. “I think it’s disgraceful,” he told Kilmeade. “I think there should be like death penalty or something.”
As a civilian flirting with the U.S.’s top job, he frequently lashed out at former National Security Agency intelligence contractor Edward Snowden on social media and in public remarks. Snowden’s leaks in 2013 revealed NSA programs that sparked a global debate about government surveillance. Trump, in reaction to the leaks, said that he was a “spy” who “should be executed.”
As President, when the New York Times reported in 2017 that his campaign had repeated contacts with senior Russian intelligence officials in the year before the 2016 presidential election, Trump took to then-Twitter to lament how “leaking, and even illegal classified leaking, has been a big problem in Washington for years” and raged that such leakers “will be caught.”
When a whistleblower came forward in 2019 with a complaint alleging that Trump was "using the power of his office to solicit interference from a foreign country" in the 2020 U.S. election, Trump told the staff of the U.S. mission to the U.N. that he wanted to know who gave the whistleblower information. “That’s close to a spy,” he said. “You know what we used to do in the old days when we were smart, right, with spies and treason, right? We used to handle them a little differently than we do now.”
But Trump has welcomed leaks that benefit him politically. Days before the 2016 presidential election, at a rally in Wilmington, Ohio, he celebrated how WikiLeaks released private emails from John Podesta, the campaign chair of his Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton, as well as emails from the Democratic National Committee. “Boy, I love reading those WikiLeaks!” Trump said. He also mused about Russia having hacked into Clinton’s email, and urged them to publish what they may have found. Trump even said that he could be a fan of Snowden if he released former President Barack Obama’s birth records at a time when conspiracy theories largely fanned by Trump hounded the Democratic former President.
Trump Administration tries to crack down on leaks
The second Trump Administration has since stepped up to limit leaks to the press. When reports of the U.S.’s dwindling ammunition stockpiles amid the war with Iran emerged, the Pentagon subjected dozens of civilian employees and military officers to polygraph tests to identify the source of the leak. Trump had called for the leakers to face long-term jail sentences.
Journalists from the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post received subpoenas after reporting on national security issues. But the news organizations pushed back against those summons, and the Justice Department withdrew them. In January, the FBI raided a Post reporter’s home, as part of an investigation into a government contractor accused of mishandling sensitive national security information.
The Justice Department has also charged alleged leakers: in April, the department announced it arrested a former Army employee, alleging that she transmitted classified national defense information to unauthorized recipients, including a journalist.
The Defense Department also threatened to withhold Pentagon access to journalists unless they signed an agreement not to publish unauthorized material. Much of the Pentagon press corps declined, and a federal judge sided with the press in March, striking several parts of the department’s press access policy.
Trump has wanted others “shot” too
It’s also not the first time that Trump has floated having certain people shot .
Three years ago, at a California lunch with Republicans, Trump said he was in favor of shooting store robbers and looters, painting himself as tough on crime before the 2024 elections. “They actually go and take everything out of the store, and then you see these guys selling stuff five miles away or selling it from behind cars. It's a horrible thing. When the police are allowed to do their job—and that means, in some cases, shoot them—this will stop immediately.”
The President has also previously pitched shooting migrants to keep them from entering the country. According to the book Border Wars: Inside Trump's Assault on Immigration, by New York Times reporters Michael D. Shear and Julie Hirschfeld Davis, Trump in March 2019 detailed extreme methods to keep them out, privately suggesting to aides that soldiers shoot migrants who cross the border in the legs. But he was told it would not be allowed. Trump addressed the allegations on social media, saying: “I may be tough on Border Security, but not that tough.”
He’s also suggested doing the same to protesters: during the George Floyd protests in the spring of 2020, Trump was reportedly enraged, and, according to his first-term Defense Secretary Mark Esper, the President also considered ordering the military to shoot the racial justice protesters in the legs.
Last week, the President approved what would be the U.S. Army’s first execution of a soldier via firing squad since World War II, and has even shown enthusiasm for livestreaming it. Trump, however, has since changed his tune, amid a chorus of negative feedback.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday. “‘Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

‘Our works are next to each other’: Art bridges Gaza and West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:37:41 UTC
17:37:41 KST

‘Our works are next to each other’: Art bridges Gaza and West Bank
Young Palestinian artists in Gaza and the occupied West Bank bring their work together in simultaneous exhibitions, despite Israeli restrictions that keep them apart.
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – Artists arrived with family and friends at the Bethlehem Peace Center, where a live feed connected them to a small gathering at an artist’s studio in Bureij refugee camp, in the central Gaza Strip.
The two exhibitions marked the opening of Anamel Falasteen, the first competition organised by Falasteen Collective, a cultural initiative launched in 2025 by Palestinian artists, filmmakers, designers and others working in arts and culture. The three-day twin exhibitions, held earlier this week, brought together young Palestinian artists whose work and opportunities to meet are separated by Israeli movement restrictions.
“In the competition, we have Palestinian artists from Jerusalem, historic Palestine, the Gaza Strip and the West Bank,” said Osama Nazzal, one of the judges, speaking in Bethlehem. “I don’t like these divisions. I want to say all of Palestine.”
From his studio at Gallery Paleta in Gaza’s Bureij refugee camp, amid Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave, painter and juror Ghanem Al Den sent greetings on the live feed.
“Greetings and peace from soul to soul, from Gaza to our sister Palestinian cities across this beloved homeland,” he said.
“In this competition, many things that were lost came together. The most important thing is hope.”
After the speeches, visitors had the opportunity to take a closer look at the paintings, photographs and drawings that covered the walls. Visitors moved between them, stopping to look closer, point and talk about what they saw.
“Artists decided to come from Hebron, from Ramallah, from Jerusalem, from Jaffa, from Nablus, despite the risk,” said Mohamed Abusrour, one of the founding members of Falasteen Collective.
“They have a voice, they want to contribute, and they want to show the world that we still exist.”
Not all the works on display in Bethlehem were originals. Because of the blockade and movement restrictions, the organisers said there was no way to transport original artworks out of Gaza. Instead, they printed reproductions of the Gaza submissions and hung them alongside original pieces.
For one Bethlehem visitor, the curation was what stood out. She assumed some works exploring similar themes were by the same artist. They turned out to be by different artists, some in Gaza and others in the West Bank.
“I sat a bit longer with some paintings, and that brought tears to my eyes,” she said. “The livestream with the presence of everyone’s paintings was a portal to bringing everyone’s essence together.”
Young artists document loss and everyday life
The works on display reflected different ways of documenting Palestinian life, from the loss of family and home in Gaza to the traditions and everyday experiences artists want to preserve.
Abusrour said the idea for the competition came from listening to artist friends describe how they could not participate or express themselves freely. He said the aim was to give young Palestinians a platform to show their work at home and abroad “without any restriction”.
The competition was open to artists aged 15 to 30. About 170 applied, nearly 60 percent from Gaza, according to the organisers. A jury split between the West Bank and Gaza selected 120 works across three tracks: memory and place, land and return, and everyday heritage.
The jury met daily by video, working through power and internet cuts in Gaza.
“Despite the lack of resources, they decided to take part, and when they decided to take part, they decided to take part with strength,” Abusrour said of the artists in Gaza.
Among the works shown in Gaza was The Vine Bears Witness, by Arwa Mukhaimer, a 20-year-old university student. It shows the entrance to her family’s home, shaded by a grapevine. It was there, on March 30, 2024, that she received news of her father’s death. He had been unable to get medical treatment during Israel’s war on Gaza, she said. Five months later, she said, the house was destroyed.
“This painting is a memorial to what we lost, a double loss, of the father and of the place,” she told Al Jazeera.
Two days before he died, he told her: “My darling, may God be pleased with you.” She wrote those words into the painting.
When she was displaced as a result of the war, she said, “The first thing I thought about was my tools.” Art supplies are hard to find in Gaza, she said, and some materials never enter the Strip.
The challenges facing artists extend beyond access to materials. Gaza’s main art spaces, including the Eltiqa and Shababeek galleries, have been destroyed as a result of Israeli attacks in Gaza.
Mukhaimer said her painting “has hope and joy in it, but its meaning is painful and moving”.
In Bethlehem, Hanan Barghouthi, 24, a visual artist from Ramallah, also chose to paint joy, but from a different place. Her painting of a Palestinian wedding is filled with bright colours, traditional symbols, and movement.
“All the art has become about people expressing sadness, so I want to reflect happiness, because I like to be happy,” she said.
Movement restrictions divide Gaza and the West Bank
Bringing the two exhibitions together required organisers to work around the restrictions that keep Palestinians in the two territories apart. Artists in Gaza and the West Bank live under different conditions of Israeli occupation, but both face barriers to meeting, collaborating and exhibiting together.
Israel has imposed a land, sea and air blockade on the Gaza Strip since June 2007. In the occupied West Bank, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented 925 obstacles restricting the movement of 3.4 million Palestinians, including in East Jerusalem, as of December 2025.
That separation is not accidental, said Rehab Nazzal, an artist and educator on the competition’s advisory committee.
“It’s a creation of the settler colonial project,” she said. “By suffocating the Palestinians with all the restrictions of movement, it intends to push the Palestinians out.”
Abusrour said spaces like the exhibition give young Palestinians a reason to stay and continue creating.
“You cannot live in a place, and be called steadfast, without having a reason to live as well,” he said.
Watching the Gaza artists on screen, Barghouthi said she felt “very sad” and asked herself, “Where are we and where are they?”
“I felt we were close to them, but at the same time far away,” she said. “But emotionally, I felt they were next to us, because our works are next to each other.”

Flemish hops receive recognition to encourage breweries to use local hops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:36:56 UTC
17:36:56 KST

Hops and hop shoots from Asse and the surrounding area have now been recognised as a Flemish regional product. The Flemish Centre for Agricultural and Fisheries Marketing (VLAM) made the award celebrating the local hop growing industry. Hops are used for many purposes but above all to make beer, and their cultivation in the region dates back to the 15th century.
Hops are also grown in Asse, but also in Affligem, Opwijk, Dilbeek, Steenhuffel, Gooik and Aalst. “Hops have a long history in our region,” says Joris Vanderveken, chair of the local hop association. “For hundreds of years, we were the hop storehouse of Europe.”
That story dates back to the 15th century. “That was when the monks at Affligem Abbey began laying out hop gardens. At first, hops were used as a medicinal herb, but people soon realised that they were also very useful for preserving beer for longer. What’s more, it had a pleasant aroma and gave the beer a lovely head,” says Joris.
Foreign competition
Today, hop cultivation has lost much of its importance. After several successful centuries, 100 years ago there were only two regions in Flanders where hops were still grown: Asse-Aalst and the area around Poperinge in West Flanders.
“Due to competition from abroad, hop cultivation here declined, but about ten years ago, the local hop association replanted several old hop varieties in a number of hop fields in the region. We now have 10 hectares of hops and hop shoots once again. We harvest the shoots in the spring for restaurants, and in September there are the hop cones, which go to the breweries.”
Breweries
Joris hopes that recognition as a regional product will encourage breweries in the region to work with local hops. “We’re already working with Affligem Brewery, Grimbergen Brewery, local breweries from Dilbeek and Asse, and a few breweries from Aalst. Things are already picking up nicely, and we think this recognition could give us a further boost to our own hopes.
“What’s more, the hop fields are a lovely feature of the landscape for cyclists and ramblers. There’s also a fascinating heritage story behind them. This is a product that cannot simply be replaced by something from abroad,” Joris concludes.

- North Korea said it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Oct. 14, without Kim Jong Un attending.
- South Korean experts believe the missiles came from Hero Kim Kun Ok, marking the submarine’s first public missile launch since 2023.
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the Korean Peninsula on Oct. 14, state media said, in what South Korean analysts believe was the first missile launch from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, the submarine Pyongyang unveiled three years ago as its first “tactical nuclear attack submarine.”
The Korean Central News Agency reported on Oct. 15 that the country’s Missile Administration carried out the launches. It did not give flight times, distances or missile names, but released photographs of a submarine and of missiles climbing away on trails of flame. Based on those images, South Korean experts concluded the launch platform was the 3,000-ton-class Hero Kim Kun Ok.
“The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions,” KCNA said.
Kim Jong Un did not attend. Senior Workers’ Party official Kim Jong Sik and Missile Administration chief Jang Chang Ha oversaw the launches together with navy underwater weapons engineers, KCNA said, adding that the test had no adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launches on Wednesday but said the next day that it had tracked the missiles from before launch through the end of their flights, using assets it declined to identify because of confidentiality arrangements with the United States. A JCS spokesperson said one missile was fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube, Yonhap reported.
North Korea launched Hero Kim Kun Ok, hull number 841, on Sept. 6, 2023, with Kim Jong Un saying at the ceremony that arming the navy with nuclear weapons could not be delayed further. Despite its label, the boat is a diesel-electric submarine rebuilt from an old Soviet-designed Romeo-class hull; the “nuclear” designation refers to the nuclear-capable missiles it is meant to carry. Until this week, the submarine had not been publicly seen firing a weapon.
Some South Korean analysts told Korea JoongAng Daily that the two weapons may have been a longer-range Hwasal-2 and a shorter-range Pulhwasal-3-31, a missile with a reported range of up to 2,000 km (1,240 miles) that North Korea says can carry its Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead. At that range, the missile could reach all of South Korea and U.S. military bases in Japan. One analyst quoted by the newspaper said firing two missile types with different speeds and approach paths at staggered times would make them harder for air defenses to intercept.
Cruise missiles fly low, often around 100 meters (330 feet) above the surface, which makes them harder to spot on radar than ballistic missiles. Unlike ballistic missile launches, cruise missile tests are not banned under United Nations Security Council sanctions on North Korea.
The previous submarine-launched cruise missile test North Korea reported came in January 2024, when Pulhwasal-3-31 missiles were fired from the smaller 2,000-ton-class experimental submarine 8.24 Yongung with Kim Jong Un watching. Earlier this week, North Korea also fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the same sea.

School roof collapses in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 33 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:30:41 UTC
17:30:41 KST

School roof collapses in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 35 people
At least 34 students and a teacher killed in incident at Al-Khair Education Centre, a private school in Peshawar.
The roof of a school in northwestern Pakistan has collapsed, killing at least 34 students and a teacher and injuring more than 45 others, authorities and rescue officials said.
The incident happened on Thursday at Al-Khair Education Centre, a private school in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
Mohammad Asim, spokesman for Lady Reading Hospital, where many victims were transported, said the fatalities include 12 girls and a female teacher. He added that some of the injured were in critical condition.
Most of the children killed or injured were between six and 12 years old, and the oldest was 14, Asim said. The hospital has declared an emergency as medical staff treat the wounded.
At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department.
“The school was very poorly built with just steel girders, mud bricks, and in some cases, wooden beams to hold the three-storey structure,” said Al Jazeera’s Kamal Hyder, reporting from Islamabad.
Television footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to waiting ambulances as residents crowded the narrow alley where the school stood.
A higher-floor roof collapsed onto classrooms below, crumpling two storeys of the building, a rescue official said.
Hours after the collapse, rescue officials said everyone trapped under the rubble had been recovered. An emergency services spokesperson, Bilal Faizi, said that nearly 100 rescuers helped in the operation, including parents who assisted the crew.
He credited the rapid evacuation with saving at least 40 lives. More than a dozen children suffered minor injuries, he said.
Peshawar’s Police Chief Saeed Ahmed said that the owner of the school has been arrested. He said the building was structurally weak.
However, following his arrest, the owner, Mohammad Khan, blamed this week’s rains for weakening one of the roofs, according to police, who said the investigation was still under way.
Al Jazeera’s Hyder said that the incident raised several concerns, as there had been similar cases in the past.
“In June, there was an incident in the city of Lahore, in the provincial capital of Punjab, which claimed 14 lives,” he said. “So there are questions as to why the government is not enforcing those building codes and rules”.
The provincial government said a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse of the three-storey building.
In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements.
“The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow,” Zardari said.

US reportedly weighs dropping 'Mother of All Bombs' on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

The U.S. is considering using its largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran if President Donald Trump revives the dormant war, CNN reported Thursday.
The military plans to use the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, nicknamed the "Mother Of All Bombs," to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, the news outlet reported, quoting officials familiar with the matter.
Trump seeks to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November midterm elections, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and resulting fuel and other price increases are hurting his Republican Party.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, which erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have stalled since the summer.
But officials doubt the bomb's efficacy if deployed, particularly its ability to destroy suspected underground nuclear sites in the Islamic republic.
"The MOAB is a massive information operations weapon that is effective for large-area clearance but not much else," a source familiar with the plans told CNN.
"It is not designed as a deep penetration warhead."
The U.S. and Israel said the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal Tehran has long denied pursuing.
Concerns also exist about potential civilian casualties from such a large weapon.
Washington has in recent weeks dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
In 2017, the U.S. military in Afghanistan dropped the MOAB to target Daesh hideouts in a complex of tunnels and bunkers, killing more than 90 terrorists.

South Korea tests vehicle-mounted laser against drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:28:02 UTC
17:28:02 KST

- Hanwha Systems said its Cheongwang laser and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser destroyed all three target drones during a South Korean Army exercise.
- South Korea began fielding Cheongwang in December 2024, and Hanwha puts the cost of each laser shot at about $1.50.
South Korea’s Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser shot down all three target drones flown against them during a South Korean Army exercise on Oct. 14, manufacturer Hanwha Systems said.
The demonstration took place during the Army TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise hosted by Republic of Korea Army headquarters, in front of about 500 attendees including the army chief of staff, military officials, academics and industry representatives. Hanwha did not say how far away the drones were, what types were used, how long each engagement took, or how the three targets were divided between the two lasers.
Cheongwang, which means “light of the sky,” is the official name of the Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I, developed by Hanwha Systems with South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development. Instead of firing missiles or shells, the system focuses a high-energy beam on a drone until its structure or electronics fail, and it keeps firing as long as it has electrical power. Hanwha puts the cost at about $1.50 per shot, in line with the roughly 2,000 won figure South Korea’s arms procurement agency has used since 2024.
South Korea began fielding Block-I in December 2024 and calls it the first operationally deployed laser weapon in the world. About five units have since been installed at major state facilities, including the Ministry of National Defense building in Seoul, and the system is rated in the 20-kilowatt class, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. The same report said engineers have since built a domestic laser oscillator, the core component that generates the beam, to replace a German-made part.
The program grew out of a December 2022 incident in which five North Korean drones crossed into South Korean airspace, one of them reaching the northern edge of Seoul, and fighter jets and attack helicopters failed to shoot any of them down. South Korea started developing the laser in 2019 with a budget of 87.1 billion won, and officials have kept its engagement range classified. The procurement agency has also acknowledged that Block-I struggles in rain and fog, a common limit for laser weapons, and plans a more powerful Block-II.
Hanwha said Cheongwang also destroyed four drones and two larger unmanned aircraft in a row on Sept. 16 at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition organized by South Korea’s defense ministry.
“Laser weapons are core assets that will fundamentally change the game of air defense,” said Joohun Shin, head of the Laser Systems Business Center at Hanwha Systems.
Hanwha is developing a 50-kilowatt laser armored vehicle with its own money, aimed at export customers, and displayed it at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which opened Sept. 8. The company has not named any foreign buyer, and it did not provide specifications for the 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser used in the Oct. 14 demonstration or say whether the South Korean Army plans to buy it.

Norway Sends $78.5 Million to Keep Ukraine’s Public Salaries Paid
Norway will allocate about $78 million (750 million kroner) in additional economic assistance to support Ukraine.
The measure was confirmed by Norwegian Minister of International Development Åsmund Aukrust in an interview with VG on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the minister, the funds will help finance the salaries of public sector workers, social payments, and infrastructure restoration.
The funding will be directed to the World Bank’s SPUR 2 support program for Ukraine. The Norwegian contribution will allow an increase in the volume of credit funds available to Ukraine.
The mechanism provides that Norway supplies initial funding, while the World Bank uses its lending capacity to raise funds on financial markets, which are subsequently provided to Ukraine as loans.
“The war is fought on the front line, but it is also fought every day—by ensuring the functioning of society, guaranteeing that children can go to school, and that nurses treating the wounded receive their salary,” Aukrust said.
In late September, Norway pledged nearly $12 million to help trace and return deported Ukrainian children, unlawfully detained civilians, and prisoners of war.
The funding was directed through UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross to support tracing, rehabilitation, and reintegration efforts.
