Backlash in Kashmir over proposal for uniform Friday sermons across mosques
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:21:36 UTC
16:21:36 KST

Backlash in Kashmir over proposal for uniform Friday sermons across mosques
Political and religious critics accuse India’s Modi government of curbing Kashmir’s freedom of religion and expression.
A proposed move by the Waqf Board in Indian-administered Kashmir to introduce uniform Friday sermons at mosques across the region has drawn backlash from politicians and religious leaders, who have accused the government of trying to assert control over Muslim religious spaces.
The Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board is headed by Darakshan Andrabi, a local leader associated with the Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, whose government stripped the region of its previous semi-autonomous status in 2019. Jammu and Kashmir was also partitioned into two federally governed territories, instead of functioning as a full-fledged state as it used to.
The board, which oversees Muslim religious endowments as mandated by Islamic laws, announced the controversial move last weekend, prompting a political controversy as the region’s top Muslim scholars slammed the proposal as “irresponsible interference into the religious affairs of Kashmiri Muslims”.
While defending the imposition of the uniform sermons, Andrabi told a leading Indian newspaper that a proposed committee formed under the board’s auspices “will be solely responsible for identifying the issue regarding the uniform sermon … [This step] is necessary to deal with issues in the [region], especially social evils, including drug abuse.”
Andrabi told the media that religious scholars will approve Friday sermons with no role for any government official in the decision.
‘Brushed aside our concerns’
On Sunday, the Waqf Board had summoned about 1500 top scholars and preachers from the Kashmir region. While some leaders were present at the venue, others from remote areas attended the meeting virtually.
A scholar from the mountainous Rajouri district, some 180km (110 miles) from the region’s biggest city of Srinagar, who had attended the meeting online, told Al Jazeera that Andrabi had passed instructions stating that only a pre-approved sermon drafted by a committee of senior-most scholars would be uniformly recited at the mosque pulpits on Fridays.
He said they were not told exactly who would be part of this committee.
“When we objected, saying that we won’t adhere to the directives if the sermon was found to be violative of Islamic teachings, she brushed aside our concerns and didn’t let us speak,” the scholar said on condition of anonymity as he feared reprisals by the authorities. “She [Andrabi] said that their decision was final as it had been four years in the making.”
A disputed region claimed by India and Pakistan, Kashmir has been at the centre of political turmoil for four decades. Years of peaceful demands for a referendum, to determine which country the Kashmiris would choose, transformed into an armed uprising against Indian rule in 1989 in response to allegations of election fixing.
In 2019, India scrapped the semi-autonomous status of Kashmir, imposing direct federal rule. The elections did not happen until 2024, when the local government was re-elected, albeit with a restricted mandate. De facto authority still rests with the New Delhi-appointed administrator.
The special conditions afforded under the erstwhile status had protected land and residency-related privileges while allowing Kashmiris to make their own laws.
One consequence of the 2019 decision was that Indigenous legal arrangements that governed the management of waqf, the charitable bequests that Muslims commit for the larger communal welfare, were replaced by those prevailing across India.
‘Trying to undermine religious freedom’
The new system gave broad powers to the federally controlled bureaucracy in the management of local religious boards such as waqf.
Since then, the Waqf Board has been accused multiple times by the local Kashmiri leaders of trying to undermine their religious freedoms or interfering with how the traditional religious practices have continued for generations.
“Centralised khutba or sermons used to take place in the name of a sultan or khalifa (Islamic caliph) during the medieval times. But that had sanctity because Kashmir was [then] an Islamic state. Today, we are supposed to be living in a secular state,” Nayeem Akhtar, a senior politician who served as Kashmir’s education minister during the previous elected government, when its special status was still operational, told Al Jazeera.
“As long as he has an audience, every cleric has freedom to speak about any topic of his choice. This freedom is enshrined in the very fundamentals of law,” he added.
Akhtar said the new instructions were coming from an office bearer associated with the BJP, which is why the latest move had provoked furious responses. “The board’s job is just managerial. It is exceeding its remit by trying to preach or guide the clerics on how they must do their job. Can a Muslim political party in India ever dictate how a Hindu pujari must conduct prayers or how a Christian pastor must deliver a sermon on Sunday?”
On Tuesday, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, the region’s top Muslim religious leader, cautioned that such a move would amount to “direct interference”.
The Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulema, a joint body of several religious organisations that he leads, said “determining sermon content was the responsibility of Islamic scholars and not of an administrative body.”
The condemnation was also shared by Omar Abdullah, the region’s elected head and member of the National Conference party that supports accession to India, albeit with the autonomous powers that New Delhi nullified seven years ago.
Following the backlash, the Waqf Board head Andrabi retracted her statement and said it had been left to the discretion of “independent scholars, preachers (and) sermonists” to talk about social issues such as rising suicides, mental trauma, substance abuse and more.
‘Exerting control on religious institutions’
This is not the first time that the BJP-led administration has been accused of trying to exert control over local religious institutions.
Earlier in January, Kashmiri Muslim scholars accused the government of discriminatory practices after the police distributed a four-page form titled “profiling of mosques” which sought intrusive details about the imams, muezzins and khatibs (preachers) of the mosques across the disputed region, including their biometric information.
For years, Muslim groups in the region have faced various restrictions on prayer, with Srinagar’s 600-year-old Jamia Masjid often being shut for important religious events such as Eid prayers or Laylat-al-Qadr, the most venerated night of the Islamic calendar, which falls in the month of Ramadan.
The administration argues these restrictions are imposed to ensure peace, but religious leaders insist that such prohibitory measures form a “systematic assault on the religious identity, dignity, and fundamental rights” of Kashmiri Muslims.
Farooq, the chief scholar, himself has been frequently subjected to such restrictions on his mobility, preventing him from giving Friday sermons on occasions when he is expected to speak on matters such as Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Previously, the Waqf Board has also sought to prohibit the practice of distributing yellow rice inside the compound of the major shrines in the region, a centuries-old tradition tied to the Sufi missionary councils that promoted Islam in Kashmir.
Religion has been a factor of political mobilisation
In 2022, the board also banned the age-old practice of collecting voluntary nazr-o-niyaz donations offered by devotees to the spiritual peers, mujawirs (attendants of a shrine) and khadims (caregivers). It cited the newly applicable federal laws as a reason for taking direct control over all financial collections and installing new donation boxes where all offerings went to the board.
Noor Ahmad Baba, a veteran Kashmiri political scientist and historian, said religion had always been a factor for political mobilisation in Kashmir, which is why attempts to manipulate or change the traditional religious arrangements evoke political outrage.
“The kind of political dispensation that we have and the kind of politics it has had with regard to Muslims is what makes the whole exercise suspicious,” Baba told Al Jazeera, referring to the BJP. “If the standardisation had come, for instance, from clerics with public acceptability, it wouldn’t have become an issue. No one can deny the need for religious leaders to talk about topics such as drug addiction, late marriages, climate change, social harmony and more.”
A Srinagar-based political analyst who has written about the conflict in Kashmir for four decades said such decisions reflected attempts to pre-emptively contain protests in Kashmir amid the rising wave of Hindu nationalism in India.
“A spate of recent mosque demolitions in cities such as Ujjain and Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh showed how vehemently the far-right strains within India’s ruling apparatus were resurfacing,” the analyst told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. “This renewed communal posturing by the Modi regime was sufficient to provoke reactions in a place like Kashmir. The attempts to assert control over mosques must be seen in light of that.”

The Dutch parliament has approved a motion calling on the government to explore ways to ensure the International Criminal Court (ICC) retains access to international payment systems despite US sanctions targeting the court.
The motion was submitted on 8th October by Hanneke van der Werf of the D66 party, alongside MPs Kati Piri of the Progressive party, Sarah Dobbe of the Socialist Party and Maes van Lanschot of the Christian Democratic party.
It calls on the government, in cooperation with the Dutch central bank and the European Central Bank, to examine ways to ensure that the ICC and other legal entities affected by sanctions can continue accessing international payment systems.
One option under consideration is routing payments through a public financial institution, allowing the affected entities to meet their financial obligations despite external sanctions pressure.
The motion argues that it is undesirable for third countries to be able to indirectly determine whether an independent international judicial body can access international payment systems.
It also stresses that the Netherlands, as the ICC’s host country, has a special responsibility to ensure the court can continue operating.
The motion further calls on the Netherlands to take a leading role within the European Union in strengthening Europe’s autonomy in dealing with other major powers.
Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen expressed a positive view of the motion. It was also supported by the parties represented by its sponsors, other parties in the governing coalition and most opposition parties.

Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:16:50 UTC
16:16:50 KST

Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
Timekeepers add a leap second occasionally to keep our clocks and the Earth’s rotation in tune. That could now change.
The world’s timekeepers are meeting on Thursday near Paris to decide whether to scrap the “leap second”, which could disconnect the clocks we use from the Earth’s rotation and realign timescales.
The world’s clocks are designed on the idea that the Earth completes one rotation on its axis in exactly 24 hours. But it actually wobbles, making the time the Earth takes to rotate less exact. And over time, the Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing.
To compensate for that, since 1972, timekeepers have added a leap second every few years – the last one was added in 2016 – to keep clocks and Earth’s rotation in synchronisation.
But pressure has been mounting to scrap the leap second since it complicates matters for financial markets and data centres, which rely on precise timing down to milliseconds.
So what is a leap second? Could it be scrapped? And how might it change our understanding of time?
Here’s what we know:
What is a leap second?
Clocks work based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the global standard that has been based on high-precision atomic clocks for more than seven decades. Atomic clocks mark time by observing the vibration of atoms.
But the Earth’s rotation works independently of atomic clocks.
A leap second is a second added periodically to UTC to make it synchronise with the Earth’s rotation. The first leap second was added to world clocks in 1972.
There have been 27 leap seconds added so far with the previous leap second being added on December 31, 2016. No further leap seconds have been added since.
According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a nonregulatory federal agency of the United States Department of Commerce, leap seconds occur at the end of December or the end of June. The NIST also cites differences between the precision of the atomic second and the Earth’s rotation to explain the need for a leap second.
“The speed of the Earth’s rotation is not constant. …. This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second,” the NIST added.
Why is pressure mounting to scrap leap seconds?
While leap seconds close the discrepancy between the Earth’s rotation and UTC, their addition has posed challenges for technology companies, financial markets and other businesses that depend on precise timings.
In 2012, LinkedIn and Reddit crashed after the addition of a leap second. The same year, ticket bookings for Qantas, the Australian airline, collapsed after the leap second was added.
Three years later, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission also issued a warning against it. And in July 2022, engineers at Meta said: “Every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures.”
With pressure mounting, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which has the French acronym BIPM, voted in 2022 to scrap the leap second by 2035. But countries like Russia have wanted to push the implementation date back to 2040. Russia incorporates leap seconds directly into its GLONASS satellite-navigation system, so delaying the scrapping of leap seconds would buy Russia time to update its satellite systems.
Despite Moscow’s concern, the 69 member states of BIPM are now meeting on Thursday in Versailles outside Paris to debate and vote on a resolution to scrap the leap second by 2027.
What’s up for debate on Thursday?
According to the BIPM, the timekeeping authorities of countries around the world will discuss three proposals at Versailles.
First, they will consider whether atomic clocks are still the most accurate device when it comes to measuring what constitutes a second. Optical frequencies are now in fact more precise than atomic clocks. If a proposal to change how time is measured is accepted, the second might have a new definition, characterised by optical frequencies rather than the vibrations of atoms.
The second, most significant proposal pertains to dumping the leap second.
And finally, the third proposal on the table is a pitch to synchronise time measurements on Earth with a new time standard that NASA is developing for the moon.
Proposals that are accepted are expected to come into effect from May 20, 2027, World Metrology Day.
What happens if the leap second is scrapped?
If the leap second is scrapped, then it means our clocks will no longer be tied to the Earth’s rotation.
According to the NIST, if this happens, “then adjustments would have to be made to time stamps and legacy equipment and software which synchronise to UTC for astronomical observations.”
“Some proposals have been made to implement larger corrections like leap hours, which would occur much less often than leap seconds,” it added.
Scientists said human routines will not be impacted and software glitches, data server crashes and network failures for financial markets will be eliminated with the abandonment of leap seconds.
But over a period of centuries, the gap between the Earth’s cycle and our clocks will become more apparent: By 2100, clocks will be ahead of the Earth by 54 seconds. In another two millennia, that gap would have widened to several hours. The result? Sunrise and sunset times that would feel out of sync with people’s natural rhythms today.

- The government says the law, which started on 1 September, protects girls and promotes equality; officials report 127 parent meetings and 52 breach reports.
- Legal action is under way, with the constitutional court expected to rule in 2027, while affected girls and families say the rule causes fear, sadness and pressure.
AI generated
VIENNA – As the new school year gets under way in Austria, a headscarf ban for girls under 14 has sparked protests on the streets and in the classroom, with dozens of pupils refusing to comply.
Austria’s conservative-led government has insisted that the ban, introduced on Sept 1, promotes gender equality and protects Muslim girls from “segregation and oppression”.
But critics argue that it disproportionately targets Muslims, infringes upon religious freedom and is forcing young girls to dress in a way that makes them feel uncomfortable.
Since the ban took effect, education authorities across Austria have held 127 meetings with parents and filed 52 reports over alleged breaches of the law, according to the education ministry.
Opponents of the ban have also held protests across the country, with several hundred people gathering each time.
‘Part of me’
At a demonstration in Vienna, Zehra, 37, who did not want to give her last name, said her two daughters, aged nine and 13, were “sad and angry” about the ban.
“We raise our children by telling them, you can decide who you want to be – and this law is the exact opposite,” she said.
Seham, 12, said she felt “afraid” to remove her headscarf at school “because I’d worn it for two years and it felt like a part of me”.
After discussions with school leaders, she said she was allowed to cover her hair with an alternative non-traditional head covering, but would still “rather wear the full headscarf”.
Roughly 8% of Austria’s nine million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.
They suffer the highest rates of racism and discrimination against Muslims in the EU, according to a 2024 report by Europe’s FRA rights agency.
In the 2024 elections, the far-right Freedom Party won for the first time even though it failed to form a government. The anti-immigration party continues to top voter opinion polls.
The new law is Austria’s second attempt to restrict headscarves in schools after a coalition between the conservatives and the Freedom Party introduced a ban for primary school pupils in 2019.
That law was overturned by the constitutional court on the grounds that a regulation targeting only Muslims was incompatible with religious neutrality.
‘Under pressure’
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria, which is supporting legal action against the new headscarf ban, said it had received around 70 reports from families about difficulties during its implementation.
“A law that was justified as protecting children’s welfare is putting precisely those children under pressure at school,” the group said in a statement.
The constitutional court confirmed to AFP that it had received a legal complaint about the law and a decision is expected in the first half of 2027.
When girls refuse to comply with the law, schools are required to hold a series of discussions with pupils and their parents before cases are referred to education authorities.
Ultimately, parents who continue to ignore the ban can be fined.
In a statement sent to AFP, Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr said the fact there had only been 127 meetings so far showed “that the vast majority of pupils and parents are cooperative”.
“In addition, the figures show that the discussions held with the parents concerned in the event of a violation are, for the most part, successful,” he added.
Education authorities in Vienna said that “on the basis of the discussions held so far, the impression has emerged that the girls wish to wear the headscarf of their own accord”.
Sandy, 12, said she began wearing a headscarf about a year ago because “I place a lot of importance on my religion and I want to be able to live it”.
A teacher who has worked with two affected girls in the capital told AFP there was no sign they were being forced to wear headscarves.
The girls had spent weeks adapting to the new rules and searching for acceptable alternatives to headscarves, said the teacher, who wished to remain anonymous.
“It is very uncomfortable for them.” AFP

ACCC takes Kmart to court over nail glue burns and button battery safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:09:51 UTC
16:09:51 KST

In short:
The ACCC has accused Kmart of selling millions of bottles of a nail glue that caused burns without adequate safety warnings.
The consumer watchdog also accused the retail chain of selling watches with button batteries that had not been tested and smart tags without mandatory safety information.
A Kmart spokesperson said it was disappointed at the ACCC's decision to take action on historical matters that had been addressed.
The consumer watchdog has taken legal action against Kmart, alleging it breached Australian Consumer law by selling millions of bottles of nail glue that caused burns requiring medical treatment.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has taken action against the retail giant in the Federal Court in Victoria, alleging Kmart sold cosmetic nail glue without warning consumers of a risk of serious injury from burns associated with it.
The ACCC said other safety warnings were set out on the packaging and bottle, which was sold individually and with a pack of nails.
According to court documents, between August 2017 and December 2024, at least 51 consumers complained to Kmart of skin burns caused by contact with the nail glues, of which at least 33 expressly referred to contact with fabric.
A further seven complaints not involving skin burns referred to the nail glues causing steaming, smoking, burning or melting when in contact with fabric, with consumers reporting suffering serious injuries including burns requiring medical treatment and, in some cases, hospitalisation and skin grafts.
The ACCC claims customers sent Kmart's customer service team photos of burned clothes and skin, and some described the nail glues causing an exothermic or chemical reaction, heat and smoke, some of which were escalated internally to senior Kmart management including the CEO.
"We consider that Kmart's failure to warn consumers of the risk of burns after receiving numerous consumer reports of burn injuries associated with the use of the nail glue exposed consumers to an ongoing risk of serious injury, as an incredibly serious matter," ACCC Deputy Chair Catriona Lowe said.
"It was important for Kmart to address this, once it was made aware of these serious product safety concerns."
The ACCC further alleges Kmart failed to submit mandatory serious injury reports to the Commonwealth minister as required.
A Kmart spokesperson said it took its reporting obligations seriously and submitted mandatory injury reports about the products to the ACCC.
"While the incidents with nail glues are also historical, we regret any injury associated with these products and apologise to anyone affected. Kmart remains of the view the labelling and warnings were appropriate to prevent misuse," they said.
Watchdog alleges button battery non-compliance
The ACCC also alleged Kmart failed to test several digital and analogue watches that contained button batteries prior to supply as legally required.
It alleges Kmart sold about 64,000 button-battery-powered watches between June 2022 and November 2024 which did not comply.
"These watches contained button batteries, but Kmart did not test them prior to supply to show that young children could not open the battery compartments. This is despite many of the watches being specifically designed for children," Ms Lowe said.
The ACCC has also accused Kmart of supplying GPS tracking devices known as Smart Tags that did not comply with the mandatory button battery information standard. The devices were recalled in 2024.
A Kmart spokesperson said no injuries were reported for any of the products and it had continued to strengthen the product safety and compliance processes.
"We have cooperated with the ACCC throughout its investigation and are disappointed at its decision to take action on historical matters that Kmart has addressed," it said.
"As the matter is now before the court, we will not be commenting further on the proceedings."
Ms Lowe said all businesses, especially large retailers like Kmart, are expected to have consumer safety front of mind.
"Withholding safety information can amount to false or misleading representations in breach of the Australian Consumer Law, but it also exposes consumers to risk," she said.
A court date for the matter is yet to be set.

UK goods trade deficit narrows to $26.2B in August, below expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:00:07 UTC
16:00:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The UK's goods trade deficit stood at £19.8 billion ($26.2 billion) in August, below market expectations of £21.9 billion, as imports fell more than exports, official figures showed Thursday.
The deficit, excluding precious metals, narrowed by £200 million from July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Goods imports decreased 2.3% month-on-month to £54.2 billion, while exports fell 3.1% to £34.4 billion.
Imports from non-EU countries dropped 6.3% to £25.6 billion, driven primarily by lower purchases of machinery and transport equipment following a record increase in July. Aircraft imports from the US and ship imports from China declined.
Imports from the EU rose 1.6% to £28.6 billion, supported by higher purchases of German aircraft and pharmaceutical products, alongside refined oil from the Netherlands.
Goods exports to the EU fell 7.3% to £15.8 billion, reflecting declines in machinery and transport equipment, manufactured materials, fuels and chemicals.
Lower aircraft exports to the Netherlands and reduced crude oil shipments to Germany, Poland and Italy contributed to the fall.
Exports to non-EU countries increased 0.9% to £18.6 billion, supported by higher shipments of inorganic chemicals to the US.
After adjusting for inflation, total goods imports fell 2.5%, while exports declined 2.8%.
 
3-month trade deficit widens
The total goods and services trade deficit widened by £1.4 billion to £8 billion ($10.6 billion) in the three months to August compared with the three months to May.
The goods deficit increased by £2.5 billion to £59.1 billion, partly offset by a £1.1 billion rise in the estimated services surplus to £51.1 billion.
Early estimates for August showed services exports increased 0.4% from July, while imports rose 0.2%.

The US is considering using the "mother of all bombs" against Iran - CNN

The U.S. military has developed new plans for strikes against Iran that envisage the possible use of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal — the GBU-43/B, known as the "mother of all bombs." Potential targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. CNN reports this, citing U.S. officials familiar with the military plans, UNN reports.
Details
According to CNN sources, one of the plans involves strikes against a significant number of Iran’s energy infrastructure facilities, with the possible use of the MOAB bomb. Another option concerns nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, where, according to U.S. and Israeli assessments, Tehran stores components of its nuclear program. President Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain. He says the U.S. goal is to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
The use of a MOAB in the conflict with Iran would mark a new stage of escalation. At the same time, according to the publication, sources familiar with discussions of the military plans have expressed doubts about whether this weapon would help achieve the strategic goals of U.S. President Donald Trump or change the balance of power in the war.
Although the U.S. military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against important Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that takes these plans into account in a way that would actually bring the war to an end — something only the president has the authority to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could serve as the "final" end to the war, at least from a communications standpoint, recognizing how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. Although some administration officials have characterized the war as effectively won, Trump has been more cautious in his latest statements, not declaring victory and saying that the U.S. still has unfinished business in the country
At the same time, over the past several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various courses of action regarding Iran.
Although Trump publicly announced that he would take no new action until the midterm elections, several advisers privately said they did not know whether this statement was final or could change before Election Day. One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets, including a "significant number of energy infrastructure facilities" and the potential use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB). The same source said the wording used was that this attack would take place "before the U.S. regression in the CENTCOM area of responsibility," indicating that the administration could carry out additional strikes, try to declare victory, and quickly withdraw everyone
We will remind you
U.S. President Donald Trump promised that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm congressional elections in November. He also said that Washington was "holding productive talks" with Tehran.

Romania’s nominated prime minister secures support ahead of confidence vote
BUCHAREST, Oct 15 - Romania's leftist Social Democrats said they will join the government of Prime Minister-designate Luca Niculescu while other parties pledged their votes, edging the country closer to ending a political crisis that has pressured its investment-grade rating.
The Social Democrats (PSD), parliament's largest party, will have 11 ministers in the proposed government Niculescu will unveil on Thursday before a parliamentary vote of confidence, PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu said late on Wednesday.
Technocrats will fill other ministerial posts, including finance, energy and foreign affairs.
While other pro-European parties refrained from joining the cabinet, many said they will back Niculescu, ensuring the 233 votes required to win the vote of confidence.
Niculescu, 55, a diplomat, former journalist and currently interim deputy foreign minister, will lead centrist President Nicusor Dan's fourth attempt to install a government in the five months since a pro-European broad coalition cabinet collapsed.
The four-party government led by Liberal Party head Ilie Bolojan collapsed in early May when the PSD quit and teamed up with the far-right opposition to file a no-confidence vote.
The PSD have repeatedly said they would form a similar coalition with a different prime minister, but the Liberals and two other centre-right parties have refused.
The months-long political crisis has pushed the Romanian leu currency to record lows while debt yields surged. The European Union state narrowly avoided a ratings downgrade from the last rung of investment grade.
Ratings agencies have all said that Romania's ability to approve a 2027 budget that further cuts one of the EU's largest deficits will be key for the country's rating.
While Niculescu's government was set to get parliament's approval, it was unclear how long it would last. The PSD will join on condition that a 2027 budget plan be unveiled by December 1, with no further tax hikes, and Grindeanu said it will assess the cabinet in six months.
Romania has agreed with Brussels to bring its budget deficit below 3% of economic output - from over 9% in 2024 and an expected 6.2% this year - by 2030. REUTERS

First swans return to Bruges’ canal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:48:22 UTC
15:48:22 KST

The first swans are back in Bruges. The swans at 't Stil Ende waterway had to be moved away during the summer because blue-green algae caused the water quality to deteriorate, but they have now returned. Swans from other Bruges’ canals will remain in the enclosure for the time being. The city is continuing to monitor the water quality of its waterways.
The number of blue-green algae in Bruges’ canals is gradually decreasing. The lab provides a weekly update, enabling the city to continue monitoring water quality. “It is the water quality that determines when the swans can return safely. We monitor the test results weekly and assess the situation at each location. The welfare of the animals is always our top priority,” says alderman Franky Demon.
“We are keeping the swans in their familiar location for as long as possible. If their health or welfare is at risk, we will take the necessary measures. Thanks to targeted monitoring and good care, all the swans are doing well.”
Removed earlier than last year
The city also took measures last year. In 2025, the swans at Wijngaardplein were able to remain where they were, but they were kept on dry land for around two weeks with fresh drinking water. In August 2025, the city removed a family of swans from the vicinity of the Carmers Bridge, the Potterierei and the Sint-Annarei because the water quality was inadequate.
In October 2025, these swans were allowed to return after spending around two months in the enclosure. The swans from Stil Ende spent the same amount of time in the enclosure this year, but the city had to remove them earlier. The long spell of warm weather early in the year encouraged the growth of blue-green algae and put pressure on water quality.
Number of swans on the rise
Bruges now has a total of 59 swans. In the swan enclosure, the city is still looking after 22 adult swans and eight newly purchased young swans for the Wijngaardplein. In addition, there are two swans from the children’s farm and seven swans from the Potterierei.
A few months ago, the number of swans fell below 52. According to a persistent legend, the city must maintain at least 52 swans on its waters. With the purchase of eight young swans, the total now stands at 59 once again.
According to Demon, the city did not buy the swans to uphold the legend. “The purchase is part of the routine management of the swan population in our city,” he says.

From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:46:52 UTC
15:46:52 KST

From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa
October 27 vote could test whether Israel’s ties with African countries withstand the fallout from the war on Gaza.
Lagos, Nigeria – As Israelis prepare to vote on October 27, African governments from Pretoria to Rabat are weighing what the result could mean for their own foreign and domestic policies.
The war on Gaza has exposed sharp differences across the continent, with some governments pursuing diplomatic measures against Israel while others maintain commercial and security ties.
Recent polling has shown a closely contested race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads and a bloc of Jewish-led opposition parties.
Neither is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with a protracted period of coalition talks expected to follow the vote.
The next government’s approach to Gaza and the Palestinian question could influence Israel’s efforts to preserve and expand its partnerships across the continent.
Israel’s relationships across Africa are shaped by competing priorities. While the Gaza war has intensified diplomatic pressure and public opposition in many countries, security needs, commercial interests and longstanding bilateral partnerships continue to influence government decisions.
Diplomatic strain vs closer ties
Since the war began in October 2023, South Africa has emerged as one of Israel’s most vocal critics in Africa. Its government brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention. Israel rejects the allegations. The court’s so-called provisional measures in 2024, including an order for Israel to take action to prevent acts of genocide, are not a final ruling on whether genocide has occurred.
In November 2023, South Africa’s National Assembly adopted a motion calling on the government to close the Israeli embassy and suspend diplomatic relations. The motion did not itself implement those measures, but it underscored the strength of political opposition to Israel’s military campaign.
Other African governments have taken different approaches that reflect national political priorities and foreign policy calculations rather than a single continental position.
Chad recalled its ambassador to Israel in November 2023, while some countries have maintained relations despite criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.
Morocco offers a contrasting example. It restored relations with Israel in 2020 under a US-backed arrangement linked to Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Despite public demonstrations opposing normalisation, Rabat has continued to pursue closer ties.
On September 16, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz. The three countries reaffirmed plans to upgrade diplomatic relations, elevate their respective missions to embassies and appoint ambassadors.
They also agreed to conclude investment protection and double taxation agreements by the end of this year, expand flights to include Moroccan airlines and arrange reciprocal high-level visits in the coming months. These were announced commitments, rather than confirmation that the changes had already been implemented.
For Idowu Johnson, associate professor of international relations at the University of Ibadan, the diversity of African states makes it difficult to predict a uniform response to Israel’s election.
“Africa’s heterogeneity means individual states have handled relations with Israel separately. Since the October 7, 2023 attacks, African criticism has focused on Israel’s denial of Palestinian statehood.
“The October 27 election will therefore be pivotal, as a new government’s stance on the Palestinian cause will shape how far Africa cooperates on agriculture, trade, security and technology, guided by self-determination and international law as well as bilateral interests,” Johnson said.
Israel’s relationship with the African Union (AU) also reflects these divisions. In 2021, the AU Commission chairperson accredited Israel’s representative to the organisation, prompting objections from member states.
In February 2022, the AU Assembly established a committee of heads of state and government to consult on Israel’s observer status. The dispute continued into 2023, when the AU moved to suspend Israel’s accreditation pending further consideration.
The disagreement has reflected wider divisions over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and the organisation’s approach to the conflict.
A new Israeli government could seek to ease those tensions, but any change would depend on its policies as well as the positions of AU member states.
Security ties may outlast diplomatic tensions
Security cooperation has been a significant part of Israel’s relationships with some African governments. Israeli companies have pursued defence and security contracts involving equipment, surveillance technology and training.
But the nature and scale of those relationships vary by country and claims about particular agreements or technologies should be tied to documented cases rather than treated as evidence of a uniform Israeli security presence across the continent.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo offers a recent example of efforts to deepen cooperation. Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi visited Israel on August 31 and September 1, meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog. Discussions covered security, defence, agriculture, infrastructure, energy and high technology. Both sides expressed a desire to strengthen their strategic partnership and expand cooperation across several sectors.
The visit followed memorandums of understanding signed on July 27. Congolese officials said the visit would review those agreements and explore further Israeli investment, including opportunities linked to the Lobito Corridor. The meetings demonstrate the potential scope of bilateral cooperation, but do not establish that a specific new security contract has been concluded.
For governments confronting armed groups, insecurity can create incentives to seek equipment, intelligence and training from foreign partners. Yet the importance of Israeli cooperation differs between countries and diplomatic tensions will not necessarily have the same effect on every security relationship.
The limits of Israel’s diplomatic outreach were also evident after it recognised Somaliland as an independent state on December 26, last year, the first country to do so. Somalia and other critics rejected the move, arguing that it undermined Somalia’s territorial integrity. The decision triggered demonstrations in Somalia and Somaliland.
Speaking to Al Jazeera this month, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country “under any circumstances”. He added that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, adding that its real aim was to get closer to the Gulf states and Iran.
According to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project (ACLED), 110 demonstrations directly linked to Israel’s Somaliland recognition had been recorded by the time of its February 2026 Africa overview. Only seven supported the move, all in Somaliland; the others opposed it. The figures cover demonstrations linked to that particular decision, not all African views of Israel, and should not be treated as a continent-wide measure of public opinion.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an Africa analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute, argues that public opposition can constrain governments even when they see strategic value in maintaining ties.
“The strongest constraint, however, may come from African publics rather than governments: the Somaliland recognition drew widespread opposition, the African Union and many governments reaffirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity, and ACLED logged 110 related demonstrations, only seven in support.
“Depending on its approach, the next Israeli government could therefore either deepen strategic cooperation in Morocco, Sudan and the Red Sea, or face a legitimacy problem if it continues policies seen as tied to the Gaza war, widening the gap between state-level cooperation and public sentiment,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera.
The Somaliland episode shows how a diplomatic move can provoke opposition when it is perceived to challenge a core principle of sovereignty.
It does not, by itself, establish that African governments will abandon security agreements with Israel. The consequences will depend on the countries involved, the terms of their cooperation and the domestic political costs of maintaining them.
Trade, agritech and the contest for influence
Trade and development cooperation offer Israel another route to maintaining relationships in Africa. Israeli firms and officials have pursued partnerships in areas including agriculture, irrigation, water management, health and technology.
Such cooperation can offer practical benefits to governments seeking investment and technical expertise, but commercial ties do not necessarily translate into public support for Israel’s policies.
Zambia illustrates Israel’s efforts to deepen bilateral engagement. Israel opened a resident embassy in Lusaka in August last year, after a 52-year absence. Agriculture, water management, health, education and technology have been identified as potential areas for closer cooperation. The move formed part of Israel’s broader effort to strengthen its engagement with African countries.
Some analysts have interpreted Israel’s renewed engagement with Zambia as an attempt to cultivate partners who could counterbalance South Africa’s influence in the region. That remains an interpretation, not an established explanation for the relationship.
Zambia has its own reasons for seeking investment and cooperation, particularly in agriculture, water management and technology; closer bilateral ties alone do not prove that countering South Africa is Israel’s objective.
Professor Iwebunor Okwechime, of Obafemi Awolowo University, points to the historical roots of South Africa’s position towards Israel.
“If we trace the stance South Africa took, it goes back to the apartheid era, when Israel backed the apartheid regime and refused to support the struggle against the minority government. This historical context is important for understanding South Africa-Israel relations today,” Okwechime told Al Jazeera.
For African governments, the challenge will be to balance security and commercial interests against public opposition, commitments to Palestinian rights and positions on international law. For Israel, the upcoming election will test whether a new government can ease diplomatic tensions across Africa without fundamentally changing the policies that have fuelled them.
As Okwechime told Al Jazeera, “There won’t be a radical change in sentiments regardless of the government in power”.

How to Turn an Attic Into Usable Living Space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

What happens to the space beneath a roof? In many houses, the answer is simple: it becomes an attic, a storage space, or a largely unused volume between the upper floor and the roof. Yet the same space can become a bedroom, home office, playroom, or additional living area if the roof and the room beneath it are considered together.
This potential matters in both existing buildings and residential architecture. Converting an attic can add usable space without extending the building's footprint, while designing a new house with a usable roof space in mind can make it more adaptable over time. The question is therefore not only how to convert an attic, but how to recognize the architectural potential of underused space created by a sloped roof.
The VELUX Design Guide approaches this through the relationship between roof geometry, daylight, ventilation, views, and indoor climate. Its guidance considers how to coordinate these factors to make spaces beneath the roof comfortable and efficient.
Making Better Use of Existing Attics
Many existing attics were never intended to be occupied, making them an overlooked opportunity for adding usable space within an existing building. A cold attic, for example, may sit above the insulated upper floor as an unheated and largely unused volume. Converting it into living accommodation means bringing that space into the building's environmental and structural strategy: insulation, ventilation, access, headroom, roof structure, and existing services all need to be reconsidered. Issues such as condensation, moisture, or heat loss may need to be addressed along the way, but the same interventions can also improve the performance of the existing building while unlocking space that was previously underused.
The gable roof is one of the clearest examples. Two sloping planes meet at a ridge, helping shed rain and snow while creating a triangular volume above the upper floor. Whether that volume becomes useful depends on its proportions: roof pitch, ridge height, knee-wall height, structural depth, and access all affect how much of it can actually be occupied. Roof pitch is particularly important. A steeper roof generally creates more usable height, while the lower areas beneath the eaves can still accommodate functions such as storage, seating, or beds.
Designing Attics for Future Use in New Homes
An attic conversion can make use of space within the building envelope rather than extending the building outward. The VELUX Room to Grow: The case for easily convertible attic design in new homes research frames this as an opportunity to provide additional living space while making better use of the land already allocated to new homes.
An analysis of approximately 669,000 homes built in England between 2020 and 2024 estimated that around 530,000—roughly 80 percent—could feasibly support attic rooms meeting minimum space standards. The assessment considered roof pitch, eaves, stairs, and a minimum space standard of 6.51 m², and found that steeper roof pitches increased conversion viability.
Existing buildings require architects to work with what is already there. New construction offers a different opportunity: the roof can be designed with future occupation in mind. A house doesn't necessarily need a fully finished attic when it is completed. Instead, the roof space can be made conversion-ready. The staircase position, structural arrangement, roof pitch, insulation, services, and available headroom can all be coordinated so the space can accommodate another use later.
The Room to Grow research estimates that the average uplift in floor area from a viable attic room can be around 31% for detached homes. Its wider argument is that adaptable roof spaces can accommodate changing household needs while using the land allocated to new homes more efficiently.
Once an attic becomes habitable, its sloping geometry should inform the room rather than feel like an inconvenience. This is why the VELUX Design Guide recommends thinking "in section, not just in plan." A floor plan shows the available footprint, but a section reveals where someone can stand, how furniture fits beneath the slope, and how daylight can reach deeper into the room.
Bringing Light, Air and Views Indoors
To make the volume comfortable to occupy, different criteria should be considered. Roof windows, such as those by VELUX, can contribute daylight, ventilation, and views; however, their effectiveness depends on how they relate to the room, roof geometry, and planned use. Daylight is particularly important beneath a sloped roof because roof windows can bring natural light deeper into the plan than vertical façade windows, potentially helping distribute daylight more evenly throughout the room. EN 17037, the European Standard for daylight in buildings, defines target illuminance levels of 300, 500, and 750 lux and provides methods for assessing daylight provision across a space.
Natural ventilation uses wind pressure and temperature differences to move air through a building, improving indoor air quality and humidity control while reducing reliance on mechanical cooling. In an attic, openings at different heights can take advantage of warm air naturally rising. Thanks to their elevated position, roof windows can support natural ventilation by allowing warm air to rise and escape, helping improve indoor airflow. However, two windows on opposite sides can support cross-ventilation, while openings at different heights can use the stack effect as warm air rises. Combining both approaches can help move air through the space more effectively. Their position also affects the view. Drawing on the principles of the European standard EN 17037 for views to the outside, the VELUX Design Guide recommends positioning the lower edge of roof windows approximately 95 to 110 centimeters above the floor to provide views from a seated position. It also emphasizes the importance of views that include different layers of the surrounding environment, ideally encompassing the sky, horizon, and ground.
The value of an attic ultimately lies in more than the floor area it adds. For existing buildings, it can unlock space already within the building envelope; for new housing, designing the roof with future conversion in mind can preserve options as household needs change. In both cases, the architectural challenge is to connect roof geometry with height, furniture, daylight, ventilation, views, and thermal conditions, making what might otherwise be leftover volume into usable, adaptable space.

Ukraine’s TENCORE and Canada’s Dominion Dynamics to Produce TerMIT UGVs for NATO Allies
Ukrainian defense company TENCORE has partnered with Canada’s Dominion Dynamics to produce its TerMIT unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) in Canada, starting in 2027, Militarnyi reported on October 14.
The companies signed a memorandum of understanding at the AUSA 2026 international defense exhibition in Washington, DC, with plans to supply these robotic systems to both Ukrainian forces and NATO partners.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the partnership, TENCORE will transfer technology and train Canadian specialists to enable full-scale serial production, scheduled to begin in 2027.
In turn, Dominion Dynamics will integrate its AuraNet command, control, and navigation hardware-software suite into the platform. The Canadian firm will also develop a specialized modification of TerMIT tailored for operations in extreme Arctic conditions.
“Partnership with Canada provides us with a scalable manufacturing base, resilient supply chains, and a reliable energy grid to launch this cycle alongside allies who require combat-proven solutions,” said Roman Tkachenko, co-founder of TENCORE, Militarnyi reported.
The base version of the TerMIT UGV is designed for battlefield cargo transport. It features an operational range of up to 40 km, speeds reaching 15 km/h, and ballistic protection designed to maintain logistical support under fire.
On July 9, 2026, building on Ukraine's rapid integration of robotic systems on the frontline, defense company TENCORE introduced AI KIT—an artificial intelligence software suite designed to enhance the autonomy of its TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles.
The technology aimed to reduce operator strain and improve combat efficiency by removing the need for constant manual control. The system featured a hands-free navigation mode, an automatic 180-degree return function in signal-loss zones, and predefined failsafes to keep the platform operating safely under heavy electronic jamming.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fears a military campaign against Iran in the two weeks before the election could undermine Likud’s chances of remaining in power, sources familiar with the matter told Maariv on Thursday.
Internal Likud assessments have fueled optimism that the rival blocs could finish tied or that Netanyahu’s bloc could secure a majority. Netanyahu, however, fears a security escalation could change the electoral picture.
A message conveyed from Jerusalem to Washington in recent days indicated that Israel would prefer military action against Iran to begin after the October 27 Knesset election, the sources said.
In private discussions, Netanyahu has raised two main considerations against launching a campaign at this stage, according to the sources: the difficulty of postponing the election and the potential toll of Iranian retaliation on Israel’s home front.
“These are precisely the scenes we cannot afford to see. A country in shelters, missile strikes, destroyed buildings, wounded people and, God forbid, deaths - that is what could lead to a victory for Eisenkot and his partners,” a senior Likud official said, adding that the remarks reflect Netanyahu’s position.
Likud fears that missile fire, casualties, and prolonged disruption to daily life would shift the public agenda in the final days before the election.
According to assessments published in the US, renewed strikes against Iran could prompt the launch of hundreds of ballistic missiles at Israel. A strike shortly before the election could also raise questions about its motives and timing.
Could renewed war with Iran cause elections to be postponed?
Netanyahu considers postponing the election because of a security emergency impractical, the sources said.
Section 9A of Basic Law: The Knesset requires the support of 80 MKs to pass legislation extending the Knesset’s term, along with special circumstances that prevent the election from taking place as scheduled. Likud officials believe they cannot secure the necessary support from the opposition.
The possibility of postponing the election also arose in security discussions between Israel and the US. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with US Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman Gen. Dan Caine about the possibility of renewed fighting within three weeks, Axios reported. Their discussions included the possibility that such a campaign would lead to Israel’s election being postponed.
Likud’s optimism rests on internal assessments, while public polling presents a mixed picture. Polls published in recent days have shown substantial differences between polling firms, with some placing Netanyahu’s bloc well short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
Senior Likud officials believe the bloc can improve its position before the election and want to avoid an escalation that could undermine those efforts.
Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot recently said he was unaware of any critical development that would justify immediate joint US-Israeli action against Iran. He stressed, however, that he has not had access to the latest intelligence since leaving the war cabinet.
The position attributed to Netanyahu in private contradicts briefings and assessments suggesting he favors a strike before the election because he believes another campaign would benefit him politically.
Netanyahu, Trump reportedly discuss resuming Iran war
Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have spoken several times over the past two weeks, with the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran coming up in their conversations, according to several sources.
The White House denied that the two had discussed resuming the war.
Israeli officials believe the denial was intended to distance Israel from the American debate over a strike on Iran and avoid reinforcing claims that Netanyahu influences Trump’s decisions. The officials said the White House recognizes that such claims could damage Trump politically at home.
The Prime Minister’s Office said Netanyahu maintains regular contact with Trump but did not comment on the substance of their conversations.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran remain high. Trump said on October 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, but subsequently renewed his threats.
At a campaign rally in Alaska over the past day, Trump threatened to deal Iran a heavy blow and said he had grown tired of its conduct.
According to a US report, the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command to complete preparations for renewed, extensive military operations against Iran.
The operational assessment in Israel, however, is that Trump has yet to make a final decision to attack and that no date has been set for action in the immediate future.
Military preparations continue amid reports that Iran is strengthening defenses around strategic facilities and restoring capabilities damaged in the previous campaign.
Washington and Tehran are also continuing diplomatic contacts through regional mediators over Iran’s nuclear program, shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz, and a possible agreement to prevent further escalation. The talks have yet to produce a breakthrough.
“Trump is Trump. With him, everything can turn around and change very quickly,” the sources said. “We do not control the situation, but the message has certainly been conveyed to him. As far as we are concerned, we would prefer quiet on the security front until October 27.”

A U.S. watchdog organization filed a lawsuit on Wednesday alleging that the current role of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as one of the administration’s leading envoys is unlawful and creates numerous risks of conflicts of interest. NBC News reports, writes UNN.
Details
Kushner wields enormous influence on the international stage "without receiving Senate confirmation or filing any declaration of financial income and assets," according to a lawsuit filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).
Kushner "has not undergone the proper vetting to perform his government duties and is evading transparency requirements intended to ensure that he uses his authority in the interests of the American people, rather than for his own benefit," the lawsuit states.
The plaintiffs are seeking to have Kushner removed from his position or, at a minimum, ordered to file financial disclosures.
The lawsuit cites numerous overlapping interests in Kushner’s diplomatic and commercial activities.
He represents the United States in the most high-profile international conflicts, including participating in the country’s efforts to end the wars between Israel and Hamas, Ukraine and Russia, as well as the United States and Iran. He holds direct negotiations with foreign leaders
"At the same time, Kushner is a private businessman. He runs an investment firm that manages more than $6 billion in assets. Approximately 99% of these assets belong to foreign investors, including sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The company has significant investments abroad, including in Israel," the lawsuit states. In the plaintiffs’ view, all of this "creates an elevated risk of financial conflicts of interest."
The lawsuit also emphasizes that "declining a salary and official title does not change the real nature of Kushner’s role: he exercises significant executive authority and has done so continuously for most of Trump’s second presidential term. And this in no way exempts him from the constitutional restrictions set out in the Appointments Clause or from the obligation to file public financial disclosures under the ethics law."
The plaintiffs are seeking to bar Kushner from holding public office without Senate confirmation. The lawsuit also states that, if he is a private citizen, "his exercise of government authority would violate the doctrine against the impermissible delegation of powers to private persons, which prohibits transferring government power to private entities."

UN-Habitat Highlights Housing Initiatives and sauerbruch hutton Completes Timber-Hybrid Building in Berlin: This Week’s Review

This week, questions about housing, safety, and the future of cities came into focus, from the impact of natural hazards to architecture's role in shaping more inclusive urban environments. The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, observed on October 13 under the theme "Resilience Starts at Home," highlighted these questions just days after a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Panama, damaging buildings and prompting evacuations nationwide. Beyond disaster preparedness, the week's developments also reflect broader efforts to address housing needs, give existing buildings new purposes, and create spaces that support education, culture, and public life.
Housing Access and the Reuse of Existing Resources
UN-Habitat has announced the five recipients of its 2026 Scroll of Honour Award, recognizing contributions to adequate housing and sustainable urban development in Brazil, Myanmar, Pakistan, Tunisia, and the United Kingdom. Selected from 101 nominations, this year's recipients include a housing organization supporting communities affected by conflict and displacement, an Indigenous village in Brazil, a public housing agency in Pakistan, Tunisian researcher Abdelmalek Ghannem, who develops building materials from local and mining residues, and London Mayor Sadiq Khan. Scheduled to open in August 2027, the school forms part of a wider transformation of Houston's former industrial waterfront.
Cultural Spaces and New Perspectives on City-Making
In Los Angeles, Frank Gehry's expansion of the Colburn School is scheduled to open on September 25, 2027, with the inauguration of Terri and Jerry Kohl Hall, a 1,000-seat concert hall. The 100,000-square-foot addition will expand the school's music and dance facilities and house its Trudl Zipper Dance Institute, more than tripling the space currently dedicated to dance. Interlocking opaque and transparent volumes, finished in a metallic pink coating, are connected by a light-filled entrance and gardens at street and rooftop levels. Inside the concert hall, an in-the-round configuration places audiences around performers, while adjustable acoustic elements suspended overhead accommodate different performance types.
Questions about how cultural initiatives shape urban environments also inform Utopian Hours 2026, which returns to Turin on October 16–17 for the second chapter of its tenth-anniversary edition. Organized by the nonprofit cultural association Stratosferica, the festival brings together architects, researchers, and urban practitioners to explore how cities can respond to contemporary social, environmental, and political challenges. The program includes a masterclass by Archigram co-founder Peter Cook on imagination and city-making, alongside an exhibition of works by Cook and Archigram not previously shown in Italy. Other participants include Wim Walschap of Herzog & de Meuron, urban strategist Zahra Ebrahim, and author Carolyn Steel. Talks, exhibitions, film screenings, and participatory sessions address public space, climate adaptation, food systems, and community-led urban development.
On the Radar
Benthem Crouwel Architects and Nieuwe Architecten Redesign University of Groningen's Learning Centre
Benthem Crouwel Architects and Nieuwe Architecten have finalised the design for the Interfaculty Learning Centre at the University of Groningen's Zernike Campus in the Netherlands. The project transforms an existing 1960s building at Nijenborgh 4 into a shared learning environment for students and staff across three faculties, combining flexible classrooms, study areas, and specialised laboratories. The redesign retains the building's characteristic horizontal façade bands, relocating building services into them to free up interior space and provide additional solar shading. The existing modular structure will be preserved, alongside materials such as natural stone flooring and stair treads, while new additions will use timber and biobased materials. Dismantling began in September 2026, with completion expected for the 2028–2029 academic year.
sauerbruch hutton Completes Temporary Office for Germany's Federal President in Berlin
sauerbruch hutton has completed the new Office Building for Federal Authorities at the Spreebogen in Berlin, which has served as the temporary seat of German Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier since July 2026. The 18,700-square-meter complex accommodates both the President's official functions and administrative workplaces while Schloss Bellevue undergoes refurbishment. Comprising two timber-hybrid buildings, the project combines prefabricated timber office modules with reinforced concrete cores and plinths. Its façade layers coloured railings over fluted glazed ceramic elements, creating a changing appearance across the elevations. Designed with circular construction principles and future adaptability in mind, the buildings can later accommodate another federal authority, extending their use beyond the temporary presidential relocation.
Henning Larsen Reveals Adaptive Reuse Plans for Perth's Mill Green District
Henning Larsen has unveiled a proposal to transform three existing office buildings in central Perth, Australia, into Mill Green, a mixed-use precinct for GDI Property Group. The project retains and adapts the buildings at 197 St Georges Terrace, 5 Mill Street, and 1 Mill Street, introducing new public spaces, landscape, retail, and hospitality programs. A network of paths and laneways will connect the buildings through a central landscaped area, with canopies and terraces designed to respond to Perth's climate. Located on Whadjuk Noongar Country near the Swan River, the precinct will be developed in phases, beginning with improvements to the ground plane and podiums.

Australian children face sharp rise in violence, sexual assault: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:27:36 CST
15:27:36 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sexual assault and family violence-related assaults involving children increased sharply across Australia between 2014 and 2024, with violence accelerating in the last three to five years, an Australian study has found.
The study found that sexual assault rates rose by 51 percent among girls aged 10-17 and 60 percent among boys in the same age group over 2014-2024. Among boys aged 10-17, rates rose sharply from 2021, at 15.7 percent per year, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Sydney.
Family violence-related assault rates also rose sharply from around 2020 among both boys and girls, with annual increases ranging from 8 percent to 20 percent across several age and gender groups, according to the study published in JAMA Network Open.
Researchers cited possible contributing factors including rising income inequality, the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, cost-of-living pressures, changing online gender norms, gaps in support services and increased reporting of violence.
Lead author Lucy Grummitt from the university's Matilda Center for Research in Mental Health and Substance Use called for greater investment in prevention and early intervention to protect children from violence.
The study found no significant change in hospitalizations for assault-related injuries among children and no increase in substantiated child maltreatment cases over the same period.
However, the researchers warned that declining substantiated cases could reflect limited capacity among child protection agencies to investigate reports of abuse, rather than a genuine reduction in violence. ■

UNDP chief sounds alarm on growing poverty after Iran war shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:27:18 UTC
15:27:18 KST

A vendor sells prepared food from her boat as she paddles past a flooded spirit house in Sena district in the central Thai province of Ayutthaya on October 7, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
Millions could be thrown into poverty by surging energy costs, the impact of an intense El Nino phenomenon and higher interest rates, with vulnerable countries being pushed to the brink by repeated crises, the U.N.'s development chief told AFP.
Global fuel prices have soared since the United States launched its war on Iran in late February, with Tehran's retaliations against Washington's Gulf allies curtailing major oil and natural gas supplies.
Fiscal deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios around the world have ballooned since the 2008 global financial crisis, with governments firefighting against a series of shocks including the pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) head Alexander de Croo said many developing countries had responded to the current spike in energy prices with blanket subsidies, but a succession of crises had left them with limited resources to keep that up.
"You have to repair your roof while at the same time your home is on fire," he told AFP, adding governments in the developing world did not have time to rebuild buffers or resolve previous shocks before being hit by new crises.
The IMF warned this week that while global growth had held up in the face of the energy crisis, that resilience was highly dependent on the boom in AI technology investments, and poorer countries not exposed to that were still struggling.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva had warned that "winter is coming" — an allusion to popular fantasy book series "Game of Thrones" — implying that a cataclysm was around the corner if the world did not prepare for it.
And De Croo added: "Some countries have a well-insulated house with money in the bank. Other countries have a house without a roof and no money in the bank.
"We're stumbling from one crisis into the other, and what countries need is some space, and some time, and access to financing."
Not getting the response right could be devastating. The UNDP warned in a new report that about 130 million people were at risk of being pushed into poverty this year if energy and food price increases were fully passed on without subsidies.
People in South and East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are at particular risk, the agency said.
With advanced economies seeing bond yields surge — owing to elevated inflation expectations, surging debt ratios and AI capital-raising activities — global borrowing costs have been rising.
That in turn, de Croo warned, had tightened space for developing countries to access the capital they needed to combat the shocks, with rising interest rates feeding into increasing debt payments.
According to UNDP, the median developing country now spends about 9.5 percent of government revenue on interest payments — the highest in a quarter of a century, and more than three times that in high-income countries.
"It starts to be a difficult situation to manage, and it takes away all their margin for policy," de Croo said.
The former Belgian prime minister said he would spend the week in Bangkok — where world economic policy leaders have gathered since Oct. 12— pushing for advanced economies and multilateral agencies to invest in economic growth, resilience and job creation in the developing world.
He also said recent stark cuts in international aid were having an impact on those countries.
The UNDP warned there was potentially more pain to come, with this year's El Nino climate phenomenon forecast to be the strongest on record.
That is expected to have widespread effects including flooding, droughts and other extreme events that are estimated to peak in early 2027.
De Croo also said private capital needed to step in to help fight some of the worst consequences of climate change.
"We see that the impact of climate has an economic cost. Avoiding that cost has a business case," he said.
