China Focus: Xinjiang's cotton fields nurturing new generation of tech-savvy farmers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:27:10 CST
15:27:10 KST

A cotton picker works at a cotton field in Donggou Village, Dianba Township of Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Gao Han)
URUMQI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- As golden October paints the Tianshan Mountains with autumn hues, cotton fields across Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China are bursting with white bolls ready for harvest.
At the "super cotton field" in Yuli County on the northern edge of the Taklimakan Desert, cotton pickers shuttle back and forth, gathering, compressing and baling the pristine white fibers into neat packages.
"We have deployed a new agricultural drone that requires no pilot operation, making cotton cultivation management even more intelligent," said Ai Haipeng, project director of this field.
Xinjiang is China's largest premium cotton production base, with output accounting for 92.8 percent of the national total in 2025. Its total yield and per-unit yield have ranked first in the country for 32 consecutive years. Across this region, smart farming scenarios are increasingly permeating every stage of cotton production, accelerating from demonstration projects to widespread adoption and giving rise to a cohort of "new-generation cotton farmers" who understand technology, excel at management and know how to run operations.
Yuli County, thanks to its arid climate and abundant sunlight, is an ideal base for premium commercial cotton cultivation, with a stable planting area of over one million mu (about 66,667 hectares). In 2021, via support from the county government, agricultural robotics company XAG launched the super cotton field project, sending Ai and Ling Lei, two post-1990s agronomists, to manage 3,000 mu of cotton fields and explore a replicable, scalable unmanned agricultural management model.
The pair began by tackling irrigation, the most labor-intensive aspect of cotton management, and continuously upgraded unmanned, intelligent monitoring technologies and equipment. This effort has made the super cotton field management model highly compatible with large-scale cotton cultivation, achieving higher yields and superior quality.
"Through years of effort, the project has achieved intelligent management of water, fertilizer and pesticides, with unmanned operation rates in management reaching 75 percent," Ai said. By the end of 2025, the super cotton field's cultivation management model had been extended to over two million mu across Xinjiang.
This year, the project introduced a new batch of equipment: the latest APC4 autopilot system enables seeders to automatically cut mulch film during planting, further saving labor. The most talked-about addition, however, is the X150 agricultural drone. This drone can automatically mix pesticides, refill, recharge, plan routes and execute autonomous spraying operations, catering to a range of field needs including weeding, pest control and disease prevention.
On Sept. 20, during the critical boll-opening period, Ai selected a template on his phone and tapped "Start." The drone then autonomously took off, landed and recharged -- with no pilot and no remote control required. On the phone screen, the status of the pesticide tank and ground chemical reserves were visible at a glance.
"In previous years, even with drones, we still needed pilots to control trajectories and handle refills and battery swaps. Now, you just leave the aircraft in the field and walk away. Go to bed at night, come back the next morning, and it has completed all plant protection tasks," Ai said. The new drone model has since been promoted nationwide.
"Our goal is to attract more young people back to agriculture. An industry only thrives when it has talent and young blood, giving it vitality and room for growth, and ultimately making Chinese agriculture better," Ai added.
In Donggou Village, Dianba Township of the city of Changji, located at the northern foot of the Tianshan Mountains, family farm owner Guo Teng, also born in the 1990s, sat watching a screen as he directed a massive cotton picker which was moving slowly through a sea of cotton, continuously ejecting neatly packed bales.
Guo, a native of Changji, represents the second generation of cotton farmers in his family. His father's generation, he recalled, faced brutal toil: one mu of cotton required enormous manual labor for management and harvesting. A single picker could harvest at most 10 mu per season, while several hundred mu required hiring over 40 workers, who started before dawn and toiled under the scorching sun. Harvest costs were high, and yet growers' incomes remained limited.
"I used to think farming was drudgery, exhausting and undignified. But now the countryside offers so much room for development that I naturally came back," Guo said. After graduating, he spent time in the city before recognizing that Xinjiang's increasingly technology-rich cotton fields were opening unprecedented opportunities for a new generation of farmers. After a discussion with his wife, Guo decided to return home to grow cotton.
Today, Guo's family farm is fully equipped with agricultural machinery, featuring four cotton pickers, six drones, over a dozen seeders and three high-horsepower tractors. Integrated water-fertilizer precision drip irrigation and drone-based fertilizing and pesticide application are used in the fields. He has also assembled long-term seasonal teams specializing in plowing, drone spraying, cotton harvesting and drip irrigation. From plowing and seeding to spraying and harvesting, the entire process is mechanized.
"One cotton picker can harvest 400 to 450 mu per day, with fuel and labor costs of just 60 yuan (9 U.S. dollars) per mu for the harvesting stage. What used to take dozens of workers an entire season can now be done by one machine," Guo said. Thanks to large-scale, mechanized operations, his 25,000 mu of cotton fields require only 50 workers for daily management.
"The more advanced the equipment, the higher the demands on the manager," Guo noted. Farmers in the new era are no longer mere manual laborers, but farm managers who understand machinery, data and business operations. Farming is now not a fallback livelihood but a respectable and promising career.
Returning to the countryside to grow cotton is becoming an increasingly popular choice for young people. Guo has observed that among his long-term collaborative teams, more and more young people are coming back. "As long as you master the skills and can operate a cotton picker, earning 50,000 yuan a month during the harvest season is entirely feasible. Working in cotton production in the countryside pays no less than working in the city," he said. ■

China 'dumped' aluminium windows and doors in Australia, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:23:06 UTC
15:23:06 KST

China 'dumped' aluminium windows, doors in Australia, preliminary trade report shows
In short
The preliminary report from the Australian Trade Remedies Commission found that Chinese aluminium windows and doors were sold here at unfair prices.
From October 15, importers must provide financial guarantees of up to 73.3 per cent of the product value when their goods enter the country.
What's next
The commission is due to make its final recommendation to the minister by December 16.
Australia's international trade monitor has found Chinese aluminium windows and doors were "dumped" here, heavily undercutting local prices and damaging the Australian industry.
Starting today, companies importing these goods will also have to put down a financial guarantee when their products enter the country, prompting a warning about higher construction costs and potential retaliation by China.
In a preliminary report, the Australian Trade Remedies Commission, formerly the Anti-Dumping Commission, found all Chinese exporters except one had dumped the goods between July 1, 2024 and June 30 last year.
The commission found the goods were sold with dumping margins ranging from 5.3 per cent to 70.4 per cent of their normal price, depending on the exporter.
Some exporters were also found to have received modest subsidies from various levels of government in China.
The commission found the Chinese imports had "caused material injury" to the Australian industry.
It estimated the local aluminium windows and doors market was worth about $2.8 billion during the investigation period.
Chinese imports accounted for 19 per cent of total sales, Australia accounted for about 79 per cent, and the remaining 2 per cent came from other countries.
According to the report, local manufacturers' sales volumes fell by about 19 per cent from July 2021 to June 2025.
Meanwhile, the value of their sales dropped about 14 per cent from a peak in the 2023 financial year, according to the report.
The commission found that half of the tenders and quotes they examined were about 30 per cent lower than the expected prices, while more than a quarter were undercut by 40 per cent or more.
It estimated the Australian industry had lost about $350 million due to undercutting by "dumped and/or subsidised imports from China".
The commission has proposed recommending Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres publish a dumping duty notice for Chinese goods, which would lead to duties imposed on those imports.
Chinese-made aluminium windows and doors currently face no tariffs under the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement.
A spokesperson for Mr Ayres said the Albanese government supported free and fair trade.
"The Australian Trade Remedies Commission initiates its rigorous, evidence-based investigations based on applications from industry," they said.
"Any trade remedies imposed are fully consistent with Australia's obligations under its trade agreements."
Securities could 'effectively lead to price increase'
While the investigation continues, the commissioner said financial securities were needed to "prevent material injury" to the Australian industry.
From today, importers will have to provide financial securities worth between 5.3 per cent and 73.3 per cent of the value of their products. The percentage will depend on the exporting company.
These securities are financial guarantees against duties that may become payable later. The industry minister will make the final decision on whether any duties are imposed.
UNSW international economic law professor Zhou Weihuan said duties were likely to be imposed, because it was "hard to change" the findings in the commission's preliminary report.
He said securities could "effectively lead to price increases" because importers would account for them in their pricing.
"The price impact would involve an increase in imported aluminium windows and doors, which in turn would push up construction costs for commercial and residential premises," Professor Zhou said.
'Protect competition from unfair trading'
The investigation began on November 25 after an application by Ventora Group and the Australian Glass and Window Association (AGWA).
The application alleged the local industry had "suffered material injury" through lost sales and price suppression.
"We're not asking government to protect Australian businesses from competition," Clinton Skeoch, AGWA's CEO, told the ABC.
"We're asking government to protect competition from unfair trading."
AGWA welcomed the securities and said they were "an important and positive development" for an industry that had faced significant pressure from dumped imports.
The ABC has approached China's Ministry of Commerce and the Chinese embassy for comment.
Professor Zhou said Chinese retaliation was unlikely, because China had historically taken far fewer anti-dumping and countervailing actions against Australia than Australia had against China.
"But it's not impossible, and if China decides to take action, then agricultural exports might be the target," he said.
Ventora commissioned testing on imported Chinese windows and AGWA made the results public.
The commission said it did not consider the testing results or other allegations about product quality or compliance in its preliminary findings.
Builders raise cost concerns
Melissa Byrne, Acting CEO of Master Builders Australia, said the group would "carefully review the commission's findings".
"At the same time, any measure that increases the cost of construction comes at a time when housing affordability and project feasibility remain under significant pressure,"
she said.
She said Australia "must not restrict the flow of high-quality, compliant building products and materials".
The final recommendations are due no later than December 16. The minister's decision is expected within 30 days of receiving them.
The final report will be published after the minister's decision.

This Spanish poet's work was banned and censored. Now it's an epic movie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:21:58 UTC
15:21:58 KST

Penélope Cruz lights up La Bola Negra, but the boys will break your heart
A titan of Spanish culture, the proud socialist, poet, playwright and theatre director Federico García Lorca was most likely executed, aged 38, by General Francisco Franco's Nationalist forces in August of 1938 as the country was torn apart by bloody civil war.
Lorca's works were banned until 1953, then heavily censored until Franco's death in 1975. Even then, Lorca's family concealed his overtly queer work for fear of tainting his legacy. The Sonnets of Dark Love emerged in 1983 against the family's will.
La Bola Negra, four pages of which Lorca penned shortly before his murder, has been adapted into an astonishing queer epic spanning 80-plus years by directorial duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known collectively as Los Javis.
Drawing on that fragment and the play La Piedra Oscura by screenplay co-writer Alberto Conejero, the Palme d'Or-nominated triumph is one of the biggest box office hits in Spanish history. It's easy to see why.
Slings and arrows
Told across three distinct storylines, La Bola Negra opens on bored-looking trumpet player Sebastián in 1937. Played by real-life musician and singer Guitarricadelafuente, replete with a mop of curly dark hair, he's part of a band tasked with musically accompanying a flyover by Benito Mussolini's Aviazione Legionaria.
But the Italians mistake the Nationalist-sympathising villagers practising the Nazi-inspiring saluto romano for Republicans, strafing the town square in a Guernica-like atrocity, leaving countless dead, including Sebastián's mother.
Sebastián goes on the run. Finding temporary sanctuary in a partially collapsed church, he scrabbles over the rubble as his lips almost touch those of a shattered sculpture of the saint that shares his name. The arrow punctures are an image that bleeds through this beautiful film.
He is soon captured by Nationalist soldiers and pressed into service as a prison guard. His ward is real-life Atlético Madrid player, actor and sometime Lorca lover Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau) who arrives, guts exposed, in a cart carrying the mostly dead.
As the maimed Rafael recuperates, a clearly dazzled Sebastián can't keep his eyes off the fallen soldier, illustrated by cinematographer Gris Jordana's aching camerawork fluttering erotically on the rise and fall of Rafael's Adam's apple.
Blackballed
Another storyline is set in Granada, 1932, before the war, and is centred on a wealthy young man named Carlos (novelist Milo Quifes, in his screen debut). Natty in a white pinstriped suit, he is attempting to gain membership of a prestigious private club. After each member votes via a white ball (for yes) or black (for no), he is cruelly rejected.
The whirr of the baubles dropping is another example of the film's potent imagery and a nod to the etymological origin of the film's title. He's barred because of his penchant for illicit meetings with men after dark and stolen glances at sunbathing sailors, which have become common knowledge.
Carlos's stern father (Antonio de la Torre) insists he must man up, explicitly linking gender to sexuality, and deny these "scurrilous" rumours and gain entry — but a subtler blow comes from his loving sister (Natalia de Molina) as she reflects on how she curbs her own wishes and hews to societal expectations, imploring him to do likewise.
The unique burble of a notification on hook-up app Grindr bursts the bubble of these historical strands.
This time it's queer music historian Alberto (Carlos González) who's cruising. It's now 2017, and he's stunned by an unexpected inheritance from his late grandfather, a man he does not know. Alberto's ferociously cranky mother (a magnificently bolshy Lola Dueñas), still aggrieved at his abandonment of their family, yells at Alberto to ignore the summons to Cantabria.
Similarly reluctant, Alberto is cajoled into going by his boyfriend, Juan (a surprisingly understated cameo by comedian Julio Torres), who points out the perversity of a historian uninterested in his own past.
What awaits him in Cantabria will tear off the scabs of his family history and that of the country, as these seemingly disparate strands twist tighter.
Face the music and dance
That La Bola Negra can paint on such a large canvas, holding close to its characters and their truths while honouring Lorca — portrayed by Alberto Cortés in black-and-white flashbacks — is remarkable. Particularly as Los Javis shoot for something grander than a bog-standard biopic.
Depressingly rare these days, the filmmakers understand that film can use light and sound in subtly destabilising ways. They know how to frame their players, adored by Jordana's lens, in conversation with one another beyond the verbal.
In union with their frequent editor Alberto Gutiérrez, they stitch these non-linear threads together in supple fashion, finding room for fireworks on the beach and Glenn Close speaking Spanish.
A show-stopping cameo from Penélope Cruz as Nené, a spectacular cupletista in the grand mould of Olga Ramos, is a performance for the ages that delivers loaded drama.
In one of the film's most tender moments, Nené encourages Sebastián to flee the army and find himself in Madrid, sharing her adoration of historic drag star Edmond de Bries, saying that his bravery, "Is the fantasy of the possible, and war is the opposite."
Snowdrifts
La Bola Negra is full of such tantalising possibility, of hope for a better, truer life, with Carlos's mother (María Morales) also begging him to leave for Madrid. It's the city where Lorca and Rafael fell into one another's embrace, inspiring those once-lost sonnets.
As Cortés's Lorca says, "This country has too many love stories buried in the fields. We have to scratch the earth so they can emerge. So more of them can exist."
La Bola Negra is such a releasing scratch, a great heaving sigh for the stories never told, for the lovers bold and lost, their stories resurfaced. There are moments, like a stolen embrace in a darkened cell, a pinprick of light piercing the dark like a Goya painting, that will wound you. It is a work of art as soft and scalding as the snow that drifts to Los Javis's majestically unmooring conclusion, then lingering on.
La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

China’s CXMT gets pledge of support as provincial party chief vows chip-industry expansion
Anhui province party secretary and former MIIT head Li Lecheng vows to foster IC ecosystem during visit to memory giant’s headquarters
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Emma Main Shanghai
Three weeks into his tenure as the Communist Party secretary of Anhui province, Li Lecheng carried out an on-site inspection at China’s home-grown memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) on Wednesday, pledging to grow integrated circuits (ICs) as an emerging pillar industry.

Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Kyiv observed the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump, only to face intensified Russian attacks and slower Starlink satellite communications.
Source: Financial Times
Details: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy said in a forthright interview with the FT in London. He also sharply criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Asked to explain the relationship between the two leaders, Zelenskyy said Trump has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and extremely wealthy people.
"He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong," Zelenskyy said.
The FT noted that Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that a moratorium on the attacks, together with an agreement to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel, is necessary to bring down fuel prices in the US.
Zelenskyy said he had suspended strikes on energy facilities for three days to accommodate the US request. However, Moscow continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure and kill civilians, with more than 100 people killed in the past week.
The president also said that, despite Ukraine suspending its strikes, its forces had been left without US early-warning systems for incoming ballistic missiles. Starlink satellite communications, operated by Elon Musk's company, had also been slowed across the country, making battlefield operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military facilities more difficult.
The FT wrote that the deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington marks the most serious crisis between Ukraine and its most important security partner since the Oval Office spat in February 2025.
"Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine's relationship with the US as an 'honest' and 'strategic' partner was essential in the fight against Russia, comparing it to Kyiv's relationship with the UK," the FT noted.
Asked whether Ukraine would stop striking oil refineries even if Russia continued its attacks, in an effort to repair relations with the White House, Zelenskyy said he would agree to do so only if the US supplied him with more American-made Patriot interceptors.
He believes that halting strikes on oil refineries could simply encourage the US and Russia to strike further deals, potentially providing additional funding for Putin's war machine.
"The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas," Zelenskyy said.
He added that the US suspension of intelligence sharing and disruption of Starlink services has become "dangerous" for Ukraine.
"We will find a way out . . . but it's better not to give him [Putin] the new life or the new will to fight," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- Later, Zelenskyy reported a Russian strike on CHP-5 [a combined heat and power plant] in Kharkiv and a power station in Kyiv following Trump's statement.
- On 13 October Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and energy facilities for two days in response to a proposal by Trump. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure.

G20 finance ministers, central bankers gather amid fallout from Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:16:46 UTC
15:16:46 KST

G20 finance ministers, central bankers gather amid fallout from Iran war
Officials meet in Thailand as conflict drives energy prices higher and casts uncertainty over global economy.
The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday amid an uncertain global outlook shaped by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meetings are being held in conjunction with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, taking place in the Thai capital from October 12 to October 18.
Here are some of the key details about the meetings:
What are the G20, the IMF and the World Bank?
The G20 is an economic forum comprising 19 large economies, including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil, India, Japan, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia, as well as the European Union and the African Union.
The grouping has an annually rotating presidency, currently held by the US.
Together, the G20 countries account for about 85 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and three-quarters of global trade.
The G20 was established in 1999 as a forum for finance ministers and central bank governors to address shared economic concerns in the wake of the Asian Financial Crisis, before expanding into a broader forum for national leaders.
The IMF, based in Washington, DC, is an international financial institution that promotes international cooperation on monetary policy, trade and economic growth.
Its membership includes all but a handful of the world’s sovereign states, including North Korea, Cuba, the Vatican City and Monaco.
The World Bank, also based in Washington, DC, primarily serves as a provider of loans and grants to developing countries. It has 189 member countries.
The IMF and the World Bank were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference in the US, convened by the Allied Powers to establish the contours of the post-World War II international financial order.
Who will be attending the meetings?
Most finance ministers and central bank governors of the G20 will be in Bangkok, along with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be a notable absence from the gatherings, as the top economic official of the world’s biggest economy and G20 chair.
US officials have cited “domestic engagements” for Bessent’s decision to skip the events, at which Washington will be represented by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke and Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne.
The G20 meeting, one of several gatherings of the group’s finance ministers each year, will help shape the agenda for the headline leaders’ summit in Miami, Florida, taking place on December 14-15.
What is on the agenda?
The economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran is expected to dominate discussions.
Attacks across the Middle East have upended economic activity across the region, while disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has driven a surge in energy prices worldwide.
Crude oil prices have exceeded $100 a barrel for much of the past eight months, placing a strain on government coffers and household budgets, particularly in the Gulf region and the rest of Asia.
In advance of the meeting, Australia’s Treasurer Jim Chalmers MP said he would use the discussions to call for an end to the conflicts in the Middle East and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz “because that’s what the global economy desperately needs”.
“The war in the Middle East is having a devastating economic impact and is pushing up fuel prices, inflation and interest rates around the world,” Chalmers said in a statement.
Other issues likely to feature on the agenda include the ballooning debt levels of many countries, which exceed 100 percent of GDP in the US, Canada, Japan, Italy and France.
In a speech on Wednesday, Georgieva warned that mounting debt posed a threat to the global economy and that there was no “magic” formula that would allow governments to avoid tax hikes or spending cuts.
G20 members will also bring more specific individual concerns to the table based on their economic and geopolitical priorities.
The US, for example, has repeatedly expressed concern about “global imbalances”, a veiled reference to China’s state-driven industrial model that has allowed Chinese exporters to flood overseas markets with cheap goods.
US President Donald Trump has long claimed that China’s large trade surplus, which stood at a cumulative $938bn in September, proves that international trade is stacked against US manufacturers.
In a statement addressed to the IMF on Wednesday, Bessent called for action to address mismatched trade balances.
“This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances,” Bessent said.
“Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment.”
Divisions and competing interests cloud the prospects for coordination, however.
At the last meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, North Carolina, US, held on August 31 and September 1, member countries failed to issue a joint communique after China objected to language to do with trade.

What is Palestine Action? Sally Rooney Books to No Longer Be Sold in U.K. Over Ties to Group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:15:15 UTC
15:15:15 KST

Sally Rooney’s publisher said the Irish author will no longer sell her books in the U.K. after the country banned a pro-Palestinian group she promised to financially support.
Rooney had pledged to donate royalties from her bestselling novels, which include ‘Intermezzo’ and ‘Normal People,’ to Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organization by the British government. Her publisher, Faber, said in a statement on Wednesday that it decided to no longer supply her work “in the U.K. in any format.”
“Current legislation in the U.K. has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on U.K. earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said.
The news has inflamed debate over the British government’s unprecedented decision to use terrorism powers to ban a group primarily known for property damage and disruption. The group describes its aim as halting the supply of weapons to Israel and ending what it describes as British complicity in Israel’s “genocide” of Palestinians.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas terror attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in 251 others taken hostage. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the Gaza Health Ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. Data from the Israel Defense Forces as of May 2025 suggested a Palestinian civilian death rate of 83%.
Israel denies allegations of genocide.
Rooney has long expressed her support for the group, and called the British proscription “a truly extreme assault on ordinary rights and freedoms.”
Here’s what to know about the group and how the British government’s ban affects Rooney.
What is Palestine Action?
Palestine Action is a pro-Palestinian group based in the U.K. that describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime.” The group has targeted facilities linked to Israeli weapons manufacturing or supplies.
“Every moment we can disrupt them is a victory, as halting production at one site interrupts their whole supply chain and has a knock on effect to other factories. If one action stops one weapon from killing a Palestinian, then it’s all worth it,” the group’s website reads.
Since its founding in 2020, members of Palestine Action have repeatedly damaged U.K. facilities linked to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems. Elbit Systems U.K. denied claims that its facilities supplied the Israeli military.
In June 2025, Palestine Action members broke into R.A.F. Brize Norton, the U.K.’s largest air force base, and spray painted two aircraft.
The British government banned the group in July 2025, proscribing it as a terrorist organization. It was the first British proscription primarily based on property damage, rather than threat or use of violence against people, although the government said the group’s members have demonstrated “a willingness to use violence.”
The group’s leaders have said it does not advocate or use violence against people.
“In several attacks, Palestine Action has committed acts of serious damage to property with the aim of progressing its political cause and influencing the Government,” then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper said in announcing the proscription.
The ban has faced a series of legal challenges. In February, the High Court ruled it unlawful and disproportionate, but the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June. The ban remains in force, with the Supreme Court scheduled to hear a further appeal early next month.
How does the ban affect Rooney and others?
Since the ban, more than 3,000 people have been arrested for expressing support for the group at demonstrations. Among these were protesters holding signs with the words, “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
The ban and ensuing arrests prompted debate over free speech and the use of counterterrorism laws against political protest. The U.K. protects freedom of expression under the Human Rights Act, but permits broader restrictions than the U.S. First Amendment, including on national security and public order grounds. Inviting or expressing support for a proscribed organization, even without inciting violence, can be a criminal offence in the U.K. Critics argued that criminalizing support for Palestine Action threatened peaceful dissent. The government, however, has maintained that the ban on the group does not prevent lawful protests in support of pro-Palestinian causes.
After the ban, Rooney pledged to donate money from her book sales to the group. In an August 2025 op-ed in the Irish Times, Rooney wrote, “I want to be clear that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can.”
“To ensure that the British public is made aware of my position, I would happily publish this statement in a U.K. newspaper—but that would now be illegal,” the author added. “The present U.K. Government has willingly stripped its own citizens of basic rights and freedoms, including the right to express and read dissenting opinions, in order to protect its relationship with Israel.”
Providing financial support to organizations designated under the U.K.’s Terrorism Act is a criminal offense. In a statement circulated by her agent, Rooney said “the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the U.K. could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the U.K.”
The decision to withdraw Rooney’s books from the U.K. has reignited debate over the ban. Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, told The Guardian that “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action.”
British Member of Parliament Ian Byrne called on the government to reconsider the ban, noting that he had “warned of the draconian consequences it would bring.”
“Now this injustice against one of the finest writers of her generation. An utterly disgraceful attack on freedom of expression,” he said on social media.
Rooney reaffirmed her intention to support Palestine Action, “which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.”
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions,” the author said. “And I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

Coalition and Greens unite to be a thorn in the government’s side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:13:55 UTC
15:13:55 KST

analysis
Government takes a battering as departing senator urges Liberals not to give up
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
As parting messages go, Jonno Duniam's was upbeat as he urged his colleagues not to wave the white flag in the battle against a rising One Nation.
It was a packed crowd for the Tasmanian Liberal senator's valedictory speech as he said farewell to the chamber he's spent the last decade serving.
Many, including Labor's Katy Gallagher, tried to convince Duniam to stay on after he came to realise the toll the job was having on him and his family following the Liberal leadership contest earlier this year.
As Angus Taylor watched on, Duniam's final speech addressed — without naming — One Nation's accession in the polls. He urged the Coalition not to stray too far from its roots as it tries to claw back support that's fallen away to Pauline Hanson's party.
"My party can give Australians what they need, not by pretending to be someone else or seeking to appease certain actors but by returning to our roots — by backing in [our values] with conviction … and explaining why it is better than the alternative," he told the chamber on Wednesday.
The question of how to tackle One Nation has plagued the opposition for the better half of the year, with some suggesting the way forward is to strike up preference deals with the party.
Others — such as the man Duniam called a "brother", Andrew Hastie — think the party should confront the issue head on.
Duniam said he could not deny the impact several election losses had, but insisted the challenge wasn't insurmountable.
"My party has been around for decades. It isn't populist. It isn't flash in the pan. It is here to stay," he said.
"Sure, we may have spent some time in the wilderness, but we have our bearings now and I know we will be able to get back over there into government."
Public shaming and Powderfinger
Small business frustration with the government has been pretty easy pickings for the Coalition.
The minister in charge, Anne Aly, was the target for much of the week, as the Coalition singled her out as a weak link. Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell went too far when she declared Aly, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, should be "shamed and stoned" over the ATO's decision.
She later conceded it was a poor choice of words after Aly, the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament, shared that she'd received 19 death threats that week couched in similar language. The opposition quickly dismissed criticism the remarks were "racist and misogynistic" as a distraction from Aly's performance as minister.
The backlash over changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, the ATO credit card ban and now the fight over discretionary trusts are adding up.
As David Speers wrote this morning, it's not been an easy couple of months for Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
The result is a jittery caucus. The prime minister tried to calm the farm this week by reviving an old slogan.
He reminded Labor it wanted to "kick with the wind in the fourth quarter" — a phrase he repeated a lot when caucus was equally anxious back when he was opposition leader.
The prime minister didn't help matters by giving the impression he made a captain's call on the ATO's credit card ban after a text message from a business leader.
Chalmers denied he'd been rolled. Albanese had to walk back the statement in question time when Taylor asked how much longer he was going to "humiliate" his treasurer.
"The whole premise of it is completely wrong," he said.
It wasn't just tension between Albanese and Chalmers on show: an old colleague came back to haunt the Liberal Party this week.
The reemergence of Josh Frydenberg, and the unanswered question of whether his recent memoir was just the first step in a mooted comeback, frustrated some within the party.
Overall, the Liberals gave the former treasurer a pretty lukewarm response. If he can win preselection and be successful in 2028, then he's welcome to join Taylor's frontbench, Deputy leader Jane Hume said.
Garth Hamilton, a backbencher from Queensland, was less excited about the prospect.
"The only comeback I'm interested in seeing at the moment is Powderfinger," he told Afternoon Briefing.
Loading
Sometimes it makes sense, sometimes it doesn't
It's not just tax changes giving the government headaches. When it comes to a contentious wind back of a Howard-era private health insurance rebate, it appears Labor is well and truly up against it.
It wants to scale back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on private health cover from next year. The changes would bank $3 billion that would then be spent elsewhere in the aged care sector.
But the bill is pretty friendless. Partially because it'll capture more Australians than first flagged, but also because about $1.6 billion of the forecast savings would be clawed back from pensioners.
The Coalition isn't for turning on this one; it'll oppose it to the bitter end, and as my colleague Stephanie Dalzell foreshadowed last week, the Greens aren't fans either. While they're against private health of any kind, they also don't want to be taking away benefits from pensioners.
Anyone closely watching this, i.e the government, shouldn't have been surprised when the Coalition and Greens teamed up with independent Jacqui Lambie to have the bill struck off the parliamentary agenda on Wednesday.
In her typical bluster, Lambie urged Health Minister Mark Butler not to reintroduce the bill.
She warned if he carried on "like a two-year-old" and did so anyway; the Senate would just "slap" it back down. Butler re-introduced the exact same bill again.
In his valedictory address, Duniam compared the Senate to a French film: sometimes it makes sense, sometimes it doesn't.
As the fight over private health showed this week, the chamber does have a flare for drama.
With three sitting weeks left, the dramatics will be on show as the government tries to negotiate its way through before the parliament rises for the year.

A 68-year-old woman died on Wednesday from injuries sustained during last week's 7.7-magnitude earthquake in Panama, officials said, marking the first death recorded in the natural disaster.
Thousands have been left homeless following Friday's temblor, which injured around 30 people and caused severe damage to buildings, bridges and roads, blocking access routes in the country's central region.
The victim, identified as Elena Barria, "was seriously injured during the earthquake," according to a statement from Panama's social security officials.
Local media reported she was a resident of Macaracas in the hard-hit central province of Los Santos.
‘Major disaster’
The shallow quake struck at 1756 GMT on Friday, with its epicentre about 10 kilometres from Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province, according to the US Geological Survey, which initially measured it at magnitude 8.0 before revising it to 7.7.
The tremor lasted about a minute and was felt across the country. In Panama City, about 200 kilometres from the epicentre, people rushed to evacuate skyscrapers as buildings shook.
President Jose Raul Mulino called the quake a "major disaster" and travelled to Penonome to coordinate the response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos were among the hardest-hit provinces, with the town of Tonosi cut off by damaged roads.
Panama City's international airport was temporarily closed, and several flights were diverted. A tsunami warning for the eastern Pacific was later lifted, while the Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the waterway continued normally.
More than 400 aftershocks have been reported since the initial quake. Earthquakes are relatively rare in Panama and more commonly occur in the western province of Chiriqui, which borders Costa Rica.

Manosphere experts warn if we lecture boys 'we lose them'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:54:54 UTC
14:54:54 KST

What is the manosphere? How can you help someone drawn in? Your questions answered
If you're worried about the pull of the manosphere, but don't know how to help someone in your life who has been drawn in, you're not alone.
We asked a panel of experts to answer your common questions about the manosphere, masculinity and how to approach conversations about it.
Read what developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey, psychologist Dr Zac Seidler from Movember and Genevieve Sheppard from Our Watch had to say below.
If you or someone you know needs help, you can click here to find a full list of resources at the end of this article.
What is the manosphere?
There's no single definition of the manosphere, but generally, it's the term used to describe online communities that promote narrow definitions of masculinity that oppose feminism and the gains of the gender-equality movement.
As UN Women describes, "these communities promote the idea that emotional control, material wealth, physical appearance and dominance, especially over women, are markers of male worth".
The ideas in the manosphere are nothing new. Misogyny has been prevalent for a very long time. What’s different today is the reach and business model. Online platforms connect these groups, algorithms amplify their messages, and influencers can profit from attention and outrage.
A recurring tactic of those who promote messages on the manosphere is to take real difficulties — loneliness, financial insecurity or uncertainty about relationships — and blame women and feminism.
That offers a simple, yet inaccurate explanation, which also reinforces male entitlement and resentment. This is a harmful message for all young people to believe and absorb.
To counter this, we need to address the challenges boys and men face while challenging the idea that women owe them sex, attention or obedience. That means well-resourced respectful relationships education in every school across Australia, supportive communities and opportunities to build belonging and connection without dominance.
What are the signs someone is in the manosphere and how can I help?
Watching out for this stuff early and discussing it in an open and curious way is the best solution to staying connected with someone skirting around the edges of this content, as it pulls you in very quickly if you are in a certain headspace.
Some things to look out for:
New language: Terms like "alpha", "high value", "red pill", "simp" or "the matrix", or talking about women in transactional or contemptuous ways.
One-source thinking: Constantly quoting the same few influencers, and treating them as the only people telling "the truth".
Rising grievance: A growing sense that the world is rigged against men, or that women, feminism or "the system" are to blame for how they feel.
Pulling back: Withdrawing from friends or family who disagree, or becoming dismissive and defensive when challenged (this can also be a sign of broader mental health challenges or a change in character).
Rigid self-improvement: Gym, money and discipline aren't bad things. It's a flag when they come with shame, contempt for "weak" men, or the idea that your worth depends on dominance.
Some recommendations for what to do:
Stay close! Your relationship is the best antidote, but it's key to avoid shocking or shaming them.
Get curious, not combative. What does he like about this guy? What does that video tell him about what it means to be successful and what it is giving him? Usually there's a real need underneath: loneliness, rejection, feeling lost or unseen.
Don't try to win in one conversation. You won't argue your way to victory. Be consistent and caring.
Offer an alternative. Take him out, show him the world, and help him interact with other people.
How can we challenge misogynistic views without alienating boys?
This can be tough, and I fail at it too. Start with curiosity because correction often leads to conflict. "What makes you feel like that, mate?" If we lecture them, we lose them.
Separate the belief from who they are. "You've got such a big heart mate, you're better than saying those things about girls and women". We hold the line while also keeping our belief in them as good people.
Look for the underlying need. Many boys are lost and unhealthy messages hook them with the promise of confidence, power and success. Once we understand that, we can offer better pathways for them to meet these needs, and help them see those voices are chasing their own money, status and control.
We can also share our own story, the traps we've fallen into, the hurt we've experienced and caused, and most importantly how we repaired and found a better way ourselves.
How can I approach this with my younger kids?
These conversations can be scary but they are already happening for our kids without us there to guide them. Our best chance is to start with low pressure, when our kids feel safe, like during a walk around the block with just us or while playing together with no-one else around.
We know body language, tone of voice and lack of judgement are just as important as what we actually say, if not more. Getting down to their eye level, sitting side by side facing the same direction, and keeping the conversation slow and casual helps. We also want to explore their experiences. "What do you think boys are like? What about girls?" is a gentle way to understand their beliefs without pressure or shame.
We can also go first as a way for them to be safe too. "When I'm scared, sometimes I get angry. It doesn't help much so I try to work on asking others for help instead." It's also important this never feels like a single conversation we need to deliver perfectly. The most important part is that over time our children feel more safe to come to us for support in understanding their world.
Is the manosphere a 'passing wave' or something bigger?
Honestly, I don't think it's either/or yet. It's going to take time to understand how the moment we are in potentially differs from the gender reckonings that have come before, but it would be remiss of me not to say that this is in no way a 'passing wave', given the volume and ferocity of online misogyny fuelled by tech platforms. The underpinning themes have not changed, their reach has.
What I see clinically is that the content itself is a symptom. Our research at Movember has told us that young men aren't drawn in by misogyny. They're drawn in by someone finally speaking to their loneliness, their sense of purpose and their worries about the future. The misogyny comes bundled with that, and therefore can probably be purposefully decoupled.
What are young men searching for in these spaces?
Many young men are lonely, often more than they'd admit, and these spaces offer an instant sense of brotherhood. You're part of something, you share a language and someone's on your side.
Then there's direction. Plenty of boys feel lost about who they're meant to be and where their life is heading. The manosphere gives them a clear script: Here's what a man is, here are the rules, here's the plan. When everything feels uncertain, that clarity is very attractive.
Respect and status matter too. Young men want to feel they count and that people see them as capable. When that isn't happening at school, at work or in relationships, someone promising to make them "high value" is hard to ignore.
Underneath many of these is a need to make sense of pain. Rejection, failure, anxiety and feeling invisible all hurt, and most boys haven't been given the words or the space to talk about that. These spaces give them an explanation and often someone to blame. That can feel better than sitting with the hurt.
None of these needs are the problem. They're completely normal, healthy human needs. The problem is that the manosphere offers a distorted way of meeting them. If we want boys to walk away, we have to offer them real belonging, purpose and respect in their everyday lives.

Türkiye, Italy seek to expand archaeological cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:49:23 UTC
14:49:23 KST

The Göbeklitepe show at Rome’s Colosseum draws 6 million visitors.
Türkiye and Italy are seeking to expand archaeological cooperation through joint excavations, conservation projects and exhibitions, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said on Oct. 14 at the opening of the 17th Symposium of Italian Archaeological Missions in the ancient city of Hierapolis in Denizli.
Noting that Italian excavations at Hierapolis began 70 years ago, Ersoy said scientists from Pamukkale University were also contributing to the work under the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Legacy to the Future Project.
Archaeology today extends beyond uncovering ancient structures to include conservation, restoration, visitor management, museum work and scientific research, Ersoy said, stressing the importance of preserving archaeological sites for future generations.
Türkiye has expanded archaeological research in recent years while strengthening cooperation between Turkish and foreign research teams, he said. Italian scientists are working at sites including Aslantepe, Hierapolis, Uşaklı Höyük, Karkamış Höyük and Yumuktepe, with Turkish academics participating in the excavations.
Denizli is also home to ongoing research at ancient sites including Laodicea, Hierapolis, Tripolis, Kolossai and Attouda. Conservation and visitor-management projects are being carried out alongside excavations, Ersoy said.
Ersoy highlighted cultural initiatives between the two countries, including the exhibition “Göbeklitepe: The Mystery of a Sacred Place” at Rome’s Colosseum, which attracted approximately six million visitors.
A subsequent exhibition, “Troy and Rome: Myths, Legends and Stories of the Ancient Mediterranean,” features 221 artifacts from Turkish museums and explores the historical and mythological connections between the two civilizations.
Plans are also underway to develop scientific and cultural cooperation between the ancient city of Ephesus and the Pompeii Archaeological Park. A joint project at the ancient city of Elaiussa Sebaste in Mersin, in cooperation with Italy’s Central Institute for Archaeology, is targeted for launch in 2027.
Turkish and Italian specialists are also collaborating on cultural heritage conservation in Cappadocia, particularly the preservation of wall paintings.
Ersoy said the return of cultural artifacts seized in Italy demonstrated the countries’ cooperation in combating illicit trafficking.
A concert featuring Italian violinist Riccardo Zamuner and the İzmir State Symphony Orchestra, scheduled to take place at Hierapolis’ ancient theater following the ceremony, was canceled due to rain.

US weighs using 'Mother of All Bombs' in potential strikes on Iran: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:45 UTC
14:48:45 KST

The US military has developed new strike plans that include the potential use of the “Mother of All Bombs” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations, CNN reported on Wednesday, citing multiple US officials familiar with the plans.
The proposed use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, would mark a significant escalation in the conflict with Iran.
However, officials have questioned whether the weapon could achieve Washington’s military objectives.
According to CNN, Trump has directed the military to prepare additional strike options against Iranian targets, including energy infrastructure and facilities linked to the country’s nuclear programme.
The plans could be activated before or after the upcoming US midterm elections if the president decides to resume major combat operations.
One source familiar with the planning told CNN that strikes could take place before US forces withdraw from the US Central Command area of responsibility, potentially allowing the administration to launch further attacks before declaring victory and pulling out its forces.
A second source said plans targeting Iranian nuclear sites explicitly included the possible deployment of the MOAB, including against a suspected underground facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Pickaxe Mountain in the Isfahan province, where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The president has maintained that preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remains a central objective of the US campaign.
Doubts over effectiveness
A US official told CNN that military planners routinely prepare a range of options for policymakers, from lower-intensity operations to more powerful strikes against heavily fortified targets.
However, the MOAB's effectiveness against deeply buried nuclear facilities remains uncertain.
The GPS-guided bomb can devastate a surface area equivalent to about nine city blocks, but it is not designed to penetrate deep underground.
Sources cited by CNN said it would likely struggle to destroy facilities protected by thick layers of granite and other fortifications.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the planning discussions told CNN, describing it as unsuitable for deep penetration.
If deployed, the bomb could cause extensive destruction at the point of impact. Its large blast radius could also raise serious concerns about civilian casualties, particularly if energy infrastructure near populated areas or other civilian facilities were targeted.
The MOAB was previously used only once in combat, in 2017, against a Daesh terror group hideout in a cave complex in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province.
Psychological pressure
Despite its limitations, US officials have reportedly considered the weapon’s potential psychological impact as part of the administration’s broader military options.
One source told CNN that Trump could face pressure to take further action against Iran despite uncertainty over whether additional strikes would force Tehran to accept Washington’s demands.
The source suggested the MOAB could be used to exert psychological pressure, particularly given the limitations of available munitions against deeply buried targets.

New artifacts unearthed at Ordu’s ancient Kurul Castle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:44 UTC
14:48:44 KST

Finds include a statue of Cybele, a figure of the child Dionysus and a representation of Pan, along with animal-shaped composite vessels. (AA Photo)
Archaeological excavations at Ordu’s Kurul Castle, which began in 2010, are continuing to uncover new artifacts at the ancient site.
According to a statement from Ordu Municipality, the 2,300-year-old Kurul Castle, located in the Bayadı neighborhood of the Altınordu district, stands out as the first scientific archaeological excavation site in the Eastern Black Sea region.
The excavations are being conducted under the leadership of Professor Süleyman Yücel Şenyurt, a faculty member in the Department of Archaeology at Ankara Hacı Bayram Veli University, with support from Ordu Metropolitan Municipality.
Finds unearthed at the site to date include a statue of Cybele estimated to be 2,150 years old, a figure of the child Dionysus, a representation of Pan, who raised him, and animal-shaped composite vessels associated with the cult of Dionysus and Pan.
Ordu Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Mehmet Hilmi Güler visited the ongoing excavation site and received information about the work from Şenyurt.
Güler said the site was an archaeological and historical treasure where discoveries were shedding light on the past.
Describing Kurul Castle as a source of cultural and historical wealth, Güler said approximately 40 percent of the excavation work had been completed and that academics were working intensively at the site.
“We have made important discoveries here dating to the period associated with Dionysus. These artifacts will both shed light on the past and add significant value to this region,” Güler said.
He added that the finds indicated that Kurul Castle was not merely a fortress but also a settlement.
Important discoveries
Şenyurt said the team had uncovered significant finds in the region, particularly the statue of Cybele.
Noting that Kurul Castle had attracted attention with discoveries that surprised the scientific community, he said the latest finds would introduce two divine figures from Anatolia to the scientific and cultural worlds in connection with the cult of Dionysus.
“With this year’s finds, we will introduce two god and goddess figures from Anatolia to the scientific community and the cultural world, alongside the cult of Dionysus,” Şenyurt said.
He thanked the relevant ministry and Ordu Metropolitan Municipality for their support, adding that the discoveries at Kurul Castle could serve as a model for future archaeological research.
Şenyurt noted that the Eastern Black Sea region contained cultural heritage sites hidden beneath dense vegetation.
“Kurul Castle has had the opportunity to make these discoveries, but it has also set an example for us. There is cultural heritage hidden beneath the vegetation in the Eastern Black Sea region. Kurul Castle has ignited the spark for future work,” he said.

An Istanbul fisheries union has sparked consumer outrage after calling for a fishing pause when a surge in bonito catches drove prices down, leading to accusations of price gouging.
The Istanbul Provincial Union of Seafood Fishers and Producers (Istanbul DEMBİR) set the requested pause from midnight until 8 a.m. on Oct. 12, saying a short break would help fishers earn a fair return without amounting to a ban.
Some social media users called the appeal opportunistic and urged authorities to investigate. One wrote fishers resented earning from one bonito what they had previously made from two.

Aksoy said bonito is a migratory fish and could move to Georgia and return, making it harder to catch in November. He urged fishers to limit catches, saying excess fish loses value and can be crushed and spoil aboard boats. He said the goal was to balance supply with demand, not make consumers pay more.
The Istanbul DEMBİR notice said lower prices led fishers to catch more to offset losses, adding to supply and driving prices down further. It called the cycle economically unsustainable.
Türkiye’s commercial fishing season reopened on Sept. 1 after an annual ban from April 15 to Sept. 1 to protect fish stocks during spawning. Fishermen along Türkiye’s Black Sea coast had forecast an abundant bonito harvest, expecting larger catches to lower prices for consumers.

3D models recreate 7.7-million-year-old fauna

14:48:23 KST

DHA Photo
Anthropologists in Türkiye’s central province of Kayseri are creating 3D miniatures of 10 animals whose fossils date back 7.5 to 7.7 million years, giving visitors a glimpse of the region’s prehistoric fauna.
The figures, made from polymer clay and based on fossils found near Yamula Dam, include four elephant models, two rhinoceroses, a giraffe, a three-toed horse, a bovid similar to a modern antelope and a saber-toothed tiger. The miniatures will be displayed at Kayseri Science Center.
“We created this display to satisfy visitors’ curiosity and show what 10 different creatures from that period looked like, both morphologically and physically,” Expert Anthropologist Ömer Dağ said.
The team sculpted the figures in clay, scanned them in 3D and reproduced them with resin printers.
Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality supplied a resin printer and the models will be painted before being placed in a miniature habitat exhibit.
Rising water levels at the dam delayed fieldwork in 2026, so the team split in two, with one group continuing excavations and the other working in the laboratory. The display will show two of the elephant models in a forest setting and two in open terrain, allowing visitors to compare their physical differences.
Shepherd Murat Adıyaman found a bone fragment near the dam in the Taşhan area of Kocasinan district in 2017. Initial tests dated the fragments to between 6 million and 7.5 million years ago. The Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums authorized excavations in 2018.

Divers have begun exploring shipwrecks off the coast of the western province of Muğla’s Bodrum district following a campaign opening the protected underwater site.

The treacherous shallows around Yassıada hold 11 sunken ships on ancient routes, including five overlapping Roman and Byzantine vessels. Documentary producer Tahsin Ceylan filmed the artifacts alongside Bodrum Coast Guard dive teams, specialist instructor Ahmet Yaşar and underwater photographer Mehtap Akbaş Çiftci. “We have always tried to open the area to tourism because it is one of the most important places in the archaeology world,” he said.
Crews excavated a Roman wreck from 1961 to 1964, while operations resumed in 1974, leading to the recovery of an Ottoman vessel in the 1980s. Experts completed excavations on three ships in total, with the site now needing international promotion. The Yassıada shallows gained international fame in the 1960s when scientists pioneered modern underwater excavation techniques on its ancient shipwrecks.

Turkish television dramas, which reach an estimated 1 billion people worldwide, are helping popularize the Turkish language and promote the country’s culture abroad, according to Murat Yancı, head of the television group at Demirören Media, who spoke at MIPCOM 2026, a major international television content market in Cannes, France.
“Turkish series reach 1 billion people worldwide,” Yancı said, noting that viewers in different countries increasingly report learning Turkish by watching the programs.
“When we ask them, ‘Where did you learn Turkish?’ they say, ‘From Turkish series,’” he said, describing the productions as a form of cultural influence that extends beyond entertainment.
Yancı said Turkish-language television dramas ranked second globally in terms of international reach, behind English-language productions. He added that international sales of Turkish series amounted to approximately $1 billion last year.
“On the one hand, we export Turkish culture and the Turkish language. Turkish series are, in a sense, a power that conducts diplomacy on our behalf,” he said, describing the productions as an important instrument of Türkiye’s soft power.
Running through Oct. 15 at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès in Cannes, MIPCOM 2026 brings together more than 10,000 industry professionals from over 100 countries to showcase television content, negotiate distribution agreements and explore international partnerships.
Kanal D, owned by Demirören Media, is attending through its international distribution arm, Kanal D International, presenting its latest dramas to prospective buyers. The broadcaster is promoting titles including “Daha 17,” “Haysiyet” and “Güller ve Günahlar,” alongside established productions such as “İnci Taneleri” (Secret of Pearls), “Veda Mektubu” (Farewell Letter), “Üç Kız Kardeş” (Three Sisters), “Yalan” (The Family Burden), “Zalim İstanbul” (Ruthless City) and “Siyah Beyaz Aşk” (Price of Passion).
Its catalog also features internationally recognized series such as “Aşk-ı Memnu” (Forbidden Love) and “Fatmagül’ün Suçu Ne?” (What is Fatmagül’s Fault?)
Promotional posters and digital advertisements for the broadcaster’s productions have appeared across Cannes as it seeks to expand its international distribution network.
Turkish dramas have developed audiences across the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the Balkans and Latin America, giving distributors opportunities to reach new markets and negotiate additional licensing agreements at the event.

Fund repayment bill clears parliamentary committee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:42:01 UTC
14:42:01 KST

Parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee approved a bill on Oct. 14 that would allow interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors in funds under liquidation.
The nine-article proposal concerns unfinished liquidations among 131 funds ordered wound up by the Capital Markets Board (SPK). It still requires approval by parliament’s general assembly.
AK Party lawmaker Ersan Aksu, one of the bill’s sponsors, said around 350,000 investors were expected to recover their net investment through interim payments while retaining their rights to a final settlement.
Interim payments would be calculated from investors’ actual cash deposits and withdrawals, without inflation adjustment, and deducted from the final amount payable.
If available cash is insufficient, the SPK could prioritize investors with the smallest net investments or set a minimum interim payment for all eligible investors.
Where fund assets fall short, final entitlement calculations would include inflation adjustments through the liquidation date, based on the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
Aksu said payments would come from fund assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses, with no public funds used.
Committee amendments clarified how eligible investors would be identified and revised calculations for the voluntary return of gains above an inflation-adjusted benchmark.
Some repayments have already been made. The Communications Directorate said on Oct. 13 that 43,643 investors in funds managed by A1, Bulls and Pardus received 6.4 billion liras the previous week.
Separately, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek authorized an investigation into former SPK chairman İbrahim Ömer Gönül following a preliminary ministry review.
Istanbul prosecutors had sought permission on Sept. 30 to investigate alleged abuse of office in connection with the fund inquiry. Gönül gave a statement as a suspect that day.

A little bipartisan bromance as Schwarzenegger, Newsom laud California's climate-change wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:32:33 UTC
14:32:33 KST

A little bipartisan bromance as Schwarzenegger, Newsom laud California’s climate-change wins
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and Gov. Gavin Newsom marked 20 years of California’s landmark climate law, celebrating a rare show of bipartisan unity amid deepening political polarization.
- The 2006 law helped cut greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels and fueled clean-energy growth, but California is falling behind its next targets.
- Schwarzenegger said the state’s climate policies show what cooperation can accomplish; California’s cap-and-invest program, extended through 2045, is now moving toward a link with Washington state’s market.
Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, celebrated the 20-year anniversary of landmark climate legislation he signed while in office alongside Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom on Wednesday.
“California is the perfect example of what can be done when people work together and when we don’t look at this as a Republican or as a Democratic issue,” Schwarzenegger said at an economic conference in Long Beach, noting that Assembly Bill 32, the Global Warming Solutions Act, had significantly reduced greenhouse gas emissions while creating more than half a million clean-energy jobs.
“This is the message that is so important for the world,” he said, because the state’s policies have become a model for other states and nations.
Newsom noted that the state had met “audacious” goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, touting 39,000 megawatts of clean energy that have been installed in the last seven years, 23,000 megawatts of battery storage created, and that no flex alert has been issued in the state in four years.
“So we’re not in the goal-setting business; we’re in the how business,” he said.
He added that the clean energy transition is “the most critical national security issue in the United States of America,” with economic and supply chain leadership at stake as China surpasses the U.S. in electric vehicles, clean-energy manufacturing and the deployment of renewables.
The state already met the climate change legislation’s ambitious target — returning emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 — four years ahead of schedule. However, recent analyses indicate California is not on track to meet its future targets of cutting emissions 40% by 2030 and 85% by 2045.
The legislation paved the way for the creation of California’s nation-leading carbon market, cap-and-invest, which launched in 2013. The Legislature extended cap-and-invest’s life to 2045 last year, and the state is now initiating the process of linking its market with Washington state.
The event as well as a luncheon the prior day in Santa Monica were rare displays of bipartisan unity at a time of heightened political polarization in the United States. Schwarzenegger and Newsom piled praise upon each other during the Wednesday afternoon discussion, hugging at the end.
At the luncheon, former Gov. Gray Davis, whom Schwarzenegger ousted from office in the 2003 recall election, as well as billionaire hedge-fund founder turned environmental warrior Tom Steyer, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, were among the Democrats in attendance, as well as former state Assembly Speaker Fabian Nunez and former state Sen. Fran Pavley, who were both pivotal in the passage of the climate-change legislation.
In addition to remarks highlighting the foundation of some of the nation’s bedrock environmental policies, such as former Republican President Nixon creating the Environmental Protection Agency and signing the Endangered Species Act, there were moments of levity.
Schwarzenegger said he told fellow Republicans “f— you” when they balked at him naming Susan Kennedy, a Democrat, as his chief of staff, he said.
During a breakout session at the Wednesday conference, he referenced his former wife, Maria Shriver, a scion of the Kennedy family, as he described his desire to hear from people on both sides of the aisle.
“So I had Democrats in my administration, and of course the Republican Party went nuts,” he said. “I didn’t care because, to me, I thought I wanted to hear what the Democrats were thinking. Plus, I was sleeping with one every night anyway.”

Istanbul floods leave two dead, force school closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:30:52 UTC
14:30:52 KST

Flash floods triggered by torrential rainfall continued to disrupt daily life in Istanbul on Oct. 15, forcing authorities to suspend classes for a second consecutive day as the city grappled with one of its heaviest downpours on record, which has left four people dead.
The downpour that began on Oct. 14 night flooded homes and businesses, inundated roads and underpasses, stranded vehicles and brought traffic to a standstill across Türkiye’s largest city.
Earlier deaths reported by local media included a 14-year-old who was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle at a park in the Fatih district, and a 34-year-old who slipped on a sidewalk in Sarıyer and struck their head.
Search efforts throughout the day uncovered another body along a stream in Istanbul’s Kağıthane district, bringing the death toll to three.
Police have launched an investigation into the death of the man, who was reportedly in his 40s.
Construction worker Faik Şentürk later died after falling into a well while draining floodwater at a school construction site in Beykoz, bringing the toll to four. Seven people remained in hospital.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gül announced that schools would remain closed on Oct. 16, following the suspension of classes on Oct. 15. He said the decision was made in anticipation of rainfall continuing for another two to three days.
Gül said Istanbul experienced its heaviest rainfall in 84 years.
Meanwhile, the Istanbul Municipality said rainfall levels reached one of the highest readings recorded since 1985.
Precipitation reached 272 kilograms per square meter in some parts of the city.
More than 1,000 flooding incidents were reported across Istanbul, leaving numerous vehicles partially or completely submerged.
Authorities urged residents to remain at home unless travel was absolutely necessary and advised people living in basement apartments to spend the night elsewhere.
Some public employees were also expected to be placed on leave, while motorcycles were banned from traffic.
Rescue operations continued throughout the city. Workers stranded overnight at a concrete plant in Sarıyer were evacuated with the help of a front-end loader after floodwaters cut off their escape routes.
One of the rescued workers, Ömer Artık, told reporters that around 30 people were still waiting to be evacuated from the facility.
“We have been stranded here for 14 hours. The loader brought us here, and we have only just been rescued,” he said, adding that the workers had also helped employees from nearby factories by taking them into their dormitories.
“The workplace was flooded, with water 2 to 3 meters deep, higher than our heads. The stream had also overflowed, so we could no longer get outside,” Artık said.
The heavy rainfall also caused the Kağıthane stream to overflow. Municipal teams rescued stray animals trapped in the courtyard of Arnavutköy Boğazköy Primary School, while construction machinery was deployed to evacuate people stranded by floodwaters near Merter metro station.
Meanwhile, 46 aircraft were unable to land at Istanbul’s airports amid the adverse weather conditions.
The torrential downpour, which began on the night of Oct. 14, is expected to continue through Oct. 17.
The impact of the flooding was also visible along the Bosphorus on Oct. 15 morning, as runoff from swollen streams flowed into the strait, turning sections of the coastal waters brown.
In some areas, the discoloration extended roughly 200 meters from the shoreline.
Following the extreme rainfall, meteorologist Professor Dr. Mikdat Kadıoğlu warned that even lower levels of precipitation forecast for Oct. 16 could trigger further serious flooding, as the saturated ground would have little capacity to absorb additional water.
