OODA Transforms a Prague City Block into a Permeable Mixed-Use Complex with a Lanscaped Central Plaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Portuguese architecture and urbanism practice OODA has released new images of an urban design project in Prague, Czech Republic. The design transforms an existing building block into a permeable site with municipal social housing, commercial units, and a landscaped central plaza. The project, titled Kodaňská 1441, prioritizes walkability, green mobility and public space. In addition to opening new connections between the existing building and the urban fabric, it includes a landscape and water management system that increases the permeable surfaces of the courtyard by 21.5%. The project is an example of urban renewal that incorporates contemporary concerns such as communal spaces, a regulated relationship with public space, planted environments, and the sustainable use of natural resources.
A cut volume defines the site footprint. The mass is divided into residential blocks, interrupted by a central void with an organic form. The incisions introduce new urban and visual connections and improve permeability, ventilation and proportion. The volume steps down toward the central void, creating terraces. The inner facade is distinguished from the exterior in geometry and materiality, while the exterior is clad in rose, cream, green, gold and blue terrazzo. Design elements such as loggias, balconies, canopies, flowerpots and shading elements add variety to the architectural language.
The central plaza is an integral part of the block redesign. It is organized into a sequence of plazas, gardens, play areas, seating, and pedestrian walkways. At the center, residents have access to a plaza and a children's playground, reached through a gated route that is open during the day and closed at night. The geometry of the planted areas and landscape design follows a radius principle, with a planting structure composed of 80% structural planting and 20% accent planting. The landscape integrates water collection systems, infiltration gardens, permeable surfaces, and bio-filtration rooftops. A second phase is planned to add more permeable surfaces to strengthen rainwater infiltration and reduce surface runoff.
Related Article
Prague Architecture City Guide: 25 Historical and Contemporary Attractions to Explore in Czechia’s City of a Hundred Spires
In terms of program, commercial units are located along the perimeter of the block, while ground-floor residential units face the interior courtyard, conceived as a quieter green space. The block is partially permeable, with passages open during daylight hours and closed to the public at night. The municipal building is differentiated from the rest of the complex. The social housing is located at the corner of the block and follows the same grid with a different architectural expression. The volume is designed with an exposed concrete facade with smooth and ribbed surfaces and a carved corner with shared spaces and community gardens.
Other recent urban design projects include Stefano Boeri Architetti's affordable housing development in Ibiza, the winning entry in Casa 47, a competition launched by Spain's Entidad Estatal de Vivienda. In Libya, a team composed of ZHA, A&O TEC, Prior + Partners, Homa, Buro Happold, Systematica and Fichtner recently unveiled its concept proposal for the "Next Generation City Plan" for Benghazi. In the United States, Heatherwick Studio unveiled new images of the redesign of Louisville's Belvedere, a 53-year-old gathering place for concerts, festivals and community events. In France, the Grand Paris Express transportation project has engaged architectural teams for the design of its 68 new stations and adjacent public spaces.

'Mother of all bombs': US potential Iran strike plans include largest non-nuclear weapon - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:29:06 UTC
14:29:06 KST

The United States military has developed strike plans against Iran that include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US arsenal, CNN reported on Thursday.
According to CNN, multiple US officials said that the plans called for the MOAB to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.
Another source said that the phrasing used in the plan was that the attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” meaning that the US might strike Iran and then immediately pull its forces out of the region.
Several of US President Donald Trump's advisors have also told CNN that, despite Trump's claims that he would not take further action against Iran before the US midterms, it remains unclear whether he will change his mind before Election Day.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN that questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
MOAB unlikely to penetrate Iranian nuclear sites
According to several sources, the MOAB likely would be unable to penetrate deep below the ground, where Iranian nuclear facilities, such as Pickaxe Mountain, are believed to be.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
The source said the MOAB's main tactical advantage in this scenario would be its psychological effect on Iran.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level… you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the source said.
When asked about the plan, a White House official told CNN that “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” adding that they do not comment on sensitive military plans.
A Pentagon official told CNN that it "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

'Completely reversed': Why more Australian households are feeling miserable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:26:24 UTC
14:26:24 KST

In Brief
- Inflation, high interest rates and rising unemployment are keeping pressure on households.
- Economic misery is expected to remain above historical averages until at least 2028.
Australians are feeling increasingly miserable about the economy, with financial pressures unlikely to ease anytime soon, according to new analysis.
New research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) found economic "misery" has returned to post-pandemic highs, wiping out improvements made since 2023 and leaving the country on track for several more years of elevated financial strain.
The think tank expects misery levels to remain well above recent historical averages through to at least the end of 2028, as households continue to grapple with inflation, high interest rates and a gradually weakening labour market.
Fresh data released on Thursday added to those concerns, showing Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
CEDA's misery index combines inflation, unemployment and interest rates to provide a broad measure of the economic pressures facing households.
"When those things go up, there's more of a financial pinch for households and there's a little bit more pressure on the pocketbook," CEDA head of economics Liam Dillon told SBS News.
Progress 'completely reversed'
CEDA says higher prices and borrowing costs have been the main contributors to the recent rise in economic misery.
"What we found is that since 2023, the misery index had been coming down as inflation was trending lower and the Reserve Bank was able to lower interest rates accordingly," Dillon said.
"Since then though, inflation's been a little bit more persistent than we had hoped. That's led the Reserve Bank to increase interest rates to 15-year highs."
"The combination of those things means that the progress on lowering that economic misery has now been completely reversed and we're back at 2023 levels."
After briefly returning to the Reserve Bank's two to three per cent target range in 2025, annual inflation rose to four per cent over the year to August.
The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates four times this year, taking the official cash rate to its highest level in 15 years, with some economists expecting another increase before the end of 2026.
The report also points to broader signs of economic pessimism, with consumer confidence remaining at levels comparable to those seen during the pandemic.
Unemployment exceeding forecasts
While inflation and interest rates have driven the latest increase in the misery index, the labour market has helped cushion the impact on many households.
But that source of support is beginning to weaken.
In the decade before the pandemic, unemployment was the largest contributor to Australia's economic misery, averaging 5.5 per cent of the population and peaking at 6.3 per cent in late 2014.
Since the pandemic, unemployment has remained comparatively low, averaging around four per cent.
But fresh figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday suggest labour market conditions are continuing to soften.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.
The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.
Employment fell by 39,300 people over the month, while the number of unemployed Australians increased by 8,900.
The result also exceeded the Reserve Bank's forecast for unemployment to reach 4.5 per cent by the December quarter.
Despite the deterioration, Dillon said the jobs market remained a relative source of strength for the economy.
"What we've seen is that even though unemployment has been rising, the labour market is still showing signs of resilience and that's really helping to support households," he said.
About 177,000 jobs have been added since the start of the year, according to CEDA.
Dillon said that had helped insulate households from some of the effects of higher inflation and interest rates, while household savings remain above the decade average in the years before the pandemic.
The remedy to misery
The report argues reducing economic misery remains difficult because efforts to bring down inflation can often come at the expense of employment and economic activity.
To return inflation to the Reserve Bank's target range, it has largely relied on higher interest rates, increasing pressure on households already facing elevated living costs.
Minutes from the Reserve Bank's September meeting, released this week, showed staff were increasingly concerned weak productivity growth may mean unemployment needs to be higher than previously thought to keep inflation stable.
Dillon said stronger productivity growth offered the best long-term solution because it could ease pressure across all three parts of the misery index.
"What we suggest and what we argue through this is that really the only way to get at all three drivers of misery is to boost productivity growth," he said.
"That's a challenge and a long-term one at that, but really this index shows why that's so important."
CEDA expects misery levels to remain above recent historical averages through to the end of 2028 based on current trends.

Israel’s voters seem more tired than engaged by crucial election

- Campaigning is unusually quiet, with fewer rallies and posters. Many voters seem fixed in their choices, while polls suggest no clear majority and a possible repeat election.
- Opposition hopes centre on Gadi Eisenkot, who promises a more transparent government. Likely changes include an inquiry into Oct 7, prime minister term limits and action on ultra-Orthodox conscription.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Two weeks before what is widely considered Israel’s most consequential election in decades, its streets are surprisingly empty of rallies and campaign posters, with voters seemingly more exhausted than engaged.
For a society that a few years ago saw hundreds of thousands pack central squares weekly to protest against the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the listlessness is noteworthy.
“It’s the most significant election since 1949 and the most lacklustre existential moment that I can recall,” said Yossi Klein Halevi, author of several books on Israel and a senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute, a Jerusalem think-tank.
“Israelis are tired after three years of war,” he said.
“They also know that the war isn’t over, that whoever wins will have to fight its next stage. It makes it hard to generate excitement for the future.”
The Oct 27 election will be the first since Hamas militants attacked Israel three years ago, killing 1,200, abducting 250 and triggering a brutal war in Gaza that the territory’s Health Ministry says has killed at least 70,000 Palestinians.
Israel has since waged further battles against Iran and groups it backs in Lebanon and Syria.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have been called up for military service, and many have spent months in uniform, away from family and work.
The Oct 7, 2023, attack inspired patriotic unity, but as Hamas held on to hostages in Gaza, fissures opened, with some blaming the government for not prioritising their freedom over combat.
In addition, Netanyahu’s ruling coalition includes ultra-Orthodox parties who have traded their votes for keeping their young men out of military service, an issue that has infuriated most of the rest of the country.
This combination of issues could be expected to inspire an impassioned opposition to make its case and get out the vote.
But that is happening far less than many had expected, although pollsters say opposition supporters will vote in large – perhaps record – numbers.
While a Channel 12 poll on Oct 12 had the opposition bloc winning 54 seats to Netanyahu’s 49, other surveys have seen a much closer gap and neither side is expected to secure a clear majority to form a government.
That is another possible factor in keeping enthusiasm low, since it could require complex negotiations or even another election to deliver a decisive outcome.
The opposition’s main candidate is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has pledged to lead a more transparent government.
He is positioning himself as a self-effacing contrast to the high-profile Netanyahu, a global figure who has been in office longer than anyone in Israeli history.
Yoel Esteron, who founded business daily Calcalist, said: “You’d expect to see Eisenkot in the centre of Tel Aviv with tens of thousands of people expressing a desperate desire for change. But he’s not a charismatic candidate and does small events.”
Esteron also noted that a lot more campaigning is done on social media than in previous eras.
Shmuel Rosner, who produces analysis and polling for Channel 13, said the low-key campaigns may be a result of most people having long ago decided which bloc they support, with little movement between them.
While cars lack bumper stickers and billboards are fewer, television and radio debates have been vigorous and intense.
Oded Ben Ami, who anchors an evening news broadcast on Channel 12, said he believes some things will change if Eisenkot wins: a commission of inquiry for Oct 7, term limits for prime ministers and an attempt to address the ultra-Orthodox conscription issue.
But Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Gaza and the West Bank, not to mention education and transportation, add up to a mountain of challenges.
Tel Aviv psychologist Amalia Rosenblum, when asked why the opposition energy seemed so low, referred to a concept known as learnt helplessness – when people stop trying to escape an unpleasant situation because experiences have taught them their actions have no impact.
“Those who packed the streets a few years ago feel increasingly that they can’t move the needle,” she said.
“Even if they win, it’s like having a disease and being prescribed medicine. You take it, but it doesn’t exactly make you excited.” BLOOMBERG

Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:24:40 UTC
14:24:40 KST

Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
At COP17 and COP31, governments must accelerate positive tipping points in energy, food and finance.
Nature is humanity’s life-support system, but it is being depleted at an alarming rate, leaving our world increasingly vulnerable. From deadly heatwaves and raging wildfires to catastrophic floods and prolonged droughts, the effects of environmental change have been impossible to ignore this year. With El Nino forecast to intensify, the risks to people, nature and economies are only increasing.
These shocks are unfolding against the backdrop of widespread nature loss, with WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026 finding that the average size of monitored wildlife populations declined by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022. Nature loss is increasingly a question of economic and national resilience – affecting food and water security, health, supply chains and geopolitical stability.
The situation is serious, but science shows there are still grounds for hope.
The economic systems driving nature’s decline can be transformed, and change can accelerate much faster than many may expect. Evidence shows that under the right conditions, positive change can cross a tipping point threshold and become self-reinforcing, making a safer, more resilient future not just possible, but inevitable.
The question is: How can we accelerate the actions needed to trigger those tipping points and accelerate the transition?
Positive tipping points and the opportunity for transformational change
In environmental terms, we often think about tipping points in terms of the threats they pose to vital ecosystems, such as coral reefs or the Amazon rainforest, where constant damage risks compounding and becoming increasingly impossible to reverse. These dangers are real and urgent. However, these tipping point dynamics can also work in our favour.
Three economic systems are driving most of nature’s decline: the energy system that fuels climate change; the global food system that leads to habitat loss and climate change; and the finance system that bankrolls it all. Triggering tipping points in those systems would see them rapidly transform for the better and reduce harm to the climate and nature. Once that threshold is passed, change can happen quickly as knowledge and technology advance, with solutions becoming cheaper and more accessible and as people learn from others. Encouragingly, progress is already under way – not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required – but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.
The world does not lack goals for 2030. What it lacks is the pace of implementation. With the Global Biodiversity Framework, the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement in place, governments have already agreed on a pathway. Focusing on implementing these agreements in full will create the conditions for rapid systemic change.
The global energy system has already passed a tipping point, with the transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy now accelerating. While far from complete, this transition demonstrates how rapid systemic change is possible, offering valuable lessons for the equally urgent transformation of our food and financial systems.
Twenty years ago, solar power was used mostly in satellites and pocket calculators. Now, it is the cheapest option for new electricity generation in most countries. Affordable solar panels are electrifying rural households and improving the resilience of food and medical supply chains. Renewable technologies are displacing fossil fuels at a pace few people predicted even a decade ago.
Changing the food and finance systems is proving slower but is no less urgent.
To progress towards a food systems tipping point, we need to hit major milestones in the uptake of nature-positive food production and see wider shifts in consumer demand for healthier, more sustainable foods to reinforce and reward this shift. Some progress is under way with efforts to tackle commodity-driven deforestation, and more than 130 countries have national strategic plans for food system transformation, but commitments have not yet translated into the policies and incentives needed to accelerate the transition.
Tipping the finance system so that more finance flows to activities that protect and restore nature than activities that harm it is a fundamental challenge. Reaching this tipping point will require a combination of regulatory change, subsidy reform, and a shift in how the sector values climate and nature as material financial risks. If even a portion of the money currently directed towards harmful activities is redirected to environmental recovery, it could shift the economics of the entire transformation.
Governments meeting at the COP17 biodiversity and COP31 climate conferences have before them a vital opportunity to work together to accelerate the actions needed to trigger positive tipping points and to build resilience into societies and the global economy.
Learning from conservation success
Hidden within the broader picture of global biodiversity decline are inspiring stories of species recovery. Populations of green sea turtles and tigers are rebounding due to dedicated conservation work bringing together governments, communities and organisations.
Creating systemic change will similarly take action from all of us, from governments to businesses, financial institutions, local communities, and individuals. We know where we need to get to and the hurdles we need to overcome together; the task now is to create the conditions in which positive change gathers momentum and starts reinforcing itself.
Building strength and resilience into our natural support system will require the courage to shift from extractive, wasteful economies focused on short-term gain to systems that are sustainable and regenerative for the long-term benefit of all. We have the goals, the solutions and pathways to get there. Yes, there might be setbacks along the way, but science shows nature and the climate can still recover and that change can happen faster than we might think.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:20:23 UTC
14:20:23 KST

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days, ombudsman reports
In short:
An ombudsman report has set out a litany of errors spanning four decades that led to a citizen's unlawful detention.
Another non-citizen was wrongfully detained for 304 days.
What's next?
The report has made three recommendations to the government, including better communication between the Home Affairs Department and the minister.
An Australian citizen is among 30 people unlawfully held in immigration detention in the last financial year, according to a Commonwealth Ombudsman report.
The person, named as Mx B, was wrongfully detained by Home Affairs for 945 days — two and a half years — due to incorrect reading of Australia's citizenship laws.
Mx B was born in Australia in 1989 to New Zealand parents, briefly left, then returned in 1992, and should have been granted automatic citizenship on their 10th birthday in accordance with the Citizenship Act. But this did not occur due to "poor record keeping".
The ombudsman report sets out a litany of departmental errors, incorrect assumptions and failed checks spanning four decades.
Three incorrect citizenship assessments
After growing up in Australia, Mx B was convicted of criminal offences and sentenced to prison in 2010 at the age of 21.
In 2018, while in jail, Home Affairs carried out a citizenship status assessment and incorrectly found Mx B was not an Australian citizen, due to their brief departure from the country as a baby.
"They [Mx B] were assessed as not having been ordinarily resident [in Australia] for the first 10 years of their life," the ombudsman report said.
"Officers failed to consider relevant case law about absences from Australia."
In 2019, the department, acting on the mistaken understanding that Mx B was a New Zealand citizen in Australia on a special category visa, considered whether to cancel Mx B's visa on character grounds, but found their visa had ended in the 1990s.
A second citizenship assessment again determined Mx B was not a citizen, which the ombudsman described as another "failure to consider all available information and relevant case law".
Upon Mx B's release from jail in 2022, the department placed them into immigration detention.
"Mx B claimed to be an Australian citizen on multiple occasions throughout their detention," the ombudsman report stated.
In 2024, Mx B's legal representative sent the department correspondence regarding Mx B's claimed Australian citizenship.
"The Department completed a further citizenship status assessment for Mx B based on existing information in its systems," the report states.
For the third time, the department determined Mx B was not an Australian citizen, "failing to take into account the new information indicated by Mx B's legal representative".
Eventual release after High Court NZYQ ruling
In November 2023, the High Court's NZYQ ruling found the indefinite detention of non-citizens where there was no reasonable prospect of removal was illegal.
That triggered the release of more than 300 people from immigration detention.
Mx B was not one of them, remaining in detention until April 2025, when the New Zealand government told the Home Affairs department that Mx B was not a New Zealand citizen.
"The Department subsequently found Mx B to be affected by the outcome in NZYQ because their removal from Australia was not reasonably practicable in the foreseeable future," the ombudsman report said.
"On the same day, the Department granted Mx B a Removal Pending bridging visa on strict conditions and released them from held detention."
A fourth and final citizenship assessment found that Mx B was an Australian citizen.
'Mx A' wrongfully detained for 304 days
Mx B is not alone. The ombudsman report found 30 out of the 4,247 people placed into immigration detention between July 2024 and June 2025 were unlawfully detained.
Of those, 60 per cent of cases were due to a delay in communicating a ministerial visa approval to the department, leaving 18 people in unlawful detention for one day.
One individual, known as Mx A, was wrongfully detained for 304 days due to a decision maker's "incorrect understanding of the law".
Of those affected, none have filed compensation claims against the government.
The report has made three recommendations, including that the department work with the Home Affairs minister to "formalise policies and procedures relating to the communication of Ministerial intervention decision".
It also recommended Home Affairs apologise to those impacted.
The Home Affairs department has been contacted for comment.

"The fact that these have now been postponed is, as Penny Wong put it, deeply disappointing."

Both nations participate in the Jordan-led Aqaba Process, established in 2015 to bring governments and security experts together to address terrorism, violent extremism and emerging security threats.
Australia said it may host an Aqaba Process meeting in 2027 focused on cybersecurity, online radicalisation and the misuse of new technologies.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Defense and transportation officials have raised concerns about Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to convert Songshan Airport into an AI park, citing military, transportation, and emergency medical needs.
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) told the Legislative Yuan’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee on Wednesday that Songshan Airport plays an important role in Taiwan’s defense in peacetime and during war, per UDN.
When KMT Legislator Huang Jen (黃仁問) asked whether the airport could be targeted in a decapitation strike, Koo said it was possible and that Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport could face the same threat.
Koo added that closing Songshan would make Taoyuan Airport even more difficult to defend. He also agreed with KMT Legislator Huang Chien-pin (黃建賓) that the risks of abandoning an airport should not be overlooked.
Koo said legislators representing outlying islands and eastern Taiwan had opposed phasing out Songshan, which provides an important transportation link for residents seeking medical treatment in Taipei. Those areas have fewer medical resources, making access to the capital’s hospitals especially important.
Deputy Civil Aviation Administration Director Yang Kuo-feng (楊國峯) told the committee that the Taipei City Government had not submitted proposals or applied for budget subsidies related to planning or research on relocating or closing Songshan Airport in the past four years, per LTN.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) asked whether the city had raised the issue during that period. Yang said former Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) had proposed relocating the airport, but the current Chiang administration had not. Yang added that the airport’s overall plan, approved in November 2023, designates Songshan as an international business airport and a hub for domestic air transport.
Deputy Transportation Minister Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) said the planned third terminal and third runway at Taoyuan Airport were intended to expand capacity, not accommodate flights currently using Songshan. After the third runway is completed, Taoyuan’s existing second runway will also need to be taken out of service temporarily for maintenance, Lin said.
Lin said Taoyuan primarily serves international routes and medium- and large-sized jet aircraft, while Songshan handles domestic and regional services, including flights by slower aircraft such as ATR turboprops.
Transferring Songshan’s flights to Taoyuan would require changes to terminal and apron arrangements and could be costly, Lin said. A Ministry of Transportation report estimated that passengers traveling on ATR-72 aircraft would add about an hour to their journeys compared with flying from Songshan.
Taoyuan Airport handled about 47.8 million passengers in 2025, exceeding its stated annual capacity of 42.8 million, according to the report. Terminal 3 is scheduled for completion by the end of 2027.
Songshan handled about 2.39 million passengers traveling to and from Kinmen, Matsu, and Penghu in 2025, the report said. It also cited 38,651 outlying-island residents who traveled to Taiwan for medical treatment and noted that nine major emergency hospitals are within a 10- to 15-minute drive of Songshan, per Liberty Times.
The two airports can also serve as alternate landing sites for each other during bad weather or other exceptional circumstances. Lin said the Songshan Airport proposal remained open for public discussion but would be considered in the next five-year plan only after its consequences and necessary supporting infrastructure had been adequately assessed.

Jonas Hejduk's blurry furnishings are deliberately low resolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Jonas Hejduk's blurry furnishings are deliberately low resolution
Designer Jonas Hejduk has released a collection of rugs and benches that have ambiguously pixellated aesthetics.
Hejduk's focus on deliberately compressed, low-resolution versions of popular furnishings were informed by his childhood fixation with video game graphics.
"Youngsters like myself were already caught in the spiral logic of infinite growth, trained never to tolerate technological stagnation," Hejduk told Dezeen.
Stools and rugs are among the French designer's output, each of which were named using computer filename formats.
In the case of the designer's rugs, the filename, initial file size and post-processing size are woven onto the surface of the piece.
Made from digitally woven wool and cotton jacquard, the designer described the Traditional-rug-1.jpeg as "poetic and gently ironic".
"Once a symbol of prestige and early global exchange, the Persian rug gradually shifted into a standardised archetype of mass culture and uniformity," Hejduk told Dezeen.
"Here, it is reduced to its own thumbnail – an enigmatic blurry image of troubled origins, copied and pasted too many times."
Hejduk's Tiger skin rug is part of a wider collection called Crash.jpeg, in which the designer explored the contemporary obsession with digital clarity and technological advancement.
"By embracing the ambiguity of the poor image, the collection presents works that are deliberately difficult to photograph and rendered anachronistic to the eyes of social media algorithms: high-definition designs are deliberately sabotaged down to lower resolutions," said Hejduk.
Similarly, Hejduk's Log-texture-1.jpeg bench recalls the nostalgia of logs as resting places in 1990s video games.
The benches were wrapped in a blurry bark skin with cut-through textures at either end, tacked together with traditional nailhead trim.
Like many of the designer's works, the logs act like an optical illusion, contrasting with their surroundings in a jarring way owing to their not-finished-loading appearance.
"Visually, it 'has no business being there', and yet, its digital nature conveys an authenticity that brings a smile, far removed from what AI offers in our daily lives," the designer continued.
In addition to rugs and benches, Hejduk produces similarly blurry ceramics, garments, bed sheets and wallpapers.
"These pieces of furniture are not just 'designer jokes about 3D', but objects of mourning and resistance," said Hejduk.
"Through the physicality of craft and raw materials, they serve as tangible reminders of the unfulfilled promises of digital modernity, all while rejecting the sanitised present that tech oligarchs attempt to impose on us."
Other products on Dezeen created in rejection of AI include a shirt that prevents the wearer from being picked up by AI video surveillance and a font that cannot be read by AI software.

The Kremlin is fabricating an offensive against Sloviansk and Kramatorsk: ISW exposed Russia’s information operation
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is exaggerating its advances in Donetsk Oblast to create the impression that Ukraine’s defenses are collapsing. ISW has not confirmed any gains near Sloviansk and Kostiantynivka.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense is spreading exaggerated claims about the advance of its forces in Donetsk Oblast, particularly near Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, attempting to create the impression that Ukrainian defenses are allegedly collapsing. However, the actual situation on the front does not confirm reports by the Russian command. This is stated in a report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), UNN writes.
Details
Analysts noted that Russia’s Ministry of Defense claims offensive operations near Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Semenivka. At the same time, these settlements are located far beyond the furthest confirmed advance of the occupying forces.
According to the ISW assessment, such reports are part of the kremlin’s systematic information campaign aimed at exaggerating Russia’s gains and creating a false impression of the situation on the battlefield.
Russians claim to have advanced dozens of kilometers
Analysts recorded similar manipulations in other areas as well. In particular, the Russian command claimed an advance near Tarasivka and Havrylivka, although these settlements are located approximately 16 and 15 km, respectively, from the furthest positions to which, according to ISW assessments, Russian forces have advanced.
In the Hulyaipole direction, the occupiers also reported combat operations near settlements located approximately 14–19 km from the confirmed boundary of Russia’s advance.
Analysts noted that Russia’s Ministry of Defense publishes some of these claims on the Russian messenger Max rather than on Telegram. In ISW’s view, this may indicate an attempt to impose an exaggerated picture of successes primarily on a domestic Russian audience.
At the same time, on October 13–14, Russian forces continued attacks on the approaches to Sloviansk and in the Kostiantynivka area, but analysts did not record any confirmed advance in these areas.
Thus, according to the ISW assessment, the kremlin is attempting to portray the Ukrainian defensive line as allegedly collapsing, although the available evidence does not support such claims.

NEW DELHI: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee is facing two separate legal proceedings in Delhi. A fresh defamation suit has been filed against him at the Saket court over a video allegedly claiming that Lord Ram and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol during their exile.Separately, Rathee has been served fresh summons in a 2018 criminal defamation case filed by BJP IT Cell member Vikas Pandey over a video titled "BJP IT Cell Part 2".
Fresh suit over Ram-Sita video
Supreme Court Advocate-on-Record Amita Sachdeva and other petitioners had approached the Delhi high court over the video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? and prayed before the court to issue directions granting an interim restraint on Rathee from creating, uploading, or publishing similar content."Some time ago, Dhruv Rathee published a video claiming that Lord Shri Ram and Mother Sita consumed meat and alcohol during their exile. We took the matter regarding that video to the Delhi High Court, and the Delhi High Court directed the Govt of India to have the video removed.""On July 15, 2026, the Govt of India directed YouTube to take down the video, after which that petition was disposed of. Following the disposal of the petition, someone extracted a three-minute segment from that 21-minute video and re-uploaded it,” she added.
According to Sachdeva, the petitioners approached the Delhi High Court again, which granted them liberty to initiate fresh legal proceedings against Rathee."We approached the Delhi High Court again. The Court granted us the liberty to file a fresh petition or suit against Dhruv Rathee and seek appropriate relief. Acting on that liberty, we filed a suit today in the Saket Court, before the Learned District Judge, seeking a declaration, an injunction, and damages for defamation; the matter was listed for hearing today," she said.Sachdeva said the petitioner's senior counsel, Makarand Natkar, appeared through video conferencing but could not complete his submissions because of technical difficulties. The court subsequently adjourned the matter to November 5."Today, my senior counsel, Makarand Natkar, presented his submissions. He appeared via video conferencing (VC), but due to some technical issues with the VC connection, the submissions could not be completed. Consequently, the Learned District Judge adjourned the matter to November 5, when we will present our fresh submissions," she added.The complainants, who identified themselves as Hindu devotees, alleged that the video hurt their religious sentiments. The suit also seeks an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Google from restoring, hosting, uploading, sharing or disseminating the video, or any video identical or similar in content, after notice and verification of the URL, during the pendency of the suit.
Fresh summons in 2018 defamation case
Separately, a Delhi court has issued fresh summons to Rathee in a defamation case filed by BJP IT Cell member Vikas Pandey in 2018. The court noted that attempts to serve Rathee had continued for several years.Judicial Magistrate Rahul Jain was hearing Pandey's plea seeking fresh summons. In an order dated October 12, the court said, "From the available record, it is clear that the complainant has been trying to serve the accused no. 1 (Rathee) since the last several years..."Appearing for Pandey, advocate Samaksh Sharma submitted that Rathee ordinarily resides in Austria and had come to India for the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in Delhi. He argued that fresh summons were necessary to ensure prompt steps could be taken to serve the accused.The court permitted fresh summons to be served through dasti service, allowing the complainant to accompany the process server. Rathee has since been physically served at his Gurugram residence. The proceedings had remained pending amid unsuccessful attempts to serve him since 2019.Speaking about the notice served on Rathee, Pandey said, "The court summons has been pasted outside Dhruv Rathee's home because he was not coming out. This stems from eight years ago when Dhruv Rathee created around three videos alleging that I offered Rs 50 lakh to someone to spread fake news against him.”“When Arvind Kejriwal amplified this fake news by tweeting and retweeting it, I filed a case against both Kejriwal and Dhruv Rathee. While Arvind Kejriwal offered an apology, Dhruv Rathee never appeared before the court. Consequently, a notice and summons were issued, which my lawyer pasted outside his Gurugram home..." he added.
The case also reached the Supreme Court in connection with a retweet of the video by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal. In February 2024, Kejriwal told the apex court that he had made a mistake by retweeting it.The cases come days after Delhi and Gurugram Police detained Rathee at his Sector 56 residence in Gurugram on October 10, ahead of his planned participation in a CJP protest at Jantar Mantar. He was released after around 22 hours.The detention took place amid protests in Delhi led by the CJP, which has been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The protests saw extensive security arrangements, barricading, traffic restrictions and the detention of protesters.(With input from agencies)

====================================================================================================

Expert says trust use to avoid tax 'bordering on a joke'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:45:25 UTC
13:45:25 KST

Proposed discretionary trust tax changes divide advocates and experts
In short:
Small business advocates say tax reforms that would see a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts are a "kick in the gut" and another cost for tradies.
One expert says the way discretionary trusts are being used to offset tax bills is "bordering on a joke".
What's next?
If the bill passes, the reforms would come into effect in July 2028.
Small business advocates say it is a misconception that trusts are only used by wealthy families to minimise tax, but one expert says the current system is "bordering on a joke" and in urgent need of reform.
On Wednesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers introduced a bill that would impose a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts starting July 2028 to try to discourage people and businesses from using the arrangement to minimise taxable income.
Discretionary trusts differ from other types of trusts as they allow the trustees to change beneficiaries and how much they receive each year.
Associate Professor Dale Boccabella from the University of New South Wales's Business School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation told The Business some trusts were being used to distribute income in a way to offset tax bills.
"It's bordering on a joke,"
he said.
"A 17-year-old beneficiary of a discretionary trust, not allocated anything for years and years, and all of a sudden they turn 18, this is a child of the parents, and they get $22,500. Now why do they get $22,500 allocated? It's tax-free. It's under the effective tax-free threshold.
"In a testamentary trust, you can have a two-day-old baby born on the 28th of June being allocated $22,500. I mean, you can see how silly it is."
He said in some cases, the income allocated did not get paid to the children and stayed with the parents.
The treasurer said the reforms would affect less than 10 per cent of small businesses; however, Housing Industry Association managing director Jocelyn Martin said there were costs beyond the tax changes.
"Even before they know whether that structure is going to impact them, they have to seek advice from their lawyer or their accountant, and our members are saying that that could cost anywhere between $10,000 and $25,000," she said.
"It's not enough to say that these changes just impact a small proportion; they impact a large proportion.
"Maybe the result might be that they don't have to restructure, but they need to do the work to find out whether that's what's going to happen or not."
Growing number of trusts
More than 1 million trusts are operating in Australia, with about 84 per cent of them discretionary.
The number of discretionary trusts has doubled since 2001–02.
About one in six small businesses used discretionary trusts in 2022-23, the last year of available data, with Treasury analysis suggesting 140,000 businesses of an estimated 350,000 would not need to pay the new tax.
Ms Martin said about three in five small businesses in the housing industry used a trust structure.
"I think there's an assumption that a trust structure is just something that wealthy people use to avoid or minimise taxes," she said.
"What we see are small businesses that are using the legitimate structure of a trust to manage their business, manage the cycles, the cash flow cycles, to actually pay themselves in a lot of instances as well, because some of our members have said they will pay themselves in good times and not necessarily be able to in bad times," she said.
Questioned on how much tax tradies currently pay, given that the proposed change introduces a 30 per cent minimum, Ms Martin said the HIA's concern was that the change was an additional cost to residential construction.
"Already we know that the tax that is paid by our residential businesses is extremely high," she said.
"But not just that, the cost that they pay to comply with some of these business measures is also escalating all the time.
"So I think our concern really when we say there's another tax on tradies is really it's just another kick in the gut."
Asset protection or 'economic injustice'?
Dr Boccabella said other features promoted by accountants such as asset protection, flexibility and succession planning were not being changed as part of the government's plan, although he believed they probably should be overhauled.
"The other thing with discretionary trusts is that you can set them up so that they have limited liability, a bit like a company," he said.
"If the small business and discretionary trust fails, you might actually end up with creditors not getting their payment.
"You can call that asset protection if you want, but a lot of people would turn around and say, 'Well, isn't that economic injustice, someone not getting paid for their services and goods supplied?'"
Property Council executive director of capital markets, Torie Brown, said the government had ignored the legitimate concerns raised by industry during an expedited consultation process.
"Industry was given almost no time to consider how these radical changes will affect their businesses. Despite the warnings from industry, the government had decided to push ahead and introduce this legislation anyway," he said.
"Changes to trusts is incredibly complex — pulling one thread unravels another. The government announced these changes without considering the impacts they would have on small business and housing supply."
There are also concerns that restructuring trusts would incur stamp duty at a state or territory level, something the New South Wales government has promised to waive if re-elected next year.
The Australian Council of Social Services (ACOSS) welcomed the changes, with CEO Cassandra Goldie saying the current system was being exploited.
"It is not fair that someone earning $200,000 or more, who would usually pay 47 per cent tax on extra income, can bring that rate down to 30 per cent or less by passing income through a discretionary trust to their adult children or a private company, while an average worker pays tax at a rate of 30 per cent of the next dollar earned," Dr Goldie said.
"This reform helps fix this severe unfairness in the system so people on higher incomes contribute according to their ability to pay."
Editor's note (15/10/2026) : A previous version of this story included a misquote which said a discretionary trust can be allocated to a two-day-old baby. This has now been corrected to state it was a testamentary trust being referred to.

Israel has detained more than 2,000 Palestinian children since 2023: report
At least 350 Palestinian children currently face “harsh conditions” in Israeli prisons.
Israeli forces have detained more than 2,000 Palestinian children since October 2023, the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society said.
In a report released on Wednesday, the Palestinian rights group said Israeli authorities continue to escalate their targeting of Palestinian children. At least 350 Palestinian children are currently facing “harsh conditions” in Israeli prisons.
On Tuesday, Israeli forces arrested at least six children from Hebron in the occupied West Bank, the report said.
The organisation said information regarding the number of children arrested in Gaza is unclear, given the thousands of missing persons in the besieged Gaza Strip, including children, and the ongoing policy of enforced disappearance.
The group said Israel’s policy of detention without charges or a release date constitutes “an additional violation and crime that leaves children facing the unknown and deprives them of family and educational stability”.
Cases of Palestinian children in prison
The report described Israeli practices that begin with “intimidation and arrest” and extend to “torture, starvation and denial of healthcare”.
The group highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who contracted scabies, a contagious skin infestation, while he was detained in Ofer Prison, where rights groups have long documented abuses. He suffered severe infections, underwent heart surgery and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition. He subsequently had one of his legs amputated.
The organisation also highlighted the case of 17-year-old Walid Ahmed, who died in March 2025 after six months in Megiddo Prison. In December, an Israeli judge halted the investigation into his death, stating that although there was evidence of starvation, no definitive cause of death had been established.
American children in Israeli prisons
Ahmed was imprisoned in Megiddo with his friend Mohammed Ibrahim, a teenager from Florida. Ibrahim was released after months of advocacy from US-based organisations and appeals from high-ranking lawmakers.
Mohammed Ibrahim was not the only young American held in Israeli prison without charge – Israeli forces reportedly took Abdalkareem Issa Ahmed Safi from his West Bank home in a late-night raid in June. He turned 18 in detention, and authorities subsequently moved him from a youth holding area into an adult section at Ofer Prison.
Similarly, Israeli forces arrested 16-year-old Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, also an American, in July. Although he was set for release in August after his family secured bail, Israeli authorities abruptly reversed the decision to free him.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society called for “real international action” to ensure the release of arbitrarily detained children, enforce investigations and end torture, starvation and the denial of treatment in Israeli prisons.
Israeli forces have detained more than 25,000 Palestinians in the West Bank, and thousands more in Gaza, since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023.

KALISPELL, Montana – US President Donald Trump on Oct 14 announced plans for what he described as a new defence “super range” in Montana for testing advanced military technologies, including autonomous weapons, space systems, electronic warfare and hypersonic weapons.
The President made the announcement at a campaign event in Kalispell, Montana, a city of about 30,000 people some 320km north-west of the capital Helena, his latest stop on a tour supporting Republican candidates in multiple states ahead of Nov 3 midterm elections.
The stop was part of a broader push amid unexpectedly tight battles in Republican-leaning states.
“I’m pleased to inform you and announce that right here in Montana, the Department of War is going to establish a new super range for testing advanced weapons and technologies, technologies including potential autonomous weapons, space, and electronic warfare technology, supersonics and hypersonics,” Trump said.
“Montana will help ensure the American military always reigns supreme.”
The state is already home to the Montana Spaceport & Test Range and the affiliated Limestone Hills Innovation & Test Campus, a public-private aerospace and defence initiative that promotes testing facilities and infrastructure for commercial, civil and military applications.
Trump did not say whether the new Pentagon initiative would have ties with the existing project.
Some military planners see autonomous weapons, space systems, electronic warfare and hypersonic weapons as central to the future of warfare, incorporating drones and AI-enabled platforms at lower costs with less risk for military personnel.
Trump has already promoted space defence, creating the Space Force as a separate branch of the armed forces in 2019. Supersonic and hypersonic weapons travel at speeds above Mach 1 and Mach 5 respectively.

"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".

In the early hours of Thursday, Russian strikes killed two people in the Dnipropetrovsk region, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Digital Affairs has asked supermarket chains to check their systems for cybersecurity vulnerabilities following reports of a cyberattack on grocery stores in France, the ministry said Wednesday.
The attack was discussed at a Legislative Yuan committee meeting, where lawmakers warned that a similar incident could cause significant damage in Taiwan, per Yahoo News.
In France, hackers remotely accessed refrigeration systems and raised temperatures to as high as 50 C, resulting in major food losses and fires at several stores, Al Jazeera reported.
Legislator Hsu Chih-chieh (許智傑) said a similar attack in Taiwan could lead to significant economic losses, given the country’s high density of convenience stores and supermarkets.

It asked them to inspect connected devices and update their firmware.
TWCERT/CC operates under the Ministry of Digital Affairs and helps address cybersecurity incidents in the private sector.
Digital Affairs Minister Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said many companies had overlooked cybersecurity when they connected their systems to the public internet a decade ago.
The global trend is now to disconnect systems from the internet unless necessary, he added. Companies can instead connect devices to an intranet and monitor access through a whitelist.

House prices are falling. So why are first-home buyers disappearing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:26:01 UTC
13:26:01 KST

In brief
- A key group is abandoning the housing market in growing numbers.
- New figures have shown affordability pressures are still biting.
Australians trying to buy their first home are being driven away by strict serviceability testing and higher interest rates, with mortgage demand in its sharpest fall since 2022.
Overall mortgage demand dropped 19.2 per cent year-on-year in September, despite house prices across the country slipping 1.1 per cent, according to data from credit reporting body Equifax.
This was coupled with a fall in new home loan applications, which dropped 22.1 per cent compared to 12 months ago.
Australian households were taking a decisive step back, Equifax chief solutions officer Kevin James said.
"This is the largest year-on-year decline in first home buyer mortgage demand since December 2022, and baseline prices for properties remain high despite recent market dips," he told The Australian Associated Press news agency.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Younger people were the hardest hit, as mortgages for 18 to 25-year-olds fell by a quarter, and those for 26 to 35-year-olds slumped 22.5 per cent in September.
Aspiring first home buyers continue to struggle in the property market, with several compounding factors such as strict serviceability testing, high interest rates, and spiralling living costs making it difficult for young Australians to achieve the dream of home ownership.
James said that unfortunately, there was no quick fix.
"There is no silver bullet solution; each element needs to be considered when looking for ways to make the market more accessible for this cohort," James said.
Even though property values had been easing, baseline prices were still high — with average first home buyer mortgage sizes hovering at record levels of $743,000.
James said many potential first home buyers were finding it hard to raise a deposit and afford mortgage repayments without institutional or family support.
Fewer people were moving to new lenders, with lender-switching falling 8.8 per cent compared to a year earlier, after a nearly flat performance in August.
"In the current economic climate, strict regulatory serviceability assessments appear to be holding borrowers in place," James said.
"Many existing mortgage holders wanting to shop around for a better rate are likely finding themselves unable to clear the serviceability needed, effectively locking them into their current arrangements."
Meanwhile, Australians aged 56 and over helped drive a surge in credit cards.
Credit card demand rose by a tenth compared to a year earlier, driven by a 36.3 per cent spike among borrowers aged 56 and above.
It's a different story for young people, as 18–35-year-olds pull back across the credit spectrum.

US considers using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:23:52 UTC
13:23:52 KST

The U.S. military has developed new plans for possible strikes on Iran that include using the so-called "mother of all bombs" against infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders attacks to resume, either before or after the U.S. midterm elections, CNN reported, citing American officials familiar with the matter.
Deploying the GBU-43/B, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a significant escalation.
However, sources familiar with internal U.S. military discussions told CNN that doubts remain over whether the weapon could achieve Trump's stated strategic objectives or significantly alter the course of the war.
One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iran, including "numerous energy infrastructure targets" and the possible use of the MOAB. The source said the wording used was that the strikes would take place "before the U.S. withdrawal from the area of responsibility of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM)," suggesting the administration could launch further attacks, seek to declare victory and rapidly withdraw all its forces.
Another source told CNN that military plans to strike Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly call for the use of the MOAB. Trump has repeatedly threatened in recent months to attack Pickaxe Mountain, where the United States and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program.
However, questions remain about the MOAB's effectiveness against Iran's nuclear facilities and other sites buried deep underground. The GPS-guided bomb can destroy an area equivalent to nine city blocks, but some officials believe it is unlikely to penetrate deeply enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite, or other Iranian nuclear sites that remain intact.
The "mother of all bombs" has been used in combat only once, in Afghanistan in 2017. It was developed in the run-up to the Iraq War and first tested in 2003. Following its deployment against tunnels used by ISIS terrorists in Afghanistan nearly a decade ago, a U.S. military spokesman said the bomb contained approximately 11 tons of explosives. Because of its enormous size, it was dropped from the rear of a U.S. Air Force C-130 transport aircraft.
Production of GBU bombs began in the 1990s, with the weapons designed to strike surface targets rather than underground bunkers. They became increasingly common with the introduction of GPS guidance technology, which significantly improved their accuracy. Development of the GBU-43 began in 2002, and the bomb could only be carried by a C-130 Hercules aircraft. Once released from the plane, it is guided to its target by GPS.

The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.

He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Too Good To Go to sell surplus household and personal care products
The Danish-founded app is introducing five new product categories, allowing customers to buy discounted goods ranging from pet accessories to flowers and dietary supplements.
Too Good To Go announced Thursday that its platform will now offer surplus personal care products, pet accessories, flowers and plants, nutrition and dietary supplements, and household goods.
The expansion marks a shift for the company, which has focused on reducing food waste since its launch in 2016.
“Too Good To Go started with food because we saw how absurd it was that something so valuable could end up as waste. Ten years later, it is clear that the same principle applies outside the world of food,” CEO Mette Lykke said.
According to the company, more than 8,500 stores will offer products across the new categories.
Approximately one-third of those retailers already work with Too Good To Go to sell surplus food.
The app currently operates in 20 countries, with 150 million registered users and 200,000 active business partners.
Through its existing model, retailers sell unsold food in discounted surprise bags, with Too Good To Go receiving a percentage of each transaction.
The company says its expansion will help businesses recover value from unsold merchandise while giving customers access to a wider selection of discounted products.
“Our partners are increasingly approaching us with challenges regarding surplus goods that extend beyond food and asking if we can help. Surplus exists in all parts of the store,” Lykke said.
Surplus stock can include seasonal products, discontinued items, outdated packaging and gift sets that are no longer in demand.

Nordea shares fell 7.3 percent by 12:50 p.m., making the bank the worst performer in Denmark’s C25 stock index.

Share buybacks allow companies to return money to shareholders by purchasing their own shares, often reducing the number available and potentially increasing the value of those remaining.

Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen acknowledged that the regulatory review was taking longer than anticipated.
“It has proven to be a long process,” he told Børsen.
Vang-Jensen said the bank considered pausing repurchases appropriate while uncertainty remained over its future risk-weighted assets, a measure used to determine how much capital banks must hold against potential losses.
Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Auto group charged with exploiting 18 foreign mechanics in Denmark
A criminal case involving workers from India, Sri Lanka and other countries will be heard at the Court in Hillerød, following allegations of unpaid overtime, threats and restrictions on trade union membership.
According to TV 2 Kosmopol, prosecutors have brought charges against two men and two companies connected to a car group in North Zealand.
North Zealand Police allege that 18 foreign mechanics were subjected to human exploitation over a four-year period.
The indictment states that the workers were required to work overtime and weekends without additional pay.
They were also allegedly prohibited from joining a trade union, limiting their ability to seek collective representation over their employment conditions.
Prosecutors further allege that the mechanics were threatened with dismissal and deportation to their home countries if they complained about their working or living conditions.
TV 2 Kosmopol reported that although the mechanics’ stated monthly salaries were 38,000 DKK, they received only 7,517 DKK after tax.
The case will now be considered by the Court in Hillerød, which must determine whether the defendants are guilty of the charges.
The court will also decide whether approximately 4.1 million DKK should be confiscated from the defendants in connection with the alleged exploitation.
Denmark introduced a specific provision on human exploitation into its criminal code in June 2022.
The provision was designed to address serious cases of labor exploitation that do not meet the legal definition of human trafficking.
The charges in the North Zealand case have been brought under that provision, with the defendants’ criminal responsibility yet to be established.

Border checks between Denmark and Germany extended for another six months
Travelers entering the country may continue to face inspections until May 17, 2027, as authorities maintain that security threats remain serious.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, informed the European Commission of the decision Wednesday, according to a statement from the Justice Ministry.
The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Reports of AI-generated child abuse material rise sharply in Denmark
Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.

An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.
The system provides limited public information about properties, cooperative housing and vehicles.
Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said he had informed the Danish Parliament about the incident.
Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.

However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.
