Copenhagen apartment prices fall as Aarhus reaches new highs
Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.
The average sales price for owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen Municipality declined by 1.0 percent from August to September, according to housing platform Boligsiden. Prices fell by 0.5 percent the previous month.
Boligsiden housing economist Birgit Daetz said it was the largest monthly decline since March 2024.
“Supply has grown significantly in 2026, and now we see a price drop partly as a consequence of more options and lower demand among buyers,” she said.
Despite the recent decreases, Copenhagen apartment prices remain 15.7 percent higher than one year ago. The average price is now 75,414 DKK per square meter.
In Aarhus Municipality, apartment prices rose by 3.7 percent in September, the third-largest monthly increase since records began in 2011.
The average price reached 50,649 DKK per square meter. This means a 100-square-meter apartment in Aarhus costs more than 5 million DKK on average for the first time.
Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.
Suspected hacker says AI created program used in Danish CPR breach
The suspected hacker behind the theft of nearly 8.75 million Danish CPR numbers says artificial intelligence created the computer program used in the attack.
“Any AI model launched within the past year or so would be able to do it,” the anonymous person told Danish newspaper Politiken.
Two experts reviewed the program, which contains more than 40,000 characters, and concluded that its code was generated by artificial intelligence, Politiken reported.
Danish authorities disclosed last week that unauthorized people accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers during approximately 10 days in September. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The suspected hacker said the program accessed the national CPR register through a website operated by Odense-based company Pays ApS. Login details were allegedly obtained from a former employee’s leaked password.
Politiken reported that at least three Pays accounts used “123456” as their password, including the administrator account. Pays confirmed to Danish broadcaster TV 2 that it was the compromised company.
The suspected hacker denied having advanced technical skills. An error in the AI-generated code reportedly caused the program to search for people born in 1877 instead of 1977. Consequently, data for people born in 1977 was absent from material shared with Politiken.
The person said they did not intend to sell or publish the information. Pays’ director did not respond to Politiken’s inquiries about the company’s security.
Greenland opposition seeks referendum on new US defence agreement
Greenland’s opposition party Naleraq has called for a referendum on the new security and defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States.
The agreement received its first reading Monday in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament.
Naleraq chair Pele Broberg said the agreement converts Greenland’s strategic importance into rights for the United States without providing comparable economic benefits for Greenlanders.
“That is the imbalance we see in the agreement. And that is what our criticism concerns,” Broberg said.
He called for a referendum after the public receives detailed information about the agreement.
Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported that Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit said the United States had made no financial offers during negotiations.
The debate lasted more than four hours before the proposal advanced to a second reading. No date has been set. A final vote will take place after the third reading.
The governing coalition of Demokraatit, Inuit Ataqatigiit and Atassut holds 19 of Inatsisartut’s 31 seats, giving it enough support to approve the agreement.
The three governments signed the agreement in New York on September 22. It updates a 1951 agreement and allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The agreement also reaffirms the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and recognizes Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. Denmark’s parliament is expected to begin considering it later in October.
Museums and animal parks are Danes’ top autumn holiday activities
Museums and animal parks are the most popular attractions among Danes planning activities during the autumn holiday.
One in five people spending the holiday in Denmark plans to visit a museum or animal park, according to a Norstat survey conducted for Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce and a major business association.
Historical attractions, amusement parks and water parks follow on the list of preferred activities.
“For many, the autumn holiday is synonymous with family time, but it is also experience time,” Dansk Erhverv culture director Michael Folmer Wessman said. “And it is truly gratifying that Danes prioritize spending the autumn holiday on good cultural experiences.”
However, 35 percent of respondents said they had no plans to visit attractions or take part in cultural activities during the break.
Overall, 58 percent of Danes are taking an autumn holiday in week 42. Among them, 45 percent will spend the holiday at home, while 16 percent plan to travel abroad.
Of those going overseas, 44 percent have chosen destinations in Southern Europe, while 18 percent expect to visit another Nordic country.
Norstat conducted the survey in September 2026 among a representative sample of 1,012 Danish residents age 18 and older.
Number of disability pensioners under 40 falls for first time since 2020
The number of people under age 40 receiving disability pensions in Denmark has fallen for the first time in more than six years, according to figures from the Jobindsats.dk employment database.
In September, 43,229 people in the age group received disability pensions, 98 fewer than in August. It was the first monthly decline since early 2020.
Jesper Brask Fischer, head of welfare at pension company PFA, said it was too early to celebrate.
“The number of young people on disability pension is far higher than just a few years ago, and the development underlines the need for a strong effort toward prevention and early assistance,” he said.
The number of disability pension recipients under 40 has increased from 29,000 to more than 43,000 over the past decade. PFA has previously identified a possible connection between poor mental health and the increase.
Across all age groups, the number of disability pension recipients has declined for two consecutive months for the first time since late summer 2021.
Denmark had 261,418 disability pension recipients in September, down 487 from August.
Fischer said further consecutive declines could indicate that fewer people are entering the disability pension system. For now, however, he described the figures as only a cautious positive sign after years of significant growth.
Renovating all public concrete shelters could cost up to 3 billion DKK
Renovating Denmark’s 1,694 public concrete trench shelters and preparing them for use could cost between 2 billion and 3 billion DKK.
Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of the Socialist People’s Party provided the estimate in a response to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, according to construction trade publication Licitationen.
The estimate remains highly uncertain and requires further assessment.
Renovating only the 831 shelters that already meet basic requirements and could be opened during an immediate emergency would cost between 500 million and 1 billion DKK.
Most of the shelters require treatment for mold and pests because they have not been used for many years, the parliamentary response said.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness began inspecting Denmark’s shelter capacity and condition in May 2025. The review of concrete trench shelters is complete, while inspections of reinforced shelters are expected to continue until 2027.
Concrete trench shelters are public facilities intended for people away from home, including road users and residents of buildings without shelters.
Most Danish shelter spaces are in reinforced rooms inside residential and other buildings. Denmark also has supplementary shelters that offer some protection but do not meet full shelter requirements.
A 2024 inventory found about 3.4 million shelter spaces nationwide. Concrete trench shelters accounted for 113,018 of them.
Danish Air Force marked squadron’s centenary with nationwide anniversary flight
Two Danish Armed Forces aircraft flew over several parts of Denmark Monday to mark the 100th anniversary of Air Force Squadron 721.
A Hercules B-537 transport aircraft and a Challenger C-215 passenger aircraft participated in the flight, which also served as a training exercise for their crews.
Squadron 721 was established in 1926 and is Denmark’s oldest operational air force squadron. According to the Air Transport Wing, the Danish Armed Forces unit responsible for military air transport, it is also among the world’s oldest squadrons still in operation.
The aircraft departed Aalborg Air Base, the squadron’s home base, at about 8:40 a.m.
Their route included flyovers near air bases in Billund, Assens, Nyborg, Korsør, Køge and Brøndby Harbor. The flight ended at Skalstrup Air Base near Roskilde shortly before noon.
The Challenger is used for passenger transport and has carried members of Denmark’s royal family and government.
The Hercules can transport up to 20 tons of cargo. For Monday’s flight, it was decorated with a winged dolphin, the symbol used on the squadron’s crest.
Squadron 721 regularly participates in international operations. One of its aircraft is stationed in Kangerlussuaq, Greenland, for about 10 days each month.
District heating prices set to rise for thousands of Danish customers
Thousands of district heating customers in Denmark face higher bills in 2027, with 10 companies so far announcing price increases, TV 2 reported.
Most of the announced increases range from six to 10 percent.
Tue Patursson, a building specialist at the homeowner knowledge center Bolius, said the increases reflect higher energy prices.
“Since district heating plants depend on biofuel, gas, oil and electricity, one must expect that the price will also rise for district heating across the board,” he told TV 2.
Customers in Præstø in South Zealand face a 40 percent increase next year. The local district heating company had lowered its prices during the previous two years.
Præstø Fjernvarme is converting its production to electricity but has been affected by insufficient capacity in the power grid.
Board chair Morten Møller Kristensen said the company had been “forced to go back to gas due to a lack of power” this year. He said the situation had disrupted its production conditions and left it dependent on fossil fuel.
Several other district heating companies converting to electricity face similar challenges.
A broad majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, approved an emergency plan for the electricity grid on October 1. The plan allows authorities to prioritize access to limited grid capacity.
The nationwide extent of the price increases remains unclear because many companies have not published their 2027 rates.
Czech man jailed and deported after drunk-driving crash into Samsø home
A 49-year-old Czech man was sentenced Monday to six months in prison and deportation from Denmark after crashing into a house on the island of Samsø while driving drunk.
The Court in Aarhus convicted him of drunk driving and endangering another person’s life, TV2 Østjylland reported.
The man drove into the house at high speed in July, causing one of its gable walls to collapse onto a 56-year-old man who was sleeping in his bedroom.
In addition to the prison sentence and deportation, the court revoked the Czech man’s driving licence for seven years and ordered the confiscation of his car.
The defendant accepted the verdict.
Danish inflation rises to 2.2 percent as fuel prices increase
Denmark’s annual inflation rate rose to 2.2 percent in September, up 0.2 percentage points from August, Statistics Denmark reported Monday.
Higher fuel costs were the main reason for the increase, with transportation prices contributing significantly to inflation between August and September.
Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organization representing managers and executives, said similar developments were visible in neighboring countries.
“But in fact, the rising energy prices do not become quite as visible in Danish inflation because the electricity tax has largely been removed this year and next year,” she wrote in a commentary.
Lower prices for holiday home rentals, package holidays and food helped offset the increase.
Larsen said there was no reason for serious concern because inflation remained close to the two percent level generally associated with stable prices. She added that there were no signs that higher energy costs were spreading throughout the economy.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, reached a similar conclusion.
However, he said the reduced electricity tax was concealing a significant rise in underlying inflation during recent months.
“In fact, in recent quarters there has been a decline in purchasing power for the Danes because precisely during that period prices have run faster than wages,” Kristensen wrote.
Danish cyber team aims for gold at European hacking championship in Germany
Ten young Danes will compete against more than 400 participants at the European Cybersecurity Championship in Bochum, Germany, from Monday to Friday.
Denmark won silver last year, but national coach Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, believes the team can win gold this year.
“Technically speaking, the team this year is completely at the top. They are exceptionally good at collaborating, and they have the will to fight for and with each other,” he said.
The competition is open to hackers between ages 14 and 25. Denmark’s participants were selected after competing in the national cybersecurity championship in May.
During the first day of competition, teams must identify information in vulnerable applications, websites and network traffic. On the second day, they must protect their own server while attempting to exploit weaknesses in other teams’ servers.
Denmark’s team has finished among Europe’s five best for the past five years and won gold in 2022.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, established the team in 2017 to develop talent capable of addressing Denmark’s growing cyberthreats.
The team is also supported by universities, European organizations and Industriens Fond, a foundation supporting the competitiveness of Danish industry.
Aarhus will host the European Cybersecurity Championship next year.
Denmark’s autumn holiday to bring sunshine, rain and overnight frost
Denmark’s autumn holiday will bring a mixture of sunny, dry periods and rainy weather, with temperatures falling to around freezing early in the week.
“It is an autumn holiday that looks really nice for most people,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Kasper Bonde Niebe said.
“There will be periods where it is a bit wetter, but there are also periods with some really nice days with sun and dry weather for much of the country.”
Light frost was recorded in central Jutland overnight into Monday. Monday morning temperatures will range from zero to five degrees in Jutland, while eastern Denmark will be slightly warmer because of cloud cover.
Showers and clouds will remain in eastern Denmark during the morning before giving way to sunshine and dry weather in the afternoon.
Temperatures could fall slightly below freezing in central Zealand overnight into Tuesday. No further overnight frost is expected during the rest of the week.
Tuesday will begin sunny before a rain front moves across Denmark from the west. Temperatures will reach between 11 and 15 degrees.
Wednesday is expected to be dry and stable, with temperatures up to 15 degrees. Thursday will remain dry but become cloudier, with temperatures reaching 17 degrees.
Another weather front will arrive overnight into Friday, bringing widespread rain during the day.
Danish foreign minister warns US-Russia diesel deal could help finance war
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates has warned that a new diesel agreement between the United States and Russia could provide additional funding for Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“It is regrettable if this secures additional revenue for Russia,” Rasmussen told Danish public broadcaster DR on Saturday.
“In the EU, we have put a lot of work into tough sanctions and into reducing dependence on Russian energy, and that work must not be undermined,” he said.
“We must continue to pressure Russia’s economy and stand together in support of Ukraine.”
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin had reached an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury Department has issued a temporary authorization easing sanctions to allow Russia to sell diesel internationally. The authorization is valid until April 7, 2027, Reuters reported.
A British government spokesperson said the United Kingdom would maintain pressure on Russia through what it called the strictest sanctions regime the country has implemented.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said the deal would provide Russia with more money to wage war.
The agreement comes after gasoline and diesel prices rose sharply across the United States, increasing costs for consumers and businesses and contributing to higher inflation.
Danish business emergency network grows to 223 members
The number of companies and organizations in Virksomhedsberedskabet, Denmark’s business emergency preparedness network, has risen from 63 to 223 in just over 10 months.
Together, its members represent about 350,000 private-sector employees.
The network coordinates resources from private companies so they can help maintain essential services during serious crises.
“It is about having this conversation about what one already has on the shelves, and how it can actually be repurposed for a crisis and support critical infrastructure,” director Maja Broløs said.
Fitness centers could provide shelter, baby stores could supply essential products and department stores could make their buildings available. Companies participating in the network include SATS Denmark, BabySam and IKEA.
Virksomhedsberedskabet is part of a broader effort to strengthen Denmark’s emergency preparedness. In February, the government launched a total defence preparedness initiative and allocated 1.2 billion DKK to the area.
Broløs said more members would be needed to respond effectively to a nationwide crisis.
“If it is a major regional crisis, we are in a pretty good position. But if it is nationwide, then those are completely different numbers we need to reach,” she said.
The network aims to exceed 1,000 members by 2029. By 2028, it plans to be capable of mobilizing members’ resources nationwide within six hours.
DTU Aqua to create 40 fish nurseries near Bornholm
DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources at the Technical University of Denmark, will establish 40 fish nurseries and spawning grounds near Bornholm over the next five years.
The artificial nurseries, known as biohuts, will be placed in the ports of Rønne and Hasle, Danish broadcaster TV 2 Bornholm reported.
The project aims to increase the number of young fish around the biohuts by 30 percent and raise local perch and pike populations by 20 percent.
Researchers will examine whether local restoration initiatives can strengthen fish stocks and reverse biodiversity loss. DTU Aqua will also develop a monitoring system for coastal and marine areas.
Bornholm is one of nine European islands participating in the EU-funded Isla Bonita project. Each island will establish a “Living Lab” where local groups will collaborate on nature restoration.
The projects will reflect local needs. Santorini will focus on reducing plastic pollution, while Scotland’s Orkney Islands will restore oyster reefs.
The islands are located across the Atlantic, Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North seas.
The EU is providing 16.2 million euros, equivalent to nearly 121.1 million DKK, for the project. It involves 51 organizations from 16 countries.
This year, oxygen depletion was recorded in 38 of Denmark’s 108 coastal waters, compared with 33 in 2025 and 34 in 2024.
`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

A 50-year-old Ukrainian man accused of leading the 2022 attacks on gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea appeared in a Hamburg courtroom as his lawyer called for the charges to be dismissed.
The defendant, identified by German media as Serhii K., will not testify because of confidentiality obligations linked to his former service in Ukraine’s special forces, his lawyer said.
Defense attorney Nicola Canestrini argued that prosecutors lacked clear evidence connecting his client to the explosions.
He also accused Russia of using the pipelines to exert political and economic pressure.
“They were a means of exerting pressure in a war,” Canestrini said, according to Reuters.
Serhii K. faces charges including complicity in war crimes, disrupting public utilities, causing explosions and destroying structures.
German prosecutors allege that he led a group responsible for sabotaging the Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022.
According to the indictment, the group traveled aboard a yacht rented in Rostock, Germany, before reaching waters near the Danish island of Bornholm and planting explosives.
Prosecutors also allege that Serhii K. traveled through Poland to Germany using a false passport months before the attacks.
He was arrested in Italy last year.
Supporters gathered outside the courthouse, questioning the war crimes allegations against him.
“Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” one protester told Reuters.
Russia has denied involvement in the explosions, although several Western countries initially suspected Moscow.
The pipelines, built by Russian energy company Gazprom, lie 80 to 110 meters beneath the Baltic Sea.
The trial is expected to continue until February.

Brazil Senate approves Bill to shorten work week in election boost for Lula

- The vote passed 75-1, and Lula said it means “more time to live, rest, be with family” and is “a victory for workers.”

AI generated
BRASILIA – Brazil’s Senate approved legislation to shorten the work week without reducing pay, handing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a potential lifeline days ahead of an election he is trailing.
The Senate voted 75-1 in favour of the Bill on Oct 14 in two rounds of votes, granting final passage to a proposal that will end the so-called “6x1” work schedule, under which some 16 million Brazilians work six days a week with one day off.
A former trade unionist, Lula has put the proposal, which will give workers subject to the 6x1 schedule an extra day off, at the centre of his efforts to mount a comeback from a first-round upset that turned right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro into the front runner ahead of Brazil’s Oct 25 run-off.
The leftist leader earlier in 2026 made the reduction in weekly working hours – to 40 from 44 – the flagship promise of his campaign.
Since finishing behind Bolsonaro in the Oct 4 first-round vote, he has challenged the Senator to back the proposal in social media videos and staged rallies in Sao Paulo and Brasilia where many attendees called for passage of the plan.
Bolsonaro, who previously opposed the Bill and sought to delay the vote until after the election, reversed course on Oct 13, saying he would vote for the legislation because most workers support it.
Investors and prediction markets consider Bolsonaro the favourite, and no candidate who trailed in the first round has won a run-off since Brazil returned to democracy in 1989.
Polls, however, suggest Lula is still within striking distance.
Bolsonaro would take 51% of valid votes, excluding blank and null ballots, to Lula’s 49% in the run-off, according to a Quaest survey released on Oct 14.
Bolsonaro outperformed Quaest’s final poll of the first round by about two points, while Lula underperformed by one.
Lula hailed the Senate vote, saying the policy is “more than just a change in working hours”.
“It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch one’s children grow up, take care of oneself, and enjoy life,” he said in a social media post. “This is a victory for workers.”
The question facing Lula is whether broad popular support for the measure will translate into an electoral boost.
Many of his major policies, including new tax exemptions for workers, debt renegotiation initiatives and a programme to provide basic medicines at no cost, are overwhelmingly popular.
But the 80-year-old President has struggled to turn that into votes, and segments of his working class base have moved rightward amid labour market shifts, crushing household debt levels and the rising cost of living.
Bolsonaro has continued advocating for an alternative proposal that he argues would provide greater flexibility in labour rules by letting employees negotiate hours with businesses, calling it a better solution than Lula’s.
Business groups have opposed the work week change, arguing it will increase costs while reducing productivity.
Lula’s government also unveiled a debt relief proposal for so-called micro-entrepreneurs on Oct 13, targeting voters who typically lean conservative. BLOOMBERG

Adelaide laneway named in honour of hip hop pioneers Hilltop Hoods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:00:39 UTC
13:00:39 KST

Hilltop Hoods honoured with laneway and mural in Adelaide CBD
Pioneering Australian hip hop group Hilltop Hoods rapped about "Goin' down a hard road" in 2006.
Now, the Adelaide trio are being honoured with a laneway in their hometown.
Clubhouse Lane, running off Hindley Street in Adelaide's CBD, was renamed Hilltop Hoods Lane at a ceremony today.
Two large-scale murals featuring the group and their associated iconography, created by Adelaide artist Vans the Omega, run down both sides of the laneway.
The Hoods, who still call Adelaide home, say it's an "incredible honour" to have their own laneway in the heart of the city they know and love.
"We have great memories of gigging in that part of town," Pressure told Double J's Dylan Lewis.
"When we were paying our dues and coming up there was heaps of old bars and clubs that we used to play. Some of them are still there, some are not."
Paying tribute to one of Australia's most successful and enduring musical acts, Hilltop Hoods Lane is the sixth addition to City of Adelaide's City of Music Laneway trail.
The growing collection includes landmarks recognising South Australian music legends Cold Chisel, Sia, Paul Kelly, No Fixed Address, and The Angels.
Hilltop Hoods even have some suggestions for the next honorary music landmark.
"I reckon Funkoars need a lane! Surely Guy Sebastian should have one," they told Lewis. "Guy Lane? Does have a ring to it."
Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith said Hilltop Hoods's enduring impact on Australian music and culture made them a worthy addition to Adelaide's City of Music Laneways.
"Once considered the Australian music industry's underdogs, the Hoods have harnessed their talent and determination to not only top the charts but build a multi-generational fan base in their mosh pits," Dr Lomax-Smith said.
"Despite their global success, they have never forgotten their Adelaide roots. That's why it's fabulous to permanently recognise their achievements on the streets."
Starting as teenagers in 1994 around the hills of Blackwood, Hilltop Hoods elevated Australian hip hop from the underground and into the mainstream. And to resounding success.
The trio — Suffa (Matthew Lambert), Pressure (Dan Smith) and DJ Debris (Barry Francis) — have released a record-making seven ARIA number one albums, won 10 ARIA Awards, six APRA Awards, and sold out multiple national arena tours.
They have made triple j's annual Hottest 100 on a record 27 occasions, the most entries of any music group.
Their 2003 breakout single The Nosebleed Section came second place to INXS's poll-topping Never Tear Us Apart in last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, in which they charted twice more (Cosby Sweater at #64 and 1955 at #73).
"Few music acts are as deeply woven into the cultural fabric of South Australia as Hilltop Hoods," said Vans the Omega, wanting his artwork to honour their connection to devoted fans and the wider public alike.
"This work aims to be both uplifting and historic, offering a place to reflect on our own lives and the journey we have shared alongside music that has shaped generations of fans of all ages.
"Like the Hoods, these walls stand as a lasting testament to what can be achieved through hard work and determination in our beautiful, humble city of Adelaide."
The first Australian hip hop group to have a laneway named in their honour, Hilltop Hoods join a growing list of musical landmarks around the country. That includes lanes named for AC/DC and Chrissy Amphlett in Melbourne, and The Go Between Bridge in Brisbane.

Architecture Between Land and Water: Design Lessons from the Bayou
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

A bayou is a slow-moving body of water, typically a creek or river that winds through low, flat terrain in a broader wetland landscape. Found throughout the Gulf Coast, bayous are distinct from swamps, which contain forested wetlands characterized by standing water, and from marshes, where tall grasses and herbaceous plants grow in saturated soils. The currents of a bayou landscape support biodiverse ecosystems of plants, trees, insects, birds, and fish, while the shifting water levels, saturated ground, humid air, heavy rainfall, and long, hot summers create a blurry environment between land and water, wet and dry, interior and exterior.
Communities have inhabited bayou environments for thousands of years, and the architectural language within them reflects generations of adaptation to unique environmental and hydrological conditions. Buildings are elevated above wet, flood-prone grounds with steep roofs and deep overhangs to shed rain and provide shade, while porches, courtyards, breezeways, and tall interior spaces move air through occupied spaces. Certain aesthetic characteristics, like earth-toned materials or broad front porches, will recur throughout the region, but beneath these elements lies a more consequential architectural logic. Bayou architecture patterns historically accommodate this variability, negotiating water, heat, humidity, and airflow through the way buildings meet the ground, shape their envelopes, and organize the spaces between inside and outside.
From Houston, often referred to as the Bayou City, to New Orleans and the landscapes of southern Louisiana, the following lessons demonstrate how accumulated local knowledge continues to inform contemporary design in the twenty-first century. As architects design for places where established climatic conditions are becoming less predictable, these projects offer a perspective on architecture with a careful observation of place and respond through adaptation. Foundations, roofs, envelopes, landscapes, and social spaces become part of an environmental strategy, revealing how vernacular knowledge translates into contemporary architecture and how buildings respond to the landscapes they inhabit.
How to Touch the Ground
In bayou environments, the ground is not a reliable foundation. High water tables, poorly drained soils, periodic inundation, and the movement of water through the landscape leave the ground saturated for extended periods, while storms and seasonal flooding raise the water beyond its ordinary limits. The first architectural question is how to touch the ground.
Across the region, buildings respond by rising above it. Slender piers and stilts allow water and air to pass beneath a structure, while more substantial columns, raised foundations, and elevated plinths keep occupied spaces above anticipated flood levels. The appropriate approach depends on soil conditions, flood exposure, building scale, and program, but the underlying principle remains the same. The foundation is treated as a negotiated edge between architecture and a landscape whose conditions are expected to change seasonally.
How to Move Air
In a hot, humid climate, an essential component of interior comfort will depend on creating sustained air movement. Courtyards, deep porches, breezeways, and other shaded thresholds extend the building outward while drawing air deeper inside. When oriented and proportioned for the scale of the building, courtyards encourage cross-ventilation through adjacent rooms and allow warm air to rise through the open space above, while vegetation and shade reduce solar exposure within the interior courtyard surfaces. Openings in the building envelope positioned across from one another strengthen air movement, allowing prevailing breezes to pass through the building through skylights, open doors or windows, and courtyards.
Deep porches perform a complementary role in drawing air movement. By shading walls and windows from direct sun, they reduce the amount of heat absorbed by the building envelope, while their depth protects doors and operable windows from rainfall, allowing them to stay open through rainy weather conditions. Porches, whether they wrap the entire building or frame the primary entrances, create a thicker, more adaptable boundary threshold between inside and outside, one that tempers sun, rain, and moving air. In the bayou, the edge of a building is an inhabitable space that helps the architecture adjust to changing conditions throughout the day and across the seasons.
How to Shed Water
In a landscape defined by frequent, intense rainfall, the roof is one of a building's most consequential environmental systems. Vernacular builders across the bayou region respond with pitched roofs and deep overhangs that move water quickly away from interior spaces while shading the walls below and protecting openings from sun and rain. The dogtrot house offers a clear example of a single pitched roof that extends across two enclosed volumes and the open breezeway between them, sheltering the passage from rainfall while creating a shaded corridor through the center of the home where air can circulate.
Contemporary architects continue this logic, using shed roofs, folded planes, butterfly forms, and clustered gables to direct rainfall, collect water, frame views of the surrounding landscape, and extend protective canopies over the porches below. Not every building in a wet climate requires the same roof form, but the movement of water is essential to shape the form and orientation throughout the design process. Roof geometry, overhangs, gutters, drainage, and collection systems work together to determine where water falls and how it returns to the ground. In this way, the roof gives architectural expression to environmental forces, turning practical decisions of managing rainfall into the building's identity.
How to Design with Moisture
In the persistent humidity of the bayou, materials and wall assemblies must release moisture, allowing walls, roofs, and other exposed surfaces to dry before prolonged dampness leads to mold or corrosion. Traditional builders relied on durable and decay-resistant materials, such as cypress, brick, and stucco, while contemporary projects expand this palette with metal cladding, fiber cement, and other materials selected for their ability to withstand repeated exposure to moisture. Ventilated rainscreens extend this logic into the construction of the wall, creating a drained and ventilated cavity behind the exterior cladding where water escapes and air circulates.
Shutters, louvers, jalousie windows, transoms, and screens are tools of operable assemblies that create adjustable layers between occupied spaces and the exterior, allowing buildings to admit breezes when conditions are favorable, reduce solar exposure during the hottest times of the day, and provide protection when storms arrive. Contemporary construction balances operability with the demands of moisture control, airtightness, and mechanical conditioning. The designers in this environment create a building envelope that is capable of responding to humid conditions.
How to Design for Heat
In the bayou climate, heat and humidity reinforce one another, making the control of solar heat gain essential to maintaining comfortable interior spaces. Light-colored exterior walls and reflective roofing materials reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the building envelope, while shade from deep eaves, porches, vegetation, and adjacent structures limit direct exposure in the interior spaces. These strategies are relatively simple, but they effectively reduce the thermal burden placed on occupants and mechanical cooling systems during the long, hot summers that characterize the region. Inside, tall ceilings increase the volume of space above occupants and allow warmer air to collect above, while clerestories, transoms, and high operable vents pull warm air outside. Even in compact floor plans, additional height creates a sense of openness while contributing to a more responsive interior.
How to Work with the Landscape
Site orientation reduces solar exposure, captures prevailing breezes, and determines interior daylight, but in cities and towns, existing street grids, neighboring structures, and zoning setbacks may limit the freedom to position a building. Even within restrictions, openings should be aligned with local wind patterns, western exposures should be shaded by trees, galleries, and deep eaves, and courtyards should be used to bring light and air into urban footprints. In a bayou environment, the site is part of a larger hydrological system. Permeable surfaces, bioswales, rain gardens, planted buffers, and areas designed to temporarily hold water will slow runoff and reduce the volume of water entering drainage systems. At a larger scale, preserving existing vegetation and maintaining connections to natural drainage patterns ensures a project participates in the hydrology of its surroundings.
How to Center Social Life
Perhaps the most compelling lesson of bayou architecture is that some of its most comfortable spaces are rarely found in the entirely enclosed, interior spaces. Deep porches, shaded courtyards, covered galleries, and dogtrot passages occupy the threshold between a controlled interior and the exposed landscape, offering long hours of shade and access to moving air. Their social value is inseparable from their environmental performance. Shade, airflow, and protection from rain make longer periods of occupation possible, while their position at the edge of the building creates opportunities for interaction that more clearly divided interior and exterior spaces may not provide. Climate-responsive design shapes how and how long people gather together, turning environmental infrastructure into social infrastructure.
Lessons from Architecture in the Bayou
The lessons of the bayou carry new weight in the contemporary practice because the landscape that shaped them is changing. Sea level rise, subsidence, coastal land loss, and increasing flood exposure alter the conditions under which communities across the Gulf Coast build and rebuild. Buildings rise above uncertain ground, envelopes open and close, landscapes hold or slow water, and air movement makes extreme climates more comfortable.
A changing climate exposes the limits of adaptation at the scale of an individual building. Architecture alone cannot indefinitely compensate for changing coastlines, subsiding land, disappearing wetlands, or increasing flood risk. Designing for the bayou asks architects to design beyond the building's boundary toward the larger systems that make inhabitation possible. The local knowledge embedded in bayou architecture is not a collection of historical solutions to reproduce, but a way of design-thinking to expand upon. Its larger lessons are of responsiveness and observation. In the bayou and far beyond it, place-based design considers the comfort, health, safety, and identity of future landscapes.

U.S. inflation accelerates in September amid high prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:54 CST
12:54:54 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. inflation accelerated in September, according to data released Wednesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) jumped a hefty 3.7 percent year on year, exceeding Wall Street estimates of 3.6 percent and rising from the previous month's 3.4 percent.
Headline inflation increased by 0.6 percent month on month, driven primarily by a 9.1 percent surge in gasoline prices, according to the data.
Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, also ticked up, climbing 2.6 percent over the last 12 months.
Price increases for shelter, car repairs and medical services rose at a time when Americans have been reeling from price hikes since inflation took hold in 2021.
Some experts noted that inflation is ramping up rather than tamping down.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua, "Inflation is getting higher, not lower and it's in the core, not just energy ... If you're the Fed looking to hit a 2 percent target, you're going the wrong way."
The news caused markets to drop on Wednesday, on fears that a rate cut is even further off than investors had expected. Some experts said the Fed would have to raise rates to get inflation down.
Gary Hufbauer, a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said "the outlook is for continued high PCE inflation, near 4 percent. To push the rate down, the Fed needs to increase the policy rate to near 5 percent."
Meanwhile, the midterm elections are just around the corner and Republicans are expected to take the brunt of voters' blame for high prices.
Some experts noted that inflation remains a risk to the GOP, the party in power.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West said "inflation remains painfully high and that poses serious risks for Republicans in November."
However, even if Democrats grab control of Congress, prices are unlikely to come down this year.
While halting the Iran war could bring down energy prices, addressing underlying inflation would require significant interest rate hikes, an unlikely move by the Fed given concerns that aggressive tightening could trigger an economic downturn. ■

8 U.S. states sue OpenAI over alleged ChatGPT safety risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:42 CST
12:54:42 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Attorneys general from eight U.S. states filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing the artificial intelligence company of endangering children through its ChatGPT chatbot and misleading consumers about the product's safety.
The lawsuits were filed independently in state courts by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana, as part of a coordinated bipartisan legal effort.
According to statements released by the state attorneys general and court filings, OpenAI allegedly designed ChatGPT to be overly agreeable and to simulate human compassion, encouraging users to develop trust in the chatbot and spend more time interacting with it.
The lawsuits allege that ChatGPT can reinforce delusional thinking, provide dangerous medical advice and, in some instances, encourage users to harm themselves or others.
The states accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety while failing to adequately disclose known risks, in alleged violation of state consumer protection laws.
The lawsuits seek court orders requiring OpenAI to modify ChatGPT's operations and strengthen user protections, as well as civil penalties and damages.
Some of the legal demands also seek to restrict the development of self-improving AI models unless their alignment with human values can be demonstrated.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had implemented age-specific safety measures, including parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections.
The company would continue working with experts to strengthen safeguards and cooperate with states on developing AI policies applicable to the broader industry, Pusateri said.
The coordinated legal action follows a lawsuit filed by Florida's attorney general in June over alleged safety risks associated with ChatGPT. ■

Feature: Winter Universiade flame reaches Changchun, passed from hand to hand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:38 CST
12:54:38 KST

CHANGCHUN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The flame lantern was carried into the Changchun History and Culture Museum on Wednesday morning, past a crowd gathered in the cold. It had come from Turin, Italy, where the flame was kindled on October 8 at the birthplace of the Universiade.
Its destination was Changchun, capital of northeast China's Jilin Province and co-host with neighboring Jilin City of the 2027 Winter Universiade.
Inside, 12 people waited to pass the lantern from hand to hand. They were chosen not for fame but for their work in the city, including a firefighter, a delivery courier, a student, a pilot, a police officer, a bank clerk, an insurance claims worker and a WorldSkills award winner. Organizers said the selection was intended to show that the flame belongs to everyone who helps build the city.
The last of the 12 to receive the lantern was Zhou Yang, a three-time Olympic short track speed skating champion. She then passed it to Changchun Mayor Gu Gang.
"The flame is very warm," Zhou said. "It represents athletes' burning dreams. The weather is cold today, so it feels warm. But it traveled thousands of miles from Turin to Changchun. This lantern is a heavy honor."
Zhou competed at the 2007 Asian Winter Games in Changchun and the 2009 Harbin Winter Universiade, where she won the 1,500m title. She said the Universiade gave her confidence ahead of the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics, where she won two gold medals.
"For me, it's a kind of inheritance," she said of going from competitor to flame bearer. "When I was a competitor, I received the baton from my predecessors. Now I've become a passer."
Among the 12 was Nilava Darya, a Belarusian sophomore majoring in Chinese language education at Jilin International Studies University, who will volunteer at the Games.
"I feel very excited and proud to witness and participate in this flame event," she said. "I welcome young people from all over the world to Changchun."
Darya said Changchun is quieter than other Chinese cities she has visited, and warmer. "I can say it's my second hometown," she said.
In the audience was 90-year-old Gao Xiangchen, who learned to skate as a child and took up figure skating at 65. He continued until he was 83, when his family persuaded him to stop.
"I'm so excited that a world-class winter sports event like the Universiade will be held in Changchun," he said. "I will definitely go watch in person. My favorite sport is figure skating."
His daughter, Gao Yan, was a volunteer at the 11th National Winter Games in 2008 and a torchbearer for the 2008 Beijing Olympics. She said the arrival of the flame symbolized both sportsmanship and Changchun's ice and snow culture.
The flame was collected in Turin, where the first Summer Universiade was held in 1959. Since 2018, Turin has been home to FISU's "Flame of Knowledge," and the flame for each Universiade is kindled there before being taken to the host city.
"The lighting of the 'Flame of Knowledge' in Turin always represents a strong link between the birthplace of the Universiade and the future host," said FISU President Leonz Eder, who attended the collection ceremony.
The 33rd Winter Universiade will run from January 15 to 25, 2027. It will be the first Winter Universiade held in China since Harbin in 2009, following the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics and the 2025 Harbin Asian Winter Games.
Changchun 2027 will feature 97 events across 12 sports. Freestyle skiing will be the only snow sport staged in both host cities. All competition venues are existing facilities being upgraded, while 8,100 volunteer candidates have been recruited.
Nan Chunhua, an executive with the Games' large-scale activities department, was a member of the team that traveled to Turin for the collection ceremony. She said the flame's journey served as a bridge between the two cities.
"When the flame was successfully introduced into the lantern, I was very excited and moved," she said. "This flame carries the hard work of the entire preparation team and the good wishes of the world for the Changchun Universiade."
After the lantern was passed among the 12 representatives, it was used to light the Games' torch, named "Jixiang," or "Auspicious Soaring." Jilin provincial governor Hu Yuting then lit the cauldron, "Zhuxue Yangyan," which translates roughly as "Chasing Snow, Raising Flame."
For Zhou, the message was simple.
"I hope China's sports, especially winter sports, will get better and better," she said. "I hope athletes coming to Changchun will feel the warmth of the people here." ■

by sportswriter Liu Yang
FUZHOU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Fujian Sturgeons have retained their core roster, re-signed head coach Aleksandar Kesar and added three imports as the young squad prepares for the 2026-27 Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) season, which marks the return of relegation after a 22-year absence.
Fujian has kept nearly its entire domestic rotation from last season. Veteran Su Ruoyu, a key offseason addition, is recovering from a preseason injury and is expected to return to team training soon. Meng Yi, the leading scorer on the club's youth team, has been promoted to the first team, underscoring the club's commitment to developing homegrown talent.
The young squad drew widespread attention last season with a series of upset victories. Fujian earned its first-ever away win over powerhouse Guangdong Southern Tigers and went on to sweep the season series. The Sturgeons also snapped the Zhejiang Golden Bulls' seven-game winning streak and came from behind to beat the Beijing Ducks.
Fujian opens its new campaign on October 17 with an away game against the Jiangsu Dragons.
"Being captain is not about glory; it is about responsibility," captain Zou Yang said. "We cannot guarantee a playoff spot, but we will fight until the final buzzer every game. I hope the fans can see the resilience and tenacity in our play."
The 26-year-old forward spent the offseason training overseas to improve his ability to cope with physical pressure, sharpening his finishing through contact and his shooting consistency.
"As captain, I need to serve as a bridge between the coaches, local players and imports," Zou added. "I will try to help our younger teammates, making sure every player understands their role during games."
Three new imports headline Fujian's offseason additions. U.S. combo guard Javion Hamlet joins after three seasons with the Tianjin Pioneers, where he averaged 21.8 points and 5.8 assists per game last season. American guard Daryl Macon, who has NBA experience, adds perimeter firepower and defensive versatility, while big man Bennie Boatwright provides frontcourt depth.
The Sturgeons finished 14th in 2025-26 in Kesar's first full season in charge, narrowly missing the playoffs. The domestic players have an average age of 23.5 this season, making Fujian one of the youngest squads in the league.
"We had one of the youngest rosters in the league and came close to the playoffs last season, beating several top teams along the way," Kesar said. "We aim to build a winning culture here. Our young players have improved through summer training and will receive meaningful minutes."
The 2026-27 relegation framework introduces a new competitive dynamic for all 20 CBA clubs. Under the new system, the bottom two teams in the regular season will face the top two National Basketball League (NBL) sides in April 2027.
Club executive director Wu Bolan expressed confidence in Kesar while acknowledging the increased pressure brought by the league's structural reform.
"We give full trust to Kesar and his coaching group," Wu said. "Our focus is on internal development, team chemistry and competitive spirit, so that we can meet the new challenges."
"We aim to compete for higher standings, and we must hold onto the fighting spirit. This team will withstand whatever pressure the new season brings," she added. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australia's unemployment rate rose to 4.7 percent in September, as employment fell and more people became unemployed, official statistics showed on Thursday.
The number of employed people fell by 39,000, while the number of unemployed people increased by 9,000, Sean Crick, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) head of labor statistics, said in a statement.
The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.6 percent, while the participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.8 percent, Crick said.
The underemployment rate, which measures people who want and are available to work more hours, rose 0.1 percentage points to 6.3 percent, according to the latest data.
Part-time hours worked fell 1.5 percent in September, while full-time hours increased 0.4 percent, Crick said.
On a trend basis, which the ABS recommends for assessing underlying labor market conditions, the trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 percent. Trend employment grew by 0.1 percent, while hours worked remained steady in trend terms in September, statistics showed.
Annual growth in employment and hours worked stood at 1.2 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, the ABS said. ■

Taiwan pineapples moving closer to US market next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:41:08 UTC
12:41:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan could begin exporting pineapples to the US as early as February 2027, with administrative preparations complete and final import rules still pending from US authorities, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said Wednesday.
The US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) published a proposal outlining import requirements for Taiwanese pineapples in the Federal Register on March 3, per SET News. The public comment period has ended, but the US has yet to publish final rules.
Chen told reporters before a Legislative Yuan Economics Committee meeting that he hoped the US would finalize the requirements before Taiwan’s peak pineapple season, which runs from February through May. Initial shipments would primarily consist of the golden diamond variety, which accounts for more than 90% of Taiwan’s pineapple production.
Under the proposed rules, Taiwanese pineapples would be eligible for export after passing phytosanitary inspections, being confirmed free of pests of concern to the US, and receiving a phytosanitary certificate, SET News reported. The requirements would not mandate irradiation, vapor heat treatment, or removal of the fruit’s crown.
The proposal would allow pineapple varieties in the Cayenne group, including golden diamond and mango pineapples. The Agriculture Ministry plans to continue encouraging farmers to grow mango pineapples because they are better suited to storage and transportation.
According to the Agriculture Ministry’s latest statistics, Taiwan exported 15,700 metric tons of pineapples to Japan this year, per UDN. Shipments to Canada, South Korea, and Australia rose by nearly 409%, 171%, and 29%, respectively, while Taiwan also expanded into markets including New Zealand, Singapore, and Malaysia.

====================================================================================================

Israel's economic future at risk as productivity falls behind G7 nations, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:21:36 UTC
12:21:36 KST

Israel has fallen from outperforming the world’s leading advanced economies on a key productivity measure to trailing them, according to a Shoresh Institution report warning that the next government must address educational and budgetary priorities that threaten the country’s long-term economic viability.
The report, published last Thursday by the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research, places Israel’s total factor productivity at 15% below the G7 average in 2023, compared with 9% above it in 1975. The measure assesses how efficiently an economy combines labor and capital to produce goods and services.
Written by Shoresh President Prof. Dan Ben-David, the report said weak education, rapid demographic change, and the departure of skilled Israelis reinforce one another, leaving the country increasingly dependent on a narrow group of workers to sustain its economy, healthcare, and defense capabilities.
“The upcoming election will determine who governs Israel, but the deeper question is what kind of country the government will govern a generation from now,” Ben-David said in a statement accompanying the report.
The historical comparison showed how sharply Israel’s relative position changed. In 1954, its total factor productivity was 27% below the G7 average. It overtook that benchmark within roughly two decades, then fell behind again.
Israel exceeded every G7 country in 1972, slides massively by 2024
A separate measure, output per hour worked, tells a similar story. According to Shoresh’s calculations, Israel exceeded every G7 country in 1972 but trailed six of the seven by 2024. Its output per hour was 34% below Germany’s and 30% below the United States'. Japan was the exception.
These are relative comparisons: falling behind other countries does not necessarily mean Israel produces less than it did in the past. It means, rather, that its performance has failed to keep pace.
Ben-David attributes the change to a shift beginning in the 1970s away from investment in infrastructure, education and public services toward sectoral interests. He said that defense spending alone cannot explain the shortfalls, pointing to decades when civilian government expenditure, measured against the size of the economy, matched or exceeded the OECD average.
Israel’s hi-tech success masks a much weaker performance across the rest of the economy. According to the report’s 2022 figures, each hour worked in hi-tech generated 22% more economic value than the average hour worked across OECD economies. But outside hi-tech, where roughly nine in 10 Israeli workers were employed, each hour generated 24% less than that average.
Highly-skilled workers incentivized to leave by taxes
The report also said the highest-earning fifth accounted for 93% of income-tax revenue in 2024, up from 83% in 2000. That concentration, Ben-David said, makes the country vulnerable when highly skilled workers leave.
Expanding that skilled workforce will depend on the education children receive today. According to the report, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) children account for 25% of first graders in 2026 and Arabic-speaking children for another 23%. Haredim make up approximately 6% of Israelis aged 50-54, but 26% of children aged four and under.
The question, Ben-David asked, is whether today’s pupils receive the education needed to become tomorrow’s engineers, physicians and other skilled workers.
Shoresh’s analysis of the 2025 PISA assessments places pupils in state-religious schools below 76% of OECD countries and those in secular Jewish schools below 81%, based on average performance across mathematics, science and reading. Arabic-speaking pupils scored below every OECD country and six of the seven participating Arab countries.
Most haredi boys, who do not study the full core curriculum, do not participate in the tests, the report noted.
When the PISA results were released, the Education Ministry stressed the wartime conditions under which students took the assessments, including displacement and interrupted schooling.
The report also points to a growing number of Israeli physicians abroad. In 2000, the number working in other OECD countries, excluding the United States, was equivalent to 0.7% of the number of physicians in Israel. By 2023, that ratio had risen to 1.9%, according to Shoresh’s analysis.
Ben-David warns that departures could increase the burden on those who remain, encouraging further emigration.
His proposed “Israel 2.0” program calls for an upgraded compulsory core curriculum for all pupils, public funding only for compliant schools, and a shift in national spending priorities. It also proposes electoral and governance reform, stronger checks and balances.
“The window for change is still open – but it is closing,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Israeli election campaigns must move past political gimmicks to tackle critical issues - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:21:05 UTC
12:21:05 KST

As the campaigns before the fateful October 27 elections head into their final two weeks, the “shtickim” and “trickim” – as Israelis refer to the shtick and tricks that typify every election and the debate in this one until now – need to stop.
The coalition has plastered billboards and issued online clips warning of “Yamin or Falestine” – a campaign without any attempt to hide its racist overtones that shows Yashar leader and primary contender Gad Eisenkot with the likes of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi peering out from behind his broad shoulders in a crass attempt to say that if Eisenkot becomes prime minister, he will form a coalition with Abbas’s Ra’am Party.
The Shinui (Change) bloc has nonstop focused on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s role in the lead-up and aftermath of the October 7 massacre at the expense of outlining and detailing their platforms and plans once they’re in power (save for the B’Yachad party, which has published comprehensive programs for each ministry).
The lack of real content is a major problem for such a crucial election, but more than that, Israeli election campaigns often rely on manufactured crises and last-minute disclosures.
Foremost is the one that could potentially postpone the election – a return to war with Iran. According to an Axios report on Wednesday, Netanyahu spoke to US President Donald Trump last week to discuss the possibility of a renewed military campaign that could target Iran’s nuclear and military sites, with Netanyahu citing alleged Iranian efforts to rebuild nuclear capacity as the reason for launching new strikes.
Renewed fighting could lead to postponement of elections
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir has warned that renewed fighting before the Israeli elections could delay them. For his part, Trump has said he would not make that decision until after the US November midterms.
We, the voters, without the information, of course, have no way of knowing whether Iran’s reported moves pose an immediate threat that would require action within the next two weeks.
But the prime minister has built his campaign and garnered loyalty among his supporters by portraying himself as the strong man who saved Israel post-October 7 against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. An attack and an election delay would certainly bolster that image.
Of course, on the other side, the pre-October 7 timeline and its immediate aftermath are what is driving the opposition. And they’re getting ammunition from timely disclosures almost daily.
Netanyahu’s former military secretary Avi Gil last week alleged that the premier presented an incomplete account of the events surrounding Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack.
In a splash on Israel Hayom and Channel 12, Gil alleged that Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Tzahi Braverman, sought to alter an official record from that morning by changing the time Netanyahu first received an update on the October 7 Hamas invasion via phone call from Gil from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m.
Major defamation lawsuit against Netanyahu by Shin Bet's Ronen Bar
Adding to the flame is Wednesday’s bombshell: a NIS 3 million defamation lawsuit filed by former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar against Netanyahu, alleging that the premier falsely accused him of knowing in advance about the October 7 attack and deliberately withholding that information.
Despite the seriousness of the accusations by Gil and Bar, the timing of the disclosure, less than three weeks before the elections, is suspect. Both Gil and Bar said they remained silent until now, hoping to testify before a state commission of inquiry that Netanyahu has refused to authorize.
But either Gil’s or Bar’s disclosure could have come two weeks ago, after voters went to the polls. These, along with the slew of other accusations that Netanyahu was warned of October 7 by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt, coming so close to the elections, can only be seen as creating an artificial crisis.
Instead, with two weeks to go, let’s hear how the parties are going to deal with education, transportation, the environment, the unequal IDF draft, the worrying wave of emigration, the future of the West Bank, and the scourge of settler violence, among others.
These elections are too critical to the country’s future for the final two weeks to focus on sensational headlines instead of the issues the country faces.

crafted from dual-tone solid oak, TUPI lamp by estudio gris resembles bird at rest

crafted from dual-tone solid oak, TUPI lamp by estudio gris resembles bird at rest
designed by medellín-based estudio gris, tupi table lamp features a hand-turned solid oak body resembling a bird, complete with a dark wooden beak that conceals the light source to project a warm downward glow.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ESTUDIO GRIS SHAPES SOLID OAK INTO A LAMP RECALLING A BIRD AT REST
TUPI is a table lamp by Estudio Gris, the Medellín-based studio led by Gustavo Rodríguez and Estefanía Agudelo. The piece starts from a single observation: the stillness of a bird at rest, that moment when it stops moving and simply watches. The body is turned from solid oak in a local workshop in Medellín, Colombia, and assembled by hand. Its tapered silhouette rises to a rounded head, where a darker wooden beak extends forward, and a small turned eye completes the figure. The beak works as the lamp’s shade: the light source sits beneath it, so the glow falls softly down the oak body instead of reaching the eye directly.
DUAL-TONE WOODS AND FLUSH DETAILS ILLUMINATE OAK GRAIN texture
When switched on, the grain of the wood becomes part of the light. The studio’s approach, which it calls introverted design, guides every decision. TUPI does not try to dominate a room. It sits on a desk, a bedside table or a shelf as a quiet presence, and reveals its character slowly, through the contrast of the two woods, the proportions of the head and the warmth of the light it casts. A switch is set flush into the base, and a beige fabric-covered cable completes a palette of natural materials. Each lamp is made to order, so small variations in grain and tone make every piece unique.

Teenager dies as heavy rain floods Istanbul
Roads collapse and hospitals take in water as floods swamp Turkiye’s largest city, shutting schools and halting traffic.
A teenage boy has died after torrential rain battered Istanbul, flooding hundreds of homes, causing roads to cave in and bringing traffic to a near standstill in Turkiye’s largest city.
Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed a surveillance camera capturing the moment the 14-year-old boy was electrocuted in the Balat area of Istanbul’s Fatih district, after stepping into a puddle during heavy rain.
The footage showed the boy walking through puddles at the entrance of a car park before suddenly collapsing to the ground.
The Istanbul governor’s office said the boy was taken to hospital unconscious, but he died despite rescue attempts, noting that an investigation into the incident had been opened.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gul urged residents to stay at home on Thursday unless travel was necessary. He called on people living in basement flats to spend the night on higher floors and to avoid creek beds, underpasses and other flood-prone areas.
The governor’s office suspended classes across the city for Thursday and banned motorcycles from the roads, the Associated Press reported. State employees with disabilities and mothers with young children were placed on leave.
The motorcycle ban took effect at 9pm on Wednesday and would stay in place until further notice.
Turkiye’s Interior Ministry warned of sudden flooding in several provinces on Wednesday and Thursday.
About 8,000 personnel, along with 2,000 vehicles and construction machines, were deployed across the city, home to about 16 million people, Turkish outlet Daily Sabah reported.
Road closures
The rain began on Tuesday evening after warnings from Turkiye’s weather service.
Water filled roads and underpasses, leaving vehicles stranded in several districts, including Esenyurt and Sultangazi.
Water also poured into homes, shops and basements.
Emergency services received more than 2,500 reports of weather-related incidents, Daily Sabah reported.
Authorities recorded 1,277 floods and 15 landslides, and 47 people were stranded. More than 800 homes, 280 businesses and 76 vehicles were affected.
Sections of road collapsed in the Eyupsultan and Gaziosmanpasa districts, the Turkiye Today news website reported.
Local media reported that passersby rescued a woman after floodwaters swept her along in Istanbul’s Esenyurt district.
Several neighbourhoods were affected, with roads submerged, vehicles stranded and homes and businesses inundated. Floodwater also reached two hospitals and poured through the ceiling of the Haciosman metro station. In Sultangazi, a primary school’s retaining wall collapsed while students were inside their classrooms.
No injuries were reported among students.
The heaviest rain fell in the Omerli area of Beykoz, on Istanbul’s Asian side, where nearly 194mm (7.6 inches) was recorded, according to Daily Sabah. Acting Istanbul Mayor Nuri Aslan said parts of the city received nearly 100mm (3.9 inches) in 12 hours.
Traffic density reached about 90 percent during the evening rush hour, and flights were operating normally, the newspaper said.

One Reddit post claimed Winston Lee was now serving in the South Korean army. Another user on X said she had received tips suggesting Lee had been spotted on Cornell University’s campus.
People with names like the other six accused also complained about rage spamming and threats.
“These social justice warriors are literally messaging and harassing the wrong” people, said podcast host Brad Polumbo.
“These things should be litigated through the criminal process or through some sort of fair process, not through a social media mob or witch hunt.”
‘Hounded’
A group of former Cornell students, who belonged to the same Chi Phi fraternity as the seven accused but graduated before the alleged incident, also complained of online smear campaigns.
“They are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement, are consequently receiving death threats and related hate mail,” their attorney Adam Ford wrote in a letter to the university that was obtained by AFP.
“Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave.”
Digital sleuths have for years misidentified accused perpetrators of high-profile shootings and other crimes, exposing them to abuse.
Such misidentification can further roil an already chaotic information ecosystem and hinder the actual investigation by generating false leads, warned Mike Rothschild, a researcher who studies conspiracy theories.
“The wrongfully accused are often hounded,” Rothschild told AFP.
“They sometimes have to go into hiding, or get death threats, or are even violently attacked themselves. And there is no penalty for being wrong on the part of those accusing them.” AFP

Trump administration seeks to strip Ilhan Omar of US citizenship: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:03:00 UTC
